This one's a weird one. It's a port of a microtransaction-driven mobile game, with the microtransactions removed. However, as it was built with microtransactions in mind, some of the game feels strangely unbalanced, such as being able to make and absurd amount of money by growing a large number of coconut trees in a short space of time (the growth of the trees and cococunts are time-gated, but the previous restriction was to do with the 'energy' of using tools which has since been removed). You'll find lots of odd little imbalances and redundancies throughout (such as the occasional quest which rewards more gems than the amount used to skip it + claim an easy reward) but most of them can be overlooked.
Balance issues aside, you're looking at the closest thing there is to a worthwhile Animal Crossing clone here, and I personally think it's worth full price. As of the time of writing, however, it's 75% off, and I very much recommend snagging it now.

The beauty of Thomas was alone lies with its simplicity. At its core, the game is a puzzle platformer with narrated rectangles. Apparently, that’s all you really need to create a fun experience.
- This game is simplistic, even with its art. Regardless, the small touches such as light, shadow, bounce animations, and background add some complexity to the style, making it more appealing to the eye.
- Simply a great narrator.
- This game is fun, intuitive, and captivating. It’s the kind of game that can be enjoyed by almost anyone.
- Each person/rectangle has a different colour, shape, and characteristics, not unlike regular people. As the game progresses you learn about each individual. Funny how human complexity can be condensed into something as simple as rectangles.
- Puzzles become harder as you include more rectangles. I believe this ties in well with the message of the game. Larger obstacles can be overcome when you work well as a team and everyone plays to their strengths.
- Fairly short. It only took me 2 hours to reach 100% completion.
- Fairly easy as well. However, I don’t think that puzzle difficulty was the main focus of this game, but rather the experience as a whole.
Thomas is alone is more than a platformer with rectangles as protagonists. It is an experience that reflects upon reality and highlights the importance of friendship. Bithell Games proves that excellence can be achieved even on a small budget (I believe less than 10 thousand pounds). Having said that, I find Thomas is alone to be overpriced for how short the game is. Definitely pick this up when it’s on sale.

I can't really say much about TWA without either spoiling the fun of it, or just sound pretentious. But whatever, here goes!
Graphically, it's... well... if you've seen the screenshots, you know what it looks like. It's not exactly gonna win any awards for visual style. (Obvious joke here for anyone that knows about the game's accolades.) But as Stardew Valley, Undertale, Shovel Knight, and an almost fûckin' literal shït-ton of other games have proven, graphics are UNIMPORTANT. Seriously.
What Thomas Was Alone HAS, on the other hand, is quite possibly the best narration in a videogame since Bastion. Maybe even better THAN Bastion. Anyone who's played the latter knows what a heavy statement THAT is. Danny Wallace, the man who narrates TWA, delivers every single line of "dialogue" with a kind of glee (in lack of a better word) that makes every single syllable a joy to listen to.
Honestly, people hold up Steve Fireman or whoever that git in Half-Life was called as some "beloved character", but frankly, I felt way way WAY more attached to Chris or Laura, or of course the best one of 'em all, Claire, because even though they were entirely two-dimensional on a visual level, they have more personality than half of the gaming world's "protagonists" combined.
Thomas Was Alone is, admittedly, "telling, not showing" in its narrative, but it's more like the sensation one gets when being read a book to. And who better to read that book than an acclaimed author and comedian?
But I digress... the music and audio in TWA is minimalistic in the best possible sense; it instills ambience, without feeling absent but also without overtaking the atmosphere of the game completely. It's like the aural equivalent of a thin mist spreading across an already spooky field on a dark(ish) night in late August.
Gameplay wise, TWA isn't very complicated, but it really doesn't need to be. I kid you not when I say that a bloody TODDLER could manage to play through the entire game without difficulty! And yet, the gameplay isn't just some thing that's tacked on to give it a sense of being a game, rather than just a glorified "narrated experience", as almost every single "story-driven" game that's released these days is. (Lookin' at you, Everybody Has Gone To The Rapture, you vomitous pile of garbage and wasted voice acting!)
Anyway. TWA won't appeal to everyone, but for those of you who can stomach a very minimalistic style in favour of a strong narration, deceptively simple yet incredibly absorbing story, and characters that may all be quadrilaterals, but has deeper personalities than just about all AAA-title protagonists have combined, Thomas Was Alone is DEFINITELY worth looking into. Hell, it's dirt-cheap even at full price, so there really is no excuse not to! 9.5/10

Full Review:
"Great action/adventure games feature stories that stick with you for years to come. Fans remember fondly stories that made them laugh, cry, and sit eagerly at the edges of their seats. The Ritual on Weylyn Island gets this half right since you will certainly laugh and cry, but for all the wrong reasons...."

Indie Survival Horror: Much like the movie industry it seems that its the indie developers who make the majority of horror titles. That means that there’s a lot of great art house style games available to buy but there is a lot of utter crap that gets published. Separating the strong from the weak isn’t always the easiest in this genre because the worst often gets heavy promotion while the good, solid, titles often get ignored. The Ritual on Weylyn Island is a game that is likely to be ignored despite it being a very solid and reasonable entry into a crowded marketplace.
Suitable graphics but a couple of minor letdowns: This is a game that does not rely on its graphics to tell the story. However, what is there helps establish the atmosphere very well. It’s color palette was extremely well chosen. It is gloomy, foreboding, etc. It is everything that you would expect a horror story located on an isolated island to be. There are a few letdowns graphically as occasionally the particular thing you need to go to isn’t very clear. For example, there is a part where you need to find a trap door in a room in order to progress through to the next stage of the story. I searched that room several times and couldn’t find anything and thus I googled the solution and a found a video that showed me where it was.  I’d also have appreciated a little bit more work into the character design. They’re not anyone that you’re going to remember after you’ve played the game art wise.
Inconsistent voice work: I must admit that I watched the Jim Sterling video on this game prior to playing. He pointed out that the voice over work occasionally sounds like it was made in two different rooms. I agree with him. The level is wildly inconsistent throughout but as he said that’s indie games for you. It’s a minor quibble but it is noticeable. I must admit that I loved the voice recording tapes that you find throughout the game. They add a tremendous amount of backstory to the game and are generally always found at just the right point of the game to make the most impact.
Enjoyable but cliche-ish story: If you’ve read your fair share of horror stories you’re bound to have come across a story similar to The Ritual on Weylyn Island. That’s not necessarily a bad thing but don’t expect the title to add anything new story wise to the genre. It’s very cliche-ish.
But I really enjoyed it: A few of the above points may sound as though I really didn’t appreciate the game yet I found that I did enjoy it. I’ve played a few horror games since I played the horror game of the year of 2015 in the PlayStation 4’s Until Dawn. Although there’s a gulf between the quality of that title and The Ritual on Weylyn Island I just have to suggest that this is a title that I will be returning to at some point with friends.
The Ritual on Weylyn Island is a very solid indie horror game. I believe that it belongs as a solid entry in a Halloween celebration gameathon. It holds its own against other horror games on Steam and is well and truly worthy of the two hours that it will take you to play through it. Consider it a B-grade movie. It’s far from trash but doesn’t have the production value of the very best titles.

Most indie horror games on Steam that are/were in early access tend to be riddled with incompetent gameplay, feature underwhelming length and show poor execution all around. Fortunately, The Ritual on Weylyn Island only suffers from one of those problems.
With a current price tag of $9.99, "Ritual" offers only about 90 minutes of game. There is no replay value - the single collectible in the game is always in plain sight, and there is only one ending. Despite those shortcomings, I find myself recommending this game purely from the enjoyable experience those 90 minutes were.
"Ritual" is an ambitious game for one of its budget and staff size. There are cutscenes, facial animations, QTEs and chase sequences. There is an overall cinematic appreciation that's missing from its "find a key to open a door to find another key" indie horror peers, and that's what sets it apart.
It isn't without its faults, of course. The voice acting quality is spotty, some animations are a bit limp, and the locations you visit often feel too empy. The presentation, while well-meaning and generally well-executed, feels "off" from time to time due to these limitations, but those limitations give it a certain charm that I find refreshing. And it sure beats the hell out of many of the bug-ridden horror snoozefests being sold on this platform.
"Ritual" won't make any horror GOTY lists, but I would be lying if I said I didn't get off this 90-minute ride with a smile on my face.

The Ritual on Weylyn Island, developed by zemaGamez, had the potential to bring back all of your favorite horror tropes, and that’s probably what the devs had in mind. However, due to poor presentation, an unfulfilled story, and hollow characters, Weylyn Island stumbles and falls before it can provide the homage it strives to represent.
You play as Moria Weylyn; a typical collage girl without any defining traits or skills. Her grandfather had recently died, and in his will, Moria and a handful of family members are given the isolated island he once called home; Blessed Island. (Odd, seeing as how the game’s title is Weylyn Island, yet it’s clearly called Blessed Island throughout the story. But I digress.)
These family members include: Uncle Brian, his two kids, Fin and Megan, and Moria’s older sister, Row. Plans were made to meet up on the island, but a freak storm delays Moria’s trip. Arriving one day after her family, she sets foot on the cold, wet dwarf and heads out.
In all honesty, Weylyn Island starts out really strong. The Island’s dark and laced in shadows, and your first few minutes are spent soaking up the atmosphere. I mean, you’ve got a bunch of unsuspecting teens (and one adult) on a secluded, creepy island. The possibilities are endless! Your first real objective is to head up to the old cabin, where your family is supposedly waiting for you. As I trudged down the trailside, bombarded by endless rain, I could only imagine what sort of horrors awaited me.
Sadly, that’s about the extent of this game’s suspense and intrigue.
Before going any further, we might as well talk graphics. And they’re… alright. I mean, Weylyn Island isn’t ugly by any stretch of the word, but its design is easily forgettable. The grey, overbearing tone works wonders at first, building upon the mood of the setting. But endless rain, pine trees and monochrome color pallets only go so far. Again, this game’s level design isn’t bad, but only decent. As for character models… well, that’s another story.
Their textures are basic at best and look far from appealing, but they manage. But it’s their animations that really bite the dust; everyone walks like they’ve got a wooden plank shoved up their♥♥♥♥♥
But let’s be real: you don’t need high budget visuals or picturesque designs to make something scary. If done correctly, a game with ugly graphics can be forgiven if its got a solid story and solid gameplay. I mean, a build up with this much potential is sure to lead to something good, right?
Right…?
As for gameplay, there’s little to speak of. Long bouts of walking and quick-time-events are in high abundance, topped off with not-so-scary chase scenes, and most of these are void of sound effects or tracks. The results are less intense and more uncomfortable (and no, not in a good way).
But despite all of this, it’s Weylyn Island’s story that ruined the entire game for me. Hell, I could forgive all these flaws had the plot been (at least) good.
But nope, it isn’t. I won’t spoil anything, but it’s got everything required to tell a lame horror story. There’s practically zero explanation until the third act, which left me more confused and less terrified most of the time. Some of these characters don’t even ♥♥♥♥ing talk! We’re watching them suffer and die but… why should I care?  One of them had little more than two lines of dialogue, and another was only capable of squealing and whining. Jesus, one of them didn’t get a chance to talk before kicking the bucket!  All of their voice actors were terrible, especially your character’s. I’ve seen sloths with more dedication than this ♥♥♥♥♥.
The game also thinks that long sessions of poetry recited by old men is scary. It isn't. This is Weylyn Island’s #1 method of storytelling, and it’s done awfully.
This game just makes me mad. God, it’s even forced me to type up my longest review yet. But when a story with so much possibility fails to strike almost every note, it just leaves me baffled. “What went wrong,” I think to myself. “What. Went . Wrong?”

Sure, the story is a complete ♥♥♥♥ing mess, and the texture work on the levels leaves a lot to be desired, and it doesnt feel at all like a Resident Evil game,  but as an action game, its suprisingly solid. The shooting (which comprises the majority of what you will be doing throughout the suprisingly lengthy campaign) actually feels rather nice, and the sheer variety of weapons for each character in each campaign keeps the shooting from getting too repeative.  And the emeies in the game are also suprisingly varied, ranging from your standard zombies, to zombies with guns (Javo),  to, in later levels praying mantis people lizard people, and some other monsters that Id rather you see than hear me describe. Overall, if you can get it on a sale, id say that you should at least try this game out.

You play a person (male or female) who is washed up on an island for whatever reason. There's no real story behind that. There are others living on this island, all of which are talking animal-people. Not much story here, but then you don't really need one unless you're morbidly curious as to why there are a bunch of "castaways" trapped on some island and no one is trying to rescue them.
Moving on, you control your new islander using the mouse. You can use the space bar as a sort of short cut to use the tool in your hand, but otherwise everything is mouse-driven. Your daily tasks include dusting cobwebs, planting trees and flowers, fishing, catching bugs, collecting shells, and decorating the town as you see fit. There are online leaderboards for things like finishing quests
+Daily quests and rewards. They're a reason to drop in at least once a day.
+Online leaderboards are neat. They're certainly a reason to do more quests and collect more things.
+The writing. It's quirky and zany--not to mention funny. I actually take time to read the other islanders' "chit-chats."
+Ability to decorate the town. You can pop down whatever decorations you see fit and make the island your own. It's a nice touch and the decorations are fairly varied.
+Dress up! I love customizing my character. An outfit a day keeps the doctor away... Or something along those lines. You can also change hairstyles, though not your facial features.
+Cute art style. Everything is vibrant and cartoony.
+Regular updates. The devs keep adding content, which is always nice.
-The game plays much like one would expects an iOS or Facebook game to play: you check in, do some stuff, and log out to wait for time to pass before you do more stuff. The game breaks this up a bit by offering a slew of quests that the adorable island residents give you, but even some of those cannot be done immediately.
-There are also some quests that cannot be done immediately because you were a go-getter and cleaned up the entire island without knowing that a quest later down the line would require you to break rocks or collect trash. So you can get stuck with certain quests unless you pay to complete them with the in-game currency.
Both are very minor gripes.
.Bottom line.
It's entirely enjoyable. Maybe not for the 14.99USD price tag, but I got it on sale for somewhere around $5 and I can't say I'm dissatisfied with my purchase.

I wrote a review for Castaway Paradise awhile back, but it's since then updated, so I'd like to renew my views on it. Originally I don't think I posted anything worth reiterating, but my main point is this: I do believe the Steam edition is the best edition to follow. I'm not sure if the Facebook and iOS/Android version still contains microtransactions, but this version does not. Nor does it contain an energy bar as of recent updates!
This is a game I was looking forwards to for quite a few years. Originally, I was very pleased with it, and for reasons I totally forgot, fell out of love with it very quickly. While it still needs a lot of love to be a nice Animal Crossing substitute ((especially now that rather certain popular farming + dating simulator game has come out)), it's not half bad. It still needs quite a few things to have a nice polished feeling, but over the years and lots of free DLC and nice seasonal updates, it's changed a lot since the last time I've poked my head in.
I haven't gotten waist-deep yet, but it's nice to have something that isn't counting down the seconds and forcing you to preplan your in-game days. It's a nice little collecting and decorating simulation with the option to quest.
These are some recommendations I have for future development, some of which are already in development or been recognized by developers. But I'd still like to bring attention to them:
-Villagers could have the same set spawns for their houses, but interchangable, which would give a slight illusion of "random" villagers. This would save the developers time considering it wouldn't be randomly placed homes that would cause obstruction of objects.
-Multiplayer.
-The chatroom feature of the mobile versions would make this game livelier. Perhaps having a minimizable, or completely optional, universal chatbox?
-Footstep and dialogue sound effects would greatly enhance the immmersion of this game for me.
-Seasonal fish and bugs, and overrall more variety.
-Rainy days, and night and day cycle. In my eyes, this is one of the most immersive aspects of Animal Crossing and simulation games as a whole.
-More music variety.
-I know it's on it's way, but controller support.
-More villagers would be nice!
-Updated and less mobile-like UI. At times, actions can be unresponsive or finicky.
-Being able to sit in chairs or lay in beds!
Honestly, it's nice to mute the music ((since there's only one track seemingly)), put on an Animal Crossing playlist, and do the dailies, quests, cleaning up the island, fishing, etc. It's not too in depth and I would agree that it's an "Animal Crossing lite" of sorts. And while I've, like many others, mentioned the AC-title multiple times in this review, it does seem to stand on it's own.
My TL;DR would be, if you can look through the rough, you might find a diamond, but it's still in the process of being polished. I like Castaway Paradise though!

I want to like this game, but I don't. I had heard about Thomas Was Alone, but never considered purchasing it until I played Subsurface Circular. I enjoyed that game so much it made me look into the developer's other games.
I know that Subsurface Circular and Thomas Was Alone are two very different gameplay style games. But I do enjoy a good platformer. I was raised on Mario and Mega Man on the NES; so I picked this up and dove in head first.
First off, the platforming is IMO off. You can't jump, land, jump, what's up with that? You have to jump, land, wait 0.5 sec, jump. THIS totally throws off the gameplay for me! I was on one level where Thomas needed to jump over a few water traps. The platforms where placed so all I had to do was jump and move. Unfortunately the delay in jump, land, wait 0.5 sec, jump, made me die multiple times. I had to jump, land, wait, jump. This game had taken out the fluid movements of a normal platformer.
There is also a bug where, when jumping off Laura, when you land on a platform, you can't move until you jump again. Also sometimes you bounce when you land and other times you don't. When platforms are moving, you can't jump, why not?!?This all compounded to one level for me.
I made it until 4.10 where you have to jump on a moving platform, it pushes you up, you fly in the air and bounce, then you need to wait that 0.5 sec to jump to another platform that is moving away from you. I couldn't make it. That 0.5 sec delay was making the jump impossible. I tried for 15 minutes. I tried bouncing, landing, moving, and jumping. I tried moving to the very edge of the ledge, bouncing, landing, waiting 0.5 sec, jumping. I tried to use coye time to get an extra pixel of space, but I just couldn't make that jump. The irritation of the broken platform mechanics culminated to that one jump and everytime I missed it made each and every negative more glaring.
Why delay the jump ability? What was the developer intending by breaking it's core mechanic? This is only made more obvious because the story is so solid. You're not playing the game for the platforming puzzles, you're playing for the story. But the platforming is the vehicle to get to the good story; so make sure your vehicle is tip top. Subsurface Circular avoided this all together and quite frankly I think it was a boon to the game.

I love art and indie games. Braid, Jason Roher, Rod Humble, Stanley Parable, Gone Home, Brendon Chung, Dear Esther, Fez, Cart Life, Glitch Hikers, The Talos Principle, and on and on. I usually afford these games plenty of patience so they can get their message across and explore their characters to a level that AAA games might gloss over. However, after spending 2 hours playing to level 5.8, presumedly a third of the game, I felt quite unsatisfied. The platforming puzzles are far from interesting. That's mostly a limitation of each character's minimalist abilities since unlike a half life game, there are only so many interesting or challenging variations of the mechanic that can be shown. At times the game resorts to dexterity based challenges like Super Meat Boy. Unfortunately, it lacks the responsiveness of other platforming games. Very often my jumps would not register. Unimaginative puzzles and poor response make for bad platforming.
Thus the platforming serves only as a delivery vehicle for plot and character development. Except narrative is delivered at a rate of one sentence per level. Sometimes that can be fine too. Bioshock or Fallout 4 can successfully delivery narrative in between chunks of repetitive and unimaginative gun fights. But unlike those games, I don't see the appeal to the plot.
By level 5.8, some half dozen characters have been introduced, each given about 5 lines worth of exposition, mostly about their angst towards each other. There's as much depth to the story so far as the number of edges each character possess. Maybe I'm being harsh by expecting more from quadrilaterals. Other people seem to think there is a valuable message from this game. I just wish I could have read the dialogue off the back of a cereal box instead of spending the time I did.

Back in 2014, when I finished the original Watch_Dogs, I thought to myself, "Boy that was trash." But as the credits ran over a giant dump of information it got me thinking... perhaps all hope wasn't loss. I began thinking about the other two IPs that also started off as Watch_Dogs did; a repetitive, mind numbing grind of terrible and good mechanics and ideas that felt like a giant exercise in patience as opposed to a game. I was given Vietnam-style flashbacks of my time with Ubisoft's iteration of the Far Cry franchise, known as Far Cry 2, and remembered just how aburdly awful the whole game was. And then I was reminded of the immense amount of fun I had with Far Cry 3. And just as I had stopped feeling like comitting suicide I was triggered once again and brought back to 2007, when I had played the original Assassin's Creed game, and was left appalled by it's also repetitive, mind numbing nature of repeating the same /seven missions/ over and over again. I was about ready to down a Max Payne martini when I remembered the copious amount of happiness I felt playing Assassin's Creed 2. Then it hit me: What if a sequel to Watch_Dogs did the same? It was almost a guarantee at this point. Ubisoft seems to be the master of emotional manipulation. They torture us with what essentially is a shameful display of AAA game development and then surprise us by taking out all the suck of the first iteration and blowing our minds with the sequel. Needless to say I was right.
Watch_Dogs 2 is phenomenal. Through and through. Although the story is generic as all hell and the characters could make up the entirety of a 20 minute cringe compilation video the rest of the game blossoms in quite possibly my favorite action adventure game in recent memory. To be honest, I almost sort of like the love-hate relationship I have with the characters. Sure, they were clearly written by a guy who is clearly out of touch with millennials and Gen X, but I'm sure if they expand on this and actually researched how kids are nowadays they could really have something special. I actually did enjoy some of the interactions the characters had... and I even kinda like Wrench's text-emote mask... even if it is a little gay and would not be possible by any stretch of the imagination. Regardless, the story and characters aren't all that important. What's important is the gameplay.
The repetitive mission design has been replaced by a much more creative and diverse main story mission structure. The side missions all feel fresh depite them all basically having you doing the same thing, and there's a ton of fun side things to do such as being an uber driver, sailing, time trials, sightseeing, parkour, etc. Missions that involve infiltration into strongholds allow the player freedom to tackle it the way they want to. The game offers 3 different play styles you can invest your points into. You can be the Ghost type that remains in the shadows and take out enemies quietly. Or, hell, not take out anyone at all. You can be the Trickster type by manipulating the game world to blow up junction boxes, overheat people's cell phones, cause cars to crash into someone, or use little gadgets and toys at your disposal to take out enemies. You can even be an Aggressor and go in guns blazing because Ubisoft realized restricting gun use in the first game was a stupid idea COUGH MIRROR'S EDGE CATALYST ♥♥♥♥ YOU DICE COUGH. They also have expanded upon the hacking too. And while it's still a bit simplistic there is definitely more variety because you now have multiple options with pretty much anything you hack. You're not limited like in the first game where x did y. It's actually really enjoyable. And as an added bonus they actually really amped up the car handling in this game. It's much more fluid, and everything feels really unique to drive. I got a huge vibe of the handling used in Driver: San Francisco. Although it's not quite the same, it's still really fun to drive now.
Oh, surprisingly, Ubisoft didn't lie about the visuals either! That's a first! This game looks the same as it did in the E3 trailer and it looks absolutely stunning. The world is so vibrant with color, life, and crisp graphics. The draw distance is some of the best I've ever seen in a video game. And little aesthetic things like leaves collecting on top of a car parked under a tree just make the world feel so rich. It also helps that this time around the NPC pedestrians all act unique. You know, like they were supposed to in Watch_Dogs 1? While it's not as extensive as the E3 presentation for Watch_Dogs 1, Watch_Dogs 2 is definitely a huge improvement. NPCs do everything from taking group photos with friends, to doing yoga and aerobics, sitting on benches and browsing their phones, sightseeing, you name it. I think so far the two most stand out moments for me was when a random NPC was beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a car on the street and screaming at her husband in the highrise above, "YOU SEE THAT HONEY? IS THIS WHAT YOU WANTED," before tossing the bat, and then carjacking me for a quick getaway. The other interaction is when I bumped into an NPC on the street and he started to trash talk. As I began to walk away he grew progressively more upset demanding I stop ignoring him and cursing me out as his loud voice grew into a soft echo that sounded like he was really down the street shouting at me. Its the world building that makes the world feel so freaking real and I love it.
And finally, we have the iconic multiplayer from the first game. It's seamless. At any given moment you can hack another player or be hacked. This means you'll have to scout the area to find whoever it is and kill them. Of course, as a hacker, your goal is to remain undetected. And if you are detected you better have a damn good escape route set up. There are of course missions that involve working together to infiltrate an area which can lead to some pretty funny moments if you think creatively with the tools at your disposal. And since there are different playstyles it can lead to some wild opprotunities. There also seems to be newer additions such as PvP Hunt, which means any time you are being chased by the cops, you can be invaded by enemy players who are rewarded for killing you. There also seems to be a different style of hacking play that involves you having to search the area for a hacker that is able to move freely around the map. It also happens in an instant. You can slip in and slip out of people's games in an instant at random and it always feels like there's something to do.
My only problem with this game, aside from the story and characters, is the gunplay. Ubisoft did the stupid thing of making it so you have to aim in order to shoot. There's no hip fire, and you can't blindfire either. And when you're in this mode out in the open you are so ungodly slow you might as well wear the shirt that makes you look like a range target because that's all you'll ever be. And trying to sprint away once you get out of aiming mode actually takes a second or two. To put it simplistically if you're a masochist like me you'll love playing this game on Realistic. There's also the issue where Ubisoft forgot to set a separate sensitivity setting for aiming so it's sluggish compared to the look sensitivity. My other problem is that the melee is still the same, "Press one button to auto-win and watch an animation," crap we see in so many games and I honestly hate it. But oh well, it's Ubisoft. I'm sure if they figured out a way to do with gunplay they would.
Overall, Watch_Dogs 2 is fantastic. I feel like I'm going to get a lot of replayability out of it unlike the first game where I beat it once and now I become emotionally distressed every time I scroll by it in my Steam library. If you have the money this is by far one of the best games you can spend it on this year.
But for God's sake buy Titanfall 2 first. That game needs love.

Before I start, here's the final thought (which will be repeated at the bottom after the whole review):
"On the whole, if you liked Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you will probably enjoy Watch Dogs 2. If you hated Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you'll likely find a plethora of things you'll love to complain about to everyone else."
For all the people reading these reviews:
A lot of the people complaining about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ frame rates are the same ones who haven't updated their graphics card drivers. This is speaking as someone who was getting some choppiness here and there, investigated, found other people saying "hey you should update your GTX graphics card drivers before playing the game", went ahead and tried it, and sure enough, my GTX 970 plays it smooth as butter.
There are some moments where the volumetric fog over the whole of the san fransisco bay will cause some frame drops, but on the whole, I was playing somewhere between high and ultra on a single GTX 970, and I'm running it just fine with almost always over 60FPS.
The gameplay is your stereotypical Ubisoft openworld game; for some players, this is overplayed, overdone. For me, I happen to enjoy the hell out of it, having played most of the Assassin's Creed Games. If you're an Assassin's Creed fan, this game plays very similarly to Black Flag (the character goes where you want them to about 95% of the time, the other 5% of the times are very frustrating). Unfortunately, just like in Blackflag, the game automatically puts your character into 'stealth mode' as necessary, rather than the more recent AC games (and original Watch Dogs) that allowed for a dedicated 'crouch to stealth' mode. The good news is that Ubisoft has learned valuable lessons from their recent The Division, especially regarding smooth transitions and cover system gameplay.
For WD2, the storyline is much better than it was for WD1, but I swear, it feels like I'm watching the grave realities brought up in Mr Robot, except presented by the Disney Channel. Some parts of the story are stale and contrived, while other parts feel authentic. On the whole, there haven't been many moments where I simply didn't care enough to continue playing (reference: Assassin's Creed Unity, FarCry 4).
The game devs did a much better job designing variability into the puzzles and interactable objects, though once you've gotten a hang of the game mechanic or interaction, it becomes pretty easy to solve the puzzles. This makes doing missions and side-missions a little less monotonous if you're knocking out a bunch.
My biggest gripes from the original Watch Dogs that made it unplayable:
* Horrible PC optimization, the game would freeze constantly, even on top of the line graphics cards
* Terrible quality graphics compared to what they had shown and advertised (thanks, Ubisoft, for agreeing to sh*t-down the graphics on PC to match the quality shown on consoles. That didn't come back to bite you in the *ss now, did it?)
* Driving engine was TERRIBLE. You shouldn't have late 80's-esque F-Zero levels of control over a vehicle that's moving through mid 2000's game engine that has realistic lighting and physics. I entered into the original WD expecting an arcade-racer style driving experience, but WTF.
* Stale gameplay
* Stale story
In Watch Dogs 2, it seems that they've taken extra care to tackle the previous game's problems as much as possible.
* PC version of the game works amazingly on my gaming rig (GTX 970 GPU, 16GB DDR3 RAM, AMD FX-8350 CPU)
* The graphics quality is typical for a game in 2016, and amazing compared to the original Watch Dogs
* Driving engine is way better, and arcade-racer-AF. That's okay with me, though, because I like both arcade racers and racing sims.
* Gameplay thus far has been entertaining and varied enough (as far as possible approaches, weapons, gadgets, attack methods, etc) that it hasn't gotten boring yet, and I'm over 20 hours in now.
* Story thus far has been overly-simplified and watered down, or (conversely) hyperbolized so the general audiences can get a pretty good understanding of what is actually going on IRL with data privacy. That being said, it's been more entertaining than Mafia 3's story, and definitely better than any of the Far Cry stories.
On the whole, if you liked Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you will probably enjoy Watch Dogs 2. If you hated Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you'll likely find a plethora of things you'll love to complain about to everyone else.

Overall, I quite enjoyed The Ritual on Weylyn Island. The game mixes itself up and comes off as a low-budget attempt to make an interesting sort of cinematic horror experience, one that has actual diversity in gameplay, setting, tasks, and knows how to pace itself and keep things interesting. A few scenes can even be startling or unnerving. This all comes with an edge of low-budget elements, including some wonky animations and a level of jank to things. However, the ambition and successful execution of many of its concepts makes it an enjoyable 1.5-2 hour experience to go through (appropriately about the length of a horror movie).
The basic idea is you play as a girl name Moira, who has come a bit after the rest of her family to Weylyn Island, an island her rich grandfather had purchased and passes down to his family upon his death (along with his riches and possessions). They go to stake claim to the place, and to help strengthen some family ties that have grown a bit distant recently. However, a strange cult has invaded the island, and now seem to want the family dead. And thus, it becomes a tiresome night of having to evade cultists, ritualistic shrines, and discover what exactly is going on here.
And it mostly succeeds. In big part due to it being able to keep the player guessing, a variety of settings, tasks, and solid core mechanics, matched with feeling involved in every moment of the action going on. Whether it be exploring the quiet coast of the island, evading a silent stalker in a basement, or investigating a strange altar with a music box, the game is full of interesting scenes matched with good atmosphere and a level of intrigue accomplished by good vision and direction.
There are a few flaws here; The story is predictable as all hell, the finale while not quite disappointing feels like it could be more. While the game is worth playing through to the end, I feel the first half of the game was better fleshed-out and realized, with the second half feeling a bit more linear and sometimes coming off as more scripted. A few areas do feel they could be tighter designed, such as a scene where you're in a house looking for a key and something is banging on the door, but no matter how long you take the door will just keep banging, smudging much of the tension there. But even despite all of this, there is a very solid little horror experience in this title. The length might put some off, but it doesn't feel they padded the game to make it longer and do keep the variety and overall quality at a higher-than-average aspect to indie horror developers. In some ways, it feels like maybe their ambition was a bit over their heads, but for this to be a mostly well-realized vision is quite an accomplishment.
But I point out these flaws as I feel the game itself is quite solid. Not the best horror game I've played, but a pretty well-done foray with a few interesting twists and turns up its sleeves to keep the 1.5-2 hour experience interesting. It's also notable the game avoids many indie horror pitfalls; the game has a good level of darkness (you never can't see what's going on and it looks like its night rather than pitch dark), your flashlight has no batteries and is actually quite efficient, there is no limited sprinting, it doesn't rely on jump scares, there isn't much in the way of key collecting, it doesn't come off as a clone of any popular indie horror game and there's no clone segments designed after Slender or FNAF or something (this comparison isn't the best, but the thing I find myself comparing it the closest to would be Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth, which it reminded me a bit of), the writing is good and isn't full of typos and grammar mistakes, the voice acting is pretty decent, among other things. But it doesn't accomplish it goals because of it not failing, it is a competent and often engaging journey on its own.
If you like cult horror (as in, literally about cults and figuratively), indie horror games with a lot of heart, don't mind a low-budgeted game with deep ambitions, and overall don't mind the price tag to the hours it might provide of entertainment, I say definitely worth checking out.

This is a review of The Ritual On Weylin Island. To simplify I have split my review into four sections; Gameplay, Graphics, Audio, and General.
Gameplay:
TROWI is a dark horror driven game, I personally enjoy the themes of Witchcraft and Satanic Rituals.  There is no combat in this game and I believe that to be a good approach stylistically.  The inability to fight the enemy adds to the overall fear and adrenaline one feels while playing, knowing your only option is to run leaves you with a slight feeling of anxiety.    Adding to this anxiety is the fact that appropriately you are not given obvious direction, giving a feeling of being lost and frightened.
Furthering to the fear aspect is the design of the witches, I find their distorted faces to be particularly disturbing.  They are quite unique and a positive artistic approach in my opinion.
I experienced some minor problems while playing.  First is that the flashlight indicates that it can be turned on with both the F-Key and with a right mouse click, however I found it did not turn on with a right click.  I also found it somewhat odd that between each chapter the flashlight would turn off and I would have to turn it back on.
I discovered a minor error with crouching.  If one crouches while stationary they cannot move while crouched, I was only able to move while crouching if I was already in motion.
The last problems I experienced were both at the pull-bridge.  The first is simply that when you reach the end of the pull bridge the transition from the bridge to the ground seemed somewhat awkward and unconnected, but perhaps that is to critical.  However after crossing the Pull bridge I discovered that your cousin Meghan became stuck and ran in place.  This was particularily bothersome as she is directly in your path and the only way past her is by jumping over her.  She did become unstuck, but I believe this error should be looked into.
the problems I experienced were all minor and did not take away from the overall feel or fun of the game, so I will give the Gameplay 7/10.
Graphics:
Overall the Graphics were smooth and an effective expression of the dark atmosphere of the Game.  I found character movement to be quite fluid for the main character, and the motion of enemies and npc's to be generally natural as well.  I particularly like the fact that you can see your own characters legs, this is an extremely rare effect in first person games and it worked well.  Leg movement was natural and well done and that left me impressed.
To contrast the positive effect of your legs I would like to point out that to me the way Moira raises her hand when passing through obstacles seems unnatural and somewhat sluggish.
I enjoyed the water visuals, I found myself admiring the graphics while crossing a bridge early in the game, I also feel that the forest, trees and paths are very well done and added to the atmosphere.
Some things I would like to point out however mostly centered around your Grandpa's house.  I found that the glass on the floor of the kitchen flickered on and off as you moved, a small bug.
The mirror effects in the first bathroom I feel needed work, as it looks more like an abstract painting than broken glass.  I would have loved to see any kind of reflection graphic, even through a broken mirror.
The next thing I would like to point out is the oddness of fluids other than bodies of water, Moira's Grandpa appears to have a jar of solidified camoflauge colored alcohol in his dining room.  Also later in the story when you reach the building that connects to the light house, there is a skeleton in a bathtub filled with what appears to be  jam, lol.
Upon first viewing the light house you are given a short clip of the rotating light, overall the effect was well done, however the leaves on the trees seem to pop into existence unnaturally when bathed in light.
One last silly thing I would like to adress is the appearance of crows over the pull-bridge. They seem to warp in and out of existence. Either this is from the witches "black magic"  or it is simply an incomplete graphic. However I will also add it is barely noticeable.
Generally the graphics were quite well done for a game of this size, and any small quirks did not effect the atmosphere much or take away from the artistic direction. I would give the graphics a 7/10.
Audio:
While first approaching the island one of the first sound effects you hear is the rain and waves. I was impressed with both of these effects and their authentic sound. The transition of the effect between being outside and inside is smooth and well done, and the effect of rain drumming on the roof is a nice touch.
Other sound effects that I appreciated were those of the frogs when passing by a small body of water, they were natural sounding and added to the effect of the forests ambience, I only wish there were more effects like this to make the forest come alive so-to-speak.  At one point there were crows crying from the trees, this effect started off well enough, but quickly became cluttered and unnatural, followed by a sudden stop in the audio instead of a more natural fading effect. I would even suggest having the effect of flapping wings indicating they were startled and all flew away.
The whispering of the witches while navigating the early parts of the forest were creepy and well done, however when they repeat the same phrase 3-4 times in a row it immediately became humourus instead of frightening.
The voice acting of the game is a bit of a let down. Moira's voice from start to finish has a reverberation that makes the voice feel very disconnected from the character, almost as if it were playing from her cassette player.  I believe this originates from the recording process and is the result of either distance from the microphone, or recording levels were not set appropriately in advance.  Regardless of where this effect originates, every time Moira spoke I was imagining the voice actor speaking into a microphone instead of the character actually speaking herself.
In general I must say the voice acting felt quite unnatural, as if it were read directly off of a paper.
There was an obvious crackling during the scene where the man was lit on fire, and all the audio surrounding that scene felt quite weak.  I personally feel that when dealing with emotions such a fear, the uninspired audio and lack of heart did in fact take away from the overal feel of the game.
Only adding to the mediocre voice acting was the uninspired music, where only simple bass notes were used during jump scares.
In light of the audio's strengths and weaknesses I will give it a 5/10
Genral:
Some things that caught my attention, I will not rate this section as not all of them need a fix, or are irrelevant. The first thing that I found strange was that Moira's Grandpa had one and a half bathrooms on the main floor, but only one bedroom, either he suffers from extreme intense diahrea or this is a design flaw.  Perhaps he suffers from gastric distress because in his cellar he appears to have jar upon jar of pickled lettuce. "C'mon gramps, you have plenty of space, how about making a garden?"
The other oddity I noticed were barrels  scattered all around the forest, what's in these barrels is a mystery. It is possible they are filled with gas, but it seems like overkill considering there is only one generator and one truck.
Speaking to the crashed truck, I also find it odd that there are far more barrels around the forest than the truck could hold.  Suggesting that the driver did not drop barrels because of fear, but instead that he is a drunk who drives haphazzardly everywhere he goes, dumping barrels around the forest as he pleases.
Coclusion
Overall I enjoyed this game, anything negative I wrote is in hopes that they can be fixed before the official release. I would give this title 7/10 and definitely recommend it to my friends. Great work Zema =)

I just finished playing the first hour of The Ritual on Weylyn Island and I'm really enjoying the story. Set on an island that the main character and her family have just inherited from the recently deceased grandfather. You are the last to arrive by ferry and find the family has gone up to the lighthouse.
The gameplay is a simple interactive first person game. You control the main character and are searching for your family and what the deal is on the island. The story so far has me hooked. The game opens with a cinematic of a man running through the woods, tripping into the center of a ritual circle made of stone. Several hooded figures start to chant loudly. A large man wearing some kind of mask stabs the man in the chest with a sword. Badass opening right?
You then arrive at a cabin in the woods and are told by the captain of the ferry how he's heard "stories" about the island that he doesn't wish to repeat. Well, screw you buddy. The character you are playing indicated they haven't been there since they were 8. So clearly I don't know these stories and furthermore, if they are so messed up why the hell wouldn't you tell the young lady you're dropping off at night. On an island. Alone.
From here you read a note indicating the family is at the lighthouse and you should make your way there. Inside you find a flashlight and a tape recorded message from your creepy grandfather being cryptic about the island.
The story is interesting to me and I'd love to know what is happening on the island. However, some of the gameplay needs tuning. There was a part where you must left and right mouse click to pull yourself across a rope bridge. It was pretty lengthy and slow. The game is also voice acted which I enjoy from my horror games. The problem is some of it is poorly recorded and mixed. There were times when the audio would get so loud I had to take my headphones off, which is a bummer. It also sounded as if some of it was recorded in a bathroom, or at the beach. All this I think can and will be fixed over time so for me, no big deal.
I'm just interested in the story here, as it's a scary story being told via first person I don't really need any fancy puzzles or gunfights. I like the idea of listening to audio logs, running from monsters, and creeping through the woods with a flashlight. Am I going to play it more than once? Maybe, I don't generally re-watch many horror movies either. As long as the story continues to be scary and well told, I'm in.

When I first tried this game, shortly after it launched, I bounced off it within an hour. The art style was great and the writing was interesting and varied. The problem was, the gameplay itself just wasn't fun. The whole 2AP per side per turn was just too large a restriction on doing anything interesting and the necessity of needing to pick up resources during combat (they weren't rewarded afterwards) further messed up the flow of combat.
HOWEVER, to their great credit, the developers listened to their customers, and have spent the past several months revamping most of the game. The biggest change being that combat now functions like most other turn-based tactical isometric games; which is exactly what most people wanted. The combat itself is a little simple, due to the lack of activity abilities (other than the battlefield-wide dozer abilities). But between 4 classes, 5 factions, and the elite units there's enough passive differences to still allow for variety in combat.
And the result is that I'm having a lot of fun with the new REDUX version of the game. I can't spreak for other people, but bear in mind that reviews of the game that came out before March 2016 were reviewing a much different game than what it is now.
I do wish there were more unlockables than just the different types of dozers (your mobile home base), but that's the nature of rogue-likes I suppose. And if the developers continue to focus on improvements to the game, I would like some active abilites for units, at least some sort of overwatch system. But even if that doesn't happen, the developers deserve enormous credit for listening to their customers and doing so much work post-release on the game.
Its definitetely not perfect, but if you're looking for another turn-based tactical isometric game this is a pretty good option.

Thought I'd give this a try after hearing it described as FTL+post apocalyptic funfun+Banner Saga. TL;DR is it doesn't live up to any of those influences, and game-breaking bugs had me restarting the game every 10-15. Disappointing. Don't buy. If you do buy, don't play for more than the refund-maximum 2 hours before you decide whether you've had enough of the bugs/wonkiness of the game design.
Pros: Art style, setting, style of game. I really really wanted to like this, for the designer's ideas To Work, especially after they took pains to push out a new combat turn system for the Redux.
Cons:
-Bugs. Crashes on ability use, on end of encounter, on character deaths, on random event proc, and most frustratingly during final narrative cut-scene dealio.
-Roguelike elements go out the window when after your first wipe your ONLY option is to "resume campaign" from your last autosave point, even more critically with a new seed on random encounters, positioning, etc. Savescumming removes what little difficulty this game could have...and the game forces you into savescumming. Hoped this was a bug. Had to reinstall to start a new campaign. Same thing. Sooo...not a bug?
-Lack of difficulty under the new combat system, frustrating-gameplay-as-difficulty mechanic under previous.
-You have the illusion of choice in your route, but to win you have to hit the same 4 points. Other main interest points highlighted on the map are Strongly Recommended, especially if you cranked the difficulty up when you started. You can go back to previous points. Less engaging than randomization of FTL path.
-Where FTL had the looming armada-catching-up-to-you to drive you forward, difficulty here is intended to gradually scale the longer your trip takes, the more victories you rack up. Longer time farming side missions/making your way=more health on enemies=hurry up, Leroy. In theory, neat. In practice, you just end up taking your high damage units and abusing abilities with the "threat bar" maxed out, with the only option to reduce "threat" being to intentionally lose fights/sacrifice units. My first few encounters at maxed threat (relatively early on the map) was challenging-ish, until I realized you could spend ability resources to reduce ability costs and out-of-combat healing time. Game then became "which I-win button should I use?"
-Cover mechanic is poorly implemented. Enemies huddled on the same side of a barrier as your Thuper Awesomesauce Unique Sniper Man take reduced damage as though they were BEHIND said cover. Shotgun pushback is the only consistent way to push a unit out of cover, and is inconsistently applied. Can't destroy said cover. Can't deploy cover.
-Lack of variation/depth in factions. Factions! NEAT! FTL had those! But here each faction encountered or played as has very little variation in playstyle, either in their units or in abilities on their faction meatwagon. Abilities unique to one faction are obtainable as on-use abilities picked up as overly frequent drops as you truck along, and didn't seem to meaningfully change how fights played out (either as or vs. said faction). Faction abilities being based on turns (every other, every third) at first seemed like a depth-adding element (FOCUS DOWN THE KILLER ROBOT BEFORE IT GOES INVISIBLE WARGLARBLE) but effectively...didn't add much at all.
-Lack of depth/variety in units. Vanilla units get better with kills, up to a rank cap- neat!!! But these levelups only add 1 more damage, some units get more health. Elite units have higher health than their normal versions, have unique looks or are at least a reskin of their baseline version. Else, just different effective ranges, movement values between classes.
-Non-elite units are meat fodder until you can replace them with elites. Some thought went into making your starter guys feel special (unique interactions with specific random events) but effectively...nope. You're going to take whoever has the shiniest damage score and the largest health pool. AKA elites, or veterans you pick up randomly and regularly.
-No ability to customize units. Not asking for X-COM 2 levels of visual or ability customization, but...damn.
-Unique aspects to each of the classes felt...half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
->Snipers: Squishy high damage, nothing to see here. Need to be positioned Just So to pull off damage vs. other games' accuracy mechanics, scaling damage based on range, etc.
->Shotgunners: Randomly (if you don't want them to/if you don't really need them to/if squint reaaaally hard at the screen before clicking attack) MIGHT push enemies back, might even push them out of cover. Woo!
->Gunslinger reactive shots: Get hit by enemy in targetable squares= counterattack tiem. Neat! No overwatch, but ok, something newish. Only...reaction shots seem to be bugged, do not proc as described/intended/with any regularity and by endgame/high levels of threat the plink damage from reaction shots doesn't stack up to merit bringing gunslingers over meatshields/snipers/shotguns.

I've watched Skyshines Bedlam all the way through development, and it's a gorgeous, richly detailed beast.  The new "Redux" update transforms the game into the deep and addictive strategy roguelike it was always so close to becoming.  The developers deserve a ton of credit and respect for sticking with it and evolving their game into a nearly perfect state.  Now is the perfect time to take the plunge and fire up your armored war wagon!
Easily described as XCOM and FTL mashed together and thrust into a postapocalyptic, Choose-Your-Own-Adventure world that would give Mad Max nightmares.  Complex where it matters, sleek and efficient nearly everywhere else.  BEDLAM takes turn-based squad combat and makes it effortless (and addictive).
The new update reworks the Action Point system in combat, leaving much more opportunity to experiment with employing different strategies against your enemies.  There's also a significant amount of new content, including additional art, many more story branches, different crew and dozer types and the addition of a fast-paced "arcade mode" as an alternative to the grueling campaign.
Bedlam strikes a pitch-perfect tone between pulpy science fiction, cutting satire and postapolyptic horror.  Challenging, unpredictable and highly recommended!

This game has very good mechanics. I played this game on launch day on the PS3 back then for almost 100+ hrs. There's a reason why I bought this game again on PC so here are my honest thoughts on Resident Evil 6.
The game would've had less flak if it doesn't have 'Resident Evil' in its name. The bad stuff I can point out on the game is the tedious quick-time events which lead to cheap deaths, sometimes unforgiving enemy damage & the lack of horror. But at the same time the game does a really good job on having an interesting story throughout 4 different campaigns & how well they intersect each other so kudos to Capcom & the devs for executing this so well. Each campaign has a different flavor & the characters are well done, old & new ones. The story is easy to follow so newcomers won't have a hard time catching up. The battle system can be difficult to pick up in the beginning but once you get used to it (especially the melee system), it will get more interesting later on. The campaigns have insane replay value so you might catch yourself playing them again possibly on a higher difficulty. AND THANK GOD THE A.I PARTNERS AREN'T BRAINLESS IN THIS GAME.
The Mercenaries is a great special mode in this game. It's the best Mercenaries yet compared to the previous ones in RE4 & RE5. You get to battle a horde of different variety of enemies in a limited time & to get the highest score possible. Unlocking the rest of the characters & costumes didn't feel tedius to me before so definitely check out this mode, solo or duo. (Also, this mode is an easy way to get more skill points to use in unlocking skills like item drop increase & more damage with melee attacks.)
My final verdict with RE6 is 8/10 for a Resident Evil game but if it's not one then it's an easy 8.5. It's really worth in the rich content you get in the game & it has great moments. The game is fun in solo but it'll be much funnier with a friend. Give this game a chance if you can.
PS: The recent reviews here are more positive so far so it's good many people are looking past the hate this game have gotten.

TL;DR: You will duck in your computer chair, lob mortars into an enemy base for lulz, and fight on foot to kill an enemy.
The best game I've ever played that combines RTS and FPS. The action is like Homeworld meets Battlefield 4, and it's a damn good marriage. Battles are fierce, especially when resources become scarce. Unit capabilties are all different, from weapons to manueverability along with the many different weapons you can equip. The multiplayer is fantastic, I've never had an "easy" game and the community is fun to play against. From players trying to snipe during a large battle with rockets and freaking laser beams going everywhere, to dropping a mega bomb at your foes base entrance to weaken the defences, there is no safe space. You will have your weakpoints exploited fiercly and deal with head to head combat when it comes to getting resources. People will treat it like gold, and rightfully so. I remember my bombers getting whipped by a fleet of scouts that flanked me -- but the balance is so well implemented with speed vs firepower, that I barely won the fight. I retreated after my victory, ammoless, only to be taken out by a few scouts chasing me.
My fondest memory was when I was literally ducking in my computer chair when a ship flew over me while I was attacking a small enemy outpost, which got ugly quickly when it became clear it was a trap. I recall knowing it was likely a trap, my ally said I'd regret chasing the bait, and even my cat said not to do it, but there's nothing more pleasing than chasing and shooting a ship running away from you if it means getting some scrap and downing one potential attacker.
There are so many ways to play the game, and so many ways to counter an enemy tactic. Each encounter is different, some more brutal than others. Such as both enemies going at it, blowing each other up, getting ejected high into the air, then floating downward towards each other to finish the fight ON FOOT. These are the moments arenas full of people would get tense over, someone will get laser beamed to death or sniped in the brawl -- perhaps by a mutual enemy watching from the sideline? Or some random♥♥♥♥♥scavenger came by making its way to drop off scrap, and creamed one of the players on accident.
Yup, welcome to Battlezone.
If you liked the original, or are looking for something with an uncommon style of play for a change of pace, this is a steal at 20 bucks.

I've played Animal Crossing: New Leaf for over 250 hours (that's about 120 more hours than I spent playing Skyrim) so I feel pretty confident that I can give an informed opinion as far AC substitutes go. If you're looking at Castaway Paradise odds are you're in the market for something that replicates the Animal Crossing experience. I've tried many different games so trust me when I say this is as close as you're going to get, but I don't mean that to carry any negative connotations.
Castaway Paradise does some things better than Animal Crossing. For instance you can place furniture anywhere on the island, even outside, and totally customize every inch of the place. Really the only thing I would say that's a bit of a bummer is that unlike Animal Crossing you're stuck with a core group of Islanders. No one moves out and people do not move in. That being said there's quite a bit more in the way of daily activities than there is in AC.
As an AC substitute this is as good as it gets, but it's still a really good game in its own right.

It's a funny quirky and lighter version of Animal Crossing!
If you buy it on sale it is definitely worth the price!
Edit: The devs have improved it even more, now it's actually worth even the full price
The Developers update it all the time, add more features and are very active in the forums, listening to gamers and improving the game.
About the game:
You can practically do all what you could do in Animal Crossing:
Fishing, catching bugs, shaking trees and collecting fruit from them, sell the stuff you find like fruit/shells/trash, plant flowers/trees, talk with the habitants of the island etc.
But! This game also has more than just these features, Castaway Paradise offers more to discover and more challenges! You can do quests for the habitants and you can plant crops! That was previously not possible in Animal Crossing. You can grow the crops and sell them. You can also invest your money into stocks and sell them when they rise. You can improve the buildings and bridges of the island with your earned money. You can also pay off your own house and unlock more rooms which you can then decorate with interesting furniture.
The developers have added lots of different theme packs for furniture/flowers/clothing/fences and other furniture for outside the house.
All in all this game is interesting and you can unlock a lot of stuff by playing for a while and earning experience points and money! Though it gets repetitive after a long while (about 35 hours in), but if you look into it every day/every other day to finish the daily quests and get some rewards you can easily keep the interest up and even get all achievements!
(That's me saying that, and i usually get bored very fast if a game is repetitive!)
Try the game, it's very fun, especially if you like decorating or doing short quests and unlocking more things for your character/ to decorate your island!

I've had my eye on this game for a while, given it's so much like Animal Crossing. In fact, that's what people are constantly comparing it to. I was excited to get it on sale for like five bucks, but...that excitement didn't last long. I had most of the island unlocked within a day of playing, and after that, things get very repetitive.
Pros:
* It is a lot like Animal Crossing, which is nice because it's a familiar gameplay mechanic. You run errands for the other villagers (quests,) catch bugs and fish to sell (or donate to the local museum,) and scavenge fruit and washed-up shells.
* You never run out of quests, whereas in Animal Crossing it can be very hard to get the villagers to give you errands.
* You can also farm crops, which is pretty neat.
* Very intutive interface, so there's no 'oops that was the wrong button' moments.
* Nice graphics that don't seem to take much to run--my computer is a joke and I've never once seen this game lag.
* I like that, the more you play, the more furniture packs you unlock. It's also nice because you get additional prizes for logging in every week.
* There's a banking/stock market system which, while simple, is pretty fun.
* You can unlock other villagers, and the developers are pretty good about adding DLC packs, which, as far as I can tell, are always free.
Now for the bad part...
Cons:
* You run out of stuff to do ridiculously fast. Once you unlock the other parts of the island, is pretty disappointing to realize that there aren't any more.
* There aren't very many villagers, which is a disappointing. I think the most you can get is six, and that's including a DLC that you have to download.
* There aren't many fish or bugs, although I think the devs are working on adding more.
* Your house is pretty small, even when you unlock all the areas of it.
* Although I laughed when I read another reviewer saying that the character interactions lack depth when compared to Animal Crossing, it's actually true. In AC, when you talked to a villager, it could be engaging or at least funny. Castaway's Paradise interactions are kinda bland. Also, there are several typos in the dialogue, which is pretty cheap in a game that costs 15$. And they're stupid types like confusing 'to' with 'too.'
* The island's pretty small, with not much to explore.
* There are ships off the pier that have no purpose--maybe the devs are planning on makng it where you can visit other islands?
*Timing seems to be unbalanced. It takes ten minutes to upgrade a neighbor's house, but 24 hours to grow an Artichoke to full size.
* Given that the furniture in your house can't be interacted with at all, it makes decorating kind of boring and pointless.
* Villagers can't move out and be replaced, and the buildings are in awkward spots.
* There's no weather/day/night cycle, which seems a little cheap  considering the game's potential.
* The statues all over town are in the absolute worst spots.
* The villagers' quests can be contradicting. One asks you to plant four flowers, the next asks you to dig up six.
* The music is a little annoying.
* And this would have to be my biggest criticism--the price. I got it for five bucks, which, yeah, that's a good price, considering it's worth about seven. But this game's full price is $15 dollars. Honestly, it's not worth that. I may change my mind if the devs ever add new content, but as it stands, this game is full of untapped, overpriced potential that leaves the player wondering 'why am I even playing this if I'm this bored?'

Before I start, here's the final thought (which will be repeated at the bottom after the whole review):
"On the whole, if you liked Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you will probably enjoy Watch Dogs 2. If you hated Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you'll likely find a plethora of things you'll love to complain about to everyone else."
For all the people reading these reviews:
A lot of the people complaining about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ frame rates are the same ones who haven't updated their graphics card drivers. This is speaking as someone who was getting some choppiness here and there, investigated, found other people saying "hey you should update your GTX graphics card drivers before playing the game", went ahead and tried it, and sure enough, my GTX 970 plays it smooth as butter.
There are some moments where the volumetric fog over the whole of the san fransisco bay will cause some frame drops, but on the whole, I was playing somewhere between high and ultra on a single GTX 970, and I'm running it just fine with almost always over 60FPS.
The gameplay is your stereotypical Ubisoft openworld game; for some players, this is overplayed, overdone. For me, I happen to enjoy the hell out of it, having played most of the Assassin's Creed Games. If you're an Assassin's Creed fan, this game plays very similarly to Black Flag (the character goes where you want them to about 95% of the time, the other 5% of the times are very frustrating). Unfortunately, just like in Blackflag, the game automatically puts your character into 'stealth mode' as necessary, rather than the more recent AC games (and original Watch Dogs) that allowed for a dedicated 'crouch to stealth' mode. The good news is that Ubisoft has learned valuable lessons from their recent The Division, especially regarding smooth transitions and cover system gameplay.
For WD2, the storyline is much better than it was for WD1, but I swear, it feels like I'm watching the grave realities brought up in Mr Robot, except presented by the Disney Channel. Some parts of the story are stale and contrived, while other parts feel authentic. On the whole, there haven't been many moments where I simply didn't care enough to continue playing (reference: Assassin's Creed Unity, FarCry 4).
The game devs did a much better job designing variability into the puzzles and interactable objects, though once you've gotten a hang of the game mechanic or interaction, it becomes pretty easy to solve the puzzles. This makes doing missions and side-missions a little less monotonous if you're knocking out a bunch.
My biggest gripes from the original Watch Dogs that made it unplayable:
* Horrible PC optimization, the game would freeze constantly, even on top of the line graphics cards
* Terrible quality graphics compared to what they had shown and advertised (thanks, Ubisoft, for agreeing to sh*t-down the graphics on PC to match the quality shown on consoles. That didn't come back to bite you in the *ss now, did it?)
* Driving engine was TERRIBLE. You shouldn't have late 80's-esque F-Zero levels of control over a vehicle that's moving through mid 2000's game engine that has realistic lighting and physics. I entered into the original WD expecting an arcade-racer style driving experience, but WTF.
* Stale gameplay
* Stale story
In Watch Dogs 2, it seems that they've taken extra care to tackle the previous game's problems as much as possible.
* PC version of the game works amazingly on my gaming rig (GTX 970 GPU, 16GB DDR3 RAM, AMD FX-8350 CPU)
* The graphics quality is typical for a game in 2016, and amazing compared to the original Watch Dogs
* Driving engine is way better, and arcade-racer-AF. That's okay with me, though, because I like both arcade racers and racing sims.
* Gameplay thus far has been entertaining and varied enough (as far as possible approaches, weapons, gadgets, attack methods, etc) that it hasn't gotten boring yet, and I'm over 20 hours in now.
* Story thus far has been overly-simplified and watered down, or (conversely) hyperbolized so the general audiences can get a pretty good understanding of what is actually going on IRL with data privacy. That being said, it's been more entertaining than Mafia 3's story, and definitely better than any of the Far Cry stories.

Essentially Puddle is a platformer game where instead of a character you control multiple fluids (sticky, explosive, you name it). You know the drill; getting from point A to B. 'DEVIL WORSHIPPERS INVADE FAMILY ISLAND!', yeah, this could absolutely be one of those weird early eighties action flicks or, if it's unlucky, a slightly more recent Steven Seagal movie.
With only the first three chapters sketched out and playable thus far, The Ritual on Weylyn Island is giving a very solid account of itself. Cult plots are usually too saturated in cheese to grind any fear from but the game establishes their brutality early as you arrive at a family residence to find blood, broken glass, defaced pictures and arcane graffiti. Your first encounter with the invaders is similarly unsettling; fleeing through a dense wood, you veer off onto narrow branching paths, forced to suddenly retreat as you almost run into the outstretched hands of robed figures.
There's no combat to speak of, aside from a QTE, and the best thing TROWI could do is keep it that way. This isn't a difficult game; there are no puzzles beyond figuring out which box to barricade a door with but it is the engaging equivalent of a walk through a haunted house.
Apart from the tightening up of interaction UI and some unfinished sound cues, my advice to the developers is mainly plot orientated. I'd ditch the opening cutscene. It looks like crap and acheives nothing. Tighten up the dialogue. Keep the cult in the shadows. I could really have done without the demonically possessed family members hissing and swearing; I think the atmosphere is better served by the hooded cultists but if they have to stay, keep their mouths shut.
