Ok proper review now since i got the game working ( the mouse and keyboard didn't work since i had a blue tooth usb game controller plugged in). So what do I think of this game, its brilliant. It has a atmosphere and plenty of freaky things happen. You have to run round a seemingly deserted island looking for your lost family members. The best thing about this game is the classic horror feel to it. 7/10 Some work still needed but for early access, this is a great horror game that doesn't make your wallet cry.

I'll be damned if I know which "classic horror movies of the early 80's" the devs of this game are claiming to be inspired by on their Store page, given that I've seen just about every horror film from that period, and the two movies this reminds me of the most are "The Wicker Man" (1973) and "The Blair Witch Project" (1999).  But let's not be pedantic, and just try to review this as a GAME in its own right, eh?  Or, to be more specific, an Early Access game, which I'll say right off the bat this most definitely qualifies as.

The Ritual on Weylyn Island is far from finished.  Some sound effects are blatantly missing, for starters, and the aforementioned Store page clarifies that all we're getting at this point is the first three chapters out of six.  On the whole, though, it's perfectly playable, and far from "broken" from what I've experienced thus far.  What IS here, in any case, is looking awfully darned promising, especially if you're into all things witch-y and demonic, like I am.  This is some spooky stuff!  The sound design, while unfinished, is a particular standout, full of whispering voices telling you that they are coming for you and what-not, and while the graphics are nothing too spectacular, they're more than sufficient to create the desired effect.  The story is building up to be a good'un, the dialogue and voice acting is adequate if uninspired (and NOT in broken English, praise Satan!), and the gameplay is certainly solid.

So what exactly does the gameplay comprise of, you ask?  Well, thus far I'd describe it as somewhere between a first-person stealth-horror game (a la "Amnesia", et al) with elements of quick-time, narrative-based events not dissimilar to Telltale's "The Walking Dead" (push a table up to a wall, climb on the table to access a high window leading out of the basement to the world outside, and press "space" repeatedly to kick your demonically-possessed uncle in the head several times as he grabs your ankle and tries to prevent your escape...that kind of thing).  It's a very story-driven piece, in other words, but one which gets down to the nitty-gritty action nice 'n' quick, all things considered.  The Store page does describe the game as "combat-free", however, so I'd think it safe to say that you're unlikely to get your hands on a shotgun and go cultist-culling at any point in the game's narrative.  But if a story-driven horror-adventure with a fair dose of stealth and running away from enemies sounds good to you, this may well be one to consider.
Now, before I continue, there is ONE thing I should probably mention.  I've apparently played up to the end of the first three chapters - the first HALF of the game, allegedly - and it only took me about an hour!  So, er, yeah...it's gonna be one of them SHORT games, unless chapters 4 to 6 turn out to be much longer and/or more challenging than the first three.  I know there's a bucketload of you people out there who object to paying decent money for such a short gaming experience - I'm not really one of you, but - should you be one of those people, you may wanna hold off for a substantial sale, even once the game's officially finished.

And there ARE, of course, other risks involved with these "Early Access" propositions.  We horror game addicts have been burned one or two (or damn well near FIFTY) times in the past, so there's always the chance these devs are gonna go bust, or simply abandon their project because one of them decides their true calling in life is to become a lonely, God-fearin' pig farmer out in Kansas or somethin' (it happens).  But I can confidently report that this DOESN'T seem to be one of those scam-happy development "companies", which are in truth probably one or two nerdy young dudes locked in their bedrooms who take all their life lessons from GTA, and thereby believe that money = ♥♥♥♥♥es = the be-all and end-all of human existence, and art be ♥♥♥♥ED.  This one, on the other hand, seems genuine.  You can truly sense the LOVE in this one, and I don't mean in a hippy-dippy, Charlie Manson commune-y kinda way (nor is that the kinda love you're gonna get from the cult members you'll encounter in the game).

For now, consider my recommendation a somewhat reserved one, based on the fact that this is very much a work-in-progress which could go any-which-way at this stage.  Fingers crossed, I'll be increasing the below rating mere months from now.  If not, well, it won't be the first ten bucks I've ever wasted in the ever-unpredictable and oh-and-so magical land of Steam...such is life...

Verdict: 7.5/10.

(PS Nice to see a new horror game where your character isn't so borderline-asthmatic that they can't run more than five metres without stopping for breath.  Thank God some devs are reading reviews, and paying attention to which recent trends audiences AREN'T actually liking!)

It's rare for a game to be so fascinating and yet so mind-numbingly boring at the same time.
7 Grand Steps is not-so-secretly two games in one. There is a choice-driven narrative, and a kind of token- and pattern-driven board game.
The narrative is the fascinating part. It tells the story of your family line spanning dozens of generations; these small vignettes give the world flavor and gives you tiny hints of insight into the larger culture surrounding your family.
The problem is, to get to these vignettes you have to play the board game. And the board game is... not great. There's some good allegory here - you're almost literally "keeping up with the Joneses", as it were, making kids and earning coin. But the actual mechanics of it make it a chore - I spent a lot of time simply muddling around on the board and not actually accomplishing much for my troubles. Sure, you'll get those short vignettes for your trouble, but they are few and far between. Making matters worse is when you finally get to a new generation and the narrative you get is a rather floral description of how badly you goofed up in raising a kid in the board game.
Even putting aside the price (as I got this game in a bundle) I ultimately felt this game didn't respect my time.

Final part, Multiplayer: This is where this game struggles the most. I absolutely love this game. It is what the latest Simcity should have been. THeres only a few minor complaints mainly about highways, but most mods plus updates from the developers help fix them.

The game has a few fancy creative sides by letting you make arbitrary roads, but I don't think the strategy tag is valid for the product. As others stated, there is no challenge in the game, unless...
...unless you want to solve the bogus traffic behaviour of the game and making a big city with a decent flow of traffic - for no other reason than to please yourself.
I have seen people writing 25 pages long tutorials about how to overcome and workaround the odd traffic behavior of the game. I spent most of my hours on record (90%+) with planning the traffic of my cities. Which I would really love, but the fact that the driver AI is so terrible that it just blows my OCD:
I had 5 layers of superhighways overground, ground & underground just to manage the traffic of a town with 100.000 individuals...
There are so many problems related to the traffic AI, I just don't know where to start?
- Car drivers don't take actual circumstances into account in decision making
- It's nearly impossible to get traffic flow on/off the highway without seriously disturbing the ongoing traffic - despite the 3 lanes
- When a car is taking an exit from a highway, it will !always! change lane at the exact distance of that exit, its not just visually unpleasing, sometimes it will be totally impractical related to the actual road conditions
- Overcrowded streets solve traffic jams by making cars disappear - one of the most disappointing feature of the game
- Roads with more lanes don't give any performance boost as drivers don't make use of the extra lanes like how it would happen in real life scenarios (I've seen so many arguments about going very detailed in planning, but the facts are there, they just borderline use the extra lanes.)
- Roads with traffic lights are completely useless
- Trucks stop on the middle of the road for loading, stopping all traffic in the area
- Train stations get terribly overcrowded, unless you spam them everywhere - then the rails become overcrowded
- Pedestrians can cross superhighways while high speed traffic is going directly over them at full speed
- I can't really tell if it makes any difference to have terrible traffic or perfect traffic, the game just doesn't tell you how much that matters...
Other things:
- pricing of small and large versions of police, health care & fire dept are just ridiculous, it feels just random how they are balanced, police stations never build big, health care only build big if you want helicopters, fire dept always go for big - this sounds totally random isn't it?
- not enough content
- nice bus system, you can put the station on the road, but the manual management of the bus paths is just repetitive and boring as there is no point to it
- your buses quickly go overcrowded and are way to expensive to run & no bus ticket income
The game is unpolished, not much thinking behind. It just feels random. They didn't reinvent the simcity genre neither implemented the original in a better way. Sadly.
I would not recommend it above 5$.

An absolute classic.
I replayed this game wanting to relive a game from my childhood, and was wondering to see how it held up. And...it did! Mostly thanks to the remastering it was given. The AI was updated, the graphics were given a nice smoothing out polish that stays true to the original game while giving it its own appeal all on its own.
The Campaigns are great. The base two that is, the expansion is another beast. The story is a fascinating concept I've yet to see anyone pull off quite as well. The Space Race was a cover to launch a new fleet of ships to gather a mysterious but powerful metal that fell to Earth in a meteor shower. America and the Soviet Union are spreading throughout the Solar System to find this new material, and slowly discover its not so benign origins.
Although it could be seen as basic in some ways, the writing and voice acting sell this story. Every VA is giving this story their fullest, and still maintains a strange sense of authenticity despite some lines or accents that are fairly cheesy in nature. The Soviets in particular are great in this regard.
The balance between the two isn't too difficult, the NSDF are a bit faster, the CCA are a bit tougher, and they share all the same units. Despite this they still manage to feel unique thanks to the great designs, and weapon loadouts. You have the ability to change loadouts as well once you have an armory, giving you any of the weapons in the game for just a bit of scrap. You can use units as they are and do great, or customize their weaponry and do even better! Or worse depending on what you give them, but still.
The difficulty is just right, as the campaign can be fairly challenging at times on the tougher difficulties, but thankfully a good strategy can carry you through the game. There's no times that not knowing what comes ahead in the mission will screw you over, and any mission that you lose will just about always be your fault, save for maybe one Soviet mission. You'll know it when you get to it.
If you're looking for the original RTS/FPS Combination, this is it baby. Great gameplay, Great story, Great voice acting, Great everything. The only gripes I would have are the AI are a bit too good at tracking your every moment before you make it, some missions are definitely stacked against the player and are a little frustrating, and ...Really that's it.
9/10 Spores, easily. Not perfect, but definitely close.
For $20, you will definitely get your money's worth.
Avoid the expansion though.

THE LEGACY IS BAAAAAAAAACK!!!!!!!!
I cannot stress how happy I am with this game. I've been playing (not to mention making mods for) the Battlezone franchise since my childhood, and while BZ2 expanded and improved on the original in almost every way the original Battlezone holds a special place in my heart, forever and always. And I am positively thrilled to report that this reboot is the very same Battlezone I came to adore back in the 2000's, albeit with improved graphics and performance.
Now, an un-biased review!
First off, graphics. The graphics are, indeed, more than a little dated. This still looks like the game that came out in 1998. That's not to say that it looks bad or anything. It just don't hold up compared to modern games, so if you're looking for something as gorgeous as Crysis 3 you'd best look elsewhere. The reboot did do a wonderful job of reworking the terrain and textures, giving the game sharper details and clearer imagery while keeping the retro look and feel of the original.
Next, gameplay. Where to freakin' start?! Not much has changed between the original and the reboot in this department. Gameplay is the original fast-paced RTS/Shooter hybrid, centering around the fleet of hovertanks you have at your disposal. Build a base, gather resources, build and command your army, all while dogfighting with enemy forces behind the controls of any one of the numerous vehicles at your disposal, from quick and nimble scout craft to meaty tanks to lumbering and terrifying walkers. Outfit your vehicle and your wingmen with a selection of conventional and futuristic weapons like anti-tank cannons, heat-seeking missiles, lasers, or that damn Thumper (an earthquake gun of all things).
The controls are rather intuitive for such a hybrid game. Sure, there are a few things that might throw off modern gamers (using E to jump and your spacebar to command units, i.e.), but once you get the hang of it the controls handle quite nicely. The UI is decent enough, with your units divided into catagories that you then select from (Offensive for things like tanks, Defensive for turrets and howitzers, utility for gatherers and such, ect.). The system is a bit limited but works smoothly enough with the gameplay.
All in all I HIGHLY reccomend this game to anyone looking to try something new. Battlezone plays like nothing else out on the market, and while an RTS/FPS hybrid does take some getting used to it is well worth a try. It may have aged a bit and might not look as good as current-gen AAA games, but this is one sleeper that will grab a willing player by the throat and keep them begging for more.

If you've ever played Animal Crossing and liked it, then you will probably like this game, and owe it further investigation or purchase.
Castaway Paradise is a cute and charming decorating game. Currently you can grow flowers, crops, catch fish and insects, collect shellfish, rebuild townies' houses, increase the size of your own house, go on quests for townies, buy outfits, furniture, carpets and wallpaper. All of these activities have level locks on the complete range of content, so depending on how you feel about content gating you'll either enjoy the farming of experience to unlock or hate it. Personally, I enjoy it.
Most meaningful actions, like growing crops, have timers attached. For instance, if you save up enough money to fix a bridge to another part of the island, you'll have to wait an hour for it to be constructed. When you evolve crops, you'll have to wait whatever minutes these take to evolve after watering them. It tends to space out your experience of the content, which is fine with me as I play it maybe half an hour in one stretch. I should mention you can pay your earned gems to skip the timers, but I've never done that... yet!
Basically your enjoyment of the game will come down to whether you find the townie characters charming, how much value you place on earning money to unlock/decorate the environment, and also how much you enjoy tasks like pulling weeds and watering plants.
Chore-based game with a community focus. The reason I come back is for helping out the island and the townies.
+ Townies are cute and have good written dialog. If you like little in-jokes about animals and pop culture, you'll enjoy reading what your townies have to say.
+ Some of the furniture pieces are really cool, and the devs seem comitted to adding more items/themes.
+ Decent variety in what you can collect and farm, as well as weekly leaderboards for fish and insects.
+ Seasonal changes, as well as holidays with special items to collect.
+ You can place furniture and floor tiles not just inside your house, but out on the island!
+ Devs that respond to the community hub, so who knows what might change later on?
+ No day/night cycle. It'll always be the same time of day, which makes the island feel a little less 'alive'.
+ Holidays and events seem to only affect the items available to purchase...
+ Aside from giving quests, townies don't do much. You'll never find them in their house, or hanging out together.
+ Only one music track that loops, which is a shame, since different theme music helps create an emotional connection in a game like this.
+ Being able to place floor tiles outside, but not being able to put anything on it, like a chair.

I was very excited to see this game come to Steam because I love the Harvest Moon and Animal Crossing series. However, I think this game needs a lot more polishing before I can recommend it to others.
One thing I like about the game is that you can buy anything you have unlocked at any time, which allows for easy freedom in decorating. However, there simply aren't enough furniture styles to make decorating interesting. For example, there's only one fridge style and one style of other kitchen furniture to match it. There just aren't many options if you like to color coordinate. Even with the theme packs obtained via DLC or daily login, decorating options feel somewhat limited.
One of my favorite Animal Crossing features is collecting all the critters. Fortunately, Castaway Paradise also allows collection of bugs, fish, and shells. Unfortunately, collecting them all is much too easy, as there are not many to collect and they are not limited to certain hours or seasons. I wish I could keep critters as pets too, but they show up on little mounts when you place them. :( (And they can't even go on the wall.)
I was excited that a farming system was included, but honestly, the clunkiness makes it more of a chore than anything. There's no real benefit to growing a variety of crops, since you can't do anything but sell them. You can't cook them, eat them, or give them as gifts.
There doesn't seem to be an affection system with villagers either. The animals have rather flat personalities and seem to like (or tolerate) you just the same whether you ignore them and dump trash on the ground or talk to them and complete their quests religiously. There's no real reason to chat with them more than a few times. You can't give them gifts, and their houses never change. The lack of multiplayer contributes to the dullness of interactions within this game.
Finally, and most importantly, the game feels so grindy that it's just not an enjoyable journey past level 15. The quests are often too annoying to bother with, e.g. "chop down your trees and destroy your flowers!", and there's no way to reject them. Money is difficult to come by, so I feel like I have to be stingy with decorations so that I can afford to get through quests. Tool stamina is annoying and expensive to upgrade. The game is essentially Waiting Simulator, as you might expect from a mobile game (which Castaway Paradise originally was).
Overall, this game just feels unfinished. I feel like I'm beta testing rather than playing a complete PC game. A price of $15 is considered unreasonable for most mobile games, as it is for this ported one. Castaway Paradise has a lot of potential and I really hope it improves to become a quality title that can compete with similar games.

I never tried any of the online components of DS Animal Crossing so I'm looking at castaway paradise and animal crossing as single player games.
The play from what I recall is very similar, upgrading house, weeding, picking up junk, etc. Let me tell you letting AC go for a few months and there were weed EVERYWHERE.
The quests in CP(castaway paradise) are pretty basic, and really seems like it would be a decent game for younger children who would probably play it more regularly as I can see myself again like in AC stopping playing so regularly after a while, but I suspect that children might play it more regularly.  It seems to be pretty safe as I haven't come across anything objectionable in the dialogs, text messages, etc.  However any child would have to be able to read or have someone else to explain things to them if they can't.

I'm remaking this review as I've finished the game.
Pros *
-Excellent upgrade from original game. Reflected on the gameplay & story flaws of WD1.
-First Ubisoft title I've played in a long time that wasn't a repetitive replay over & over. Missions were sometimes similar but for 90% dynamic and new every time.
-Map size is enormous and full of life. No vacant or bland areas to be found.
-Gameplay was really fun overall. From trolly sidemissions like ♥♥♥♥ing over company CEOs that had it coming to them to infiltrating the FBI. Never gets boring.
Cons *
-This title as of right now does NOT truly support SLI. There was 0 fps increase on my end whether I was using two cards or not.
-In general, the performance isn't complete garbage, but it's bad. I'm running an i7-6700k clocked at 5.2ghz with two GTX 970s FTW Edition (Highest OC out of box) and 16g of ram and I get 30-43 fps anywhere in the city.
-Depending on how you like your narratives, this time around Watch Dogs is more of a trolly/fun take on hacking. Personally I love that, but others might not.
-Driving is a trainwreck, if you want a general idea of how vehicles handle in WD2, think of GTA : Vice City. It's bad.
-Physics are meh. The toothpicks from WD1 have carried over.
-Firearm combat is garbage. I got to the point of upgrading my stun grenade capacity asap to completely avoid it.
VERDICT *
Good gameplay, fun story, bad performance, mechanics are so-so, no SLI.
Buy it on sale, they'll probably patch the performance issues by then if they aren't autistic.
Worth a buy

Tfm is a game you have to put a lot of effort into and i have to say it might be stressful at first but over time you'll get alot better. No instore purchases are necessary and your able to obtain any item you can afford and enter any room. In this game their are mini games where you have to advoid the cannons the sham is summoning inorder to survive and obtain cheese that allows you to buy items for your mouse. Their are also other mini games where you could race other mice to get first status and over time you could earn titles. Their is even boot camp where you would play complex maps that are also saved onto your status but i dont recomend doing boot camp right when you start. Instead play in the Vanilla rooms, the most basic and simple maps to help you get use to the game it's self. To top it off their are Transformice rooms with maps that other players made that you could play. Now that the rooms are out of the way, lets get onto the shaman bees wax. Being shaman means that you have to distroy the mice around you or you would have to build structures for the mice around you to help them enter the hole with their cheese depending on what room your playing in. X  and Z is rotate your items, B is for red nail, V is for blue nail, C is for green nail. Green nail is used to link items together and Red is used as a base to start your build off, V is not useful and is only their for players on Divine mode. On easy your able to use all nails, On hard your only able to use green and blue nails and your equpied with a feather that allows you to use a totem ( A premade build ), and on divine your only allowed to use blue nail. You start off with easy and once you save 2,000 mice in easy you'll obtain hard mode and once you get 5,000 easy saves and 2,000 hard saves you unlock divine mode. Every round you play on is timed depending on what your playing ( Many rooms are timed by 2 min per a round ). Rooms like the village arent timed they are rooms where your able to buy things like cheese, titles, etc. With the basics out of the way, you earn titles by earning or achiving something. For example, you get the title Fastmouse for getting one first, Pirate mouse for 100, and so on so forth. I recomend clicking every button on the screen when you first join to know where every thing is located like the shop, the forms, the tribe info, your friends list, etc. To talk with your tribe write, /t in the chat bar and say what ever you would like to say to the tribe after; For example, /t Hey guys how are you doing?. You could make your own tribe or join one, it costs 500 cheese to make a tribe and inorder to join one some one will have to send you an invite. To leave the tribe click the tribe icon on the bottom left corner with a crest resembeling a cheese, once you click that click the gear icon and click "Leave tribe". Communication is a thing in Tfm of corse and cussing is allowed, your able to enable cussing by clicking the options icon under your mices actions tool bar and clicking enable language filter for younger audiences even though the game is recomended for 13 and up. People can be bitter and brutal and i recomend to ingnore any one who trys to hurt you peronally or spams you. If you left click on a persons user name you have the option to trade, Block, and  wisper. Wispering is a personal chat between you and that person, no one is able to observe the conversation besides the mods. Their is also an cafe where you can post topics and you can say your opinions on topics, I recomend not saying any thing offensive unless you want to be burned to death by every one else in the cafe that takes offence of it.  Thank you for reading this review <3~

While I didn't cry, the "twist" in the plot was unexpected and made me feel things for what are essentially "only" colored bits of pixels.
Controls are functional, but could have been a little tighter here and there. While I didn't run into many issues, the timing of some jumps may be frustrating to some people.
The game isn't very long, clocking in at only a few hours playtime, but with how huge my "stack of shame" is getting, I consider the short length a plus. Achievements were also a breeze and can all be completed on the first play-through, or easily gone back to from the level select.

The new update simply gives each unit 2 action points, making that aspect play more like XCOM. Loads of people were moaning about the fact that the game played differently from XCOM and, well, they got their wish, I guess. Fortunately, you can play using the old combat system, and it's really fun and challenging. You should check that out, too.
I've put in some more time since I first wrote the review, and I've actually reached the end of a few runs. It's lots of fun. I like the setting of the game and love the 2D art. Sound and music are good and unobtrusive. The strategic map offers interesting choices: do I go here and proceed with the story, or perform a side mission? Do I engage in a small battle for some resources? If I win, the threat level goes up and the difficulty increases: is that worth the rewards? Lots of interesting choices to be made.
In short, I thoroughly recommend this game if you're into turn-based strategy games. But please realize that Skyshine's Bedlam is its own game, and don't fault it for not being like any of your other favourites. Despite the changes, the tactical battles are still quite different from XCOM, since e.g. all units have a minimum and maximum range for attack, making positioning much more important.

Call of Duty Black Ops III is one of those game that gives you an ultimate experience. Ending the game, unlocking everything will take you a LOT of time, if it is even possible. The game is separated in a multiple modes. Campaign, Multiplayer, Zombie, Bonus.
The campaign has nothing to do with previous Black Ops stories, except a reference to BO II antagonist. Your character is a soldier joining a high skilled spec ops team, which will investigate about a catastrophic event that occured years ago. But you may find clues about them beeing traitors. A man hunt will begin, trying to figure out what’s happening, in the middle of a war for petrol. Terminating with a mind blowing ending, the campaign can be replayed to unlock special camos, weapons, equipements, as well as hidden documents and items. You will also be challenged with a hard "Realistic " difficulty mode. The campaign is ok, with explosions and action everywhere, but you might do it 2 or 3 times at best. Also a very good point, you can do it in cooperation with friends.
The multiplayer, one of the two biggest feature in the game, will let you join 6v6 (or more) fights in some fast action battles against other players. The modes are variant, Team Death Match, Domination (Classics), but special modes like Unreal Tournament’s Bombing run exist. Even if not many players are on them. The progression is never ending, you will firstly grind levels, unlocking weapons, equipements, scorestreaks, etc, then once level 55, the prestige race begins. You can choose to gain one prestige, locking back every weapons, and starting again. Each new prestige allows you earn more experience, and choose one weapon/equipement to keep. Once prestige 10 if done, you can move on the "Prestige Master", allowing you to move to level 56, in a long long long road until lvl 1000. This will unlock you more customization as you raise level. There's a money in multiplayer, which you earn by finishing games, allowing you to open loot box with camouflages, taunts, calling cards in it. There are also a lot of challenges to unlock.
The zombie mode. Now that could sound goofy, but honestly, the Zombie storyline made by Treyarch, is deep, interessting and even if you don't care about history, each map has it's own gameplay and ambiance. If you want to discover the story, DLC 5 Zombie Chronicles will let you play the World at War and Black ops 1 maps. Concretly, in this mode you will be dropped in a map, with neverending waves of zombies, becoming more and more strong and numerous. You can use points you earn by killing zombies, to open new areas of the map, activating traps, getting more powerful weapons or even upgrading them. The same system than multiplayer stands, in terms of progression. Prestiges, ending with a long Master prestige. Also with all the secrets ad strategys to do, you will never be done with the zombie game.
TL;DR
+ Campaign is OK
+ Multiplayer is nervous and enjoyable
+ Zombie is the next chapter in a storyline begun 9 years ago
+ Full zombie experience with the 5 DLCs
+ Zombie gameplay is deeper. Simple and complex at the same time
+ 800 hours of game time, far from beeing done yet !
+ Mod tool / Workshop on PC
+ Game in parts, but you can get them extremily cheap now, on websites everybody know, but noone talks about. ;)
+ Funny bonus mode: Time attack wall run, parody of retro arcade game (Dead Ops Arcade 2), remake of the campaign with zombies
- Huge place on disk with all the added content
- Beginning in multiplayer now with all the experienced player might be tough
- Joining a game i multiplayer were your team is beeing crushed is common
- Zombie with only the free map isn't funny
- Zombie publics can be frustrating
- Game in parts

I've had Rayman Origins on the PlayStation 3 since it first came out, and it's given me hardly any disappointment. It's a fantastically fun game!
There's no need to complain about the lack of a story simply because this game is emulating the good ol' days where it was just about the gameplay and fun and not necessarily about the story.
Rayman Origins is a 2D platformer, and the control in this game is very smooth and responsive. The game boasts 60+ levels of awesomeness, and players get new powers from the nymphs as they go along. Yes, you have to win the power of punching and kicking. But that's a callback to the first game! And the third! The levels are differently themed. You will travel through jungles, oceans, mountains, frozen tundras, musical lands and even an infernal kitchen! The game is designed to be relatively easier to just get through, however the game does get a lot harder as you progress. Plus, the major challenge in the game comes from gathering the collectables. Electoons can be found in cages or won by collecting hundreds of Lums, which can be found scattered throughout the level, obtained from defeating enemies or finding Skull Coins. The Tricky Treasure levels provide the second-biggest challenge in the game, as they are frantic chase-the-chest levels where the stage pretty much falls apart even worse as you keep going, and you earn Skull Teeth from these. The boss fights are not as difficult as I expected them to be, but they still provide a good challenge. However, once you complete the game there are a few very interesting twists that I will not reveal. Play the game to find out. :P The hardest challenge, of course, comes from The Land of the Livid Dead, a level that is unlocked after gathering all 10 Skull Teeth.
[EDIT: I have played this level, and GOSH DARN IT is it hard! I lost track of how many times I died just trying to complete one section of the stage, but it's a lot of fun, and worth it, too. :) ]
But it all gets a lot zanier and crazier if you bring some buddies along! Up to four players can play this game at the same time. I've only done co-op with one friend at a time (I only had 2 PS3 controllers), but even that gets nutsy after a little while. The players have free reign to slap each other without directly hurting each other (however that won't stop you from accidentally launching your buddy off the cliff or into a trap). I have, however, done a whole bunch of friend co-op in the game's sequel, Rayman Legends, and if that mayhem was any indication, you're gonna have a great time with this one!
The Windows/OS X port was done pretty well. The only gripe I have is that it doesn't appear to be optimized TOO well, as occasionally it will skip a frame or two. It's nothing terrible, but to me, it's noticeable.
Now, people may want to draw parallels to Legends. Is it better? Well... To be honest, I found Legends to be a little too easy. Origins packs more of a challenge from what I could see, and, honestly, I kinda prefer the cartoony art over the more realistic rendering of Legends. And it had an anti-climatic ending that wasn't funny like this on--
In fact, screw it. This game is miles better than Rayman Legends. To be fair, Legends has more content, but something just feels...off about that game compared to this one. This game has lots of character, bright environments, upbeat and fantastic music and, well, the entire game is amazing!
If you love platformers and/or Rayman, GET THIS GAME. You will NOT be disappointed! As you can see, I had no problem buying another copy of this game, so even if you have this game on a console already, get it for Steam.

Absolutely the best computer game ever written - here with a beautiful face lift. No other game ever came close to combining a first person shooter, inside a real time strat with online play.  The flight mechanics were always fantastic, and you'd have fun just flying arounf the moon and doing sideway slides, but combined with such a clever and intuitive user interface Battlezone really hit all of the marks. The only thing that was ever wrong with Battlezone, was that because it was an unusual mix - most people never even tried it.
So this is what it is.
Imagine a strat game - in the style of things like command and conquer, or something where you're building resources and one or more enemies is as well. Now imagine that instead of being a god like figure looking down on that game, you're actually inside it. You can run around, jump into vehicles, eject and so on - but more importantnly you can still command an array of ships and resources as the battle rages around you - almost as simply as pointing at something.
The AI of your ships and enemy ships is great and large battles can unfold - but then take that online - and suddenly you have a dozen people all doing this in a strat game, or simply battling it our like a roman gladiator.
In the last 20 years this game is still unsurpassed in the in game user interface, flight mechanics, first person strat - and potential for online fun

I am an experienced player of the original 1998 game and I still play it on occasion to this day. This is one of the greatest video games ever made and possibly the best tank real time strategy game ever made. It is legendary. Now onto the review of this Redux remake:
First thing, I appreciate that they kept the opening theme of the game, that was a nice touch. The rest unfortunately needs work. This does not look much better than the orignal game with the HiRes texture pack installed. I was expecting the graphincs to be much more polished but I was dissapointed. The vehicles (Tanks, turrets, etc.) have been improved only slightly, they are still blocky/geometrical. I was dissapointed with the sounds (Gunshots, explosions) as well, they are the original ones and sound exactly the same. The explosion graphics look the same as the originals with the HiRes pack installed. A few more things worth mentioning: When you first open the game the small launch screen looks like the work of a 2 year old, very crude. The fonts of the in-game menus do not look good. Also, the original game has a built-in cheat code to enable access to all the maps. You would choose your side (Either US or CCA) and then type:  iamadirtycheater and the map list would appear. It doesn't work on this remake. Since it was part of the original game, it should have been included.
I would not recommend this remake. Stick to the orignal w/ HiRes texture pack installed. Works and looks flawless, even on a modern system.

This and Battlezone II were some of my favorite games as a kid, and I'm so very glad the series is once again getting some attention!
The core mechanics of this game remain unchanged from the original. Which is good, as they (mostly) still hold up 19 years later. Zipping around in your tank of choice still feels good, as if the vehicles have weight to them. Weapons still have a punch. Commanding multiple units is still easy enough to figure out from the start, though doesn't get much more in-depth than what you get at the surface.
As for the remake, almost all of the changes have been cosmetic. Upgraded textures, visual effects, some touches to lighting. A proper, full-on remake could have seen multiple Quality of Life changes, or changes to things like the shape of terrain, additional units/buildings, or changes to the way pilot movement and combat functions. I just wish Big Boat Interactive had done
.
As it stands, it seems as though this project was given to a small team to test waters, and the new Battlezone VR game appears to have been the focus of Rebellion's use of the IP. The game is still fun, and I'm eager to see what else they have in store for the series.

Great third-person shooter mechanics, a complex but incoherent storyline, tons of minigame-like sequences, level design ranging from decent to painfully bad, and almost no fear-inducing elements whatsoever: that is Resident Evil 6 in a nutshell.
Resident Evil 6 was ambitious; it wanted to surpass all of its predecessors at once. To this effect, it features four campaigns, each with their distinguishable gameplay styles:
Despite this variety, all campaigns share many common elements—for example, movement and aiming is fast with fluid controls, while combat also offers a wide range of melee options.
On the negative side…
The user interface is catastrophic. QTEs plague every step. The story is disjointed with gigantic plot holes. The unlockable system is so limiting it is nearly useless. The game reuses bosses so often that it not even funny. Even Mercenaries has some issues with spawn triggers, despite being one of the acceptable elements of RE6.
Admittedly, while RE6 as a whole is still an acceptable action game, these issues are still big enough to consider it the weakest entry in the core series even to this day.

What is Castaway Paradise Complete Edition?
Castaway Paradise, for short, is a casual game where you land on an island and just help rebuilding it. For that you earn gems and puzzle pieces that you can get by doing various actions. Since there is no real objective to the game, it is very much a decoration sandbox game where you can unlock parts of the island and decorate everything at your will (provided you have the gems first).
Controls:
The game is completely controlled with the mouse and in most cases this goes very fine. When it doesn't, you just need to be careful. There are cases where icons appear that you would not want to click - for example, after digging a hole the game usually suggests you to plant a bug you caught earlier in the hole, instead of the flower seeds or fruits. So you must click one or two times extra. No big deal, but annoying.
Gameplay:
There is no way to permanently mess up, and so there are also no missable achievements. When you first start the game, you get a tutorial quest series, and you will want to just do quests for a while to learn all the basics of the game. There are various activities you can make, such as catching bugs and fish (and donating them to a museum), planting and harvesting vegetables, growing fruit trees (and of course also harvesting them), and rebuilding bridges, gates and houses. On top of that, you can decorate the island at will.
The game is definitely not made for someone who wants a deep story or gameplay, but aimed at a more casual audience, although it will require quite some time to achieve everything.
I heard comparisons to Animal Crossing, but as the versions I have I didn't play much, I can't tell.
Here is only one example, the most rewarding and involved of the various things you can do: You come across a field of 4x3 squares. First you remove the weed and stones (only once before you use it). Then you rake the field and plant seeds in it. You get seeds by buying them in the shop or the store menu. Everything is bought with ingame money, and even the VIP status is reached by leveling up enough. Conveniently you can access that store at any time - and that means also while you are at the field and just looking at the raked square, so you can buy and plant seeds with one click (two or three if you must choose another seed first) without having to enter the actual store menu. After that, you need to water the plants. Then it takes some time for them to grow. Then you water them again. Possibly you repeat that once more. Then you harvest the plants (or at any step before but then they give less plants), go to your silo and sell them (again, conveniently without having to go to the actual shop). You can expand your silo to hold more plants, which is highly recommended at least once. As a tip, I found peppers to give the best reward (508 gems profit per field in 30 minutes, possibly plus water refill time or minus water refill gems if you have many fields). You read the last sentence right - instead of waiting for the water to fill up in your can, you can also buy that with the ingame money. Convenient!
Of course you can upgrade the can to have more maximum water or deliver more water at once. When you get to the VIP status by reaching level 15, you have infinite water, but delivering at least 3 water at once still is useful.
On top of everything, the game doesn't take itself too serious - the characters are over the top, and that is a good thing. The always grumpy Angus who hates flowers, the partying Mayor Viktoria, the francophil baker Gustave - the characters you meet are all lovable!
Music and Sound:
Unfortunately, at the music it falls badly. Sure, the sound ingame is nice, but the music is too few. You hear the same music over and over - especially noticeable when entering and leaving a building.
Graphics:
The graphics are in two distinctive styles. First there is a 3D blocky style for most objects and subjects, without ever getting pixelated as in Minecraft (see the screenshots on the store page for how it looks like), second there is a 2D style for the rest, such as flowers and the ground. With everything it does, the game looks not bad but could be better. Probably it was made to resemble the abovementioned Animal Crossing games.
Recommended?
It is really hard to give you advice. I love the game, but I also see that beyond the humor the mechanics are relatively simple and shallow. For me it was worth the money (I paid around 5 Euro in a sale), and I got over a dozen hours out of it so far and will spend more, probably until I have all achievements.
If you want a game that you can return to every now and then, but then also are willing to invest some time to do the daily quests (that are optional but help you, and also reward you with badges not gotten otherwise for an optional collection), like half an hour for three or four times a day, then you have a small gem that can give you joy.
If you however want to explore a lot, do epic quests, save the world, have battles - no, this is not for you then. Go back to Skyrim! Here you can only save a small island and spend all the time on it.
PS: From some of the ingame things it is obvious that the developers might have wanted to make a F2P game ot at least modeled some mechanics after that. It is good that they didn't. There are no real money transactions inside the game, everything is bought with ingame money or - the VIP - by just leveling up, i.e. playing the game. It is only the second game from the developer that I find on Steam, and the first one that is a major project. The developer loves this game, he makes events for it, gives out free DLC every now and then. So as far as I can tell by this review, it would just be worth buying for that reason, just like Nation Red was back in the day.
As for the recommended price at which to buy, I can't tell. Personally I feel fine with the 5 Euro I paid, but depending on what you expect and how much you get involved in such games - or if you like it at all, it is as much a hit or miss at all or at any price I would tell. You must decide for yourself.

A casual game where you control a villager on a small island. The island has multiple NPCs who all give you quests, often of the type of 'collect three apples' or 'plant four flowers',  and the occasional fetch quest.
This is very much a mobile port, all the controls are done by big buttons and there are cooldown timers on just about everything, but the developers have removed any microtransactions and there is a lot of free DLC.
The development team is also active on the forums.
It has a cute art style and soothing background music, there is no voiced dialogue but there are good soundeffects to make the world seem more alive. As usual for games in this genre there are a lot of incentives to keep you playing, free items, lesser cooldowns, etc.
Another nice feature is that the game continues playing when you're logged out, so if you have to wait for a particularly long cooldown you can just quit and come back later, to find it completed.
I like what I've seen of this so far and will keep playing it for a while. It's currently still on sale, don't skip it!

A really nice action platformer with gorgeous 2D visuals depicting interesting and creative themes, solid controls and a gameplay that, while based on the first rayman from the PS1 era, is a lot more refined and fast paced, with great flow and bringing concepts from other modern games in the genre.
The painting-like maps and characters look like moving, playable concept art, with an enormous amount of layers, effects and animated elements. Some areas are more detailed than others, the first being one of the best, but even the simpler ones still give an amazing feel.
The music stands out with some really catchy tunes, but in a number of instances focuses a lot on childish sounds and themes that may become irritating to some people after a while.
The story, at least the part told directly in the form of cutscenes and dialogue during gameplay, is extremely simplistic, childish and minimalist, but hides lots of details and connections to earlier games in the franchise for whoever decides to look for extra material on the internet.
I felt a few pacing problems around the 60-80% mark, where the game was starting to feel longer than it should be, but after that it got me glued again until I finished it.
Highly recommended!

If you're a big fan of Call of Duty Zombies, this is definitely the "definitive" game to go to, which is what I'll sum up each of the maps in this review:
Shadows of Evil is a great and challenging map for fans of the series; however, for new players this could be a frustrating experience. It's best for new players to play The Giant first.
The Giant is a basic remaster of Der Riese from World at War. This is great first map for newcomers to the series, as it lets you learn the basics and mechanics. I recommend you get this map, either standalone or with the season pass.
SEASON PASS MAPS:
Der Eisendrache is like an extension of The Giant. It's possibly the best map of the Season Pass maps because of how accessible it is. The map will teach you the more advanced things of zombies, like buildables, easter egg quests, and strategies like training or camping strategically. It will really let you understand the bulk of what zombies is today.
Zetsubou really tests your patience and such. I think of it as a great map to practice multitasking and how to use your points wisely. Overall though. the map is not as great as the others.
Gorod Krovi is definitely the most challenging of the Season Pass Maps. There's just so much to do. With a challenging easter egg and tons of things to do like the little upgrade steps and such, this map will test your skills.
Revelations is the easiest of the 4 maps, hands down. Treat it like a giant version of, well, The Giant. Myster box wonderweapons, and tons of open areas makes this a map to either grind XP or just mess around and have fun.
And finally, Zombies Chronicles are remakes of classics that fans loved throughout the series. The maps here are vastly different in terms of how they play from each other. Have fun playing these maps!
Oh, I forgot about Custom Zombies as well! Those add a whole new layer of replay value to the game!

It's been an awfully long journey. The initial rollout of BEDLAM was to lukewarm reviews and to muted user response, largely because of a very polarising core mechanic which encouraged some very specific and exploitative play (the long and the short was that it encouraged some very specific team configurations and relied too heavily on you getting an elite that you could power through the game with).
That version of BEDLAM remains, for those that enjoy that style of game, however, there's a new mode, called "Campaign", and with that comes a completely new BEDLAM, one based very much on the XCOM:EU 2 AP per character approach. This completely flips the game on its' head, encouraging a balanced team of rotated characters where each individual link in the chain needs to be as strong as the next, lest you start leaking team members due to people getting smooshed by elites in the late game.
Skyshines' BEDLAM is a blend of a few different games - FTL and The Banner Saga probably being the most prominent titles that would make the most sense to suggest, having a flat overworld map made up of nodes that you can explore, a lot of which have choice based text adventures, along with a smattering of isometric tile based combat encounters where you move your combat pawns around and fight against your opponents. In this game losses are permanent, so there's a touch of the rougelite about it as well, along with persistent meta-progression as you complete runs and unlock more dozers and more options to start your loadout with.
The theme and lore of the world is absolutely excellent, seriously, it is. A bone dry wasteland that is filled with some memorable characters, a lot of backstory to each one, and a pulpy, comic book feel to the whole thing. The world building has been very well thought out, and is consistent enough that it could easily be built upon in other games, the lore is strong enough to serve as a platform for books and stories, if the game is able to keep going. The art style equally has this pulpy comic style that serves extremely well, and helps set the tone for the game in general, you really do get immersed in this somewhat askew look at the apocalypse. It's more Borderlands than Mad Max, and that's entirely to its' benefit.
Mechanically, the game plays out somewhat similar regardless of Arcade or Campaign mode. You'll be moving from node to node on the overworld map, and then exploring minor nodes with your outrunner car as you see fit, sometimes this will result in a fight, sometimes this will result in an adventure encounter. Either way, there's a LOT of content to digest, it's easily on a part with FTL post it's advanced edition patch, if not moreso. You'll be working your way through the badlands of Bedlam fighting the various factions, each have their own little quirk which adds flavour to the combat, as well as figuring out the best build for your playstyle (since each of the classes have their own way of fighting, and mixing them gives you a very different approach depending on what setup you run with).
With the advent of the Campaign mode, there's now two very viable choices for players. Arcade mode satisfies those who enjoyed BEDLAM at the point of release, complete with the BLITZ-o-meter and the original 2AP per side regardless of how those AP were spent over the turn. The Campaign mode satisfies the tactical thinkers who prefer the XCOM:EU style of approach with AP on a per character basis, and means that encounters are far more about teamwork and thinking ahead in a group sense, rather than an individual sense. These two very seperate modes actually work to the benefit of the game, opening it up to a much wider audience, and giving the game life where previously it would have been restricted only to very specific fans of the lore or the style of game.

Overall, I really liked this game. The world is open right at the start. There's no need to climb towers, and you have to explore the world to find collectibles and side missions by yourself. Because of this playstyle I chose, the game was more like a puzzle game. Sometimes, I felt the game became too easy because of the RC car and drone. The capabilities of them are so great that it was bordering on OP. But still, I feel that this is how Watch Dogs 2 should be. It shows how a hacker can thrive in a world where everything is connected and can be hacked. Of course it's not as simple in real life, otherwise how can Marcus put all the stuff he holds in that bag of his.
The only thing I didn't like was the driving. Feels like too much grip. But there's fast travel and car chases are minimal. So it's a minor issue.
I can't comment on the graphics, because I have a GTX 770, so everything had to be put on low. I'm playing at 1080p resolution, so occasionally the frame rate drops to 40, just for a second or two. The Redux patch brings Skyshine's Bedlam from the world's most confusing game of doubles tennis into the realm of an actual strategy game. While many people may have liked the two actions per side each round design, it seems far more flocked forth to give Skyshine's Bedlam a bad review.
Personally I held off on writing a review, because the Early Access portion of the title's existence was a week that existed only in an effort to avoid offending those Kickstarter backers who had paid extra to get the title early. I get the feeling that they may have had financial need to release the game when they did, and so I wanted to give them time to straighten the game out.
From what I have seen so far the Redux patch has made what was always a gorgeous strategy game into something a little more similar to games that have come before. No longer do you have to sit and watch the enemy take a step toward your highest level character, and then instantly kill them in one shot over the course of their "turn". There's a reason chess has people move one piece at a time, the potential for two successive moves to put someone in checkmate would be insane. I feel like Skyshine did the right thing here, there was no need to reinvent the turn based strategy wheel.
Another complaint I had about the game as it had existed was you were forced to choose, do you act and kill your enemies, or do you gather supplies for the long road ahead and likely suffer deaths. For some reason you're apparently not allowed to scavenge the battlefield after the enemy lies dead at your feet. The entire team moving allows you to split up the duties, acquiring more resources and killing enemies at the same time. Troops are more durable as well, no more will a character who has been the focus of all your efforts die in one hit despite being behind cover. There's still a risk/reward balance here, but it's no longer an 80/20 split.
The art of this game was always beautiful, and that was why I backed it on Kickstarter. I'm glad to see that with the Redux patch the game has conformed to strategy genre standards. They're standard for a reason, two actions per side was by far the strangest attempt to innovate I have ever seen. I am personally very glad they ditched that, because the AI had a clear advantage in the sense that they have legions of fodder, and your troops were always very finite and easily killed. This new system will likely take a little tweaking to balance perfectly, but Skyshine has shown dedication to making their game as enjoyable to play as it is to look at.

I'm very close to giving this game a recommendation, but I think it needs a few tweaks/more content to be worth it, even on sale. I'm a long time fan of the Animal Crossing franchise, so I was excited when I heard that a clone of it was available for mobile and PC. Castaway Paradise has all the right features, but they lack depth:
-I can upgrade my silo to hold more food! But why would I want to when all I can do is sell it anyway? I can't get more seeds, I can't use it as fertilizer, and I can only use it for quests once in a  while. It'd be nice to be able to choose between selling, turning into seeds, and something else.
-There's a catalog where I can order most items I need right away, which removes the challenge from it. Even a minute wait with a delivery animation would be nice. Also I don't see much point to using the shop when I have the catalog everywhere and I can sell all my items for the same price in many different places. Cheaper prices in-store would be nice, as well as specialized vendors who will pay more for certain items
-I like how fruit is automatically added to my inventory when the space is occupied by flowers or something, but it would be nice if I didn't have to click the green check mark every time I pick a fruit. It would probably be best if the green check mark step were removed altogether.
-There's a nice selection of items, but I don't just want to look at my house, I want to interact with it too. I can't even sit in my chairs or bed.
-The VIP section of my house looks nice, but it's totally out of place inside of what's supposed to be a tent... and why is part of MY house roped off? Give me a model home to tempt me and make the VIP section an upgrade like the other (but still needs VIP to unlock). I'd like to add more space to my rooms and add rooms, not just remove stuff blocking existing rooms.
-The stock market is very cool, but 3 stocks isn't enough and a buying limit of 20 is too low. Make it a single screen/chart with lots of stock options and/or add 2 stock tables for less advanced players.
-[Edit: This has been fixed/added] The graphics look nice, but could use an update considering this is PC. At least let me run it in a window
-I like the idea of the investment system, but needs rebalancing. I don't want to wait longer for less interest, either increase the % as time goes up or show the difference in terms of gems to make it feel like more time=more money.
-The high score table is kinda nice, but when people have maxed it out just in the past week for every insect/fish, it could use some work. Add a greater variation and increase the rarity of getting a really big one.
-It's nice that tools are separated from my inventory and can be upgraded, but I don't want to use the axe often, let me store it or something so it defaults to the water can when near a tree
-High scores seem to be the only multiplayer feature. Please add online multiplayer at some point
I think this game would work best as a mobile, time wasting game. Make the mobile version the same payment model as Steam (one purchase, gems instead of gold, VIP unlock at level 15) and I'd recommend that instead of the Steam version. Make the other changes I mentioned above, and I'd highly recommend either version.
As it is, I'd say just stick with Animal Crossing New Leaf.

The long and short of it is, this game just fell short and wasn't much fun in execution.
I enjoy both Animal Crossing and many of the Harvest Moon/Rune Factory games and it looked like this game might be a game with aspects of each.  Sadly this game has neither the charm nor the fun of any of it's predecessors.  Most of the aspects of this game are unnecessarily grindy and tedious with little reward.  I realize this had once been a Free2Play microtransaction nightmare, and the one thing going for it is that they removed the real money payment type but they left all the extra time sink requirements in.
As far as a farming and life sim goes, the controls are just too awkward to make doing anything a pleasure.  The targeting is a chore, especially if you are trying to put down a fence behind a house that you can only barely view behind.  And the farming and planting takes just a few too many clicks to select your actions all so that after a 10-12 min wait (and a few extra clicks) you can harvest a vegetable from a plant and then turn around and sell it for exactly what the seed to grow it costs.
There just isn't enough personal customization to really make doing all the chores (tasks the other inhabitants want) and waiting around to be able to do more chores, worth it.  Everything on the island is already in its place and just requires you to raise gobs of gems to fix up and make them useful.  The house you start out with is a tent and requires another gobfull of gems to turn into a house, but when you go inside said tent, it's just an interior of a house with the back rooms already visable and just roped off with an "under construction" sign.  If I'm living in a tent, my room should look like a tent so that the reward of raising all those gems really adds up to something.  Somehow the whole thing just feels like a community service simulation executed in real time.
Maybe it's because there are no good Animal Crossing or Harvest Moon Games available on Steam that this game has gotten such raving reviews, but this game just didn'y scratch that simple, life-sim itch like it's 3DS predecessors do.

After 2 hours of gameplay I felt as if Castaway Paradise had taken a giant dump on my childhood.
If one was to remove RNG, item scarcity, and complexity from Animal Crossing then add in pay to win elements you'd have something similar to Castaway Paradise.
If you are looking for an Animal Crossing clone for PC you'll be disappointed.
Pros:
- The building, environment and item art captures the essence of animal crossing 'cutesy'. (sadly I disliked the art for the characters which is very boxy and frankly kind of ugly.)
- Has character levels which add an extra incentive to do things around the town.
- 'vip' (the ios/android 'Pay to Win' premium account status) is awarded for no cost at level 15.
Cons:
- All the buildings and townsfolk are pre determined, gameplay is clunky and buggy.
- Game play feels mindless, every townsfolk quest is spoonfed to you. Buildings are predeturmined and in shambles and visible until you finish building them. Farming currency is a game of waiting for your watering can to spawn more water.
- The UI is still optimized for the phone and is thus needlessly large and clunky.
- With the exception of wasd for walking you must use the mouse for everything.
- All items are available from your inventories 'catalog', rendering the town store pointless. Infinite numbers of items can be purchased removing any sense of 'item scarcity' and adding to the feeling of a spoon fed mindless game.

In a nutshell, its a somewhat entertaining freemium game with infinite use - no paying real cash to speed up events or ridiculous long waits.

- Lacks day and night cycle

- Although decent enough, character customization could be better

Verdict: Castaway Paradise is the best (if not only) poor man's Animal Crossing, which is not a bad thing imho. Is not as quirky and downright adorable as its source of inspiration, but it has a charm of its own that works well enough. One of the main problems is that it was originally developed for smartphones, so the PC port doesn't translate well with its interface and timed actions. It doesn't have microtransactions at all and all of its updates are entirely free, which says a lot about the development team. Worth the price if you can understand that it's not meant to be the next Animal Crossing, but rather a charming tribute with enough cotent to keep you coming back.

Thomas Was Alone, by Mike Bithell appears to be a typical puzzle platformer with simple, narrative design and a captivating aesthetic minimalism.
Creating  short story fragments from the simplest of movements. It's original, and when something has personality, the flaws become peculiar; even, in a way, essential. That game i must say, has a lot of personality.
Thomas is just a red rectangle, as simple as that. Your friends are also blocks, each with a different way of jumping. Chris, Claire, John... are the names of some blocks that we control, and the most amazing thing is to refer to them as "characters." This is because the philosophical essence is not a limit for the player to establish identifications with the agents he controls, laughs at the situations and thoughts of each character or even lets a tear escape.
The quality of the soundtrack makes you melt, i liked the idea of playing as rectangles and squares, by the fact that we hear them narrated as we play, also the control of the "characters" are a reflection of human concepts.

Its minimalistic design really didn't deliver. Everything was very plain. And even the above average soundtrack couldn't elevate it to something greater. The puzzles were tedious and I couldn't give a damn about the 'story'. I feel like ''thomas was alone'' would be more at home on a flash game website. Also it is completely unacceptable that a game as graphically demanding as minesweeper has constant framedrops.

Overall this game gave me a great first impression this morning. The one thing I would ask is for a way to rotate the camera with my mouse, preferably with the right button of the mouse. On the PC the middle mouse button works to rotate the camera but it doesn't work on my Razer on my iMac and the Magic Mouse doesn't have a middle mouse button. Beyond that I'm very happy with the game. It is what the Sim City reboot should have been.
One final note to the game developers. Please make use of more cores on processors that have them. I have a 5930K and two GTX 1080 cards. I get 40FPS at Max 4K settings. The CPU usage is at 20%. If more threads can be run to make use of the processing resources I think the frame rate could go up and increase the ceiling for even more detail in the simulation model.

A great 2D platformer, capturing the original Rayman style with some of the elements from Rayman 2, 3, etc. The characters are quite creative and humorous, the music is nicely orchestrated and occassionally silly, and the environments are fun to explore around and find hidden coins and areas.

This makes it even harder in cases like the boss levels, as you try to remember the pattern on how to defeat them, the Treasure Chest chasing levels, and for those who want to complete every level with the highest amount of Lums and Electoons. Beautiful. Vibrant. Humorous. Brutal. Fun. Special. To me, that is what sums up "Rayman Origins" in the best way possible. In a time where platformers have stopped showing up as often as they did in the 90's, it's very refreshing to see and play this game. I only wonder why I did not purchase this game on it's initial release date in 2011. So, I may be late to experience the joy that is "Rayman Origins", but I can say that it is a good quality platformer. There seems to be arguments on where in the Rayman timeline this game takes place. It was originally planned as a prequel to the original Rayman PS1 game, but it was scrapped at the last minute in favor of a new "story" (if you can even call it that) and is now mostly viwed upon as a reboot to the original Rayman. There is no meat on the story at all; just a pile of bare bones. But, who plays a platformer for the story, anyways? Just look at Mario. The visuals are absolutely breathtaking! The colors are vibrant and the animation is as smooth as butter. It may be nice on the eyes, but don't let that fool you into thiking it's going to be an easy or friendly childs game. I would say that the vast majority of levels are set to an "average" difficulty, but there are some that are much more unforgiving. Timing, momentum, and precision are key to succeeding these difficult areas. If you don't gain enough speed, it could lead to failure. If you run and jump, you could miss your target completely and fall to your demise. Even pressing the "A" button to jump, or lightly tapping it for a short jump can make the difference in hopping around pointy shards. In a screen-scrolling section of the game, I went through the whole level perfectly and just one little thing messed me up completely. As I was sliding down a tunnel, the end collapsed ever so slightly just before I got to that section and bonked Rayman on the head, resulting in a restart of the whole annoying level. The solution? Pressing down on the analog stick to make Rayman slide on his belly so he won't bump his head. It's those small things that can make the difference, and you have have to be fast to react. Also, it never feels cheap; you are always in control of whatever happens. The feeling of accomplishment is very great; just as you have FINALLY succeeded on a level that you have died on over and over again. To make it a little more fair, co-op is an option and it is a blast! Co-op is not something that I am very fond of, but in this game it works very well. This game may have some of the best controls of any 2D sidescrolling platformer out there; they are top-notch, very reactive, and tight, which is a very good thing for this type of game. The music is pretty nice, too. Maybe not as atmospheric or trance-like as the Donkey Kong Country series, but very nice, funny, and relaxing all at once. The only complaint I have is that the structure of the game feels a bit inconsistent at times. Instead of the levels going from easy, easy, hard, harder; it can be more like hardest, then easiest, then hard, then easy. The same applies for boss fights. The challenge posed by these bosses holds little correlation to the sequence through which they're unlocked. You may complete an absolutely horrowing level, only to fight a more-than-easy boss. Other times, you will beat an extremely easy level only to be pitted against a very difficult boss. But, I guess this concludes my review. Rayman Origins is a game I recommend to fans of 2D platformers and players who LOVE a challenge! Absolutely anyone can pick up a controller and learn to play this game within minutes, but it takes patience to complete it!
RATING - 8/10

It's hard not be charmed by Rayman Origins. It has a sort of party atmosphere, with its bright colors, upbeat music, and surreal shenanigans that keep it charming almost all the way. Almost. The graphics are probably some of the sharpest 2d environments seen in a platformer, with a bizarre cartoony look that's not like much else.
At its heart, Rayman is a collecting platformer, where you try and collect thingies (lums) to free thingies (electoons), though there's a secondary thingie (skull teeth) you can collect in special challenge levels to unlock another thingie (an extra hard series of stages). As such, if you want to hit every note, you'll be repeating stages to make a better time or to collect more thingies, and your opinion on that may very. Overall, though, you don't have to sweat that too much, and those that can put their collection impulses on hold can charge through the game for the most part.
With a variety of moves and skills to unlock, most of the levels become a breezy delight, hovering, running up walls, bouncing off of enemies, etc. In my opinion, it comes very close to dethroning the kings of platforming, save for two issues: the levels can be long, and towards the latter half the game can lean towards being surprisingly tough. Seperately neither of these would be an issue, but together they can deal out some real frustration towards the end of the game. The long levels mean it can lean on being repetitive within a larger world, but each world is varied and often come up with some really great gimmicks, floating through updrafts or sliding down waterfalls. (Note to the developers, though: ice levels where you slide everywhere are not fun.) Annoyingly, the game has a tendency to ask you if you want to switch levels if you die too many times, which it will do over and over - some of the final levels had that pop up occur six or seven times, and when you're just trying to progress, it's rather irritating. An option to turn that reminder off would have been pretty welcome. Contrary to that, though the challenge levels can be similarly tough, their short length and breakneck pace thankfully turn them into one of the highlights of the game. At its best, the game has you charging through areas in a fashion you'd expect of a AAA theme park game, while at no point holding your hand.
Ultimately, though, whether you just get a taste or collect every bit, Origins is worth your time. If you can affort Legends, it's a better game that mitigates many of Origins' flaws, but since Origins is often available for just a few bucks during the seasonal sales, it's absolutely worth it. For those with a distaste for UPlay, you can also relax in the fact Origins doesn't use it at all. It's a rare "pure" sort of game from a big developer, with no DLC shenanigans or anti-piracy measures. (This may also be due to the fact it got a government grant for its development...)
Give it a shot, you should at least get a smile out of it.

Jagged Alliance is a very fun game if you like old school squad-based action that takes a good amount of skill and preplanning.
Upon starting, you create a character and have enough funds to hire a couple of mercenaries to accompany you on your missions. When recruiting, you can select whether you want a mercenary to join you for a day, week, or longer. You can also choose to outfit them with their preferred equipment, or equip them from your own stock. Each mercenary comes with a specialized role and relevant skills (+ equipment if you choose to pay for it).
I've played a lot of Fallout, especially Brotherhood of Steel, and I am fairly adept at those games.
In Wildfire, not so much.
Action points limit how far you can move/shoot, etc per turn, and fog of war prevents you from spotting any enemies outside of your party's field of vision. The feedback for weapon accuracy/chance to hit is very helpful, however, it should be noted that on Windows 7 and above you need to manually patch your game in order to fix the bullet drag animations (it is REALLY slow otherwise).
Aesthetics provide a good deal of nostalgia for veterans of older squad-based games, and the comments each mercenary makes when you are attempting to hire them adds nice flavor. The learning curve can be a bit rough if you are not already familiar with playing squad-based tactical games, and the tutorial definitely does not hold your hand. Character death is brutal, as there is no way to revive your downed teammates.
Character skill upgrading is pretty diverse, allowing you to completely remove skill from an area if you do not care about it (ex: putting first aid at "0" will effectively make your medkits useless).
Recommend giving it a try if you want a real challenge and do not care about dated graphics.

BATTLEZONE IS AWESOME.  It has always been awesome, and this Redux version does a great job of breathing new life into it.  When it comes to these nostalgic remasters and remakes, sometimes I have a hard time determining if a game was truly great, or just seemed great at the time and I was too young to really know the difference.  Rest assured, Battlezone deserves its legendary status.
Playing this game reminds you how great gaming can be, and why you've been a gamer all this time.  Most games have obvious inspiration from other titles, and generally follow the same formula within their genre.  Battlezone is a true original, there are very few games even remotely similar.  It's still the best FPS/RTS hybrid, and one of the best RTS games of all time.  The controls are unique, but instantly intuitive and very effective.  I don't understand why nobody has even attempted cloning BZ over the years.
All in all I'm very happy this "redux" version was made, and very happy I picked it up.  Battlezone would have been a legend in my memory either way, but nobody should miss this chance to relive one of gaming's true gems.
