Update:
I have now owned and played this game for a while and there was a patch recently that fixed a lot of the baisic bugs. Every month there is a new patch and every month this game looks a little bit more like what it is supposed to be. This game is not a simple indie project and honestly it would take a AAA game company ten years to develop something on the scale of what Dragon: the game is promising. Anyone who thinks this game should be even close to finished after two or three years has no idea what it takes to build a game.
Some people will fire back that the developers should not have released the game in early access at this stage. I disagree, Red Level is a brand new developer with very few recources and they are tackling an immense project while having to maintain their lives. Puting this game out in early access is a way to generate revenue and allow those who are interested in this type of game to check out what Red Level has done so far as well as get involved with the development process.
Giving this game a bad reveiw because it is unfinished is like being upset that you got fish from a fish market. It is still in its very early stages of development and as i said before it shows. however early access is not for people who want a finished game.
In the end:
Buy this game if you love dragons and like to watch as a game grows from idea to fully realized universe.
Dont buy this game if you are impatient and want a finished game.

7 Grand Steps is weird. I don't really have a better way to describe it, because it aims to be a life simulator in the strangest way possible. You guide the lives of a family through many generations of early human history, raising them up through the ranks of society from farmers to rulers. The way you do this is by feeding tokens into a fancy machine that moves your little people along an ever-turning wheel. The wheel turns counter-clockwise towards the crocodiles (representing death in the fine Egyptian tradition) every turn, and spending a token on your character moves them ahead to the next instance of that symbol on the wheel. You can also have your characters make new tokens, which keeps them stationary or moves them backwards depending on the proximity of other pieces, so you have to balance spending and making tokens. There are other characters on the wheel representing neighbors and acquaintances, and they have their own agendas as well.
You also produce children who become your new characters when the current ones die, and you can spend tokens on them to train them for life. The token system is a very clever representation of wealth and resources. Trying to balance their uses gets really tricky, especially when you get the chance to move to a higher ring on the wheel (representing higher society) and have to start collecting and using different tokens. As you move you also collect counters towards a life goal, which has dramatic effects on the wheel like changing token symbols or opening up new rings. There's quite a bit of storytelling to it as well, with some Crusader Kings-style choices to make about your family. Additional gameplay systems come into play as you ascend through society as well, such as ruling over others, and the game purports to have 15 hours worth of content. I didn't get that far because honestly this doesn't feel like my kind of game, but it's unique and worth trying to see if it's the kind of thing that clicks with you.

It is amazing how squares and rectangles can have this much personality. Wow...
Thomas Was Alone is a platformer where you play Thomas. Yes, that square is Thomas. And at the end of the game, you will not see it as a giant square. You will see him as a fully fletched character. The same goes for the other characters.
The narration makes this game. It tells how the characters feel, how they react to eachother. And he tells it oh so well. You feel sad when these little pixelboxes feel sad. You feel happy when they feel happy. It is truly amazing how well the writing is for this game.
The puzzles aren't too hard and I think that is actually a good thing for this game. It keeps the game going, so you can learn more about the personalities of all the characters. There is some more challenging platforming here and there, but they never frustrate because you respawn very quickly and can try again right away.
The only negative thing I have to say about this game is a music glitch that constantly happened during play. Every time I died, the music would reset, but would continue playing at the same time. Eventually, when it reset enough times, it sounded like a horror-mess which was unbearable to hear. Playing like 6 or 7 instances of the same music, but all messed up. Which was a shame, because the music really fits the tone and atmosphere. Restarting the game fixed this issue, but it hindered my experience a bit.
Still, I would recommend anyone that likes good characters in their games to play this. It proves that you can give anything emotion and character if you write and tell it well enough.

It's a Rayman game (I loved the first one on PS1), it's often good, sometimes great... so why I am so bored when I play it ?
Two expressions come to my mind to try to get to describe the feelings i have regarding this game: "Soulless" and "Paint-by-numbers".
Many of the levels feel empty. You go from platform to platform, you meet some enemies, but most of them are immobile, or even sleeping. They don't feel like enemies at all, they are not here to hunt you, they don't care about you at all. They completely lack personality. Good platformers have enemies that have an interesting behavior that give them personality. Even Goombas in Mario are memorable with their mean looking eyes. In Rayman, in many cases, that's not the case. It's so bad that sometimes it's hard to tell if something is here to help you or kill you (i made a few mistakes that way).
Story-wise it's the same. It's full of holes. After a hilarious 5 min cartoon intro, the game tells you "ok you have to fetch electoons again. Go for it". It's almost like there is no relation to what you just saw with what you have to do. Most of the characters you will meet have no name, and will usually don't utter more than one sentence. Sometimes it feels like there are 2 distinct stories and none of them was completed.
That's really disappointing, because technically the game is top notch, with colorful environments and very nice animations. And sometimes, the Rayman's magic is back. In a few levels, (particularly the water world levels), enemies actually have personality, the environments are full of life, and the music nicely complement the action.
Nowadays AAA studios have mostly abandoned platformers to the indie scene. So i was happy to get a new Rayman from a big Ubisoft studio. I suspect many of you feel the same.
However, I can't forget nor forgive the fact that, after 2 or 3 levels, i usually quit the game because i was bored. Worse, i also used the "skip level" functionality several times when i didn't feel like completing that level right away. That's not things i would get in a good game. I did finish the game, including the awesome bonus level (by far, the best level, and really enjoyable), but i really had to force myself to play many of the levels (particularly the wind world).
Sadly, there are too many boring levels where I'm just going through the motions. "Been there, done that", was a recurring feeling. Most levels felt like the 1000th iteration on the same stuff from countless platformers. There are too few memorable/good levels for me to recommend this game.
Maybe some of the problems come from the added multiplayer. I only played the game solo, and i guess with friends, it would get more chaotic, but also more fun. Maybe that would alleviate some of the issues i had with the game. It would explain why the levels sometimes feel empty and the enemies are too passive: with 4 players it must already be very hard to get to the end with everyone. But I'm unable to test that theory.
PS : For achievements hunters, be warned that the game doesn't include Steam achievements, even though the console versions have them.
PS2 : Regarding difficulty. Some reviewers state that this game is the toughest game they've ever seen. That's not my opinion. 2D Platformers have often been challenging games. Considering that fact, i think that Origins is not easy, but it's not hard either.

Rayman Origins revives a character we have maybe not actively seen in games for some time now. When I was growing up, Rayman was my absolute hero. I will never forget Rayman 3, and Rayman 2, where colourful characters came to life and took me on amazing adventures. Rayman Origins however goes back to old, old Rayman games, in which the character is barely larger than a pen and often finds himself dodging household utensiles.
Rayman as a character is a colourful little guy without arms or legs, who can make a helicopter out of his hair and traditionally throws his fist at enemies. He is often assosciated with his best friend Globox, a blue frog who loves to dance raindances.
Rayman Origins creates a beautifully colourful world, with fun music and great level design. The art in this game is absolutely amazing, and it all comes together in such a delightfully colourful way that it is a real joy to play through the levels.
It is also notable that Rayman Origins is a very quick paced jump'n'run, and when you find yourself used to the completely adaptable controls, you can go through a level with great momentum, never really stopping for anything. This makes the levels even more fun, as once you replay them and get the hang of them, you can just glide through them, reminding me very much of the old slide levels.
The game is quite replayable (as I just noticed myself by returning to the game after some time). You can free 5 Lums in every level, and whilst it is not necessary for game completion to get all these Lums, you can unlock new stuff and further levels by getting them all. It is therefore worthwhile to repeat older levels and look cloer for the cages of the Lums, or collect more points throughout every game.
There is not much of a story to the game, as expected maybe of a simple jump and run game, but generally the characters are charming and the environment is so friendly and vibrant that the story is not so much necessary.
My only gripe with the game is, that, as a longtime rayman fan, i find myself not recognizing the main character very much. To me, Rayman had always made a friendly, confident, cool expression, where as in Rayman Origins he very much becomes a tongue-stuck-out crazy silly kind of guy.
The game goes for a very silly reprensetation of the characters, which is certainly fun in the general feel of the game.
What is completely missing however is Rayman's traditional fist throwing mechanic. This came as a disappointment to me because I was so used to using this special,personal technique in most of his other games. Rayman no longer throws fists, instead he kind of just slaps his enemies, or tornadoes through them, or kicks them, or stamps them, which is all very fun, but I miss his trademark technique.
Overall I can absolutely recommend this game. If you can ever get it in a sale and maybe get it for a bit cheaper, it is definitly worth it. Lovely Art, lovely Music, fun and unique level design, charming characters, definitly replayable, even if you dont have a lot of time on your hand. Quick paced and lively. Whilst it is not the continuation of the rayman franchise that I had maybe hoped for, it is certainly a great Jump'n'run more like the very old original rayman games.

UPDATE 3/31 - Version 3.450860234??? something like that...is out! The developers spent a ton of time rebooting the game and changing the mechanics from the two guys move per turn setup to the more standard XCOM style of move each of your guys then end turn. You can still play in the original mode via the options menu if you so choose.
The update also brought in a number of tweaks and additional content as well as a slightly altered path to victory that makes the game seem a little less grindy.

Kudos to the Dev for not jumping ship when the initial run of poor reviews came sliding in btw.
OG REVIEW:
Your ability to get enjoyment of this game will start and end with the combat. Since the combat style/mechanic is different than any other tactical style game I can think of you really need to spend a few minutes at least watching a "let's play" and go from there.
Personally I enjoyed the combat style a great deal and it helped me to get over a number of blemishes I found along my journey through Bedlam.
Pros -
Solid Tactical Combat Puzzlesque Fights
Unique (as far as I know anyway) mechanics
Colorful artwork helps bring the bleakness of the game world to life
Unlockable dozers for future runs
Ac/Dc -
Extreme Challenge at Times (more on this later)
Violent
VERY Grindy
Cons -
Repetitive Gameplay - There are some choices to be made that can affect your journey via text choices but 90 percent of this game is going to be on that combat map.
To elaborate...
-Units and their abilities are very much interchangable same stats for all units within a class (only 4 of those) regardless of whether you start the game with them or pick them up along the way
there are Elite Units that contradict this with boosts in HP and damage but slower overall progression
Lack of individual skills makes many of the fights nearly if not exactly the same. If you do not mind grinding a bit this might not be as much of an issue.
-Replayability is Low
-The method of unlocking the Dozers are completely random
BALANCE - The begining of the game - Brutal
After a few runs - You realize that your gonna lose some people early on for most of
You can and should shrug these losses off.
Middle - Long and gets pretty easy once you have the hang of it.
End - Pretty tough again unless you spent about 8 hours or so grinding to get there.
So I would give this game a 5/10 but would recommend it if your a fan of tactical turnbased games and want to try something different. The combat mechanic is pretty intersting and takes awhile to get use to. Once you do your going to see a surge in success rate.
I hear there are still plans for substantial improvements to the games content and have some fixes in the works to restore balance. I would say this game probably should have be considered an Early Access Title until they come get through a couple more updates. There's potential for a much bigger game with more depth that could show up here in the next few months.
In the meantime its not a bad tactical combat game....its just not really a rougelike.

It's an alright game. Just be aware that the combat system is like that in The Banner Saga, not like that in Shadowrun / Fallout 1/2/Tactics / Divinity:Original Sin / etc. - your characters don't have individual action points, but each side in the conflict get 2 moves each round, to spend on moving or attacking.
Well, and sometimes your enemies get 3 moves if you don't kill any of them over enough turns in a row, presumably to keep you from just sitting there doing nothing while your enemy has to spend all their moves to get in range to attack you - only to not be able to attack because they're now out of moves - allowing you to blast them to pieces effortlessly during your turn since now they're in range.
Anyway, it's just sad that it gets so annoying a few hours in. Sure, if you can deal with the combat system, it's a pretty good game for the first few hours. Pretty simplistic, but entertaining enough. Then you make it to the aztec city, and turn around to fight king viscera. He's pretty hard, but you manage to beat him, probably at the cost of a good chunk of your stored up power and probably a couple of your best fighters. Then you face him again. And again. And again. And by the third or fourth time, you're either completely out of characters strong enough to actually fight him, or you're out of the power required to use the 'equalizers' necessary to have king viscera not just kill one of your characters every turn.
The game's combat system reveals itself to be very broken in situations where one side has a character vastly more powerful than anyone on the other side. Your characters have 5-20 health and do 5-10 damage per attack, while your enemy's character has 60+ health and does 10+ damage every attack.
So what happens is just he walks up to your characters with his 2 action moves, you shoot him twice with your action moves, then the next turn he kills 1-2 of your characters (unless you spent moves running out of range of him, in which case you weren't shooting him, never mind how you just have him BLITZ points, which generate when you're not attacking, so if you do that enough he gets a 3-move turn), then you shoot him 2 more times, then he kills your 2 remaining characters and you lose. Only way to actually beat him is use 'equalizers' that keep your characters from dying every turn, but those cost power and power is limited.
Only way I can even imagine being able to beat the game is by, in a very un-roguelike fashion, literally spending hours (with no savegame feature as far as I can tell) grinding in the wasteland to gather enough power to be able to spam equalizers constantly during the king viscera fights.
Overall... I want to recommend this, but I just can't. The first few hours are pretty good, but the final part of the game is just, well, not very.

I will update this review with each successive update to the game.
If you find this review unhelpful, tell me why and I will try to fix it.
Revised 7-8-2016
It is evident from the blog and other resources that the focus right now is on game function and code stability, mostly under the hood stuff, the kind of stuff that matters much more than how pretty it looks. Nobody gives a damn about your Corvette if there is no working engine, and nobody cares about a game with underdeveloped code. In that regard I think Red Level has its priorities straight, and in the play-through my priority at this phase in development was to look at code stability, controls, and interface. Stability and Control score a solid OK, it took me only about five minutes to figure out the basics of movement and flight and after ten was able to fly around without crashing into anything. 
 For those thinking of buying now, the dragon maneuvers like you are flying a helicopter, gravity is irrelevant once you hit the space-bar and continues to be irrelevant after you let go, which causes you to slowly float back down to the surface. A The W key allows forward flight, with a momentum dynamic like you would logically expect. Turning is instant and mouse directed, but you will tend to drift like a Ford on ice while cornering even if your dragon faces the desired direction instantly so plan ahead. Be aware that the game does not bind the mouse to the game screen, so long turns in one direction will cause the mouse to drift off screen and will close the window when you click any mouse button.
 Combat is very one sided, both in terms of damage taken, and physical damage dealt since you can only swing your tail to one side or your dragon, so make sure the thing you want to kill is on that side. Fire breath is hard to aim at first so be careful using it on the ground or you will burn yourself before anything around you. Think like an airplane when using this, you want to strafe a target with fire if you can, before landing to collect it.
 As of right now navigation is line of sight only, you get a look at a map sketch when you first drop in to the game but you have no mini-map in your interface so plan on getting lost. Right now having your bearings doesn't really matter since there is not all that much to do. .
 The quest system did not load during my most recent playthrough and is likely being rewritten.
 Currently you get three small circles in the lower right had corner of the screen which tell you what powers or attacks you have. There are "Roar" "Tail Swipe" "Bite Attack" and "Fire Breath". Roar did not provide audio feedback when used, and I could not observe any notable effect to things on the surface. Tail Swipe/Fire Breath controls are functional though there are some quarks to be resolved as the game progresses. A Three button mouse is needed to use both bite and tailswing. There is a hunger readout on the bottom right which gives access to the upgrade menu which is currently in development and not working. A new menu tree is in process which looks promising.
 Vast improvements to terrain and graphics quality were included in the most recent update. The framework is there for high poly models but they have not been applied yet.
 Mostly placeholder sounds, they have good ambient noises but the looping soundtrack can be a bit annoying. Improvements to come, but likely not until after Alpha.
 In shooters this would be like bullet holes where you shoot walls, or dynamic destructible vehicles. In dragon this is most notable with fire breath, where your fire can spread from one part of a building to the whole. You can burn down trees, or knock them over with your tail.
 Physics modeling for a dragon in flight is helicopter based, you will drift in the direction you are leaning when not using the throttle. Glide dynamics have been added, but gravity is weak for your dragon and allows for unrealastic floating, and are now fall/impact deaths for you or NPC's, but collision mapping is buggy and can cause models to drop through. The glide dynamic has improved somewhat with the most recent update, and is being dialed in progressively.
 Villagers become hostile when you get close enough, and are harder to kill. They will always take the shortest route to you, and will stack up beneath you if you fly just right. Animals are neutral, (except for bears) but will run away if you get too close. The recent update has reduced the amound of ambient wildlife, making eating more difficult.
 Beta, not optimized. You will have low frame rates regardless of your system power. I maxed out at 32FPS but dropped as low as 12 at near max graphics, which did not strain my system. Pre 3-29 update I was lucky to get 12FPS max, so there is improvement. There have been a series of small un-announced updates which have improved overall stability.
 A quick twenty minutes of game play did not result in any crashes or game breaking glitches. I did not get stuck in a cave, or get caught under the map. When grabbing objects you are almost guaranteed to experience a glitch known as the "runaway rag-doll". This glitch can happen as a result of poor collision mapping, or can occur if the engine thinks the object its grabbing is weightless and therefore has no inertia. You get an explosion of flailing limbs that can be distracting, but that’s about it.
Another prominent glitch occurs when two animated objects collide on uneven or akward terrain, resulting in one or both objects being thrown violently out of map or straight into the air. This glitch occurs in nearly every game in development, and was made popular by Skyrim's "hammer spike" in which being killed by an overhead swing from a giant launched your character straight up into the air. You will see this in Dragon if you land directly on a live deer or wolf. Sometimes the both of you are thrown, or sometimes only one of you. This is more likely to happen on hillsides or in rocky terrain. It also happens if you tail swing a sheep, deer, or wolf into another object without killing them, resulting in a violent but non lethal vertical launch.
 Red Level Games as an upstart has an opportunity to fill the general void left by developers like Bungie, EA, and even Microsoft. All of these companies have had rather lackluster recent releases that have underperformed in some way, they have become victims of their own success and now sell titles based on their franchise hype.
Red Level Games has all the attributes of a good developer, they:
1. Operate an independent website that isn't an eyesore, and was reasonably easy to navigate.
2. Have an easy "contact us" section which allows anyone to email them directly.
3. Post blog updates to their website and Steam (recently on a monthly basis)
4. Allow the community to contribute to game mechanics where applicable.
5. Are honest and forward in their efforts.
6. Clearly communicate update goals and priorities.

After getting my early access key, I jumped straight on the computer and played the game for a bit. It's a good start, but here are the first things I feel like are missing from playing the game for the first time:
- Directional controls are a bit funky. When I try to walk backwards, that's what I expect. Not the weird twirl that my dragon does, facing me away from what I'm fighting.
- Not sure who is losing health, me or the wolf. Perhaps putting the health numbers of the player in a different color?
- There's no good sense of aiming. A crosshair or something similar would be extremely helpful.
- Looking around is clumsy. When the mouse is in the center of the screen, the camera is not. This is a huge problem and could also help with the aiming issue.
- Quest markers were really all over the place. It told me to go kill a deer and the marker was floating 100 feet over the ocean.
- Lag. Obvious thing to fix.
- Upgrading stats wasn't working. I could only update the passive skills at the bottom.
- Movement speed is terrible. I know that you eventually level up speed, but the starting walking speed is absolutely horrendous, there's almost no point to walking, except that flying is the same. I feel like it takes a long time just to fly over to the next wolf that I should be walking towards.
After a quick play, these are the issues that I noticed immediately. I'm sure that there's a lot to get done, but this game has a ton of potential. With work and passion, this could be a fantastic game. Good luck, developers!

I sat my girlfriend in front of the PC and she played for ten hours straight.
"Castaway Girlfriend Paradise," should be the game name.
10/10, would distract girlfriend again.
In truth, she's made many comments while playing Castaway Paradise:
- She enjoys the 'Animal Crossing' style game play where you want to come back each day for a "refresh of the world" and continue playing.  Areas unlock as you collect Puzzle Pieces.  You can decorate and expand your home.  There's a Museum you can submit collectibles to.
- She has already collected everything the Museum needs in 20 hours playtime, which leads her to the impression that there's not a lot of content overall.  Of course, with the game in EA state, this is expected to change.
- She does not overly enjoy the questing system.  Most quests reward you with a pittance of currency and restoration projects to expand the city cost thousands.  They are also repetitive and sadly necessary to make any progress (Growing crops take real-time hours and net little money, too; in addition collecting things from the shore or ground reset each real-life day, so there's no other way than questing to make your cash - at least this is her belief).
- She gets frustrated at the time barriers, but has come to accept them, as Animal Crossing does the same.  The only difference here is that she can *cheat* in Animal Crossing by changing the date/time of her Wii or 3DS.  Although we haven't tried changing the PC time and relaunching Castaway Paradise, such an action usually has far more consequences than doing that on a console.
At the end of the day, any complaints aside, she does keep launching it and playing it each day and that's good enough to get a positive review.  If a game keeps drawing you back, then it's worth it.

I heard about Pony Island while looking for innovative horror games, and my expectations were equally met and disappointed. Disappointed regarding the "horror" aspect, as it was not really a game that scared me - and trust me, I'm a HUGE weenie - but met regarding a good and enjoyable game experience. Pony Island is cheeky, amusing and thoroughly fun; I often found myself grinning at some events during the game, thinking about how much the developer must have giggled while implementing those ideas.
Still, I have to say that while the game is certainly entertaining (and has a super catchy soundtrack) and innovative in some aspects, I found some design choices to be rather foreseeable and cliché, maybe because I've read too many creepypasta already. I think it works if you see this game as more of a comedy thing that pokes fun at those tropes, but if you are expecting to be seriously creeped out, it might make you groan at some points. I also found that it could've been a bit more unconventional and daring in its actions... this way, it was fun, but there are some points where I thought the whole shtick could've been taken a little further.
Also, I highly advise you to play the game in the language your operating system is set to, or some errors will occur that will definitely have a negative impact on the game's enjoyability. I can't delve into it further, but it's a thing.
Either way, all in all I recommend Pony Island if...
... you enjoy games with a distinct Indie flavor that toy with conventional game mechanics
... you think you'd have fun going through an easy-on-the-skills mix of logic puzzles and jump'n'run
... you want to jam to some 8-bit-y tunes accompanied by the nostalgic whirring of an old computer's fans
... being pranked and fooled makes you laugh along
... you love adorable ponies!!!!!
On the other hand, don't spend your money on this if...
... you're looking for a good scare that leaves you sleepless
... you want gameplay that challenges your skills
... you expect a deep, thoughtful and elaborate storyline that stays with you for days after completing
... you hate being the butt of a joke
... imagery and topics related to the devil, demons etc. have a serious negative impact on your health (I'm serious, I know some people who have a problem with stuff like that)

Deathspank is one of my favorite games of 2010. It combines the mechanics of Zelda and Diablo with the sly humor of Monkey Island's Ron Gilbert. A silly, forgettable, but altogether enjoyable storyline for this first installment of two will run you about 20 hours to fully enjoy. Combat mechanics work great when paired with the X360 controller, as that's what the game was actually designed for.
Deathspank is a must own -- and since it's indie, it's cheap. While it's not your standard $50 experience, it's definitely worth the ~$15 or so it usually sells for. Pick up both Deathspank games for an interesting and humorous gaming experience you may actually enjoy playing.

DeathSpank is a fairly ordinary Action RPG. In fact, call that ARPG lite because the loot system is fairly lacklustre, character development is narrow, and game replayability is virtually nil. Sadly, the humour tends to fall flat, at best the game dialogue tries to be funny but ends up being lame. About my only real laugh was Bong's Potion Store, with a little spaced out gnome. Otherwise, no other diaglogue or game event could be considered memorable for the laughs.

“Minimalist” is a term that can be interpreted in a bunch of different ways. A lot of the time it’s all about a lack of material possessions, keeping only what you really need to live a good life. At other points it’s the absence of complicated visuals; the presence of something that is simple yet appealing to look at, with no sharp corners or brash colours to distract the eye. Or sometimes it can go to the extreme, as is the case with Thomas Was Alone; a game that’s mad enough to consist of nothing but simple lines and rectangles.

I’m honestly not kidding – that’s pretty much all that’s on show here. Apart from a few subtle lighting effects working away in the background, this is very much a textbook example of what you see is what you get. Yet the overwhelming simplicity of this world isn’t as bad as you might be coming to expect; what really matters here is how the story builds up what this world and its inhabitants represents.

You see, this is a tale of AI programming becoming self-aware, and via some brilliant and funny narration by Danny Wallace (Whose works you should check out, by the way!), each little AI block you control is given their own distinct personality. The main character of Thomas, for one, is naturally inquisitive and logical. Others you meet along the way have their own unique traits; there's a deeply cynical square, an arrogant yet caring tall rectangle, and another bigger square that has delusions of being a super hero... On and on it goes, with new faces appearing all the time. It's done to such a level that as the plot moves along you actually start to care for each of them in a weird little way. It's never to the extent that you're going to shed a tear for their plight, but it’s enough to keep you engaged with them throughout their journey – even though they’re just little coloured shapes. It’s ingeniously done.

So your gang of crazy characters is set up, but what exactly are you doing with them? Puzzle platforming, that’s what. It’s up to you to switch between all of them, using their unique abilities to navigate through each level, and getting everyone to their respective exits. That’s it. If anything, the gameplay is as minimalist as the art style – but again, that’s by no means a bad thing. Thomas Was Alone’s main strength when it comes to its gameplay is in the way its difficulty and pacing is second to none. Each and every level presents a challenge that is both not so hilariously simple that you can cruise through it in two seconds, but also never hard enough to create a situation where your progress comes to a screeching halt. The game also introduces new ideas and character abilities at a steady rate, keeping things fresh and entertaining, but never at a pace where everything feels overwhelming.

The process of actually navigating your way through each of these challenges, however, is where the cracks begin to show. For one, the act of switching characters is cumbersome, requiring you to cycle through all of them in turn to reach the one you actually desire, the camera trying to zip towards every character in turn at an almost nauseating pace. This isn’t too bad when there’s only three shapes to control, but when there’s six or seven, the endless cycling can start to infuriate somewhat. Couple that with a soundtrack that I found so incredibly annoying I proactively sought out the sound settings just to turn it down, and you can perhaps see how the blood pressure can slowly start to rise.

There are a few other minor factors that also don’t help. The jumping mechanic, for one, feels at points oddly heavy and stiff, creating situations where I felt I wasn’t fully in control of where my jump was going – with a missed jump often wiping out a hefty chunk of progress in an instant. The level design at points also didn‘t help my mood, and really dents into what is otherwise flawless pacing – you can complete the bulk of some levels, only to realise you need to backtrack and do something with a character near its beginning.

Perhaps I’m just rubbish, but whether you attribute these problems down to poor play or not, they still lead to situations with feel unnecessarily annoying. All these minor niggles created a situation whereupon, once I realised I was nearing the end of the story, I was quietly hoping it would hurry up and end already, just so I didn’t have to put up with another inconvenience. Considering the game itself is only three hours long, however, and… Well, you can perhaps see why that might be a bit of a problem.

Thomas was Alone is far from perfect, then, but that doesn’t mean it’s inherently bad. It’s still perfectly playable, and the charming narration and story do a lot to help plaster over the faults that might rear their ugly head as you move along. It’s a fine example of how much you can do with so very little, and also stands as a perfect counterpoint against the sheer flood of lazily made indie games with tiny budgets that flood the market every day. So don’t be a square – check this out.

As an added bonus I got a decent story mode with great production value. Missions get a little repetitive but that is to be expected. Still there is plenty of variety and different ways to go about finishing missions which makes me keep coming back for more.

+ Great music / sound effects
+ Excellent attention to detail
+ Amazing atmosphere
+ Cool gadgets and skills to cause chaos and mayhem or use it to stay steathily in the shadows
+ Fun online multiplayer 'Hacking Invasion' mode (Choose to hack others or unexpectedly get hacked anytime during your singleplayer gameplay)
+ Interesting gameplay to find hidden collectibles (Research points and money across SF)
+ Fun Co-op mode (But only 2 players I think)
+ Seamless multiplayer / singleplayer gameplay
+ Multiple ways to complete missions - be stealthy; or go in guns blazing, take your pick
+ Great production value
+ Decent Optimization (Frame rates drop to around 40-50 on 'Very High / Ultra' in the city sometimes on my GTX 970 but it is mostly playable and looks gorgeous so I will give it a pass)

For the longest time, I felt rather odd around this game. I never bothered to buy this rather affordable title for years since it came out, and despite its popularity, I just didn't feel like getting it for some reason. Then one day, a sale came around, and as I was looking around for bargins, I came across this title for a nice little price. I was torn between a few other titles I wanted, but then I decided to get out of my comfort zone and try something I never was too interested in.
Turns out it was worth it, even if it ticked me off near the end.
In an age full of mindless shooters, zombie surviver deathmatches, and "retro" games that hardly feel retro and more lazy in the art department, Rayman Origins is a game that shows us that you don't need any of that rubbish to be a good game. You can be a 2D platformer and still look good at the same time, and best of all, it has difficulty that scales with the levels, so the further you go, the harder things get. None of that so called "hardcore" platforming crap where they claim they designed the levels poorly intentionally.
Ranting aside, this truely is a nice return to form for Rayman, even if the story is rather confusing and the gameplay, while it starts out fun and simple at first, soon gets really hard and demanding as more mechanics come into play, sometimes to the point that you die over and over again at a single point of the game until you either master it or get lucky.. But thankfully, there are plenty of save points, so it at least reduces the frustration, even near the end of the game.
Now, the game isn't perfect, sure. As I said earlier, sometimes you'll come across levels that'll kick you in the balls over and over again, turning your happy little mood into a mood of pure annoyance, if not rage due to the near-percise actions needed for some parts of the game (as one person noted, it is almost like a quick time event, but without the "Press x to not die" system in place). However, as♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off as I would get at these levels, I still powered through, and even if you couldn't, the game will allow you to skip some levels if they prove too hard for some players, which is a kind gesture I suppose, if sometimes insulting.
In short, while I don't recommend this to casual gamers, those looking for a real, honest challenge might find this a lovely title to invest in. And best of all, you can play with your friends, should you have any, which might make the game easier or harder, depending on if your friends are jerks or not.

I love squad based TBS games (Fallout 1 + 2, XCOM, etc etc) and I like the post-apocalyptic art in this game. What makes this game different from similar games is that instead of a turn order, you have two actions per turn to use per turn, and then the enemy makes two actions, etc. (Like Chess). The result of this is that even though you will be heavily outnumbered by the AI later in the game, it really doesn't matter as the AI can't move all its troops anyway. A lot of people complained about the game's difficulty, pointing to things like the AI faction teleporting units (this has been somewhat nerfed in the 1.5 patch), but I thought it was a suitable difficulty curve.
The game features four classes of units: Deadeyes (snipers), Frontliners (tanks), Gunslingers (pistolers) and Trenchers (shotgunners). With three kills, a rookie levels up to a Veteran (and gets a change of outfit to white), giving more hp and damage dealt. With every five more kills, the Veteran levels up, doing a further point of damage. This means that by the time you reach Aztec City, you should have Veterans at level 20-30, dealing 20+ damage per hit. To me this is an imbalanced mechanic as it favours certain classes over others. Deadeyes are close to useless in the late game due to their pitiful 5 hp as Veterans, meaning that they will be one shot killed regularly. Gunslingers I have found of limited value too. Trenchers are the stock troop of your army and you'll rack up a lot of kills with these guys. In my first successful playthrough, Maygrim reached level 30+ and had something like 150 kills. But now I've realised that Frontliners are BY FAR the best class due to their 7 movement and 12 hp as Veterans. Early they only do 2 damage, and then 4 after reaching Veteran, but if you nurse them through to level 10 or so they become godly, one shot killing anyone. In my second successful playthrough, I had Den on level 30 doing about 35 damage. That's overpowered and basically breaks the class system, as leveling up only gives more damage, not hp.
Travelling around Bedlam is relatively fun, but lacking variety. There are four enemy factions (Mutant, Marauder, Cyborg and AI) and some variety in the battles as each faction has a different mechanic, but once you learn what these are the variety fades. You'll need to upgrade your dozer to improve various efficiencies, but here I found that I maxed out the upgrades WAY too quickly, like within the first 30 mins of play. You'll encounter Elite enemies (helpfully signposted on the map when available), which join you when you defeat them. They are bigger (take up four squares), stronger (more dmg and hp) but seem to level up slower, so increasingly I have been using the normal units instead. It's harder to get them in cover too, on account of their size. Various random events will get you more units along the way, but you can't otherwise buy new units. As this is an Ironman game, you really need to babysit your team.
And this is where I encounter my main problem with this game and the thing that will kill its long term replayability unless patched somehow. There's a Bedlam meter rapidly increasing that encourages you to get to Aztec City quickly, but NO consequence if you don't do so. Sure, at Bedlam level there are more enemies, but due to the 2 move mechanic this really doesn't matter very much. It just makes the battles longer. The enemy troops basically DON'T get stronger, just more numerous. Because you need to level your guys up to 20+, and because you need a lot of power cells to defeat King Viscera, you basically need to grind your way around the map. In my first successful game, I spent over 600 days in game and explored basically the whole map, and in my second game I got bored by around 400 days. Just by exploring every side point of interest, you'll collect passengers, crude, meat and most importantly power cells. I had over 4000 food and crude and 600+ power cells by 400 days this time, meaning I could either grind some more or go straight to Aztec City.
One of the replayability factors is the unlocking of new dozers, but this is very hard (and random) to do. I unlocked my first dozer (Cyborg) after 27 hours, even after completely scouring the map on my first playthrough! And the dozers themselves aren't that interesting. I still haven't unlocked the other three dozers. There are some bugs, such as when you defeat E-Radik-8 and he's supposed to join you. He doesn't appear in your roster but DOES interact in some quests. This game needs more variety, more rewards for playing. Some of the achievements didn't work before the patch, and some aren't working after the patch. There needs to be some reason to stop trawling the map, because currently that is the way to win. The Bedlam meter goes up far too quickly, the upgrades are far too easy to get, and once you get your guys levelled the game is too easy and grindy overall.
These caveats aside, for a game I spent $16 on, 28 hours of play is a big win, even if I never played again. And I will. The devs addressed some of the issues in the 1.5 patch, and I'm hopeful that in time they might add more variety and spice to the game. Skyshine's Bedlam is a good indie game in the squad based TBS genre, and I've enjoying playing it and can recommend it to fans of the genre!

This is a very good game. Not easy, but hours of fun and replayability. It dispenses with a lot of the standard BS and dumps you right into the action.
There is a significant learning curve to battle and you have to figure out how best to use the different types of fighters you have or you will quickly deplete your snipers and gunslingers (don't let Frontliners get too close to your Deadeyes and have Gunslingers behind cover nearly always). If you do not click on enemy soldiers to see how far they can move their next turn before you make your moves then you will find out that one of your hard earned upgraded fighters can get killed because you didn't move him far enough out of range from the enemy (the game is very much like chess in this regard). You also have to upgrade your Dozer carefully so you don't run out of crude or food. Along the way you try to pick up upgrades for your ride and new soldiers to fight for you in battles. The key to the game is gathering as many power cells as you can to use in battle and to upgrade your Dozer.
Graphics are pretty cool (Borderlands cartoon style). I have not yet come close to finishing the game on normal, but I just keep restarting and employing the tactics I learned the last time I got myself killed in Bedlam. All in all it is a pretty sweet little game to consume yourself in for a few hours at a time.
A lot of reviewers have criticized this game for its repetitive style and difficulty. Both are legit complaints, but I still enjoyed playing the game even though I was often frustrated. Plus, it's not like you're dropping $60 on a bad game, and upgrades and fixes are supposed to be coming.

Let me begin by saying the game is a port of a mobile ap so the interface is not really designed for mouse+keyboard [though it is getting better patch-by-patch]. If you can get past that, this is an enjoyable though quite simple casual RPG/farming game. Trees of various types and a variety of vegetables all have the same essential mechanic: water them, wait a bit, possibly repeat, and harvest the results. There are also fish to catch, quests to complete, insects to chase, buildings to repair, etc.
Absolutely not a deep game in any way, but if you like decorating your house or playing dress-up there are tons of items to unlock/collect.
One of the best features by the way: The developers are *very* responsive in the forums and such. The game has improved massively from beta to release because they listened and adapted to what PC players said they wanted.

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game
Castaway Paradise is an interesting take on the Animal Crossing formula. Much like it's inspiration, you go around your island home, doing various tasks, such as gardening, clean up, fishing, and quests for your friends. Through these activities you'll gain XP and currency to help progress, and customize both your character and your island home. It's a pretty simple premise and should be pretty easy to grasp for all gamers of all age and level.
The game isn't hard to learn, and it's not one I would say it's focused on player skill. Rather, it's fairly relaxing, and could be argued as mindless, but I'd like to call it simple. The controls are all through mouse clicks, from moving your character to watering your plants. Accessibility is one of the game's biggest strengths and the learning curve is very easy going and should be able to be enjoyed by even the youngest of audience.
Though the game is simple, I do feel it to be fairly satisfying. Earning xp to unlock the next set of things to customize my island and character with, purchasable with the ingame currency earned, there's something really addictive about this formula. I found myself endlessly checking on all my plants, constantly chasing the next quest, and doing it over and over again, Castaway Paradise has mastered the endless loop design of Animal Crossing. Because of this, it's arguable that the game can start feeling grindy after a while, but I don't think it was designed for long stretches of play, rather, like it's inspiration Animal Crossing, really meant to be visited for an hour or just a few minutes each day.
In Animal Crossing there is a pile of incentive to keep playing, or at least to visit each day. You can unlock mini-games, trigger events in game during real time holidays and celebrations. In Castaway Paradise I've yet to see any of these elements. I've only played for about 3 hours on the game's launch, so since this genre requires real world, time commitment over months, if not years, it's difficult for me to say if these elements are apart of the game. I'm of course hoping that these interesting tidbits spearheaded by Animal Crossing is also included into Castaway Paradise in some way. If there is a lack of mini-games to be unlocked, or if it isn't real world holiday sensitive I feel the game would be lacking some of the most charming elements that made Animal Crossing so memorable. Again, these are elements that I simply can not comment on for Castaway Paradise, as I do understand will require time to fully flesh out, if it's there at all.
Overall Castaway Paradise is a charming little Animal Crossing-like, that seem to be doing a pretty good job at emulating it's inspiration. Only time can tell the true quality of the game, as this genre is really meant to be played over long periods of real world dates. But speaking solely from the 3 hours I've experience, it won me over.
Pros:
- Charming visuals
- Addictive gameplay
- Lots to unlock
- (so far) does a good job at emulating it's inspiration (Animal Crossing)
Cons:
- Can be considered grindy
- Might be too simple for some

It is hard for me to say that I strongly recommend this game, but I don't dislike it enough to say don't get it either.
Overall, I think this game has a TON of potential.  Think animal crossing mixed with some Farmville mixed with some harvest moon.  Don't expect the addictive game play of Harvest Moon or Animal Crossing.  Those games have deeper characters and game play where you feel personally attached to the game and characters, this game makes me feel more like an errand boy who washed up on an island where people are more concerned about their own inability to get simple tasks done instead of why you washed up on the shore covered in seaweed.  The game feels like it is a money grabbing Facebook game like Farmville, but I have yet to hit a wall where I have to buy anything with any form of "premium" currency.  So far it feels more like someone had me pay upfront to unlock all the premium items instead.  Two things that REALLY makes it feel like a Facebook game more than a purchased game, for me at least, is that you get a daily login bonus and you have to wait until a higher level to become a "VIP".
The game play is pretty basic, and at times the "quests" seem pretty repetitive.  There will be times where one character asks you to deliver an item to another character who is literally standing 3 steps away, but I can't fault the game for this because the character wander freely.  I do wish there was some more diversity included with regards to crops, tasks, other aspects.  Don't have me run back and forth 80 times delivering items from one random character to a different random character while I'm waiting for crops to grow.
I also don't really like the fact that actions (like watering) is limited by "stamina" that regenerates at a rate of 1 per 50 seconds.  This seems trivial of me to pick on, but I feel like the reason I paid for a game like this was so that I wasn't stuck waiting on games that Facebook has for free which limit your actions due to energy or stamina.  You can refill "stamina" by using standard in game currency, but it gets a little frustrating.
I know so far I mentioned a lot of negatives, but there are also positives.  The game itself is cute.  It's a good concept that mixes Harvest Moon, Animal Crossing, and Farmville.  I like that you can buy things from a catalog instead of waiting for items to randomly be in stock at the store.  I also like that there are areas of the island to unlock as the game progresses.
I have to also say it was nice to play a game of this style where you aren't stuck at the beginning playing a really long tutorial or having to hoard items to reach the next point.  Goals (such as upgrading buildings and unlocking areas) are easily attainable so you can enjoy the game more than worrying about hoarding an item just to get to the next part.
I have to say that the game has it's positives and it's negatives.  If I had played this game first would I have still purchased it...... maybe if it was on sale for a bit more off...

Stolen Couch proved to be a step above the rest of the social/mobile game developers.
The original development plan for this game was merely to be a PC port of the mobile/social version: a free-to-play microtransaction disaster. To my surprise, however, Stolen Couch Games actually listened to user feedback and ultimately removed the pay-walls entirely from the STEAM version. Because SCG knows that the F2P microtransaction model is far more profitable than the premium model, the fact that they still chose to go premium is that much more commendable, and deserves a lot more attention than it is getting.
If you like Animal Crossing, buy this game. Hell, even if you don't like Animal Crossing, buy this game just to support honest developers, and show that good games are sustainable, without the freemium model.
Kudos to the entire team at SCG for having artistic integrity in what is turning out to be a fantastic game.

The gamemakers claim this is an interesting tale of families and dynasties with multi-layered gameplay and board-game like mechanics. In reality it is a game about game pieces moving on a quarter wheel using tokens, to keep away from crocodiles,  to pick up beads, to make tokens, to make kids that you give tokens to, to increase their token making abilities in order to level up from getting beads. The story is delivered in tiny random pieces that are really boring. The game is super repetitive and the only thing that changes from leveling up and moving to a different tier of the board is there are more symbols of tokens you can make. The makers claim 15 hours of gameplay, but I was already bored after 30 minutes, I can’t imagine sinking that much time into it. Instead of actually playing like a fun interesting board game, it plays like a casual budget game. There really is no incentive, because you’re just going to do the same thing with your kids that you did with your parents before. There really isn’t much of an element of surprise, besides the random shadow people that move around the board. The game talks about all these choices and decisions, which basically boils down to: do you want to make tokens or move, and which space will your person move to based on the tokens you have, and which ability you want to level up in your child. I guess it never gets old that everybody bangs everybody almost every turn. The best part is the price of the game is 20 dollars, which is absolutely hilarious, as it is honestly worth about 2 dollars. Buy this game if it goes 90% off and if every other game on steam is out of stock.

TL;DR - A game that has awful game mechanics, ridiculous combat scenarios, and a poor excuse for the Resident Evil games that I grew up with. Don't waste your money, and be prepared to consider this a waste of time.
So... where to start. The first campaign seemed alright as it revisited combatting the undead (since Capcom has gotten onto this kick of battling creatures that have nothing to do with the undead) while still maintaining the mutant bosses and occasional set of minions. It still takes an absurd amount of ammunition to kill a basic zombie even though a head shot should be the end all. The skill point system makes it difficult to expand upon your character's assets as you simply cannot get enough points to obtain noticable increases in performance. In addition, you can only have 3 of these skills equipped at any given point in time. It is aggravating to say the least.
The next campaign was more aggravation in the sense that, once again, we are battling a foe that has nothing to do with the undead. Furthermore, the thing that robs this game of all fun is the sense that you can never get enough ammunition. With an enemy that requires everything you pick up to bring it down, you are constantly trying to save up anything you can get only to have it stolen away as soon as you get it. I don't particularly like being reminded of my financial performance everytime I get into a battle, which is pretty much the entire game.
As I stand now, I have stopped in the middle of the third campaign to write this review. We start off with this supposed badass who prefers to use his hands to fight people... with guns. I can appreciate these kinds of stunts if one actually had more moves than the one-two punch and a flying knee. Seriously, Capcom couldn't have come up with a better set of weaponry? As if I want more aggravation in my life.
There are countless other complaints that I have with this game, but there really is no point in listing them. I have not continued further into the campaign simply because the storyline is not worth the aggravation. I do not know of a game that I was more irritated with the programming and design than this one. I enjoy challenge, but not being constantly short-handed and given nothing to make it better. Save your money, buy something else.

It's hard to recommend RE6 as a good addition to the series due to capcom's many developmental mistakes further emphasized by their decision to make RE7 more of a  (hidden) objective survival horror. My biggest issue with RE6 are the un-skipable dialogues, mini-cutscenes, and walk-only parts that riddle the game only serving to lengthen your game-play time. The adage, "once is enough," is only too true in RE6 making co-op a nightmare that makes you want to immediately quit or sigh, and think to yourself, 'not this again,' due to how much time you spend during these mandatory and tiresome sequences. So lets get into what  they did right...
+ Multiple Campaigns, without this RE6 would've been more negatively received.
+ Co-op, a recent hallmark of the series that brought a bigger crowd into the game, but lessened the atmosphere into what it became - action horror though the horror was extremely limited.
+ Agent Hunt, aside from the horrible monster controls, this game-mode is intensely fun once you gather a few other hunters together to ruin other people's final game score. Alone it is frustrating due to how often it requires perfect timing to kill the player. [Hint - A.I. Partners cannot die]
+ Skill system, a good addition, but infinite weapons shouldn't be included as skills also props for the quick change system that isn't really quick[maybe utilize the f1-12 keys next time though this allows for abuse easily solved by a time required change].
+ Pill system, a good addition removing the need for them in the inventory.
+ Stamina system, until you're low.
+/- Mercenaries, staple of the series, but no significant changes here.
+/- QTE, there's a setting to remove most qte, but it is requirement for grabs.
- Same Old Same, Another virus outbreak story, U.S.A. x2, Africa, Spain and Asia off the top of my head.
- Co-op, forced to deal with mandatory scenes that riddle & damage the overall game in my opinion.
- Agent Hunt, the bad controls, possiblity of hunter farming due to players not advancing & forced hunter spawn.
- No microphone control, I don't want to hear every sound you/others make on your side.
- No inventory control, I actually enjoyed RE5's inventory system as well as how I squirreled away extra ammo to help on higher difficulties.
- Spy sequences are annoying & often unable to keep concealment due to camera switches [i.e was proning across a guard rail walkaway, view changes & my character stands up, wtf, all while i'm still holding prone button]
- Camera view switches on a dime completely changing your control layout [ffs who thought this was a good idea]
- Some search sequences confuse people.
- Not enough inventive melee sequences
- No mini-tutorials for those that don't know how to beat mini-bosses and the such. although it's intuitive that when a boss puts his hand on a roof & you climb on it...
- How fast Shotgun wrecks your accuracy score as long as a certain %[like 40%] of pellets hits then it should be considered 100% accurate instead of counting each pellet as a hit/miss. Reducing how many players will actually use a shotgun, most just dump the shotgun ammo for another type.
- can't really play w/ other countries due to lag problems even on 2 bars.
- How the basic zombie is a major threat on moderate/higher difficulties not only did they remove the fact that a headshot[unless it's critical] won't kill a zombie anymore now it won't even stagger zombies + it leaves a hole in the head that you can miss through. [FUUUUU]
- How common/easy it is to get shot/thrown weap. @ and impossible for your partner to help you in time on higher difficulties during those separation sequences.
- Laser disappears after a few consecutive shots.
- How those pesky mandatory grab sequences remove your hp crazily on higher difficulties.
- They kill off your friendies in the same damn way almost everytime. b00m, gg, no re, friendly a.i.
- how hard is it to introduce text chat?
- Overly complicated Co-op Search.
- The voice command of your character is too hard to use now.
- Partner Attack, just why?
- Elena has 2 shotguns dafaq.
+/- No Wesker [:eng]
-/+ First aid Sprays are rare.
-/+ Infinite Ammo system, It's negative for me since it's rare for someone to enable infinite ammo, and then you have to give up a skill slot for a single weapon, prefer RE5's way.
- Ada Wong, no particular reason why she was helping everyone/character changed despite being a mercenary; though, the fact that Simmons was delusional and cloned her personage onto another person likely tilted her motivations.

TL:DR: Great game to play with friends, interesting plot and good gameplay, hours of fun.
After two runs and a half on this game, I can tell that I really enjoyed my time on it. I cannot tell about the single player experience however, because I haven't played the game alone, I always played it on coop, the only difference is that the guy accompanying you is a friend, and not an AI.
The gameplay is really good to me, being a fan of QTEs, I really enjoyed it, it's fluid, the difficulty rises with the levels, and it keeps a great interest with the different characters having different ways to be played. You'll be sent through hours of epic action that would, according to "purists", not suit the saga of Resident Evil, well, no offense, and with all due respect, screw them. This game may not be Resident Evil 4, but if you want more of it, just play it, it's a new game with new mechanics, a new plot, and a new way of being played.
Multiplayer modes also offer some versus modes that are interesting to play if you manage to gather enough people. It's not groundbreaking, but you'll be able to have so fun alltogether. Also, the possibility to accept players as special zombies is really fun and increases the difficulty at some points, if you're a tough player and get bored of slaughtering brainless meatpacks, you'll want to try this out.
Really, I can't find any real trouble about the game, it's not the game of the year, far from it, but it'll provide you with hours of fun to play with a friend, and if you want challenge, difficulty levels will provide you some, with less than 0.2 seconds for a crucial QTE, and if you have a hard time with them, you can still use something to lower the difficulty of these.

I've played this games a few times back in the PS3 era. Let's make it clear; it is a great game, but definitely not the strongest entry in the franchise. I dare to say RE5 surpases this by a bit, and here's why: I feel RE6 is overly done. It tries to offer too much, but doesn't really bring anything new. The game has an amazing intro and first chapter, but that's where it all ends. Finish Leon's chapter, and then you find yourself with a very repetitive and tedious game. In comparison, were RE5 shines is in how simple it is and its perfect balance of length and variety.
The other three chapters do have their moments, but by the time you reach Sherry's chapter, you'll be bored to death of doing the same stuff over and over. Ada's chapter feels like a chore.
I feel this game could've been great with only Leon's chapter, even if extended a bit more, with ocassional appearances from the other charactes.
As for the technical aspects. I was a bit surprised (or disappointed) that RE5 manages to look a bit better than this game. Sure they are old games, but for anyone who played RE5 for PC, they might know how amazing the graphics look, and how well the game runs. It still looks current, despite is nearly a decade old. RE6, even maxed out shows very dated textures and toned down light effects.
Controls are a bit wonky. RE4/5/6 are known for their tricky controls that lack a proper aiming system. Forgivable for RE4, somewhat passable for RE5 which at least made the movement a bit smoother and added strafe. But the third time around, it is unforgivable. RE6 is a bit too sensitive, in my opinion. Gets some time to get used to.
Other than that, it is not a bad game. Not the best in the franchise, and the weakest entry of the 'Action' RE bunch, but worth having if you're a RE fan.

This game is difficult for me to review, and I'll explain why. I have dreamt of this game concept for YEARS. I have told all my friends about this "idea" I had about a game where you played AS a dragon. Where the game was a mix of RPG/Action/Strategy/Open World/Co-op and PvP. A game where you started off as a baby dragon, heading out into the world. You would set up a lair, and then proceed to level up and grow as you saw fit. Maybe you'd be a typical giant red dragon breathing fire on all the nearby villages. Or you could be a diplomatic dragon who forged alliances with humans instead. Each level would allow you to customize and upgrade various aspects of your dragon. Etc...I could go on all day about my ideas (Been thinking about them for years as I mentioned.) Reading the description from the developers, this game COULD potentially BE my dream game, finally realized.
On the one hand, I want to enthusiastically recommend this game so more people will support it and it can grow into the game of my dreams. However, I have to be honest and tell people what they are getting into before they spend their hard-earned money. I have barely started the game up, and quit after a minute or so because the controls were so un-intuitive and I couldn't figure out how to switch them. The graphics were poor, and no amount of messing with the settings would improve them. Obviously this is still in early access, so there is still hope for lots of improvement. With such a limited amount of experience in the game, I can't talk about any of the deeper mechanics, etc...but the small amount I did experience was hard to endure. I am planning to not ask for a refund in the hopes that this game will continue to grow and adapt into a game I can love. I bought it on sale for $15 ish, normally it goes for $17.99 I think. If you love dragons like I do (and like the developers, from the sound of it) this game could very well be worth supporting. If you're kind of "meh" on the subject of dragons, maybe wait a few months before purchasing.
I will continually check up on this game and revise my review as time goes on. Thank you for reading!
END OF OFFICIAL REVIEW

9/10 - Clever, witty, full of charm and tons of fun. I find myself laughing out loud quite a bit while playing DeathSpank. A solid yet simple and memorable Action RPG. While the gameplay is nothing new, the humorous story, characters and stylish graphics are what makes the game unqiue and fun.

The overall art style is very nice indeed, and the combat system might be a nice idea on paper - sadly said combat system results (at least for me) just in an overall frustrating experience.
There is a difference between difficulty of a game and simple unfairness. Overcoming difficulty can feel even more rewarding, while overcoming unfairness - without a certain degree of influence on the outcome - just feels like, well, being lucky. If there was a combat system with strategic depth, where you really could make use of the different classes, weapons and cover on the battlefield I am sure this would be an enjoyable, interesting game.
Edit: The redux version changes the combat system substantially to the better. Recommended!

-Great concept. The idea of travelling in a mobile fortress, trying to reach a utopia and save the people you have with you is awesome, and in this era of post-apocolyptic games everywhere, it's different enough to stand out.
-The writing. There's a lot of flavor text, for pretty much every event. The fact that even the most generic of this text is well written and very thematic speaks volumes about the care that went into this game.
-The events. This ties into the writing, but the events, for the most part, feel very fleshed out, and your decisions feel like they have meaning.
THE EHS:
-The combat. Now, don't get me wrong, I love tactical combat, and I think they handled it fairly well. Unfortunately, due to the "two moves a turn" system, you feel punished for bringing lots of people into combat, as most of them won't be able to do much. There are still some balance issues to work through as well, as some classes (like trenchers) are generally much more useful than others (like gunslingers). Sure, a gunslinger can hit from slightly further away, and counter-hit for 1 damage, but trenchers push enemies back, can hit targets in melee range, and do more damage with their attacks. You only need to bring gunslingers when you're out of trenchers, for the most part, or as a warm body during a tough fight. It's still fun though, and that's what's important, it just doesn't feel as good as it could be.
-The Bosses. The bosses are all well designed, and fun to use once you recruit them after beating them (a system I enjoy). Unfortunately, most of them are fairly easy. Every boss I beat during my first run was taken down using the same strategy: use my Dozer weapon (the one that makes enemies hostile to each other), watch the boss take damage and destroy their squad, kill boss with one or two attacks as they try to close distance after drunk effect wears off. There's no reason to do anything other than this, no reason at all. The bosses all have cool abilities, but you don't really see this in their fights.
THE CONS:
-The music. Now, the music isn't bad, it's just very, very, very forgettable. If you heard a song from this game by itself, you most likely wouldn't be able to identify the game, like you could with, say, Binding of Isaac, or Fez. Soundtracks are super important to me, and this one just doesn't stand out. Most people would put this under EH, but coming from a musical background, I count it as a CON.
-The bugs. I know the devs are working on this, but I still need to count it, because they are glaring. I had one fight that had half my squad all occupying the same space just off the movement grid, and later, after using an ability on my Dozer that makes temp clones on my units during battle, the unit I cloned disappeared from my Dozer, despite ending the battle with full health. These were both during the same run, and if they hadn't happened as late into the run as they did (when I could recover from them easily), I might have lost the run overall.
FINAL VERDICT
Skyshine's Bedlam is a diamond in the rough. It's great in a lot of areas, but the few flaws it does have are major ones that hold it back. As a KS backer, I'm not disappointed, nor do I regret my backing, but I do feel Skyshine has their work cut out for them. I don't like numbered ratings, but if I absolutely to give it one, it would be 7.5/10. It's solid, it's fun, and it's beautiful, but there's a lot left to be worked on that, once completed, will make this a much better game. Give it a try, but be patient. The devs are being very responsive to the community (something I love, especially in indie devs), so if you have a complaint, give them a bit of time, and it'll likely be fixed quickly.

Castaway Paradise is a clear port of a tablet/phone game. I mean it even says so on their website.
However, don't let that dissuade you from giving the game a chance though. There was a lot of work put into this game by the developer and I'd like to point that out.
Free to play games on a mobile platform tend to be frowned upon, however, you have to remember that this is a business. There is just more money in a freemium version of a game and the reach it gives is ten fold. Allow anyone to jump in and get something out of a game for free, then setting up options for a way to accelerate at what ever pace they're comfortable at is perfectly fine.
Now, this becomes an issue when porting a mobile freemium version of a game over to a paid platform like pc. When you charge for a game you have to remove all that. Which is what Castaway Paradise does.
Everything that was once a paid for option is available in the game, you still have to earn the money to purchase everything, but it's there. (Insert applause track) so many games don't do this. They still try to keep the pay to play options in WHILE charging you. Which the folks at Stolen Couch Games didn't do.
Onto the gameplay!
Castaway Paradise is a fun 'Animal Crossing' like game. If you like exploring, farming, questing, and just generally living an alternate life like you're a traveling salesman with a family in Albion and Pittsburg then you'll be right at home.
You wash ashore as a lost hopeless human on an island full of anthropomorphic creatures and must assimilate to their ways. Plant flowers, catch bugs, do whatever you feel like doing at the moment.
The controls are a little janky, but I have faith the developer will work that out. As they've already patched in a way to zoom in and out.
If you need a little Island of Dr. Moreau in your life and like 'Animal Crossing' then Castaway Paradise is your game.
