So, Skyshine's BELDAM. Where to begin...
This game, as with many others like it, falls into the cracks made by FTLs earth-shattering redefinition of the roguelike genre. It's so painfully, agonisingly close to a good game but for me it just doesn't quite measure up. Let me cover this bit by bit so I don't miss anything out.
The Dozer. You'd think this'd be a decent chunk of the game considering the amount of work that's gone into it's art and how it's front-and-centre of the games lore, but it doesn't feel like you're in one at all. It lacks primarily in two ways.
First, the dozer is presented as a sort of Ark for people looking to make it to Aztec City. The number in the dozer menu says you have 1,000 souls on board, but it might as well be zero as they don't have any bearing on the gameplay. They can be traded away to various encounters just like fuel, meat or power cells. The Banner Saga wracked me with guilt and anguish by visibly seeing people abandoning the caravan or starving to death. In this? Gimme the power cells!
Secondly, the dozer has very limited gameplay influence. Outside of bombardments, it's absent from combat. You frequently fight inside it, but this just means you can't use bombardments and if you lose this particular fight it's game over (negative reinforcement gaming booo). You can (re: must) spend power cells on upgrading various efficiencies, but there's no choice here, no interesting decision to weigh up. Your best choice is to upgrade them all when you can. This is neither FTL nor Convoy in highlighting strengths and weaknesses of a given vehicle. It's just a thing you see on a map.
The combat. The difficulty spikes and troughs are gargantuan. The early-game is incredibly difficult. You'll lose virtually irreplaceable rookie units at a steady rate through no fault of your own. The enemy plays by the same rules as you do, but with a much less greater sense of self-preservation. They'll move their guys into suicidal positions to kill someone on your side, and while it's no big deal for them in this random battle, steady losses means your guys don't live long enough to level up and be useful. Playing in any way other than perfectly defensive will lead to heavy losses that you can't claw back from. Better units are recruited only by defeating them, so if you've already got a depleted roster and lose a few more trying to recruit a heavy hitter...
If you're able to keep one or two rookies alive long enough to get 3 or more kills, they become significantly more useful. Recruiting said heavy hitters then become much easier, who drastically improve your roster further, and from then on until near the end of the game it's easy street. I've only encountered the end few fights once but holy Moses does the difficulty explode to astronomical levels again.
Both ways that the game handles increasing difficulty are unpalatable. In one way they turn guys into massive bullet-sponges (which is unsatisfying as you've worked so hard to have upgraded soldiers to just have it negated ) and the other by drastically increasing the number of enemies (which is also unsatisfying because they still only get two actions a turn, so you end up churning through a steady trickle of weak enemies, which make you a lot stronger a lot quicker). The enemies themselves stay the same in terms of weapon and movement range.
My overall impression of the combat is that there is one correct way to win, not many ways to win.
Don't even get me started on how the Robot AI enemy-type blatantly cheats. They can teleport to what appears to be anywhere else on the map for an action. So while you've got a front line of defenders and you've made sure that your heavy-hitting snipers are well out of the way of suicidal dives by the enemy, they'll teleport well beyond their movement range and one-shot the sniper. Thanks, game! Super jerk-like of you.
The story stands on it's own two feet in terms of having its own tone in a crowded genre, but the presentation falls flat. In FTL you come across encounters that are risk/reward based on who you've got on your crew and what type of ship/weapons you've got. So far I haven't encountered a single negative affect from investigating every text-based offer presented to me. Many encounters will just be story with no choice and no resources gained or lost, so it feels like a waste of time. You don't really encounter stores, just people willing to trade, but you're never told how much you're going to get or how much you're going to trade.
tl,dr: Garhhhh this game has so much potential! So many things are already there and in place and working that could turn this into something fantastic. Certainly not FTL level, but at least up there with The Banner Saga. But alas, no. The 'base' of the dozer is very underutilised in gameplay, the combat frequently feels cheap and lacks a lot of strategy found in similar titles, the encounters feature heavy repetition and little if any risk...
I can't recommend this game even for fans of the genre as you're better off playing something I've mentioned earlier. It's so bloody frustrating, this could've been great! I can see it through all it's shortcomings, it's 95% of the way there... But no, it's not. This isn't the game I hoped it would be.

Skyshine's BEDLAM can be summed up in one word: rewarding. The game is very challenging, even on easy. Victory becomes a true accomplishment, not merely an expectation one gets "putting in enough hours" into a game. BEDLAM won't let you off that easy.
BEDLAM merges several genre's together as a cohesive unit. The art style is "retro" in that it's very artist rendered. Yet the art is not pixelated. Much care was taken in the art process to build the set pieces and characters within this universe. Is the game fun? Absolutely. You will become invested in your heroes. You will scream in agony with them when they die, and cheer them on when they win. While the Dozer may appear to be the heart of the quest, your true emotional attachment goes to the men and women (and mutants!) who defend your hulking machine from the denizens beyond.
If you enjoy roguelikes, you will enjoy BEDLAM. If you enjoy turn based combat, you will enjoy BEDLAM. If you enjoy quality gaming, you will enjoy BEDLAM. Do yourself a favor and grab BEDLAM: a game that is sure to attract your attention, and test your skill.

Thomas Was Alone's strongest point is its story and character with a brilliantly narrated script. It's a simple story told with a lot of heart. Gameplay mechanics help to emphasize each of the characters actions and motivations. By the end, I wanted to care about these characters. I wanted to see what the little rectangles would do.
The emphasis there is "wanted to care," because, frankly, I couldn't, as in the later sections of the game, every section of narration (the primary means of telling the story) is separated by repetitive, uninteresting, and incredibly unchallenging gameplay. I only sort of recommend this game... The graphics, music and level designs range from good to amazing, that alone makes it well worth playing, but... (There's always a but.) The controls and boss designs leave much to be desired. Bosses move in completely fixed patterns that are pretty unforgiving and extremely boring once you know the patterns. In other words, bosses are trial and error until you've learned the patterns. That gets tedious real fast --- especially so on the final boss, where the bad controls and poor boss design clash in such a way that it's actually possible to go too fast and die because of that, which seems counter-intuitive when you're chasing the bad guy. The same thing goes for a few other levels, where you can build up enough momentum that the game can't keep up, which is extremely sad to have happen in a platformer. And then there are the controls that don't really feel tight enough for many situations that you are put in. Constantly I caught myself thinking "this wouldn't be a problem if it was Super Meat Boy or Mega Man". It's not that the controls are downright bad, they're just not good enough.
If you can overlook the flaws, it's a very good and extremely entertaining game.

Fantastic game. Definitely one of the best city sim games ever. The only problem I have is that the traffic can be a bit frustrating sometimes and the roads can be a little silly to snap.

I really love this game, and am very happy about the passionate modding community behind it. They add so much replay value, allowing for smoother gameplay as wel as more ways to express your creativity with all the extra assets. If you're solely looking for a city builder that challenges you in a managerial or strategic way, I would pass. Cities Skylines is however one heck of a creative city builder!

Cities: Skylines is the city builder that SimCity (2013) should have been. Skylines simulates traffic and people incredibly well and although using the Unity engine, the game looks great and is very immersive. Skylines has a lot of options of how to build and the workshop is full of mods to make the options of detailing seemingly endless.
Skylines is not the easiest game to play and there's a slight learning curve if you don't use the Unlock All mod when playing. In the same sleeve, if you don't have Unlimited Money mod, then $70,000 is a tough start. It is very fun though to watch your town grow. Although the game can handle 1,000,000 population (it can take quite a toll on your computer, though) the population is more realistically simulated than that of SimCity.
Skylines improves all areas where SimCity failed -- one aspect was the development in your city. In order to get education in SimCity, you had to add an expansion to your city hall. In Skylines, it's just a matter of increasing your population and if your city can afford a new service. That kind of style is a better route. You had to open multiple cities in SimCity to have the ability to drop all the services. In Skylines it's based purely on population.
Now even though Skylines operates better in all aspects compared to SimCity, one problem I find with it is that you can't get to 1,000,000 population on one area or several for that matter. You can build a giant city on 6 connect areas, but you won't see the population in porportion. Instead it will probably take 9 areas or all 25 (mod) areas to get to 500,000 even. There is a mod that increases population, however, for people who want a realistic population to go with their giant city.
Cities: Skylines will be the measuring stick for city builders for years to come with its vast improvement on gameplay. So in-depth the game has a very high replay value. Once I upgrade my rig to a better processor and graphics card, I will be logging much more time on the game. Currently, $40 may sound like a lot for this game, but it's well worth it. If you can wait for a 75% off deal (which come out often) you can snag this for a steal.

Needless to say, my original review was not positive, but as I as I said, after the patch I will be updating.
I want to first give credit where it is due. The devs said they would address some of the biggest concerns and I feel they have done enough to justify a change on my review. (which you can find below)
If you are enjoy rouge-like/lite games then this should fill your need. There are enough elements to the game to make learning the best path take a few runs. After which you will be working toward getting the ending.
I want to point out that my only minor complaint is with the fact the game gives you plenty of champs to fight with, but for the most part they are useless still. This doesn't really impact the game in a negative way, so I can't take points off. Just would be nice to see each of these champs be unquie or give value to them other then wasted meat to sheild my elites.
- In combat there is a 50/50 chance every encounter that enemies will be placed right next to you, or one of your champs is placed right next to them (this is not a good thing). Nothing you do, sort of cheesing (using an OP item) will prepare you for the end game. Getting extra characters is almost pointless (nothing will replace the guy you just lost with 23 kills).
I was expecting some RNG tactical game where you build up a squad of fighters to go toe-to-toe with a big bad boss. After an epic battle, I would get a gratifying feeling knowing that I played my cards right with progression, that RNGesus blessed me just enough and my tactics were sound.
At this point, I feel no sense of achievement. On my first play-through, I did not lose anyone, had a badass sniper that did 12 damage (thats alot) and a squad of strong champs. Then the ending happened.
****spoilers****
form is unreasonably strong. I didn't have the one equalizer that heals when you get hit (didn't even know it existed on my first play) and I got rekt. What is worse? when you go to fight him again your whole epic party is gone and the whole fight starts over. You literally have 1 chance to beat him. There is no battle of attrition.
I like the 2 turn thing. More realistic then a whole team moving.
The rock, paper, scissors feel to each character is alright.
The blitz mechanic gives a feeling of pressure to keep moving
Biggest game ruiner for combat is the random placement at the start of combat. I can deal with not being able to place my team exactly, but the idea that the enemy can be placed behind my line is absurd. Imagine starting off where you are in a position to lose two champs at the START. I echo what someone else said- "I would never place my team like that" and add how did they get that close without getting shot first.
Pretty much everything else in the game is exactly as you would expect. I really enjoy 90% of the game. The look is great. The resource system. The map etc...
Until the issues above have been corrected though, I just cannot recommend the game. The devs say they are listening and plan on releasing an update. I will be back and will change my opinion if things change to fix these heart breaking issues.

I really wish I could recommend this game but I just can’t. My expectations for this game were fairly hi which is suppose is my own fault. I was expecting combat to be tactical like Banner saga or Fire Emblem instead your units are dropped in a random cluster. Melee units do pretty much nothing they die to fast to be effective tanks and don’t do enough damage to kill even snipers. Even after units level up pretty much all of them die to one or two shots so investing time in leveling units is meaningless. Aside from the poor combat the game is ok at best. The art style is interesting and fun, there are plenty of cool death animations you will see these a lot. The wastelands themselves leave much to be desired. At a glance at the map there are a number of unique zones with different factions and interactions. Upon closer examination every zone is pretty much exactly the same with enemies being graphically different and that’s it and the events themselves are all pretty much the same regardless of the zone you are in. This game had a lot of potential it just failed to deliver combat was bad the events were boring really the only thing this game delivered on was a cool art style.

Battlezone 98 Redux is set in a alternative version of 1960s whereby the USA and Soviet Union have secretly deployed armies into space for an extra-terrestrial substance that can be forged to craft weapons and armour that is powerful. Obviously other Nations are going to fight over this substance, so the National Space Dfence Force and  Cosmos Colonist Army battle over control of this substance.
This game is a blend of RTS and FPS elements that really seem to fit together and join together as one rather well. With the game primarily taking place in space with a sort of futuristic style it really takes upon the genre rather well. You can play as a hover tank that you can view from the cockpit, hunting down enemys with the hovertank destorying enemy crafts is rather satifying and brings back memories of when I used to play Starwars battlefront II.
Although the game looks rather nice and seems like a pretty strong build from the earlier version of the game, sometimes the AI on the game seems a bit unresponsive and just sits there. Sometimes their pathfinding of where they are actually suppose to be moving can be a bit weird and obserdly different than what you would expect them to do.
Anyways, the game is a really good source of what a RTS game should be all about. Being able to deploy your recycler at a power source to collect bio-metal that are used in the base in order to build defensive structers and wingmen into the battle. You are able to build towers to help you in the battle, with things such as Comm Tower which can take control of a satellite and you are able to view the battlezone. This gives you the added advantage of being able to command your wingmen in the traditional wya that you would normally in other RTS games.
With the graphics remasterd from the 1998 version of the game, it looks very nice and sharp which is what you would expect a game to look like in todays standards. With the hovercrafts and towers looking very futuristic and nicely detailed, I feel like the game was refinely detailed in every way when this game was being developed. The textures look very smooth and the explosions on are very nice.
+ Detailed graphics
+ Fun gameplay
+ Shows what a RTS should rally be like
+ FPS in a RTS game is very unique and hard to come by on steam
- Weird AI at times
My final thoughts on this game are pretty high. They really took the original game and made it into a modern version, with the graphics of everything and the amount of towers you can build to help you win the battle it really shows what you can do with a RTS game. If you can get past the weird AI at times, then I would definatly recommened this game.

This is the best game you've never played. It's the hidden gem of hidden gems.
Set in an alternate 1960s where the space race is just a cover for a cold war turned hot, the United States and Soviet Union secretly deploy massive armies into space in pursuit of an extra-terrestrial substance,
, that can be used to craft amazing and powerful weapons of war. The National Space Defense Force (NSDF) and Cosmos Colonist Army (CCA) do battle over control of the
throughout the solar system using hover tanks crafted from the precious material. Battlezone has some of the best sci-fi lore of any game- don't skip over the briefings and debriefings!
Battlezone has always had interesting gameplay because of the way it blends RTS and FPS elements. You primarily play the game from the view of the cockpit of your hover tank: you can hunt down enemy craft yourself and blow them away, OR, you can deploy your
(main production unit) at a nearby geyser power source and being collecting
using
in order to build a base, defensive structures, and wingmen to take into battle with you. If you build a Comm Tower, you can take a satellite view of the battle
zone and command your wingmen in traditional RTS style, but you don't need to have a Comm Tower to effectively command all of your units (in fact, most often it is better to NOT take this approach).
Battlezone 98 Redux (BZR) has received many improvements over the original game. These include highly improved terrain textures, models, lighting, menus, and more, and these alone make the game worth a purchase and play through. However, because BZR is built on the code of the 1998 release, some of the baggage from years ago has made its way into this game. The net code, though improved, still struggles from time to time, and having a good connection can be important to having an enjoyable online experience. (Overall this is has never been a problem for me, though.) The sound system also struggles mightily when there are many units in play or in a battle- it will eventually just choke and cut out completely until there are fewer units. The sound cutting out is a scenario that you're for the most part unlikely to encounter during regular gameplay, however.
Keeping these small qualms in mind, the game is absolutely a steal at its current price, and will buy you hours and hours of fun in space. I SAID FUN IN SPACE!
If any 90's game deserved a Redux, this was it. Especially if you never played the original (but even if you have!), this is a must buy.

It is an embarrassment on my part for paying for this game. The animations are goofy, the dragons themselves have so few polygons they look like something out of a PS1 game and they have the low resolution textures to match too. One of the features of the game is "destructible environments" where the destruction is limited to burning down some stuff like houses and trees to a crisp... in exactly the same way every single time. The fire graphics... oh my god... seriously, it's on the same level as Quake (the original one). "Towns" are basically agglomerations of houses sitting on the grass on some prairie or field. Nothing you do in this game makes any difference, you might as well just do nothing at all.
The only thing that seems like it might be a good idea is the concept of flight as you get to flap your own wings at your choice, this means you can control flight much better than other games where there is no difference piloting a flying animal and a jet plane. All in all, a very bad game and the developer excusing it calling out early access and alpha as some sort of excuse for the very poor quality this game has is an indication that this project will never see completion. The mechanics of the game are floaty and unappealing, the graphics are horrible, the textures are low resolution and just ugly, the effects for fire are amazingly bad (and this is a game where you'll be using fire as your main weapon mind you) and I say amazingly because there are free games out there that have better effects for fire. A quite unique game with a strange combination of tactical board game and roleplay & story-telling. As first side, the game seems like a "Monopoly": you start by moving your character-token and gathering ressources (token and achievement points). But you'll quickly discover that the gameplay mecanism has quite some depth: how to optimize your itinerary by minimizing ressource-token used and by maximizing achievement points gain, how to use "boost" of movement etc etc... There are a lot of tricks that can give you some tactical advantage over AIs.
However, this gameplay discover phase may take you 2 hours or so, and then you may start to feel some repetitiveness: the game has 3 main phases (copper age, bronze age and iron age), all of them have absolutely the same gameplay mecanism. The only thing that changes with the ages is the "ruling game", which you gain access by uplifting to the highest rank. Honestly for me, the ruling game is the true shining point of the game, they are kind of "management & simulation" like mini-games. I found them pretty well thought, as they fit very well to the historical aspects of each age.
One major default is that the "random side stories" you can encounter. The problem is that... well they are random, but the pool of available events are extremely low... If you chain several "heroic deeds" quests, it's very likely you'll get the same story twice or more. For a game which is supposed to centered on developping a story of a clan/family, I found this very annoying.
Overall, I rate this 7/10. Repetitiveness and the lack of variety in "random events" are the major default, but it is still worht playing if you seek an unique game with an enjoyable board-game gameplay and interesting story.

What a truly fascinating game! A someone who is new to PC gaming one of the genres I was most looking forward togetting into was that of metagames. Specifically, this refers to games about, well, games and do so by playing with genre conventions often humorous and occasionally dramatic effect (bizzarely, these almost never seem to get console ports). Undertale was first on my bucket list, for obvious reasons, and Pony Island drew my attention next thanks to its low price and a similarly strong reputation. I made a point to avoid as much information as possible about the game, not even reading the full steam description, and I feel I made the right choice in that regard. Pony Island exists for the sole purpose of surprising you and it does a fantastic job of it. What surprised me greatly was that the game was a rather strong example of psychological horror and its tricks truly got under my skin at times. However, it is flawed in a rather significant way: the actual gameplay is not very fun. Much of the game is based around a very typical 2D runner minigame and though I am aware that it is poorly designed on purpose you have to spend a very significant amount of time playing it, more so than I feel was necessary. I have similar issues with the puzzle mechanics: they are not bad, but at times they feel they are present merely because the game feels like it needs to have something for you to do. I would have prefered a slightly shorter, more refined experience with no filler, but what is good in Pony Island is not only really good but utterly unique. All this and a bargain price and you have a great storytelling experience that is an easy recommendation to all. Before I finish I must give a warning: the game is meant to be played in one sitting. Considering it's length of about two and a half hours this should be managable, but it is worth keeping it mind.

I really love this game, and am very happy about the passionate modding community behind it. They add so much replay value, allowing for smoother gameplay as wel as more ways to express your creativity with all the extra assets. If you're solely looking for a city builder that challenges you in a managerial or strategic way, I would pass. Cities Skylines is however one heck of a creative city builder!

Cities: Skylines is the city builder that SimCity (2013) should have been. Skylines simulates traffic and people incredibly well and although using the Unity engine, the game looks great and is very immersive. Skylines has a lot of options of how to build and the workshop is full of mods to make the options of detailing seemingly endless.
Skylines is not the easiest game to play and there's a slight learning curve if you don't use the Unlock All mod when playing. In the same sleeve, if you don't have Unlimited Money mod, then $70,000 is a tough start. It is very fun though to watch your town grow. Although the game can handle 1,000,000 population (it can take quite a toll on your computer, though) the population is more realistically simulated than that of SimCity.
Skylines improves all areas where SimCity failed -- one aspect was the development in your city. In order to get education in SimCity, you had to add an expansion to your city hall. In Skylines, it's just a matter of increasing your population and if your city can afford a new service. That kind of style is a better route. You had to open multiple cities in SimCity to have the ability to drop all the services. In Skylines it's based purely on population.
Now even though Skylines operates better in all aspects compared to SimCity, one problem I find with it is that you can't get to 1,000,000 population on one area or several for that matter. You can build a giant city on 6 connect areas, but you won't see the population in porportion. Instead it will probably take 9 areas or all 25 (mod) areas to get to 500,000 even. There is a mod that increases population, however, for people who want a realistic population to go with their giant city.
Cities: Skylines will be the measuring stick for city builders for years to come with its vast improvement on gameplay. So in-depth the game has a very high replay value. Once I upgrade my rig to a better processor and graphics card, I will be logging much more time on the game. Currently, $40 may sound like a lot for this game, but it's well worth it. If you can wait for a 75% off deal (which come out often) you can snag this for a steal.

At it's core, a 2D platformer. A few mechanics beyond running, jumping and attacking are unlocked as you progress - swimming , wall running, flying - however they're mostly only used in the world that you unlocked them in.
The combat is very simple, most enemies die in one hit, apart from the bosses which have some originality, but like much of the harder portions of the game, the bosses just need lots of repetition to get muscle memory and knowledge of attack patterns.
Each level has a few "electoons", which are mostly quite easy to acquire. The fun part in getting these is in the little challenge each section presents, but due to limited game mechanics, I can't remember any distinct ones.
The hard parts, such as bosses and the levels where you chase a treasure chest for a secret *thing*, are like quick time events without the visual cues - and if you're just a moment off even though you made a good recovery, the design of the game forces you to play again, getting a microsecond closer to the speed they want you to get to.
The visuals are quite nice, but you only notice them in the calm before the storm because otherwise you're too busy running around or trying to not die, which is a shame.
The music was unique, but the loops caused by dying repeatedly mean that any nice melodies are quickly forgotten.
The sidescrolling shooter parts are fun and a good challenge, and there aren't too many, which means you can accept that they didn't give the separate costumes (oops, I mean characters) distinctive playstiles.
As far as I noticed, even in the walking part of the game, the different characters did nothing either, apart from help you identify you and your friends apart.
Without co-op I probably wouldn't enjoyed this game enough to bother going very far. Co-op mechanics were decent and allowed for coordination and teamwork, however guacamelee did it better - in fact, I think Guacamelee did everything better, apart from on incomparable things such as artstyle.
tl;dr unless you're a big Rayman fan, play Guacamelee instead.

Skyshine's Bedlam is a strange, strange game, with cool ideas, great game feel, and a completely anti-fun combat system. This game feels like it should be in early access. Videos of my run will follow, to prove my points.
It's odd limitations make it beneficial to bring nearly no soldiers into battle. I found that 3 soldiers were enough. Until the near end of the game, I brought 3 soldiers every fight, and had so many resources I couldn't use them all. the core thing to realize is that bringing more troops DOESN'T make you more safe. It just means you lose more troops. You'll generally end each fight with 3 troops, whether you bring 3 or 6. The way the engine works is simple. 2 actions for me, 2 for you. Any of my pieces can use the actions on my turn. This means that numerical advantages really don't matter at all, and in fact are a kind of disadvantage. A force of 3 can move together, cover themselves, and pick off the flanks. The large force can only move, at most, 2 pieces a turn, meaning it's esstially a Thermopolae situation every fight. The player forces stand back, hold position, and let the opponents run into a gauntlet of fire until they're all dead.
The class system is a good idea that is executed poorly. The sniper class is literally useless. They start with 2 HP, and can move 3 spaces. They do good damage, but it doesn't matter, because the next class makes them useless.
The Frontline can move 6 squares, has 10 HP and does 2 damage. One hit from any enemy kills any rookie sniper. And the AI targets them 100%. I actually started bring rookie snipers to bait the trap for the AI, because they make it the top priority to kill them, ignoring everything else.
The shotgun class often ends up killing itself, by blasting targets out of their own range. Basically useless.
The only class I found really useful was the Gunslinger, who had decent range and decent damage, although the class ability (When attacked, you return fire) never worked properly. It would happen sometimes, but not others, with no explanation of why that would be.
The random placement of your troops, often within shooting range of the enemy, leads to a mad scramble that results in multiple deaths on your side before you even get to fire a shot.
On my first run, I made it across Bedlam, but by the 30 minute mark I found that I didn't care. The upgrades to the dozer were maxed out in the first province, and the few people who survived their first encounters were far too strong.
The designers realized, or course, that this game would revolve around players biding their time and waiting, as the enemies charged at them (as seen by the Blitz meter at the top of the screen, more on that in a minute), but the AI is so useless that turn after turn, 2 enemies would move into range, and both would be immediately killed on my turn. On the next AI turn, they'd send 2 more to their doom, for no reason. Some of the enemies have grenades (which you don't have, by the way), and when they target 3 of your people, you don't get to attack that turn. You have to move 2 people out of the way, and the 3rd still gets hit.
This game has a lot of cool ideas. I like the Dozer, I like the resources, but again, I was never even CLOSE to running out of any resource. EVER. Except power, which I spent carelessly and freely the whole game long.
Upon fighting a named boss, you will, guaranteed, lose a crew member. The bosses do 7-9 damage, and the only member of your crew that has more than 9 health cannot do enough damage to kill a named boss. There are just so many problems. I want to like this game. I think it has great combat animations, and the grid system and cover mechanic is nice, although I wish they had a % chance to hit shown, instead of random guess. I also wish cover worked sensibly, where you could shoot over your cover on your turn, and hide during the other side's turn. I wish that being "in cover" didn't help you when I'm shooting you in the back from the same side of the cover.
Now, let's talk about the Blitzmeter.
The game teaches you NOTHING about it. There's a random tip on the loading screen that informs you that when it fills up, the enemies get 3 actions, instead of 2. It doesn't tell you that killing an enemy resets the counter. It also doesn't tell you that enemies can move farther during their blitz action. This is not the kind of thing that is "a cool trick" that players need to learn by playing, it's a frustrating mechanic that the game doesn't tell you about. Ever. There's no notice that you're resetting the counter, not even a sound effect. The bar goes down in silence, and it doesn't tell you why.
I played one run, and the game crashed after I made it to Aztec City.
Also, achievements are broken. Unless not one person on Steam has won 3 battles in a row.
P.S.: This game uses ellipses where it should use periods.

**Updated 4-1-16**
The last time i played this game was 11-7-14. At that time it was little better than a tech demo.
I have redownloaded the game. This is my new impressions.
I'm going to compare what was, to what is now:
(Note, i played on "good" setting for graphics).
The UI prior - Seem to be well made for the starting screen where you pick your dragon/map and hit the play button. The background was equally nice. Over all, I liked it. When picking your dragon you could look at stats and what could be skills/powers. Detailed, very easy to read. This alone I'd say was very well put together and awesome at that.
The UI now - The starting screen where you pick your dragon. First impression... Green neon grass/ground. Picking your dragon button over lapped the play button so all you can see of play is LAY. Which is fine since you can put together that it is a play button. Picking dragons, the details of the dragons you can pick from are lost on the right side fo the screen into the neon green color. Leaving you guessing as to what it is saying.. I think i saw the word Ox for one of the dragons.. not sure what that would be.. maybe fav food? Really not sure what happened here. Hard to read, buttons over lapping. Step down from last time i played. Real disappointment. Almost feels like they went backwards here.
Map prior - poorly put together, could tell it was either rushed, or someone new to map making had put it together. Lots of seems where you could see the parts that were put together. Things would randomly fall through or if they walked into a seam, they'd fall through. Going too far in one direction would unload the map from where you were. Once unloaded, the map wouldn't reload. You were left with "dead zones" where you couldn't go back to them. Few trees. Villagers and their homes were bunched together like small villages (this is a plus). Over all, really drove home the feel that the game was a Tech Demo.
Map Now - Improved, smooth, no seams, nothing falling through the floor. Map doesn't unload and fail to load again when you come back. Rather odd coloring, kind of a neon green or off green for the "grass". More trees. Trees look nicer now. Villagers do not appear to live very close together. Takes away from the feel of villages. Over all, makes the game feel like an Alpha so a step up for sure.
Mobs prior - Few villagers, chicks with swords and guys with pitch forks (and of course the villager of doom, but he was a bug/glitch), cyclops, wolves, ents (or where they giants?). AI wasn't that good, simple see and attack. Passive mobs, cows, sheep. Easy to kill.
Mobs now - Same types of villagers, plus man at arms (or what i'd call them since they had shields), Didn't play long enough to find many other types of mobs. But i did take note there are now deer, and rabbits. Wolves are still in. AI is still rather basic. Though now they don't all attack on sight (but should in cases like the wolves who sat there and let me fry them for one of the quests)
Dragon Prior - Going to be honest here. The dragon we had access to when i first played was awesome looking. Really made me think Dragon. Handled ok, would go lopsided every once in a while. Could even change it's face a little.
Dragon now - While it does offer i think premade dragons? Not sure as it wouldn't let me actually pick anything. I was able to change the color of my dragon with sliders. Didn't have that option prior. You could make a pink dragon if you wanted to now. However, the body of the dragon as well as head leave me thinking lizard then dragon. They did it the right way the first time. Though to be fair, i heard we'll be able to have more control over what our dragons look like... hopefully. Otherwise I'd say a step backwards here with the shape.
Quests prior - there were zero quests.
Quests now - very simple quests at first. I didn't put a lot of time in this time around, but i get the feeling the questions are going to become more and more involved.
Combat prior - We had claw/fire to use for weapons. Pretty simple to be honest. shoot some fire, or hit them with your claws. I never found any bugs or problems with it when i played then.
Combat now - Able to use fire or a tail whip. Tail whip doesn't always seem to hit. Fire will fly off into the distance and cross the map. I found this out by ranging in the direction i had sent some flames doing the quest to find a chest. Actually seems more buggy then it did prior.
Over all prior - I felt the game was a tech demo and nothing more. I wouldn't have recommended the game to anyone, but didn't want to leave a poor review as it's not a finished game. I wanted to wait until the game is finished, then give it a real review that may or may not be positive.
Over all now - I don't feel like the game is a tech demo anymore. If i were to gage it's "age", i'd say it's early to mid Alpha. It's gettingn a lot of factors together now. The map is for sure cleaned up. Just needs more TLC. Combat and UI needs some heavy work. The game does though seem to flow better. There are some real possibilities for this game if it ever gets finished.
Do I recommend the game? My answer is still sadly no. Not because it's an early Alpha after 1.5 yrs. Nor because of the remaining bugs, and unfinshed features. It's not even the snails pace it seems this game is being developed at. The reason why I am not willing to recommend this game is simple. Commuication. The developers made a promise to maintain that with us. They failed to keep their promise. I will not move my recommend to a not. Because the game is not finished. As such, there is still a chance the dev's will turn it around yet again. But we'll see how that goes. I will be uninstalling the game now. I'll load it up again when there appears to be either some heavy updates or the game is finished or in another 1.5 years ;) Which ever comes first.

Perfect mozzarella recipe:
Prep the Ingredients
Fresh mozzarella is made with four simple ingredients: milk, rennet, citric acid, and salt. It's especially good made with whole milk—just make sure it's not ultra high temperature (UHT) pasteurized. Both liquid rennet and citric acid can be purchased online or in specialty cheese shops. Start by combining 1 cup water with 1 1/2 teaspoons citric acid in a bowl until dissolved. In a separate bowl, combine 1/4 cup water with 1/4 teaspoon liquid rennet.
1/9
Add The Rennet
Pour 1 gallon whole milk into a large heavy pot. Stir in the citric acid mixture and heat over medium-high heat until it reaches 90°F on an instant-read thermometer (it will feel slightly warm to the touch). Remove the pot from the heat, stir in the rennet mixture, and continue stirring for 30 seconds. Cover and set aside for 5 minutes.
2/9
ep_07132015_mozzarella_003 / Photo by Chelsea Kyle, food styling by Katherine Sacks
Cut the Curds
After 5 minutes, the mixture should be set with a gelatin-like texture, and pull away from the sides when you jiggle the pot. (If it's still a liquid, let it sit for another 5 minutes). Once set, use a long knife or large offset spatula to cut the curds: Making sure to reach all the way down, make vertical and horizontal cuts at 1/2-inch intervals across the surface to form a crosshatch pattern.
3/9
Cook the Curds
Set the pot over medium heat and cook, stirring gently every once in awhile to avoid breaking up the curds too much, until the curd mixture reaches 105°F. Remove the pot from the heat and set aside for another 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
4/9
Separate the Curds From the Whey
Dip a fine-mesh sieve into the pot and use it to separate the curds from the thin yellowy liquid (the whey). Clump the curds together and drain off as much whey as possible. Discard the whey (or reserve for another use).
Reheat Curds
Bring a second large pot of water to just below boiling, about 185°F. Put the curds in the strainer and lower into the hot water for 2–3 minutes. Wearing food-safe rubber gloves, fold the curds several times, then check the internal temperature of the curds. If necessary, return the curds to the hot water in order to reach 135°F.
6/9
Stretch Mozzarella
Sprinkle 1 teaspoon kosher salt over the cheese. Working over the pot of hot water, gently fold the curds over itself, stretching as you fold. If the mozzarella gets cool as you stretch it, return it to the pot of hot water for 10–20 seconds, then continue. Repeat folding and stretching until the curds becomes smooth and elastic.
7/9
Shape The Mozzarella
To finish the mozzarella, shape it by pulling the edges in towards the base to form one large ball, two smaller balls, or many bite-sized balls. Seal the shape by placing the finished mozzarella ball in a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes.
8/9
Enjoy!

Okay so I am revising my old review, because I have gotten quite a few more hours on the game since. The graphics are good, they aren't amazing, but it certainly is a beautiful game. Then there are the hacker bases, which you can unlock one from a mission, but all of them are full of character, with a lot of graffiti, sculptures, artwork, and overall location. And I think all of the bases, maybe one doesn't but all of them have 3D Printers, which you can use to print the jumper and quadcopter drone, and you can use it to print weapons, including DedSec weapons and military weapons(the DedSec skins can actually have paints on them military can't). Which brings me to another point. Scattered throughout the map, a lot of them you have to discover are bags of money which lunch bags give you about 4000 dollars while the duffle bags give you about 18 thousand, then there are also paint jobs for cars and drones scattered throughout, along with research points and key data which unlocks the some of the skills. Then there is of course the drone races, motorcycle races, boat races, and e-kart races. All of these give you money(assuming you win) and all of them are a lot of fun, and can inspire some competitiveness between you and your friends. This is a huge improvement over the first game for those who played it, and will def. be a fun journey for those of you new to WD.

So far the game has really blown me away, I felt like I was taking a big risk pre-ordering the game but it was so worth it.
Theres tons to do in the game, Go-Kart Races, and drone races, you can practically be an intense Uber driver, or you can sight see throughout the map and take pictures and selfies and post them online for all of your followers to see, its really satisfying seeing your numbers go up. In open world games I usually dont want to just casually walk to the objective... but in this game I'm totally fine with popping in my headphones and making a 2000m jog to the next objective. I always find myself taking selfies at landmarks or with random people. Or just watching all of the civilians go about their days (While I hack their bank accounts and read their texts and intrude on phone calls) and with the custom playlist you can set a certain tone to your surroundings and just makes for an all around fun and intriguing experience.
The story is all over the place, but most missions all are done with the end goal in mind, getting a big enough following to take down Blume. But it's enjoyable and it's made me laugh a lot as well.
The detail in the game has amazed me too, I've never seen so many NPC idle actions in one game... Everywhere you go feels alive and thriving, people will be chatting and doing their own thing, they could spill their coffee, even sneeze. I even found an angry spouse smashing the windshield of her mans car with a baseball bat while he watched terrified. I pulled out my phone and took pictures and she got mad and literally attacked me. It was hilarious. If a car is parked under a tree, the leaves that fall from the tree actually will land on the car and blow off when you start driving it. It's the little things like that that make the game really enjoyable to play.
The various gangs and police will have shootouts and sometiems you get stuck right in the middle of them, even choose who you want to help out. I witnessed a drive by, and the ambulance showed up while the guys friend stood crying off to the side. You see civilians actually getting handcuffed and shoved into police cars for commiting various crimes. Ubisoft really nailed making the city feel alive. Civilians photobomb your selfies, or try to fight you or talk to you outside of your cars if you get into an accident.
The game is great, and I still have plenty of side missions to complete, so I'll edit this as I go if I feel like I need to add anything.
Edit: Just finished the game, and I have to say the ending felt a bit underwhelming. But overall I really enjoyed the game. Ill give it a solid 9/10!
Edit: With the new update, you can now 3D print fully functioning AK-47 assault rifles. Oh, and replay the really fun missions too !

This is hands down my favourite card collecing type game around. The fact that duelyst mixes cards with a strategic gridded arena give this game depth which no other card game can even come close to.
The good?
-Awesome pixel art, every card looks great and has a bunch of smooth animations.
-Well balanced races, every race excels in a few things, every race can be countered, there is no real "go to" race which is refreshing.
-The amount of cards and strategic options is amazing
-A very nice mana ramp system with mana pools on the map. This lets the game naturally progress from small openers to huge game enders and also rewards good players with extra mana if they can play around the pools properly
-For each race (4) there are 3 general to choose from, each with their own abilities which lend strength to varying strategies
-Every game feels different, it always plays out differently. If you build your deck right you never really feel like you lost because you got bad RNG. If you aren't drawing things you can use it's likely your deck design that's flawed not the RNG. If you really hate RNG there are cards that let you replace multiple times/draw more cards so really there is no excuse to be hating on this game's RNG.
-Cards aren't "better" or "worse" in a general sense. They all are balanced to their mana cost. They may be better at certain things but that is always at a cost at other things. At the start you'll have very basic but good generalist cards. You can play all the 6 mana legendary cards you want but the starting 8/8 Stormmetal Golem is still one of the best. You can't dispel it to remove it's abilities, it's just going to come at you with it's massive 8/8 stats and there are few options to deal other then fighting it.
Cons
-There are so many cards now that the learning curve is immense. While card to card the game is very balanced you will find that seasoned players have better decks since their decks are tailor made to follow a specific strategy and they will be more effective because of it. While this is a con you can get over it easily. Do some research, find out what deck you want (mech decks are good starters as they can be used for any race/general) and then just recycle all cards that you get that aren't the ones for that deck. You'll have a top tier deck in no time, I ranked diamond (2nd highest) in my first month because of this. After you have your one "good deck" you can start collecting cards as usual and branching out.
-Microtransactions, microtransactions as far as the eye can see. Want an emote? That's a microtransaction. More cards? Microtransaction. Skins? Expansions? Player Icons? Card backs (really guys?)? Keys to open crates you've already "earned"? All microtransactions. This game is fun without paying for extra content but be aware of this. Pretty sure the Duelyst devs snort microtransactions before work every day to get "in the zone."
Overall, if you have time to spend this game will be very rewarding. If you just want a pick-up and play type game it'll be awful as it does take some time to get a competative deck.

A very limited game because of many 'problems'.
First off the 'compression' of the maps makes it very limited building areas, with many towns & resource locations all most right next to each other.
The second problem is related to the first problem, in that with such small maps & everything so close to each other, it makes it very hard to lay tracks between locations.  Some of the issues are when laying double tracks, then trying to connect them with crossover tracks.  Many locations are so tight, that there is just no room.  And the track laying has no apparent "undo" button, so if make a mistake (or more likely a track won't connect correctly), then often have to delete surrounding sections of trackage, just so you can finally click on the original bad track section.  Then you have to re-lay those tracks you had to delete to gain access to the one you actually wanted removed.
AI routing of trains is also very messed up at times, with trains crossing over to other tracks, just to re-crossover a little bit further down the track.  Sometimes the trains even crossover tracks onto the same line as other trains, which then they have to stop to wait for that train to pass (which would not have been required if they stayed on the original trackage).  Also, it is not uncommon for trains to run down a track, only to turn back on itself & return the way it came from (& have seen numerous times where AI trains seem to get stuck in "loops", where they run down a track, double-back, then go a little ways to once again double-back again).
Game also crashes a lot for no apparent reason.  So you are forced to constantly use the 'save game' button, to possilby allow you to finish a game after it crashes.
AI Players trains also don't seem to be affected much by grades, since they will build tracks up & down hills or other extremes, but trains will still haul a lot of cars (even for very early locomotives), & their speeds don't seem to be affected at all.
This game may be good for multi-player with friends, but even then the very 'compressed', small maps limit any real opportunity for a lot of repeated gameplay.

Great game, especially if you've played the others and want to see more of the characters.  Admittedly, the plot plays out like a fanfic (i.e. convenient timing so the main people can run into each other - but the individual stories are good) and is totally action-based with little 'horror-style' tension.  You'll have a huge arsenal of guns and this really damages the horror atmosphere.  If you aren't afraid of zombies running at you, this game will not change your mind.  The J'avo enemies are more like the parasite-infected cultists from RE4, but the shambling zombies are still there too.  Certain undead of both kinds can shoot at you - this can be annoying if you aren't using cover, which is rarely necessary.  For classic RE fans, know that this is closer to Uncharted than those older games.
Now that that's all out of the way: the good stuff.  The movement system is deep and liberating.  There's nothing I wanted to do that I couldn't: from jumping rolls, to advanced melee-weapon moves, to quick from-the-hip shots, to a huge number of contextual attacks.  There's real variety in the combat and the characters.  There are tons of different enemy types, so it doesn't get repetitive.  And this is a long game, too: four fully co-opable campaigns took me more than 40 hours to get through, and that's not counting the excellent Mercenaries mode.  Do yourself a favour and play on a hard difficulty - my first playthrough was on No Hope with a buddy; it verged on frustrating, and we died a lot, but winning felt really good.  Play on at least Veteran for a tense experience, or Professional if you're gutsy.  No Hope is a trial on NG, because it is truly, truly hard.
All the stories are worth experiencing.  Leon's plot includes throwbacks to RE2 and RE4, with city-based and ruin-based zones.  His areas are generally dark, claustrophobic and grim.  Jake's (alongside a grown-up Sherry Birkin) has the most variety, with a hilariously effective snowmobile waiting in a snow area, and an unarmed stealth section.  Surprisingly, it works, and Jake has some memorable lines; he's more laid back and arrogant than Leon (stronger sarcasm, amazingly), and the antithesis to blunt, serious Chris, but the biggest badass is hard to call.  Chris' campaign has the most emotional impact if you can get invested in a 'band of brothers' type of plot - the BSAA is made to seem much more important than RE5 ever made them.  Piers Nivans' giant gauss rifle is amazing, so consider playing Chris' campaign from his perspective.  Ada appears in all those stories, so her extra (DLC) campaign reveals what she was doing in-between.  Finally, I recommend switching between campaigns using a chonological order guide for your playthrough.

Thomas Was Alone is a game that should not be judged by its cover.  Mechanically it is a straight-up platformer with minimalist rectangular graphics; the main gimmick is swapping between characters to solve jumping puzzles, and it is not notably difficult or even memorable.  But then these rectangles are given names.  They are given inner monologues.  They are given personalities, desires, and existential crises.  The player will follow their journey, their struggles, and their triumphs.  Friends will part ways, and be rejoined.  A story is created as emotional and philosophical as any big-budget movie.  And it does it with rectangles.

Thomas Was Alone is an amazing platformer in the way it makes you feel. This game is cute and fun and the narration draws you into the graphics so well that it becomes secondhand to refer to each quadrilateral by its name! I'm so happy to rediscover it in my library, so I downloaded it and played it again. Most recent playthrough took me about 4 hours, so could be a one-sitting game depending on the length of time you're willing to stay seated!
The game has very minimalistic graphics and simple gameplay, making it such that it has a small filesize (yay for great games under a gig!) yet the story and the way that the developer's used those minimalistic graphics paired with professional narration to represent dynamic relationships between... well, blocks. Thomas Was Alone offers a good experience and I would recommend it.

Thomas was alone; I was bored. A short review for a short game: while it does have a peculiar postmodern charm, I hadn't sufficient enjoyment from the game to offer my recommendation.
The experience is a bit shy of 3 hours in total, including the bonus missions separate from the main story. Ostensibly a puzzle-platformer, the puzzles are too rudimentary to engage, and the platforming similarly lacks challenge. Consequently, the primary challenge offered is exercising the patience to slowly move each of a half dozen pieces one at a time to their obvious positions, cycling slowly through them with unnecessarily awkward controls. The game uses a sparse visual style that is inoffensive, but certainly does not impress: it's a 2D game made up of moving blocks and very limited animation. A visual force this game is not. The ambient, often shoegaze-styled score is somewhat enjoyable, but I encountered frequent audio bugs which marred the experience. I'd often hear duplicated background music playing with a slight offset, and the previous level's soundtrack would often fail to stop, leaving a cocophonous overlap blaring until I restarted the game. Given the mediocre gameplay, the spartan visual style, soundtrack, and narration are the main feature of the game. Unfortunately, I found the narrative similarly uninspiring; you simply push your quadrilaterals along their predetermined paths while a narrator intones their thoughts and feelings. It perhaps resembles a primary school teacher reading to young children; perhaps an audience of a younger age group may delight at the motivations of this animate geometry. Alas, I did not.

Battlezone was released back in 1998 and was one of the first action-RTS hybrids - it has all the usual elements of an RTS, but you command from the ground in a vehicle, fighting alongside your troops. The genre never really took off, but because Battlezone was bundled with a lot of graphics cards it reached a wide audience and gained a cult following.
If you are someone who's considering buying this having played it way back when, do it. It's a reworking, not a remake, so the real BZ atmosphere is still there. The ships and buildings are all heavily redone, with much more detailed models and much larger textures. They look excellent. The terrain looks very much like it did back in the original, so it's still behind Battlezone 2, nevermind more modern titles. But all things considered, the graphics do a good job today with the update. The gameplay is as rich as ever. Multiplayer is now handled through Steam within the game, which keeps things nice and simple, with all the old options. A bomber DM is still a thrill after all these years.
If you are someone who's never played the original and are wondering whether you should buy this, well don't expect it to look fresh. The developers of this update have done an incredible job hauling parts of the game into the 2010s, but there are engine limitations. Firefights are limited to a few hundred meters in distance, and don't expect detailed ballistics or other physics.
The real joy of Battlezone, however, was always its gameplay, and its blend of FPS and RTS that has never really been replicated since. In each mission you will be dogfighting and base building, often at the same time. A selection of ships can be built, each of which offer different benefits, and you can kit them out with a variety of weapons. Your resources ("biometal") are gathered by Scavengers which have an annoying habit of wandering off into dangerous areas and so need to be constantly protected. Two single-player campaigns are included, so there's a hefty chunk of content for someone who has no plans to dabble in multiplayer.
At the price, this game still delivers eighteen years after its original release, whether you're looking for something new or a satisfying hit of nostalgia. Buy it.

I'm a sucker for mystery Visual Novels, so this one caught my interest by default. And while the game has its less appealing sides (like the art; or some awkward grammar here and there), I actually found myself enjoying it quite a lot.
At first, I was surprised about the pacing of the game. A single playthrough consists of 7 days, but each day goes by pretty quickly with basically just a single scene revolving around a character of your choice. Things almost feel rushed at times, but it makes consecutive playthroughs smooth and you don't get the feeling that things are starting to drag on. I suppose that can be both a good or a bad thing, depending on your approach. Personally, I didn't mind it.
The game has 6 endings, and 4 of those reward you with items that you get to keep permanently across your save files. You need all 4 of those to unlock the True Ending - which is the most fun to experience with some twist and turns and definitely worth the effort to unlock it. Once you get the True Ending, you also get a little bonus in the extras gallery which I found to be a nice touch from the creators. :)
I also liked the music in this title a lot; it works nicely to give that kind of eerie/mysterious atmosphere that I love to experience in games such as these.
So, kudos to the creators for bringing out quite a unique mystery Visual Novel! Playing this one convinced me to check out their 2nd ~Cafe 0~ title and I'm excited to see what it has in store on the mystery side, too.

To give you an impression, I played this game on Desura, a long time before it came to Steam. The game hasn't changed, and though there are now Achievements I am probably bound to not replay this game.
What first comes into my mind playing this game is, okay - it is a visual novel, probably of the Otome kind - this often is promising a not so good game. I won't indulge that VN aren't games, because some VN actually are very decent and playable games, a lot of them are not.
First we get to the story, A girl died, and now she has to relive the last seven days of prior to her death, sounds a bit scary, right? Wrong the story is quite naive, it's more a dating sim where you have to chose interests and try to uncover the whole story - if a story is really well written, then this can be fun - but not so here. The game doesn't exactly know where it wants to go, it's like a fluttering butterfly eratically being blown by a strong summer gale. And that is really bad. It's more a dating sim than a supernatural, mystery and the story actually suffers from this. It might have to do with the original target audience of the VN in this case, but that explanation is much too cheap to really matter.
Second Atmosphere. The game actually fails here on a whole new level, I never had a game which I actually did loathe to start (even back on Desura) this was the first game that did create this feeling for me. It was a ruined atmosphere, by the narative, the sound of the game, the ... action sound (footsteps, bubbles... whatever), probably because I am not just a 14 year old kid trying to get the best out of this. In my youth there were books that had a similiar ring to it, and one reason I preferred Fighting Fantasy from Ian Livingston and Steve Jackson over the CYOA-Books was the element of chance, over prewritten content - this plays like a very, very boring CYOA-Book.
The next is the technical and graphical implementation, and that is a bit more on the positive side - but doesn't save the game as a whole. The graphics are not really well made, but not too shoddy either.
The game has some nice concepts, but ultimately fails to transpose this to a general audience, the game is really more like niche product, built for a generation of entitled Smartphone users, who didn't had the experiences and the troubles of the generation of pre-millenials... if love becomes the naive topic of a childs play, it isn't simulating love, neither it's simulating friendship or relationship, it just creates more feelings of entitlement because life isn't working in the way it's shown in games like these - not even close.
There are VNs that at least try to take their topic a bit more seriously, and aside of that are more fun to play, this game is at times too depressing or too enervating and boring.

I reinstalled the game to check out the latest beta patch. I wrote my previous review months ago, but now I figure it's time to come back and readdress some things with a bit more clarity.
I purchased this early access game in April 2015. It is now currently January 2016. There have been very little changes since I bought it. Certainly not enough to "wow" me yet.
1) Previously, I made mention that the flight controls were sickeningly sensitive to the point of being out-of-control insane. With the 8.3 update, it's not as bad. I was able to move without throwing up in the process. That is one thing I can say has noticeably improved. It was so terrible before that I couldn't play the game at all.
2) The terrain seems more lush than before. All I remember was long stretches of blank ground with barely any trees or mountains or much of anything.
3) You can grab people and animals and carry them into the air and eat them. If you can manage to get it to work properly, that is. I'll get to that later.
4) You can now color the dragon. This wasn't an option before.
5) Flying around in circles is fun, even if I'm not really doing anything important. So, ponts for being immersive.
1) They said the optimization was improved, but it still seemed pretty poor on various settings. The funny thing is, the lag and stuttering happens the most when running on the ground, and it's smooth sailing (no pun intended) when you're flying over miles of forests. This happened to me before the patch, as well, on the fastest graphics setting on a brand new gaming machine with a more-than-capable graphics card. This needs some serious tweaking before it's playable for a wider range of people.
2) While the flight controls were easier to deal with, the other controls were a bit of a mess. I tried like hell to pick up people off the ground in mid-flight. I managed to successfully do it once, then proceeded to drop said human because I'm spamming the Q button like crazy trying to snatch him up. It barely works. I was more excited than I needed to be when I finally managed to get it.
For some reason, the flight controls were automatically selected as inverted when I reinstalled and restarted the game. I'm used to normal flight controls. This isn't a big complaint, because that's an option you can change.
Grabbing things will sometimes just bug out the dragon or the enemy you're picking up to where they're almost melting together like in The Thing.
3) The envrionment is hilariously glitchy, as are the enemies and objects. While flying the dragon around, I couldn't count how many rocks, trees, tree stumps, houses
people were either stuck halfway through the ground and peeking up through a mound of snow like they got trapped in a snowbank, or were floating in mid-air like they were caught in a time-warp. I almost don't want to call this a "negative" because I laughed whenever I saw it. I actually got stuck underneath a floating rock at some point.
Sometimes you'll get stuck on a piece of the terrain-- say, a house or a tree-- and you'll suddenly and mysteriously get launched backward several yards as if you had been rocketed off of a pine tree trebuchet. This also made me laugh. "Where are you going, Dranonimous?!" I yelled.
The LOD is a mind trip. In the distance, the envrionment is just one giant oil paint color blotch, which really negates the look of the piece of the map you're currently standing in. It makes you think that if you go anywhere near the color blotch, you'll disappear into the gaming void. I didn't want to go past the borders of the snowy forest, which I figured was the least glitchy part of the map. I did fly somewhat away form it to check out a badly-rendered lake. Then I turned back because the rest of the map had also turned into a lake somehow.
4) I never lost any health. Or gained any. I don't think you can really get hurt yet. I understand that eating is meant to replenish you, but that doesn't seem to have a purpose. Not yet, anyway. And your enemies are clones of one pitchfork-wielding dude and cows. Or cottages.
5) Maybe I'm not the first to say this. If I am the first to say it, then let it be known: The dragon... is ugly. I'm sorry. But it just is.
The dragon's front arms look like they should be socketed on a G.I. Joe. The back legs belong to some kind of alien frog. The head... well, I can barely look at it, because whenever I try to, the dragon shoves his face in the ground like an ostrich. The tail is three times as long as its body.
The running and flying animations aren't very fluid. Instead of running on its bulging soldier arms and amphibious hind legs, it does this sort of "hop" that really reinforces the whole "Frog" concept. Maybe there'd be a different animation for walking, which would follow the stride of most other four-legged creatures. Right now, it just looks awkward and weird and not at all aesthetically pleasing.
The flight animations aren't much better. The body is sort of stiff as its airborne, sans the waving, flapping tail, and the wings resemble cardboard.
Overall, my opinion is mixed. It's starting to show a
bit of potential, but the updates have not been very grand since I bought this, and they state it should be ready for release and out of Early Access in two years (and they said this when I bought it). Yeeeah, I don't think so.
Dragon The Game is in
, and this should be considered when making the Early Access purchase. It is barely even half ready after nine months. With how slow the game is updated, and the lack of massive improvements, I'd say it would take more than two years to make this game bug-free and good enough to buy.
Does that mean you shouldn't support it? Eh. If you think it'll go anywhere, be my guest. I still feel like my money hasn't gone to anything worthwhile.

I haven't played very much of this game at all, but in my opinion this game is a fun game. When combined with a good playlist on Spotify or while listening to a podcast while playing this game really just allows you to get lost in this game.
Reasons why I love this game:
1- I really enjoy city planner games in general.
2- Lots of things to micromanage, so I can obsess on the most efficient way to possibly have my hospital buildings situated in relation to all of the environmental obstacles and city streets.
3- You can mess with tons of modifiers, like being able to raise taxes from 7% to 50% or lowering the budget for education from $10,000 to $1,500.
3b- When you mess with modifiers it really does affect the game. Such as if you were to raise taxes, households would become angry and move out, causing your city population to fall, effectively lowering your total tax income.
4- Atmospheric sounds and graphics go really well together, be careful because you might get sucked into the game and forget about real life for a weekend because your eyes were practically glued to the screen.
Downsides:
1- On my Mac, the game would crash randomly about 4-8 minutes into a session. (My Win10 laptop runs the game fine, it has never crashed on my laptop.)
2- If you mess with the water- such as by destroying a dam or terraforming land on the coast- the water will look all glitchy and if you don't go back without loading an earlier save it will look wierd and take a long time to go back to looking normal.
3- Traffic is hard to manage. (Just like in real life, not really a problem but can still be a nuisance.)

So I just finished my first trek down to Aztec City and I have to say I had a really fun time with it. Like a road trip with your friends! Through a desert! Oh such antics you and your friends get up to along the way. Like watching Bill get eaten by an acid-spewing mutant, or selling Ted and his buddies off to a group of nomads for some fuel. You know, typical road trip shenanigans.
But seriously, Skyshine's Bedlam is pretty darn fun once you adjust yourself to the difficulty and figure out a few reliable strategies. My first run ended in a fit of desperation as I had a mere two units left from the rather large stock the game provides for you at the start and I just barely made it. I was saved by the simple fact that I had squirreled away enough resources to pelt enemies my dozer weapons and shield my two remaining veteran badasses as they tore through everything and everyone. Hugely satisfied when I finished my first run.
The combat is something I see a lot of mixed feelings on in the other reviews and I certainly see some of the concerns that people are bringing up. Often times in the early stages of the game it can feel like units just get chewed up before they can do very much and I think that's at least partially intended. If you could pimp out every single unit Bedlam would probably end up being far too easy to clear. As to whether or not it's fair...you can certainly move to minimize casualties through liberal use of the dozer's equalizer abilities (Shield!) and holding the squishier units back. I found that a veteran frontliner can be a rather useful shield/feeder for your rookie units. Regardless, I didn't find the game to be unfair most of the time.
One thing I do wish the game had was a way to get a lay of the land before each encounter, just to plan out which units to take. The random placement of said units took some getting used to but I don't mind it too much, a simple lay of the land would suffice.
There is also the willingness of the developers at Skyshine to keep tweaking/improving the game as demonstrated by their swift response to player feedback. That's probably the most comforting thing a new game could possibly have, attentive devs.
So, in sum the pros and cons!
Pros:
-Variety of Races/Dozers lends to replayability
-Unit ranking/leveling system
-Tons of different routes to take and dozens of events/points of interest to investigate (or run away from)
-Equalizer/Dozer Weapons add tactical depth
-Resource management creates a nice air of tension in both battles and travel
-Element of chance keeps things interesting
-Excellent Artwork/Animations
Cons:
-Difficulty curve is a bit rough for new players
-Two turn system can feel a bit restrictive
-Tons of exposition for the lore
-Tough to retain units and the ones that make it, may end up overpowered
Overall: Worth playing if you like strategy games, roguelikes, and/or trading innocent passengers for fuel!

STRONG POINTS: elegant and steeped in metaphor. The game tells a story while you play. The actions from one generation build upon (and perhaps hamper those) of the next. Lots of interesting strategic decisions: when to marry (and gain an additional pawn), which pawn to move first to maximize your chances at points. The game expands impressively the further you advance, and when I first landed in the ruling class my jaw dropped.
WEAK POINTS: Those who dislike randomness will become frustrated with the inscrutable child-bearing mechanics. Sometimes you try and fail every time, sometimes your pawns won't stop having kids no matter how many you already have. :)
TO SUM UP: An epic strategy game that doesn't end up overwhelming. You stay focused on the here-and-now, even though the ramifications of the player's actions stretch beyond the immediate.

Ubisoft seem to be putting themselves back on the right track.
Firstly with Rainbow Six Siege and now Watch Dogs 2, both games are very enjoyable and fun to play while still having good graphics and optimisation. As for Watch dogs 2 it runs great on my PC (4790K + 1080 @ 1440P) where i see highs of 120 FPS and Lows of 55 - 60 in some areas of the game. Thats with my settings on Ultra apart from Shadows (Medium) and MSAA + HBAO disabled.
Gameplay wise the game has a great mix of stealth, hacking minigames / puzzles and combat, while still maintaining an interesting story with diverse missions without being repetitive. The multiplayer aspect helps to give some diversity between missions while they can be annoying sometimes. COOP missions are rather lackluster and remind me of Far Crys outposts, that being said with the right people this game is a great laugh with friends.
The combat may be fun but the game still has its issues. Guns unlike melee takedowns feel realtivley lackluster and not very impactful, this directly takes away from the combat but i still enjoy it non the less. Another problem i have is the CRAZY long animations to enter and exit hideouts, especially when compared to areas like shops where you can just walk straight through the door it'd be a lot better if this unlock animation was shorter. All in all for Ubisoft have done well with this game especially when compared with their previous track record.
Bonus - The ragdolls in this game are absoloutley hilarious and you can take equally hilarious selfies.
I reluctantly spent £40 on WD2 (Which i don't do very often for any games)  however i feel it has not been wasted, i wouldn't recommend it to many people while it is still at its high price point, if for some reason liked the first game you'll love this one.
Overall i'd give Watchdogs 2 a good 8.5/10 there are still some aspects to improve upon but it's nice to see a big games company taking steps in the right direction.

Strike the perfect balance between a strategy game and a somewhat casual game. Pickup and delivery game mechanic with transformation of resources (ex: coal -> steel -> cars), cities are growing and demands more diverse goods as they grows. Spawn a vast range of history from very small and slow coal engines to more recent electric engines. Multiple scenarios available with differents objectives. Grow your train company from a single track between 2 cities to an empire across the whole map. Once your routes are setup it's fun to watch your trains go around the map and check your bank account filling up. You can optimize your routes if you wish but it's not obligatory. Really the spiritual successor of the previous Railroad Tycoon games but with much better graphics. Small downsides includes the sometime clunky track laying (but you get used to it) and the somewhat limited number of scenario. I played a lot more hours with the standalone game than indicated on my Steam profile.
