One of the best platformers I have ever played. The Donkey Kong Country series was the one I always considered the best, until I tried this one. The main thing I like about this game, is that you move at a much faster pace, compared to something like the DKC games. There are optional challenge levels that will test just how good you are at controlling your character at its max speed. If you can complete those, you earn the right to play the Land of the Livid Dead level, which is the most challenging stage in the game.
All the secret/bonus rooms in a stage, have their own unique platforming segments that you must get past, in order to get the reward from it. I enjoy that a lot more than how the DKC bonus/secret areas usually are (just collecting the bananas). The boss fights are also a lot more difficult and better designed. The art and animations make the boss fights look so good and those water stages also.
The difficulty is also great. Nothing is cheap and unfair. Everything stays the same for a stage and you will never feel like it was the stage's fault for dieing, but your own. The game also has fast respawns for when you die and automatic checkpoints per stage. You will never have to start back at the beginning of the stage (unless you die there) and you will get to keep everything you have collected so far.
The game will last you 10+ hours, if you plan on trying to unlock all the levels. If you like this game, then check out Rayman Legends, which I think is even better.

My experience with this game is a little different than most reviewers.
For one, i really liked the battle system. Sure it makes no thematic sense to have just two actions for the whole team, but there is a lot of strategy and risk management involved. Apart from the last battle, i didn´t find the game´s difficulty to be unbearable.
However, when i FINALLY defeated the last boss, guess what? The game froze. That´s it, no ending score, no achievements, nothing. I turn to the forums and find out that EVERYONE WHO BEATED THE GAME IS HAVING THE SAME PROBLEM.
So, to sum it up:
PROS:
+The art style is really well done. The characters are stylish and each drawing is a joy to see.
+ I loved the battle system. It´s tense and makes you think. Most people won´t like it though.
CONS:
- The writing is terrible. 80% of the words in each paragraph are made up. For people that do not have english as a native language, it´s almost incomprehensible. Plus, the lore and events are bland and uninteresting, and do not impact the gameplay in any meaningful way.
- The events are also poorly scripted. You get a lot of items in your journey, but very, very rarely get the chance to use any of them. And when you finally do, the payoff is disappointing. The events also often repeat, so there´s not much replay value.
- After a lot of hours, and tense battles, when you finally complete your mission, THE GAME FREEZES WITH NO VICTORY SCREEN. And this is not an isolated ocurrence. Honestly, this is unacceptable.
Conclusion: Unfortunately, this game is simply not worth the asking price. Even if they fixed the problem with the ending, it would still be advisable to wait for a major sale before you consider buying it.

A bit late to write a review for this game but I think it's time. A longer one than I usually write too. TL;DR will be at the bottom.
CAMPAIGN:
Personally I wasn't a fan of the singleplayer, most of the missions bore the crap out of me, the dialogue is bland, the characters are boring and don't really offer much in terms of learning to bond and loving them, AND THE CHARACTER YOU PLAY AS IS LITERALLY REFFERED TO AS "PLAYER." That doesn't seem like a big deal, but when you're playing a nameless character throughout the entire story, it creates a bland experience. And it's quite a mind♥♥♥♥ of a story to wrap your head around at first. The plot thickens by a large margin as you progress, it's psychological journey. I've heard lots of people praise this story for having a lot of depth and tiny details, maybe a bit too much depth for my liking. If you criticize the story, people will liklely tell you "Well that's because you don't understand it." I understand the story, it's just uneccessarily confusing and when I finally realized what it all meant my first thought was "...wow. That was pretty undewhelming for all that mind ♥♥♥♥ery." That's just my opinion on the singleplayer, some people like that kind of depth and story telling, and that's fine. Then again most people I know don't play the singleplayer regardless.
MULTIPLAYER:
It was fun while it lasted. DLC maps were DOA, Treyarch's balls were being squeezed by the greedy money whoring publishers which resulted in TONS of RNG loot via supply drops being added to the game (despite them saying the loot would be cosmetic only, and then going back on their word and adding stat-changing weapons into the mix despite the community clearly not wanting that.) The first RNG weapons that were added weren't necessarily OP, but it was annoying being killed by all kinds of weapons that you knew you either had to:
A: grind an EXTREMELY long amount of time to gain crypto currency for the black market to have a less than 10% chance for a weapon (to make matters worse, Treyarch even nerfed the rate you could earn cryptokeys.)
B: buy COD points in bulk with actual money.
Or C, what I did: Admit the fact that your luck is♥♥♥♥♥♥and don't even bother trying to get any weapon anymore.
Now, the devs added some redeeming qualities to the black market system to ease the grievances we had, such as Contracts and daily challenges to earn some cryptokeys throughout the day/week, and even some "bribes" that guaranteed you a ranged and melee weapon in a supply drop. But by the time this happened, the playerbase on PC was already dying, dropping from an average of 30,000 players to less than 9,000. I myself was tired of the insane amount of weapons and goofy taunts (specifically the "dab") being added to the game and dropped multiplayer for a good while. That, and the obsession PC players have of ONLY PLAYING TEAM CAMPMATCH.
SERIOUSLY, THIS HAPPENS IN EVERY COD GAME. YOU GUYS REALIZE THERE'S OTHER GAME MODES TO CHOOSE FROM, RIGHT? MODES THAT ARE BETTER, LIKE DOMINATION OR KILL CONFIRMED?
In all seriousness, you can still have some fun in multiplayer. Just be prepared because the only game mode you're gonna find is TDM, and you can only play the same game mode for so long before getting bored (TDM being incredibily boring already.)
ZOMBIES:
At this point, Zombies is the only real reason to buy this game. Incredible story, maps, weapons, good fun with friends, mod support, and the upcoming Zombies Chronicles DLC with remastered classic maps. If I ever open up BO3 nowadays, it's to play some god damn Der Eisendrache <3
I almost forgot, there's a bonus mode to this game called "Nightmares" once you complete the singleplayer, which I will also review.
NIGHTMARES:

Multiplayer: It's alright, it used to be a lot better, TDM only
Zombies: 10/10

7 Grand Steps: What Ancients Begat is a game made essentially by one man (he outsourced music and art assets, I believe). Originally, this game was meant to be part of a seven part series. The developer has mentioned however (in early 2014), that the second step (game) won't be coming for "several more years".
The game is stylized after the old coin games in which you insert a coin into a machine which triggers movement. Game play is relatively simple to understand, but is complex enough so that there is a layer of strategy involved.
The game is relatively simple. Through the use of coins and choices made during game play, you influence a family through the ages, determining how educated the children become and how powerful the family becomes. Play the game right, and your family could end up ruling over their city as high priest or even king.
:
:  You start in the bronze age as a new family. Throughout the game, you'll be presented with story cards through which you can sometimes influence the fate of your family. There are several Ages through which you must progress in this game. Each Age follows several generations of your family. Some generations manage to reach high society while some struggle to survive as simple peasants. The story cards are very samey throughout a given Age, which can make the game a bit boring at times.
: The art assets are very well done in this game. Similar to the story cards, there aren't many different assets, but that's to be expected, given what the game itself is a relica of (old fashioned coin fed theatric game machines).
: The music and sounds in What Ancients Begat are superb and really add a lot to the overall ambience and immersion of the game. They're not over done, but are instead rather subtle, which is exactly what a game like this needs to make it shine.
: According to the forums, the length of this game varies according to each person's play style. Some people manage to finish the game in less than 5 hours, while others take closer to 15 hours to reach the end. Personally, I got about 13 hours worth of play time.
: There is a bit of replayability in this game. In my opinion, it's well worth playing through at least twice, as the first time can be seen as an opportunity to learn the mechanics and work out a viable strategy for the second playthough.
Overall, I recommend that you purchase this game if you enjoy simple, historical, slow paced games with strategical elements and few art assets. It's definitely worth getting on sale, if nothing else.

Thomas was alone; I was bored. A short review for a short game: while it does have a peculiar postmodern charm, I hadn't sufficient enjoyment from the game to offer my recommendation.
The experience is a bit shy of 3 hours in total, including the bonus missions separate from the main story. Ostensibly a puzzle-platformer, the puzzles are too rudimentary to engage, and the platforming similarly lacks challenge. Consequently, the primary challenge offered is exercising the patience to slowly move each of a half dozen pieces one at a time to their obvious positions, cycling slowly through them with unnecessarily awkward controls. The game uses a sparse visual style that is inoffensive, but certainly does not impress: it's a 2D game made up of moving blocks and very limited animation. A visual force this game is not. The ambient, often shoegaze-styled score is somewhat enjoyable, but I encountered frequent audio bugs which marred the experience. I'd often hear duplicated background music playing with a slight offset, and the previous level's soundtrack would often fail to stop, leaving a cocophonous overlap blaring until I restarted the game. Unfortunately, I found the narrative similarly uninspiring; you simply push your quadrilaterals along their predetermined paths while a narrator intones their thoughts and feelings. I haven't played very much of this game at all, but in my opinion this game is a fun game. When combined with a good playlist on Spotify or while listening to a podcast while playing this game really just allows you to get lost in this game.
Reasons why I love this game:
1- I really enjoy city planner games in general.
2- Lots of things to micromanage, so I can obsess on the most efficient way to possibly have my hospital buildings situated in relation to all of the environmental obstacles and city streets.
3- You can mess with tons of modifiers, like being able to raise taxes from 7% to 50% or lowering the budget for education from $10,000 to $1,500.
3b- When you mess with modifiers it really does affect the game. Such as if you were to raise taxes, households would become angry and move out, causing your city population to fall, effectively lowering your total tax income.
4- Atmospheric sounds and graphics go really well together, be careful because you might get sucked into the game and forget about real life for a weekend because your eyes were practically glued to the screen.
Downsides:
1- On my Mac, the game would crash randomly about 4-8 minutes into a session. (My Win10 laptop runs the game fine, it has never crashed on my laptop.)
2- If you mess with the water- such as by destroying a dam or terraforming land on the coast- the water will look all glitchy and if you don't go back without loading an earlier save it will look wierd and take a long time to go back to looking normal.
3- Traffic is hard to manage. (Just like in real life, not really a problem but can still be a nuisance.)
Great idea but plays like a electronic board game, a boring board game.

The mechanics are unique, which makes learning them a lot of fun.
There just isn't a lot of depth or quite enough going on to really keep you coming back.
Worth a spin at a discount.

Here's the thing. You pretty much have to review a game at the full price. That's the value of the game in the eyes of the publisher.
In that case, 7 Grand Steps fails utterly.
Graphics, audio, story, documentation. No aspect or combination is worth the full price.
The game concept and overall execution isn't bad, but suffers from simply pretending to be more than it is. A lack of documentation that serves to feign complexity.
Example: You're given 4 questions with 4 options each. The degree of success determines how well you will do in the new age, while complete failure will outright kill the character. That sounds fair.
However, picking the exact same options on a second playthrough might result in different results. Why? The stats or family of the character? The reputation of the character? Wealth of the character? Any missions undertaken by the character? Pure chance, possibly with a greater chance of success for certain options?
Yeah, good luck figuring it out, because the game doesn't tell you. Initially that is of little consequence, but it becomes more important as the game proceeds through the ages.
Overall, not recommended. Perhaps on a 90% sale, if you can handle the frustration.
Look at earlier Mousechief games, that have a good deal more to offer.

This second otome visual novel from roseVeRte feature a female protagonist Marin Umino, a former swimming ace at a school who finds herself at Cafe 0, a place where the recently deceased full of regrets arrive at and would be attended by a different waiter for each different person to advise them on returning to the living to uncover pieces of their past, discover more about themselves and eventually find peace in their journey after death which is unavoidable and will always occur within 7 days at the time of returning back to the living world. With the Cafe 0 waiter Sui attending to Marin, Marin finds herself waking up from a near drowning incident at her school's swimming pool where she was introduced to her best friend Ami Kawase, her ex-boyfriend Tooru Mizutani and her school's doctor and counselor attending to her Shou Takizawa with no memory of each character's role in her past. As Marin attempts to find out more about her past through each character, she will return to Cafe 0 and back to the living again, reliving the same 7 days prior to her death with additional mysterious items from her death appearing in her room drawer each time before eventually dying without returning to Cafe 0 in a tale of mystery, intrigue, subterfuge, love, lust, honour, jealousy, betrayal and vengeance.
The game has plenty of save slots to allow different gameplay and dialogue choices to be made during the game, with a black or gold butterfly popup icon to reach a different storyline branch, Marin taking on a white, black or green appearance, additional mystery items to make enquiries on after each playthrough and the option to skip and fast-forward any part of the game. Background music and overall game presentation are good after factoring in chibis for each of the main characters and constantly moving zero symbol in character selection screen. Recommended when at discount or in bundle offer as it takes less than 10 hours to unlock all mystery items, reach all endings and unlock all CGs and achievements.

is RoseVeRte's second visual novel and the first game in the CAFE 0 series so far. It is most certainly no masterpiece, yet it is a satisfactory supernatural mystery with an eerie feeling, accomplishing more than many others of its competitors for the genre in a limited game time.
In this eerie little adventure, our protagonist is Umino Marin. As the game starts, the young high school student finds herself in an odd little cafe in the middle of nowhere. Once within, she is attended by a weird waiter with the worst kind of manners: Sui. Sui presents Marin a glass of water and obscurely wishes her a good journey. Only then Marin wakes up, apparently just saved from drowning in her school's swimming pool. The most alienating of all these uncanny events, is that we remember nothing from our previous life and we bear no reflection before a mirror anymore. It's as if we do not exist in a physical manner. As the game progresses, Sui appears again to inform that this is the last week before we died. We are solemnly living through the last week of our lives, in order to come into acceptance of our dying. We will have a week to learn about our past, come to meet with the people that we deemed important for us and find a way to deal with what actually happened to us.
The narrative within the game is not extraordinary, yet it's chosen topic and the specific way that its mystery ends up revealing itself is more than charming. Marin's character and her way of dealing with the impending doom waiting for her at the end of week, the constant suspicion she endures for everyone and the sense of loss she goes through, change in every playthrough according to your choices to establish a unique, supernatural sense. Marin's nickname at the school - The Mermaid Princess - is a direct reference to Andersen's elegant, yet grim fairytale. The titular oxymoron - The Drowned Mermaid - is a most fitting metaphor for the storyline too. Characters themselves tend to end up on the superficial side due to limited game time, yet you still get a solid sense what type of people they essentially are.
The CGs and the artwork are most certainly not the strong suits of the game, yet I ended up liking them a lot anyhow. The amateurishly drawn manga depictions of all characters felt like a solid art choice for me. They are eerie, anatomically wrong and far from being appealing, but their eeriness, especially the glassy, cold look in everyone's eyes - very like dead fish eyes - felt like fitting allegories, as if every one of them are dead on the inside, including Marin herself. Sad, but beautiful.
Most people in discussion forums got sincerely annoyed that the Japanese voice acting is presented as a bonus DLC rather than being a part of the original game, but the developer explained that the original version lacked any voice acting at all. So, them being a later add-on, you gotta pay for it. I played the game with the voice acting, and I'd vote that it is worthy of your 5 dollars. Voice acting is really well-done, enhancing the mood of the game wonderfully and adding character to all personas.
At the end of the day, this was one of the visual novels that grasped me as I went for the bed. I found myself thinking about the tragedy poor Marin ended up with. I do recommend the experience for the ones who enjoy the genre, and maybe all others that would appreciate a good but short supernatural mystery.

I will admit, I bought this game on the Halloween Steam sale because I had been watching some YouTubers play Co-Op in Insane Mode (when you die the level restarts) and it looked really fun. I have a great fondness for platformer games, and a growing love of puzzle/obstacle based games.
This is a good combination of both, with an unexpectedly entertaining story to go with it. The controls on mouse and keyboard work well, as I don't have a controller to set up as recommended, and the levels do increase in difficulty at a pretty decent pace. Sometimes I do have to step away and attempt a level at a later time as I grow frustrated, but that tends to occur when I've been playing for an hour and a half and my brain gets a little fried on the puzzle aspect.
The narration by Stamper is what helps sell the comedy aspect of this game, as well as the storyline. Without the narrator, this would just be a platforming game with no real purpose. There are some mysteries, such as the origins of the cats and why the titular Battleblock Theater was created, and there's worldbuilding in the asides from the narrator about these subjects.
There's also the option to play levels built by fans, and there are some very creative levels out there. Someone literally recreated the first few levels of Mario!
Definitely would recommend, if interested in a comedy platformer with some puzzle elements. Favorite bit would be one of the cutscenes where the Narrator talks about how he would leave after showing the cats his favorite finger (his thumb).

Ubisoft seem to be putting themselves back on the right track.
Firstly with Rainbow Six Siege and now Watch Dogs 2, both games are very enjoyable and fun to play while still having good graphics and optimisation. As for Watch dogs 2 it runs great on my PC (4790K + 1080 @ 1440P) where i see highs of 120 FPS and Lows of 55 - 60 in some areas of the game. Thats with my settings on Ultra apart from Shadows (Medium) and MSAA + HBAO disabled.
Gameplay wise the game has a great mix of stealth, hacking minigames / puzzles and combat, while still maintaining an interesting story with diverse missions without being repetitive. The multiplayer aspect helps to give some diversity between missions while they can be annoying sometimes. COOP missions are rather lackluster and remind me of Far Crys outposts, that being said with the right people this game is a great laugh with friends.
The combat may be fun but the game still has its issues. Guns unlike melee takedowns feel realtivley lackluster and not very impactful, this directly takes away from the combat but i still enjoy it non the less. Another problem i have is the CRAZY long animations to enter and exit hideouts, especially when compared to areas like shops where you can just walk straight through the door it'd be a lot better if this unlock animation was shorter. All in all for Ubisoft have done well with this game especially when compared with their previous track record.
Bonus - The ragdolls in this game are absoloutley hilarious and you can take equally hilarious selfies.
I reluctantly spent £40 on WD2 (Which i don't do very often for any games)  however i feel it has not been wasted, i wouldn't recommend it to many people while it is still at its high price point, if for some reason liked the first game you'll love this one.
Overall i'd give Watchdogs 2 a good 8.5/10 there are still some aspects to improve upon but it's nice to see a big games company taking steps in the right direction.

Rayman Origins is a platform game.
A reboot of the classic Rayman game (the 2D one, not the 3D games), Rayman Origins is an excellent addition to the franchise.
Rayman and his friends are all relaxing on the Snoring Tree. But their snoring disturbs an old granny from the Land of the Livid Dead. She sends out an army of Darktoons across the Glade of Dreams, who capture the Electoons which inhabit it. You, as Rayman and his friends, must go out across the world and free the Electoons to restore the Glade.
Although the story is great, the game's aesthetics and soundtrack is where it really shines. The beautifully crafted world, accompanied by the brilliant musical score, is what really sucked me in. The visuals are absolutely gorgeous, and the soundtrack is superb.
Gameplay is excellent too. The animations are fab, and the game overall feels very fluid. I am not a huge fan of platformers, the gameplay usually fails to entertain me, but I absolutely adored Origins. You start off with just the ability to run. But as you progress you unlock more abilities, such as wall-running. There are also certain levels in which you ride a mosquito. You can either shoot enemies or suck them up to fire them.
The game comes with 4-player local co-op. This is great, but it would be even better if it included Online play too. This is the only downside to the game.
One of the best PC games to be released in 2012. I recommend this to both those who adore platformers, and those who do not.

Hilarious fun for 1-4 players. This game isn't plagued by some of the annoying aspects of platformers like Mario.
There is no timer except during an optional (but highly recommended) second level run during which you try to achieve a time goal. The lack of a timer allows you to explore as much as you like without feeling pressured. Also, one of the most annoying things about Mario games is absent from Rayman -- collision detection between players. In Mario, you feel forced to stay clear of your co-op partner as much as possible because bumping into him or accidentally jumping on his head (or visa versa) usually sends you flying uncontrollably to your death. In Rayman, there is no collision between players except when the players choose to boost each other or intentionally slap each other. There are no "continues" in Rayman. You're not going to have to start the game over because you run out of them. If it takes you 10,000 lives to finish a level, then so be it.
I had to restart several levels simply because I was laughing to hard to play. The game is downright hilarious, and the platforming is challenging without being irritating.

Solarium is a very cool way of teaching about various types of plant life ands its uses over the years. the idea is a very good way of teaching about something while keeping your attention. while i'm not very interested in plants myself, if you are i highly recommend trying this game.

Solarium isn't so much a typical game as it's more of an educational experience. You take the role of a student in space who is essentially studying to become a botanist.  You can visit various locales such as a desert or the alpines.  Or even time periods such as medieval.  Each area has 10 different questions associated with that environment and clues nearby.  Answering correctly will give you points which you can put towards making your own crazy plant designs.

This was my first minimalist platforming game since the old days of the Atari 2600. In a lot of ways there were parts that reminded me quite a bit of those old games, from the graphical style to the sound effects. Not bad, but not really great or really very much fun.
The only striking part about this game was its narrative. I enjoyed the story, which felt a lot more present than game play or visuals, but as a game that feels wrong. A good story is fine, but when t is the showcase of a game, especially a platforming puzzler, I feel like the point is missed. This isn't to say that it is right or wrong in this respect, this is just my own perspective.
The narrator does a pretty good job of giving these colored and named blocks their own personality, though listening to him speak at times had me feeling a bit like I was listening to a post-modern “The Adventures of Milo and Otis”. I rather enjoyed some of the elements of the story, but even that aspect felt really skeletal.
The game play is pretty straight forward. Each block as its own ability, name, and purpose for a puzzle. One can float, another can hop twice before landing, and so on. Their sizes and shapes are utilized well for solving a few of the more complex puzzles, but there really isn't a lot once you’ve figured things out.
The controls are quite easy and work very well. I used a keyboard and my controller and had no issues with either.
Overall this was an okay experience, but not really much of a game. There really was a lot of missed potential. The presentation served a purpose and did so well, nothing about this game feels cheap or lazy. It is unfortunately very short. As of this writing I'd clocked in less than  90 minutes but I think I played closer to 2 hours, all achievements unlocked and all parts of this game experienced. I would like to have seen more, but as it stands I just can't recommend this game, especially at full price.
There really isn't much, but what is there isn't bad.

Thomas Was Alone has the bare bones of an interesting takey-turney teamwork game in the vein of The Lost Vikings. Each of its little coloured blocks has a different ability (small size, double-jump, inverted gravity...) and a wry, twee little characterisation of its own. The game is pleasant to look at and has good-quality narration. If you happen to die, the respawn is very quick which helps avoid frustration.
However, you never really feel like the game is letting you off its rails. The puzzles are almost all so obvious that they're tiresome to complete, especially given that the jump button is finicky and unresponsive. The one solution that struck me as being interesting and clever was telegraphed by the blocks' starting positions, which seemed like a bit of an insult to the players' intelligence. There are very few sections where you get any freedom to go platforming. Maybe this is part of the story/metaphor/thing, but frankly that isn't really interesting or coherent enough to sacrifice fun anyway.
There's a good game concept and a nice little story in here somewhere, but sadly it's chopped off at the knees by dull level design and some slapdash writing.

If you're a fan of rogue-likes and/or turn-based combat, you can't go wrong here.
The two-turn battle system was the biggest "whaaa?" when I first started playing, but it actually does a great job of making the combat feel unique. (And stressful!) Rather than the standard "queue up all your players to barely avoid being attacked next turn" that we've done a million times before, Bedlam's encounters force you to think differently about who moves where, and when, and attacks what. It also forces you to not coddle your characters; they will die, and sacrificing them becomes part of your strategy. That's not the way I usually play these kinds of games, and it's cool to play something that keeps me on my toes.
There's also a lot of strategic choices and risk-taking to be made as you travel the wasteland. Should I risk some potentially rewarding or deadly side missions, or stick to the road? Do I help this group of nomads, or attack them and take their stuff? Should I risk taking on this boss battle? (Because if you win, the boss joins your crew!) Should I spend some power cells to upgrade my dozer, or save them for encounters? (Where you can use them for dozer-specific AOE attacks that kick all sorts of♥♥♥♥♥during battle.) Each run through Bedlam always feels different.
Top that all off with a cool post-apocalyptic world full of grotesque, yet charming, characters and I can easily recommend this game. Good stuff!

Early on in the marketing for Bedlam the devs mentioned they were influenced by FTL (along with four other games), a very popular rogue-lite space exploration game. Since Bedlam is described as "strategic" and "set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland", I naturally thought it was going to be exactly like FLT in every way.
Well, I'm sorry to tell you that despite Skyshine's massive and scurrilous campaign of disinformation to trick everyone into thinking Bedlam was a reskinned FTL, IT'S NOT!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
So for the teeming millions of gamers out there who thought they would be buying a second copy of FTL, RUN AWAY! It's a horrible trick! You will discover shortly after you start playing, that it's NOT actually FTL. It's not even made by the same people. It's different.

My team set up feels like it matters more and each character has their use. Rather than a wait till your useful approach. The death animations are still glorious and now I get to see many more of them. The combat feels much better when everyone can act. The old system made it so whoever was closer or got in trouble first was the one you played until they basically died or someone else was in more trouble. Serious kudos to the dev for listening to peoples feedback and making it a choice so you can either play with the new redux rule set or the legacy ruleset. Seriously awesome work. I loved the look of this game when I first saw the title. I'm a fan of rogue like games & the stories they can create comapred to someone else. Bedlam was looking to be a strong game with some great design. I love the combat animations and the environment. Sadly the main part of this game the combat feels dull rather than strategic. You get 2 actions across your entire team as does the enemy. So that one move one attack or 2 moves etc etc. However I often find both me and the AI are using one character for both our action points until one of us  loses that fighter then we move onto the next. The rest of our team just waiting patiently in the corner watching the action happen until it's their turn to be thrown into slaughter. The game is hard I won't deny which I do like. Leveling up a character if you can make them live that long and get enough kills will gain veterancy and start to just become all round better fighters. The challenge is a good challenge but where I thought I'd find myself loving the wasteland combat and losing my mind if I scored that lucky headshot or one of my best fighters just got butchered I'm finding myself sighing whenever combat begins. Not what I expected at all and it's a shame. The animations in combat are great so not getting to see them at their full potential kinda saddens me. As much as I want to I generally don't think I could recommend this game. Hopefully they make a seperate combat mode as a difficulty setting or their future games take a longer look at their combat.

Having played a lot of strategy games Duelyst looked like a fun game, after playing it however, I see why it died. The cards you initially get are pretty awful, which means you'll be grinding for commons that can even do anything productive.
Unfortunately, typical rewards for grinding are "specials" which are just coupon packages that you have to pay for. You can earn a decent amount of cards by simply playing, but you'll soon be getting crushed by epics and legendarys that have little counter play if you don't have those cards yourself.
This wouldn't be so bad if the grinding wasn't so brutal. It has a purchase system inline with Hearthstone's, but missions give only you 10-15 gold, as do solo adventures. That means you'll be sinking a lot of time into this game just to get basic packs (orbs).
Also, the game doesn't seem very balanced. There are cards that literally have no value, and some that break the board and are severly undercosted.
After only a year this game is pretty much dead. You can find games, but next to no one streams this on Twitch. There is no reason this game shouldn't have a lot more content. The cards and models look very simple, and the more you play the more you realize that you just need more options strategically, as well as more synergy between cards.
No one wants to get into a dying game, and the devs aren't trying to save it. That's games these days, get in, get paid, get out.

What a strange and fascinating game...that was literally my first thought when playing this game and it still accurately describes what i think of it now.  Even after 20+ hours of gametime I cannot think of many other experiences as unique and interesting as 7 Grand Steps.
But is it fun?  Yes...if you are into this sort of gameplay...which I now realize is probably difficult to pinpoint the audience for this game.  It is probably most accurately described as a storytelling boardgame that lets you build generations of your family trying to achieve advantages to overcome "challenges of the age," which are basically disaster events that wipe out most everyone but you (if you pull it off).  Strangely enough, the gameplay sort of simulates the constant struggle of trying to stay ahead in society and still provide a better future for your children (basically by teaching them better than you were tought).  It works extremely well at keeping a feeling of tension and accomplishment throughout, and I found it pretty addicting.  It is definitely a game that warrants a few hours each time you play instead of one to two hours.
However, my biggest complaint with the game is...the sequel.  Or rather the very low chance of getting one.  I would LOVE to see this game continue,  and I really hope it sees more attention.

How can i put this Masterpiece, This Treasure,Into words?
When someone asks me what my favorite game is. or what the best game i ever played was,
It is this game and only this game I talk about,
I was first introduced to battlezone at the age of 7 In 1999, My dad had found this gem in a clearance bin at Big Lots, and had bought it with the intention of playing online over our dial up connection with his Installer Buddies from work.
At the time Joysticks as they were called were the best way to experience any simulator and fortune would have it dad had a Thrustmaster Fox 2 Pro at the time one of the best joysticks available(Having 3 Axis Or a Throttle at all Was a feat to be recoginized for controllers at this time).This Controller and Battlezone would come to be my church as I took my first steps as a gamer, And what a leap it was.The strategy,The vehicles,The ACTION! To this day I can remember it all.
Some of my best memories are of playing this with my dad and his friends and the journey it took me on as i developed my skills and mindset towards becoming Better and better,  Every match utilized a different  strategy there were so many different vehicles and weapons loadouts you could use that it provided endless challenge and excitement Even though I lost almost every match,
Just as the year ended I donned a New mantle that would come to be my gamertag(ReaperX2000).
Moments before the new millennium I defeated My father and his friends in a brutal day wrecker victory I built and ammased an army of scouts and an armory quickly hunting down my opponents by carefully placing my troops i ejected so i could overlook the enemy base, launching 2 day wreckers onto seperate targets so the blasts would overlap and cause the most  widespread havoc,
I waited with my sniper prone trained on whatever red dot i could find as the bombs reached the peak of thier arc i waited anxiously counting down the moments before they would be in range, as they approached just above his base i took the shot sniping one of his scavengers to draw his attention.Perfect, Just as he had time to turn around the bombs dropped destroy his entire offensive wing most of his scavengers and almost all of the buildings lay in critical condition.
"Time to send in the dogs." I ordered my wing of scouts to attack his recycler, it was a crushing blow, as the scouts many miniguns quickly lay waste to what was left of Dads installer buddy.  I quickly ordered my scavengers and a couple defense turrets into the area to collect the salvage, It was time to take on the real threat, Dad himself.
My attack had been successful but in order to accomplish this task i had left myself open to attack at my original base, Fortunately i had already tucked my recyler away in a different geyser, calling it and the constructor it had built i quickly began raiseng defences for my new base, i built several powerplants and guntowers surrounding and plugging the perrimiter turrets,
I had recyled most of my scouts and sent a few to scout for the enemy repurposing all the metal i could find into tanks and walkers, and of course switching to my own walker with my favorite choice of weapons,(Flash & Mag <3) Dad had already utilized the time to construct his own army of tanks but he lacked defensive structures, With my earlier attack run i had gained advantage by collectiong far more scrap far quicker, He put up a good fight, Our tanks clashed in a battle of explosions for what seemed like an hour. But in the end my resources allowed me the victory, Sending in wave after wave of tanks as i established defenses on his doorstep to reclaim my lost scrap, Eventually he lost out and I claimed Sweet Sweet Victory.
This victory would be the driving force to push me to succeed in any and every video game,Memories of the different odds i have overcome would give me the confidence to take on any new challenge,And the theme of this game would place space simulators action and strategy games in a special place in my heart.My 7 Year old Mind would grow to use battlezone as the basis to judge every game upon, And to this day, No game i have ever played,(And I have played ALOT) compares to matches in this game,
This to me, is simply the best game that was ever made, and seeing it here in steam(WITH MODS!!), remastered beautifully, Leaving the real joy to this game completely untouched, Because it was just so masterfully done the first time. is a dream come true,
I would reccomend this as a 10 Out of 10 But this game is so wonderful it would simply take its score Divide by zero and multiply by infinity, Not only do I reccoment this game, this is THE game I reccomend For gamers at any point in thier lives
Thank you for reading.
TL;DR: Buy this game, It could change your life.
P.S. If you have the means, USE A CONTROLLER/JOYSTICK, its where the magic of this game really is,

First off, I would just like to address that as the indicator states above, THIS IS AN EARLY ACCESS REVIEW, and will be assessed as such.
Dragon: The Game has great potential, great conceptualization and fantastic ambition. The idea behind an open world MMORPG/RPG that puts you in the position of being one of several fully customizable dragonkin is an amazing push towards online gameplay and single player experiences alike. Putting you at the helm of fully designing, developing and modifying your dragon-sona is something that hasn't been seen in the field.
However, the development team is relatively slow compared to similar major Early Access games such as StarBound or The Long Dark, and more importantly, THE PRICE FOR THE EARLY ACCESS IS RIDICULOUS. Yes, it's wonderful to contribute to new developers, as the gaming field is a large and quickly growing industry that should be open to anyone who so wishes to explore it, but $17.99 for a game that is currently unplayable is not appropriate.
That said, it's hard to see why such a basic game in this current stage is suffering from such a dramatically poor run-state. As you will see in other reviews, along with my own input, you really do need a near top-of-the-line operating system. Don't be fooled by the pretty commonplace system requirements - I apologize for not being able to tell you exactly why it doesn't run, but the performance, even at literally bare minimum skeletal optimizations, runs at about 8 fps at best on your average to decent gaming computer or laptop.
However, I still am very excited to see the completion of the game. I am hoping that this problem array be addressed so that the game doesn't get criticized and ridiculed, but rather fixed and allowed to live up to its full potential. I still support this game, but cannot recommend it at this point in time. I do however, recommend that you keep up with this game!

I haven't found Bedlam fun.  Which is a pity because it had huge potential.
The graphics are great and the animations are fluid.  The random encounters are exactly what I expected from a Rogue-lite style game.  Sometimes they're fair, sometimes they're not but that's just that way the dice rolls.
My complaint is with the tactical combat mechanics.  They're honestly stupid.  Each side gets two turns.  It doesn't matter if you've brought one unit or six.  You can move the one unit twice or two of the six units once.
Think about this for a moment.
Most of the units will be unable to move in any given round.  There is no numbers advantage; a small team tends to be superior as their members don't stand around like numbskulls whilst getting shot-up.  No team composition will give you an advantage until you start getting high health and high damage veteran and elite members.  That's not tactical play.
There are four classes of combatant scaling from high health and low damage melee fighters to low health high damage snipers.  A melee fighter can attack someone adjacent to them only - which makes sense.  However their low damage means that attacking with a melee fighter is a waste of a precious turn.  They're meat shields in the purest sense.
Ranged units can attack only at a very specific distance.  A sniper unit can attack someone seven paces away.  If the enemy is six or eight paces away they cannot be shot at all.  How does this make any sense?  Why doesn't damage or to-hit probabilty scale with distance?  A lot of the gameplay reduces to hoping an enemy will run into the narrow band of a ranged unit or trying to coax them into one with a sacrifice.
Nothing in the description, video or screenshots indicates that this is the tactical style.  That no real gameplay is shown is very telling and should have been a huge warning for me.
Still complaining about the tactical game.  Units are not placed at the start of battle they're dropped in randomly, a melee unit could start well behind a sniper unit who is too close to shoot the enemy.  Why - when I am instigating the attack - would I possibly want my units deployed like that.
Bedlam could have been a great FTL / XCom mix but as it stands it's a game of chess where your opponet randomly kicks over your pieces.  It's not fun at all.

In short, this game is all about sacrificing your units so some of your units can get strong enough so they can start 1 shotting enemy units. You also need to manage your power usage so you can prevent your OP leveled units from getting one shotted from bosses with 60-100HP+ post-Aztech.
That's my experience from playing this game for approx 10 hours on Bedlam Mode (Hard Mode)

This is a re-review of the game, on 3/30/2016.  I'll be keeping, adding, and removing to my original review as needed.
What is this game?:
Basically...  Xenonauts + FTL + in a wasteland = Skyshine's Bedlam REDUX.  The premise.. you have a giant map with a bunch of winding roads.  You load up a massive APC-like super vehicle of your choosing, then trek off across the map to reach the end.  As you travel between nodes along the road paths, you will often have to choose which direction to take at crossroads and what detours to take, in order to collect resources like fuel, weapons, allies, and special storyline objects needed to complete the game.  However, the more stops you make, the higher your threat meter becomes, making tougher enemies appear, and in larger groups.
Along your journey, you will run into many randomized events that may help you, or try to stop you.  Many of these will be battles which take place in isometric "Tactics" style randomized battlegrounds.  If you have played Xenonauts, Final Fantasy Tactics, Ogre Tactics, Front Mission 3, etc etc, you'll know exactly what kind of fighting I'm talking about.
If you succeed, travel the lengths of the map, and defeat the boss at the end, you are rewarded with unlockable vehicles for future playthroughs.
Pros:
- Turn based combat system resembling classics like Final Fantasy Tactics, Fallout Tactics: BoS, Front Mission 3, etc
- Very cool Art
- The game seems a lot more polished and easy to get into now.
Cons:
- RNG Heavy.  This can lead to stressful games, as there is a large amount of luck involved before a fight begins.  As an example; just like my previous review of the game, I ended up in a battle semi-early on against 5 enemy frontliners that immediately surrounded me and were far tougher than I.  It was also taking place inside my vehicle, so I couldn't use vehicle weapons to AoE/soften them up.  Despite having 4 veterans, the 4 enemies also were nearly 1 hitting my guys, which was making my vehicle heal ability pointless.  Up until this battle, I was doing quite well, having not lost a single unit.
- Tiny battlefields.  This makes attempting strategic fights sometimes impossible.  Often enemies will spawn already in weapons range and/or so close to you that you can't back up out of their move/attack range due to an invisible wall directly behind you.
- Very little cover.  Each fight, a random assortment about 2-8'ish cover blocks will spawn, sometimes far enough away from you that you don't get to use them before already taking fire.
- 4 units per fight, with no AoE units.  This requires some explaining.  You can build up a fairly huge roster, yet only 4 can ever come out at once.  The enemy however, will start greatly outnumbering you, the further you make it on the map.  If one of your unit's HP hits 0, perhaps due to a rush of enemies that focus fired all on one ally, the unit is dead.. no knock outs, no bringing it back, no salvaging anything from it, all it's hours of kills lost in a single turn.  This creates a scenario where you end up choosing 4 units to be your main force, and focusing all your leveling into them, to stand up to these overwhelming odds.  Which in turn, makes losing one to RNG or a bad battle decision, all the more catastrophic.  You'll be stuck having to relevel a new unit against stronger enemies, in greater numbers, before the end of the map.  You do get AoE abilities in your vehicle which can help deal with huge numbers.  But that's assuming you can get them into range, have the spare energy cells, and can target the enemy without hitting your own units.  This is probably an intended gameplay mechanic, but it's a very high stakes one that may leave you flustered when a unit gets assassinated, extremely dropping your chances of success.
Summary:
I feel like the game has gotten a lot easier to play since my last review.  Enough so, that I can see some people enjoying it.  I myself, will probably put some more time into it.  The RNG aspect has gotten seemingly a lot better than it was previously...  as it feels like I can now work out strategies to combat really bad luck situations.  But that's assuming I haven't just gotten lucky so far in my recent games.  The restrictive battles also make me feel like the available strategies for use in a fight are pretty limited.  But that simplicity can also be a plus side to some.  Shoot stuff, bigger numbers win, use cover/buffs/AoE to shift numbers in your favor when overwhelmed, rinse and repeat.
All in all, I feel I can recommend this game now.  Much less infuriating lol.

After 10 Hours. I have learned a few things but First the Pros,
-Not Overly bad for micromanagement.

- Simplistic Controls, you could actually get a mmo mouse, and never have to touch your keyboard.
- Train models, seriously, if you want anything for a modern Diesel, you have ONE choice, Newer Electric. Hope you like the TGV Because that's it. (Even by 2006 standards its barren)
Cons
1.) Crash fix Patch, go get it. Seriously, All of the problems stem from when this game came out, games would only take 2GB of Ram, because 32bit Windows was standard, (4gb max) so they limited the game so it can't crash the system. Go get the patch, it will make the game use 4Gb. Much More stable. If you don't do this this game can be crashed out by simply having trains get stuck. GET IT.
2.)Clipping, bridges have NO regard for what they do, they will build supports in the middle of existing track, clip with each other when splitting off or running a double track.
3.)Tunnels are hard as Hell to make unless you want to dive straight down. (mountains are "okay")
4.) Dense Stock maps, Hard to get everything in, either you end up with bridges everywhere, trains waiting (sidings are almost impossible to do as cities are literally, a 8 car consist away from each other.
Everything from here has to do with Realism, or actually controlling your trains. If this doesn't concern you then skip to the Finale.
5.) Realistic Routes are not a thing in this game. Trains take the shortest available route, Period. Including Running backwards on a track, so it will drive head onto another train because shortest route.  (Signaling issue). This is a hard mode problem FYI, If you don't mind magic 8 car consists just suddenly facing the other direction, or trains passing on a single line track (oncoming and overtake)
6.) Signaling
- There is no dedicated way to place a signal. Best way is to make a dead end 'Y' and delete the dead end, which leaves the signals behind.
- There are no settings for signal at all. All signals are Two way. Period

CAFE 0 ~The Drowned Mermaid~ is an average Visual Novel that tells us the story of Marin, a girl who died a miserable death, going seven days back into the past with the help of a mysterious waiter from a weird cafe. She tries to uncover the reasons behind her death, since she has no memories of who is she or what happened.
The player must complete four endings in order to be able to get the true ending, that explains what really happened with Marin. The Novel mechanic is kind of strange. I don't want to spoil your playthrough, so I will not give anymore detail. The graphics are really above average, the BGM is repetitive and the plot in general is a bit poor.
Even though the game is really short and a bit repetitive (I took like 3 hours to get all endings and achievements), it's true ending can be a little unexpected and make us think twice before trust into someone else. As we see in the game, people can be selfish and blinded by their own desires, being true monsters sometimes.

This Visual Novel is based on the discovery of a story to learn it and understand You have to start it a few times from the beginning. Gameplay time is something about 2 hours. The drawings seem to be okay just as soundtrack. Unfortunately, Japanese Voice pack is in the form of paid DLC. As for me, this is a game for fans of the genre, or for those who are looking for some kind of existential thought. I don't think that this Visual Novel should be so expensive ... so I recommend to buy it with a good discount.

Ushio Marin wakes up in front of a café, in the middle of nowhere, without any of her memories. This café, however, is not your regular run-of-the-mill café: it lets you re-experience the last 7 days of your life.
As one comes to understand pretty quickly, our MC is a young woman who just died, and whose last 7 days will be our case of study. How did she die? Why did she die so young?
Right from the get go, this visual novel does a good job of setting up the mystery scene and making ourselves ask the right questions.
...Maybe it did too well of a job compared to the rest of the VN, though. The prologue set my expectations a bit high, so the development, which can arguably be described as a pretty cheap dating sim, disappointed me greatly.
The true ending is decent enough. Without saying too much,
It does suffer from the short length of the VN though (less than 3 hours), which greatly cuts and rushes character development and cheapens the true ending a bit by making its execution a little bit cliché.
Overall, a good setting that could have offered much more if the execution was more fleshed out. The art could be better, but it does its job well enough to be experienceable in my opinion. 6/10, would half-heartedly recommend on sale or in a cheap bundle.

There's some great and quirky story-telling, too, about what all the rectangles are doing together. As a platformer, most levels are pretty straightforward, but a few of them provide distinct challenges. Other platformers would have all these abilities present in a single character, but by having each character represent exactly one ability (e.g. swimming or double-jump), you have to think in slightly more creative ways to get around problems, particularly as not all the abilities are always available to you. It's definitely a fun and silly way to spend a few hours. :)

A bit late to write a review for this game but I think it's time. A longer one than I usually write too. TL;DR will be at the bottom.
CAMPAIGN:
Personally I wasn't a fan of the singleplayer, most of the missions bore the crap out of me, the dialogue is bland, the characters are boring and don't really offer much in terms of learning to bond and loving them, AND THE CHARACTER YOU PLAY AS IS LITERALLY REFFERED TO AS "PLAYER." That doesn't seem like a big deal, but when you're playing a nameless character throughout the entire story, it creates a bland experience. And it's quite a mind♥♥♥♥ of a story to wrap your head around at first. The plot thickens by a large margin as you progress, it's psychological journey. I've heard lots of people praise this story for having a lot of depth and tiny details, maybe a bit too much depth for my liking. If you criticize the story, people will liklely tell you "Well that's because you don't understand it." I understand the story, it's just uneccessarily confusing and when I finally realized what it all meant my first thought was "...wow. That was pretty undewhelming for all that mind ♥♥♥♥ery." That's just my opinion on the singleplayer, some people like that kind of depth and story telling, and that's fine. Then again most people I know don't play the singleplayer regardless.
MULTIPLAYER:
It was fun while it lasted. DLC maps were DOA, Treyarch's balls were being squeezed by the greedy money whoring publishers which resulted in TONS of RNG loot via supply drops being added to the game (despite them saying the loot would be cosmetic only, and then going back on their word and adding stat-changing weapons into the mix despite the community clearly not wanting that.) The first RNG weapons that were added weren't necessarily OP, but it was annoying being killed by all kinds of weapons that you knew you either had to:
A: grind an EXTREMELY long amount of time to gain crypto currency for the black market to have a less than 10% chance for a weapon (to make matters worse, Treyarch even nerfed the rate you could earn cryptokeys.)
B: buy COD points in bulk with actual money.
Or C, what I did: Admit the fact that your luck is♥♥♥♥♥♥and don't even bother trying to get any weapon anymore.
Now, the devs added some redeeming qualities to the black market system to ease the grievances we had, such as Contracts and daily challenges to earn some cryptokeys throughout the day/week, and even some "bribes" that guaranteed you a ranged and melee weapon in a supply drop. But by the time this happened, the playerbase on PC was already dying, dropping from an average of 30,000 players to less than 9,000. I myself was tired of the insane amount of weapons and goofy taunts (specifically the "dab") being added to the game and dropped multiplayer for a good while. That, and the obsession PC players have of ONLY PLAYING TEAM CAMPMATCH.
SERIOUSLY, THIS HAPPENS IN EVERY COD GAME. YOU GUYS REALIZE THERE'S OTHER GAME MODES TO CHOOSE FROM, RIGHT? MODES THAT ARE BETTER, LIKE DOMINATION OR KILL CONFIRMED?
In all seriousness, you can still have some fun in multiplayer. Just be prepared because the only game mode you're gonna find is TDM, and you can only play the same game mode for so long before getting bored (TDM being incredibily boring already.)
ZOMBIES:
At this point, Zombies is the only real reason to buy this game. Incredible story, maps, weapons, good fun with friends, mod support, and the upcoming Zombies Chronicles DLC with remastered classic maps. If I ever open up BO3 nowadays, it's to play some god damn Der Eisendrache <3
I almost forgot, there's a bonus mode to this game called "Nightmares" once you complete the singleplayer, which I will also review.
NIGHTMARES:
♥♥♥♥ing garbage. Don't even bother.
TL;DR:
Singleplayer: I hated it, maybe you'll like it
Multiplayer: It's alright, it used to be a lot better, TDM only
Zombies: 10/10
Nightmares: No

It's not true to the original games.  It is, however, an extremely fun and well produced game in its own right.  This game surprised me when I sat down to play it with a friend on the XBOX 360, and it was some of the most fun I've ever had playing a game.  I'm not in the camp that thinks ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jumpscares are the pinnacle of horror, and RE6 diverts from the earlier entries in that regard.  Tension in the game varies by campaign, but it's almost always situational tension rather than a petty attempt at startling.   You won't be anxious because a pop-out shouted BOO!, you'll be anxious because there's zombies pouring in from 6 different windows and you're low on ammo.  Combat feels really gratifying, with a focus on brutal combos that have you destroying your enemies with melee after you weaken them with your guns.  There's also tight controls (for a controller, a bit akward on keyboard) for rolling and dodging attacks, and even countering melee attacks if you have nearly frame-perfect timing.  The combat depth in this game is insane, and can be extremely rewarding for those who take the time to master it.  Some of the most fun I've ever had playing a game with a friend, heartily recommend playing co-op.

Tl;dr: Weird but evocative.
An interesting game that plays pretty much like a cross between a board game and a poker machine. The basic idea is that you try and elevate your family through ancient society to accept challenges related to technological discovery, prestige and heroism by gathering tokens and using them to advance yourself while educating your children - heavy stuff for what looks like on the surface to be a casual puzzle game.
Some people have an issue with the random number generator suddenly throwing your family back amongst the peasants through misfortune, but I feel it encapsulates the idea of struggle - and once you get a feel for the best strategy you can reduce the likelihood of that happening. In one instance, the parents played favourites too often so the next generation was plagued by a sibling rivalrly when my useless brother kept stealing my tokens.
If you get to the top rung it opens up another game-within-a-game depending on the era, at one point I was a general (and was really bad at it), on another playthrough I got to play senator with all the powerplays and shenanigans that involves.
All the individual game elements are pretty basic but they form a quite evocative experience, much of this down to the excellent writing of the challenge scenarios. I should note that this is apparently the first of a series of games, so this particular episode stops kind of abruptly after a few eras with a "to be continued" placard. Even so, you might start off thinking it's a bit lame but then hours later...

I kind of have mixed feelings about this game. I would give it 5/10. Good, playable, but with serious drawbacks.
Upsides:
It does give you a strangely epic feeling - you do feel like a part of history itself, looking at stories of families not at the level of each individual, but ultimately, for the entire family bloodline, as a whole. I would say that this epicness is the most unusual part about this game, which no other games I've ever played offers.
The graphics and music is also not bad for a game of its size.
Downsides:
The biggest problem is the disconnect between player's choices and their consequences, and the lack of any coherent logic as to how and why to make decisions. For example, when your family is facing a crisis of the age, you are given 4 questions, each with 4 choices - and after you choose all 4 answers, you kind of get a "score" on how you did. But there is absolutely no prompts as to why one answer may or may not be correct - and the worst answer kills your character outright, and the previous 2-3 hours of your gameplay is wasted. What the hell?! This happens in other places too...
To make this even worse, there's no SAVE functionality in this game - just Pause/Continue. I understand that history cannot be rewinded, and that decisions are decisions. It makes sense, but this is a game, for people to play. It is not meant to punish the player harshly. If the character you control dies, you lose your previous 2-3 hours of progress; If all you characters of the current generation dies, you are dead. Your game progress is completely erased. What the hell?!
Overall, I like this game for what it's good for, but I hate it for what it's bad for. I'm not playing it again.

Now go forth and do what you do.
***UPDATE 1/5/2016***
The game has gone through a considerable amount of updates since my last time playing and last review, and it has improved. However, this improvement is still not enough to render the game playable.
In my initial review, I discussed framerate and blamed my computer for it. Playing now, the framerate is considerably better even though the game has had a significant amount of content added. This tells me that it was not, in fact, my computer being lazy, but the poor optimization of the game.
Sound has been added, the camera is slightly less wonky, and it's actually possible to navigate menus now. But this is still FAR from a playable game. If you decide to buy this game, consider it a long term investment. This product should be considered no more than a tech demo in it's current state.

TLDR: Game is very good.  Think early stages FTL with a different setting and XCOM-esque combat.  It's getting a lot of bad reviews and that feels unfair, especially since they're already addressing the things that everyone is downvoting for.
Pros:
-Soldier classes and leveling: Would be nice to choose the stats to level, but it's plenty rewarding as is.
-Concept and setting:  It's basically post-apocalyptic FTL, what's not to love
-Replayability:  It's hard to unlock new dozers.  I mean like scouring the correct regions AND getting a little RNG love hard.  Similar to a few of the ships in FTL, where you have to get the right event in a specific race's region.  That said, I totally want to try the other dozers and this gives you subgoals aside from just beating the game.  There are also dozens of different weapons and boosts you can find in your travels, making each game a bit different.
-Combat: Combat is fun and gratifying.  A lot of reviewers seem to hate it, but if it was too easy to outsmart, then it would be dumb.  You'll likely have to sacrifice some soldiers to get levels on others, or to simply beat a battle.  Don't buy this game if the thought of playing god and having to sacrifice soldiers for the sake of your masterplan is an absolute deal-breaker for you.
Cons:
-Troop placement at the start of combat:  Honestly, this one isn't that bad.  Reviews keep saying you insta-lose snipers etc because they spawn nearest to the enemy.  While this does happen, you always get the first move.  So really, at worst you're losing a turn relocating your troops.  This is something they are updating anyway.
-Dozer upgrades:  Resource management in BEDLAM is pretty good.  Not overly complex, but managing fuel and food requires some forethought.  That said, there are dozer upgrades to reduce your food and fuel consumption that are pretty much completely necessary to survive.  You just end up leveling those to max before you can even consider your other options.
Last Thoughts:  If you really like FTL, even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ RNG and the sometimes unfair boss fight, and $20 isn't going to make or break you, then pick this up.  It just released, it is good, and the cons listed here are already being worked on.

This game is a solid tactical roguelike with interesting combat that's great for quick and fun play sessions.
The art and presentation is superb. I expected not to like the art, but it grew on me right away. It's closer to Borderlands than Fallout in tone, and that's not a bad thing.
The game is fast-pased enough that taking early loses is not overly punishing. And you will take loses, in your first fight. The combat is well balanced, but does not work like XCom or Fire Emblem, and if you try to play it like those games, you will certainly lose. It's closer to Chess, you will lose units, often in a single hit, but that does not mean you fail the battle. You don't have a ton of units to spare, but a single veteran unit can often carry an entire fight on her own, so once you start leveling up, the game gets more forgiving. Though losing a veteran is incredibly tragic, which, honestly, is why we play games like this right?
Overall the combat feels more like a puzzle than other tactical games. Because units will die so quickly, figuring out what units counter each other is very important to succeeding, and a large part of the fun.
The overmap portion is not incredibly deep, but still more fleshed out that something like FTL, and is beautifully rendered. Resources are rare enough that it's worth taking risks to gather more, but I didn't feel like I was running on empty the whole time. You start out with a good deal of breathing room, but bad choices and lost battles will quickly erode your supply.
If you like the look and setting of the game, enjoy interesting and new tactical challenges, and don't mind learning by losing a few battles or a few games, Bedlam is worth picking up.
If you were looking for XCom with a Fallout skin, this is not that game.

It's not even close to being as bad as many other players say it is. It's not THAT hard and they're already working hard on the balance. It has some pretty cool ideas and is a lot of fun.

But once you get a hang of the combat system, its a lot more manageable and you get to see what this game is about, each battle is a mini puzzle, essentially how to get through each fight without losing a crew member and using the least amount of resources.

What a great way to learn some really cool songs. I'm not an expert guitarist, but I was able to learn several of these songs in full, because of this. The side games modes are a great way to learn beginner, intermediate, and advanced techniques used in every song, which is what some people (such as myself) need to get through some of these more difficult songs (and learning your own songs outside of this game).

Now, I can't speak for Rocksmith from a beginners perspective, because I had already been playing guitar for roughly 10 years before I bought it.  However, from an intermediate guitarists perspective, I think it's a great learning/practice tool.
The "Guitarcade", while pretty gimmicky, is a pretty good way to focus on specific skills/techniques.  Although I found that unless you're tuned in JUST right the game has a way of missing certain notes you hit, or catching them too late to trigger that note you so desperately need to hit to get your new high score.
Session Mode is a great tool for practicing improvisation, and I find myself there quite often brushing up on my scales and improv skills (Of which I have very little, admittedly, so I'm quite fond of its inclusion).
For the meat of the game, you have "Learn A Song", which, for the most part, acts like interactive tabs that automatically play the song along while you're playing.  It's an amazing way to work on learning new songs, or brushing up on old ones.  Although I find that sometimes it chooses to play things in less than efficient ways, it's a minor gripe, give than as long as you play the same note, even if it's on a different string, the game will recognize it.  Being able to slow the song down and use the Riff Repeater's options to cater your practice experience to yourself is a boon for learning that tough solo or technical rhythm part.
All in all, the game does have some bugs and some quirks, but for what it is, it's a great tool for beginner and intermediate guitarists.

Thomas Was Alone is a very good game. The storyline is quite good, the characters are very well developed, and the gameplay is really well done.
The storyline of Thomas Was Alone is about
. The storyline is not just encompassing the situation, but also the characters. Along with the storyline, the character design comes along. The character design is quite good, each character is a rectangle or a square, each of varying sizes, this is how the
is repersented. The game itself is not too long, but doesn't feel too short either.
The character development is really good in this game, as each individual character have thought processes, and each character has their own little insecurities, hopes, dreams, and interests. This is contrasted beautifully with the minimalist character desgin in the game. The game includes female characters as well are male characters, and they are both written equally in depth. Each character has a name, which should not be odd for games, but the addition of names really does help to build the character's personality, making them less of just shapes and more of actual characters. Despite what the title says, there is no real protagonist (at least not from what I could see), each character was as important as the last, and probably appeared just as often as each other. As in this game each character has a special ability, it becomes impossible to create favourites, as they all are very useful and have their own traits.
This game is a puzzle/platformer game. You need to solve the puzzle of getting all of the characters to their little glowing boxes (which reinforces the idea that all the characters are equally worthy), this is often done by using the special ability of each of the characters to your advantage, this makes the game less of a puzzle game, and more of a teamwork game. Despite the changing between characters being slightly tedious, the overall gameplay is quite smooth. There are no levels that I got stuck on that made me dread continuing the game, quite the contrary, I felt compelled to continue to play more and more, to the point I had to limit my sessions. Along with the gameplay, the achievements in the game are quite nice, they provide more replayability, and revisiting of levels, and are not too hard to achieve, but not stupidly easy.
Thomas Was Alone is quite a good game, it's not too long. The game has brilliant character development, and the gameplay can be tedious, but is quite natural. I would recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a nice game to get them thinking, but also to calm down and enjoy a really good story.

There is a lot to like about this game. It's relaxing, and it's interesting. It's kind of like taking part of the transit management from Cities Skylines and making it a separate game--which is great, because for me that it one of the most fun parts of that game.
Unfortunately, however, this game really feels incomplete. It emphasizes multiplayer so much that it really feels like single player runs out prematurely. All of the maps also feel too small; even the largest maps have lots of empty area around the edges. Thus you don't get that really epic game that you want. Games tend to be short and easy; relaxing but not altogether satisfying. The maps also cover such large areas of land while including so few cities. Many important cities are overlooked. So it's not as great for learning geography as I would like.
You can try expanding the game through mapmaking, but the map editor is hidden and extremely buggy. It crashes so often, no wonder there are relatively few user-made maps available for download on the Internet. Downloaded maps also seem to crash fairly often.
The AI is terrible, of course (who would expect anything else from a Sid Meier game?). The interface is also rather poor, and it's not possible for example to get an easy view of all of the trains departing or shipping to a particular city, or carrying a particular commodity. Going back through old routes to made sure they are still relevant is difficult.
This game is worth a little waste of time if you get it really cheap, but in general I don't recommend it.
Also, in case you're wondering like I was, it is not a suitable game for very young children. Not that it's inappropriate at all, but I mean that it's too complicated for the youngest kids, no matter how much they like trains. I'd guess that a smart 8 year old could pick up the game, maybe.

Duelyst however, with its liberal redraws and a boardgame layer added to the matches, winning or losing can often depend entirely where you put and moved your units. It creates an environment where simply having a netdeck doesn't help enough, you must master the positioning of your units in various matchups, and missplays will spiral into entirely different board states, where somebody may end up literally cornered.
This is a game you might want to look at if you want Hearthstone with a new dimension added in, thus a higher skill ceiling.
It is also a game with much more generous progression, although that's not exactly a high bar.

I have never played anything like this before. It plays like a casual, strategic peg solitare board game, but it produces engaging, thought provoking stories. In the game, you guide a family's journey through thousands of years of history. You set their aims and decide how they handle their fate.
To give you an example, I played as the Archian family named after the family's discovery of the Arch building technique. The first child of the family remained an only child despite the parents' many attempts to become pregnant a second time. The child became known as Raziya the lovable, for she was much loved. Raziya married Amen and started trading in pottery. Her first born, Kawab, grew up to have  a very pessimistic view of life. As he was gathering courage to propose to the love of his life, she went on a boat trip where she married his best friend. Kawab felt his pessimism confirmed and became a fatalist: All that happens is meant to happen and cannot be changed. Kawab's friend knew of Kawab's love and felt immensely grateful towards Kawab for giving up his own happiness. He became Kawab's most loyal friend and ally. Kawab married a woman whom he did not love, but who was deeply in love with him. He later became a local hero as he stopped a massacre on his village. Kawab begat two children: Etan and Osahar. Kawab was a genious irrigator and ran a very successful farm. He gave both his children the opportunity to study, but Osahar also followed his father into the fields and thus learnt from his genious. Kawab tragically ended his days, when his was killed by the city guards on a false accusation of stealing. His wife struggled as a sole provider. Etan became head of the family, for Osahar loved his brother and would never speak out of turn against him.
Etan entered the family into the trading business and they rose in society. His father's irrigation geninous, however, was not carried on. Etan married the love of his life, but she did not love him. She only married him because he was rich. Thus Etan in a way ironically suffered his fathers's fate reversed.
All this from only 3 hours of gameplay and the game has barely started. I warmly recommend this game.
