I am recommending Bedlam for one reason, really, and that is that it's a fun, challenging game that will serve you hot death from the RNG gods more often than not. It's a game that will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, and for a lot of people, after a few rage quits they'll be done with it.
However, should you stick around, you'll find that it's not actually a tactics/strategy game. I mean, it is in a sense, but the combat is almost a puzzle game. While random unit placement can put you in awful situations, with planning and proper management of your resources, you can overcome huge odds. In fact, I'd say Bedlam's strong suit is in how it makes you feel like it's impossible, but as you play and learn the mechanics, you start to really improve. Bedlam will drag you through it's brutal world with style, visceral brutality and a ton of character.
Skyshine is currently looking at ways to make the game a bit more accessible, so if you're on the fence because of other reviews, give the game a 'Follow' and see how things pan out. And while the 'FTL meets Mad Max' thing is not wholly far off, it's also not very accurate. Bedlam obviously owes a bit to both entities, but truly it's its own beast. I'm having a lot of fun with it, but I also enjoy the trial and error aspect of learing the ins and outs, and I absolutely adore the setting. If I had to give it a score, it would be a solid 7, if not an 8. It's a good game for those who are willing to try something new but at the same time familiar. While it's no FTL, it's a strong showing for Skyshine and I will gladly support any future endeavors by the team, especially if one was a full blown RPG set in the Bedlam universe (hint/hint).

Good game - just don't expect X-Com style combat since while it looks similar the experience is pretty different. Since units have specific ranges they can shoot at (they get more options of shooting ranges as they level) it has something of a puzzle aspect to it. Has quite a lot of FTL style random events (about 350 I believe currently) and it's important to visit the (!) points of interest to build yourself up rather than making a beeline for Aztec City. There is no real pressure to go directly there anyways aside from the difficulty rising as the days pass.
Art style and graphics have a nice look to them, and I like that veteran units get a different look to their armor. The sound and music compliment the game nicely too.
Overall a good game, that I feel is being a bit misunderstood. I can certainly see that the game could have unfair moments which would be frustrating, but I also feel that as you learn how to play it more it feels pretty rewarding to get farther than before. Judging by the dev posts currently on the forums too there are changes planned to make the easy mode (which is recommended for learning the game although unlocks aren't available there) more welcoming to new players, as currently it isn't really much different from normal outside a slower escalation of the difficulty level.

Thomas Was Alone is a very good game. The storyline is quite good, the characters are very well developed, and the gameplay is really well done.
The storyline of Thomas Was Alone is about
. The storyline is not just encompassing the situation, but also the characters. Along with the storyline, the character design comes along. The character design is quite good, each character is a rectangle or a square, each of varying sizes, this is how the
is repersented. The game itself is not too long, but doesn't feel too short either.
The character development is really good in this game, as each individual character have thought processes, and each character has their own little insecurities, hopes, dreams, and interests. This is contrasted beautifully with the minimalist character desgin in the game. The game includes female characters as well are male characters, and they are both written equally in depth. Each character has a name, which should not be odd for games, but the addition of names really does help to build the character's personality, making them less of just shapes and more of actual characters. Despite what the title says, there is no real protagonist (at least not from what I could see), each character was as important as the last, and probably appeared just as often as each other. As in this game each character has a special ability, it becomes impossible to create favourites, as they all are very useful and have their own traits.
This game is a puzzle/platformer game. You need to solve the puzzle of getting all of the characters to their little glowing boxes (which reinforces the idea that all the characters are equally worthy), this is often done by using the special ability of each of the characters to your advantage, this makes the game less of a puzzle game, and more of a teamwork game. Despite the changing between characters being slightly tedious, the overall gameplay is quite smooth. There are no levels that I got stuck on that made me dread continuing the game, quite the contrary, I felt compelled to continue to play more and more, to the point I had to limit my sessions. Along with the gameplay, the achievements in the game are quite nice, they provide more replayability, and revisiting of levels, and are not too hard to achieve, but not stupidly easy.
Thomas Was Alone is quite a good game, it's not too long. The game has brilliant character development, and the gameplay can be tedious, but is quite natural. I would recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a nice game to get them thinking, but also to calm down and enjoy a really good story.

An extreme disappointment and I don't understand how it can be so "Overwhelmingly Positive" in reviews.
I put off the game for many years after watching what the gameplay is many times. Eventually, I caved in and decided to be more open. Turns out that I should have stuck with my initial expectations.
There are two main aspects to the game - the general story/narration, and the actual gameplay itself. For the story, at least of what exists, it is somewhat interesting and I definitely enjoy the narrator. Some of the things that are said are very nice and interesting, and kept me a little devoted to keep going.
However, the story sort of falls apart and becomes incomprehensible around the latter half of the game. Note that the game is not that long and took me less than 4 hours to 100% it (i.e., finding those little collectibles as well). And by the end of the game, I did not really feel much connection or accomplishment with what was going on.
For the second aspect of the game, it is extremely weak. The actual platforming puzzles overall turn out to be not much fun at all. While there are a few different capabilities of the rectangles you control, and a few puzzles here and there are nicely made, the majority of them follow a lot of the same, monotonous work.
I would say 4 out of every 5 of the puzzles are not actually "puzzles" and just require meticulous, nail-biting perfection of stacking the correct rectangles in the right order, and jumping over obstacles or edges at the right time. It was killing me to keep playing by the time I finished Chapter 5, which was easily the worst with the focus on the upside down gravity and requiring very annoying angular jumps.
Again, I am really surprised at the high ratings for the game. Maybe the people just give the artsy narration of AI some perfect review - but the game overall is not anything I'd recommend. It really wears down on you and loses any actual enjoyment, which is really bad for a relatively short game.

CAFE 0 ~The Drowned Mermaid~, while a story of tragedy and more grim than usual otome games that focus on romance and whatnot, is one of the rare games that really left a lasting impression on me because of its unusually pessimistic approach in the psychological makeup of its characters. I actually played the voiceless version ages ago, and recently got the deluxe voiced version as a part of an amazingly cheap bundle (which is still ongoing on
if you guys are interested, 3.99 for ALL 7 games by this developer!!!).
First lets discuss the game mechanics without giving away any spoilers. You are Marin Yumino (default name, can be changed but I keep it because people pronounce her name if I do), who has been given the chance to redo the last 7 days of her life to get closure on her death.
There is the added challenge of the heroine not remembering anything about her life, and there are 3 main characters you can interact with while trying to figure out the details of the life you had led until now.
The 2 men are potential "romantic interests", and each of them have 2 possible endings-one where you pick all the goodie-to-shoes choices and use this limited time to fall in love, and the other where you pick all the interrogating/suspicious choices and try to figure out if they had anything to do with your death. Like this you play 4 times (sounds tedious, but each route is pretty short so it doesn't take even half an hour to finish one), every end will give you a plot item, and then you play the game for the 5th time you take those items to the 3rd character, your female friend, and manage to figure everything out and get the "true end".
To be honest I can't review the story itself without giving too much away since the storyline is mysterious and interesting but short. I felt like the main concept of this game is how people can become twisted when they let their desires control them. There was a few things about the characters' motivations that confused me, but in general everything started to make sense once I started playing the true route and although the end was not 'happy', my character got to do what I wanted to and that's what is important to me.
So should you play it? Depends on what you are looking for. If you are looking for a visual novel with a short but intriguing story that involves psychological analysis of the dark side of human nature, then HELL YEAH get it on sale right now! But if you either don't like visual novels in general or want a happy and fluffy romance, this is not the game for you.
The one thing I want to say to the developer- THE LAST MINUTE OF THE TRUE END WAS EPIC  10/10 CAN'T WAIT FOR MORE CAFE 0!
P.S. I want to punch Sui /^/^

This game is... weird. It's a mystery visual novel with some horror touches. I can't really write more about it without spoilers, so...
Ok, so I leant towards Not Recommend because overall this game is depressing as ♥♥♥♥. Aside of the helpless heroine every single character is an abusive a$$hole, who coerce, injure and eventually try to kill her. There's also teacher-student sexual abuse and blackmail. Lovely. Even the god-character, Sui, is an a$$hole, though at least he's a bit less damaging than the rest of the cast.
You can follow various decision routes: on the 'Good' one you end up as a very trusting person full of love towards others, on the 'Evil' one you end up as a distrustful and cold person, suspecting the people around you used and killed you. Then you can unlock the 'True' route, and guess what? Your suspicious version was right all along...
Overall I'm not sure of what to take away from this game. I mean, I guess it's possible that the creators just wanted to tell a story without further meaning, but I miss some kind of message or conclusion from it. The message would be what? Your best friend hates you and is plotting to kill you, the guy you grew up with as siblings is secretly lusting over you and pulls you into a relationship with wide age and power difference, only so when he gets bored of you he can pass you over to the popularity-chasing a$$hole who blackmailed him...? As I said, quite depressing.
Technical quality-wise the graphics are okay..ish, seen much better to be honest, and some of the CG screens have weird anatomy.
The sound design is okay, the voiceover is a nice addition, it sounds professional.
The UI could be a bit better designed - that sizeable block of menu options permanently placed on the screen is kinda pointless and unnecessary. Those options could have gone in the top menu with the others.
The text sometimes has weird phrasings, it feels like the writers are not fluid in English.
Honestly the most enjoyable part of the game is the Extra, after all the endings are unlocked. Sui does some fourth wall breaking. But even then there are some dialogue options to ask about the more confusing aspects of the plot (albeit we don't get answers) -  I guess the developers felt it too that there were some gaps in the plot.

Let's think about this for a moment here.
The story involves The Cold War cover up where the actual battles took place all over space. Space tank space race.
The gameplay is an incredibly well thought out combination of a squad based fps shooter with command and conquer-esque rts elements which has only been done just a few times, none of which has come close to Battlezone in execution.
Because let's face it, there is no reason to attempt it again. It was done perfectly the first time and all future attempts will fall short of greatness.
The base building is satisfying as you go from a small recycler to a full-on citadel of gun turrets and mines as you balance a need to finish off the mission as well as keeping your scrap intake moderated so you do not inadvertantly starve yourself of resources. That's where the first-person squad based gameplay comes in. There are a wide variety of different tanks to choose from with a varying degree of playstyles between them, starting from a nimble and weak Scout/Fighter to a slow, powerful Walker/Golem. Bread and butter Tanks to niche fillers such as Rocket Tanks and Bombers to tackle specific situations that may arise as you fight over a planet. No one tank feels completely useless and all feel as if they can be useful in a one-on-one fight if used/maneuvered correctly. If you choose that the fps gameplay isn't exactly your sort of thing, there exists more traditional RTS elements through satellites that give an overhead view of a map where you can micromanage your tanks effectively rather than blow things up yourself.
It is legitimately my favorite game, and now it has an HD remake and runs perfectly on a modern PC.
This game and all it offers deserves a playthrough, because it never got a fair shake when it initially came out. Think about it for a moment, Atari released boatloads of reboots of their old franchises and most of them were terrible because it did not do anything remotely interesting. Along comes another old arcade reboot which served as the antithesis of everything Atari was churning out. It not only features the badass story that hooks you on its sheer craziness, the gameplay has also aged incredibly well.
Infinite recommends, you should play this and experience one of the most unique games to come out of the 90s. As jaded as I've become over video games along comes this one title I fawned over as a child which shows me that yeah, video games are still pretty great, and Battlezone is just as unique and entertaining as the day it came out.
Battlezone revealed to me that I love video games, and it deserves to be your favorite game, too.

Really wanted to like this game as a nostalgic lover of Battlezone 2, and if they make a Battlezone 2 redux I will buy it in a heartbeat, but I REALLY don't see the appeal to this one.
I'm about the second Mars mission in and the game is way too micro-managy to understand what I should and shouldn't be doing. The game gave me a Recycler, an Armory, and ONE Geiser to make use of, so I placed a recycler down, then it told me to go check something out and then when I got there the comms told me "Ok, cool, lock it down".
HOW!?
Was I supposed to build an army before going there?
Was I supposed to setup a defense so that in the minute I was gone 5 russkies didn't blow up my recycler?!
This is my problem with this game over Battlezone 2 negating the fact it lacks a further in-depth base-building mechanic; it doesn't help you whatsoever and often failing can result in waiting ~5 minutes for a specific wave of enemies to arrive just to trigger something over and over again.
I feel like i'm missing specific important controls that are vital to me controlling things, like a command view, but the game doesn't even have a full list of keybinds!
The redux devs completely left out all of the important controls (though i'm not sure if even the original had it).
Not to mention this game feels repetitive.
Every mission so far has been:
-Escort
-Defend from enemy waves, escort.
-Setup base, defenses, defend base, escort.
Personally I just hate escort missions in games overall, especially when the vehicle you are escorting seems to be made of paper mache.
The story seems decent from the first two hours i've played but it really does feel like basic 1960's sci-fi stuff, which is awesome for some people, and dreadfully boring for others.
It's really slow and lacks life.
Battlezone II jumped into the more "character-based" story-telling at just the right time, when it was starting to become a popular thing to do, and is better for it with memorable characters like Braddock, John, Sharbayev, and Cooke.
There's a set-up, an investigation, defense, build-up, and full on attacks with a farily detailed environment.
I realise BZR's setting is based on the fact that it's the 1960's and they've JUST basically landed, so there's not going to be much in the way of detail, but christ the landscapes are boring to look at.
I don't know, I came in expecting an enhanced BZ1 that is also leagues ahead of BZII, but honestly it isn't.
It's certainly enhanced in ways, but the game is too blurry for me to notice unless I downscale 4k to 1080p which completely destroys my performance somehow on my R9 380.
If I had another hour to play before my refund, I would have tried the Russian campaign to see if that makes up for it, but honestly I just want to go play something else.
If Red Oddyssey expansion comes out (they are "discussing it") I may choose to rebuy it and judge the game on that, because that's appearantly the best BZ out there.
But not if I have to shell out extra cash for it, it should have came with the game or had compatibility for it in the first place.

What an amazing game.  I played the original version for 300+ hours.
If you've played this before, then you already know how incredible it is and have bought it.
If you haven't, this version of Battlezone is a hybrid FPS/RTS sci-fi tank/battle Cold War simulator... in space. It's every bit as awesome as it sounds. Basically, imagine a really excellent, top-notch RTS with a fantastic interface in which you get to play as one of your own units while directing the battle. It sounds complex, but the UI is so excellent that neither part of the game, the tank simulator or the RTS, loses anything in the translation; it's two first-rate games in one. You play as a pilot who can switch ships and even snipe enemy pilots and take over their vehicles.
I still remember the amazing adventures I had playing this game. The heart-pounding race to escape  a planet about to explode in seconds, being chased by alien superweapons all the way. Escorting my Soviet scientists across a bridge above the fiery lava of Jupiter's moon Io, getting blown out of my tank as it's destroyed by superior American forces, sniping the pilot of an American rocket tank who attacked me, stealing his vehicle and using it to fire upon my unsuspcecting foes, saving my forces. Sneaking into a heavily defended Soviet base on Europa to see where they've hdiden the stolen plans. Being ambushed by Soviet forces on the plains of Venus. They simply don't get any better than this.
The emergent gameplay situations, the enormous tactical flexibility afforded by the strategic layer of the game, the first-rate physics and satisfying gunplay, the huge variety of weapons and vehicles- even nearly 20 years later, this game remains unmatched I truly wish more people would try to rip it off! To try to compare it to some more modern titles if you haven't played this, imagine melding the seamless tactical interface and large-scale battle control of Sins of a Solar Empire with the visceral action and FPS excitement of Call of Duty, plus the open-ended battlefield and branching combat options afforded by Crysis or Far Cry. All with a cool sci-fi story in space. I am not exaggerating. It truly is that good.
And all this before I even get to the beautiful, loving restoration this game has been given!
All of the above refers to the 1998 "vanilla" edition. But in this 98 Redux edition, the game has been given a complete makeover and beautifully brought up to date with care and devotion. The developers really layered on an extra level of polish along with all-new graphics and options for modern PCs. New, Steam-based online multiplayer? Check. Brand new HD graphics and textures? Check? New mod support? Check. In my brief time to date with the new version, AI also feels like it's been improved and bugs have been fixed. It really feels like a whole new game with the excellent graphics update. This is NOT the shovelware, throw-anything-on-Steam junk that most developers throw up onto the Internet when they get an old license- this is the remastered, restored edition, presented with the care and attention that all developers should lavish on a game rerelease. It truly is worth a buy even if you've played this as many hours as I have.
Until then... I'll see you on the Martian battlefields... or the Moon.... or Venus....

Visually beautiful handcrafted adventure with hacking elements that I can't get out of my mind even long after I finished it. It may take a while to get used to the art style and it definitely has its share of problems.
During the course of the game you learn how to modify and create ingame software using a custom language called "Sprak" which not only can print text on screens but allows you to modify the game world itself. If you know what to do you can immediately reach the end of the game by accessing a computer and typing in the right commands. Though you'll have to get familiar with the language and the architecture first. The story doesn't hold your hands at all and requires you to pay attention to what npcs are saying. The world isn't too big so you can always find a way to advance the story through exploration, though. There are notes and hints hidden all over the world that give you tips on hacking as well as as a large part of the story, so the game definitely rewards exploration.
Admittedly the game feels incomplete in the end. Just when you really start to get familiar with the hacking aspect, you reach the end which seems rushed and doesn't completely account for all the ways you can reach it. I encountered a game breaking bug (so save often) that will likely never get fixed. While it feels like the developers ran out of time/money  and didn't get to finish/implement/add all the things they had originally planned, it still gripped me all the way to the end and left me wanting more and I would cautiously recommend this game to you if you were interested enough to read until here.

A game with so much potential that ultimately falls infuriatingly short of what it could have been.
First thing's first - the hacking system is excellent.
Hacking keys to brute force numerically-locked doors.
Hacking password computers to unlock doors.
Hacking coffee to be so powerful you don't need to sleep.
Hacking doors to connect to other places.
The narrative is weak, loose and confusing.
Ordinarily I could look past that, but it gets worse.
The game actually starts off more fun at the beginning.
Nearing the end, I find myself wanting to go back to before things started going downhill.
Past a certain point the narrative funnels the player into following it and doesn't give the player time to explore. If anything it punishes the player for following it by forcing them to choose between the narrative or their world-hacking exploits.
Furthermore the plot doesn't even advance at the start unless the player is in the right place at the right time and turns up at a series of parties (which isn't exactly an obvious thing to do - hackers aren't exactly known for going to parties and mingling with people).
There are a couple of glaring bugs in the quest system.
I know of at least one quest linked to the main hacking group that the narrative entirely skipped over in my game (specifically the Casino Heist).
And when I was trying to complete a quest to find out the Mayor's secret, one of the hacking group burst into the room, interrupted my conversation and started me on the next story quest.
I haven't quite reached the end, so I looked up the various endings.
None of them feel satisfying. There's no deep meaning or plot pay off.
I hardly feel anything for the characters anyway, most of them spend most of their time obsessed with drinks, drugs and parties, and the one character I did like (because he was the one who kindly taught the main character how to program) hardly features in the story.
All in all, this game is a glorious mess, which is so sad because it could have been a glorious masterpiece.

7 Grand Steps: What Ancients Begat first impressions after 2 hours.
This is a good game, however I can't recommend it.
Please hear me out.
This game is a computerised board game, the advertising boasts that it is part board game, part real time strategy and part interactive novel. I guess they are somewhat correct, but the ratio is more like  95:1:4.
The board game part of this game works like a dynasty simulation. You start off as an adult of very low social standing and have to find a partner and have a child to continue the blood line. The board  is like a big disc with 4 rings on it, and you start at the lower ring. Most of the disc is off screen but you see from the 3rd quarter to about 3 O' clock.  There are crocodiles just below the disc and after each turn it rotates around, moving all the playing pieces with it. If you get nommed by the crocs then your character dies. The board has these symbols on it and you gain tokens throughout that you spend to move your pawn to the next segment with that same symbol. There are also other pawns on the board that the computer controls.
When the new generation starts the first thing that you really need to do is find a partner and start raising a family. This is important as the disc eventually runs out of segments and only a new generation can start on the reset disc. You also want to do this early because each turn you can give the child a movement token to train them in that profession. When your 2 married pawns are on the same space then a little flame comes up which allows them to try for a baby. This seems to have a very high chance of success, at least 3/4. The other way to bring about children is “accidentally”. If you run out of tokens you can instruct your pawn to generate more. This makes them fall back towards the crocodiles but they will be “caught” by another pawn assuming that there is one between them and death. Based on the skills they have been taught as a child they will have a chance to generate new tokens based on each of the labours that they have trained. If you are caught by your spouse that is optimum as they can both generate tokens meaning you will get a higher yeild, but after work they get in the mood if you know what I mean and you have about a 25% chance of having another baby.
Children are a real problem. The most optimum solution is to have one and only one because it is in your best interests to spoil that child rotten with tokens so you will have a powerful pawn for the next generation. The game adamantly warns you about having a “favourite” as the children will get pissy with each other if there is a golden child, but really the benefit outweighs the risks with that. I understand that it is a board game and you have to use your imagination, but the families are so similar and you go through so many generations that they become so bland and are almost interchangable. I got to about generation 7 on my play through and I can guarantee that if I was to take a break and you hacked the game so that I was playing generation 3 pawns, I would not notice. This is where the interactive novel part of the game comes in though, as your children are given a few tidbits of backstory as they grow up, it says if they are playing nicely or breaking each others toys, unfortunately that's about all it says, the interactive novel is surprisingly repetitive. Later on they may annoy you as adults but the most they can do is remove a few of your tokens and they will do that at most two or three times per generation, but it is much more powerful to generate new ones with a buffed spoilt golden child then it is to have a half cocked character with a little insurance.
If this were a real board game then the families would feel like this for sure, but that's not really an excuse. Don't get me wrong, I adore board games, I prefer spending time around a board game with friends then any computer game (although there's still over 500 left to review at time of writing so I might end up eating those words) and I understand that this is a dynasty simulation and in real life you would not be like this towards your children, but you are most likely a gamer like me, and you want to win. This isn't like the sims where you can see an abused child crying, every 10 or so turns you might get a small text box that says she had a crappy day but really that is your only motivation for caring for them outside of your own imagination.
I think the object of the game is to become the ruler of the bronze age, not that it tells you that until the late game. You see, there are mini objectives that you choose to fulfil, these are a choice of a heroic deed, an invention or an upgrade in social class. When you have chosen your mission you try and pick up a certain number of beads that are on board segments, the npcs can take them too though.
A heroic deed is a gamble. You are given a text based multiple choice quiz and you will try to come out with more beads than you lose, unfortunately the text is extremely vague and it ends up being just luck if you choose the right things. I had one where I had to write a book, at the end it asks if I should give it to the mayor, a scholar, a priest who trains scholars or bury it. I gave it to the priest who told me it was crap and that was that. An invention will replace a certain segment with a more upgraded version, I.e masonry becomes arch building. As the inventor you get a load of that token. This is quite a tactical decision to make because it will obsolete everything you have taught your child of that profession, but it can give you a boost in movement and training. Its a real pain if an npc does it though as you not only lose your obsolete tokens but you don't gain an of the new type. And this is really a problem because as you raise through social status jobs less befitting of you are slowly lost from your bloodline, which actually happens quite organically which I thought was a nice touch. And finally there is a raise in social status, this allows your pawn to advance to the ring above it where you can learn new trades and have a much better quality of life.
I managed to get to the highest ring which made me a very noble person, so much so that I had responsibilities for the community. This however was incredibly confusing to me as suddenly I had 4 sliders I needed to keep in check. They had something to do with the amount of farms that the city builds and how many tokens I can skim off the top in bribes but the game didn't explain it very well and I just kept clicking okay on the default one. At the end of each turn I was getting a boat load of tokens and getting some very vague text box like the villagers are working hard, or the villagers are content. Unfortunately though, ♥♥♥♥ing bandits came and burned the entire city down!? o.O
Was this my fault. I guess I will never know. This demoted my character back onto ring 3 giving me a massively long quest to grind up again to have another go. It was at this point I closed the game and wrote this review.
Now call me thick for not knowing how to balance this game properly, and yeah you are right. I'm an inexperienced noob but I don't really feel like taking the time to master this. Maybe you would. To me the game isn't quite as arty as it thinks it is. I wouldn't go as far to say it is pretentious but I would hear you out if you told me you did. The story is just too vague and brief and could really do with fleshing out way way more in order to train the player a little more. Some of it is pretty interesting though like when you mouse over the crocodiles and they tell you what each represents.
I realise that I have complained a lot but the game does have some really good parts too. First of all. It is fun. It is time eating fun. I played it for 2 hours without realising how much time has passed which actually kind of shocked me. The style, graphics and sound effects are really quite lovely and fit

Good mechanics, but bad storytelling.  You want to buy this game because it seems like it'll pioneer choose-your-own-adventure storytelling into a strategy game, but it ultimately fails.  The CYOA is often linear and random in that you don't even get to choose among options or the options you choose among don't have sensible consequences.  Furthermore, if you try to influence those consequences through preparation, your preparation doesn't seem to help.
I played the game up through the Bronze Age's "Challenge of the Age", and had to stop because of this.  After invading all of my neighbors for 20 turns straight and improving my cities infrastructure and roads, I died because my invading forces fell apart and couldn't regroup despite how I previously got the regular army upgrade.  In other words, everything I did up to that point was completely meaningless.  Yea, I could have taken the conservative route, but I thought my mechanical preparation would have made that unnecessary.  On top of that, in the Copper Age, I took the conservative route in the "Challenge of the Age" when subduing colonies that weren't tributing resources any longer, yet that penalized me by making the invasion of my main enemy more difficult since it had more time to prepare.
This ignores other problems like how the king gave me only so much time to "conquer a city", but despite how I won so many invasions where I got sued for peace, the king still didn't recognize my conquests and even ridiculed me instead.  Other times, the king would build me monuments but still keep the clock ticking.
I mean the mechanics in the lower three social tiers are easy enough to grasp as long as you play a balanced strategy between using the ingot to get more tokens versus jumping on victory point chips to achieve heroics, discoveries, and social status.  Don't breed too many children either or else you'll end up with sibling rivals in the next generation who make your life a pain.  You can be sure of this by using the ingot back and forth between your partners in moving backwards to make more tokens while the other one gets victory point chips...
...but ultimately, the storytelling just falls flat.  Decisions don't make sense.  Sometimes, you don't even get to make a decision, and half the time, the story doesn't even seem important.  This especially happens when choosing a personality for your next generation after finishing a rite of passage.  What's the difference in the game between being virtuous versus benevolent or miserly versus petty?  The game is never clear about this.
All and all, interesting concept, but poor execution.
___________
EDIT:  I have since completed the game since my last playthrough had a dimwit sibling, so the game let me play as him (or her since I don't remember).  Luckily, I managed to get a lot of tokens by playing the ingot over and over, so my next generation lead the country to success...
...upon which I became a hermit shepherd who never got married and had to start over in the bronze age again...
...so I did, and again became a shepherd, but got married and had too many kids that constantly got in fights, but I eventually managed to reach the ruler class in the iron age anyway.
The game ended with the empire splitting up after I consolidated all the power of the (Roman) Senate, and my family forgotten in the original part while remembered widely in the new part...
...and then the game tells you there will be a part 2 and that your family's history is saved in your documents folder...
...except it wasn't.  :-\
The Iron Age ruling period is weird since you have to vote for bills alongside your political party to maintain support among constituents even if the empire suffers.  My party got so small at one point though that I had more politicians supporting me than my party size was, so I had no idea how to vote.  Thankfully, I finished the game before getting removed from power and dumped back into the noble class.
I dunno about you, but the game seems like it needs a lot of work to me.

Excellent multiplayer 2D platformer.  Unlike many in this genre, players won't bounce off of each other, or generally get in each other's way.  (Though you can hit each other, which may be used to assist in finding the secrets/exploration.)  There are no limits to lives - as long as any single player is still alive, the other players can continue.  You only need to restart the level if everyone dies at the same time.  This makes it possible for widely varying skill levels to still have fun together.  The skill progression is also nicely balanced - you aren't given new abilities until the prior abilities have been deeply explored and mastered.

Full disclosure: I backed the Kickstarter and I know the devs on Skyshine’s Bedlam (great people, in my opinion)
Skyshine's Bedlam is a passion project by three core dev's. These guys are all industry vets with a ton of game experience. What does that have to do with anything you might ask? Well, it means they care and want you to have the best game possible. Simply put, they continue to listen to the community well after the initial release.
Bedlam is tough for sure and there are many awesome ideas in it. The thing I would like to impart in this review versus the many others is you are dealing with a top notch crew making the game. Since Early Access they have been active in the community and provided feedback as well as game updates.
If it looks interesting and you have done your due diligence – I recommend checking it out. It’s a great ride and I hope to see more from the team.

Update: I have had a chance to play since the fixes and Skyshine has basically redone the game. The new version(s) do not appear to have any of the old bugs and it actually quite an enjoyable experience.
It really is nice to see a company go back and fix things that were broekn and improve a product this vastly.

One of the most underrated CoD games around.
Albeit having a controversial advanced movement system, I've found it very easy to get used to after spending a lot of time around FPS games. After playing Counter-Strike for 3000+ hours, I've found every gun battle easily predictable, however this can take some time to get used to for new players.
Pros:
- Great Multiplayer:
Always has a thriving playerbase. A lot of DLC weapons and camos you can get for free by just playing the game (or by spending money on CoD Points, which is also questionable for those Activision money ♥♥♥♥♥s). Most of the MP maps are flawless however some of the base game maps just are straight up dumb and have some graphical bugs/malfunctions (sorta segways into the cons as well I guess). Lots of replay-ability because of the high-level cap and Prestige modes (not to mention the VERY regular Double XP/Double Weapon XP/Double Cryptokey events they have almost every weekend).
- Amazing Zombies Content:
Even the base map alone (Shadows of Evil) has a very intricate design and very fun layout, which is hard to get right after having such a dreadful flagship map in the 2nd Black Ops game (Tranzit). Also, the DLC maps are f*cking incredible, each map telling stories from different iconic Zombies character to expand the storyline of the franchise. With the additions of Gobblegum machines and Weapon Kits, the Zombies on this game has been flawless. (Not to mention Zombies Chronicles/DLC 5 launching on PC next month, which is surely going to be incredible).
Cons:
- Mediocre Campaign Mode:
From what I played of the Campaign, it was okay. Interesting ideas were used because of the futuristic setting, however it's plain to see that Call of Duty's major amount of funding and attention goes elsewhere (into Multiplayer & Zombies mainly because that's what people want). As far as campaigns go, it should really be left to Infinity Ward because I don't remember a time when they undelivered in a Campaign/Story environment (even Ghosts had a great Campaign too!).
- Gun Balancing is dreadful:
The multiplayer gun balancing is so far out of whack that it's actually infuriating the majority of the time. Specialists were a great add to the Multiplayer, however Specialists weapons like the Purifier that can 1 shot you with so much ease and range, and the Ripper that can just bounce and lunge between player to player and easily hit 6-mans with little to no effort is just hilariously dumb.
Like every game, shotguns are really hard to get right, they're either a useless disadvantage or just break the game entirely, there's only a few games that do it right. However the shotguns on this game are broken beyond repair (by the likes of the Brecci and Haymaker). With the advanced movement system it makes it so easy to get kills with shotguns (especially on maps like Nuk3town).
I still feel the LMGs, SMGs and Melee mechanics still needed to have been messed around with a little bit more before release, but they are manageable.
Nevertheless, this game is amazing (aside it's gun balancing, which you do learn to deal with). I recommend it to everyone who's just tired of the basic same-old same-old FPS games (like Modern Warfare, CS:GO, Battlefield, etc.).
It's Pros heavily outweigh its Cons (even though it doesn't seem like it on paper).

What makes this card collecting game different from the others is that you play your cards on a board. This way, along the standard card collecting game mechanics, the game has a whole new dimensions: unit positioning. The board-centric gameplay makes the game a lot more strategic (and fun!) than most card games.
Duelyst has two main play modes: ladder and gauntlet. In the first one you play decks built from your own cards and try to rank as high as possible. In gauntlet you build your deck from randomly presented cards and try to get 12 wins (more wins means better in-game rewards).
This game uses pixel art, so if you like that art style you’re gonna love the images and animations used in Duelyst.
Even though the game is F2P it’s not pay to win! For new players I suggest focusing on one faction and to craft cards just for that faction.

This game shares many mechanics with Hearthstone.
This is because Hearthstone touched all the bases before anyone else could. They thought of everything a card could do first, and I mean everything. "When this card is played", "When this card is dead", "When someone else plays a card", "At the start of your turn", so on and so forth. Hearthstone invented the inevitable, and while they DO deserve credit for inventing it, saying that other games rip off the mechanics of Hearthstone is complete and utter nonsense, because as I said before, it was inevitable that SOMEONE, SOMEWHERE, will invent it.
That being said, this game takes that, and shakes it up a little. By adding a 5x7 grid that you can play cards and move your units around on, it took a little bit of weight off of having the "Better" deck, the "I Payed $100 and now I have five legendaries in my deck and you still have the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ starter deck" deck, and instead now adds more skill to the game by having you plan strategies around where your opponent is. Of course, there are still games where no matter how you dice it you will lose, it makes those far less often. Add in a free card every day and it goes a little bit beyond "Spend $100 dollars and hope for the best". Maybe that card will be your coup de gravy, but maybe it won't.
I have much more to say about this, but it would just turn into a tutorial about the game, so I'll let you play it and figure everything out. My point is, by adding this seemingly meaningless mechanic, it gives new players a better chance at completing their daily missions, and getting new card packs, to make a better deck, instead of being stuck in Hearthstone's loop of "Just buy cards and you might have a chance".

Do you like trains? Actually that's not even a prerequisite for this game because I don't care about trains one way or another and loved playing Sid Meier's Railroads!
But wait, what is this? As of the date I'm writing this review the steam reviews for Sid Meier's railroads is mixed? Why? How? Do I agree?
It's because the darn thing crashes, like a lonely teenager playing halo in 2001 at midnight with an unlimited supply of full throttle energy drinks.
And yeah, on my windows 10 machine the game crashes after an hour of play. I haven't done any research to see how to solve the crashes, I suspect it might have something to do with it auto saving every minute... but at least with the rapid auto saves you're only losing convenience with the crashes.
There's not really much to say in the story-category for this game, in the opening cinematic it's hinted at that this can be viewed as an old grandfathers hobby-train-collection, or a model for the same grandfather as a railroad tycoon.
There are several scenarios and objects you can play though, but story-wise it's left up to the players imagination.
To simplify the strategy, this is the goal: You build railroads, then buy trains to move goods from one city to another.
The game is much more complicated then that... but for a starting point that's the best way to think about it.
To elaborate on the complexity, you need to keep in mind the supply of goods, the price to keep your trains running and how much proffit they make from moving goods, you need to sometimes move goods to a refinery and then move the goods again for an even higher profit.
The game really shines when you add other players, because now you're competing with others to move the supplies in the same cities, and you need to build OVER other railroads, and you can buy other players stocks and then buy them out! But the whole game becomes much more complicated and much more fun to play.
I have little to no doubt that if Sid Meier's Railroads User Review score would be much more positive if it wouldn't crash and would just run the way it's intended to.
Regardless, you can make your own mind up if you want to get the game, I would expect that running Sid Meier's Railroads on windows 7 or earlier Operating systems might negate the problem, but even if you can tolerate the game crashing and just rebooting, this is a solid Train simulation Management game.

I am not entirely sure I know what this game is. I am also not sure if I actually enjoyed playing the game.
The overall goal of the game is that to lead a family through various generations, and by your decisions lead them upwards from common laborers to become artisans, merchants or even priests and kings. A turn based game, you either move your charges to new positions on a spinning wheel based on a variety of tokens you have on hand, or spend a turn earning new tokens. Ultimately, you character will have children, and these tokens can also be used to teach these descendants new skills, which will - once they have grown up - limit where they can move on the game- board. It is a unique game and for that alone is worth the price of admission.
I'm just not sure it's really that much fun. Game mechanics are poorly explained, and too much of the gameplay is determined randomly by the computer. This makes it exceedingly difficult to create any sort of long term strategy and - especially as the game progresses - advancing the characters upwards through the social ranks takes more and more time and becomes increasingly onerous. I suppose this bears some resemblance to real life but since I use games to escape this sort of drudgery, it doesn't entice me to keep playing. It doesn't help that there is precious little visual chrome, with little variety to keep up interest. Ultimately, "7 Grand Steps" is  an interesting but sadly flawed experiment that failed to keep me entertained.

Let me pre-face this with Skyshine's BEDLAM is a hard game. It is not easy, and it is made that way. It is punishing, brutal and difficult. It will chew you up and spit you out a thousand times over, and I like it for that. If you have read the reviews you will see a lot of complaints about the combat and that is what I would like to address for the most part in this review, becuase beyond that the game is entirely amazing.
COMBAT: Essentially BEDLAM is a game that takes a lot of inspirations from games like FTL, Banner Saga and XCOM. First and foremost, those who are comparing this combat to XCOM obviously haven't played Banner Saga, or they would see the clear translation to this game. Don't treat the combat in this like XCOM. If you do, you will die. The combat in BEDLAM needs to be treated more like a game of Chess. You need to find synergy between your units, and utilize them according to their strengths. For example, synergizing your trenchers and their knock back ability is essential for maintaining control of the map and positioning enemies where you want. Enemy just out of the range of your deadeye? Push him into range with a trencher and synergize your units. Play to your opponents weaknesses. Does your enemy have 3 deadeyes? Close the gap and play close. Get in their face and play smart so they can't make a play without getting punished. The combat is difficult and brutal, you WILL lose units, it is made this way for a reason. My only major complaint that I can't justify is the Blitz-o-meter. In my opinion the blitz function is what makes the combat over the top difficult. It basically takes the game from an 8/10 on the difficulty scale to a 9.5/10. If the enemy is going to get a blitz, I should too, or no one should get one at all. Also, unit placement. There is no unit placement prior to engagements and that is a major no-no considering how vital positioning is in this game. The positioning of your units its CRUCIAL, especially given the fact that if your unit is "in the open" and not utilizing cover, it is a 100% hit. I think if Skyshine implemented a pre-combat positioning system, this would solve A TON of peoples complaints about this games combat.
EVERYTHING ELSE: The other meaty chunk of this game is the overworld map and dozer management. All of which I find awesome. It is very FTLesque and definetly feels like I am struggling over those same risk/reward issues that FTL would slam in your face, and it is great. The music it atmospheric and sets the scene, the voice acting is gritty and fitting, the artstyle is attractive and the animations are nice and provide some gruesome deaths. The Dozer upgrades are cool and can provide some help in combat, although you will often time not have the resources necessary to use them because you are either...
1) using the in-combat heal function too much because of the unforgiving combat
2) trying to upgrade your crude effeciency, because good God crude is a ♥♥♥♥♥ and a half.
What is boils down to. Skyshine. Listen and implement a pre-positioning system for combat. I think this will drastically improve the combat as is because it is beyond frustrating to be hot dropped into a combat scenario against a group of enemies and your 3 deadeyes are right up front, meaning you have to take a very very very very valuable turn to move them back, knowing 1 of those 3 are probably going to die because of the 2 action limitation.
I recommend this game for those who are seeking a challenge and who ARE NOT looking for XCOM combat.
WARNING: THIS GAMES COMBAT IS NOT LIKE XCOM AT ALL, IF YOU ARE LOOKING FOR XCOMS COMBAT YOU WILL BE VERY VERY UPSET.

The characters and dialogue in Watch_Dogs 2 are so cringey and under developed that I find it very hard to grasp the serious topics in the game, including gang violence and mass hacking fraud, just to name a few. As a result, the story is much worse than that of Watch_Dogs. For instance, Aiden Pierce was clearly a nice guy under the cold hearted killer facade aiming to get revenge for his niece and to help his sister and nephew, but Marcus Holloway is a young man with his whole life ahead of him who choses to partake in, at times, blatently criminal activities for what seems like no other reason that "for the lols", as the youth may say. In my opinion, you shouldn't be completely changing the direction of a franchise like this. Ubisoft should have created a sequal with the improved hacking mechanics in Watch_Dogs 2 but still maintained the dark and sombre tone of the original, yet all I see if I search for Watch_Dogs 2 on the internet is colourful and vibrant images.
I find it quite annoying that the taser is so powerful. It can take out enemies from very far range with incredible accuracy and even enforcers with just one hit - the strongest enemy in the game. In Watch_Dogs, these bad boys would take a couple of grenades and multiple headshots before dying. I think Ubisoft may have some kind of hidden agenda to push non lethal weapons, because who uses those in an 18 rated video game if they aren't incredibly overpowered?
Also, the missions are frankly stale, with the goal for most of them being to get the drone inside, hack the FBI, get out and bish bash bosh you're done! The missions really need to be improved next time. The minigames and collectibles strewn around the map are a waste of time with very little reward from the cash ones and you can already buy a big variety of clothes from myriad of shops around the bay area.
Ubisoft may have removed you having to climb towers to unlock parts of the map to allow you to do whatever you want right from the start, but I don't think this is true. If you want to max out one of the skills in the skill tree, you have to explore the world (or just the specific areas it tells you to) to unlock the ability to unlock the new skill. You may have removed towers, but you have added limitations to what you can do from the start of the game. This means that when you collect research points which can be used to buy skills, you will probably have less choice than before, and are constantly bugged by the highly irritating popup that tells you that you have unspent skill points, if you are saving up for the big skills that require up to 8 research points. In the big picture, this means you will end up with a balanced skill set, which is not good considering Ubisoft wanted to support many different and unique play style. The balance of the skills most players would achieve through these limitations mean it is harder to specialise in one aspect that you might prefer. This would be easier achieved if they allowed you to fully master any skill as long as you have the research points.
But what Watch_Dogs 2 lacks in its dialogue, character development, tone and atmosphere, repetitive missions, overpowered non lethal weapons, useless collectibles and poorly thought out skills it makes up for in its stunning visuals, sort of. The graphics aren't terrible, but they aren't perfect if you intend on actually playing the game at a decent framerate. If you want SF fog on, and perhaps some of those nice Hybrid Frustum Traced Shadows, you'd be looking at a loss of around 30-40 FPS. I guess you could just turn them off though...
Furthermore, I played the game again just for research and received a message from the Uplay overlay that my GPU was below the minimum requirement. I have a GTX 980 Ti! And then, about 10 minutes into playing the game, it just crashed, without any warning. I have very capable parts in my computer and am only playing at 1080p (4k monitor coming soon). This hasn't happened for any other games, either.
Overall, Watch_Dogs 2 is a bad sequel that most people seem to like for ditching many parts of the original. I'd rather have a linear story if it means the story can be told better and with more depth. It also just got a price increase, so there's even less incentive to buy it.

Tl;dr - It's good, but you'll still need a real teacher if you want to progress beyond just "getting by".
(From a bassist's perspective)
Good stuff:
- The difficulty curve is excellent, starting off similar to Guitar Hero easy mode, but adapts during the song to your progress and gradually increases the complexity of the song in a logical fashion, eventually hiding the making the notes transparent as you master and memorise the songs.
- Riff repeater is a great tool for practising a song section, independently altering the speed and complexity until you're comfortable.
- Score attack gives a consistent goal to shoot for - rather than just learning a song, you can play the song at a constant difficulty level and try to make the fewest errors.
- Minigames help to drill a particular aspect of playing, like scales (both in ascending/descending order and jumping between notes in a scale) and harmonics.
- It's really fun!
Bad stuff:
- While it does try to teach basic theory, it doesn't push you to actually memorise any of it; it's possible to gloss over most of the theory and still get high scores. I'm 80+ hours deep and it's not once taught me the relationship between notes (like octaves, fifths etc).
- Sometimes crashes AMD Radeon driver when quitting the game.
I'd definitely recommend playing this in addition to finding a proper music teacher and theory books. It's main strengths lie with finger dexterity and keeping the playing fun, which is crucial to avoid getting burnt out learning a bunch of theory.

One of the most underrated CoD games around.
Albeit having a controversial advanced movement system, I've found it very easy to get used to after spending a lot of time around FPS games. After playing Counter-Strike for 3000+ hours, I've found every gun battle easily predictable, however this can take some time to get used to for new players.
Pros:
- Great Multiplayer:
Always has a thriving playerbase. A lot of DLC weapons and camos you can get for free by just playing the game (or by spending money on CoD Points, which is also questionable for those Activision money ♥♥♥♥♥s). Most of the MP maps are flawless however some of the base game maps just are straight up dumb and have some graphical bugs/malfunctions (sorta segways into the cons as well I guess). Lots of replay-ability because of the high-level cap and Prestige modes (not to mention the VERY regular Double XP/Double Weapon XP/Double Cryptokey events they have almost every weekend).
- Amazing Zombies Content:
Even the base map alone (Shadows of Evil) has a very intricate design and very fun layout, which is hard to get right after having such a dreadful flagship map in the 2nd Black Ops game (Tranzit). Also, the DLC maps are f*cking incredible, each map telling stories from different iconic Zombies character to expand the storyline of the franchise. With the additions of Gobblegum machines and Weapon Kits, the Zombies on this game has been flawless. (Not to mention Zombies Chronicles/DLC 5 launching on PC next month, which is surely going to be incredible).
Cons:
- Mediocre Campaign Mode:
From what I played of the Campaign, it was okay. Interesting ideas were used because of the futuristic setting, however it's plain to see that Call of Duty's major amount of funding and attention goes elsewhere (into Multiplayer & Zombies mainly because that's what people want). As far as campaigns go, it should really be left to Infinity Ward because I don't remember a time when they undelivered in a Campaign/Story environment (even Ghosts had a great Campaign too!).
- Gun Balancing is dreadful:
The multiplayer gun balancing is so far out of whack that it's actually infuriating the majority of the time. Specialists were a great add to the Multiplayer, however Specialists weapons like the Purifier that can 1 shot you with so much ease and range, and the Ripper that can just bounce and lunge between player to player and easily hit 6-mans with little to no effort is just hilariously dumb.
Like every game, shotguns are really hard to get right, they're either a useless disadvantage or just break the game entirely, there's only a few games that do it right. However the shotguns on this game are broken beyond repair (by the likes of the Brecci and Haymaker). With the advanced movement system it makes it so easy to get kills with shotguns (especially on maps like Nuk3town).
I still feel the LMGs, SMGs and Melee mechanics still needed to have been messed around with a little bit more before release, but they are manageable.
Nevertheless, this game is amazing (aside it's gun balancing, which you do learn to deal with). I recommend it to everyone who's just tired of the basic same-old same-old FPS games (like Modern Warfare, CS:GO, Battlefield, etc.).
It's Pros heavily outweigh its Cons (even though it doesn't seem like it on paper).

tldr; Game is overall good with reasonable ways to get cards for free but has high learning curve as one should expect; be careful when and who you use your dispel/removal cards on.  Stupid microtransaction monetary system makes buying packs have uneven pricing.
The game has a great art style and with 18 Heroes (you unlock some by playing each faction) to choose from each with their own unique hero spell to build around you'll get plenty of variety and possibilities.  It plays with a grid based system with heroes and minions moving and attacking on the board so positioning is important like blocking your general or high value minion from attack with even a crappy minion in front could be the difference between victory and defeat.  Games usually take somewhere between 10-15 minutes.  There are some RNG cards but not nearly as bad as Hearthstone on average and they've actually toned down the RNG from before with their newer sets so it feels more skill based which is a plus in my book.  There are some randomness cards particularly with specific egg based cards that the Magmar faction has but for the most part isn't complete cancer.  Especially after nerfing Meltdown and Chysalis Burst
It takes a lot of practice to get a feel for when to use a card and when to save it for a bigger threat but the tutorial and training modes do a good job of teaching you the basics of how the game works.  As with any TCG its all about the cards and opening packs to get better cards to hopefully build more effective decks.  This is where some people may view it as a p2w scam or a standard card game business model.  Personally I don't think its that P2W if you take the time to learn the game and understand the strategies but I can't fault new players for having that knee jerk reaction if they get stomped by being matched with experienced players early in the season or didnt save a removal spell or a dispel type card (works like Silence in Hearthstone) and got smashed by an "OP" card because they had no answer to it at the time.  Some cards will be innately strong but I've never encountered a card that didn't have any ability for counterplay that wasn't available in the common or rare card pool.  There are plenty of reddit users who make easily obtained budget decks that go to Diamond League or above so it really boils down to how good of a player you are more so than throwing money at the problem.  That being said there are some cards that could use some slight balancing like Thunderhorn for 5 mana or as a 4/4 would be good, are poorly worded that make what they exactly do a little confusing, and having access to wider ranges of cards does make your deck building options flexible but that's innately in any card game.  The game suffers from the usual early player learning curve like any competitive card game out there.  You can't expect to go to Worlds Cup after playing a weekend of Magic the Gathering at your local game store.
To help new players the game does give you 1 free generic common a day to help build up your library.  It's not much but it helps and if you do the daily quests you net about 100 gold a day which equals to a pack of your choice.  Every 3 wins on ranked also gives you 15 gold.  With the introduction of a set rotation, some of the sets like Shimzar will rotate out next year so if you're new and wondering what packs to get Core set is a solid pick since that will never rotate out and then probably the newest set Immortal or second newest Unearthed Prophecy once you get a good collection going.
Another way to get packs is by beating some arguably challenging Weekly boss fights.  These can be tough starting out since your deck building options will be limited but if victorious it will reward you with 1 free pack of core set and a Boss Box that lasts 48 hours.
which to some people may be a deal breaker but at least they do give you a free pack so think of it like doing a whole days daily quests.  The Boss box has 3 packs of Prophecy, a Hearthstone Arena format ticket (normally $2) which nets you at least a random pack regardless on how well you do, a negligble loot crate key, and a random Legendary Card which is almost like a pack itself since legends are the rarest cards in the game.  So its like $8-9 of value for $5; take it for what you will
You can craft cards via spirit essence and usually disenchanting a legend will get you enough to make any epic, an epic enough for a rare, a rare enough for a common.  So even if you get a POS legendary you know you won't ever use you essentially got an epic which you DID want which is  honestly in higher demand since you usually need more of them.  They also have "Chromatic" versions of cards which you get from packs and crates and are supposedly supposed to have an extra sprite effect but I don't see a difference. They are worth the full crafting value of the card when disenchanted so if you get a chromatic Legendary then you essentially just got a regular legend card of your choice.  I'd say if you already have a full regular set of a card or know you don't need that many then trash your chromes and duplicates and craft away
Before the Bandai Namcom merge they used to do flat prices like $4.5 was 3 packs, $15 was 10 packs etc but now they do this garbage middleman currency thing you see in mobile games where you buy diamonds and you use diamonds to buy packs.  But the costs for diamonds dont add up to the cost for packs.  450 diamonds is $4.50 which is the same as 3 packs so thats the same but to get 10 packs you need 1450 diamonds.  Do they have a 1450 diamond option?   Nope! $10 is 1050 diamons and $25 is 2750 diamonds.  There isn't a $15 price point like there used to be so the game forces you to either buy 3 at a time or buy in bulk which is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid and is most likely some bullcrap tactic Bandai told the game studio to do since they are now the publisher.  Bottom line if you plan on being loose with your wallet then it doesn't really matter but if you only want to dip in every now and then I'd just stick with Boss crates.  Get yourself $10 of diamonds and you'll get more value from 2 boss crates unless you're looking for specific sets in which case not much you can do except shell out the $25+ and nab an uneven amount of packs.
You also get chromatic cards from unlocking common, rare, or epic crates you randomly receive while playing using keys you pay to get but crates are mostly esthetics like emotes and different general/background skins so if thats your thing by all means go for it but they aren't cost effective ways to get cards.
As for the packs themselves I feel like the rarity of a legendary is about 20% and an epic card is like 33% so thankfully at least this game is more generous than some drop rates in other card games like 5% for a legendary in Hearthstone.  I feel chromatics show up 1 in every 3-4 packs but thats just an educated guess.  You can have up to 3 of the same card in a deck including legendaries so technically you may need duplicates which can be tough to get without dust crafting unless the RNG gods look favorably upon you but Id say most decks really only need 1-2 of any specific legendary so for the most part you should be fine and let's be honest, its the commons and rares with a handful of epics that make the REAL power since they make the bulk of your deck.  Like I said before there are plenty of budget decks you can check out that are very effective without having to break the bank  so ultimately I think this is a game that any TCG fan should give a try despite the dubious microtransaction structure.  Its a game that can be incredibly rewarding and fun if you're willing to put the time to learn its intracacies.

Before you read this review, I ask that you know and understand that I was fully prepared to deal with any glitches, bugs, problems, or lack of content in this game, knowing that it is in early access and certain there was an idea here to be built upon. Flight is as about as smooth and simple as dancing the can-can with a pitchfork shoved firmly up your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the graphics are about as appealing as the head of medusa if the snakes on her head suffered from projectile vomit, and I have to be incredibly careful where I fly lest I fly out of the flat world, where I ended up spending more than half of my time despite being more cautious than my mother on my first day of school. The "goblins" and "people" might as well have been dots on the screen, and the quite sparsely spread excuses for structures might have fallen over if I farted in the wrong direction- I'm not quite sure what I did, they were always falling over anyways. I understand that this game is in early access, but I don't know if it's worth the money. I'm glad I spent it so they can work on it some more, but I'm having doubts. This game definitely has a cool idea, but it's not quite ready for anyone to play right now. In fact, there's almost nothing to do but fly around. Don't get me wrong, I absolutely love the dragon concept, but I don't know if they have a good enough foundation to get this off the ground (I made a pun because the dragon can barely get off the ground). Here are some ideas to make this game awesome:
1. Better flight controls - It's very clunky and full of bugs. I found this nifty little nook on the top of a mountain and I tried to get to it, but my dragon kept falling backwards for some reason. No idea why. I would like to see something like Zelda: Skyward Sword. The birds in the game had very simple, but easy to use flight controls. Flap the wings, they'd go up. If you were high enough, you could coast on the "wind". I'm not looking for realistic, I'm looking for fun.
2. Better ground movement - Dragons are mythical creatures, so I can't never know for sure...but I'm fairly certain that they aren't supposed to move like that. Also the body of the dragon doesn't interact well with the ground, and I'd like some motivation not to crash my animal into the ground. So far, the only way that's possible to land your dragon from high up is to do a death spiral to the ground.
3. More interesting landscape - I get that they are trying to be realistic, but I'd almost prefer if they focused more on mechanics and less on landscape. Plus, the mountains are kind of boring at this point. In the future, I'd like to see snow on top of them, and forests so thick with trees that it is almost impossible to land among. Also, rivers and lakes.
4. Dragon Territory and Hoard- I think the game makers are going for a territorial/combat/choose your destiny kind of game. I'd like to see some caves where I can store all my treasure and princesses.
5. Better dragon customization - enough said. I'm glad I have an option to explore as a silver dragon, but I'd like a little more detail than that.
Once again, I understand that this is a work in progress. But they aren't moving very fast and I don't know if they have the foundation for this to succeed. I will remain hopeful, however. So buy the game if you can afford it, but think of it like a donation right now because it's not much of a game at all currently.

Intriguing concept with not that intriguing execution. We play as a girl, that find herself in weird, under water place, called Cafe 0. We meet equally weird blue-haired waiter, drink glass of water and then... We're back in reality and it turns out that we've almost drowned in pool, during swimming competition. The thing is... We don't have any memories. We don't know who we are and who are people around us. We can't even see our reflection in the mirror. If that wasn't bad enough, blue-haired waiter shows up again and inform us, that we will die after seven days and that we have to prepare ourselves to our journey into the afterlife.
Since then our task is to speak with of the three other main characters - our, supposedly, best friend Amy, our ex boyfriend and school doctor, who is weirdly close to us. Endings depends on who will we choose as our company and what kind of answers we will give them. I think there's a six endings total. Of course all of those characters are clearly hiding something.
Good thing about this game is that it does not give us schematic characters and non of the classic love story. It's a little deeper and a little darker (though not deep and dark enough, when you consider it's potential). Bad thing? It's short. Really short. And not realistic the slightest. Hey, I get it, it's a game, but if someone finds out that they have only seven days before they die, they won't just limit themselves to one short talk with only one important person during a day. And protagonist doesn't have her memories. She should be focused on getting as much information as possible. Protagonist's reactions to certain situations also aren't very realistic - though, sadly, it's a plague of visual novels, that take many serious or shocking revelations with merely a shrug. Protagonist of this game, for example, does not protest the slightest about the fact that she is supposed to day in the seven days. In theory, it's kind of explained by her "feeling" that it may happened, but it actually make it all less believable, not more. It's worth adding, that all of the endings are linked to each other in some way - you need to go through them all to have the full picture before you. After each ending you get a special item, that you get to keep during your next play - it almost creates an illusion that we're in the never ending cycle and that was definitely a good part.
The biggest flaw of this game is the fact that it doesn't truly exploit this intriguing premise. Instead of giving us something really deep, a picture, that we, as the player, will reveal slowly by getting each ending and this way we will solve our own murder, it gives us almost a few unfortunate coincidences, that ultimately doesn't feel relevant or satisfying.
In general... If you'll find this game for a very low price (in a bundle or during sale) and you are fan of visual novels, give it a try. Otherwise, you don't lose anything.

I often find games that give me conflicting emotions are far easier to reccomend, and this is such a case. For the majority of my playtime, I absolutely loathed this game; the characters, the dialogue--all amounted to some of the most infuriatingly childish attempts at romance and edginess in a game with some very straightforward choices that lead to almost the exact same thing. I almost gave up, writing it off as another game more catering to tweens and their fledging libidos, and I am so glad I didn't.
You see, this is an otome visual novel; basically, this is meant for girls, and in just about every way, The Drowned Mermaid is that. At a lot of points especially I was put off by the main character and the choices offered, and all of the endings at first seemed extremely shallow, going the "I love you forever~~" route or the "burn for all eternity" route (which were always far more interesting). However, without giving too much away, this shallow presentation to some extremely shallow characters is actually a partial ruse for something much more intricate and sinister. While this does not discount the dialogue as being amateurish, somehow it adds to the intrigue this game builds up. With each ending, you get closer to the true one, and believe me when I say it won't take you long.
By the end of my little journey, a game I thought I would hate for its pandering had me wrapped around its little finger as I tried to piece together what actually happened, and once the real truth comes out? You will find even the most innocent and cringe-worthy romantic endings will carry a very different weight by the time you see the true ending.
Cafe 0 is a unique enough concept that manages to surpass its own failings, even though as a Visual Novel it leaves something to be desired. However, if you really take a moment to see this fairly short game through, you will be surprised as to how wonderfully put together this story is. For the price and for the length, I can say without a doubt that this little gem in the rough is more than worth your time; just don't be afraid to use the skip button after your first time through.
Edit: A good two hours were not recorded on this log because of my finicky internet, so what you see there is only about half my playtime, just to give you an estimate on how long it took me to see everything.
