First of all, I played the game before its release on steam thus explaining my playtime. Also, I voluntarily will not speak of the game's details because it's not what I want to defend in this review.
Café 0 ~The Drowned Mermaid~ perhaps isn't the best visual novel ever made nor the prettiest.
It's probably one of the ugliest but, as a wise and just as ugly man once said, what matters is what's inside! And what's inside is okay! It offers an average and, somehow, a bit compelling story focused on characters interesting enough for you to keep on playing the game.
I went through several states that I'd like to develop from before playing to reaching the true ending:
1) The discovery: I was truly amused, mostly by the graphics (just like you I assume) and yet was curious about this setting (like you once again, explaining why you are currently reading this review).
2) The purchase:  I ended up purchasing it due to my curiosity taking over my reasoning I guess (not that I regret it today), and felt this feeling ,which was a mixture of both amusement and a bit of nervousness, just like before you go on exploring the complete unknown of a safe experience.
3) The playthrough: I played for a straight 4 hours (as I remember), at night alone in my house and went through a rollercoaster of feelings mainly composed of inquisitiveness and mockery at times which truly fulfilled those 4 hours I spent on the game. I was also really satisfied by the endings delivering something that can rarely be found in gaming experiences in my opinion.
4) The post-experience: I went from making fun of the game, upon discovering the game, to making fun of the game and defending its qualities, because it deserves it. I even lost some credibility in some friends' mind but it doesn't matter because not only did I have a good time but I also became wiser as of judging one's book by its cover and therefore, by extension, learning to give a chance to everything and everyone.
Some might point out the price of the game, perhaps a bit expensive for its content, and I can only agree but once it goes on sale, I truly hope that this review would have convinced you to give this game a chance. A chance it really deserves. Thank you.

The game is moderately interesting to begin with, the concept itself is quite appealing: this mix of tabletop game and an arcade machine, the artstyle and so on. It, in fact, could have been a nice game... if it were about 5 times shorter and 10 times cheaper.
One playthrough takes wa-a-a-y too long, even if you don’t take into account the possibility of your family dying out halfway through, which of course makes you start over, as there is only one save. For the first couple of hours planning on your family’s development, balancing between producing tokens, spending them and moving forward is interesting, even fascinating – due to the novelty of this experience, probably – but it gets old really fast.
You rise up to the very top of your ancient society, become an ultimate ruler… and then the Age ends, and you find out that you have to do the same thing yet another time. And again, in the third Age. The art changes from Age to Age, the icons on the board change… everything else remains the same, over and over again. Once you start climbing up the social ladder during the third Age, the routine gets depressingly, brain-curdlingly repetitive and boring. The ruling mini-games are the only thing that is different among the three ages, and again, after you organize your city’s grain supplies for 30-odd turns, repeating the same set of actions…
The title implies that the developer plans on continuing the series, this time showing the way of a family through the Middle Ages. If the sequel ever gets around to being released and it will be similar to this game in terms of game mechanics, well… I can only say that the developer is really, really optimistic if he plans to keep it up for all 7 steps.

Rayman Origins, the first remake of the Rayman games, is one of the best platformers I have ever seen. Why? Read this test to learn more!
First of all I want to talk about the atmosphere. You play in different worlds and their "Dark" World types. The worlds are completly different (Forrest, African, I won't spoiler more...) and have their own music and graphics. You see  Dust flying up in the African styled maps and after a time this even becomes a part of the Gameplay!
The Graphics are just awesome. Hand-made worlds create a feeling of really being in the Rayman World. Together with the fitting sounds and music, this creates a very good atmosphere.
Also: When I played the first levels of Rayman, it made me really happy. I played and was happy. I even had to stop myself from playing too much, because I did not want Rayman's adventure to go over too fast!
Now to the Fairness and sticked with that: The Controls.
The Controls are intuitive and easy-to-learn. After some times, you get new abilities, which though do not make the game confusing. You understand them and they stay in your brain.
The game is pretty easy if you just want to play it through. You just have to get through the levels with the (sometimes not so many) checkpoints. But if you want a challenge, ok: Collect over 300, or even 350 points in the level, complete it with the best time possible or even find all of the hidden emoticons!
Anyways, sometimes the not so good spreaded checkpoints are a little annoying or the unlimate pro times in the time challengers mode. You have to complete the level in a certain time (may sometimes even be 3 minutes!) AND not die AND be as fast as somehow possible. This is sometimes annoying, but I mean: it is optional, so...
I already talked about the Gameplay a bit: Different worlds, different challenges, new abilities, time trial,...
The most fun though is exploring the level. If you just up in the "wrong" way that you should and then do a bit of this and that...Hey! There is a mini game for an emoticon! And if you try to just go under the collapsing bridge...50 points in a coin! Nice done, Ubisoft!
Also, you unlock new characters and racing levels with the emoticons. The characters are just for the optics, but the races are really fun! With the pursuit soundtrack you run behind a running Chest around a collapsing level, split up, come to him again, etc etc. It is just like a much better time trial mode!
Anyways, the Longness is not so long if you just play the game through without secrets, time trials and so on. You can be through in 7 hours. If you do the time trials and the other stuff, Rayman can take like 25 hours. This is up to you. For this huge difference there is a minus in the points rating though...
The Multiplayer is the only thing I would critise in the game: You may play local Co Op, but there are no Local Co Op levels, and in a time in which everything is connected to the Internet, an Internet Multiplayer is actually a must-have...
TL;DR: If you want to play a platformer which makes you happy while exploring wonderful levels with atmospheric music, you should buy this game! Just if you need a Multiplayer at all costs though, you should think about getting the game.

The characters and dialogue in Watch_Dogs 2 are so cringey and under developed that I find it very hard to grasp the serious topics in the game, including gang violence and mass hacking fraud, just to name a few. As a result, the story is much worse than that of Watch_Dogs. For instance, Aiden Pierce was clearly a nice guy under the cold hearted killer facade aiming to get revenge for his niece and to help his sister and nephew, but Marcus Holloway is a young man with his whole life ahead of him who choses to partake in, at times, blatently criminal activities for what seems like no other reason that "for the lols", as the youth may say. In my opinion, you shouldn't be completely changing the direction of a franchise like this. Ubisoft should have created a sequal with the improved hacking mechanics in Watch_Dogs 2 but still maintained the dark and sombre tone of the original, yet all I see if I search for Watch_Dogs 2 on the internet is colourful and vibrant images.
I find it quite annoying that the taser is so powerful. It can take out enemies from very far range with incredible accuracy and even enforcers with just one hit - the strongest enemy in the game. In Watch_Dogs, these bad boys would take a couple of grenades and multiple headshots before dying. I think Ubisoft may have some kind of hidden agenda to push non lethal weapons, because who uses those in an 18 rated video game if they aren't incredibly overpowered?
Also, the missions are frankly stale, with the goal for most of them being to get the drone inside, hack the FBI, get out and bish bash bosh you're done! The missions really need to be improved next time. The minigames and collectibles strewn around the map are a waste of time with very little reward from the cash ones and you can already buy a big variety of clothes from myriad of shops around the bay area.
Ubisoft may have removed you having to climb towers to unlock parts of the map to allow you to do whatever you want right from the start, but I don't think this is true. If you want to max out one of the skills in the skill tree, you have to explore the world (or just the specific areas it tells you to) to unlock the ability to unlock the new skill. You may have removed towers, but you have added limitations to what you can do from the start of the game. This means that when you collect research points which can be used to buy skills, you will probably have less choice than before, and are constantly bugged by the highly irritating popup that tells you that you have unspent skill points, if you are saving up for the big skills that require up to 8 research points. In the big picture, this means you will end up with a balanced skill set, which is not good considering Ubisoft wanted to support many different and unique play style. The balance of the skills most players would achieve through these limitations mean it is harder to specialise in one aspect that you might prefer. This would be easier achieved if they allowed you to fully master any skill as long as you have the research points.
But what Watch_Dogs 2 lacks in its dialogue, character development, tone and atmosphere, repetitive missions, overpowered non lethal weapons, useless collectibles and poorly thought out skills it makes up for in its stunning visuals, sort of. The graphics aren't terrible, but they aren't perfect if you intend on actually playing the game at a decent framerate. If you want SF fog on, and perhaps some of those nice Hybrid Frustum Traced Shadows, you'd be looking at a loss of around 30-40 FPS. I guess you could just turn them off though...
Furthermore, I played the game again just for research and received a message from the Uplay overlay that my GPU was below the minimum requirement. I have a GTX 980 Ti! And then, about 10 minutes into playing the game, it just crashed, without any warning. I have very capable parts in my computer and am only playing at 1080p (4k monitor coming soon). This hasn't happened for any other games, either.
Overall, Watch_Dogs 2 is a bad sequel that most people seem to like for ditching many parts of the original. I'd rather have a linear story if it means the story can be told better and with more depth. It also just got a price increase, so there's even less incentive to buy it.

TL;DR -- If you're trying to figure out which game is the best in the Sid Meier's Railroad series, look no further. It's this one, by a mile.
It's also more designed around multiplayer than any of the other games. The single player campain is very short (not a lot of content there), and it's really built around being a skirmish-based game. You can actually drop in with a buddy and go head to head in games that will only take an hour, and its great. If you've ever played Offworld Trading Company, the victory system is identical. You win by buying out your opponents company.
This game is VERY streamlined compared to the earlier games, but in my opinion that is what makes it so good. The economic side of things is simple, but they decided to make everything revolve around moving particular commodities to where they need to go. This is a massive streamline in terms of making money. I'll be comparing it to Railroad Tycoon 2 because I skipped 3 (it sucks).
The biggest difference is that stations will ONLY accept cargo they have demand for. If there's no demand they will NOT buy the cargo. On top of that, stations no longer have demand "quotas" or numbers that can run down. If something is in demand, its ALWAYS in demand, and will not turn off. This is a welcome change because there's nothing more fustrating than having a car full of cargo arrive to see you used up the demand already and you get paid diddly squat for it. Frankly, I thought that was a stupid system (A real city would never run out of "demand" for goods). In this game demand is constant and only supply will get used up.
Another large difference is how much is centered around making things grow! Cities grow very fast, and you actually have to grow them yourself. The maps will only have a handful of established cities when you start off, the rest being small villages that have demand for an industrail cargo type but no passengers or mail. So for instance a village might have a paper mill. You find the nearest logging camp and connect that to the village, and start bringing in logs. The paper mill will turn the logs into paper. You will get paid for the logs even if the paper isn't being moved yet, but you'll see the paper being added to the villages supplies. You can then move that paper to somewhere else that demands it. Only cities with newspapers will demand paper! You might have to move the paper a few cities away to sell it (or you can build a newspaper yourself in any town or city with an empty industry slot).
Any activity whatsoever will add to a village or cities growth points, and once you have enough growth points it will grow into the next stage (village>town). Once its a town, it will have supply and demand for passengers, and you have more options open up for making money.
Now the cool thing about this is that you decide which cities grow based on briging them industry. So you have to think several steps ahead of yourself, to decide which supply chains are going to be the easiest to set up, and which cities are easiest to grow. This more than makes up for the streamlined economic system. I read some other reviews where people said this game was "too easy" or "for kids" or whatever. That's not true, you can play this game as an intense skirmish RTS if you want to. Just crank all the difficulties up to hard and play with a buddy. I guarantee you it's fun as hell and not easy.
Now you see the economic aspect is just superior in every way, but I haven't even touched the main thing about why this game rocks. The Railway building system is extremely well done!
See I haven't played Transport Fever yet. I've heard its great, but this game came out 10 years ago and the railbuilding system still shines today. The map is dynamic and everything on the map will morph around your railways. I personally think this is just better and more realistic since you're looking at a graphic representation of thousands of miles of land. Anyway you can terraform the landscape to make your lines perfect, and you even get complete control over it. Using the + and - keys will terraform the land up or down so you don't need to rely on the game's auto terraforming system. Anyone with experience in these games knows that track inclines (whether its uphill, downhill, or flat) are a REALLY big aspect of this game. If you try to run a railway through a hilly area, it will automatically carve a valley through (like in real life, they would use dynamite to blow a valley through some hills). If its deep enough underground it will build a tunnel. If you try to connect to points of high lattitude (like 2 hills or mountains), it will make a bridge. You also have complete control over all of this. Say you want your line to be totally flat between two large hills with a valley in the middle, even if its a super wide valley, just set the height up and it will make a bridge. Vice Versa for any hill you want to tunnel through. You can build bridges or tunnels over/under your own railways. If you want to spend boatloads of money making your tracks super flat over long distances, you can do that. The possibilities are endless.
Thats just the terraforming system. Another big aspect is the unlimited railway dualing. You can use the "double railway" button for not just doubling. You can add as many as you want. Stations will only allow up to 4 "lanes" for incoming and outgoing, but for the rest of it there's no limit (not that you'd normally need more than 4). So you can have lanes just for passengers, lanes just for shipping, you might even have shipping lanes only for specific cargo. Proper design of your shipping lanes is a really cool aspect and a big part of the game. To top it off the trains are fairly smart, and will automatically detect which lanes to use if they're connected to more than 1. I found most of the time, it's better to try to keep your freight trains on completely seperate tracks from the passengers so they never block each other, but thats not always feasible (especially in multiplayer when you're trying to build as fast as possible)
Honestly I would keep writing my review about how great this game is, but at this point I'd rather just go play it. You should too.

-----------------------------
UPDATE 19/9
-----------------------------
So the devs just recently patched in some changes based on community feedback and I thought I'd give it a shot again - and it feels so much better! The initial difficulty curve has been smoothed out a bit (and having played a few runs prior made me more thoughtful before even clicking my first POI).
The game still retains its tough-as-nails difficulty, but now instead of a 0.1% fighting chance, it's bumped up to 1% and for a game like this, that is enough to turn it from frustrating to satisfying.
I now recommend this game but it's definitely not a game for everyone. You must really take the effort to invest in learning the game because its strength (the 2AP combat system) is also its weakness (if you don't get to know it properly).
If you are considering buying this game, I strongly urge you to check out some Let's Plays of other people doing runthroughs. But if you decide to get it, then welcome to Bedlam!
-----------------------------
ORIGINAL REVIEW
-----------------------------
The current iteration of Skyshine's Bedlam is not recommended for most people unless you live purely on the thrill of dying repeatedly due to factors outside of your control (and a very small segment of the gamer population does thrive on this!).
I'm REALLY trying to like this game because the art and concept is so amazing, but it's such a shame that the combat gameplay is a letdown.
I feel that the combat is too random such that your victories and losses have a lot less to do with your skill and more to do with your luck (namely initial unit placement or deployment phase, rookies dying too easily but not as easily replaceable). This game would often be compared to the new XCOM and FTL, but both managed to hit the mark on letting you feel you can usually triumph with skill.
This game would also be compared with chess, but whereby the latter has a consistent deployment layout and a strategy develops over time as you play, this doesn't happen in Bedlam as combat is too short to have a sense of chess' grand strategy, and the deployment issue has been mentioned earlier as well.
The good news is that this can be rectified by balancing the stats and lowering the initial difficulty curve so that rookies are slightly beefier and easier to level up, as well as letting melee units have some stopping power to delay enemy advancement into your squishy damage dealers.
Essentially, instead of feeling satisfied and enjoying that you one-upped against all odds of randomness when you win, you just feel disengaged with your units and just cross your fingers that they don't die each time. Outside of combat, the Dozer has no character and is simply a fancy looking stats-tracker (which is fine if the combat is improved).
If you look at the forums, the above issues are generally consistent with why people are unsatisfied with game, so hopefully the devs consider how to balance the hard roguelike intent against user enjoyment. I hope the devs are not discouraged by these feedback and see that a lot of us really want to enjoy the game, but certain aspects of it must be significantly improved to entice us to try it again.
I hope I can return to it later once some patches have gone through to help improve the above issues.

Don't buy this unless you fully researched how combat works.  It is not what I thought it would be so - make sure you know what you're buying before you drop cash on this one.  A lot of people like it, a lot of people hate it.  I want to like the game, but as the combat currently stands, I don't.
You get a team of up to 4 to take into a fight.  You have to collect resources during the fight, you don't grab them before you kill everyone on the enemy team then you don't get them.  Yeah, that's ridiculous, I know.  Somehow they're available while the team I field is being shot at and stabbed, but as soon as it's safe - they're gone.  Makes no sense.  Nevermind the fact that there's a resource "multiplier" meaning if I take a smaller team than 4 and win, and manage to collect something, I get more of it.  That's just as dumb as it sounds.  Imagine the reverse - three people go into the field first, the fouth guy got lagged behind tying his shoe, or something.  Suddenly he appears at the edge of the combat just before the fight starts.  The lookout says "Gee, guys, I could have sworn I saw four barrels of oil there two seconds ago, but since Jeb just caught up, now I only see three."
Makes no sense to me.  There are either 100 units of oil, or there aren't.  It does not matter if one, two or twenty people tag along.  A restaurant won't have more burgers in the kitchen if I show up with two friends instead of three.  The bank won't have more money in the vault if I show up with two other people with me instead of three.  The grocery store doesn't suddenly have 25% more product for me to purchase if I go shopping alone rather than with a group of four people.  The volume of items should be static.  It should be there regardless of how many characters walk into combat.  Plus when the fight is over, you should be able to loot any items that you didn't pickup during the fight.  As it stands, you can't.  Even if you're standing right next to it.
You get two activations per combat round regardless of team size.  You got one guy, he goes twice.  Four guys, two of them can go once, or one guy can go twice.  Whole team standing in the open?  You're probably going to lose someone, or two someones.  I expect any turn based strategy game to either give you enough activation points to move everyone at least once, or give each character a turn every round.  That is *NOT* how this works at all.  Oh, and want to move one character, then shoot?  Sure, go ahead - but that's *TWO* activations so your turn is over.  Yup, can't even move and shoot, or move and stab, in one action.
Some people seem to like this set-up, some don't.  I'm in the don't camp right now.
Otherwise, passable graphics, poor voice acting, passable animations, pointless back story.  This wants to be a cross between FTL and Banner Saga using the Banner Saga engine.  It's also got some humour, but I don't particularly enjoy the writing.
I want to like this game.  But I don't.  Do your research.  Do I recommend this?  Yes - as long as you know what you're getting into.  Just because I don't like it doesn't mean someone else won't enjoy it "as is".  I just have much higher expectations out of a turn-based, perma-death, choose your route, get to the promised land, resource management game.
The combat is frequently compared to chess, but it's nothing like chess.  I honestly think most of the people who compare it to chess have never actually played the game.  Chess is a completely balanced game with two equal sides on a static playing field.  Each piece is only as strong as the position it occupies relative to all the other pieces on the board.  The strongest piece, when in the wrong position, is useless.  Also, each side sets up exactly the same way ever single time it's played.
This game isn't like that at all.  Random starting positions.  Different playing fields.  Resources you have to capture during the fight.  Perma death.  In chess all your pieces are available for the next game.  In this game if someone's lost, they're gone forever.  The only resource you "capture" in chess is an opponent's chess piece.  You don't locate more "food" or additional "energy" for your knight in chess just because you occupy a certain square.  I think you get the point.
I want to like this game, I just don't.  Primarily because of combat and how it works.  I wanted it to be so much more than it is.  I hope it becomes something great, despite disliking it, because I do like the concept.
Recommended: Yes - but know exactly what you're paying for.

I absolutely HATE the time system in the game. There's absolutely no reason to be so unforgiving to players. I had a dialogue, had my main plot forwarded, and then fell asleep in the streets. I woke up, and now I can't further my plot without going back to a considerably older saved game.
==== After spending tens of hours playing ====
Once I was able to get the Modifier, the item in game that allowed me to get to the coding portion, I had a lot of fun programming. However, I absolutely would not suggest this for someone that didn't already know how to program.
I found that I spent probably thirty hours exploring the world using techniques that were obviously not intended as the plot was not being pushed forward. Once I was finally done creating a library of all utility functions I thought I would need in the game, it took me only a few hours to actually beat the game. By the time I got to the last mission (Saving Private Ivan), I did not have to sleep anymore due to some trickery. However, there was a dream one had to have by sleeping in their own bed that was required to finish the game. I had spent days trying to figure out what I had done wrong for the game to not finish. Finally, after having to read through the discussions of others who were in similar situations, I figured it out and was able to finish.
Overall, I still wouldn't suggest this game. It was fun for me only because I already knew how to program and I like to delve into these sort of things head first and stay there. If you want to learn how to program, pick up an intro book.

An interesting game about hacking the world.
The game plays like an isometric adventure. After a while, the main character gets a device that lets him modify the objects in his environment. The behavior of (almost) each interactive object in the world is implemented with a programming language called SPRAK and over the course of the game, the main character (and the player) learns to make changes to these programs.
Being able to program helps while playing this game, but it teaches basic programming concepts and it certainly can be finished by people who are not programmers.
The game's setting is a small city. It is completely open from the beginning and serves as a sandbox to reprogram.
The programming part of the game is well done. The only negative thing is that the ingame code-editor is not very good.
Less well done is the writing and the plot. I did like the main characters, but the plot takes a while until it gets interesting and shortly after that it just stops. There are so many unfinished threads and open questions at the end, that at first I believed I had triggered some sort of premature ending. I was disappointed by that.
But still, the way to that point was interesting, and I enjoyed my time of reprogramming trash cans, cigarettes and fuse boxes.

Cafe 0 ~ The Drowned Mermaid,
Is not a Visual Novel for just anybody. The subject that's being brought up in this VN is a bit different. It's about dying and finding peace in the fact itself.
The story itself is quiet interesting from time to time, but if falls short on depth in my opinion. The conversations with the "important" characters are too shallow compared to other VN's of the same price. So, I would have expected more on that part.
The graphics are a bit different also. I can't say they're good, but they arent bad either.
Gameplay, hmm, without trying to spoil anything, it's basically a good ending / bad ending thing. You make some choices and get some progression "stat" throughout the game so you're able to see how you're doing. That's the part I liked a lot, because it's done in a different way than just displaying some numbers or bars.
The one thing I didn't like at all is that at the beginning you've got to enter a name. But, you're not told that you're supposed to enter a female name. So, if you enter a male name it feels like you're some kind of shemale. A bit weird..
Another negative thing about this VN is the fact that it falls short on length. It doesn't take that long to complete a path and the fact that there're several endings doesn't make it any better. It feels like a cheap way by the developer to stretch the game time.
So to put it all in a list:
Pros:
-Interesting/different subject.
-Interesting story.
-Nice music.
Cons:
-Too short.
-Repeating dialogs.
-Lack of information when entering a name.
-The different endings feel forced.
-Towards the end of the story it feels like a rushed product.
As you can see there're more negative things than positive aspects about Cafe 0. The thing is that I don't regret buying this Visual Novel, but I don't recommend it to people who're looking for a more fleshed out product. (e.g. Katawa Shoujo, Narcissu, Yandere, etc.)

Cafe 0 ~The Drowned Mermaid~ is a short shoujo/mystery visual novel. You play as Marie Umino, a deceased girl who must find who killed her 7 days earlier. There are several suspects that you can meet to try and find out who the true culprit is.
The story branches out in "routes", that lead to several ends : 4 "main" ends, one "true" end, and one "bad" end
In order to get the "true end" you need to finish the story at least 4 times, to get all the items needed. That means you have to re-read dialogues you've already read, which can get quite monotonous. At least you can use the "skip" function, although in the end, that makes the game very short.
It's not really hard to figure out what to do, as the choices you can make are fairly limited and rather simple (you can be "good" or "evil", basically), and the writing isn't stellar, though it kept me entertained.
I wouldn't really recommend it, unless you're a diehard fan of visual novels or mystery novels, because there are far better visual novels out there (and with better art, too), and the price is quite high right now (luckily I got it in a bundle).
But for 2 or 3 euros, you might consider it...

TL;DR: sandbox game for creative players. If your creativity is channeled through problem-solving, then this game will leave you wanting.
I have tried so hard to like the game.
Hands-down, technically the
. The problem is: I don't have the urge to come back to it. 5 hours in, lack of interest settles in, I just give up and start over. Rince and repeat. I
though I'm looking hard.
Therefore it's aimed at
players, who just play on unlimited resources and invest time in designing a beautiful city.
Lack of challenge makes you fail to see the point of anything after a couple hours. "Ok, I can improve traffic, but what's the point, people still come to my city and budget is fine anyway". "Criminality? Okay, whatever. Budget's fine".
"Cool, I can fine tune the budget with all the sliders!... I can make tax-free zones for specific industries!... but I don't care and won't ever use it because there's absolutely no point".
If you're the kind of person who just wants to design stuff, then you'll have a blast. If you channel your creativity through problem-solving, then boredom will settle in quickly.
If you're anything like me, then you will find that there's no point in moving away from the "grid" city-design. Every block is a square, crossroads are crosses, because that's the more efficient choice. So if you're a problem solver, all your cities will look the same.
That may sound stupid to Americans, but here in old Europe, cities have grown organically over the course of millenias: cars are barely allowed in medieval city centers, which have tons of pedestrians-only walkways; low-rent flats are usually in the cities' outskirts; then, further away, the big business center with highrises, accessible by road or public transportation, built in a very windy spot or on an old marsh, because that's the only spot where our ancestors didn't build anything...
I dream of the day a city-builder will have us build a city through the ages. Imagine the challenges! Your 1200 AD city needs wall for defense, but cannons will soon render this useless and you'll be left with crumbling walls dividing your city between center and outskirts. Industrial revolution comes around and now you need housing for workers, railroads for supply: means you have to burn down some of those outskirts houses and decide what to do with their poor inhabitants... Enters XXth cenury, in order allow cars into the city you need larger avenues, so then again you need more space! Residents won't be happy... Then, fast-forward 2010, there is so much traffic that you need to reshape everything around cycling and public transportation...
You could choose to start in the New World around 1600 AD, where challenges are entirely different...
If you built your city originally on a marsh, or trapped between mountains, or in windy plains, then you would have different challenges and opportunities, renewed every new era.
Now, THAT would keep me playing till 4am. Cities: Skylines? Sadly, no.

tldr; Game is overall good with reasonable ways to get cards for free but has high learning curve as one should expect; be careful when and who you use your dispel/removal cards on.  Stupid microtransaction monetary system makes buying packs have uneven pricing.
The game has a great art style and with 18 Heroes (you unlock some by playing each faction) to choose from each with their own unique hero spell to build around you'll get plenty of variety and possibilities.  It plays with a grid based system with heroes and minions moving and attacking on the board so positioning is important like blocking your general or high value minion from attack with even a crappy minion in front could be the difference between victory and defeat.  Games usually take somewhere between 10-15 minutes.  There are some RNG cards but not nearly as bad as Hearthstone on average and they've actually toned down the RNG from before with their newer sets so it feels more skill based which is a plus in my book.  There are some randomness cards particularly with specific egg based cards that the Magmar faction has but for the most part isn't complete cancer.  Especially after nerfing Meltdown and Chysalis Burst
It takes a lot of practice to get a feel for when to use a card and when to save it for a bigger threat but the tutorial and training modes do a good job of teaching you the basics of how the game works.  As with any TCG its all about the cards and opening packs to get better cards to hopefully build more effective decks.  This is where some people may view it as a p2w scam or a standard card game business model.  Personally I don't think its that P2W if you take the time to learn the game and understand the strategies but I can't fault new players for having that knee jerk reaction if they get stomped by being matched with experienced players early in the season or didnt save a removal spell or a dispel type card (works like Silence in Hearthstone) and got smashed by an "OP" card because they had no answer to it at the time.  Some cards will be innately strong but I've never encountered a card that didn't have any ability for counterplay that wasn't available in the common or rare card pool.  There are plenty of reddit users who make easily obtained budget decks that go to Diamond League or above so it really boils down to how good of a player you are more so than throwing money at the problem.  That being said there are some cards that could use some slight balancing like Thunderhorn for 5 mana or as a 4/4 would be good, are poorly worded that make what they exactly do a little confusing, and having access to wider ranges of cards does make your deck building options flexible but that's innately in any card game.  The game suffers from the usual early player learning curve like any competitive card game out there.  You can't expect to go to Worlds Cup after playing a weekend of Magic the Gathering at your local game store.
To help new players the game does give you 1 free generic common a day to help build up your library.  It's not much but it helps and if you do the daily quests you net about 100 gold a day which equals to a pack of your choice.  Every 3 wins on ranked also gives you 15 gold.  With the introduction of a set rotation, some of the sets like Shimzar will rotate out next year so if you're new and wondering what packs to get Core set is a solid pick since that will never rotate out and then probably the newest set Immortal or second newest Unearthed Prophecy once you get a good collection going.
Another way to get packs is by beating some arguably challenging Weekly boss fights.  These can be tough starting out since your deck building options will be limited but if victorious it will reward you with 1 free pack of core set and a Boss Box that lasts 48 hours.
which to some people may be a deal breaker but at least they do give you a free pack so think of it like doing a whole days daily quests.  The Boss box has 3 packs of Prophecy, a Hearthstone Arena format ticket (normally $2) which nets you at least a random pack regardless on how well you do, a negligble loot crate key, and a random Legendary Card which is almost like a pack itself since legends are the rarest cards in the game.  So its like $8-9 of value for $5; take it for what you will
You can craft cards via spirit essence and usually disenchanting a legend will get you enough to make any epic, an epic enough for a rare, a rare enough for a common.  So even if you get a POS legendary you know you won't ever use you essentially got an epic which you DID want which is  honestly in higher demand since you usually need more of them.  They also have "Chromatic" versions of cards which you get from packs and crates and are supposedly supposed to have an extra sprite effect but I don't see a difference. They are worth the full crafting value of the card when disenchanted so if you get a chromatic Legendary then you essentially just got a regular legend card of your choice.  I'd say if you already have a full regular set of a card or know you don't need that many then trash your chromes and duplicates and craft away
Before the Bandai Namcom merge they used to do flat prices like $4.5 was 3 packs, $15 was 10 packs etc but now they do this garbage middleman currency thing you see in mobile games where you buy diamonds and you use diamonds to buy packs.  But the costs for diamonds dont add up to the cost for packs.  450 diamonds is $4.50 which is the same as 3 packs so thats the same but to get 10 packs you need 1450 diamonds.  Do they have a 1450 diamond option?   Nope! $10 is 1050 diamons and $25 is 2750 diamonds.  There isn't a $15 price point like there used to be so the game forces you to either buy 3 at a time or buy in bulk which is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid and is most likely some bullcrap tactic Bandai told the game studio to do since they are now the publisher.  Bottom line if you plan on being loose with your wallet then it doesn't really matter but if you only want to dip in every now and then I'd just stick with Boss crates.  Get yourself $10 of diamonds and you'll get more value from 2 boss crates unless you're looking for specific sets in which case not much you can do except shell out the $25+ and nab an uneven amount of packs.
You also get chromatic cards from unlocking common, rare, or epic crates you randomly receive while playing using keys you pay to get but crates are mostly esthetics like emotes and different general/background skins so if thats your thing by all means go for it but they aren't cost effective ways to get cards.
As for the packs themselves I feel like the rarity of a legendary is about 20% and an epic card is like 33% so thankfully at least this game is more generous than some drop rates in other card games like 5% for a legendary in Hearthstone.  I feel chromatics show up 1 in every 3-4 packs but thats just an educated guess.  You can have up to 3 of the same card in a deck including legendaries so technically you may need duplicates which can be tough to get without dust crafting unless the RNG gods look favorably upon you but Id say most decks really only need 1-2 of any specific legendary so for the most part you should be fine and let's be honest, its the commons and rares with a handful of epics that make the REAL power since they make the bulk of your deck.  Like I said before there are plenty of budget decks you can check out that are very effective without having to break the bank  so ultimately I think this is a game that any TCG fan should give a try despite the dubious microtransaction structure.  Its a game that can be incredibly rewarding and fun if you're willing to put the time to learn its intracacies.

My favorite game apart from maybe Interstate '76, and it's based upon that game's engine anyway. One of the defining games of my childhood and well deserving of this re-release.
Originally released in 1998, this take on Battlezone was itself a re-imagining of the 1980 arcade game. It blended first-person vehicular combat with real-time strategy elements to create a revolutionary hybrid game experience that has only been briefly revisited since, in games such as Sacrifice and Brutal Legend.
In 1952, as the story goes, a meteor shower in the arctic circle brought a previously unknown organic material to Earth. Simultaneously discovered by scientists of both the US and the Soviet Union, this "Bio-Metal" was soon discovered to have the unique ability to remember shapes it had previously assumed. From this material, the superpowers created hovering tanks and weapons centuries ahead of anything they could have otherwise made at the time. They quickly ran out of it, and turned their eyes towards the stars in search of more. In secret, the two nations sent thousand-man armies into space. Thus began a new, hidden chapter of the Cold War- the one too brutal to televise. You will journey to the moon, Mars, Venus and beyond in search of the bio-metal, and the truth of its origins.
You take the role of a soldier of either the Americans' National Space Defense Force, or NSDF, or the Russians' Cosmo Colonist Army, or CCA. You begin most campaign missions, as well as multiplayer strategy matches, with your own tank and a Recycler- at once your core base structure, your resource depository, and a factory that produces all other essential units. It exists in a mobile or deployed state, able to travel (slowly) about until you find a geyser over which to deploy it, whereupon it becomes able to build. You have two resources: scrap, and pilots. The former are gathered by scavengers, autonomous resource-harvesting vehicles built from the Recycler that will wander the map gathering bio-metal scrap, found lying around in fields on most maps, or generated from destroyed vehicles and structures. Controlling these scrap fields and assigning escorts to your scavengers is crucial in more difficult missions, and in multiplayer.
Combat vehicles include nimble scout craft, light and medium tanks, rocket tanks, bombers, and walkers. Defensive units include mobile turrets and artillery that must deploy to fire, as well as minelayers. Offensive vehicles for the most part are fast, turn quickly and can strafe, allowing you to maintain fire on a target while avoiding return fire, though the bombers do not turn quickly and are more adept at long-range strikes on static structures. Combat is fast and chaotic- focused fire can destroy most vehicles in seconds, and battles can involve upwards of twenty tanks at once- more in the campaign. You should quickly master the ability to group your units using Control plus the Function keys, and commanding them to focus-fire individual enemy targets, lest they haphazardly engage multiple enemies at once and lose the advantage of their numbers. The scouts and turrets are built from your Recycler, while the rest are built from your Unit Factory, a more specialized builder vehicle that is also built from the Recycler. If a vehicle is destroyed, including yours, fear not- the pilot will eject, and have the opportunity to return to their base and be put in a new vehicle. While on foot, you are extremely vulnerable, but not defenseless- you have a low-damage plasma gun, as well as a sniper rifle you can use to snipe out the pilot of an enemy vehicle and steal it for yourself. Be wary of enemy pilots in multiplayer!
You may also build a Constructor vehicle from your Recycler that can build fixed structures, such as powerful gun towers, repair and resupply structures, and a communications tower that grants you access to an overhead satellite view in the vein of a traditional RTS. It can also build a barracks- the only way to increase your pilot count. Protect your Constructor well- it's often a priority target for AI enemies, and getting a network of gun towers up is crucial for fending off regular enemy raids in the later campaign missions. You will also want to build an Armory, a third mobile base vehicle that builds and launches repair, ammo and weapon pickups, as it is your only means of repairing structures and allows you to resupply in the field, as well as launch bombs on enemy bases.
You can command your units either by looking directly at them and pressing the space bar or by selecting them using the number keys from a list. Units are organized into offensive, defensive, utility, with an extra section for available navigation beacons, which also function as cameras when selected, to give you remote viewing of that location. Offensive units have the most diverse range of orders- they can be commanded to move to a specific location, attack or defend your current target, follow you, defend a key friendly, or to move to a selected nav beacon, as well as to get repairs or ammunition, or to recycle- refunding a portion of scrap used in their construction, as well as returning their pilots to your global pilot count- this is good, because you have a finite cap of 30 pilots per level and they cannot be replaced. This works both ways- target enemy pilots to deny the AI access to replacement units- I think. The computer probably cheats on both scrap and pilots, and they most certainly can spawn near-infinite waves of harassing attacks on your base. It works in multiplayer though.
Aside from the two story campaigns, there are a variety of multiplayer modes, including deathmatch, strategy, and "MPI", a form of co-op strategy versus AI. This Redux includes extensive Steam Workshop support- you can download maps on the fly even in-game. It also includes updated models and visual effects, trading cards, achievements, and other niceties- aside from running very smoothly on modern systems, more so then it ever did in the old days. However, it is a essentially a straight re-release, and does not attempt to address any of the game's existing shortcomings- save the netcode, of course.
You are limited, for example, to only ten units of each type, since that's as far as the number keys go, as well as the hard pilot cap of 30. The AI is single-minded at best and suicidal at worst, with frequent issues with pathfinding, often getting stuck trying to scale inclines the player would have no trouble at all with. Scavengers are completely incapable of not only defending themselves but even of reacting to being attacked, and will continue on their merry way scavenging in the face of certain destruction. Artillery units will fire at will regardless of the risk of hitting your own forces and cannot be set to hold their fire. Your offensive units also require careful management ot get the most out of their attacks. The walkers are also so painfully slow that their use in most campaign missions is extremely limited- its entirely possible to finish CCA Mission 6, for example, without the use of the three Golems you are given. Most campaign missions also have only one or two safe methods of completion, with very little room for experimental tactics.
However, most of these flaws are attributable to the limitations of the original game engine, and and while they are even more glaringly obvious all these years later, there is something to be said for bringing the game to Steam and a new audience as is, the way we enjoyed it 18 years ago, and it is certainly easier to forgive then a brand new game with these same flaws. Battlezone was something completely new and any problems it had were excusable in the face of how much fun I had with it, and it was a great pleasure to revisit this landmark title in both my young life and the history of PC gaming. I urge newcomers and old hands, shooter and strategy fans alike to pick this one up. You will not be disappointed.

Rating: 7.5/10
Overview: Third Person Shooter
The Good:
+ 4 campaigns each with 2 characters to select from (except for one campaign). Each campaign has a different feeling to it and depending on which character you select allows you to experience certain parts of the game from a different perspective giving you an incentive to replay the game. At certain points, the campaign stories arc will cross each other which is cool and gives you a different perspective. Each campaign is roughly 5-8 hours long.
+ Lots of graphical/gameplay/camera options
+ Lots of different weapons. Certain characters have their own unique weapons
+ Combat has been modernized. You can now move while aiming, roll, dodge. The most flexible combat in a main title Resident Evil.
+ Mercenary mode makes a return and its probably the best yet given the new improvements to combat. Plenty of levels and characters to choose from.
+ Agent Hunt mode allows you to invade another players game as an enemy.
The Average:
+/- Game has some neat gameplay mechanics that are never explained properly or not at all. Checking a guide will help.
+/- Cover system is poorly implemented and feels clunky compared to almost every other third person shooter on the market.
+/-The story like every other resident evil game is stupid, crazy, over the top non-sense. It serves to hold all the campaign stories together and shoot monsters.
+/- The game really holds your hand the whole way through. Need to open a door, no problem, the game will pinpoint where the keys are, need to pull a lever, the camera will zoom in on the exact lever etc. The developers don’t seem to trust the players to figure things out on their own.
+/- Killing enemies and breaking crates allows you to collect skill points which allows you to upgrade a variety of skills. You can equip 3 skills allowing you to choose the ones that fit your playstyle. A good system but feels like a downgrade compared to Resident Evil 4/5 where you can manually upgrade each gun’s damage, accuracy, reload speed etc.
+/-The Bosses are big, ugly and feel epic to fight but they go on for far too long to the point where its no longer fun.
The Bad:
-This game is littered with quick time events. You can’t play for more than 5 minutes without being bombarded with a quick time event. This game came out at a time when almost every developer decided to abandon qte’s because of how bad they were. Resident evil 6 doubles down on them.
- There are certain sections of game that are terribly designed. Worst of all these sections seem to drag on for far too long. This game has a lot of content but not all content was created equal.
Conclusion:
Resident Evil 6 throws everything at you in the hopes that you will end up liking something it has to offer. This is a difficult game to review because for everything this game does right it has equal parts that are just as bad. After replaying all the resident evils multiple times, this game doesn’t hold up all that well despite the improvements to combat.  This is a game that is a jack of all trades and a master of none.

I'm posting my final verdict of the game up here because the rest of the review is filled to the brim with spoilers.  Pick up this game.  It's short, sweet, and yet, somehow very involved with plenty of secrets.  In the playtime overall listed for me, I have 100% completed this game.  BUY IT!
Now then, on to the main review:
Allow me to be clear, this game is not entirely about ponies.  If you're considering it because ponies, look elsewhere.  If you're looking for a puzzle platformer that messes with your head, you should pick this up.
The game's story isn't flat out told to you, however there are clues if you know where to look.  You play as Theodore, a crusader who died and was sent to purgatory.  While there, you are forced to play a poorly programmed video game.  You recieve help from a hopeless soul, who is likewise trapped in the computer.  As you play, things deteriorate as you match wits with 1u(c)if#r, the programmer of (the In-Universe) Pony Island, and his 3 daemons (Incedently, I love that pun.  Well played Dan).
The game centers around 2 main concepts, the puzzles and the platforming.  Each of these is very well put together, and leads to an enjoyable gameplay experience.  The game is best played with a wired 2-3 button mouse, but you can also use Space and Right Alt (Option).  The puzzle difficulty is staggered very nicely and, with one notable exception, make you feel very smart when you solve them. (At least, that's my subjective view)
The visual style of this game is remenicent of DOS-era PC games, featuring a lot of vector-based artwork.  At least, at first.  One of the greatest things about this game is how it almost perfectly mirrors PC game advances, adding an overworld and eventually full 16-bit color graphics.  The music and sound design is also fantastic.  I purchased this game and the Soundtrack DLC, and both are worth the money.
This game has 24 tickets to collect and 20 achievements.  Be prepared once you get that 24th ticket though.  Once you do, you get whisked away to the true final boss, unless you are playing through the game for the first time, getting every ticket on the way.  Then you will have to wait until the end of the game.  This boss has 3 phases that reflect what you have learned in the platforming portions of the game.  While I'm talking about bosses, I should bring up the daemons.  The first one tests your puzzle skills.  The second one tests your platforming skills.  The third one messes with your head, and it is glorious.  It even tricked me once, and I knew it was coming!  I love when bosses break the 4th wall creatively, so this boss was a nice treat.
Overall, this game is amazing.  If you need another reason to pick up this game, just look for the 200+ post discussion in the community hub.  Give it a read, and you'll see just how much love went into this game.  This game gets my Seal of Recommendation.  GIVE IT A TRY, MORTAL.

As a result, progressing as far as the story actually starting is often the result of accident at best. It took me 4 hours of just wandering around, not knowing what I was supposed to be doing or why.
Once you're able to program there's a bit more direction and less frustration, but you're still not given much reason for doing it until later on.
All in all, stick around if you're really invested in getting to the programming. Otherwise, it's an exercise in frustration and shallow conversations that's not really a lot of fun.
Art's gorgeous though, so the game has that going for it at least.

It's been nearly a year since I bought it, and I have not regretted my purchase at all. It's like Rock Band or Guitar Hero, but you use your own guitar and actually play the songs. And there are plenty of songs to choose from. The base game has a decent enough selection but DLC is where you get the most out it. It's a little expensive though... Three bucks for a single song? I know I'm effectively buying interactive sheet music and the "genuine" guitar tones (most sound REALLY close, but a couple make me wonder if they're actually the real thing or just imitations), but OUCH, my wallet hurts.
Make no mistake, this game is not just the price listed for the base game. You need a guitar, first of all ($$$). You'll also need the Rocksmith cable to hook your guitar up to your PC, sold separately (I think it's like $35). And of course, most of the songs you actually want to play are separate DLC ($$$$).
Despite the overall cost, I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who plays or wants to play guitar. This is a fantastic learning tool, especially in combination with taking guitar lessons from a tutor. Just do yourself a favor and buy it when it's on sale. Go through the DLC page and add songs to your wishlist that you want and pick them up when they're half off. They are still regularly adding songs to the list, and they have a webpage where you can make requests if you don't see a song you were hoping for.

It will not replace a metronome and proper practice though. Much better UI than the original Rocksmith.

Feburary, 2015 was when I first gave this game a review.
I gave it a thumbs up because it had potential.  Sadly I'm going to have to update this review, as of January 2017, and change it to a thumbs down only because I just remembered that I backed this disgrace on both Early Access and then on their (somehow successful) Kickstarter.
I bought this game initially when it first crept onto Steam in Early Access form.  It was a little square of land floating in the endless void where you got to move around a shoddy looking dragon asset, fly around haphazardly and burn some villager and goblin assets.  Even then, in the most barebones, tech-demo-y existence of this game it was more playable then than it is now.  Let this sink in.
Two years ago, the game was more stable than it is right now.
These days, despite a few additions of enemies and ground textures, the game has made almost no positive changes.  But it has made changes.  Oh yes, the game's stability has actually degraded over the last year or so.  The dragon controls terribly, buttons simply do not work, commands are mapped to mouse buttons that don't exist on most commercial mice, enemies still try to kill you long after you killed or even ATE them, the game crashes frequently and such a simple looking game runs awful on even high end computers.
Did I mention there was, or might still be, an achievement that's granted if you go into a cave lair and get stuck there?  Because that's acceptable.  The lair isn't there anymore, to my knowledge.
There is nothing redeeming here.  There's no fun gameplay loop here.  It's a herculean effort just to get the game to work on your computer.
The thing that really stings the most is the complete lack of communication from the developers to their EA Steam community.  Long bouts of silence broken up by non-updates if the community got too silent and goes so far as to childishly insult its concerned stakeholders because they are rightfully upset about the product they might have double-dipped funds into in hopes it would become their dream dragon game.
I really wanted this game to be good.  I still do, in fact!  But honestly, if its incredibly small but incredibly dedicated fanbase tried, they could probably make a far better game in half the time.
Pros?  Nothing.  Cons?  Everything.
Avoid.  The Dragon Dream remains a dream, for now.

It's a pretty neat game that feels very much like a strategy board game with (mostly) pretty good mechanics. The "board" is this sort of spinning wheel that you move across each turn by spending tokens. There are 4 lanes representing social castes, you start on the inner most lane, the labor caste, and can build up points to move out one track at a time.(artisans, noble professions, ruling class) Each track up increases complexity slightly until you reach the top rank where an additional mini game begins each turn you have to make civ-like decisions on how to distribute grain through the city or how to use troops to attack neighbors, etc.
I had fun for a few hours until I reached the end of the first age, the copper age, and once the bronze age started just got sent back down to the artisan caste to work my way back up again. Soon after this I realized the game was just going to be this same thing pretty much over and over until whatever "age" it decided it was done. (description on steam says it's 15 hours and I played about 9, I'm not sure I'm really up for another 6.
Anyway, the game is fun for a few hours but compared to other games you can get for the price I think $15 is a bit steep. I'm pretty sure I picked it up for ~$1 in a humble bundle sale. If you can get it cheap it's worth checking out if you like a good strategy board game.

Removed at the request of developer. Will be updated at a later time when I get around to playing the improved REDUX version,

== Update for Redux ==
This update is amazing. Each squad member having their own set of actions is exactly what I thought it would be from the beginning and I love it. Arcade and Campaign modes are both great ways to replay the game with different pacing. The reworked health and damage is nice since you don't have to worry so much about your units getting one-shot. Being able to finally choose your starting crews and factions is great. This feels like the game that should have been released from the start.
I can't give the devs enough credit for their response to player feedback. They've been awesome.
== Update 02-11 for Patch 2.0 ==
Bleh. I still don't like combat, and now you're forced to waste you're already limited actions per turn to farm resources on the battle grid because of the loss of the resource rewards after combat. I hate that change. Should I attack the enemy in the middle of combat or should I run to some corner of the battlefield to collect some steaks? It's completely anti-fun to me to do that.
Thumbs back down.
== Update 24-09 for Patch 1.5 ==
Patch 1.5 is a big improvement for perceived difficulty caused by RNG. Board placement is fair, though I'm not sure if completely eliminating ambush maps was necessary. It was bad getting them 3-4 times in a row, but now it doesn't seem to ever happen. Achievements seem to work now (aside from the high score achievements not also counting for the score achievements below it) and now you can actually complete the game after you kill King Viscera's 4th form.
The cover change is great since now you can rely on it when planning your two moves. It seems to be a really harsh penalty to Gunslingers though since after rounding their damage becomes 1. You can pretty much ignore enemy gunslingers in cover now. Frontliners and Trenchers can ignore cover at point blank and Deadeyes at rookie still do at least 2 damage. I never see my Gunslingers retaliate either; they might need some kind of buff.
I'm so far not really liking the leveling changes. It was already grindy to me before and now it seems more so. Elite units take 8 kills to level now instead of 5, which wasn't in patch notes. With reduced numbers of enemies and the elimination of the mandatory fight, there is less kills to get before you get to the first elite. A lot of times I get to the first elite without any veterans now, which makes that fight pretty rough. Badlam difficulty is slight easier to level than Normal now because there are slightly more enemies - which seems backward. Recruiting new non-elite units still feels like a waste; like I want to bring some rookie unit into a Severe/Bedlam threat level combat. With the normal unit leveling change, it seems like more level grinding now to fight KV.
The loss of the x2 Power bonus kind of sucks. Power seems much harder to get now and reliant on risking units to collect the map powerups. I'm not sure how I feel about it yet, but KV fights still seem reliant on hording a lot of Power before Aztec City (based on continuing the unfinished game I had pre-1.5 waiting for the end game bug to be fixed). This combined with the leveling change maintains the POI grind you have to do before Aztec City. I'm not sure if that fits with the fast-paced rush to AC that the developers seem to want. I feel like leveling should be either quicker or easier to spread among units (instead of funneling kills into a few units). Farming every POI you can to gather Power shouldn't feel necessary either. KV still has a crap-ton of HP, so fighting him still requires equalizer spamming and hoping that you find the good ones by then.
Overall, I really like this patch. I think it just needs a little more tweaking to the pacing (i.e. grinding), maybe slight balance tweaks to KV (which would decrease grinding and improve pacing), and some improvement to the random events to make the decisions you make seem more impactful. Even though I'm still not much of a fan of the 2AP system, I'd be more inclined to recommend the game to people who like roguelikes and chess so I'm flipping my thumbs down to a thumbs up. Developer response to feedback has been awesome; they deserve a lot of credit.
The Good:
* Post-apocalyptic setting like Wasteland/Fallout/Mad Max always makes my nipples hard.
* Graphics and animation. Nothing is more satisfying than melting people with Chunderok's barf attack, blasting the flesh from their skeleton with a Gunslinger, or kicking someone in the nuts and elbow dropping them as they double over.
* Losing due to randomness is much less decreased, and more likely your own fault now.
* Turn-based combat (with a caveat below).
* Developer response to feedback and patching.
* Seeing my name in big gold letters in the credits.
The Bad:
* 2 actions per turn isn't my cup of tea and not generally well-received by players. It resembles chess and I don't like chess. If you do, this isn't really a bad point.
* Random event decisions don't really matter much. Some events have no impact at all except for wasting your resources to get there.
* Leveling and farming Power Cells is tedious, despite the intent for a fast-paced game.
The Ugly:
* My pants after I rage-sh!t myself because I made a mistake that kills one of my Elites or high level Frontliners.
== Update 18-09 ==
Recent patches made the Blitz much less catastrophic, so it's not as punishing anymore. I still wish it was a usable mechanic for players and not just CPU. The limited actions still makes it seem like chess to me (I hate chess). Patches brought much improvement though.
I'd say if you like roguelikes and chess, this is right up your alley. If there was a rating between "yes" and "no" I'd upgrade to that, simply because devs are so responsive to tuning yet not giving in to lowering difficulty. I was always fine with the difficulty; it was just the random elements that crush you were too annoying. I feel like the game could've used more time in Early Access for tuning, when people may be less critical of flaws. Games like this are hard to evaluate in the 2 hour limit that Steam gives refunds, so that first impression for a final product probably brought a lot of negative response.
== Original Review ==
It sucks not liking this game when you're a Tier 7 backer. I just can't recommend it because the combat system is so abhorrent. Having just two actions to split among your team is so crippling. Even if the difficulty was drastically lowered, I can't imagine having two actions will ever be fun. It ensures that only one of your units can move into position and attack per round. It forces you to choose just 2 units to move into cover after RNG surrounds you with enemies from the start of combat. It makes having a team of more than 3 or 4 units useless. It's hard trying to convince yourself that there is strategy when there's so few options on what to do each turn - either move 2 units, move and attack with 1 unit, or attack twice with 1 or 2 units. And the Blitzmeter just punishes you for even participating in combat. It might as well be a random tornado that kills 2 or 3 of your units. It's a horrible mechanic. It makes you want to avoid combat as much as possible, but unfortunately that's 90% of the gameplay.
It plays similarly to FTL, but in FTL failing felt more like my fault rather than just being a victim of randomness and the Blitzmeter.
Nice graphics and animations though.

Fans of Judge Dredd / 200AD, turn-based strategy games / tabletop games, and anything with a wasteland/apocalyptic setting will feel right at home here :)
This is quite a challenging game. It's of that genre, and you will die! Not every run will be successfull, and sometimes RNG will cause your veteren sniper to be killed in 1 hit  (delicious permadeath) - with no possible way of you avoiding it. Yup, these things will happen, so if you are fine with that and enjoy games of a simular nature (X-com being a good example), then this game could be for you.
The actual gameplay comes in two halves. The first involves navigating the worl map and essentially plotting the course for your 'Dozer', choosing which path to take and where to stop and explore. Travelling the waste will use resources, which you can restock during your travels. These resources (meat, crude and energy) can also be used to upgrade and enhance your Dozer / units throughout your journey.
The other half of the game is combat. It's turn based, and uses a 2AP/moves per turn system. It's worth noting that unlike X-com where you can controll/move your entire squad each turn, this game just allows the use of those two action points. So after selecting a unit, moving it, and then ordering it to fire. Your turn will end and the enemy will then do the same. Those 2 action points may be spent however you wish (moving the same unit twice, ordering a unit to fire twice, making one guy move and another fire, etc). As a result of this you really do have to study the battlefield and consider your movements before doing anything, acting too hastly can have serious consequences (did I mention delicious permadeath?).

Regardless of any of its merits, the fatal flaw of this game is simply terrible performance - as the game progresses laying track & stations becomes increasingly more laggy, to the point of absurdity (e.g. following behind the mouse cursor by tens of seconds).  This is somewhat inexplicable, because while not ugly, the game is quite old at this point and very undemanding graphically.  Perplexingly, animations remain smooth even while it descends into hellish control lagginess.
In any case, even if that were fixed, it'd be just an okay game at best.  It is indeed a dumbed-down version of the Railroad Tycoon series, of which I was very fond (particularly Railroad Tycoon 3).  Unfortunately there were some poor choices made as to
to simplify it.  You can't zoom out to a decent level or otherwise see a usable overview of goods availability & demand, making route planning unnecessarily difficult & tedious.  Cities move magically out of the way of your tracks & buildings, which seems convenient at first but also makes it excessively easy for competing companies to lay track right into your cities, creating almost comically over-complex networks of overpasses.  Constructing your own industry buildings is, according to the tutorial, prohibitively expensive, but it really isn't, which makes it very easy to just build convenient routes out of nothing, undermining one of the fundamental gameplay premises of rewarding careful analysis & forward planning.
I could go on.  Granted it's a cheap game, but having spent just a few hours playing it, I'm done.  There are many, many far more entertaining and enticing games available on Steam.

If you like puzzle platformers and snarky British narrators, I cannot recommend this enough. Each shape has a special ability (except Chris, poor Chris): Thomas jumps high; Claire swims; Laura is a trampoline; etc. The level organization does a near-perfect job of introducing the shapes, letting you use them, and familiarizing you with their abilities with the group. The group completes a puzzle when each one reaches their goal: a white portal specific to each shape. The variability with the portal locations and the shape mechanics creates interesting and challenging puzzles.
Did I mention the narrator? Other than quotes shown at the beginning of each chapter that explain a major AI malfunction, he's responsible for progressing the story. And he's wonderful. He shares the shapes' thoughts as they meet each other, judge each other, fall in love, pretend to be superheroes, and everything in between. These shapes have better character development than I've seen in AAA games.
I do have a few quibbles. Alternating between the shapes isn't consistent. Some of the cooperative mechanics between shapes were cumbersome, which is fine for one puzzle. When you require that solution for multiple puzzles, it gets repetitive and frustrating. Such small critiques. Go play the game and enjoy its charming and simple nature.

Thomas was Alone, and then he wasn't.  There is good and bad to the game sadly.  This game gets a load of hype about how it's fantastic and full of feels, in some ways it is but in a lot of ways it isn't.  The beginning, introducing the main characters is done very well, full of smiles and fun and you think that this will eventually lead to a great pay off or bittersweet ending.  Unfortunently it kinda doesn't ever really pay off.  With as few spoilers as possible, game tries to give a meaningful payoff and TRIES to have some kind of feels, but I just never really felt it.  In that way it dissapoints, and not by a little.  I want to reccomend the game for the beginning, but the ending just never does it.
In addition, as much as I hate to trash a story-based game for its gameplay, however it IS the foundation to the core game.  The gameplay can get annoying and resulted in me having to turn off and come back later.  What's wrong with it?  In the beginning of the game only two characters are introduced, and the only controls that are TOLD to you is to press Q or E to swap between them.  This can get annoying because the other of the characters can change, and just scrolling through them can leave you on the wrong one.  When the character count increases to 5, 6, 7?!!  You cannot play this way, and I learned that each character, when loaded to the level, is assigned a number and you can select the character through that number.  The other problem, none of these are labeled.  So I had many times where I thought a character was one number, then had to AGAIN, scroll through numbers to get the one I want.  When some levels are time-based, this is not fun, and I smash the game for it so much because it would be fixed BY JUST LABELING THE CHARACTERS.
But yeah, it's a good game.

This could be a very good game, fast paced lots of weapon selections etc.  But the problem is most people purchase this game for its multiplayer aspect.  This is where the problem lies.  First dedicated servers are far and few between.  Those that do exist are typically empty.  There is currenty 10 times more action on COD4 servers today then there are on this games dedicated servers.  The next problem is rampant cheating.  You will find at least one cheater in every two or three games.  The most common form of cheating in this game is wall hacking.
