7 Grand Steps is an ambitious game. It provides a single-player boardgame experience against computer-controlled AI characters set amongst the classic ages of history. Unfortunately, the experience is enormously crippled by the random elements of the game. Progress often feels the benefit of luck, and the frequent impediments to your progress are frustrating and feel beyond player control. While the various storylines you'll encounter are somewhat engaging, they are often hopelessly vague. Character choices that work for one individual utterly fail for another. While training children is an important part of the game, the parents can reproduce beyond their means, such that nurturing each child becomes impossible. Should you choose to dote on one child, rivalries will develop which hinder progress down the line.
While progress is exciting, especially from Age to Age, due to the strange and random nature of the game, you could be forced to play one Age for a great length of time. As you are forced to make the same choices again and again, the tedium weighs the experience down, such that slogging through the wheel becomes a chore. While you may find the game has an instant surface appeal, it doesn't ultimately hold up. The lives of the characters in the game feel beyond any meaningful influence, and each turn eventually feels mechanical.
The initial wonder of the experience was greatly muted after a few hours of play, to the point that I couldn't explain why I continued to play. The structure of 7 Grand Steps is intriguing, but sadly, it is a flawed creation. "Winning" the game is an empty achievement: the end result of many hours of token creation in a blind universe.

Human history is often presented as a grand story of great individuals. Movements and ideas are humanized, given life. But for many years history was defined more about the ties of family. In 7 Grand Steps you start as a couple living hand to mouth in the fields of the Copper Age. These two are married, have children, work with and against their fellows to survive and perhaps thrive, and then they die. But their death is only the next step as you take the role of one of their children and continue the story of this ancestral line and, in doing so, you continue the story of the human race.
The grand wheel of life is represented by a playing mechanism where your descendent and their spouse are placed along with other "families" along a track in a quarter of a wheel. The wheel contains spaces with pictograms, and you move you and your spouse ahead (literally symbolizing "getting ahead" in life) by playing tokens matching those pictograms. Each turn you make your move, and then the wheel of life makes it turn, pushing you back. You must keep ahead of the end of the wheel, lest your mother and father tokens meet an early end. You must decide when to not move forward but make an investment in order to have the tokens to move later. You must compete with the computer-controlled players for "advancement discs" that allow your tokens to become a hero of legend, make a new discovery or raise their social status. And when the wheel comes to an end for your husband and wife, you must pass your inheritence onto your children and hope they can achieve what their ancestors left undone.
The game is clever in how it creates metaphors through game mechanics. For example, one goal you can set for your family is to rise in social status. If you do this, your characters move to a different, literally high track on the game wheel. There's a new set of pictograms on this track, and you may find your characters transitioning between classes for a generation or two. The higher the track, the more diverse the pictograms (representing more varied economic opportunities for those in higher social classes) and the track of the wheel goes longer per generation (representing the increased life span of those in higher social classes). The central conceit of the game - using early 20th century carnival game machines to represent the "wheel of life" - is an interesting take an old and hackneyed cliche, thanks to the strangely nostaglic feel achieved in reproducing an analog machine.
7 Grand Steps has that addictive "just one more turn" quality of a game like Civilization. However, it does not have the kind of strategic depth of Civilization, or at least not the breadth of strategies. There's certainly strategies to be a more effective player of the game of life (lives, really, untold generations' worth), but the core mechanics of the game are fairly narrow. The game mechanics open up when your family reaches the ruling caste level (the highest level), but for the first three castes the game focuses on the push-and-pull of investing tokens to achieve your family's goals while having enough tokens to move where you want to move on the board and avoid being pushed off the wheel to your death. Random events occur that can result in your family gaining or losing tokens, which can be annoying as you have no control over when these happen or whether they are positive or negative effects. You play this over and again until you reach the "Challenge of the Era", a scenario where your current family member must survive a catacysm of the era using the legend status and inventions of their family. Survive and you move onto the next age. Fail, and you'll go back to an earlier ancestor so they can try to succeed where the other branch of the family could not.
This is the first of what seems to be poised as a series. Despite the title, I don't think that having seven games in this series is going to happen. A sequel to the game is promised at the end of this game, which contains three eras, and functionality that will allow you to import your family from the first game is promised. In fact, a file is saved at the end of the game for this purpose. I'm not aware of any date of release for the second game, but 7 Grand Steps: What Ancients Begat stands on its own as a fun game for those who want to chart the course of human history through the struggles and triumphs of a single family line. If it sounds dry and academic, I assure you, it's not. It's maddeningly addictive as you become attached to the family you've created, generation by generation.

Battlezone is a game that was way ahead of its time when it was first released in 1998. It seamlessly blended FPS and RTS gameplay in a way that has yet to be matched by another game (apart from the sequel: BZII). Not only can the player build and direct units in battle, but they can participate directly in those battles themselves.
I remember playing Battlezone consistently for several years, until I got my hands on Battlezone II: Combat Commander. My grades suffered because of this obsession. To see that it had been remastered was exciting. At only 15 dollars (20% off sale), it was an easy impulse purchase.
Rebellion has done a swell job of remastering this game. The gameplay is essentially the same as it was in 1998 (apart from bug fixes). Everything just feels right. With the substantial graphical overhaul, the style of the game has been neatly retained. There is no dissonance between my nostalgic memories of the original and the improved fidelity of this remaster.
The story is an incredibly captivating Cold War era sci-fi alternate history. Rebellion has also bolstered the mod support of the game with Steam Workshop integration and mod tools. Mods from the original can also be ported into the remaster. I'm eager to see what the community can do with this new opportunity.
I look forward to playing this for years to come.

So I'm going to start with the criticisms first.
The "Joystick" controls are not very good.  You have a bunch of default settings for some Joystick types, XBox Controller and Steam Controller but none of them are re-bindable and a prime example is the self-destruct button is bound to X.  There seems to be little support for modern HOTAS joysticks like the X55 (and I enjoyed playing this game back in 1998 with my Throttle joystick, I would love to be able to do it again). I would note though that keyboard bindings are fully configurable.
I also forgot how annoying the *beep* *beep* noise is when an enemy approaches, and firing this up near midnight the misses wasn't too happy with the annoying noises.  Would be nice to have more options to turn that stuff off.
HOWEVER other than this, really it's the same great game that is was 18 years ago but looking a bit sharper. The only thing that hasn't transfered well is the FMV sequences but that is to be expected for a retro title like this.

You know what is the saddest thing of Battlezone Redux? That they do not make games like this anymore.  I will try now to stay away from my 18 years long nostalgia and do an accurate review.
Battlezone is a mix between RTS and FPS/Simulation, as you will probably know. The gameplay mechanics are very well integrated into this concept: While piloting your hovertank through several solar system worlds, you can control your production ships, combat units, defense, support vessels.... Anything simply with your numbers, tab and space. It is a system that requires a bit of playing to learn but, once you do, it becomes really intuitive.
From an strategy point of view, you have a very limited number of units in play. That is, 10 offense, 10 defense, 10 support. With those, you must overplay your opponents to actually win the game. If you combine that with limited resources (in the form of biometal) and ships that, when destroyed, become a little ammount of biometal, you have the key for very dinamic multiplayer games. A failed attack against the enemy base may mean that your enemy will get extra resoureces, while you will loose yours. Tough decission, right?
The simulation and FPS system is a combination of your piloting skills, the tank you have and how you outfit it, specially in the latest game. The best definition of it is "ground based dogfight": To pilot a hovertank that flies at about 3 feet from the ground, jumping over the obstacles and maybe flying over your enemy to rain death on him... That's majestic. Of course many players will feel confused with the handling, as this game represent very well the "hovering" mechanics... but that's part of the fun. A direct hit may send your tank flying away, and you may need a moment to retake control of it.
About the rework: I love it... but the nostalgic kid inside of me tell me "that's not my game!". I really like how it looks: the new models, explosions, particle and light effects... It is really a HUGE improvement, profiting the potential that average computers nowadays can offer. But old players as I may find it... strange. The feeling is the same than when you watch your favourite movie dubbed in a different language. It may be very good but... it's not the same.
And about the campaigns:
The campaign story is amazing.  New players may find it linear (yes, it is) and a bit topical for the first 2 or 3 missions. All this changes when you find, in Mars, an alien relic... that relates directly to an ancient human civilisation. And I will not spoil anything there, but if you like mithology as I do... You will be mind-blowed. Specially when the real enemy shows up in the end!
My recommendation for new players: Give battlezone redux a try. The mix of RTS and FPS may feel strange at first, but when you get a handle on it you will be amazed of the epicness it can handle! Deploy your recycler and get those scavengers! Get the biometal while defending them with a few scouts! Get your defenses, but move closer to a new biometal deposit! Get your army, and lead them into battle, charge against the enemy while the bomber's missiles fly just over your head! And find out no pilot, not even you, is good enough to win every battle alone!
Battlezone is a relic, one that has not been repeated since its sequel "BZ2 battle commander"... so try it. It is really worth the money.

Usually when a game gets released during Q1 of the new year, there aren't high hopes for it succeeding due to the intense Q4 of the previous year with massive triple A titles coming out the cut and wanting all the attention. However, for Pony Island, this caught my attention after watching the Yogscast do a short episode about it. I was intrigued that some guy decided to make a game titled Pony Island.
But here's where I went wrong...
Pony Island isn't some happy go-lucky game where you control some person riding a pony and frolicking in the wilderness. It's a game where you know that the decisions you make impact you as the player and the character you are mimicking. When it comes to indie games, they love using dark themes because it provides that depth most games don't have. In Pony Island, there is no such thing as a linear story. There is reason behind each statement and it's a psychological thriller. Yes, clicking and shooting lazers is all fun and games, but when you are trying to secure your own freedom from the grasp of a devil like creature (Satan, in this case), you will do anything in your power to be freed from the oppression.
This is why I'm giving this game a definite 9.5/10. The story, art style, and music mesh really well together and gave me a positive experience despite the fact that some parts are really repetitive. I hope you guys enjoy the game as much as I did because man, this is one of the best games I've played so far that came out this year.
FULL RATING:
Story: 9.8/10
Gameplay: 9.4/10
Music: 9.5/10
Art: 9.2/10

A rare occasion in hacking games is playing a normal guy/girl. You are not an elite hacker, or activist making clandestine moves against the man. At least you don't start that way, which allows you to get into the role a lot better than being told who you are. Sebastian starts out completely in the dark, just as the player and with all the cheering about games that don't hold your hand, this one has gotten a lot of flak for that very same reason. I think it's really the camera that will break your heart though. Replayability is pretty much required as it will take a lot of time just to get a sense of the city.
Hacking/Programming is also very unique compared to other hacking games as everything from coffee, to doors, to turtles are open for your crazy experimentation.
* Find song names scattered around in jukeboxes and discs and program your hand radio to play your faves!
* Low on cash? Repurpose an arcade cabinet into an ATM! (one of my favorite projects :)
* Looking for someone you can't find? Hack into one of the tourist placefinders and program it to lead you to him/her!
The possibilities may not be endless, but you aren't likely to run out of things to do. Just make your own fun and don't blame the game for not 'giving' you a purpose! It's kind of a life simulator in that way and you need to make your own path. It can undoubtedly be frustrating, but there is a lot of reward and fun waiting on the other side of that.
TL;DR - Try again.

Rayman: Origins is a 2D side-scrolling, platforming adventure with full four-player local co-op.
Rayman accidentally started a war with the Livid Dead, the monsters lurking beneath the otherwise peaceful Glade of Dreams.
The protagonist must work his way through a series of themed stages, collecting floating objects called "Lums", and rescuing critters known as "Electoons" from hidden cages. Reaching certain Lum targets can earn extra "Electoons", which unlock new levels and characters.
Besides of jumping Rayman learns new skills such as hovering, swimming and shrinking, bringing a compelling variety to the action, and testing your dexterity to the limits.
On your way you have to cross floating platforms, dissolving platforms, platforms that twist and turn, that bounce you into the air or slowly fall and fade.
Rayman: Origins has impressive graphics, the backgrounds are beautifully drawn and has multiple layers of action.
The levels vary from familiar takes on platforming staples – cloud levels and underwater levels – to such oddities as a world based on didgeridoos.
Alongside the standard platforming levels, there are boss encounters, and scrolling shoot-'em-up challenges in which you leap on to a mosquito and fly through formations of angry birds and spiky puffer fish.
Rayman Origins features drop-in/drop-out cooperative play for up to four players at a time and as long as one of you stays alive to free injured players from bubbles in which they become trapped when hit, progress through a level remains possible.
Everywhere there is humour and whimsy, every screen a feast of bizarre scenery and weird inhabitants.
Rayman: Origins is one of the best platforming experiences you are going to have on Steam. The game is crafted with so much love, so much humor, and does so many things right, that it is impossible not to have a blast. It is definitly worth the money.

Ok so first off, I did not like Watch Dogs 1, I think it was pure trash but the concept was nice. Watch Dogs 2 on the other hand takes what they tried to do with the first one and improves on it a lot, but there are still some issues. Here's how I feel so far, this may change after I've progressed further into the game.
-The opening mission and the cutscenes following it are fantastic
-Optimization is decent, I have 60+ fps on a mix of high and very high settings.
-Graphics look great, the exact same as the first E3 showcase
-Stealth gameplay has been improved
-Story so far is surprisingly well-written and is filled with satire, the comedy style is very similar to GTA V but with more focus on tech and other nerdy things like corny 80s action films. Main characters can be a blend of funny and cringe-worthy, but I kinda do expect a bunch of social outcast hackers to be cringe-worthy at times.
-The game seems to be FILLED with unique side missions with their own little stories
-San Francisco looks fantastic and the game world is way more alive this time, people walking their dogs, random deer on the outskirts of the city, hacking into random phone conversations and listening to strange and interesting little stories, people being stopped by police, more world interaction in general.
-Fair amount of good music on the radio (Danny Brown, Run The Jewels, M|O|O|N, Aphex Twin etc)
-Hacking is improved LOADS from the first one, with way more opportunities.
-Parkour system is improved
-Gunplay is also improved from the first one
-Even though it is improved, the gunplay is still quite mediocre (especially compared to games like GTA V)
-Movement can feel a bit wonky at times (Some have compared the character movement to the handling of a shopping cart, which is kind of accurate, but it's not THAT bad)
-Driving is still god awful for the majority of vehicles
-Enemy AI can be pretty stupid at times
-Occasional FPS drops
Atm I'm feeling a light

Pros:
1.  The map : You can roam around all of SF, it's huge and it's lively. Devs must have put in a lot of work mapping a whole real city in a game.
2. The phone's music feature is kinda new, usually you can listen to songs while driving right ? well guess what, in WD2 you have a music app that you can play throughout the game (you can't put in your own songs but WTH it's still cool).
3. Story rich.Characters are cool, especially Wrench and Marcus' duo.
4. Parkour is great, and if you go out and do the side missions, like collecting money bags or skill points, trust me some of them really take a lot of work and thinking, it gives me a weird sense of satisfaction when I collect a difficult to reach item.
5. The online part, the hacking invasion part is the same as Watch Dogs 1 but adding the drones to the equation makes it a whole lot interesting, it's hard to do if you are up against a skilled player but nevertheless it's a thrilling experience to not be caught.
Cons:
1. Even on the best of PC hardware the FPS is limited to around 60-ish (I have a GTX 980 and i6 4690K with 16 GB Corsair Vengeance RAM)
2. The nudle map is kinda annoying to me, I mean it's all great and all but it's difficult to locate yourslelf given the really small and indistinguishable blue marker.
3. For most part the online part works good, but it's still a little buggy.
4. Not much detail given to driving and cars. I mean if you compare it to GTA V, it just doesn't feel all that great to drive.
My score : 8.5/10
Overall : Definitely a good game and recommended.I hope some performance patch is released soon.

Thomas Was Alone is a puzzle platformer I've taken my time getting to. It's been on my radar for quite some time, but only this steam sale did I finally decide to pick it up and play through the game. What greeted me was something quite... Unexpected. I had no real idea what I was getting into aside from shapes and platforming puzzles, but the narrative, sound design and colourful (quite literally) cast of characters kept me invested through my three hour play time.
The gameplay of Thomas Was Alone is simple. Each level, you will start with a set amount of rectangle/square shapes of different colours and you use them to move throughout the environment to portals at the end of each level. Each shape has it's own portal to get to and all shapes must touch the portals at the same time to move on. Each of the shapes have unique characteristics and personalities. For example, the red rectangle, Thomas, is a hero who's got average jump height. Then there's the orange square Chris who can't jump as high. John is a yellow rectangle with a massive jump height and the rest of the cast adds more to the mix (Swimming, Bouncing, Double Jump and reversed gravity).
Each of these new power ups are easy to understand, hard to master. But lucky for you guys, the difficulty in this game doesn't go too steep. Very rarely did I find myself using the restart level function. There are ten main chapters of the story, segregated into 10 levels per chapter. On top of that there are two bonus chapters featuring another character, Benjamin, who uses a jetpack to fly through the levels. The jetpack mechanic takes a lot of getting used to and doesn't handle very well, it made these extra chapters an absolute slog to play through, but the story kept me going.
So let's discuss the story in minor detail. Thomas is an AI that becomes self-aware of his environment. We get little quotes at the beginning of chapters detailing the events of the game as historic events. Thomas is apparently known as an "Architect" and the seven shapes you encounter throughout Chapters 1-8 are important in this regard. The characters are all fun and memorable from the miserable Chris, the Wonder-woman Claire, the frantic Sarah and the sinister Gray!
This game isn't perfect though. The final chapter feels extremely rushed from a narrative standpoint. It tries to tie up loose ends a little too quickly and some characters literally just drop of the face of the earth, like they were never relevant. The puzzles do get more difficult, yet the difficulty spike of the game is very much a rollercoaster. Some levels are easy to cruise through, others not so much.
But overall, this is a game I would very much recommend. If you haven't already, pick up this game and give it a shot, you might find yourself caring about these little coloured shapes afterall.

Another update 18/09
So after putting some more hours into it, I have a gripe that stems directly from the combat system. The longer you roam the wasteland, the more notoriety you have which is reflected by levels of threat (low -> guarded -> eleveted -> severe -> bedlam), akin in theory to the FTLs chase system, where it discouraged 'farming' or basically taking too much time. However, in practic, the threat level of bedlam does not coexist with its combat system, through which threat is represented. For each threshold you surpass, the battles are supposed to get tougher by simply putting more enemies on the battlefield. You face the same type of enemy units throughout the game, so they have the same health and damage throughout your whole journey. What is broken here, is that late in the game you encounter the same weak (as compared to your badass elite units) henchmen, but there are just way more of them, however, the numbers advantage they seemingly posses is mitigated by the two moves per turn system. Therefore, out of 15 enemies, only two, or even one move towards to attack you - easy pickings for your hardened lot. The rest is just grouped in the corner waiting their turn to enter the meat grinder.
The only battle headache is the random placement system, which can really put in a tough predicament right from the start. Still, you always go first in battle so you can immediately activate shields, damage absorbers or flat-out nuke clustered enemies.
In essence, you just drive around wasteland, hoping to unlock a new dozer (I didn't unlock anything yet), and scoring levels (= more damage output). And boy, you'll need your elites levelled if you are to have any chances with boss. What does it mean? If you manage to survive your first 20 minutes, you're rolling and the game gets grindy fast. Still, the potential is there, the game just needs tweaking.
Update 17/09
So I kind of finished the game on normal.
Let me say this. There are two difficulty bumps after which the game is a breeze (at least on normal). You hit the first bump right after the start - you only have rookies, who, for the most part, won't withstand more than one shot. Keeping them alive and leveling them is the tricky part. Some of them will die, but their sacrifice allows you to keep a force of capable veterans. Then, you gonna find the first elite recruitable. After the moderately hard battle, he/she joins. Elites are powerful units - they have more health, and their damage output raises each time they level. By the end of the game, one of my elites dished out 16 damage per shot (which means one-shotting regular and elite enemies, the only exception being the boss). I'd say that's pretty deadly.
The second difficulty bumps comes right after you established a foothold with your now veteran troops. The resources. All of a sudden, your fuel and food are almost depleted. If you manage to gather some, you good. But that's random, as most of it comes from points of intrests that hide a random encounter. It could be your precious fuel, or a band of cyborgs.
After that, you just steamroll. More elites join you, they level, you gather more powerful equipment for your dozer to use in battle (like a nuke, or a shield granting immunity to damage and regenerates your health each time someone hits you for one turn), etc. Most of the time I fielded my 3 elites and they mopped the floor with like 15 enemies without taking a scratch.
As for the random encounters, I'd like to see more crew-specific, contextual interactions. There were only a handful during my 3 hour playthrough, and I'd would greatly enhance the feeling of accomplishment and connection to your crewmembers if they had more options to interact during encounters. As it stands now, half of the encounters don't even give you any option to pick - just a quick, flavor text and that's it. Hell, I don't mind losing my guys because of a choice I made in a random encounter!

---- Original review ----
I cannot recommend Bedlam in its current, underdeveloped state, as it lacks certain, IMO, fundamental features.
I do not share many reviewers' concerns about overall unbalance of the combat mechanics. I think two moves in a turn spent on whatever by whoever is an interesting concept. It just requires getting used to. However, I do have an issue with how uninteresting and not varied the characters are mechanically-wise. I.E. You start with 4 snipers, each of whom has the exact same stats. Like carbon copies. Same for your 4 gunslingers (each has 5 health, 3 damage, 3-4 range, 4 move). A wasted opportunity right from the start, a little mix up in the roster would greatly improve the decision-making process. Said gunslingers should all bee a wee bit different. Like imagine, one gunslinger with 4 health and 3 range, but 3-5 damage. Another one with 5 health, 2-4 damage, 2-4 range, and 3 move. You know, some tactical flavor.
Once a character levels up (after scoring three kills), their combat usefullness increases dramatically, and their stats go up in a fixed manner, which means we do not get to allocate any skill points. A real shame - the way it was in Banner Saga kept things interesting - there you could specialize classes, having direct control of how and what function a given unit would perform on the battlefield. What a wasted opportunity! For instance, I would heavily invest in health for my sniper given the chance, granting him survivability, but at the cost of lower damage output. I would increase the range and quickness of my shotgun unit, making them glass cannons, etc. Choices is what we need, to further adjust the characters to our playstyle.
Unfortunately, there are no active/passive skills either (sniper is the most 'exciting' class, as they have a passive chance for a headshot each shot), so there is no incetive to use your lesser units, as they are prone to dying extremely fast and cannot really dish out any proper damage. If the vanilla troops had a skill, like for instance your tank having a charge, or granade to use once per battle, that would justify using them in certain situations, even if they do not scale to the enemy stats-wise. Currently what happens is you end up using your two moves on your badassest guy, and reasonably so! A skill-tree, like choose one skill out of two per level - that's what Bedlam needs.
Same goes for equipment. It's all bound to a character and is unchangable. Your frontliners will use a simple melee weapon, always dealing 2 damage. After the level up, the damage will increase, but it's always a fixed value. You cannot influence it in any way, your troops gonna deal the exact same amout of damage each time they attack. Instead of a boring 3 damage each shot, why not introduce a 2-4 mechanics? What about finding weapons as you travel along the wasteland? We don't need an abundance of them - just a few to spice it up.
Apart from combat and character progression, the Dozer's upgrade system seems to be lacking. There are four areas of research - bio research (slower food consumption), armory (less power cells spent for using dozer's special equipment), barracks (faster soldier recovery), and engineering (less fuel used). By spending power cells, you can improve each, up to a level 5. Each level grants a % improvement in efficiency. And that's it. It could have been a small research tree for each research area, with at least a few passive bonuses to choose from, maybe an active bonus here and there. As it stands now, it just feels underdeveloped.
Nevertheless, the art, the feel, the world, the atmosphere, it's all here, and it creates a fantastic coherent entity.
In essence, the potential of Bedlam is huge, it may even surpass FTL, but as it stands, I cannot recommended it, even though I wish I could.

The font is supremely readable. The fact that I'm calling that the absolute best thing about this game says more about most strategy games than this particular strategy game so I'll review the thing properly too.
Bedlam is Banner Saga (engine and all) meets Mad Max meets roguelike. It's a largely randomized game where your goal is to get from the top of the screen (a city called Bysantine) aaaaall the way to the bottom of the screen (Aztec City) in a Dozer... which is a tank. Sure it might sound like a bulldozer but I assure you it is not. You must upgrade your Dozer with power cells, feed refugees with MEAT, and keep your fuel gauge as full as possible with CRUDE. You've also got soldiers who fit neatly within four classes: Deadeyes (squishy snipers,) Frontliners (tanks with bonesaws and riot shields,) Gunslingers (adaptable mid-range damage dealers) and Trenchers (close-range shotgun specialists.) These soldiers are renamable and have unique backstories that you will not read because they will die very quickly. Oh yeah, this game is HARD! It IS a roguelike after all.
During battles, which are faster paced than most in the genre, you and the enemy can move twice per turn. Not per character ala Banner Saga, per turn. Everyone is randomly placed too so you'd better move your squishies to cover so they'll get a 50% dodge chance. Along with cover, there are also MEAT, CRUDE, POWER, and explosive boxes littered around the map. Pick up some of those and you'll get more supplies (which you will need.) If you've got the power and the enemies are tearing you up, your dozer can fire off huge weapons or bestow helpful boons to your party. As you need that power to upgrade your dozer, though, you'll want to think carefully about deploying it. Soldiers can die in Bedlam. It's a roguelike after all. Guess what, though? There are elites! They suck! They can murderlate the holy hell out of your team but if you beat 'em, they (and their mighty abilities) join you... because MAD MAX, amirite?
All in all, Bedlam is a brutally difficult game that is also rewarding for anyone who, like me, enjoys brutally difficult games. It has twists and turns that I sure ain't spoiling here and like I said in the beginning, the text is infinitely readable... so YAY for accessibility.
Oh yeah, it's not accessible for newbies yet. There are tutorials and they do their job very well but the game is blisteringly hard, even on easy. The devs have said they might fix that. Here's hoping. No game should be painwalled after all. Inclusiveness for newbs and pros alike, right?
So that's my review. I recommend the hell out of this game.

So this game had been in my library for ages after I had either picked it up with a coupon or during a sale (it's been too long). I've finally played it and was delighted. We get to follow a bunch of colourful squares who have loads of personality and different skills. There's pensive Thomas who is rather average, Chris the pessimist (who has a soft spot somewhere in his heart) whose skills are more of a supportive kind, sporty John who can take enormous leaps, Claire the super hero who can do something none of the others can and a few more. Working together, they happen to stumble into changing the world, as we learn from the enthusiastic and loveable narration.
The levels are bite-sized so you can stop playing at any time without losing too much progress. Difficulty varies between easy, just right and the slightest bit hard. If I got stuck, it was never for long: Usually I would find the solution rather quickly, and if the characters died, it helped that savepoints were distributed fairly whenever necessary. One has to do it correctly for sure, but one doesn't get punished for messing up 1 of 20 steps in a sequence.
The game gets bonus points from me for allowing the player to return to each and every level to pick up missed achievements.
Addendum: After completing the game, I found that a free DLC had unlocked in the shape of a new scenario called "Target". That one is definitely harder than the main game due to two things in combination: 1) Wonky flight controls , 2) oh so many spikes. Less of a thumb up for that part from me.

Battlezone has always had a special place in my heart since I first piloted a Grizzly tank, on Mars, with an army at my back, facing an enemy just as powerful as I was. The concept is flawless- a masterful FPS and an intuitive RTS cleanly blended together in a hovertank space shooter. Remastering this timeless classic is one of the greatest revitalizations I've come across.
The game offers a unique environment where standardized FPS elements are challenged and redefined. I am a huge fan of ammo shared between all of your weapons. Combined with the mobile, dynamic RTS that forces you to make decisions based on the type of terrain you're in and what the enemy is building, just like any RTS. However, the only thing I find lacking in the entire game is the RTS itself as I personally find it quite simplified, but in exchange for the complexity of strategy there is a first-person combat experience to steal the focus from.
As a modder for the original game from 1998, I am enthusiastic about the capabilities the Redux has, especially Steam Workshop support. The unified and proven system Workshop offers will give my creations more exposure than ever before, something I look forward to and intend to make the best of.
The game has survived eighteen years of existence. Some said Battlezone was "the best game you've never played". With the Redux, that will change. Battlezone is better than ever before, and it is destined to bring both old and new players back to the front lines.

Duelyst is a fun game, very strategic and much more deep than the more popular Hearthstone.
This game falls under the format of "action card game" in which it is not a real card game, but rather you build decks with creatures, spells and artifacts which you can use in a battlefield to defeat your opponent.
The cards are varied, the generals are each unique, and the match diversity is very high.
Even if every opponent you ran into opponent used the same deck, same general and drew the same cards as you, each match would play out differently. This is mainly due to the combat grid, positioning and hand recycling which essentially eliminates mirror matches.
My favorite aspect of Duelyst is the card animations, and card feel. Each spell and each creature is animated while in card form with a preview of the attack animation making the game pretty cool to watch. However this is also a gripe, because while they show they can animate every creature, spells are only animated in your hand. when you play them they are not animated nearly as much as the card.
Yet like all games Duelyst has some serious flaws, the main one is more of a professional one, the player base. There are not that many players which is unfortunante because this is a great game. The second one is the Lore and Fluff.
The lore in this game is good if you seek it out and force yourself to read it, which can be a very dry read.
and then the fluff, very few cards in this game have any fluff, aka flavor text.
Those who do have terrible flavor text.
Personally i enjoy flavor text on cards because i feel it gives them a little bit of soul.
all in all this is a great game, you should try it if you enjoy strategies and card games.

Great game. Kudos to Ubisoft for a well optimized PC game, hopefully you guys will keep this up and your sales on PC go up again.
Things that I have enjoyed:
+ Game performance is SUPER! Although i dint max it out, i played the game on High settings (which looks to me like Medium) and the game runs at 70-85 fps on my underclocked CPU (specs below)
+ The protagonist, Marcus, is likeable. Not my favourite character design but he is OK, there is unexpected humour in him and the characters around him are also not boring so that makes the game very chill in a way.
+ No map lock. The entire city is available to explore from the start of the game and you can go where ever you want, and just like real life, all clothing shops/vending machines/car shops are already marked on your map and you can fast travel to them without destroying any "Templar towers" if you know what I mean.
+ Unlike older Ubisoft games where you are forced to play the story to unlock "necessary" gadgets, this game asks for no such thing, you can unlock all your skills just by exploration/side quests, the more you explore and do stuff, the faster you can gain XP (followers) and the faster you can unlock the skills of your choice.
+ Side missions are really fun, I loved that ATM Hack mission where you can just go around and give/take away money from random strangers and see how they react to it (really giggled me up). The spray paint missions are also fun because its always a puzzle to figure how to physically get on top of the building roof tops without any flight access, so far I jumped off highways, use forklifts and even construction cranes in the most creative ways to get things done.
+ Lively and rich atmosphere. Although the streets sometimes feel a bit deserted and traffic is low, the NPCs are more realistic in this game, feels like they are more aware of what’s happening around them. The cops are great too, placing APBs on your targets (or anyone for that matter) will make the cops chase them until they are taken down.
+ Seamless multiplayer. You can jump in and out of multiplayer without any loading screens which I thought was really cool.
Bugs that I encountered:
- Vehicles would spawn 250 - 300m away from my location when I request for my vehicle delivery through the "car on demand" app.
- Driving is still a little bit wonky and nowhere close to the comfort I get on GTA 5. The car crash animations are really lazy and I don't understand why there is so much dust every time you collide with other cars.
- If you die and respawn, or drive like 200m away from where you left any local street vehicle (not your personal vehicle), the entire map just resets, dont know why they did this. It bothered me because I would use those trucks to create a ramp on the highway then bring my car around to the highway to make the jump but only to see that the truck has disappeared -_-

i5 4670 (underclocked to 2.7 Ghz from 3.4 Ghz)

I am an avid fan of xcom style of games. Currently clocked at 110+ hours on both Xcom 2 and Xenonauts with many more hours off steam which is unaccounted for so I feel I have a good grasp on the genre.
Current relevant cons are:
- Although the devs have been attempting to balance combat prior to release, difficulty ramp is still exceptionally difficult. You go from 1-2 enemies to 5, to 9, then +11 very quickly. This coupled with -

- The turn system is unlike xcom etc, where your whole team takes a turn and then the enemy. You each get two "moves" in rotation, move move or move shoot etc. This discourages you against bring more troops on the field as a "bodies I can lose resourse" since you can't use them all in a given turn. In addition to this you get more rewards the less units you have in the field (and you really need these bonus resources to get through the game) meaning, when you be bring 3 guys against 9+ and you lose a guy to oneshots things get hairy real fast.
- End game is still broken. Fighting Freeza going through all his forms as say Krillin you know your gonna have a bad time. Didn't stock up on energy cells before you got to the end? Tooooo baddddd.
Lastly my biggest gripe with the game is that, its mechanics is against all the turn-based games it associates itself with in the genre. The most loveable aspect about its kin is the attachment you grow with your units that you have kept alived through the entire game. That feeling of naming yourself and your friends ingame and you try to keep your guys alive through it all. However with the randomised spawns and the current design of everyone being oneshottable it is impossible to keep anyone in this game alive to grow any sort of attachment to. Your guys spawn in a cluster facing a crossfire of the aforementioned 7-13+ enemies with only 2 moves before the enemy gets to act means every battle you bring someone to the field as a throwaway meatshield which I myself find extremely unfun and is against what I look for in such a game.
TL:DR. As of this date I do not recommend purchase of this game if you someone that plays the genre for the attachment value of your troops.  + End game broke.

Summary: This game is kind of slow but mesmerizing. You're turning the massive gears of a beautiful clock. It oozes one-more-turn once you figure out what's going on. I recommend it for patient people who enjoy working out intricate single player puzzle systems. If that's not what you want to do, you will bounce right off.
In this game, you move a married couple individually, Candy-Land style, along a wheel of a few tens of spaces marked with symbols. You move by spending coins with a matching symbol, which represent skills, or maybe technologies, like Brewing, Sailing, Writing, and so on. Other people, basically your neighbors, are also moving along the wheel, spending their coins. Some spaces contain points that fill up a "legacy" meter. So first, you are basically racing your neighbors to them.
The way that you get coins is by moving backwards to your previous neighbor, then teaming up to do work together. Each person has individual skill levels and produces different coins based on those skill levels. If one spouse you control teams up with the other one, they both produce coins at once. When you meet different neighbors, you can also trigger random events that may affect your people's personalities and stockpiles.
Each turn you have to decide whether to go forward or back, one move per person. After every turn, the wheel rotates backwards toward crocodiles, death. So there is first this balance between exploiting and replenishing your resources.
If that were all, the game would still be pretty simple and your decisions would be pretty constrained. But then you have babies.
When the married couple meet as they journey on the wheel of life, they may produce children. Children are stupid. They have no skills. Each turn, you can decide whether or not to train your children by spending coins on them. Trained children can themselves be used to produce coins in skills they are especially good at, which can become critical if you need a particular move.
Every turn of the wheel, the biological clock ticks down. Eventually, the current generation ages and cannot advance for more tokens (death is a wall), and doesn't have room to go backwards to do more work. So you have to pass on your family legacy to your chosen heir. If their skills suck, then when they take over the game, they will have a harder time succeeding.
So each turn becomes a series of agonizing tradeoffs. If you train the kids, you can't move out for points. If you go backwards and fall behind the group, you have to spend a lot of worthwhile tokens just to stay alive. It's a diabolical resource management puzzle.
If there's one thing I would change, in contrast to other fun dynasty/legacy games like Crusader Kings II, you don't usually get to make choices for your characters. Usually in an event there is one option to click on, which violates my sense of role playing and agency. Or in the succession event, all the options can look crappy. Are you: a) evil; b) dumb; c) cowardly? It could be improved by making the pros and cons of each option a little more visible, or a little more obviously pro.
Also, the progression can feel pretty slow, especially when there are no points in sight on the board. In such a case, it can feel pretty grindy to train up the chosen heir as much as possible and squeeze every drop out of the parents. After a succession you can feel like you're not going to make much headway if your heir is crappy. In general, you feel like you're working a lot for rewards that are few and far between.
At the top of the progression there is even more game as you become a city administrator and make even more decisions. I've just gotten into this, but it promises the same interlocking connections between the different levels of the game.

Basically Rocksmith is guitar hero but for actual guitars. Whole songs are tabbed out for you to play and practice. Rocksmith 2014 is an improvement over its predecessor Rocksmith with much better UI and the songs are tabbed out more completely (all or most parts included). I will say though that the original Rocksmith has a better tracklist but that is easily fixed. For just $10 you can import the entire 50+ song Rocksmith discography into Rocksmith 2014 using the Disc Import Tool on this page. And if you really get into this game, Rocksmith 2014 and its "NoteTrackers" have produced sooooooo much dlc content. Theres songs for pretty much any genre and most popular bands. Foo Fighters, Black Keys, Tame Impala, BTO, Tom Petty, Stevie Ray Vaughn, etc. etc. etc.
The only con of this game is that there is the possibility of technical difficulties with your guitar. I've ran into them myself but have figured them out for the most part. This game picks up your audio signal from your electric guitar's pickups. Sort of your typical DI output using the rocksmith cable. Point being, if you have very thin gauge and/or old and worn out strings, the volume from those strings is going to be quiet and the rocksmith cable is going to have trouble picking up your guitar. It may not even playable if the strings are quiet enough. So I recommend changing strings,  switching to the treble (Bridge) pickup and possibily even getting slightly higher gauge strings if Rocksmith is having trouble picking up your guitar. Hmm...this game is Marmite. You will either love it or hate it. First you need to be aware that it is never a case of "this is what you need to do to progress to the next segment" it's ALL about the aimless wandering around..and DISCOVERY (and later about your own creativity and ability to think outside the box). The negative reviews I have read are all by people who have totally missed the clues the game throws at you or have simply not understood what it is and how it works. Case in point are those that say what is the point of the Wellspring contact and why is it a chore to find him in the first place. Well both finding him AND selling soda afterward is a device meant to encourage you to wander around talking to every single person you can and, of course, it is the premise for you being there in the first place. The whole "what's going on here?" and "I don't know what I'm doing" feeling is there DELIBERATELY. It is not a design fault; you are MEANT to feel this way...then when you do eventually get involved with the in-crowd..or discover how to hack..it is all the more rewarding. It's not perfect for the very fact that many will not realise these things and simply give up on it. It's not perfect for the fact that, despite the many reviews saying that you can learn the basic principles of programming with no prior knowledge, MANY of the people who even persevere enough to get that far will find actually changing the "code" overwhelmingly confusing. It IS a good game, it IS a completely original game..it's also a game that will never suit the impatient. As one character tells you at a certain point "You need to loosen up a bit man" because if you don't go into this game with a chillaxed attitude then you wont like it. I did and I do - despite its issues.
If you aren't quite clever and quite a creative thinker then you wont get the best out of this game. That does not mean you can't enjoy it at all.
If you are impatient for "progression" you will either not like the game or distill it to a useless object lesson in trawling for how other people have played it. It's the Journey not the destination. ENJOY the confusion..soak it in..it is part of this game's atmosphere.
A very rudimentary understanding of the computer language BASIC will definitely help make things go more smoothly but is not a pre-requisite.

I anticipate this will get a lot of flack from people that like the game. This review isn't for them. It isn't for people looking be outraged that I disagree with them. It's for people wondering if this is a good programming game.
tl;dr: I haven't found it to be a game of any sort at all, nor have I found a programming interface of any stripe within the program itself.
You've probably read that this game has a cyberpunk element. You've probably read that it involves programming and hacking things. But the worst deception is that this game is educational, and can teach programming.
I've found the SPRAK manual, and it does offer a modest and orthodox nod toward the rudiments of programming. But I would never point anyone interested in programming toward this game.
It could do with a smidge in the direction of hand-holding. I've spent over 20 hours playing this game. I've wandered every pixel of Dorisburg I could get to, at least twice. I've read dozens of found floppies. I've compiled pages and pages of notes, observing how the world works and noting there are at least two naming conventions in use for things. I found the useless contact for the laughable MacGuffin of a soda salesman job.
I haven't found a way to see let alone modify the code of anything. The closest I found were register overflow hacks, and a few specialized computers scattered around town that could do something vaguely interesting that could be made more interesting if a modder were ever to surface.
I know there are modders and I know there are supposed to be at least two available to acquire. But what I haven't found is an in-game whiff in their direction.
Meanwhile, I've entered every unlocked door, social engineered my way past a guarded door, and hovered over every pixel in Dorisburg, though after awhile, I admit, I stopped checking trashcans and just started using them for excess inventory. About the only items in game I didn't find multiples of were keys and modders--the latter of which, I reiterate, do not exist in my game.
At this point, some people might be tempted to leak info about the location of the modders. Don't bother. I'm done. I've given this game more than I usually give to a game that doesn't start having a payoff in the first hour or so. I've got too many good games, and too many unplayed games to waste time on games that aren't working toward what I see as their fundamental purpose. In short, if a game doesn't at least live up to what I was anticipating when I bought it, I ain't got time for it.
There are two reasons I put in as much time as I did. The main reason I overlooked the hideous flaws (camera and building design are frequently at odds with each other; inventory management is from the stupid age, and painful; dialogue seems to have been written using a something like a magic 8 ball; if you have the misfortune to look at someone's face, you're left wondering how much they've been drinking, for how long, and what the hell they jammed into their eyes; navigation is seriously unpleasant; for all the objects in the world, there really aren't that many objects in the world; it's fundamentally pushy about being a partying extrovert; etc), is because I like programming games, so I really wanted this to be one.
As far as I'm concerned, it isn't one. It's a sham and a fraud. You'd be much better off looking at Human Resource Machine or TIS-100. Those are actual programming games where from the very beginning, you will be shown an interface and language for programming, and (for the most part) gradually fed more difficult problems and complexity. Fair warning: both those games are more assembly language type programming, where as Else Heart.Break() promises a high level C-like language with a frill--per my reading of the in-game SPRAK manual--that you have to discover on your own because...
From one perspective the approach is a metaphor for self-taught programming/hacking. Unfortunately, the adherence to that metaphor kills the game for me.
About the only thing I haven't done in the game is talk to everyone. Or at least, I don't know if I have. I just know every "conversation" I had in-game was irritatingly stupid, and a waste of effort because it yielded nothing of value. It's not the sort of SmallTalk I'd be interested in seeing in a programming game.
At this point, I'm pretty sure the whole thing is a giant hoax. I want my twenty-some hours back. I suspect if everyone who got this game gave an honest review of their experience with it--and no one resorted to Googling walkthroughs to get past the utter lack of presenting an actual game to the customer (as I have not and will not as IMSO, if such is required, the design is a failure), the reviews would be Overwhelmingly Negative.
I'm surprised I never found a music token with Rick Astley lyrics.

If you're going to design an open world game, you have to do it in a way that respects the player's time. Else Heart.Break()'s visually cluttered but scarcely interactive world and its timed events do not.

I'm all for games that break the mold, but that doesn't make them any less disappointing when they don't pan out. The pitch for Else Heart.Break() is pretty great, offering you a dynamic, open-world adventure full of drama and hacking. The art style is fascinating, the interface is clean, and the whole thing just drips with potential. And then you sit down to play it, and you wander around a city for 20 minutes, either waiting for a timed event to roll around or to stumble across something interesting. Even after two hours I could get no deeper into the game than this, being constantly rebuffed in my efforts to dig in by empty rooms, locked doors, and silent people.
You play Sebastian, a young adult with fine taste in clothes and horrible taste in eye shadow who's just scored his first job in a distant town. The intro at his home eases you into the simple point and click interface that powers the game, and then moves him off to the unfortunately-named Dorisburg to make it on his own. With only a hotel room and a vague hint at a business contact, it's up to you to help Sebastian find purpose and meaning in this strange, bitty city.
This really is how the game starts, leading you to your lodgings at a hotel and then telling you that maybe you can meet the guy who hired you at a nearby cafe. For any other adventure game in existence this would either lead you to meeting the dude or finding a clue that leads you to him, but here that plot thread pretty much dead-ends. At that point you're on your own, roaming the twisting streets looking for something to do. You might find it as I did eventually, or you might check out the weird shops and houses around town, or you might take to rummaging through garbage bins. It's the promise of that open, dynamic world to explore, but as you might have expected already it's pretty well at odds with having a tight narrative to follow.
The "dynamic" aspect of the game is in how all the characters have schedules they keep to. There are no random NPCs here, everyone you see is a citizen of Dorisburg with things to do and thoughts to have. NPCs get up in the morning, go to work, take breaks, go shopping, hit the bar, and go to sleep, just as you'll have to. There's a clock ticking away in the top left that tells you what time it is in the city, which will be important when characters ask you to meet them somewhere at 10pm or get coffee at lunch. Again, this gives the city the impression of being alive, but also makes it harder to find people when you need them, or events that actually progress the plot.
That right there is the real heart of the problem, really. The folks behind Else Heart.Break() made a dynamic world but didn't give it a dynamic plot. You can stroll wherever and talk to whoever and pick up beers and floppy disks but the story isn't going anywhere unless you meet specific people and do specific things with them. Instead of creating some bold new point-and-click hybrid, the developers just made it harder to play through a pretty standard one. And the worst part is, it's not like a standard one where you can keep fiddling with a puzzle you're stuck on. I lost the plot about 45 minutes ago and really have no idea how to get back on it, despite finding neat new things like a ministry of computers.
I haven't touched on the choices you can make in the game or the supposedly extremely powerful hacking systems you can dig into to alter things about the game world, because I never triggered the right events to get to them. My two hours in Else Heart.Break() were spent wandering the city, waiting for parties, and navigating some awkwardly-translated dialogue. That's another important note, for a game that leans so heavily on drama and relationships, the writing is stiff and unnatural. Interactions between characters always feel rough and shallow, and in an effort to capture the pathos of unemployed youths they end up overloaded with "whatever" and "I dunno" and "that's cool" instead of anything useful or interesting.
I know there's something special in here. I've seen it in the trailers, and I've heard tales of it in the rare positive review. But you REALLY have to put in the work to find it, work that's probably not going to be very engaging or gratifying on its own. You have to work against the open, dynamic grain of the game to follow the breadcrumb trail of events until... I don't even know how long for. What I do know is that it's longer than I'm willing to try, and surely longer than most people would be willing.

I have to admit: the first time I've played this game I got stuck on
quest to find
person. I got so tired and sick of trying to find him that I uninstalled the game and had to give it
4 months later.
And, as you can see, this is the only reason why this isn't the end of my review.
This is a nice sandbox game with a meh story loosely added on top of it (which IMO isn't the point of this game anyway) where everything can be programmed (hacked, cybered, pwned or whatever word you want to use) using in-game programming language called SPRAK. If you're here only for the story, pass this game. If you don't like long walking sequences, pass this game. If you don't like reading large amounts of text, trying out new things and appreciating art and lore, pass this game.
And if that didn't convince you, you might actually like it.
can potentially spark your interest in programming. You can control a nearby street lamp by drinking your hacked booze. You can teleport from an electricity box to a broken TV in some apartment
. You can write your own OS for a computer without having any background in programming such things and then control any in-game object with it.
Personally for me, this game scratches the itch that I've had since I first saw what you can do with a computer. Art in this game is both minimalistic and rich at the same time. Soundtrack is amazing (some of the music is made by El Huervo!) and I still often find myself listening to some tracks from it on repeat.
This game gives me a nostalgic vibe of a depressing alternative era where USSR didn't fall, but instead developed super advanced technology for tracking and controlling of everything and everyone.
Oh, and if you like to search for easter eggs and hidden jems, this game has more of them than you could ever want. To this day I still sometimes find things that I haven't noticed before.
As you might've already guessed from my review, this isn't a game for everyone. You WILL get lost
, you WILL hate this game for taking its time and you might not even try to program anything using the SPRAK language, thus missing out on a huge chunk of this game. The story is honestly bad, you can
through it as soon as you reach a stage where you can hack into everything and/or learn how to teleport. A mindblowing amount of content isn't even shown to you in the main story, and unless you go exploring on your own you may never even see any of it. Most puzzles don't utilize the full potential of the underlying (and powerful) engine. I'm honestly disappointed because this game does have the potential to be something amazing, but it just doesn't go anywhere, leaving the player hanging more often that it should.
I have a love/hate relationship with
. On one side, it changed my view on the world and made me rethink my life. On the other side, this little-known game needs many improvements to become somthing that I could even consider giving a 10/10 to.
Overall though, I still like this game, but the same might not necessarily apply to you. This is a niche game that requires a certain mindset to be fully appreciated in its current form.

Not going to spend a lot of time writing a review for this game, it's simply not worth my time. Apologies for the shortness... 3.5/10 for me. I did enjoy the graphics, but that's about it.
I bought this expecting a roguelike Xcom. But basically they throw you on a very small map with zero ways to prep and you get 2 moves. For those 2 moves you typically dive behind some cover if any randomly spawned around you. Then the computer takes it's 2 moves and kills one of your guys. Since you only had 2 moves you can't save everyone I guess. then you take your 2 moves and kill one of theirs. It gets old fast, zero strats involved.
Then you finish killing all the enemies, you get in your truck and randomly spawn on another small map and  guess what? Lose a guy, rinse, repeat until you're out of guys. There is some skill involved and a very slight learning curve, but only being able to move 1 single guy (out of your entire army) 2x, or 2 guys once, really doesn't give a lot of options or enjoyable game play. What can you really do with that? You can't really get a game plan together on such small maps, or devise any tactics. Maps are about 20x20 tiles. You pretty much count on the luck of the draw, where your troops randomly spawn, and where the enemy randomly spawns. You have zero control over what happens!
Then let's talk about troop combat. Your troops all have places where they can attack. Melee can attack adjacent which is fine. Shot gunners can attack a couple spaces and knockback, which is also fine. But anything else is complete garbage. Let's say you have a guy who can attack 6 spaces out in a circle around him, not 4, 5, or 7 mind you, it's exactly 6, otherwise you cannot touch him. Lets say you want to cover a tank as backup. The enemy just walks to 5 spaces shoots your guy and stands there. Now you have to waste both moves on your turn taking one step back and shooting him. There is no overwatch, so it's not like your sniper can sit there guarding someone. No, he has to waste his entire turn moving a single step back and then shotting the bad guy who is now exactly 6 blocks away. Most games you play, the shots get easier as you get closer and a higher chance to hit, not so in this game. you actually have to be the exact # of blocks away to make the shot. The enemy understands exactly where this range is and makes sure you have to waste both of your turns moving and shooting. It's probably one of the worse game mechanics I've seen this year in a turn based strat game.
So in closing, I should have watched a couple more youtube videos before purchasing this. I would have seen this game breaking flaw. Hopefully you can now learn from my mistakes and avoid this game until it goes on sale for $3.99 or something. Good luck!

It saddens me to give something this new a negative review.  I'm sort of new to the whole XCOM-type combat system, but I've played a little bit of it and it's very simple to figure out.  It's literally chess.  Some units can attack with only 1 space of range, some give you a much broader attack range (like a shotgun, for example), and some require a certain distance (a rifle unit cannot attack unless they are a certain number of spaces away from the target).
Well... the idea, and the combat, is fine... but the problem I have is how the game progresses.  There's no skirmish mode, campaign mode, or any of that stuff.  There's only one type of game mode, and that's the roguelike thing where you drive around this big truck on a giant map with a countless number of random events.  In between battles, your units basically don't heal at all.  It says like, 25 days to heal each unit, so basically do not expect a single hit point to be healed ever.  If they die, they're dead forever.  You have a limited number of units, fuel, and meat.  You can pick up fuel and meat on the battlefield, at the end of the battles, sometimes in random events they are given to you, and you may even find a meat/oil trader along the way.
You are given meat and oil bonuses if you take a fewer number of units on the battlefield, but since you can take as long as you want in between turns, I always take the full 6 units out with me, this gives me a much broader choice of actions.  So your 6 units are placed on a battlefield against their 6 units.  The amount of damage each unit does and the amount of hit points they have varies, but you and your opponent are equally matched.  Often times I would lose 2 or 3 units, since they die on 1 hit most of the time!  Some enemies doing upwards of 5-6 damage, when your units may only have 2-5 health.  The units which have 10 health, which is actually a pretty decent amount, only 2 damage to your enemy, and can only attack one single space in front of them.  Since they'll have to attack numerous times to take anyone down, you can expect them to be at least half dead after each enemy.  Remember, there's no healing in this game either.
Let's say you played a game of chess against someone, and you lost half of your chess pieces, would you feel confident enough to face another opponent using your remaining pieces?  I don't think anyone's ever tried doing that before, a sort of 'survival' chess...  Probably because it's not that good of an idea.  Yet this game embraces doing exactly that.
You start with 16 units.  After 3 or 4 battles, you'll be lucky to have 6 good ones left.  The enemies will slowly chip away at your team.  And so far the only way I have found to recruit extra team members is to defeat a boss, then the boss joins you.  This is a really cool feature, actually, but those bosses do like 7-9 damage per hit.  You might be able to take him down with 3 well placed rifle shots but they are not easy to kill, and you may end up losing half your team in the process.  It sounds easy enough, right?  Shoot him a few times.  But the unit movement is very awkward, you will lose turns trying to line up your shots.  Sometimes you can kill them with ease, but they also have equal opporntunity to kill you with ease.  And they do.
So basically, I have not survived more than 18 minutes before getting a game over.  I'm not big into reading the long dialogs so I just skip them and get right into the combat as soon as I can.  When it's 6 against 6, there's a good chance I lose a unit or two in battle.  After 4 battles, I barely have anyone left.  Then it's game over.  Is this really all there is to this game?  I think this game would be better off if I had twice as many units, or twice as many hit points, or something.  I'm playing on the easy difficulty, too.  Never tried normal.  And I still can't seem to last 20 minutes.  The gameplay isn't rocket science.  You move into range, click to attack, then they do their turn, either killing you instantly or cutting your health in half.
I wouldn't recommend this game.  Seems a few other reviewers are also having the same experience, but not all.  The developers have even said in the discussions that they are working on balancing the combat system...  They should have done that prior to release in my opinion.  I can't give them tips on how to improve it, though, as the concept sounds great but it's just awful in practice.  I didn't even get into detail of the limited fuel and how annoying it is to get a game over because you run out of fuel.  You have 1000 fuel to start.  It takes anywhere from 30 to 200 fuel to move your truck a space.  That's another aspect to manage and it runs out very quickly.  Move your truck 5 times and then it's game over, play the whole thing over from the beginning!  Rediculous.  Just play XCOM, if you are into these types of games, at least that game gives you a fighting chance.

My review will be divided in two parts: in an opinion as a gamer and in an opinion as a fan of Rayman.
As a gamer, it is definitely a game worthy of the prizes that received back in 2011 by several identities including BAFTA, as "Best Platformer" and "Best Art Direction". It features more than twenty hours of longevity thanks to its 60+ levels, full of detail thanks to the wonderful job of the artists at Montpellier. It is a breeze of fresh air in the market of platforming games as an alternative to Mario, Sonic, etc. This game also supports cooperative gameplay. Chances are low that you will regret purchasing this, just check by yourself by playing the free demo!
As a Rayman fan, I honestly think the game had really a lot of potential to be better than what it turned out in the end. The game suffered significant changes during the development, ending up in something that wasn't quite "promised" back in the E3 of 2010. Keep in mind: "Origins" for the 2D side-scrolling gameplay (like Rayman 1), not "Origins" for the backstory of the most important characters. Don't expect the existence (and especially a coherent) of a story, since this pretty much lacks it. The levels are too linear and easy to overcome  especially if you have a sharp dexterity from Rayman 1. While the artwork is impressive, I think the artists were chosen bad for the background treatment, with just one or two exceptions. For me it is the least good Rayman title out of the four currenty existent, and after finishing it you won't wish to replay it very soon. In short, it is a good game but not as fantastic as the other main titles released before.

This is a gorgeous, personality-filled, light-load, fun packed game.
I first played this title a decade or so ago, and I knew from the moment I first opened a map and started building my own little railway network that this would be a title typical of the Sid Meier games (Pirates!, etc) - a polished, balanced, aesthetically pleasing game which takes the concept of relaxing gameplay into active consideration.
You take on the role of a railroad tycoon, unleashed into various theaters and tasked with fulfilling certain rail objectives. You start with one town and a single station from which to grow your empire. You connect to another nearby town and start shuffling wheat back and forth. Soon you spot a third town and head off to it, gambling on a long stretch of track that you have to borrow to afford... Connecting to the new location and the huge herds of beef cows it boasts, you realise with a jolt that you have nowhere to sell the cows. Frantically you search around the map for a town which buys them, realising that the nearest market lies three or four cities away. The size of your task has grown, the ambition of your railway firm has grown, the scope of the gameplay has grown, the payoff in economic fun has Doubled, Tripled, Fourbled and Fibled!
You can't reach the far cattle buyers just yet, but you are able to shuttle passengers between your little network of towns, so you build a secondary line to your freight route and get shuttlin'. You spot marginal gains in the buyers and sellers of nearby hamlets and pounce, connecting them to your network, watching them grow and provide more returns! You upgrade trains - such speed! Such pulling power! - and soon hills are as easy to scale as descents, and suddenly you finally deliver those 12 cars of cattle to the distant metropolis that is dying for them and your bank balance goes ka-ching!
Dem monies, tho.
This game is just solid gold fun. An elaboration on typical economic management sims, the ability to custom build your own rail routes and work out new and efficient track layouts and schedules makes you really feel like the original Isambad Kingdom Brunel. The formula wears thin once you have conquored all you can, once you have maxed out every advance and the finite maps are chock full of railway lines, but the race to this endgame is just so fun that you keep on coming back again and again. Then restarting. The wide range of maps is also quite nice, since each map is of varied difficulty and houses a goodly chunk of play hours and replayability.
It's dirty cheap so buy it, and enjoy it, I love it to bits.
9/10.

An old gem from my childhood, Battlezone manages to perfectly merge RTS and FPS elements creating a kind of field commander experience that has yet to be effectively reproduced in the 18 years since its inception. Coupled with one of the best stories ever to be written for a video game, this is a game you absolutely can NOT miss out on.
As for this specific re-release, it's as well done as anyone could ask for a game that's nearly 20 years old. Rebellion has seamlessly integrated the game into Steam's workshop and brought the graphics engine up to speed (or close enough for my liking, anyway) for modern systems, and brought everything into high resolution since we no longer run 640x480 on our systems any more.
I cannot thank Rebellion enough for this!
However, I must venture a warning. If you see this game and automatically think "Activision? CALL OF DUTY!" you're in the wrong market. When this game first came out, Activision made GOOD games. Do NOT buy this game if you're looking for a call of duty-esque game.

Battlezone 98 has always remained one of my all time favorite games.  It was before it's time, coming on to the scene during a period when Mechwarrior 2 was still fresh in the minds of PC gaming.  It combined RTS and first person (both vehicle and on foot) in a really fascinating package of the secret war between the US and USSR over the mysterious bio-metal that was spread throughout the solar system.  The RTS aspect was solid and setting up bases worked well in that you never left the action, the game was seamless.  Thanks to Rebellion, we now have Redux, which updates the game and brings it out of the shadows again (there has been an active community around this game for years!), and the various enhancements along with release on Steam will give this gem another shot in the modern gaming world.  Absolutely recommended!

Great game, highly recommend this. Get better at guitar and have fun doing it.
Basically Rocksmith is guitar hero but for actual guitars. Whole songs are tabbed out for you to play and practice. Rocksmith 2014 is an improvement over its predecessor Rocksmith with much better UI and the songs are tabbed out more completely (all or most parts included). I will say though that the original Rocksmith has a better tracklist but that is easily fixed. For just $10 you can import the entire 50+ song Rocksmith discography into Rocksmith 2014 using the Disc Import Tool on this page. And if you really get into this game, Rocksmith 2014 and its "NoteTrackers" have produced sooooooo much dlc content. Theres songs for pretty much any genre and most popular bands. Foo Fighters, Black Keys, Tame Impala, BTO, Tom Petty, Stevie Ray Vaughn, etc. etc. etc.
The only con of this game is that there is the possibility of technical difficulties with your guitar. I've ran into them myself but have figured them out for the most part. This game picks up your audio signal from your electric guitar's pickups. Sort of your typical DI output using the rocksmith cable. Point being, if you have very thin gauge and/or old and worn out strings, the volume from those strings is going to be quiet and the rocksmith cable is going to have trouble picking up your guitar. It may not even playable if the strings are quiet enough. So I recommend changing strings,  switching to the treble (Bridge) pickup and possibily even getting slightly higher gauge strings if Rocksmith is having trouble picking up your guitar. It's also just a good idea in general so that Rocksmith picks up your signal better and you dont have to worry about your streaks being broken from faulty readings lol
So in conclusion I give this unique game 9.5/10. If you enjoy playing guitar and want to have fun getting better, this is definitely worth picking up.
