Time trials and alternate dinos give you more reasons to replay the game.  Collect hidden eggs, fight bosses, and defeat a variety of enemies, what's not to love?  I'd suggest this game for old school platformer lovers to beginners.  Iggy's has that classic feel you love, but a modern approach that beginners will like too.

Paradox Interactive and Colossal Order have an unexpected hit on their hands, with Cities: skyliness garnering over 1 millio sales. The game was labelled as one of the best city-building experiences to date, and the debut trailer certainly made the game look gorgeous, massive and entertaining.
I questioned whether Cities: skyliness could succeed where SimCity ultimately failed, and the question is answered with a resounding yes. Where SimCity faltered in terms of map size, controversial always-online requirements and a lack of mod support, Cities: skyliness allows gamers to have a much larger map, no online requirement, and works with the Steam Workshop to allow players to create their own assets, visuals and mods within the game(Los Santos map is amazing).
As soon as players enter the game, they’ll see an interface that will be familiar to all city simulator fans: roads, power lines, pipeworks, zoning types and specialized city buildings are immediately available to select. Though users can only place zoning 3 blocks wide along each road, as opposed to filling whole sections of area, it’s easy to adjust to the tighter spacing and design ethics this decision brings. As the population of a town grows, users will unlock new zoning types, city service buildings and unique structures – or, of course, they can just go full-on sandbox and enable the game’s own in-game money and unlock cheats, a handy tool for those just looking to create the most beautiful city they can.
Speaking of, this is the absolute highlight of Cities: skyliness – creating huge, gorgeous cities on a scope never before seen in a city builder. The game eclipses all other city builders in sheer land mass, allowing gamers to create a cities that looks about twenty times as large as SimCity Cities. Gamers can even download a modification to go beyond this limit, with the only functional downside being they might have some framerate issues.
Exploring cities is easy, and players will likely find themselves in awe watching commuters go about as firetrucks struggle with six lanes of traffic during a high-rise fire.
The game also adds new elements to mix, like one of my favorite new features that allows users to designate certain areas of the map into ‘Districts’ and subject them to special rules. This feature makes it easier for players to put more tax on a wealthy subdivision, pay to hand out smoke alarms and reduce the change of fires, or even designate that a certain industrial area ignore safety concerns to increase productivity. The Districts feature adds a unique element to areas of the city that might have been somewhat repetitive otherwise, and being able to label neighborhoods helps add to the personality of each city.
There’s also new city services which must be considered. All city simulators have healthcare, but skyliness introduces deathcare. Cities must have allocated graveyards, but those fill up, which prompts he use of crematoriums to service the city. The same goes for garbage collection, where landfill areas have limited space, but the pollution-pumping incinerators will help finally get rid of the garbage. For a price, mayors can use the district tool to enable a better focus on health or recycling, which help out and keep the game interesting with more areas to focus on and ensure the city has good coverage.
One of the only downsides to Cities: skyliness is that it ultimately fails to provide much of a challenge in just about anything. The hardest portion of the game is waiting for citizens to move in and keeping areas well patrolled in terms of city services like police, healthcare, deathcare, and fire control. Within about 9 or 10 hours of playing, I'd reached the end-game status with a city raking in millions of cash with low crime, high health and a happy populace. That said, the gameplay was consistently fun the entire time, and Cities: skyliness delivered an unexpectedly smooth and wonderful experience from start to finish.
The game also includes an Asset Editor, so players can start creating their own building designs and easily add them to their gameplay experience. The tools are relatively straightforward, and the Steam Workshop is already full of hundreds of pieces of user-made content. Custom maps can also be designed, so players can start planning their cities from the terrain up. From our own experience, topographically-extreme maps deliver the most fantastic, albeit challenging design experience. Though the gameplay itself features no online component, gamers likely won’t notice the absence of neighboring towns as they expand their own borders over and over.
Conclusion :
In short, Cities: skyliness is everything that a city builder should be. Coming in with the affordable price of $29.99, HGunified recommends Cities skylines to every gamer who loves city building simulation games. Cities skylines is best city builder available in market. (9/10)

My review will include comparing Six Siege with CS:GO since both games have similarities and are very popular.
Unlike CS:GO which is a lot more fast paced and easier to master, Six Siege is quite the opposite. It's easy to get into and harder to master and very much a slow paced - mind game where each sound you make could make the difference.
It has a lot of operators (heroes), each one unique and new ones are out regularly. The game also offers a lot of map variants as well as day and night versions of each of the maps. After 50 hours in I still can't consider that I know even all the basics of the game. Every day I learn something new or how to do something better.
The game also offers skins and "loot boxes" in the form of alpha packs which, optionally, could be purchased with real money currency or you could also buy them with the in-game one. Unlike CS:GO which doesn't reward you anything outside of a simple blue skin for winning a match, in this game you could buy 90% of the available items just by playing the game and you don't even have to get lucky from opening an alpha pack, if you like an item you can straight up purchase it separately without needing to gamble.
The game offers a few different editions, each with it's own benefits.
The Starter one is the most basic edition and it's exactly as the name suggests -- You start with only 4 operators and the price tag for the older ones is 12,500 instead of  500-2,000 renown in the Standard Edition. So it will require you quite a bit of grinding to get them, but if you think you will enjoy and play the game a lot and want to save some money then this might be for you. Standard would be recommended for most people since it will give you a lot of options in characters to choose and you will unlock older ones easier. And the complete edition gives you basically everything + additional benefits such as 10% shop discount and additional challenges to do.
My suggestion is to wait for a discount and purchase it then. And if you're unsure wait for a free weekend like I did and decide for yourself if it's worth your money and time.

My Pros and Cons with this game. *Warning: small biased opinion in here and a bit of a read*
Prerequisites:
- If you want to learn the basics of guitar/bass, try this game with the Real Tone Cable. If you are just starting, you might have a beginners/starters guitar kit. Try getting Rocksmith 2014 with the Real Tone Cable.
- As you progress, you can venture in other areas of guitar/bass, and it's pretty much an open path to where you want to go. If you want to mostly play metal, pop, punk, rock, jazz etc. there are a lot of options to choose from. Just know that certain genres use certain techniques usually not used in other genres, so take a look.
Pros:
-- With the Remastered version, most annoying bugs are gone, and you won't need a Real Tone Cable for the game anymore. You might want to get a decent mic if you want to play it like that (you will also need a good amp to blast itinto the mic).
-- Beginner friendly, and there are songs to everyone's liking.
-- After almost 7 years, they're still making DLC for this game! As of now, there are more than 900 songs to download, and 266 Song packs (Some are not available in EU, so try setting your location to USA if you want those certain DLCs)
-- Arcade modes to practice Hammer-ons, Pull-offs, Sliding, natural harmonics and more!
-- If you by any chance have the 1st Rocksmith, you can buy a pass to transfer all of the songs from Rocksmith one to the Remastered version.
Cons:
--Not all techniques are available in Rocksmith 2014. The one they teach/showcase here are the ones that are most commonly used in most playstyles of guitars.
--After 7 years, all the DLC prices are still the same. That is complete crap to be honest. 1 song is $2.99 (or €2.99) and is very expensive. If you plan to buy ALL DLC in the game, it would tally up to ~$4500 (or €4500). That is jawdropping!
--Some songs are exclusively in DLC song packs, and there might be a song that or two that you like, but you dislike the rest. I have this situation wiht a 5 song back, and only like 2 songs in there. It discourages me from buying the pack.
Small fix:
Reduce DLC that have existed for over 18 months to $/€1.99, and 36 months by $/€0.99. It is really a bummer to find a song made in 2012 and still costing €/$2.99. Or have a anniversary DLC sale!
Wrap up:
Overal, this game has a few flaws that can be ignored, but the rest of it is great. They should really fix that DLC pricing.

After playing the game for some time I can tell that it is really cool. It is my first game of the hacking "genre", but I do have experience in software development and I am somehow familiar with the topic.
The beginning is quite straight forward and you get along pretty good. However as soon as you get to the main city where the actual story (for what I can tell atm, I haven't finished yet) takes place.
A problem that you may face if you have absolutely no idea of what "hacking" is about, that even if you do not have to do any hacking yet, you are already expected to have the right mindset for doing so. The nature of hacking just is about finding a way how to get to a solution and in the case of the beginning it is just about getting to know the right people at the right time. This does require some skill set like having fun with exploring new areas, keep on pushing again and again until you get the result you want - like advancing in dialogues- and last but not least the patience to keep up with the task. But what is the task? This question will become clearer the more you move on. This is part of the game.
To sum up, you will need about 2-4h to get to the part where the "actual" game begins (the hacking part). If you get there, the rest will mostly be learning new stuff (like simple programming and manipulation) and a nice story. But you have to have the patience to get there - if you don't then probably the hacking part may not be your biggest satisfaction, neither. So you may just put the game aside and don't "waste" time on this game. On the other hand if you do get there you are most probably going to have a lot of fun with the rest of the game as well.
This may also be the biggest criticism: The game is not there to "teach" you patience and since it does not have the claim to be an educational game it somehow fails to introduce todays average/casual gamer to the required thinking (no offense to both parties :) ).  So I would definitly recommend the game but beforehand I'd make sure the player does know what to expect.

Bullets are weak. Explosions have no splash. People reload, heal, and regain thrust faster than a cheetah on steroids. Everyone seems to know where the enemy is, thanks to overpowered perks, skillstreaks, or downright cheating (historically common in CoD).
Half of my hits don't register. A lot of my great shots show on my screen but not the kill cam. Even if I manage to land 4-5 shots center mass, they'll just turn and one-shot me (most people use sniper rifles). Getting the jump on someone isn't even a guaranteed kill, as they can just fly around after getting hit (and players can magically withstand multiple headshots). I almost always get traded after a kill; I've only unlocked one scorestreak so far. Some of my perks literally don't work, and I don't know why. I know some can be countered but not everybody can have the same countering perk. I hate having to give up important tactical equipment just to keep up with those who use 4-5 perks. To make matters worse, the wildcards enabling over-perking take up an inventory slot themselves, which makes little sense. I try to stay quiet and under the radar, but silencers nerf the damage and range to an unusable degree.
Beginners like myself are always pitted against the literal John Madden of CoD, with little hope of a positive K/D. It's not fun, the constantly getting shot out of nowhere and the resulting humiliation. Paying customers should not feel embarrassed and harassed for starting out. The campaign and bonus content offer very little preparation for real engagements. Core team deathmatch is the only mode people play, and it's only about kills. And the zombie mode is a joke compared to other CoD titles with said game mode. What bugs me most is I can follow perfect tactical procedure, only to get butchered by someone sliding in like an idiot, or bumrushed by a random spawn in the relatively small maps. The kill cam fails to show what I did wrong, if anything.
To succeed in CoD BO3, you must learn to spray, jump spam, and stare at your radar. Then you'll carry these bad habits into other games (that take real skill) and get rightfully pwned. To me, it is not worth forgetting everything I learned in much more realistic military shooters. I actually feel sorry for those who spent hundreds or thousands of hours in this game, as their skill isn't transferrable to other games or real life. This is not only the worst CoD title in the series; it is the worst modern AAA shooter. I am done with CoD for life, and the desperate attempt to rebuild the fanbase with a WWII version will not save it. If you want to experience the campaign, it is barely worth it at 50% off ($59.99 retail at time of review). As a whole, at full price,  I obviously do not recommend.
P.S. If the developers make CoD WWII's combat anything like BO3's, it will not only be disrespectful to those who actually fought in that war, but it will give kids a distorted view of history and reality. War is not some arcade game. While I don't think video games contribute to violence, I think telling a youngster headshots are non-lethal is asking for an accident. Ironically, Call of Duty fails in it's "duty" to depict weapons as the dangerous tools they are. Heck, maybe kids these days will want to join the army after playing, but a good CoD player does not a soldier make.

This is frustratingly close to being a uniquely great game but just manages to make it as a worthwhile one due to a multitude of bugs and oversights in the story. It's a memorably vibrant, youthful, digitally fanciful journey worth exploring if you can navigate your way around the worst of the bugs and handle the juvenile relationships.
+ a beautiful, eclectic look and atmosphere, and lots of suitable tunes to go with it (grab the soundtrack! get googling)
+ a very cool digital, modern take on the classic adventure game
+ a fun hacking element that requires minimal involvement if one so chooses, or can be taken a fair bit further
- there are a number of potentially story stopping bugs, and a very rigid story structure that's easily derailed
- a frequently terrible script, even when it comes to sentence composition and spelling (it's been translated, poorly)
- an often hard to navigate world
- very flat endings
A guide exists (which says a lot but doesn't give away absolutely everything..) to ease the pain but otherwise keeping in mind a few key things will make the game flow a lot more smoothly:
> the plaza has a compass around it to aid with navigation
> really try not to miss scheduled dates with characters
> make your own notes of what's been said, requested, arranged
> coding yourself a better drink will help with falling asleep at inconvenient times
> don't stress too much about flogging those Wellspringer drinks (they are terrible after all!)
> you can find a modifier without progressing the story, e.g. if the story stalls, just go exploring
> as of writing, I've reliably found myself to become stuck after being caught by Longson and his guard - avoid!

I discovered this gem when it first launched it's early access on Steam, and I was instantly convinced that I would buy it - some time. So I wishlisted it, being a sceptic towards early access and all. But ever since I did, I've revisited the gamepage frequently, rewatching the trailer dozen times every week, reading reviews, searching for more footage from the game. 2 days ago I couldn't resist it anymore and I just HAD to buy it. And boy am I happy I did!
If you're like me, and enjoyed the post-apocalyptic atmosphere and badassery of Lucas Arts' "Full Throttle" and Double Fine's "Brutal Legend", and don't mind this game being neither 3rd person 3D or "point and click", then this might be something for you.
You traverse in a "semi-openworld" game, and by "semi" I mean that there's a map with locations that you can choose and instantly travel to with your motorcycle, meaning that you don't partake in the actual travelling. To be an actual "openworld"-game IMO would be if the game had several different routes interconnecting the world that you would either have to travel manually or at least be given the choice alongside a fast-travel option. Personally, I don't mind really. In fact, for this game in particular, I prefer it this way. And maybe you do to. ;)
When travelling to different locations you'll encounter alot of interesting characters, some of them just there for the sake of giving the game more depth, many NPC's for subquests, and others further developing the main story of the game. So nothing out of the ordinary there compared to other games, but you're actually given dialogue-choices, so depending on your answers, the outcome is changable, and I think it's AWESOME!
Many interesting locations to discover! Keep in mind that it's early - VERY EARLY - access, so there aren't too many locations yet, I've been to all the current locations in just over 2 hours of playtime, but those locations that are currently available are some next-level eyecandy! There's some platforming, enough to keep the leveldesign interesting, but not too much. It is mainly a 2D brawler with grinding-features and an actual story. Now, what I mean by grinding is that you travel back to areas you've been to, just for the looting from foes and staged away throughout the areas, so that you may craft new items from all the scavenging and looting. If you don't care much for crafting, then stay clear of this game. But if you don't mind that extra feature, then go for it! :)
To sweeten the deal, there are voice-actors for every NPC's I've encountered thus far. Most of them are decent, while some of them are just terrific! As a matter of fact: the voice of the narrator (and also the protagonist's stepfather) is one of the many reasons why I ended up buying the game. To sum it up: although early, and even though combat might feel a bit clunky and lacking finesse, some of it might feel unpolished and quirky, but still I am happy I bought this game. It's truly unlike anything I have in my library, even though it can be compared to other titles in terms of core mechanics and gameplay. I have high hopes and expectations for this game, only by experiencing it in it's current state, and you should too. ;)

Seeing as this is an early access title, I will just post some issues that I had and believe should be noted:
1) Difficulty level is high mainly because of damage from earlier waves if enemies stacking up, you are often left trying to fight a new wave of enemies with just a slither of health left that you have no way to heal before the new wave. This causes the correct form of play for players to be quite odd... losing on purpose the moment they take damage to prevent losing in the next wave.
2) Healing over time doesn't work with screen transitions, the health you didn't wait for is lost forever. This will make players wait without doing anything before moving from each screen.
3) There are some minor animation glitches when moving from one idle animation to the other, not sure if there is much to do about that, but it isn't a big deal.
4) It is hard to understand how to drop items, inventory get's cluttered with crafting ingredients that might not be useful.
5) When dropping items next to an item pickup, which seems like it will be a common practice, you have no way to not pick it back up before engaging in the next pickup.
6) When inventory is full and you are trying to pick up an item, i would suggest the default option to be closing the menu or opening the full inventory to give an option to throw things.
7) Junkyard level- insanely hard, no checkpoint for like 5 waves of enemies. I had full health and when i finally got through i was out of ammo...
8) You can skip fights by running to a checkpoint. got to the elevator in gutless while being chased by enemies, was killed on the elevator and when i respawned i was surprised to start there. Maybe checkpoint shouldn't count when there are still enemies around.
9) I was told to go to the greenhouse, I did but there was nothing to do there, so i stopped playing, is this the end of the content for now or was there a bug there? (or maybe i'm dumb)
10) This might be only relevant for the parts that I played, but combat seems pretty repetitive. You mainly need to position yourself correctly and keep using melee attacks to prevent them from attacking. That isn't bad, but since lots of waves of enemies are pretty similar, this tends to get dull.
Even though I did have a bunch of issues, I did enjoy my experience. The game really shows heart, and the changes that I feel need to happen are not big changes.
I wish you the best of luck with this game and I am waiting for future updates to see where this goes.

Quit after the first 10 minutes, but returned to finish the game in order to see if it did something interesting later on for the review. About 1h of the recorded time was alt-tabbed because "escape" didn't open up a menu to exit the game, didn't think to try "enter" for it.
The game could be somewhat enjoyable if the controls weren't as clunky as they are. You can only press one button at a time - 4 direction movement with no smooth transition. Also it seems that whoever designed the menus has never played any other video games. Took a good while to actually navigate the in-game pause menu to exit the game. The way dialogue popups pause the game doesn't feel good for the flow either, subtitles or narration would work much better. Didn't bother me too much, but would have left a better overall impression.
The weirdest decision the game makes is having stealth gameplay with a timer ticking down to your death. Good stealth games are all about observation and calculated movements. However the aging gimmick requires you to rush through the levels so it rather becomes a boring grind of trial and error.
As for the aging idea, it seems interesting at first, but the only actual gameplay function it has is that you have to be this tall to pull a lever and can move faster at some ages, that's it. Some checkpoints also seem to reset your age while others don’t, so there’s an inconsistent “your choices matter” – “your choices don’t matter” thing going on, probably in order to prevent the player getting stuck. The aging mechanic is never a tradeoff of "I will have less time but have these new options", it's always "you need to be this tall to proceed" Once you reach your first lever you HAVE to age up in order to use it, once you hit a big movable box you HAVE to age up in order to move it. The only actual tradeoff moment I noticed was that as you age, you get slightly faster. The "Portal instructional video" artstyle made me think of clever puzzles, but the hardest puzzle in this game was figuring out how to navigate the menu. All other puzzles boil down to "Press every button you see and carry on".
Off the top of my head, they could have made the aging two-way, have some certain points where you can change age and stuck a whole lot more age-related puzzles in between. Maybe have the child fit through small spaces, have an actual purpose for the elderly, had a bunch of Portal-like puzzles where you have to wait to age up at certain points and use different ages to solve a single problem etc. But right now it's a couple of trivial puzzles and some stealth segments.
Feels more like a gamejam game or a prototype than a finished product.

Since this game was just released as a super early♥♥♥♥♥alpha recently, it's not completed (obviously). There's not much to do and not much to see. It's a starting point and the devs are pretty keen on working on stuff (and did some pretty immediate bug fixes so that's a pretty good sign). Here's the preliminary barebones review, to be updated as the game does.
UPDATED - NOVEMBER 12TH, 2014
Notes: It's really hard to actually split some of these things into pros and cons at this stage of development because everything, depending on what you value or how 'done' it is could go in either category. Until the game is further along, I'll keep the various points in a numbered list here, irrespective of pro or con.
ONTO THE THINGS--
1. Lots of potential.
You're in a sandbox world as a dragon and theoretically, you get to help shape the landscape (metaphorically). Hopefully before too long we'll be able to interact with humans, have enemies, etc. At the moment, as of the latest hotfix, there is a lot more life to the map. Humans (some that attack you with spears), cows, deer, trolls, move houses, lots of trees-- It's not much yet, but it's getting there, especially compared to what it was on release day.
2. Graphics aren't half bad though not spectacular. A little dated at the moment.
They'll probably get better and could use some optimization work (but so could the whole system and that typically comes with time). There are still some problems with screen resolutions and rendering, but killing something no longer causes the Peasant of Doom glitch (I.E. killing a peasant would cause them to erupt with red blood gibs that formed an FPS-murdering column to the point where you ought to restart your game and think about what you how murdering peasants is apparently bad). Also the status bars and some of the buttons (like the map selection button that looks a bit like a loading screen) could use some polish.
3. Dragons are customizable and can age.
While that's not fully implemented yet, it's on the way, bro. There is some current customization and stats (but they don't seem to have much effect at the moment). At the moment, customization is limited to changing colors, but entire different species of dragon and adaptations are planned.
4. Linux and Mac versions.
They were released pretty quickly along with the recent hotfix. There seems to have been some issues with getting the Linux version to play straight from Steam for some users, but the devs posted a workaround for it in the meantime while they fix up their Linux upload.
5. Very active and respectable developers.
They've been very active in the forums, very polite in how they handle criticism and feedback of all sorts, and have shown zero leaning towards any sort of censorship. They're chill with anyone wanting to review or add suggestions or doing letsplays. They're also working on cataloguing known bugs to quash as they can while working on implementing new mechanics. So far, they've been very on top of things and have been amicable. They are some of the best behaved Early Access developers I've ever run across.
6. Unity engine.
Not really a con unto itself so much as Unity can be a buggy pain but it can also do some cool stuff. There are people that really don't like the Unity engine. That's entirely fair. However, it can be done well. In the meantime, it's going to be its own pain in the♥♥♥♥♥while the devs work to tame it. It also just doesn't seem to like some computers which can be a real off-putter to some gamers.
7. Nothing much at the moment to do.
You can fly around (the mechanics of that were improved with the recent hotfix, but it can still be a bit wonky-- I'm bad at it and faceplant into the ground a lot). You can light things on fire, especially now that there's a lot more to burn: several villages from small to large (though some are unpopulated), a small amount of people (women with spears and screaming men), trees, and apparently trolls. You can also eat the gibs that drop to help you grow. Unfortunately, there's nothing more than that yet. That and the growth mechanic isn't exactly implemented yet either and it needs a lot of tweaking.
8. The tutorial is virtually non-existent.
A tutorial itself hasn't really been implemented but some helpful hints when you start a world are shown on the screen. Unfortunately, due to earlier mentioned resolution problems. There is a list of current controls pinned in the Steam forums, but that's another temporary workaround until things can be more solidly implemented.
9. No save/load feature.
When you start a world, you always start fresh. You cannot save and you cannot load. This is only temporary, but at the moment, there isn't much you'd want to save anyway. Your dragon's stats at the moment are carried over through the playthroughs anyway. Just every time you start the game, you basically refresh the map so you can burn the same villages over and over again.
10. Pricy, somewhat.
For the level of early access that it is, it's a bit high, but they made no pretense about how much it would be when they posted their pricing model in the forums here on Steam. However, in the long run and for being a part of the development process, that's not so bad. It just depends on what's worth it more to you, the customer, to pay now to be part of the development process or to pay later (at a possibly higher cost) when the game is more complete or entirely complete. The developers have stated that they are encouraging people who aren't sure or who have been burned by Early Access debaucles before to please wait to purchase until their trust can be earned.

It's a game that's really only worth playing if you discovered it already in your Steam library. The great soundtrack and sweet analog media aesthetic don't balance out the uninspired puzzles. The game's primary gimmick involves collectible cassettes which take you to these screensaver / music visualization worlds. These are very pretty but gameplay wise there's no depth to them. You pop in, you see if there's a green thing to click and, if not, you run a magnet over the thing and you go back in and find the green thing to click on. It's rinse and repeat from there until the game is over (in about 1.5-2 hours). There are a few align the gears, rotate the water valve puzzles to open doors in order to progress but these are all either way too easy or challenging simply because there's not enough signposting for the player to know what they're meant to do. I also had some frustrations with rotating the gear arms. It's physics based and I found it twitchy and obnoxious.
Overall:
It's very pretty, sounds awesome, worth downloading if you already own it or maybe if it's in another bundle but honestly it feels like a polished browser game with enough artistic merit to grant some attention but not enough legs to actually carry a steam/console release. A meatier version of this with trickier puzzles and a less Anonymous-voice plot sprinkles could be a sweet little indie gem. This isn't quite there.

This game is like an analogy of modern art for videogames: it's objectively bad, without any purpose, meaningful gameplay or whatever but nonetheless since this kind of games are gaining momentum you can't actually say it's bad.

NOTE: I received this game as a gift from a friend who had found himself in possession of an extra Activation Code – I hereby send him a symbolic thanks!
Small Radios Big Televisions (hereinafter "SRBT") is a game about exploring worlds composed out of psychedelic imagery which are locked inside a series of audio-cassettes (or "tapes" if you will); and trust me when I say that visually speaking, SRBT is unlike anything you have ever seen. (Unless, of course, you do drugs on a regular basis.) The game's basic premise is simple: you move around deserted oil rigs and other increasingly mysterious abandonned structures and click your way through a series of interconnected rooms, within which you usually do one of three things – you either find a tape (and explore it), magnetize the tape (and explore its distorted version) or solve a thematic puzzle. The audiovisual side of the game is absolutely brilliant and mind-boggling, which is exactly what its creator, Owen Deery, had intended. And yet, SRBT is the first time I found myself hesitating before posting a recommendation. While the experience is undoubtedly unique and definitely worthwhile, some design choices are questionable or outright bad. I have to mention the fact that the maps of the levels (displayable when pressing 'M') are absolutely useless and confuse you more than they help you. Other unfortunate decision on the author's part is a late-game puzzle where you turn wheels to raise/lower the water levels – this is terribly designed and frustrating in that the game is unable to properly explain to you how it works (usually done via invisible tutorials and clever environmental design). I shan't pretend I have any sort of proficiency in playing puzzle games, but I am yet to see a player recording a walkthrough who didn't just randomly stumble upon the solution while having no clue as to its explanation. SRBT's full price (12 €) also seems like a buggerance since the game offers only 2-3 hours of gameplay. Luckily enough, SRBT's unprecedented overall atmosphere outweighs its small but significant imperfections.
TO SUM UP: If you like experimental games with genuinely interesting ideas and don't mind the occasional surge of frustration, then you should definitely consider buying Small Radios Big Televisions and paying a few tapes a visit. However spending the full price of 12 € is unwise as the game simply cannot offer enough in return to compensate for it.

My Pros and Cons with this game. *Warning: small biased opinion in here and a bit of a read*
Prerequisites:
- If you want to learn the basics of guitar/bass, try this game with the Real Tone Cable. If you are just starting, you might have a beginners/starters guitar kit. Try getting Rocksmith 2014 with the Real Tone Cable.
- As you progress, you can venture in other areas of guitar/bass, and it's pretty much an open path to where you want to go. If you want to mostly play metal, pop, punk, rock, jazz etc. there are a lot of options to choose from. Just know that certain genres use certain techniques usually not used in other genres, so take a look.
Pros:
-- With the Remastered version, most annoying bugs are gone, and you won't need a Real Tone Cable for the game anymore. You might want to get a decent mic if you want to play it like that (you will also need a good amp to blast itinto the mic).
-- Beginner friendly, and there are songs to everyone's liking.
-- After almost 7 years, they're still making DLC for this game! As of now, there are more than 900 songs to download, and 266 Song packs (Some are not available in EU, so try setting your location to USA if you want those certain DLCs)
-- Arcade modes to practice Hammer-ons, Pull-offs, Sliding, natural harmonics and more!
-- If you by any chance have the 1st Rocksmith, you can buy a pass to transfer all of the songs from Rocksmith one to the Remastered version.
Cons:
--Not all techniques are available in Rocksmith 2014. The one they teach/showcase here are the ones that are most commonly used in most playstyles of guitars.
--After 7 years, all the DLC prices are still the same. That is complete crap to be honest. 1 song is $2.99 (or €2.99) and is very expensive. If you plan to buy ALL DLC in the game, it would tally up to ~$4500 (or €4500). That is jawdropping!
--Some songs are exclusively in DLC song packs, and there might be a song that or two that you like, but you dislike the rest. I have this situation wiht a 5 song back, and only like 2 songs in there. It discourages me from buying the pack.
Small fix:
Reduce DLC that have existed for over 18 months to $/€1.99, and 36 months by $/€0.99. It is really a bummer to find a song made in 2012 and still costing €/$2.99. Or have a anniversary DLC sale!
Wrap up:
Overal, this game has a few flaws that can be ignored, but the rest of it is great. They should really fix that DLC pricing.
My grade: 8.6/10
Main issue: DLC
Minor issue: none

Godot is a meticulously crafted piece of software.
Just imagine you want the latest dev build on ANY platform you are just two commands away. Git clone, scon platfrom=x11; and then run the fat binary.
It doesnt stop there the fat binary then crosscompiles your games from linux to the supported platforms.
In achieving this Godot places itself amoung a select few softwares of excellent quality; software such as Steam, Source engine (undoubtedly unfair comparissons as neither of these publish their code publicy), Firefox, Inkscape to name a few. It is a massive achievment.
It is very similar to unity in that it makes developing games accessible and takes care of many of the crossplatform hurdles.

Genius software here. As a systems programmer I know how much content this engine has that would take ages to do from scratch. On that example alone, it shows just how crazy it is for this to be MIT licensed.
Godot 3.0 features a renderer similar to that of Unreal Engine 4's. You now may ask yourself, "Why not just use Unreal Engine 4?" Well, obviously because you know you can make a game in Godot, but you should be prepared for reality when you work with Unreal Engine 4.
As a pro game-dev tip: don't choose the engine for what you believe it can do. Choose the engine for what you *know* you can do.
Godot is free for all, and all for free.

Heart of Ember is an amateurish casual little RPG.
Sure, this part-time project could use better quality control (text escapes its boxes, you can get stuck in scenery, and you need to scroll to see major options like "Exit"), the stats are rather simplistic (we don't get to distribute ability points when we level), the prince is in our party but we can't see him unless we're fighting, the save system (interact with a save point or you won't be saved) and the mostly featureless landscape - all of this makes Heart of Ember an amateur production. But the writing and world-building, with backstory and secrets hinted at (and good BGM), is, while not epic, sufficiently enticing to me to not want to not recommend this game. It's not much of a challenge, but it's
, and it doesn't feel dumb. Chapter 1 is all you get right now (it ends on a huge cliffhanger), and it takes 1-2 hours to complete.
You might find the price a tad high for a small amateur production, but if you catch it in a bundle or it is on sale, give it a look.

Hello everyone I play Guitar and still  learning new things every day I will update this more as time gos on to tell you the truth I'm absolutely in love with this game. Learning to play guitar or bass has never been more fun than this. All you need is your electric guitar or bass of choice, the game and a cable that you can buy in a lot of stores that sell things related to music or just electronics in general.
When you first start up the game you get to set up a few things just so that you get the most out of your Rocksmith experience. I went with the option of starting out as someone who has never played guitar previously although I did have some knowledge about how to play. If my memory isn't failing me you get to calibrate and tune your guitar before the game lets you continue onwards. The game then explains the basics and how the layout of the so called 'Note Highway' will show you what notes to hit on the guitar. After you've made it through the basics you're ready to go!
At the start menu there are a lot of options to choose from such as 'Learn a song', 'Lessons' and 'Guitarcade'.
As most other people I went with Learn a song instantly because I was so excited to start playing songs. If you chose the option of starting out as a complete beginner the game will take it easy in the beginning by only giving you a few notes now and then. It will feel slow but it was still enjoyable for me. The way this works is that the more notes you hit and the better you do will increase the amount of notes you get on screen. This is called 'Dynamic Difficulty' and is one of the main reasons Rocksmith actually works as well as it does.
I would recommend starting out in Lessons learning some more of the basic stuff like posture, picking and how to use a strap if you want to play while standing up. I think that most people, like me prefer sitting down when playing Rocksmith or they just don't have a strap to stand up. There are a lot of great lessons ranging from the more simple techniques like chords to the advanced stuff like tapping.
Something that a lot of beginners tend to neglect is the Guitarcade, I really think that the Guitarcade is one of the most important features of Rocksmith as the mini-games are fun and help you build up muscle memory that you will need if you want to play the guitar. One of the best mini-games for me is the 'String skip saloon' as it helps you learn to hit the right strings without looking. 'Ducks ReDux' is another important one teaching you the distance between the frets of your chosen instrument.
The most commonly asked question is probably: "Does Rocksmith 2014 really work?"
Yes! It most definitely works. It provides the motivation and fun aspect needed to learn to play the guitar and your favourite songs. If you are thinking about buying this game and your biggest concern is "does it actually work?" then buy it and see for yourself, I can guarantee that you will atleast to some degree improve your playing and general technique.
Rocksmith 2014 has to be one of my favourite games of all time just because of how detailed and enjoyable it is. A function that I didn't even discuss but is a great way to get better is the 'Riff Repeater'. It lets you slow down and practice certain sections of a song or a lesson and really fiddle around with a lot of settings to make it easier for you to learn. Also in 'Session mode' you can jam with AI musicians playing scales at your own tempo and with a lot of different instruments.
10/10

-Talk to everyone you see.
-Keep an eye on the time (it's a 24 hour clock in the top left of the screen).
-Be sure to make it to every apointment, especially parties (and try not to get too drunk and pass out at parties).
-Read all floppy discs you find, copy and paste useful information to one disc to save space and stay organized.
-Use floppies to take notes.
-Test yourself, be clever and don't give up!

PROS: Its a very good game - from a stategic card game point of view. There are dozens of possible decks to play, and each turn theres lot of decision making. A lot of options how to screw up or turn the tide of the battle. The system that lets you mulligan a card every turn prevents unlucky draws being a major factor. Even though theres lots of decisions, the game is relatively fast paced and comebacks are viable (in some other games you just know youve lost after few turns - not in Duelyst).
CONS: This is the big dealbreaker. Duelyst is one of the many games that sprung up around the time Hearthstone gained mainstream success. And the playerbase of Duelyst is actually very small. Meaning that you will get constantly matched against players whove been playing the game for year or longer and have all the cool epics and legendaries and all the combos and synergy. So unless youre ready to spend a hefty sum of money to get yourself up to speed, prepare yourself for a beating of a lifetime. Youll get smacked around every single game - which gets boring extremely quickly.

The voice acting and dialogue could be a bit better, and the controls can be buggy (but it's early access, so I think it's fair to assume that will be fixed in due time), and the story -- while interesting -- could be more engaging.
That said, BUCK is loads of fun! The art style is interesting, the atmosphere is intriguing, and the gameplay is addicting sidescrolling brawling. While the voice acting, dialogue, and story could use some work in some places, in other places it is quite good. The crafing mechanic of the game is neat and fun to play with, scavenging for supplies makes what at first seems like mindless beat-em-up brawling more high stakes, requiring more finesse, skill and strategy as you progress in order to defeat your enemies without being defeated yourself.
While, as I said, the story could be better, it is however intriguing and does keep you engaged overall, it is just that at times it seems cliche and uninspiring.
The pacing of the game is good, with always something new to do, and a new challenge to overcome, with a reasonable progression of difficulty.
This game isn't perfect (and in its current state, a bit buggy, which is to be expected), but it is loads of fun and quite enjoyable to play. Happy to have Kickstarted it.

Buck is a well constructed game. It has a rich envoirnment, a well suited soundtrack, and delightful gameplay mechanics. The story is well driven, and the characters are all fitting, (if not slightly exaggerated in their characterization). However, there were a few flaws that I noticed within the early-access portion of the game. None of them particularly major, but noticable enough.
To start, the tutorials are decently constructed in-game, but whenever I looked at the tutorial menu, the first page with the 12 slots was hard to read, and I couldn't zoom in on it. The icons themselves were divided up nicely, so if there were a way to divide that up into separate pages for an easier read, that would be a nice touch. Also, if the background music of the current location could continue playing in the menu screen, that would keep from breaking away from the envoirnment Buck is in at the current time.
Second, the combos are tricky to master. I like the idea of needing to execute a combo with the right timing, and different timing for each combo. However, this wasn't exactly easy to do, and it would be nice to have a better indicator of when to press the next button in the combo, or have an broader time range to execute the combo.
Third, the character interactions were believable, but the the dialogue itself between the characters didn't exactly seem to flow. Nibbler the Salvager, for instance, was a stark contrast to Buck. One of the things that threw me off was how loud the audio was between them. Nibbler was more animated in his voice as opposed to the gruff softness of Buck, and while this is fantastic for the diverse character interactions within the story, it fell into the uncanny valley of one recording not syncing with the other.
Fourth, the envoirnments are incredibly detailed, and are beautiful. The dark tones are fitting and pleasing to look at in the post-apocalyptic world. Every now again, however, even with my brightness turned up high on my laptop, the visuals seem to fade into dark values a little too much, and became hard to focus on whenever Buck travelled from place to place. The main area where this was present in The Junkyard level.
Fifth, the battle mechanics are well constructed, and provide a great challenge. However, this is sometimes unfairly so. For instance, if you have two slow-moving shooters, and one fast melee opponent, whenever you manage to dodge one, you could be instantly shot at by the other, and lose health, and when on low health, this can be rather trying. This is avoidable, and there are tactics to manage the battle. It would just be nice to have an easier way to dodge attacks or manage the battle.
Sixth, the crafting is a wonderful touch, but I did notice that in order to create some items, you needed five slots, which didn't make sense, when you only use four different materials to craft a single object.
The last "major" thing that threw me off were some of the dialogue options. This game poses the idea that your choices matter, and that's a fantastic idea, especially with the various dialogue options given. However, sometimes the dialogue choices mean little to nothing, and other times, it progresses the conversation. What I would like to see here is a color code to indicate what dialogue options can be chosen again, like in the beginning stages when talking to Mug about Jodie or asking about the Mongrels, and what are a one time decisive option, like when talking to Zoe for the first time. A way to do this could be a green color to indicate that you can come back to this question or conversation, while blue could indicate that this will be a "choice" or a one time dialoguue option. Futhhermore, when I first started the game and was under the impression that choices define you, I thought this was a relation to looting items as well, which made the game progressively harder (not necessarily a bad thing, just misleading).
The only "bug" I ever came across was right after the discovery of the murder of the scout Mongrels in the first mission, when leaving the building. When I dodged the final enemy in that small area, a bulky, club weilding dog, I was shot, and the game kept respawning me at that point, causing me to constantly die, and I needed to restart the game. This also occured in the Gutless Gultch, coming down the elevator towards the entrance of the 1st area.
Buck shows a lot of promise, and I fully enjoyed the game for its early access. Here's hoping for a brilliant final product!

So, this is a weird one. Mechanically, you explore a set of facilities hunting for tapes (i.e. Memorex style blank audio cassettes with labels scrawled on them) then exploring the small vignettes inside each tape for keys (actually glowing green orbs but they're used as keys) that let you access further into the facility. There are mild environmental puzzles to solve and each facility has a couple of tape scrubbers which corrupt the tapes you're carrying and reveal further keys inside them. None of that probably sounds too odd but it's the aesthetic that makes it. Everything is viewed through an odd filter that makes it looks both new and old at the same time. Similarly the sound track is made up of a bunch of hazy dream-like ambient pieces which don't force their way into your perception but are instantly noticeable when they change or stop. This extends to the tapes themselves which, in their vanilla form, are usually clean-ish and normal looking scenes (e.g. a mountain, a forest, a river) but which are warped to varying degree by the scrubber to become weird and twisted versions of themselves. There's an over-arching story which is alluded to in cut scenes between levels but it's not fleshed out enough to become particularly meaningful to my mind. The game itself is slightly let down by the fact that in a couple of parts you waste lots of time just navigating the levels and the gameplay itself isn't strong enough to stand that but it only happened a couple of times and not enough to colour my overall positive experience with the game. If you're looking for something short and weird with a unique aesthetic then it's definitely a goer.

The campaign is long and deep, but multiplayer is another story. And many would argue that is the real meat and potatoes of a CoD game. (In fact, Xbox 360 owners were cheated out of the campaign entirely.)
First off, coming from competitive shooters like CS:GO and Insurgency, it is very unrealistic both in gameplay mechanics and visuals, and a lot of weapons and skins are downright ugly. I would prefer a battle-scarred sand dune to the "best" ones in the game. Everyone is Ussain Bolt. Snipers can fly around while shooting with Annie Oakley accuracy. Guns recoil like Airsoft. Bullets are weak. Explosions have no splash. People reload, heal, and regain thrust faster than a cheetah on steroids. Everyone seems to know where the enemy is, thanks to overpowered perks, skillstreaks, or downright cheating (historically common in CoD).
Half of my hits don't register. A lot of my great shots show on my screen but not the kill cam. Even if I manage to land 4-5 shots center mass, they'll just turn and one-shot me (most people use sniper rifles). Getting the jump on someone isn't even a guaranteed kill, as they can just fly around after getting hit (and players can magically withstand multiple headshots). I almost always get traded after a kill; I've only unlocked one scorestreak so far. Some of my perks literally don't work, and I don't know why. I know some can be countered but not everybody can have the same countering perk. I hate having to give up important tactical equipment just to keep up with those who use 4-5 perks. To make matters worse, the wildcards enabling over-perking take up an inventory slot themselves, which makes little sense. I try to stay quiet and under the radar, but silencers nerf the damage and range to an unusable degree.
Beginners like myself are always pitted against the literal John Madden of CoD, with little hope of a positive K/D. It's not fun, the constantly getting shot out of nowhere and the resulting humiliation. Paying customers should not feel embarrassed and harassed for starting out. The campaign and bonus content offer very little preparation for real engagements. Core team deathmatch is the only mode people play, and it's only about kills. And the zombie mode is a joke compared to other CoD titles with said game mode. What bugs me most is I can follow perfect tactical procedure, only to get butchered by someone sliding in like an idiot, or bumrushed by a random spawn in the relatively small maps. The kill cam fails to show what I did wrong, if anything.
To succeed in CoD BO3, you must learn to spray, jump spam, and stare at your radar. Then you'll carry these bad habits into other games (that take real skill) and get rightfully pwned. To me, it is not worth forgetting everything I learned in much more realistic military shooters. I actually feel sorry for those who spent hundreds or thousands of hours in this game, as their skill isn't transferrable to other games or real life. This is not only the worst CoD title in the series; it is the worst modern AAA shooter. I am done with CoD for life, and the desperate attempt to rebuild the fanbase with a WWII version will not save it. If you want to experience the campaign, it is barely worth it at 50% off ($59.99 retail at time of review). As a whole, at full price,  I obviously do not recommend.
P.S. If the developers make CoD WWII's combat anything like BO3's, it will not only be disrespectful to those who actually fought in that war, but it will give kids a distorted view of history and reality. War is not some arcade game. While I don't think video games contribute to violence, I think telling a youngster headshots are non-lethal is asking for an accident. Ironically, Call of Duty fails in it's "duty" to depict weapons as the dangerous tools they are. Heck, maybe kids these days will want to join the army after playing, but a good CoD player does not a soldier make.

I have to say Sword of the Stars II: Enhanced Edition is - far and away - the best space 4x game I've found. I have a couple dozen games in my collection, so I feel confident saying that.
It's not an easy game on any dificulty setting. You have to manage your research to be able to compete with your neighboring races' military while earning enough money to sustain your empire. That fleet you just swept an entire sector clean of the enemy with will be decimated if you don't upgrade the weapons and armaments at an apropriate starbase before it enters battle again.
There are planets which will be stepping stones for your empire's expansion, while others will be the economic and industrial powerhouses which sustain and drive forward everything - once you find them and colonize them. It takes *fleets* of colony ships working for many turns (typically) to establish a colony, then more turns for that colony to reach it's potential.
The game has an evolutionary feel. The early ships you begin with will survive combat with a neighboring race only 50% of the time - you will take losses even if you win. Careful research choices and economic management will give you an advantage - for a while - then your enemy will bring up their newer designs and it will be an even fight again, at best. If you know military history that should sound familiar. You also have to plan how to build your fleets, remembering to include supply ships.
Lastly, many of the technologies will not be available to you (randomly, every new game), so you have to adapt to what you can research. Maybe you'll have point defense lasers, or maybe point defense cannons. Maybe energy weapons or kinetic. Missles function as artillery, devastating in certain circumstances but are slow to fire, large weapons systems that require a lot of supply. Kinetic weapons also require more supply than energy weapons - which require energy. Each ship will be a balance between energy produced and supply capacity versus available weapons and armor systems - and crew requirements - and the range your fleets need to operate at. You might want that new weapons system as much for it's battle winning power as the automation improvements which reduces crew requirements - and allows you more flexibility with design. Only in the late game will it be possible to field a powerful warship that can range further than neighboring systems.
SotS II is a deep game, and well worth it to learn how to play. There is too much to mention in an already long review whcih gives SotS II a lot of depth and replayability.  Oh - did I mention that each race has it's own unique drive system? so you have to have a different play style with each race, especially since one race will be more likely to have energy weapons while another will be more likely to develop kinetic. There's just too much to say about this game, it is a classic, and well worth your time to learn.

TLDR:  I absolutely recommend Rocksmith to anyone who wants to enjoy practicing/playing guitar and/or for someone who enjoyed guitar hero games and want to take it up a notch.
I've been playing guitar/bass on and off for 10 years or so.... including 2 summers where I took lessons.... I've never been good enough to feel comfortable playing in a band, but I've always enjoyed jamming and playing tabs by myself and very rarely with friends.
I grabbed this game on summer sale after watching it for years... I wish I would have gotten it so much earlier.
I've played more guitar the past few weeks in Rocksmith than I had the past 5 years combined.  I have really enjoyed playing guitar again and it is super helpful for feeling like you are progressing each time you sit down.
I've personally had more satisfaction playing bass than guitar at this point... the bass lines are super fun to sightread and many of the tracks have been easy enough for me to master in a few sessions of practicing.  But guitar is great too and I look forward to bouncing back to it after I get bored with the bass lines of my favorite songs.
The only cons I can think of:
- As others have said, this is not going to TEACH you proper technique of how to play guitar.  But I think if learning guitar from scratch was your goal, you could surely tandem Rocksmith with some lessons/youtube to make it work.  This game will help more in making practicing/playing fun than anything else.
- The way the game senses your playing seems to be very favorable... so if you are really trying to dial in a song, at some point it is on you to hold yourself accountable.
- Unless I am missing it, it doesn't have a 'career' mode like Rock Band... that I personally loved a ton.  It's very much a self-driven game/tool.
- I've already spent more on DLC than the game itself  :D
Overall, I am loving the game and highly recommend it to any aspiring/amateur guitar players.

Ever wished Watch_Dogs focused more on its hacking and less on its Ubisoft, open-world AAA desires? then this is the game for you! Really interesting and enjoyable open-world hacking game, where you can hack a turtle (or was it a tortoise...)!
The game is great with it's hacking. There's so many secrets and hidden webs for you to follow if you use some intution and it's one of the most rewarding parts of this game. It has a very hands-off approach when it comes to telling the player what to do, which is what makes it so satisfying when you run into something really interesting and cool..cus you did it yourself, not cus the big marker told you to do the thing. Congrats! I was also surprised by how much I could do with the hacking. The coding language in the game isn't going to turn you into a real life world class coder, but it's a great tool for beginners to pick up and advanced enough to let people with experience to make some pretty cool hacks (i know there's a way you can exploit the finance PC for infinite $$$...never could work it out).
One of the other's strengths of the game is it's music. One of the main dude's on this game, El Huervo, contributed tracks to the Hotline Miami soudntracks and him (and other contributers) have created a fantastic OST. Music isn't used too much but when it is, it hits the feeling of the world and the atmosphere just right. Whenever I was walking around the town, I liked to carry a radio just so I could help immerse myself in the world that little bit more.
The game does have some negatives though. There's some bugs in the game that can get you stuck (watch out for desks. seriously.), NPCs don't really react to you much (both friendly and hostile) and the ending of the game is a bit limp and unsatisfying, with relationships and characters just feeling...unresolved...
...but if you can deal with all those things and willing to be a bit more forigiving of a small indie team making a game of this scale, then you'll find a game that's totally worth your time. Fresh, unique and BE CAREFUL WITH THE REGISTER COMMAND.

A really fun, smart game. The art is gorgeous, the world is intriguing, the dialogue is realistically awkward and endearing, and the developers are Swedish. And then there's the hacking: real, creative programming.
You can hack almost any object in the game, and construct intricate networks of computers conspiring to transport you around the town and unlock doors for you at will. I love the way the game allows you to remove roadblocks from the early game through hacking - no need to sleep when you can hack a can of soda to give you -1000000000000 sleepiness.
My only real complaint is that the camera controls are a bit clunky, but you'll get used to that in your first couple of hours.
As someone who does coding as a hobby, this was a fun and creative experience with character and depth. Get it in a bundle if you can.

This game is a brilliant premise, and for the most part is quite well executed. There's a fair amount of freedom given to you, and no pressure on time. The hacking part of the game, for someone with no programming skills (i.e. me) is simple enough to get to grips with, although I suspect someone with more knowledge would find it easier and be able to do more. What lets it down is that it's often hard to know what you are doing or supposed to do - there's no log of your conversations which means that you can easily forget things people have told you, particularly if you come back to the game at a later time. There are also a few glitches I've found, and it's difficult to know whether it's a problem with the game or if it's supposed to happen.
Overall, Else Heart.Break() is a really good idea which is done well enough to get you to come back after your first few sessions, but not quite well enough to be a game that is something you can't wait to get back to. As it progresses, you might find yourself more frustrated with it.

Don't get me wrong, this is an impressive game. There are just a few things that break it /just/ enough for me that I can't recommend it at full price.
1) This game does not have a learning curve. If you don't have much city sim experience, you will start at a significant disadvantage. There are no tutorials, no directed quests (unless you count scenarios, which aren't included with the base game), and no way to learn except by trial and error. Sandbox mode is great, but I expect a little more with my $30 game.
2) The bugs. This is the big one. The bugs vary from person to person, computer to computer, but there will be bugs. Some people have 6 lane highways where drivers will only use one lane. For me, power lines keep going bad for no reason, which basically kills a city if it's one that goes to a water distribution plant. Sometimes deleting a broken line would fix it, sometimes not. Restarting the game didn't fix it, and I didn't have the funds to completely replace the electrical grid, so when it broke for good, that entire save file was ruined.
I don't want it said that I had nothing good to say about this game. It looks beautiful, it performs admirably, and I can see tons of strategic depth to it. That makes it all the more disappointing that random chance keeps interfering to prevent me from experiencing it.

I feel very rude and it frustrates me to write this, but I do not recommend Cities: Skylines unless it is at a good sale price.
I love simulation games, but this one grew stale and was not for me.
The first several hours were really enjoyable and I even went as far as to get the After Dark DLC at a sale price since I anticipated I'd be addicted. But only a few hours later did I realize I wasn't enjoying the game anymore. There are no "scenarios" to play, adding actual goals to the game, unless you get the Natural Disasters DLC (and there are apparently very few). You're just left to endlessly build a city with intricate micromanagement. If that sounds like your type of game, buy it! If that's all you want, this game will be perfect.
My major complaints that led to me stop enjoying the game began with the lack of customization. For the first while, before your city's population adds up and you unlock more features, there's not much to add personalization to your city to make it feel like your own. Different types of roads and other customizations are blocked off arbitrarily in the early portion of building a city, and you'll only get access to these by boosting your population by a stated amount. It makes sense! It really does, but it made the first hour or two of starting a new city absolutely boring. I feel the game would have benefitted from loosening these restrictions.
... and to follow that up, you may say "there are mods, though!" Yes, there are, and I was very excited to try them. However, the community proves that there are troubles with every update. Mods become incompatible, unsupported by the developers, and as a new player, lots of research will go into finding out how to use these mods and have them appear in your game, like custom buildings or styles. Many times, just trying to make sure custom content appeared in the in-game "Content Manager" would crash the game just after a few items. I thought it was just because I originally ran the game on an external hard drive, but I eventually tried it on my internal SSD, and the mods just seemed to hamper the game.
If you have a lot of patience to learn the sciene behind the custom content of the game, and don't mind the aimless city-building with not much else to look forward to but "more, more and more". This is a sandbox game for you, no question.

I understand why some people like it, but after the amount of time I played, I just feel exhausted and need a long break. The pleasure of growing my city sort of numbed itself.

One of the best games ever made in the 4x genre, I can not stress this enough.
The ship upgrades, tech trees, weapon combinations, realtime battles, completely different races ...
It will look difficult to some people at first, and trust me, it is, but the time investment is so worth it in the end.
There are a lot of negative comments, but most of them stem from the fact that most negative people only played for half an hour, or in general a way to short time. You can't really learn this game in that short amount of time, especially not a game as big as this one. Reading through every item on the tech tree alone would take more than a half an hour :P
Looking at a couple of ships in the editor, and equipping different weapons, engines, etc will also take more than half an hour... So how can you base your review on 30 minutes played time? It boggles the mind...
I've played this game for just over 140 hours, and in all that time, the only bugs I encountered were an end game crash when I fought a specific incredibly dangerous space monster. So people complaining about constant crashes, need to take a look at their system.
All of the recent 4x games pale in comparison to this masterpiece. Sure some might look very pretty and have an awesome shiny interface, but are shallow and boring (Endless space series) or perhaps they're very easy to play and require really no 4x knowledge to get going (Moo3) but are ultimately very forgettable.
This one however will kick your behind, eventually you'll figure out a powerful tech path leading to great weapon loadout and engine tech that gives you an edge, only to be kicked in the posterior again by the AI's response in 50 turns.
In conclusion:
Do you want a hard game?
Do you want a deep game?
Do you want an unsimplified game?
Do you want tons of research options, tech, ships, etc.?
Did you answer yes to the above? Then go ahead, try one of the best 4x games on steam.

Transformice is one of those games that takes time to get addicted to but once you do, it's a never ending binge of enjoyment.
~~~~~~~~
I've been playing Transformice since around 2013. I must have over 300 hours on this game outside of Steam. It's one of those games where you can just kind of relax and play without having to strategize too much. Let me go over some pros and cons.
PROS:
It's free. There isn't much of a comitment. You don't like it, you uninstall it, you love it, you get to keep it forever, free of charge. There are some P2W features for clothing and such but none of which are demanding.
It's addictive. I've been playing this game for around 4 years and it still isn't utterly boring. You can kind of just sit there for hours without getting bored.
It's creative. The idea of Transformice is unlike any game I have personally seen before. There's plenty to do. Many different gamemodes, custumization, and a huge community that always keeps the game interesting.
CONS:
The community itself isn't the best. There aren't any chat restrictions so one moment you could be just doing your own thing and the next you could be getting in a vulgar 'roast' battle with some snotty 12 year old. If you're bothered by language, I suggest ignoring the chat completly.
Kind of gets repetitive sometimes. For me, I need a month or so break from the game every once in awhile to keep the gameplay fresh. Don't get me wrong, there's still a lot to do but once you're at a certain point in the game where you own pretty much all the features and skills, it does get a bit dull. Nothing a short break can't fix though.
Advancment is kind of slow. It takes awhile to level up and earn in-game currency referred to as cheese as time goes on. You just have to be willing to spend a lot of time and or money to purchase clothing and or objects you want.
DO I RECOMMEND?:
Yes. Transformice is a creative, unlike any other type of game where you just have to try it to understand the enjoyment of it. It's also free so the only thing you have to loose is time. Go for it.

So lets take a look at the call of duty black ops 3 starter pack. For those wondering what that is well its a purchasable content copy of black ops 3 that provides strictly multiplayer. I will be looking over the game on a pro/con style and end it with my final thoughts of the game.
Pro:
The game provides many different main menu musics ranging from zombie songs like lullaby by a dead man to what ever songs that play for black ops 3 zombies. The choices are even bigger with the inclusion of songs from multiplayer and a few from the campaign. Needless to say i really enjoy the zombie songs so it makes chilling waiting to join a match or relaxing at the main menu pretty enjoyable.
Freerunning is a bonus mode where you race time with your freerunning skills and a few target practice. Its not a very big deal in the games case but i find it somewhat welcoming.
Many guns and weapons to use in the game. Most guns are obtained through normal level progression but other guns are earned from this game's lootbox system the "Black Market". I dont mind it personally it is nice to see a variety of guns but it is nothing that i find really necessary or worthwhile. The black market also causes you to get clothing for your character and calling cards too.
Con: (Here we go)
With the starter pack copy it eliminates any offline experience. I dont care if i dont get zombies or the campaign but taking out the custom match mode is pretty low down. The backs the player in the corner to do online multiplayer and it is a pretty sink or swim tactic. This makes any and all offline practice with bots impossible unless you pay for the full game.
The multiplayer has multiple different characters. That is not bad at all but the issue is the characters have special abilities, some are really cheap and definantly kills any enjoyment that the game can provide. One imparticular is the character that has the clone special ability. He spawns 4 or 3 clones that doesnt sound so bad but it makes things cheap or how about the flamethrower guy that has a flamethrower that has a huge range and kills fast. Balance is what makes the game fun. If you boost something for some offensive use bring down their health then. It produces a balance and does not break the flow of the game. Another suggestion is that each character had a counter character like in games such as overwatch or seige. That is blance for players.
Killstreaks are very annoying to deal with. Theres these things called raps which really suck. Technically they are explosive spike drones that act like the swarm in black ops 2. Needless to say they take some hits to destroy....i dont know because i never happen to destroy one. I put in maybe a half of a clip and they kept rolling towards me. Needless to say dying because of that is something no one really enjoys and really makes me want to uninstall the game.
Remember when call of duty was all boots on the ground and killing an enemy was something of skill or better map navigation. Pepperage farm remembers. haha jokes aside this game is far from what made a good multiplayer fun. I dont mind the wall running that is cool and can lead to some interesting level design. My issue is with the boosting in the air and how it makes things much more tedius when it comes to pvp. In a sense when playing a fps like call of duty back in the day all you had to do is focus on things at eye level. Players didnt have to focus on enemies dropping from above on them. In black ops 3 thanks to the boosting; now players can fly over their enemy and get some sneaky shots off on them. As a player you now have to focus not only on potential attacks that can be viewed at eye level but you must look directly up at times. All of this focusing is not fun and will get you the player killed pretty easy since with the more ways one can get gunned down in a simple fire fight the higher chances you will get to see that lovely killcam more than you play.

I'm not one for lengthy reviews, so I'll dive right in.  This is awesome, but the default way that it wants to teach you how to learn a song is going to be bad.  Music is muscle memory.  The game wants to slowly add difficulty to a song by adding more and more of the actual notes as you improve (Think Rock Band or Guitar Hero difficulties).  This is the default option.  If you learn this way, you'll constantly be unlearning the bare bones of a riff to relearn the slightly more beefed up version.  It's also super disorienting when you're making a ton of progress on a song mid-play and it suddenly is far more complicated after half of the song has passed.
Do yourself a favor.  Override dynamic difficulty and set your difficulty to 100%.  This will show all notes at all times and grade you accordingly.  Learn it this way, no matter how daunting songs seem.  If you're struggling, bring up the options and use the riff repeater to slow down a section and practice it over and over and over and over and over and you get the idea.

Rocksmith is an excellent piece of software but poor value as a game. I'm an intermediate bass player and self taught at guitar.
Good:
Interface and options.
Riff repeater. Press space to loop a section or sections. You can set the difficulty, which the song retains after exiting RR, and speet to practice at
Neutral:
Accuracy. For the most part it's pretty good and detects if I'm playing the right note on the default sensitivity. It starts failing on drop Db but that could be my guitar's intonation or pickups. There's many false positives and ways of tricking it into reading a correct note, but it's acceptable in my eyes
The difficulty level up is slow. Even on the increased level up setting and decreased level down setting, songs often stay on simpler difficulties for too long and can take three or more playthroughs to get reach 100% difficulty. For example, in the song "Closing Time" I figured out how to play the melody in no time but the game didn't show the notes until the end of the second playthrough. You can however easily adjust the difficulty of the whole song using rift repeater, and this might be a personal issue. The game is very flexible so it's not fair to call this a negative
It might be easier to learn to play a song with Rocksmith, but learning a song with tabs helps me play by memory much better
Bad:
Price. The game + cable costs about $75 retail and features very limited content in terms of songs. DLC songs are a bit pricy at $3 each. This is fair since you're investing in learning a song through this platform, which is excellent and intuitive for many people, but value becomes dubious with songs that are simply repeated chords. Personal value is subjective though
