Kind of have a love/hate relationship with this game.  For myself, it is an addicting little title.  It is fun to play for a few hours and come back to a few days later.  The game doesn't have much depth, however, and mastering it takes very little time.  It is a fun little Stratedgy/Sim but has a ton of flaws as well.  Being an older game, some of those can be forgiven.
So, the Pro's.
As mentioned, I find this title to be a bit addictive.  The map randomization allows for a different game each time you play.  The graphics aren't bad, considering this came out in 2006, and it's one of the newest Train management games out there.    The game runs very smoothly and is fun to watch.  You're always looking for new resources and at your existing track, looking for the best routes and tie-in's.
Now, the Con's.
Crashes on Windows 7 unless you get the Patched .exe from the forums.  Online multiplayer service is no longer supported.  Cheaty and annoying AI, which isn't very smart and tends to build track which would normally be impossible for you to do so yourself.  Very limited city management.  Games run on a timeline which makes everything feel very linear.  No real Sandbox mode.  Winner is usually determined by who starts out in the "sweet spot" with best resources near them.  Map edges are not very well utilized and you tend to have everyone too close when starting.
Sometimes, the AI in the game becomes really annoying.  They'll neglect resources which they could use and instead lay track to a city you are already running a line to, hindering both you and themselves.  Also, like most AI, they do as they please and it makes me wonder if they actually have the $$$ to do what they did.
In the end, it's a very simple game mainly about train management, routing, and gaining $$$ the fastest in order to win.  It would be nice if it had much more management, maybe maintenance costs or random events on your tracks.  Once you route to many of the resources in your area, the game can play on auto-pilot, somewhat.
Is it worth $10 which Steam has it listed for??  If you like trains, like to play new Sim/Stradegy games, then probably.  However, it is an older game and a simple game, which can grow old fast.

Else Heart.Break() is a beautiful game, both aesthetically and mechanically, and is completely deserving of your time.
Although a little slow to start, Else Heart.Break() picks up dramatically once the programming and code aspects are discovered. Upon acquiring a “modifier”, the player character can waltz around the small town of Dorisburg changing the functionality of various objects and interactions found within the world. From hacking coffee to top-secret computer mainframes, the game’s coding system provides an interesting means of progressing its story. This code system is so robust that it allows for multiple solutions to many of the plot points that you’ll run into, allowing you to stretch your creativity and solve challenges in a personalized manner.
This hacking system lends itself well to the narrative of the game, as nearly every major plot point requires you to go out and find it yourself. You’ll often find yourself running around town talking to every NPC imaginable, attempting to find some hint or direction to advance the story. Although this can be frustrating at times, the majority of the time I found exploring Dorisburg and learning about its characters to be exciting and fun. This game rewards you for delving into its secrets by presenting you with humourous side-stories or new functions to augment your programs and hacking ability. It is extremely satisfying to work off of a small hint given to you by an NPC and hack your way to the next objective.
That said, if you are looking at this game as a non-programmer, your experience with this game may be completely different than mine. Although this game does a good job of introducing you to the concepts needed to use its language (if you manage to find the floppy disks ridden about the world), it may be a bit overwhelming to wrap your head around. It doesn’t take much hacking to advance through the plot and beat the game, however, I think that a major part of the experience lies in exploring the hacking system and messing around in the digital playground that the game gives you.
Additionally, the dialogue system that the game revolves around is extremely rudimentary. Although you are presented with many options to choose from when conversing with NPCs, I found that not many of my decisions actually mattered. The way that NPCs would interact with my character was hardly different based on the decision I made, aside from a few lines of dialogue. This definitely detracts from the overall experience of the game, as you’ll be encountering a heavy amount of dialogue.
These gripes aside, I believe that Else Heart.Break() is a fantastic game that is worth every bit of time that you put into it. Dorisburg is a lovingly-crafted playground that begs to be explored.

I tried Thomas Was Alone because I wanted a short game, and this made a lot of "Best short games" lists that I found across the Internet. I had no idea what to expect going into the game. I hadn't read anything about it. Needless to say, I was quite surprised when I started the game off as a little red rectangle. What the heck was happening? Then I began playing and started to understand the game. At that point, I was hooked. Here is my simple review of this indie gem:
Graphics:
Basic. Very basic. You play as geometric shapes after all. But the graphic simplicity is part of the game's charm. Thomas Was Alone proves that an indie developer can make a compelling game by keeping things simple and focusing more on story and gameplay than on flashy graphics and effects. Don't get me wrong, I like a AAA title with killer graphics, but I also like to take a step back at times and play games like this that are visually simple.
Sound:
The music is great, but where the sound really shines is in the narration. Much like Bastion, the narrator in Thomas Was Alone is at the center of the experience and a key reason why the game is so enjoyable. It is through the narration that you get the game's story and you will find yourself wanting to play through just one more level to hear what is going to happen next.
Controls:
I played with an XBOX 360 wired controller and found the controls easy to pick up. You will find yourself cycling between each character/shape to solve the different puzzles presented in each level. The game does a great job of easing you into the game and helping you understand each shapes movements and special abilities which is important in the later levels where you will be using a combination of abilities to solve the puzzles.
Story:
The story in Thomas Was Alone wasn't particulalrly deep in my opinion, but it was very engaging nonetheless. What made the story great was the different shapes/characters each with his/her own personality. I was amazed at how these personalities shined through both through the narration as well as in the way the shapes moved and behaved. You genuinely will find yourself caring for these shapes. It sounds weird, and it is. It's also freaking brilliant!
Puzzles:
The puzzles struck a good balance of super simple to moderately difficult with no puzzles cuasing me to get to the point of utter frustration or tempting me to look up solutions online. The puzzles become more fun as you progress through the levels and begin using a combination of characters each with different abilities that will need to be used in tandem to progress. Not a deep or extremely difficult puzzle platformer, but a fun one nonetheless.
Overall experience:
This game made me genuinely care about shapes. I never thought this was possible, but it is a testament to the developers and their creative use of the medium. I enjoyed the simplistic graphics and controls along with the fun but not overly difficult puzzles. What stood out the most to me was the narratorand he is a big part of why I played this game from beginning to end. And yes, the game is short with about 3-4 hours playtime in order to complete, so it's not a huge time commitment either. I definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun experience that shows off the power of simple indie games.
TLDR;
I thoruguhly enjoyed Thomas Was Alone. Play for the characters, the narration, and the fun but not overly difficult puzzles. Don't play if you get hung up on simple graphics.

This is a weird game to talk about for me. Not because I was weirded out by it, but because I found this game so aggressively middle-of-the-road, I can't recommend for or against.
Here are my thoughts:
Firstly, 13$CAD for this is far too much. This is a 5-hour tops point-and-click.
This game, along with many other puzzle games nowadays suffer from "ambiguitis", when it comes to storytelling. "What happened here?" You'll find yourself asking. Well, SRBT won't tell you, not in the slightest. This isn't always a bad thing, but when it serves no purpose, it's not really an addition to the story. Or lack therof, I guess.
A few of the earlier puzzles don't follow the rules of the game. Because this game has no tutorials, it expects you to make jumps in logic that you may not always get. I'm not the smartest, but when a system previously introduced to us can't be used in a certain location, I feel cheated. This problem fixes itself in the later levels.
It's boring. The Witness is an interesting game because its world is set up to be explored, and with so many *different* options for what could happen, it keeps you engaged with the game. SRBT presents itself as linear, and doesn't allow for those "oooooooh" moments other games have.
I hate the name, it's very annoying to say.
The visuals are pretty to an extent, I have a few screenshots of particularly nice scenes. The effort the devs made to make the game look older but new was best done in the loading gif. That is aesthetically pleasing, far more than the actual game.
The music is alright, but it wasn't for me. Experiences may vary.
So I guess I didn't really like this game. Maybe you would though.

Long time user of Unity3d.  My initial impression of Godot Engine is good.  From what I've read the engine's scripting langauge (GDScript) is not good for things that demand performance (pathfinding, procedural generation, etc.), but it's great for gameplay logic or other things which do not require optimal performance.  Godot provides a module system which allows us to plug in and compile our own modules written in C++, and 3.0 will introduce C# and other features providing us with everything we need to work around GDScript's performance concerns.
The user interface is easy to navigate and easy on the eyes.
The software itself is lightweight and portable.
MIT license, no strings attached, no royalties.
I designed my Unity3d game's code to not be reliant on UnityEngine.  When Godot 3.0 comes out there's very little reason for me to stick with Unity3d, and I will heavily consider porting over to Godot.

It's a real shame that this game is total garbage, because I love platformers and was looking forward to this one's unique mechanic. Looking back, that mechanic isn't unique at all, but regardless, even though I got it in a humble bundle, it still felt like an enormous waste of time, money, and potential.
First of all, there is no Steam controller support. It doesn't recognize the Steam controller as a 360 controller like NEARLY EVERY OTHER GAME WITH CONTROLLER SUPPORT, and for whatever reason, Big Picture also won't allow me to import configs, so I was stuck using a mouse and keyboard, which is a big "no-no" for platformers of any kind.
Secondly, the design of this game is absolutely disgusting. They throw so many cool mechanics your way, like the ability to take off your head and throw it, or the ability to keep going after you hit an obstacle (I'll get to that in a bit,) but it never really makes any good use of any of these mechanics, and just sticks to the same 3 obstacles with different coats of paint throughout the game (at least, in the 3 chapters that I stomached before giving up completely.) The coolest part of this game is that your limbs can fall off and you can keep running. Your body has 11 individual sections which all can detach when damaged. However, 99% of the obstacles in this game are spinning blades which spin at chest, neck, or ankle height, so you rarely see your limbs flying off like you'd expect. Also, when you hit any obstacle (there are also swinging hammers and lasers,) you fall to the ground and, after a short time, press a button to get up. NOTE: one of the most frustrating parts of this game is that, unlike ANY OTHER GAME IN EXISTENCE WHERE YOU CAN FALL OVER, you can't press the jump button to get up. You have to use WASD. You can also take off your head and throw it, but I only ever had to do this in 1 level before I was ready to throw my keyboard across the room in frustration.
As far as level design goes, this game falls flat again. Like I mentioned before, there are really only 3 main obstacles: spinning blades, swinging hammers, and swinging lasers. Many of the levels have a unique mechanic that separates them from the rest, such as balls rolling down a hill or faces that eject themselves from walls next to you, but these are either incredibly frustrating to avoid or frustratingly easy to avoid. This game has no middle ground. The swinging lasers, as well, swing randomly, and are placed randomly. One of the levels has a "stay in the spotlight" mechanic, but it's never really clear where the spotlight is going to go, and the darkness often hides obstacles that would've otherwise been avoided had I been actually able to SEE them, and the spotlight radius is so small that it almost feels like I keep getting cheated out of my gametime.
I only fought one boss through the entire thing, which was a giant, robotic clown. Which sounds awesome and intimidating, until it starts laughing this annoying, squeaky giggle every two seconds. THen, it's just annoying, especially since that boss has a lot of BS mechanics, such as a platform you have to jump over that randomly switches directions often.
Overall, I hate this game. Couldn't even complete it, don;t want to get invested in its unfair ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Don't buy this game, even in a humble bundle.

Transformice is one of those games that takes time to get addicted to but once you do, it's a never ending binge of enjoyment.
~~~~~~~~
I've been playing Transformice since around 2013. I must have over 300 hours on this game outside of Steam. It's one of those games where you can just kind of relax and play without having to strategize too much. Let me go over some pros and cons.
PROS:
It's free. There isn't much of a comitment. You don't like it, you uninstall it, you love it, you get to keep it forever, free of charge. There are some P2W features for clothing and such but none of which are demanding.
It's addictive. I've been playing this game for around 4 years and it still isn't utterly boring. You can kind of just sit there for hours without getting bored.
It's creative. The idea of Transformice is unlike any game I have personally seen before. There's plenty to do. Many different gamemodes, custumization, and a huge community that always keeps the game interesting.
CONS:
The community itself isn't the best. There aren't any chat restrictions so one moment you could be just doing your own thing and the next you could be getting in a vulgar 'roast' battle with some snotty 12 year old. If you're bothered by language, I suggest ignoring the chat completly.
Kind of gets repetitive sometimes. For me, I need a month or so break from the game every once in awhile to keep the gameplay fresh. Don't get me wrong, there's still a lot to do but once you're at a certain point in the game where you own pretty much all the features and skills, it does get a bit dull. Nothing a short break can't fix though.
Advancment is kind of slow. It takes awhile to level up and earn in-game currency referred to as cheese as time goes on. You just have to be willing to spend a lot of time and or money to purchase clothing and or objects you want.
DO I RECOMMEND?:
Yes. Transformice is a creative, unlike any other type of game where you just have to try it to understand the enjoyment of it. It's also free so the only thing you have to loose is time. Go for it.

This game is a steal for the current sale price of $8.39.
And yes I meant the $8:39 because the main game (great Co Op experience) and the extra game modes are fun and are worth getting.  So grab Resident Evil 6 Complete, grab a friend, play all 4 of the main campaigns, play the extra game modes (the more people that hop on the more people we have to play together, but even with a just a few of your friends the extra modes are fun), and thank me for it later ;) .
This game never deserved the hate it got back when it came out nor does it deserve it now.  Is it maybe left a little unpolished here or there?;, yes, but what it lacks in polish in some areas it makes up for in sheer content and new fun concepts/gameplay.
This game is like getting 4 games in one!
Seriously though it is.  And people that don't really really try the game enough, don't understand just how great the combat/movement is now.
I know the changes in RE 6 take some getting used to and personally I think that's a big reason why people don't give it enough of a chance. The demo does a poor job of showing the game's potential.
The controls are a little different now (coming from Re5) -not having the knife handy felt odd at first but for the trade off of being able to roll out of the way to either side, being able to slide, being able to quick fire, being able to duck, being able to jump to your back, roll foward, run+slide+quick turn around (can run from an enemy slide then turn around fast to fire on him while on the ground), etc. it was worth it.  NOTE: that Leon's story angle starts off not letting you use all controls right out of the gate, give it a second and they become available so don't play it for five seconds and go, "these controls suck", calm it down wait for them to kick in ;) .
Also at first the Healing/Herb Use set up feels weird but once you understand how it works it's actually pretty cool and doesn't stop the action, which I believe is the point of the new inventory set up:
1.) There's a button combo you can use to automatically combine your best herbs without even opening the inventory.
2.) As you combine herbs the dots you see on the herb result are how many life blocks that get added to your case for instant use. Put one herb that has one dot in your case and it gives you the ability to instant heal one life block (via heal key), combine a red and a green herb and it gives you a 6 dot herb to add to your case and thus you can heal 6 heal blocks just from it; the more herbs you add to your case the higher your instant heal potential can be.
Also I think People complain because starting with Re5 they think that the games moved away from what the series was, but infact the series was morphing into something that fit the storyline perfectly like it or not:
-Umbrella was looking for a way to weaponize biological weapons to their fullest and what better way than to make creatures that can do even more but will listen to what they are told to do.  Thus as much as we didn't like it, half smart zombies that could efficently use guns, axes, etc. showed up as they fit Umbrella's agenda and thus the story line.  And with more crazy badies the action picked up and thus became an action co op horror instead of just lone wolf survivial horror.
However that does not mean Re5 and 6 are bad games, quit the opposite really they are plain Action Co Op fun taking down horrible monstrosities.
Back on track though More on RE6-
What Resident Evil 6 is, is really a love letter to it's previous games, to it's fans, and an ode to one of the other greatest zombie killing Co Op games of all time, Left 4 Dead.
Where Resident Evil 6 may lack some polish here or there it makes up for in the meatiness of the game; your basically getting 4 games for the price of one.
You play through 4 different angles of the storyline (which at some points intersect, and thus your game could have 2 other real people playing with you and your buddy, if they are playing their game and are at the same story line point your team is at the same time) with each angle being Co Op and having different partners for that angle:
Leon and Helna Campaign- an ode to oldschool RE Style (slow moving, not so smart, back to basic zombies) and an ode to one of the other great zombie games of all time L4D (Church, Ammo shop Areas, etc).
Chris and Piers Campaign- Re5 style action back in play(run and gun), cranked UP and with a more military twist (Chris finds out it's hard to be a leader of a squad, and he's struggling getting over the emotions brought on from Re5).
Sherry and Jake Campaign- an ode to Resident Evil Nemesis (Run!) with a touch of martial art super human fun (I'm lookin' at you Jake, good thing you got your Dad's blood or that injection might not of went so well huh?).
Ada and Agent Campaign- ode to 2 of the greatest known yet unknown characters of the series (atleast till now; I'm lookin at you Ada...I mean you are wearing tight leather pants after all, erh I mean...your story is expalined more in this game, erh umm yeah that's it), Ada and Hunk, erh umm Ada and The Agent, which is clearly Hunk to me (note Agent is not totally fleshed out as Ada's mission was at first just set as a single player experience, as in he's not in the cutscenes with Ada and he kinda teleaports to where she goes when using her zip gun, but still totally worth it to have yet one more Co Op Campaign; he was thrown in extra for that exact reason last min. and he's still cool as hell---love his freaking punch in mercs mode).
I won't spoil the storyline, but I will say this is a Resident Evil game so you gotta expect someone trying to destroy stuff and a little cheese, but all Re Games have that horror/slapstick aspect to break it up, but that's what makes it Resident Evil imo.
Then there's the extra game modes!
-Oh and I almost forgot once you beat the game with any of the three starting Campaigns, Leon and Helna, Chris and Piers, or Sherry and Jake (Ada and The Agent's Campaign is an extra Campaign that used to be an unlockable as well, but now is available from the start I think), you'll unlock Agent Hunt mode.  Agent Hunt mode allows you to control various monsters throughout another person's playthrough of their Campaign (at certain points) if they have it checked as an option when they start their game!   And you don't have to go it alone, there can be more than one human controlled monster via Agent Hunt mode so you may have another person join up as a monster as well and together you can cooridinate an attack.
Just like Resident evil 5 this game has an extra mode The Mercenaries. In The Mercenaries mode, you have a set amount of time to try to stay alive and kill as many monsters as you can till the chopper arrives, shooting for a high Grade rating, however you can up your timer and your points per kill in various ways.  There's also The Mercenaries No mercy mode that's pretty much just like The Mercenaries mode, but a lot tougher and has the option to play as the characters from Left 4 Dead 2 and has some of the boss type character from L4D2.
Not to mention the Predator extra game mode from the DLC (if you listen to me and get the Complete version for the $8.39 sale price right now), that's a lot of fun, where you can run around as the big baddie from Jake and Sherry's Campagin trying to catch the other players or vice versa depending on how it starts, but no worries everyone gets a turn ;) .
-And as a sweet extra feature you can unlock extra costumes for these modes as well.
There are a few other extra game modes as well both from base game and dlc's I believe, but those I mentioned were the most fun to play to me.
Anyways it's getting late here now, but this game is TOTALLY worth the sale price, and especially if you play it Co Op.
If you've been on the fence just grab it, enjoy it, and thank me later by up voting this review.

Rayman has been around since the mid 1990s but the rapid success of the spin-off Raving Rabbids had left the main character behind and stuck in the background. But then one day, original creator Michel Ancel decided to bring the character to give the team a break from developing Beyond Good and Evil 2.
The return of the character as well as its return to its platforming roots has been very much celebrated. This is probably as good as platformers are ever going to get. The game has a fun, cartoony look and atmosphere to it, it doesn't take itself seriously at all and it completely blows away anything Sonic and Mario have done over the last 10 years.
The difficulty is spot on, no lives system here you just keep going, with checkpoints that are places so the game remains challenging without being frustrating, you'll never be wasting more then a minute of your time getting back to the point where you messed up.
The level environments and music are so well created its surreal. You can revisit any level you want to play from the game menu and the flow of the levels are so smooth. The game is long too, expect it to take a good 10 hours to get through, if you pace yourself.
Highly recommended if you love great platforming, wacky fun humour and a great art style to fit it all together with. No DRM either!

Rocksmith is an excellent piece of software but poor value as a game. I'm an intermediate bass player and self taught at guitar.
Good:
Interface and options.
Riff repeater. Press space to loop a section or sections. You can set the difficulty, which the song retains after exiting RR, and speet to practice at
Neutral:
Accuracy. For the most part it's pretty good and detects if I'm playing the right note on the default sensitivity. It starts failing on drop Db but that could be my guitar's intonation or pickups. There's many false positives and ways of tricking it into reading a correct note, but it's acceptable in my eyes
The difficulty level up is slow. Even on the increased level up setting and decreased level down setting, songs often stay on simpler difficulties for too long and can take three or more playthroughs to get reach 100% difficulty. For example, in the song "Closing Time" I figured out how to play the melody in no time but the game didn't show the notes until the end of the second playthrough. You can however easily adjust the difficulty of the whole song using rift repeater, and this might be a personal issue. The game is very flexible so it's not fair to call this a negative
It might be easier to learn to play a song with Rocksmith, but learning a song with tabs helps me play by memory much better
Bad:
Price. The game + cable costs about $75 retail and features very limited content in terms of songs. DLC songs are a bit pricy at $3 each. This is fair since you're investing in learning a song through this platform, which is excellent and intuitive for many people, but value becomes dubious with songs that are simply repeated chords. Personal value is subjective though

To hell with this game. It was, for a time, the best of the Hearthstone-based (no interaction on opponent's turn, automatic resource gain every turn, creatures which don't regenerate HP, a lot of shared or basically identical keywords) digital CCGs out there thanks to its simple chess board mechanics which added a LOT of strategic depth, but it's also one of the MOST pay-to-win CCGs out there (simple explanation: you can have up to THREE copies of any card in your deck rather than 2, Legendaries aren't restricted to 1 per deck, and almost all competitive decks REQUIRE multiple Legendaries) and the release of the last expansion was the last straw. Since they were bleeding players already, the developers made a deal with the devil and sold the game to Namco Bandai, who promptly demanded every player sign up to their stupid online service to keep playing (for no reason), added a new premium currency to buy packs with instead of just using real money (always irritating and inefficient when you have to buy more currency than you need) and, worst of all,
the drop rate for Epics and Legendaries in boosters to a FRACTION of what it had been. Hey, pro tip of the day: when your game is losing players, the smart move to make is NOT to screw the ones you still have HARDER! Once I worked out what they'd done (it wasn't hard, it was a STUPIDLY obvious change to notice) I just made my displeasure known on the forum and uninstalled without a shred of hesitation. Really is kind of a pity because the game IS fun, but I refuse to be screwed by any developer. See ya, Duelyst, it was nice knowing you, but whatever happens to you next... you brought on yourself.
EDIT: I actually just went back to the game again to see whether I'd been too hasty; whether they HADN'T in fact massively slashed the drop rate of Epics and Legendaries and I'd just had a streak of appallingly bad luck. Several Orbs later I had my answer: nope, I was 100% correct. Be a Wallet Warrior or be a loser. Screw this game. It's dying, and it deserves to die.

Imagine an LSD fueled retro-futuristic combination of the game Flower and a point and click adventure. It's fantastic, but make sure you go in knowing that it's about the experience, not challenging puzzles or length.

Received from Humble Bundle.
Small Radio Big Televisions is a simple point and click puzzle game that, although doesn't offer much, is a compact visually-appealing experience. The player's job is to explore vast abandoned factories to find tapes that play a looping visual that requires you to find a green gem in order to open doors that lead to the progression of the level. Puzzles are in♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ed through gears, water amounts, buttons, and other simple contraptions.
I can definitely say that, visually, this game excels. However, even in the visuals, and as a guy who has zero optical issues, I would find myself with a minor headache from even a quick session of gameplay (30 minutes or so). But most of the time, the environments and music tied well together, and I screenshot quite a few scenes simply because they looked astounding. The subject of puzzles isn't really something to talk about, since it's quite easy to figure them out, sometimes even on accident.
SRBT does come with it's flaws. For instance, the camera movement revolves around the tracking of your mouse, and I found myself spinning like crazy a good portion of the game. This is only present when you're allowed to spin 360 degress, which is always when viewing the tapes, so it's not entirely often. Another thing I discovered was the price of this game. I completed this game, lacking only one achievement, in only 2.2 hours. $12 for an around three hour experience is ludicrous. I had no idea about the price, for I purchased this game from the $1 portion of an Adult Swim Games Humble Bundle, which is probably what this game's price should be, $5 maximum.
With my experience, I can say I enjoyed this game for what it was. The "psychological" aspect of it all was honestly a little boring, but I did like going through and exploring the detailed and nice-looking factories and environments, as well as the kooky and crazy distortions that were the tapes. Really, it's less of a game, and more of something easy to play when one's bored.

A really short narative/non-narative of an experience(?) Not sure how to describe it other than strange and interesting the whole way through. It uses some basic puzzle elements to take you on a short but sweet ride through what appears to be something of a drug induced haze or fever dream of a world. I liked the use of magnetization of tapes to alter the experience. I don't think I can really describe much of the content in my limited vocabulary as a human being other than a disjointed puzzle game from a non character perspective on the exterior and a first person perspective on the interior of the tapes. It's truly strange but fascinating and well worth a play through if you don't mind a really short romp. Small Radios Big Televisions has a title which basically says nothing at all about the actual game. It is an unique blend between a point and click adventure, a puzzle game, walking simulator, partially rotatable levels like in FEZ a physics simulation and a quite mysterious indie title, story wise.
The main selling point here is "unique", as the gameplay itself is rather simple, but the combination of elements, blended in a way never seen like this before, makes this an actual fun journey. The level designs are nice (and sometimes confusing), the collectible tapes are interesting, the magnetic reshuffling mechanic of found tapes is downright brilliant and the different worlds all have a touch of their own. All in all it's a rather short experience of a few hours with zero replayability whatsoever and I'd wait for a sale to pick it up, but it does very well as a little gap filler for a long evening or a not too challenging yet interesting game to wind down.

A lot of people complain about the traffic. I find the ridiculously stupid traffic patterns to be HELPFUL, as it allows me to teach myself how to solve its problems.
Such as, a roundabout directly off the main starting highway.
The game is extremely satisfying, because even though you don't actually construct the buildings on your own, its great to zoom out, look at the "skyline" and say, wow, I made that.
The extreme level of detail in the game is astonishing. Each and every specific citizen has a specific job, a specific house, and sometimes their own car, that only they drive. Some citizens have dogs! The fact that you can literally follow a citizen throughout their daily life gives you a sense of godlike power.
I don't play the "progressive" game. I have both the Unlimited Cash and Unlock Everything mods enabled. I attempt to model my in-game cities off of real life cities. It has actually helped a ton with traffic issues, because obviously roads that work in real life would work in a game. It's great seeing the city build up around you as you place roads, name districts, provide services, design transit lines, and of course, stalk your citizens.
The mods in the game make it even better. Its really nice to not have to click the annoying Chriper chrips away when a mod disables them. Or, go into a first person view.
In my opinion, the graphics are absolutely beautiful. I've read other reviews saying the graphics are not that great, but the stalker in my goes to their Steam profile to see if they posted their PC specs. Obviously the game runs like crap on a Mac! And, if your using your moms old laptop from '06 the game will look like crap! My new PC is so high-end I can have the graphics on MAX with frames near 120. (While previewing this I guess that last sentence isn't very helpful, but whatever)
What is my final verdict? Get this game. Now. Who cares about IRL car payments when this game is ready for download RIGHT NOW? It is the best city builder game of 2015/2016/2017. But with the traffic, it's also the best PUZZLE game of the year. Hehe.

I really want to love this game, but I can't. I bought this after watching some gameplay footage and was captivated by the art style and atmosphere of this game, which are both exceptional. However, the game has some issues which I can't ignore.
It's poorly optimised. During some sections on high settings, the game runs flawlessly with 60 FPS, on others it gets barely over 35, even on the lowest settings – even the menu runs poorly! I'm running an old-ish AMD GPU.
Secondly, the controls are just unfair. They're not inprecise per se, but whenever you get hit, your character turns into an uncontrollable ragdoll until he stands still again. Combine this with a very whacky physics engine and you'll go flying into the abyss over and over again.
The concept of losing a limb instead of dying when being sliced and being able to continue to play is so unique and cool. But every third time when this happens you instead go flying thanks to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ physics, completely destroying the very  concept of playing as a deformed zombie.
Your character runs automatically, and while pressing down shift you will walk. While unconventional, this is something I can get used to. What I can't get used to however is the controls getting stuck in "walking mode" without me pressing anything sometimes.
But the most frustrating thing of all is that this game regularly minimises itself for some reason (using Windows 7). While continuing to run in the background. So often was I about to cross an obstacle, and boom! There's my desktop. Alt-Tab – I'm dead.
The concept has much potential, but needs a lot of refinement. Not recommended in the current state.

Transformice is an adorable romp of chaos and cheese. The game revolves around (relatively) face-paced matches, with most of them lasting no more than 2 minutes (sometimes less, depending on the skill and malevolence of the individual selected as "Shaman" for that round; the one responsible for getting the rest of the players to the cheese). The game is straightforward and simple, but learning curves and advanced technique do exist. Sadly, the game doesnt give you much direction outside of the barest tutorial, so a lot of the learning is trial and error.
The game is a good time waster if you're looking for only a few minutes of playtime, and you like cute mouse sprites. However, the gameplay can be a bit slow at times. Even with the wide variety of level designs the game will begin to feel repetative after longer play sessions. There is a general area for more relaxed conversation, if gameplay becomes stale. Overall, it's something that's not bad to have in your inventory; its fun, its free (beware the micro transactions!), and it has a low MB cost.

Don't get me wrong, this is an impressive game. There are just a few things that break it /just/ enough for me that I can't recommend it at full price.
1) This game does not have a learning curve. If you don't have much city sim experience, you will start at a significant disadvantage. There are no tutorials, no directed quests (unless you count scenarios, which aren't included with the base game), and no way to learn except by trial and error. Sandbox mode is great, but I expect a little more with my $30 game.
2) The bugs. This is the big one. The bugs vary from person to person, computer to computer, but there will be bugs. Some people have 6 lane highways where drivers will only use one lane. For me, power lines keep going bad for no reason, which basically kills a city if it's one that goes to a water distribution plant. Sometimes deleting a broken line would fix it, sometimes not. Restarting the game didn't fix it, and I didn't have the funds to completely replace the electrical grid, so when it broke for good, that entire save file was ruined.
I don't want it said that I had nothing good to say about this game. It looks beautiful, it performs admirably, and I can see tons of strategic depth to it. That makes it all the more disappointing that random chance keeps interfering to prevent me from experiencing it.

I feel very rude and it frustrates me to write this, but I do not recommend Cities: Skylines unless it is at a good sale price.
I love simulation games, but this one grew stale and was not for me.
The first several hours were really enjoyable and I even went as far as to get the After Dark DLC at a sale price since I anticipated I'd be addicted. But only a few hours later did I realize I wasn't enjoying the game anymore. There are no "scenarios" to play, adding actual goals to the game, unless you get the Natural Disasters DLC (and there are apparently very few). You're just left to endlessly build a city with intricate micromanagement. If that sounds like your type of game, buy it! If that's all you want, this game will be perfect.
My major complaints that led to me stop enjoying the game began with the lack of customization. For the first while, before your city's population adds up and you unlock more features, there's not much to add personalization to your city to make it feel like your own. Different types of roads and other customizations are blocked off arbitrarily in the early portion of building a city, and you'll only get access to these by boosting your population by a stated amount. It makes sense! It really does, but it made the first hour or two of starting a new city absolutely boring. I feel the game would have benefitted from loosening these restrictions.
... and to follow that up, you may say "there are mods, though!" Yes, there are, and I was very excited to try them. However, the community proves that there are troubles with every update. Mods become incompatible, unsupported by the developers, and as a new player, lots of research will go into finding out how to use these mods and have them appear in your game, like custom buildings or styles. Many times, just trying to make sure custom content appeared in the in-game "Content Manager" would crash the game just after a few items. I thought it was just because I originally ran the game on an external hard drive, but I eventually tried it on my internal SSD, and the mods just seemed to hamper the game.
If you have a lot of patience to learn the sciene behind the custom content of the game, and don't mind the aimless city-building with not much else to look forward to but "more, more and more". This is a sandbox game for you, no question.

I understand why some people like it, but after the amount of time I played, I just feel exhausted and need a long break. The pleasure of growing my city sort of numbed itself.

This is one of the most interesting games I've played in YEARS and I don't believe I will stop talking about it for a long time.
-- SUMMARY --
It's weird and different in all the right ways with an incredibly open world. And what is lacks in size it makes up for in rich, detailed environments. In fact, it might be the most open game in existance since you can, and are encouraged to, literally hack and mod the game itself. Which unsuprisingly also introduces some complications with the gameplay.
Nonetheless I'd recommend this game to anyone with a general interest in programming and adventures games. Especially to anyone liking that 8-Bit, nerdy, quirky atmosphere similar to other media like Scott Pilgrim and Fisheye Placebo.
-- PROS --
From the atmosphere to the innovative gameplay to the intricate level design, I loved it all. Else Heart.Break() manages to create a world worth exploring populated with lovable characters.
The developers went to great lenghts to create a living and breathing city. Each and every of the characters and even random NPCs(!) have their work / life routine and their own individual home. Honestly, just checking out all the interesting apartments was a treat in and of itself.
And figuring out which people you would meet at certain places and hours of the day was rewarding. The game successfully conveys the helplessness of being the stranger in a new city which makes settling in and slowly joining a new social circle that much more enjoyable.
The main game mechanic, programming, introduces a new dimension to an already interesting point and click adventure and you're given so many possibilities that you'll be spending hours just messing around, trying to exploit the game in creative ways. Discovering secrets on floppy disks at hard to reach locations, that sometimes give hints about the main story and sometimes more information about the inner workings of the games' ingame programming language SPRAK.
The coding concepts introduced are basic, easy to grasp and well explained with lots of ingame examples of working scripts than can be reused and experimented with.
In general, the developers seemed to put much emphasis on experimenting and learning on your own, which I believe to be a risky decision, possibly scaring off players who are very used to long tutorial missions and being held by the hand. But personally, I found being thrown into a world without clear objectives liberating and in combination with the beautiful city and it's mysterious hints I was instantly intrigued and intent on getting behind the secrets of Dorisburg.
-- CONS --
The biggest issue is that the game creates huge expectations.
You'll be left wanting more more more, and while that sounds like a good thing, you might be disappointed if you're expecting all of your actions to create a new storyline or dialogue options.
In a ridiculously open environment like that it's impossible to account for the myriads of possible scenarios and it shows at times. When you finally managed to break in a previously inaccessible building with an ingenious plan, you might be taken aback by discovering that this changes nothing about the main storyline. You can't even tell any of your friends about it.
That lack of interaction devaluates your impact as a player on the game and I believe that is the single issue everyone is talking about when they complain about lacking content or story.
In an AAA game this would have been a major concern, but seeing how an indie dev team works on comparably much more limited ressources it's understandable that they simply can't create hours of content for each and every possibility just in case a handful of players choose that exact route. And creating content that only a small minority of players will experience is a pretty wasteful endeavour.
My only hope remains that this is the first of many games using this engine or some ambitious players will be building mods expanding this world that I can't seem to escape from.

SMALL RADIOS BIG TELEVISIONS
PUBLISHER Adult Swim Games
DEVELOPER Fire Face Corporation
GENRE Indie, adventure, surreal, puzzle
THE BASICS:
You're exploring an apparently-abandoned complex of buildings (which are shaped like, and named after, a number of basic 3-D shapes), dealing with the overgrown plants, diverting power, solving a few simple puzzles, and opening doors so you can get further in and do it all again.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
I'm sure there's a story in here somewhere...Maybe I left it in my other pair of jeans...About all there is, is the subtle mystery of why these towers were (apparently) abandoned and left to go to seed, yet they still have power. Not much else is evident while the game is still interesting.
The gameplay is basically point & click. Items such as doors, gears, etc. that you can interact with get highlights on mouseover, allowing you to lug certain items from room to room in order to move the items and use them to solve some simple physics puzzles. You also find a bunch of items that look for all the world like old audio cassettes, but contain data used for immersive VR-like worlds.
These worlds allow (more or less) 360-degree views while you either remain still within them (for some), or travel through (on rails), looking for green gems which you can retrieve and bring back with you into the “real” world. Said gems are then used as keys within the polygonal rooms, unlocking new sections of the buildings in question.
Run out of keys? No worries! Each building also has at least one set of devices that have a strong magnetic field. Running a tape over these devices corrupts them (remember to snag the gem first!), making it possible to them delve deeper into each tape's world. The thing is, the worlds within the magnetized tapes are now corrupted. Sometimes they go black & white, or some bizarre amalgam of color and b&w, or simply glitching out the worlds themselves and the objects within. Trippiness aside, the corrupted worlds will also (eventually) yield more gems to put into more locks.
CONTROLS:
Mouse controls to move to new rooms (your “character” may or may not be physically present) – you see entire 2-D “rooms” at a glance, and moving the mouse mostly allows you to slightly alter the angle from which you can view the room.
GRAPHICS:
Crisp and clear, no-nonsense, but not exactly eye-popping. Nothing to complain about here.
SOUND:
Mostly environmental. In the “real world,” sounds are generally subtle, ambient sounds and tunes, along with appropriate beeps, bleeps, and dings when activating widgets, opening doors, etc. Sounds within the VR realms provided by the tapes – both pre- and post-corruption, feel much more surreal and strange at times, helping to sell the idea of the bizarre, limited VR environments.
OVERALL:
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Win 7+ 64 bit; Otherwise minimal. Geforce 500 series recommended
REVIEW BY: Eric_Kei

I go into most games expecting to be either disappointed or to come out with a negative experience from playing the game. I've been playing games long enough to grasp the reality that very few games are worth playing. Those that
worth playing, however, make all the turds worth wallowing through. When I saw that I got a game called "Small Radios Big Televisions" in a Humble Bundle, I rolled my eyes, installing it and figuring I'd play it for perhaps fifteen minutes then give it a negative review, because the title sounded dumb and I hadn't heard of it.
Within seconds of starting, I was hooked on the game. The music is some lovely and powerful synth stuff, with graphics that range between simple to pretty good, and the "simple" graphics are deliberately so, for very good plot reason. Yes, the game does have a story, and it's a bit interesting, but I wouldn't recommend focusing on it, if only because the ending is rather confusing (it was to me, at least).
Small Radios Big Televisions' gameplay consists of seeing a large factory from a distance with doors to its interior, going inside said doors, solving fairly simple puzzles, finding tapes with hidden green gems you use to unlock doors in the factory, finding routes outside the factory to new sides so you can rotate to different entry points, and once visiting all the sides of a factory, that factory is complete, and you go to a brief story/dialog thing in between levels.
There are a total of five levels, and I enjoyed all of them. Check the vents on the first four factories if you want to find hidden lenses which you can use in the story/dialog things between levels to get an achievement. If there is an impact on the ending, I do not know. New puzzles are introduced in each factory, but none of them are stupidly difficult.
I only have two complaints. One: the game has some mouse sensitivity issues when trying to move big metal arms with a gear on the end to line up perfectly and hold it there, because the motion either sends the arm flying past where I'm trying to hold it, or it doesn't quite reach. And two: the game has a map but it was useless for me, as I couldn't make sense of it, and finding my way around was fairly hopeless since everything is shown from a flat/2D view of walls in rooms. Luckily, you move so quickly from room to room, that it doesn't take too long to get where you need to go from randomly clicking until you find the room you're looking for again.
I would say that the ending being confusing was a complaint, as it normally would be from me, but I wasn't put out by it at all. It's certainly a sensory delight from music and visuals, and is far longer than most games' endings. Also, it wasn't the end of a 60-ish hour game that concluded a trilogy of 60-ish hour games or anything, so the ending wasn't something I was on the edge of my seat to witness.
This game only takes about 2 or 3 hours to complete, I found it to be fun, colorful, it sounded great, I liked its look, and even if the story didn't feel to me like it had a lot of closure, it was a nice addition to the game. I am very glad that I gave this game a try, and the developers should be proud of what they've made here.

Back when this was released in 2016, I remember always wanting to play it, but I couldn't because I would spend all of my money on tf2. But now, in 2018, I played Hyper Light Drifter for the first time in my life.
And it was beautiful.
Everything about the game is so tweaked and fluid, it's hard to believe it's an indie game. The combat is surprisingly Souls-like, but it manages to separate itself from the hardcore gamer stigma surrounding the Souls series. The added feature of a gun adds this unique rhythm to the game. Slash, slash, slash. Shoot. Dodge. Rinse and repeat.
This is most evident in the bosses. Oh, the bosses. I've only beaten two bosses so far, the north and the west bosses, and I can say that they test your skills in the most fair and funnest way possible. I vividly remember getting the west boss down to a single point of health, me on my second, and us charging at each other to see who's the quicker draw. Needless to say, I was faster.
The music is another amazingly strong point of the game. Every single track in the soundtrack for HLD is a masterpiece, with my favorite personally being Vignette: Panacea. Whenever I listen to that track, my mind instantly floods with memories of Dark Souls II, and how much I loved and adored that game. Now that I compare that game to this, I can safely say Hyper Light Drifter is better than Dark Souls II.
I have to say though, the story is simultaneously one of the worst and one of the best I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. The story is heavily convoluted, with absolutely no dialogue spoken throughout the entire game. It's sometimes hard to piece together what's going on at times, and it's frustrating for me to figure out what's happening.
But at the same time, it's amazing. Instead of using dialogue like any sane person would, they use context clues, cutscenes, and even THE ENVIRONMENT to tell this story. Whenever you travel to any environment in the game, you can see corpses and other somewhat disgusting things all over the place. This naturally gives me the feeling that something went wrong and the world is falling apart slowly, if not already fractured into a million pieces.
By cutscenes, I don't mean CG ones like in Fire Emblem, or like Dark Souls where there's a predetermined cutscene with your character slapped onto it. No, when I talk about cutscenes, I mean horrible visions that happen to you randomly throughout the game, about your character becoming overwhelmed by the darkness. I won't explain any further, for fear of spoiling the whole game.
To summarize, Hyper Light Drifter is an amazing indie game, quickly being my favorite game to come out of 2016. I highly suggest that anyone that likes difficult yet fair games like Dark Souls, Cuphead, or NieR should try this game. Even if you're a casual player, the scenery and amazing views will captivate you. I immediately and sincerely recommend you buy the soundtrack edition, because the entire soundtrack is on par with Mozart in terms of quality.
TL;DR Go buy this game, it's amazing.

Lightweight, Free and OpenSource, Easy Node system, Great UI.
Godot is made for people who:
like building their games from stratch.
Enjoy a diverse script languages
Custumizing their game engines
Prefer linux over every other platform
Publish to html
low spec computers
Dive into other people's opensource projects and change them for the better.
Godot however is not for everyone, especially those that:
Prefer toying with assets (Unity is for you)
want to easily make games (Gamemaker, Construct2)
Use a lot of tools to make things shiny (Unreal)
Have a specific game genre in mind (various, like RPG maker) (However Godot does have Escoria Project, Which is for Point and Click Adventure games)
And have a huge library of tutorials to teach you (ANY OF THE ABOVE)
Godot's power is what you'd call a double-edged sword.
It's for those that at least have a half idea of what they are doing (Don't worry I am exception. Just look up the Q&A), beginners are welcomed to try, but it is not the easiest to learn. Gdscript is undoubtably easier than C++.
My favorite part of Godot is the Node system. Organized, and simple. I can call a node function, get a node variable, load a script in, instance a scene, or signal it on command. With very little hassle. The list of node types and their node family inheritants are quickly understood.
Because Godot is FOSS it is customizable for everyone, If you prefer C# over the default gdscript, gdscript can be replaced, prefer to work on linux over windows? No problem. (infact it seems like that was the targeted audience.) And if you don't like where the engine is going, you can fork it. (Also if you do that, PLEASE CALL IT GODOT MATE!)
The Escoria Project. To me this changes Godot completely. I'm still using that familar UI, but with very powerful point and click adventure tools, I especially love the dialog system. esc script can make really complexe dialog trees, and I love it! I've been wanting to make a point and click adventure ever since I started using game engines, and now I got the best one for the job. It's a dream come true!
But not all is good. My biggest complaint with Godot is the lack of tutorials, and those that exist need improving, But that's a community issue. Of a community driven engine.
It's also Still early in development. A lot of stuff is missing. Infact very recently enumerators were added to gdscript. STINKING ENUMS!
Plus The lighting is awful, like other game engines, it does not spread out, annoying hot spots are frequent. It's a disaster when making dark areas.
overall I do recommend Godot, if it appeals to you. I came because of the node system, but stayed because I felt I can help shape a community, Thanks to Escoria and Dolphin Island 2.

I've been playing around with Godot for nearly a year and it's a fantastic piece of kit:
It's not as well known as Unity and perhaps not quite as robust as Gamemaker, but both of those tools are either premium or require royalties. Version 3.0 is out soon with a revised UI and some great new features. If you're a pro or experienced developer, you may find Godot lacking in some areas, but if you're curious about making and programming games then definitely give it a shot.

A flexible and customizable game editor that can be powerful in the right hands.
There's a lot of capability and can make some visually stunning effects without being too taxing on the CPU/GPU.
The node system paired with the screens system allows for ease of use and the scripting system paired with the signal system allows for a variety of possibility inside the game as well as in the code.
At the moment, the language available is GDscript which works a lot like python, but in 3.0 they'll be unveiling C# as another possible language for even more accessable code.
It allows you to be really creative, but it will take a while to learn. Luckily, there are enough video tutorials online where people that have played around and gotten more acquainted with the software that it's easy enough for a beginner to learn and play around with to get just as acquainted.
As long as your mind is open, and you're willing to learn, you'll have a great time with this.
Edit: My hours are low since I use the version offline of steam, but I have played around with this software for about 24 hours.

This game outshines more recent clones like Train Fever by a long chalk!  Gameplay is easier, more logical and intuitive, and the graphics are much, much better.  The constant crashing mentioned by other reviewers -- runtime errors, the software algorithms run into logical defeats -- can be reduced greatly if you daisychain your tracks as per the turorial and don't try being "too clever" with collection/dropoffs on extended lines, or completing (quite by accident) a "circuit", since the calculation tables used are flat arrays, not paradox-susceptible loops.  Playing with an AI oponent also increases chance of crashing, as the AI is essentially stupid. This means half the supplied scenarios, which depend on you buying out all the stocks in AI opponent companies, cannot be played beyond sandbox mode. Using older graphics cards can make the animation jumpy, so you'll need a PCI-express based system at the very least.  My best AGP card, an ATI Radeon 1650 Pro, had trouble keeping up.  This is a wonderful "update" on an old PC title from the DOS era, and worth looking into, whether or not your played the original.
One small niggle: no "passing time" control beyond normal and ffwd, the set scenarios are time-dependent (in game years) and this ticks away faster than you can build up your empire to the required "win" standard.  A "llama" or "tortoise" speed would be helpful.  Otherwise you have to put the game on pause to assess your next moves, and on pause you make no profit.
Another niggle: not enough single-player scenarios.  Once you've learned how to play without crashing every five minutes (it's possible, I've done it), you work your way through the provided quest maps very quickly.  But hey ho, play them again for a higher score in the Hall of Fame.
It's enjoyable, but it's crashy as hell if you aren't using Windows XP.

As the introduction suggests, this is less a tycoon-esque game and more like a giant toy train model track.  Only it costs you ingame to add more rail (as oppose to real money in RL).
I have some criticisms;
-The maps too small/cramp, everything is too close to each other with not much space to breath. This is not a problem early on but later on when you have a lot of trains it doesn't give you much room to give them room.  This is likely why theyimpliented a system where building move to make way for you, if it wasn't like that there would be  lot more problems.
-I often find after a while about 4-6 trains just glitch and end up in a part of the map where their routes are not located bugging out. Only way to solve the issue is get rid of the train and replace it. (edit: turns out like Transport tycoon, hich had the same problem, if you keep trains on their own tracks and DON'T link to toother tracks, they never got this bug.  So a cattle train must not connect to a passenger rail, it works anyway as the trains rarely also get in each others' way)
-Ugliness.  Once you start building 4 track stations your map begins to really look an eyesore.
-The double rail system is annoying.  Once you connect a double rail track to another rail you can't continue to make that track double rail.  Transport Tycoon never had this problem, its an older game.  And Railroad Tycoon doesn't bother being overcomplex. Both have better rail systems in game.
Those are the things I've encountered.  Still the game is fun and a attractive alternative to playing the Railroad Tycoon series, its fairly simple.
Some advice;
-For those who cant make a buck; ignore passengers, they get you no money.  Even if the train hs to come back empty in one direction, it will often make far more money then city to city passenger and mail services. I figured this out after two games and now just ignore them unless the goal of themap states to do a certain amount. Processed goods should be your main focus of set up, the sooner you get drugs to hospitals and things like that, the sooner you make big bucks.  The game tries to push you to shift this inthe tutorial as  early train load, but I've encountered more profit at the begining regardless ignoring them.  Passengers and mail are easy, hence why its a lot profit service, as you're justgoing from town to town. Even later on, trains will not provide much profit even when faced with a 100mph train attached.  You cn earn a buck with these, but this involves setting up a single train to go around every town.
-If a industry is going to even hint it will mke money before you start a train unloading there buy it; usually within 15 years with regular supply by your trains it earns back the cost and goes into profit.
-If a trains says it handles "frieght" stuff, but its slower then that passenger train capable olf 100 mph, still buy it.  The ideal cargo thing actually pays off, for 20 less speed it often hauls just as well or slightly better speed.
-If you can afford a train and the maintance cost of id train is cheaper, upgrade.
-You don't have to upgrade every train to the latest model, but bare in mind their cheaper and if you have the cash its best to.  Short of money?  Ether you've set up your trains wrong or just resort to every other model upgrade until you have millions in pocket.  But don't ignore upgrading completely. The newer trains haul cargo at a faster pace.
-Invest in patents even if your the only player in the game.  That early purchase often hs huge benefits and later on in the game, you will soon back tht 50,000 you spent on it within seconds often.
If you have enouh room to create a short cut rail between different stations, do it.  the fastest single problem this game has, particular when faster trains come out is the overload of trains to every station.  If you have find room for a rail that will avoid a train being somewhere it doesn't need to be thisis great.

Its not really a bad game, more like a precious gem in need of some polishing.
The bad:
-Lots of bugs, although plenty have been fixed with various patches but many more still remain, none are really gamebreaking though.
-Unoptimized. At later turns, 500-900+, you'll see a substantial lag when ending turns, i've had turns taking 5-10 mins to cycle. Also it doesn't run well on most PC setups, even high end rigs, its all in the game coding, engine and optimization.
-Cut content. Its very obvious. Some features are implemented half complete, certain basic features are missing, we also have content and assets in game that do nothing.
-Too combat & war oriented. Personally i like having a good mix of empire management, combat, diplomacy, trading etc. SotsII main focus is war.
-SotsII has flamboyant lore and backstory but lacks a full fledge story mode or campaign which is a shame.
The good:
-Gfx are amazing, for its time. The ship models, laser beams, projectiles, armor, modules and whatever visual assets and effects are stunning and beautiful. The different designs & styles created by the devs fit perfectly into the lore & game, very pleasing to the eyes.
-Music, SotsII has arguably one of the best OST though its has a very war-like theme.
-Combat. Its a turn based game but with real time tactics combat. Combat is one of the bigger strengths of SotsII. Although its small scale tactics but theres reasonable amount of tactical elements like formations, armor/shield facing, firing arc, special manoeuvres etc. Granted half the time i'm in cinematic mode just spectating the gorgeous space battles.
-Ship design & customization. Very modular, flexible, balanced and makes a lot of sense. Its also one of the few space games that take scale seriously. A Dreadnought is visually much, much bigger than a Cruiser while a Leviathan is exceedingly massive making Cruisers look like tiny fighters and fighters look small like missiles. Goes the same for weapon and module loadout. A Cruiser might have 5-10 turrets of various sizes(PD,S,M etc) while a Leviathan has a realistic whopping 70-80 turrets. All turrets have their own targetting, physics, firing arc etc which makes combat very tactical.
-Tech tree, this is a hit or miss. Personally i love the RNG Tree format, it forces the player to adapt and get creative if you get locked out of certain progression path, also makes every playthrough unique. But since its RNG it can get frustrating especially in a multiplayer game, you might end up being locked out from majority of the techs and have to resort to hardcore salvaging.
-Distinct and unique faction/races. Both lore wise and empire & combat mechanics. Very vibrant backstory for each of the races/factions. They all have their own special FTL method of travel, various strengths and weakness, very different playstyles too etc etc.

Lowriders aren’t a common presence in video games. Most car customizations and the certain subcultures which might entail them, rarely go beyond scratching the surface. Ride ‘em Low wishes to combine the hydraulic system competitions with more conventional street racing. It succeeds in a large part and despite not aging so well (2013 release), it’s still among the few titles focusing on this particular type of cars. It was the Steam debut of Red Dot Games and this is quite obvious even if in recent years, the developer has shifted towards comprehensive and far more entertaining  Car Mechanic Simulators than the game I’m writing about today.
Much like the hot rod/rat rod car customization style and subculture, the lowriders also trace their origins in Los Angeles, California and share a similar time frame, even if the similarities end there. Lowriders never go to the same extremes of stripping an old car apart and keeping just the essentials which are also exposed to the elements, most of the time. No grandpa’s car which youngsters decided to “freshen up” and also offer an entirely new look. Low rider vechicles focus more on what’s under the hood than the aesthetics. In case you’re wondering, I’m a fan of any type of customization, cars included. Stock parts and looks, simply don’t offer owners the same satisfaction as an object which they took an interest in and decided to add a personal touch to it.
I first came in contact with the term and the (digital) visual representation of lowriders in 2005, while playing Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. The slick maneuvers and stunts which were achieved with those custom hydraulics as well as the subsequent portrayal through rap music videos, captivated me. Back to Ride ‘em Low, players get to forge their own tales in real time. As with the older titles within the Need For Speed series, you also get to name your in-game avatar and have the freedom to choose which car model you want and then go crazy with the customization of it. The car brands themselves aren’t named as such, for obvious reasons. Time has proved that even more established series such as DIRT and GRID, may suffer from costly licensing issues. So naming the car as “Caddy” instead of Cadillac, makes sense in the long run.
American car brands, naturally. Even if you have limited interest in automobiles, you’ll still recognize the form factor on those generic names used in Ride ‘em Low. For some weird reason, opting for the Metric unit system instead of Imperial, also changes the currency from US Dollars to Euros. A career mode is implemented in the sense in which players shall have to earn cash through racing events before even having a large enough budget to install a noteworthy hydraulics system and participate in the traditional lowrider competition involving that iconic bouncing and “dancing”.
From the looks of it, Ride ‘em Low features a proprietary graphics engine. The cars are rendered quite nicely, with both the textures and reflections to show off the attention to details. If only I could say the same about the racing tracks or the fonts and scaling within this game. Those are abysmal. Playing in my monitor’s native 4K resolution, I had to choose between downsampling  enough until the cars looked like they came from a PlayStation 2 port or accept the glitchy fonts to all the in-game text which had line collision or even fused sentences & words. First time I experience this with a Steam game and I’m quite disappointed since I couldn’t find a workaround.
The sounds are all repetitive and forgettable. Take my advice, mute them altogether and blast off some old school rap to your heart’s desire. It will make those races and hydro competitions far more enticing.
What more can I say of the gameplay? It certainly offers a challenge at the very start of your lowriding career. The stock car you purchase is underpowered and no matter how much you cheap out, you won’t be able to afford crucial upgrades until you grind those race tracks and up the ante by betting on yourself. Not a exactly the definition of sportsmanship but hey, these are street races afterall. I doubt something like this would be legal in real life. I would have enjoyed some more details relating to the mechanical upgrades instead of just naming the next upgrade which seems like an improvement only because it costs more than the previous one. At least you can customize the exterior as well. Don’t expect the absolutely bonkers customization from the Saints Row franchise though.
If I didn’t find the lowrider topic and the classic cars even remotely interesting, you can bet I would have rated down Ride ‘em Low. 60/100 is my minimum prerequisite for recommending a Steam title and I felt generous enough since my scaling issue can’t be replicated by those which play in lower resolutions. Your mileage may vary and that pun is intended. I’m also not gonna act as if Steam game from 2013 absolutely had to include Cheevos and Cards. It would have been a nice touch, if added in a future update, but even as it is, you almos get your bucks’ worth out of this title. Waiting for a Steam Sale or bundle is ideal and the game shall certainly entertain fans of the lowrider subculture.
+ Pleasant graphics.
+ Decent customization options.
+ Sufficient racing track & vehicle diversity.
- No Steam Trading Cards nor Achievements.
- Resolution and font scaling issues.
- Limited sound selection.

Okay...I did NOT see this one coming. I got it in a game giveaway and picked it because it had cutesy graphics. I didn't expect much from it (or anything), but as it turns out, this game would've satisfied me even if I had paid full price for it (only six bucks? that's even a lot of buck for your money).
But honesty first: the first impression wasn't good. The game ran slow and crashed a lot. On two different computers. But as I found out, all I had to do was change one 1 to a 0 in a file (C:\Users\<my username>\AppData\Roaming\offspringfling\Local Store\config\config.cfg..."enableController=1" should've been 0), and all issues were immediately solved. Those with negative reviews: do at least a SLIGHT bit of research, mmkay?
What we've got here is actually remarkably reminiscent of what the trailer promises: an awesome puzzle platformer game that has its home on a nintendo system. This isn't just in the graphics and sounds that wouldn't be amiss in a Kirby or bubble bobble game but in the level design as well. This is easily up to par with games like toki tori, lost vikings or the mario vs donkey kong games, and for those unfamiliar: these are games with some BRILLIANT level designs.
The main mechanic (picking up and throwing your children) is also something the devs picked up and ran with as far as they could. Not only is it funny (OF COURSE throwing your children against the walls and enemies is perfect parenthood ;-) ), but it's used in switch mechanics and for breaking rocks. You can pick up multiple children, but this makes you taller and reduces your jump height. All in all, it flows naturally and intuitively.
I already mentioned the main flaw in the second paragraph, but that solution didn't 100% solve it. At times things feel a bit slower than they should be to properly flow. And while the game itself lends itself to decent controller support (and can probably be circumvented), the menus are mouse driven for some reason. That's a bit of a pity, but it'd have to do. I can't but presume the game engine (adobe air) is at fault, but can't say for sure.
But in any case, this game is well worth its money and perhaps even more than that. :-)

The first hour or so of this game is terrible, but it exists to really emphasise how important the hacking is. Once you get to that stage, the world becomes flexible and the game becomes fun. That said, I didn't think much of the story, but it was worth it to get the satisfaction of creating a bottomless cup of coffee and stealing from everyone across the city.
The programming is easy to understand, but the documentation is deliberately hard to get, so you "level up" through organic discovery, which is a nice mechanic.

Else Heart.Break() is awkward. The camera takes some getting used to (and forgiving acceptance.. just wait until you're told to find a 'tall building' but you can't actually look up), the art style is unique but strange, the event triggering and dialogue paths are often awkward and you'll spend a decent portion of time being confused about where you are in the story line and what you're supposed to do next or if you've already done it and whether that mission you just did was a success or not.
That being said, I absolutely love else Heart.Break(). I would buy an expansion or sequel in a heartbeat (Heart.Beat() ?). I spent a leisurely 28 hours on the first playthrough in three days (got snowed in), and plan on going through it again and tinkering around with more stuff and trying for alternate endings and just practicing building scripts.
Its awkwardness eventually becomes endearing, the strange art style becomes a cherished world, the programming aspect is surprisingly robust, and the bugs and quirks become part of what you would expect in a fully hackable world. I wish it were longer, but I honestly have no idea how the developer crafted it in such a way that even it holds itself together for 28 hours. Once you learn how to modify the world around you, you're limited only by your programming skills and curiosity. I have a bit of code experience and definitely ended up in some places I shouldn't have before I was supposed to, but for the most part the game still kept up with me.
###
Speaking of programming skill, if you have some coding knowledge, I bet you will enjoy this game. If you have no skill but really want to learn, you should certainly play it. I've learned a bit and gotten good practice just hacking around and building scripts in this. I recommend taking some programming courses online along with playing the game. Being able to apply your knowledge to the game will feel awesome.
If you have no programming skill but enjoy logical problem-solving, you should be able to tinker your way through this and have a good time. If you don't enjoy problem-solving, you're probably in the wrong place.
Lastly, if you actually are a professional programmer, the sky's the limit for the wacky awesome sh*t you could build in this game. There are a few Github repositories and gists that could use more advanced contributions, and a Sprak syntax package for Sublime Text that's handy for working on and saving scripts outside of the game. I would love to see a bigger Sprak meta out there.
###
Some people have complained that the game is too slow in the beginning and turns them off, and I won't argue with them. It didn't bother me while playing it, but while researching before purchasing, most of the let's play videos on YouTube involve someone playing through the first couple of hours and honestly it didn't look very enticing. They made me worry that programming really wasn't a major part of the game. The few YouTubers I could find that actually show some hacking were doing pretty basic stuff.
So just trust me that you should stick through until you acquire the ability to reprogram the world around you, and you won't be disappointed. Programming is the real meat of the game, and you
feel like a god.
