That is about all I can think of. Oh, and don't give up if you give it a try. Stick it out until you meet a girl named Pixie and a little while after that. Once you get a Modifier is when this game shines.

Else Heart.Break(). What can i say. If the coding from this was in Watchdogs, it would be on of the greatest games ever made. This has the type of hacking Watchdogs should have. There is a linear story you can follow, but there are also ways you can completely skip the story after a bit and immediately end the game. Multiple endings to find, multiple ways to get there. Want to hack something but cant? Hack your hacking machine. Want to go through a door you dont know the code to? Bruteforce it! virtually anything you can interact with in this game, you can hack. I HIGHLY reccomend anyone with any sort of knack for any form of programming (not HTML/CSS) check this game out. I put a few hours in on my friends account at his house, and many more on my own after buying it.

Else Heart.Break() is a great game and for me reminded me of playing "Little Big Adventure" as a kid, it invites you in to explore its world. Slowly you realize that exploration follows a fragmented linear path using hacking to jump the gaps, this type of storytelling I enjoyed immensely and once completed felt the need to load an old save and go down some of the paths I didn't complete first time around.
However, it could be improved in a number of small ways,
- Inventory, it's too simple and clunky, a grid with stacking items, previews and images would be much easier to navigate rather than having to hold things and put them back to interact (at which point the item changes position in the list due to usage).
- Something like a vague storage of important things you have been told or seen, not necessarily a quest log, just a journal of some kind that is controlled by the game like "X told me there's Y over there, perhaps I should check" since I tended to forget some important paths I didn't go down in sake of others, in the end I played the game with a text file open in the background to keep track of information, that's not the end of the world but I think it would make the accessibility a little better.
I'd say those two things were my only gripe, I had a few bugs where I couldn't move, couldn't talk to NPC etc but they were fixed with a restart.
Overall this is a really enjoyable game that challenged me and rewarded me, more please! :)

I have tried my best to review various game engines, and Unity is unrivaled in functionality, with deployment on many different platforms and development on both Win, Mac, and Linux (Linux client still beta, but fully functional). If I would pick anything else than Unity, I would pick CryEngine because of its beautiful 3D rendering, or Lumberyard for both CryEngine beauty and Amazon Web Services.
Godot looks great if you didn't look at Unity or any other options. But after looking into the different engines that are available at this time (2017), Godot is just left far behind on so many things. The only thing that Godot has going for it is the MIT license which makes it completely free, compared to for example Unity where you need to pay some licensing if you start making more than 100'000 USD per year, at which point you really should reward the game engine developers anyway, unless you are a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Speaking of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, it is my impression that the Godot community is rather hostile and not really nice people. Maybe I was just unlucky in my interactions. Without naming any names, just look at this Steam review, which previously pointed out a bug that made Godot entirely unusable. One of the comments said that "this negative review doesn't count because bugs are not part of a programs functionality" [slightly edited]. So apparently, having a bug that renders a software impossible to use is not part of that softwares functionality?!? Anyway, I mentioned this bug in my first review, which made one of the developers respond and work to fix it, so great job on his part. However, while I reported a bug that made the software impossible to use and while that report resulted in a developer responding and fixing said bug, 83% of the Godot users came in to say that my review was "not helpful".
So according to the Godot user community, bugs that render a software useless should not be part of a review because it has nothing to do with functionality, and reporting those bugs so that they can be fixed is "not helpful". This is just one example of my interactions with Godot users, but I really don't have any kind of positive impression of the community. Meanwhile, other engines have users that produce tutorials and act generally friendly with advice and help. Again, this may be some unfortunate and unlucky things that only applied to me, but it is my own experiences and impressions. You might be more lucky, if you want to risk it.
To sum up, I don't think Godot is bad software. It's just not even close to other software, and the user community appears to be less friendly and helpful than what I have found elsewhere. Therefore, I would recommend anyone to try out Unity, Lumberyard/CryEngine, Unreal Engine, and the other options out there that are most likely better than Godot in every possible aspect.

This game tries really hard to explain things only through environmental cues. At times it may fail to convey the message. It is definitely pretentious, don't get me wrong on that. Things are deliberately unexplained to hamfistedly add "mystery" and at times they are altogether nonsensical. But, in this way it is very similar to Myst, in fact there are many similarities between this game and Myst. I won't get into them, but thematic elements like world creation and instant travel to synthetic worlds are present throughout the entire game. I see this as a good thing personally. You may take that as you wish.
All that said, I think this is a great example of a new way to do adventure games. The most interesting part of the game is the environmental storytelling which, while not adding up to anything too amazing in my opinion, does provide a curious driving force throughout the experience. The themes it touches on are both realistic and fantastical, blended by digital retro-3D abstractionism. In fact this game feels almost more like a proof of concept than a game, that there could be a massive game like this and it could go far more into detail about the worlds you explore. Alas, it was developed with an extremely small team (I haven't looked too much into it, but it's all credited to one man, which is actually quite impressive in it's own right).
In the end, is this fun? Yes. Is it deep? No.
Will you be entertained for a couple of hours? In all likelyhood, yes.

( The game itself seems alright. I like the look of it, and the music is also pretty good! )
The controls are a bit annoying. Which is a bit of a feat given their simplicity. The problem is this: you have to pick things up. The developer mapped it to the "Down" button. The controls are rebindable, but pick-up is
the same as down.
It could be fine, but no: this is a speedrunning game (a bit too forceful in that regard too), so your constantly incentivized to optimize all the little actions at all times.
As is it, I'd like to pick things up without having to move the movement analog. It's just awkward. And it's not like there aren't extra buttons for it. On a controller, I think I only use the analog and 2 other buttons (jump and throw).
It's a detail, sure. But in a game that right from the first level is pushing you toward golden (and beyond) medals for speed, it's a detail that comes right into the vanguard.
I'll probably update the review if I have anything relevant to say. As the previous reviewer wrote, the game really pushes you into the speedrunning side of things. It's not Super Meat Boy (so far) in that the game itself is difficult and challenging, but after (or while) mastering it, you find the fastest paths, etc.
In here, the levels are fairly easy (at the start, at least), but also rather straightforward. The speed isn't as much in finding the right path as much as timing jumps (it's a pressing-time sensitive jump) and throws.
So beware. If you don't want a game that pushes time optimization, probably good to look elsewhere. Sure, you can ignore the timers, but the game seems very focused on the time, so there's that.

Ok, I've "finished it, now". Well, not really, but for my purposes. I've finished the main 100 levels, all with Golden Flowers (beat the time limit).
This unlocks another 10 levels. If you really, really like Speedrunning, you can try to beat the Dev's time (<=) for the Rainbow flowers (which I didn't pursue and only got on a few levels (<10)), which grants you another 10 levels for a total of 120.
These last 20 levels are far, far harder than the other 100. In a way, I really like it. In another, not really.
The main 100 levels are rather bland. Completing these levels is never an issue, they aren't very interesting. Their value is mostly in beating the time. Most of the time, it comes down to optimizing the small movements to an infuriating level.
Occasionally, though, it's about the subtle techniques that could make this game awesome!
Warning: this section probably makes no sense to people who haven't played the game (or at least aren't familiar with speedrunning platformers, in which I assume these subtleties are commonplace).
There was one level, for example, with a long, narrow, horizontal corridor. There were also pursuers that killed you on contact.
Given the normal mechanics, if you tried to go through it, the pursuers would catch you. If you took a detour to attract the pursuers somewhere else, though, your time would be
higher than the target. This large interval in the times is important, because it suggests there is a way to get through the corridor faster, since that's the only plausible way to get the golden flower.
Through it, I discovered you get a speedup when jumping - and, I believe, a speeddown when falling. Because the ceiling cancels the falling speed-down, spamming jumps in that corridor will make you go a bit faster - enough to get through the corridor in time!
Another level had to do with jumping while carrying offspring. These slow you down, and lower your jump height. One level, though, had a golden time of 1 second. The "normal" way of doing it was 10 or 20 seconds. Again, this huge difference is important.
The trick was to jump
grabbing the offspring, and grab it in the air, without reducing the jump height and managing to go over a platform that would otherwise be too high.
These things were very interesting, to me! I'm not too into speedrunning, so I'm not used to these subtle mechanics.
Unfortunately, the main game barely uses them, and also teaches them way too late in the game.
Maybe they're useful for beating the dev's times, but very rarely do they help in getting the golden flowers.
The point is that the game could have been much more interesting if the levels relied on these more than they do. Because, as it stands, the levels are not noteworthy at all (with some exceptions). It's mostly filler with a very narrow window for innefficiencies to get the gold medals.
The last levels go the complete other way. They rely on most of these techniques, but also with a very precise timing and familiarity with the game's controls (which I've mentioned I didn't really like) to even finish.
It really lacks the middle ground, in my opinion.
I'll leave it as positive because the game isn't really bad at all. But I didn't enjoy most of my time with it.
The fact that just finishing the levels wasn't challenging or rewarding at all created a huge pressure to finish the game within the specified time. This something requires incredibly precise timing on most of the low level activities instead of clever paths and subtle techniques.
Despite that, I really like the look of the game (very nice choice of colors and shading!) and the music was quite alright too.
I'd advise to get it only if you're into the speedrunning. As a more general-purpose platformer, it's probably not a good choice.

I had an amazing time playing Offspring Fling.
I dare say it's the best time-attack/puzzle platformer I've ever played. Yup, I do think it's better than Super Meat Boy.
Why ? First, it's got nothing less, artistically-speaking. The universe, cutscenes and music are wonderful, and give the game a genuine, cutesy atmosphere which I find really enjoyable.
Besides, the controls are irreproachable, and allow/reward pixel and frame-perfect action, for the most hardcore players.
The level design is awesome too. Even among the hidden levels, which are diabolically difficult, none is unreasonably long, like in most SMB-like games, which makes the die-and-retry experience a lot less painful and frustrating, while still as rewarding.
Finally, you can really play the game two ways. If you don't care about beating the best times on each level, you should find the game quite easy and refreshing, and you can enjoy the various changes of atmosphere as you make your way through the 100 first levels. Hence this game is perfect for kids and people who enjoy themselves some relaxed, casual playtime. It succeeds where most games fail miserably.
Or you can try to beat all the dev times to unlock everything. It's a total new experience, and oh boy, that guy's serious. But I can tell you it's definitely worth it in the end.
Plus you get to throw cute animals in the face of a dinosaur.

Offspring Fling is the most fun I've ever had throwing babies. That's partially because I don't get to throw babies very often, but also because it does what it does quite well. Every puzzle game needs to make the most of whatever portion of the genre it carves out and this title does just that, forcing you to push your understanding and mastery of its mechanics to their limits. What it lacks in scale it more than makes up in heart and polish, which are often in short supply on the platforming side.
I'm not sure what you play as in Offspring Fling, but whatever it is it's adorable and has tons of tiny adorable babies. Some damn dinosaur thing comes through and scatters them though, so you've got to help your bunny-mama-thing round up her childrens. This happens over a hundred levels that are mostly single-screen puzzles but pack plenty of tricks and traps into that space. Along the way you'll deal with deadly pits, switch blocks, monsters, and other hazards to complicate saving your little ones.
The main mechanic of the game is throwing your kids around, unsurprisingly. Pressing down next to one of your tiny offspring hefts them over your head, and pressing C pitches them in a straight line either right or left. You have to get them and yourself to the exit and the easiest way to do that is to chuck them through the door, but of course it's never that simple. Holding a baby raises the height of your character, slows them down, and limits their jump, meaning that you have to strategize how you move them around and make the most of your throws. This is even more important in levels with three or four offspring to transport.
Very quickly you'll start coming across levels where a simple obstruction like a one-block space or a slightly too-tall wall force you to come up with complex maneuvers to get past. They're clever puzzles, ones that appear simple but build difficulty outward as you keep running into little snags in your plans. The puzzles that introduce new gimmicks like pits and switches do an excellent job of easing you into dealing with them as well, so the overall difficulty curve is quite smooth. Be aware that much of the challenge in Offspring Fling is based on timing and reflexes, though. Some puzzles will require you to outrun enemies or traps, or catch a baby in mid-flight to prevent its heart-wrenching demise.
With timing challenges come timers, and it's here that Offspring Fling allows you to go as hard as you want. Beating a level at all earns you a flower, needed to unlock further sets of levels. But each level also has a target time that requires an optimized solution and earns you an additional gold flower. Early on these will come easily but soon start to get away from you, forcing some brain-wracking to earn. And then, if you're a true offspring-flinger, you can go for the rainbow flowers which are only awarded for beating the level in the fastest time possible. These are absurdly hard to get on anything that isn't a tutorial level and sometimes require far more clever and less obvious solutions to reach.
It's all wound up in an adorably fluffy package with some Yoshi's Island-style sketch graphics and pleasing sound design. Honestly between the sharp puzzles and charming aesthetic there's not much holding it back, aside from the lack of story depth. Be warned, though, I wasn't able to get it running on my Windows 10 system so you might have to pass it over if you're fully upgraded. Aside from that it's an easy sell to fans of puzzles, cute games, and throwing babies. And everyone likes at least ONE of those.

This is a fantastic experimental game. The graphics are effective and have an interesting style, the sound works well, the gameplay is smooth (although there are a few problems with the camera and getting caught on objects) and the basic idea - of a world in which you can "hack" literally anything - is fascinating and well implemented.
Where it falls down a bit is as an actual adventure game. The story's rather badly paced and seriously dissonant with the abilities and scope you have in the game. I spent 3 hours (!) wandering around looking for a modifier (the item which lets you hack), couldn't find anything or indeed any interesting items other than a bunch of disks and a teleporter that sends you back to the hotel where you start. I practically quit in frustration before I Googled and found a review article that happens to mention the name and location of the one place and one time you have to be at to meet the one girl who advances the plot.  Once I'd done that and gotten the modifier, was I interested in the fetch quest I was told to do next? Nope, I went off and hacked everything in side, in doing so finding the name of the master villain, blundering into an encounter with them that was apparently supposed to be much later in the game (in which they yelled at me for all the trouble I'd caused them when I hadn't done anything yet), and then finding a terminal that blew the whole game wide open.
It's fun, but it's not really an adventure, and the facade of an adventure tremendously fades when you consider that the hacking in this game is supposed to be in-character (other characters have modifiers and talk about being hackers), which means it makes no sense that anyone ever does anything else. Oh, there's bad guys using secret methods to track people's location? Gee, that would be scary if you couldn't get anyone's location anytime you like with two function calls. Worried about your job? You can hack yourself a million dollars in 30 seconds.
So, if you like the idea of a game where you can be curious and experimental with a simple programming language and build up to having the feeling of AWESOMA POWAH then this game is great. As a story, though, maybe not so much.

As far as I know, there are three Sid Meier railroad games out there.  I like each one, but this first one -- simply entitled "Railroads" -- is my favorite.  I guess when it comes down to it, it's the simplicity I like; #2 & #3 are definitely more complex and are really geared for people who like to mess with numbers and markets and such.  To me, #1 here is more about the building of railroads, which is really the point, right?  There is a market system, yes, but it's clearer and more manageable than the two successors' are.  And I have to say the actual building of a rail system is a lot easier and clearer as well.  Building a railroad in #2, for example, seems to be taking a step back in terms of graphics and ease of controls.
The one (MAJOR) downside of this first game is that it seems to crash quite often.  I've tried it on three computers, each one noticably different than the others, and the game just crashes at seemingly random points on all computers.  If it weren't for that, this easily would be one of my favorite games.

I really enjoy this game - I'm especially a fan of the multiplayer. My family loves to play Ticket to Ride (boardgame), but my brother and I live on opposite sides of the country; we're able to connect playing Railroads.
The single player campaign, if you can call it that, lacks depth. I found it was generally very easy to beat the computer, even at high difficulty, and there isn't much variation to the gameplay. I also found the maps to be, generally, far too small - there are no opportunities for long stretches of track. There is also no economic simulation like one would find in the older Railroad Tycoon series - here you simply pick up cargo where it's produced and hual it to where it's consumed and get paid.
All of the above being said, I still come back and install the game every couple of months just to scratch that itch (or spin up a multiplayer round with my bro). For the price difference, pick up the Railroad Tycoon collection.

Watch Dogs 1 was a dreary, glitchy mess with a severe lack of polish and mediocre gameplay. I'm happy to say the sequel is a much, much better game, in fact one of the most improved sequels I've ever played. The stealth, the driving, and the story have been improved tremendously and the world is much more fun to roam around in with the new hacking features. You can do stuff like send cars careening off the road, make people's phones electrocute them, lure people to a generator before blowing it up, or call in gang hit squads on random passerby. Much better than the "press q to hack" gameplay of the first. The missions are very good and allow for lots of freedom, every approach is viable. You can even complete some missions without ever entering the mission area, by sending in your drones to do the work! There are some flaws such as weird and buggy movement as well as poor gunplay, but as someone who didn't like Watch Dogs 1 very much I can recommend the sequel.

Right, after playing the game for a couple of hours, I have to say that I am impressed. Watch Dogs 2 feels a lot better and looks a lot better than the original Watch Dogs. == Long Review (please select a different one if you want only a short overview) ==
Let's start with the positive aspects:
- There are three different campaigns  plus a forth one featuring the all-mysterious Ada Wong which was originally a DLC
- the total length of all campaigns is okay => For the first play-through it took us around 25 hours to finish.
- the graphics of the game are decent
- the soundtrack is okay
- the co-op play is really great
- there are hidden emblems which unlock additional story content like secret files or collectibles
- different skills can be purchased and upgraded, too
- the cinematics / cut scenes are good
- there are some truly epic scenes in this game, but I will not spoil them for you here.
- the difficulty level on normal is acceptable for an average player.
- the story is complex, but good: All four campaigns are woven together and the protagonists often cross their paths.
- there's competitive multi-player modes
So far, RE6 looks like a decent sequel to RE5 (which was an excellent game IMHO).
Here's the part that can break an RE fan's heart:
In essence, RE6 miserably fails to deliver a good gameplay.
1) I have always liked the RE cut scenes and I think they are a vital part of the game. But interrupting the gameplay every two minutes simply ruins the atmosphere. I cannot even begin to fathom why the devs chose to script virtually everything in the game. And it's not just the cut scenes: In almost every level you will find that your protagonist struggles to keep on his feet: Ground shaking, ceiling collapsing, plane crashing, diving, sliding, etc. While that may be realistic, it really bugs me if the surroundings constantly throw off my aim when I am trying to survive through a nightmare of collapsing scenery.
2) You will be set under pressure. A LOT of times. Generally, enforcing time limits on the player in certain scenarios can help to invoke a dramatic flair and it will get your heart pumping. However, if you constantly put the player into hour-long scenarios where you have to run / escape because virtually everything around you collapses / explodes / gets flooded is a sure way of ruining any meaningful gaming experience. Exerting some pressure is okay, but please - for god's sake - let me look around the world. Take in some of the details. Let me do some strategic planning and not wildly running off from one cinematic to the next.
3) You will be forced along a very narrow road. In many of the action sequences when there is a time limit, you will be forced to follow a fixed path which is often not clear to you. Instead, you will often barely notice that the camera perspective is shifting, and that you have to run somewhere before you notice that you actually took too long and - of course - die instantly.
The problem is not that it is actually difficult to survive the countless Quick Time Events, no. It is that you often do not know what you need to do before it is too late.
4) For some reason the devs thought that it would be a great idea to erratically and unpredictably fix the camera in a completely different perspective from time to time. Of course, that means that your character will automatically change direction if you keep your buttons / keys pressed while the camera changes. This is simply ridiculously bad.
5) Countless times, you will find yourself in a situation where you are fighting an infinite number of enemies, forcing you to quicken the pace and find a solution to one of the game's (mostly) lame puzzles or to quickly leave the current part of the level. This is both mindless and boring at the same time while adding virtually nothing to the gaming experience.
6) Where are the Zombies? Though you will face some of RE's most-famed enemies during the first campaign, you will suddenly find yourself fighting "mutated people / soldiers / mercenaries carrying firearms" almost all the time. This is one of the most criticized facts about the game that partly it feels more like a generic shooter like COD than like any RE part prior to it. The fact that you can also (slowly) move while aiming / firing your weapon and even dodge to the side / to the back does not really help matters. In fact, in earlier RE games I rather enjoyed having to weigh the consequences of fighting off an opponent with my weapon (but having to stop running) or running away to get in a better position to fight him.
7) One of the strongest aspects of the RE series are the bosses and the boss fights. While RE6 certainly comes up with some of the meanest, biggest and most impressive monstrosities of the series, the actual boss fights are either:
a) totally lame (because you have to wait for a stupid NPC  to finish something)
b) totally scripted
c) totally counter-intuitive (because you have not the faintest idea on how to hurt the boss)
d) totally ridiculous (because the boss is invincible)
8) Skill System. The game offers you to select up to three different skills, improving your damage, aim or abilities.  Skills can be unlocked and upgraded using skill points found during the game. While this sounds interesting at first, it gets boring quickly: You will soon notice that many of the skills are simply too ineffective or too specific to be useful on more than one occasion.
9)  The menu system is needlessly cumbersome.
10) To find all the hidden serpent symbols which unlock the collectibles of the game is quite difficult. That was the same in e.g. RE5 and is not a bad thing in itself. What I truyl disliked is that at least one symbol is hidden in an action sequence where it is pure luck whether you initially pick it up or not. Missed it and wanna go back? Forget it. You have to restart the whole level again. Frustrated? Angry? Be my guest!
11) While trying to tie the four campaigns together in the story, the devs have decided to have many overlaps in the level structure of the game. While this helps to certainly invoke a feeling of familiarity, it gets boring too quickly: Fighting the virtually same boss twice (just controlling a different character) is lame. Ironically, this will happen numerous times.
What really frustrates me the most is this: RE6 does have a huge potential.
The first campaign of Leon and Helena is really good (leaving out the final levels, of course).
Why Capcom has chosen to abandon the mood and atmosphere altogether in the subsequent campaigns will remain their secret.
RE is about having a great atmosphere. There's almost nothing left of that in the game.
Once you have finished the whole game and watched the credit roll (which you cannot skip and which takes approx. 5 minutes, by the way), you will realize that many dozens of people were involved in making this game.
Didn't they ever realize that RE6 falls back behind its predecessor RE5 in purely every aspect of the game play?
Didn't they ever realize that the replay value once you have soaked in all the cinematics is minimal?
Didn't they ever realize that constant pressure on the player and endless quick time events cannot compensate for a lack of atmosphere?
We will never know.
I can recommend RE5 without hesitation to you and had RE6 been at least half as good, I would have recommended it, too.
If you are a die-hard RE fan, you might want to get this game anyway, but honestly you can also look up the story in a let's play and you will not miss much.
I can only pray that Capcom will turn back to make RE7 more like the earlier titles of the series...

It seems that retro-style games have resurfaced from its pixelated past. Swordlord will cater to those who love these types of visuals from the 80’s and 90’s, and it does not disappoint! There are subtle details and animations that make the game visually pleasing, like the clanging of swords, and the various boss spells, to the blood-stained targets that leave a trail behind them when their health is low.
The game is a classic top-down view, and the player selects from 4 characters which doesn’t affect play-style. It would have been great to see various play-styles based on the character or class.
The game’s music adds a nice touch, and the multiple soundtracks keep the incoming waves refreshing. The voiceovers, though few, enhance the quality of the characters and enemies, and typically aren’t expressed in games of this sort.
To control the character, use the WASD keys to move, and use the arrow keys to swing left or right.
At first glance it may seem like simple mechanics; swing, slash, kill. However I found myself using avoidance and proper swings to initiate the targets for successful strikes.
It’s important to avoid targets while they have momentum, and strike when they slow down.
The boss fights have unique spells that change the fight mechanics a little bit so it doesn’t feel the same.
Enemies also drop currency and/or health after they are killed, so remember to utilize this!
The reward system is very satisfying as the player undergoes a sense of progression through the game. Characters gain strength and armor, and it’s quite gratifying even though upgrades aren’t too difficult to attain. The waves of enemies that appear feels as if there is a sense of urgency to upgrade, as enemies gain health, armor, and stronger weapons over time.
My only major gripe with the game is the lack of a save feature. This would be highly favored! I want to be able to save all my phat lewts! :) I would also love to see some story development for these characters, because visually they are unique, and it would be interesting to know who they are and where they come from! Maybe the developer can shed some light on them! ;)
Overall, this game is awesome! It’s simple, fun and can be challenging! I highly recommend it!

If you are looking for a great budget game with a retro art style and goofy physics based swordplay, I highly recommend Swordlord! You fight waves of enemies, and can upgrade your weapons & armor as you progress. It's a simple fun game, yet the bosses can be a good challenge with some interesting mechanics. It also has a really excellent soundtrack!

I really wanted to like this game, but there are two issues which kill this game for me. The first one is the interaction of health, health packs and save points. There are plenty of save points in the game, but each also saves your HP and number of health packs you currently have. This means, you can easily get stuck in front of a particular difficult section with just 1 HP and no health packs left. The only way to get out of this is to warp back to the town, farm health packs in easy areas and then back track all the way were you got stuck the first time, this time being very carefull not to lose too much HP on the way there, reloading every time you lose too much HP. I really don't mind difficulty and dieing a lot if I can try again fast (I have 100% Hollow Knight and love games like Super Meat Boy). But requiring large backtracking every time you get stuck is just boring and additionally you alwyas realize too late you ♥♥♥♥ed up before, because you don't know if the hard parts of the dungeon are still ahead. In practice this lead to never using my health packs in dungeons because I was afraid I would get stuck without any HP left again.
The second issue was a lack of direction where to go next to advance the story. It is often required to find secret areas to advance the game, but you are not really told where to search next. This would result in just aimless exploring, uncovering a lot of secret areas providing power ups, but not the one secret area required to advance the game. I like some exploration and uncovering secret areas, but the game doesn't really distinguish between optional secret areas and mandatory ones. I solved this problem by liberally using walkthroughs, so this alone wouldn't have killed the game for me.
The rest of the game is really nice though. The sound track is great, the art style is distinct and unique, although not fully my taste. The combat and enemy design is satisfying and fair. All enemies have clear telegraphs of their attack. Overall, I'm really sad that the developers killed this game for me with a few bad design decisions.

As much as I'd love to rave about everything great about this game, I'm going to narrow it down to the one thing I noticed above all else. The game was difficult. Not hard. Difficult. Important distinction. games that are supposed to make you rage or pit you in a competitive online enviroment are hard, like the browser game Cat Mario and CS:GO. Games that will punish you for making a mistake but give you an opportunity to avoid all mistakes are difficult, like dark souls, which is insanely difficult, but all attacks are broadcasted with long animations before your enemy finishes striking, giving you a chance to avoid it. If something is hard, it has the possibility to be unfair or you cannot avoid being punished. If something is difficult, your not going to have an easy time, but you can negate all damage or punishmnt with enough practice, and everything is made to be fair. Now, just to clarify really quick, I don't hate hard games. Hell, as of writing this, CS:GO is my most played game on steam by a lot. But back on track, Hyper Light Drifter isn't a hard game, it's a difficult one. You will probably die alot, but almost none of the deaths are able to be considered unfair. As I played through it, I noticed something; I wasn't getting mad when I died, mainly because every time I died, I knew that it was me making a mistake and I knew what that mitake was and how not to do it again. I love multiplayer games, but they make me rage more than any other type of game because by nature of you fighting against other people and not a precisely designed and tuned AI, the games are bound to have moments when I die or lose unfairly. This game didn't, which I am immensly glad for, because it gave me the courage and sanity to check out other difficult games I didn't really want to get into before. It's like old school games; you don't get to easily regenerate health, but the enemies attack in such a way that it's possible to never lose any health either. I do hope I don't sound like an obnoxious nostalgic. I was born after the time of ye old retro games, and when I have played them I found them to feel rather clunky to control, but I still enjoy the idea of their design. Well, theirs that ramble of a review. Hope you enjoyed.

As has been mentioned by many others, Offspring Fling lives in a couple different houses. It can be a basic puzzle-platformer or a kind of time-attack frenzy. My play was solely comprised of the former, so that is where this will briefly focus.
I have to admit that the game feels a bit like the sort of 'flash game du jour,' a puzzley platformer where you must get from A to B while negotiating a twist or intermediate objective. Where this differs from the "Hi, I just learned HTML5" personal project is the polish––the controls are decent, the physics make sense, and the levels are well-considered. I'm sure this becomes more apparent if the player delves into unlockable content, extra levels, etc. The base difficulty is pretty approachable and all the variations on the central theme are pleasant surprises. Additionally, the art design is well-appointed and captures the target SNES-aesthetic. Except for the menus––they look weirdly sloppy in a "16-bit zoomed in" way.
That all said, my recommendation is tempered by what you want out of the game. A basic play-through of the levels is ~2 hours. So if you plan not to do any of the "beat the clock" attempts at the levels, then please keep it in mind.
EDIT: It's also worth noting that, at least in my experience, achievements do not work on macOS.

Working with this engine has been an absolute pleasure. Steam has only recorded a fraction of the time I have spent with the engine - I've easily sunk a couple hundred hours into this engine.
Pros:
**Clean interface, that's easy on the eyes.
**Built-in Code editor/Compiler that's easy to work with.
**Great Engine developers that actively listen and work to keep the engine moving forward with bug patches, feature updates and promotions.
**Don't need to pay any royalties if you release your game commercially.
**Huge library of "nodes" (elements of your game) that make development much easier.
**Very powerful 2D engine that is capable of creating any 2D game you can think up.
**Open-Source Engine
**Multi-platform support (PC, Mac, Linux, Console, Blackberry ect)
Cons:
==You have to learn GDScript (which is very similar to python)
==The 3D engine is a bit lacking in some areas. (still very capable for most indie projects and there are often workarounds)
Notes:
As of this post the engine developers are actively working on a new 3D component. From what I have read so far, the new 3D component will feature a more modern OpenGL renderer with Physically based shading. This is excellent news in my opinion that's worth mentioning - because it shows that the guys behind godot are pushing the engine where the community wants it to go.
Overall, an excellent engine I'd easily recommend.

This review was *almost* a positive recommendation.  You can read a lot of the other positive reviews to learn why it's a really good development framework.
I was about to choose Godot as the engine for my next game, but then my partner noticed that there were posts dating from over a year ago reporting screen tearing and frame stuttering, and these reports continued up to the present.  (Search for "godot screen tearing" to see some of the posts.)
I had not noticed the problem because the scenes we had made for our evaluation project did not have scrolling.  As soon as I added some scrolling to the project, I saw the problems.  Unfortunately, there seems to be no workaround.  Even Godot's own Space Shooter demo has the problems.  Neither turning VSync on (or off) nor enabling pixel snapping helped.  It would sometimes look so bad that one could clearly see the seam flicker between two triangles of a texture.
Once Godot fixes the screen tearing and frame stuttering, I will gladly change my recommendation to "Yes", but for now, it's not good for commercial use.  It's still good for personal projects, prototyping, and game jams.
UPDATE (25 Feb): As another test, I created a project with no scrolling.  It was simply a 4-color Sprite node that one could drag around the screen, and the background was a solid color.  If I dragged the sprite rapidly around the top 1/3 of the screen, I would see weird ripples inside the sprite. Slower movement minimized the rippling, but it was still noticeable.  I don't think it's simply a hardware issue because similar behavior does not happen if I recreate the demo in GameMaker, Corona, or Unity.  It seems like a renderer issue to me.  I hope Godot 3's new renderer fixes the problem!

I've used a lot of game engines in my time. Unreal, Unity, Game Editor, Love2d and out of all of them Godot has become my favorite engine. Considering how simple it is, it's wildly powerful. Once you learn how to use it you feel like you're using a well tuned instrument. I find myself working on features I've never made before and just *knowing* what I need to do to make them.
I'm not saying it doesn't have a learning curve. It's Scene-inside-a-Scene workflow definitely will take some getting used to. But it helps to just think of Scenes as containers for things that you can use to group stuff into one inside another scene(container).
After that you can learn to use GDscript and signals in a day. After that you're on your way to being a game dev wiz. I can't wait to see how this engine grows.

Ok, first an anecdote, skip to [PROS & CONS] if you don't want to read it:
I first came across this game while stumbling around the internet, in one of my routine "StumbleUpon" binges before insomnia succumbs to fatigue. I didn't hit it directly, I hit some other game from the same publisher or something and then a link to it from there. It was pre-release at the time and not being promoted anywhere else. I read enough to be excited by the prospect of it but fell asleep or got distracted or something without making a note of the name.
Fast forward a few weeks till I thought of it again and I was driving myself nuts trying to remember the name of this brilliant experimental adventure game I had found... I got so frustrated I almost had myself convinced I imagined it, dreamed it or fantasized it.
I was pretty sure it would be released on Steam eventually if it wasn't a delusion, so I waited, stalking the coming soon and new release listings on the Store page. And finally here it is, snapped it up real quick and I'm glad I did.
[PROS & CONS]
Pros
- Highly experimental game mechanic (A pro in my book)
- Vibrant and creative art style
- Brilliant "chiptune" soundtrack, appeal for retro gamers
Cons
- Not polished like a AAA game (not that you should expect it to be)
- Writing could be stronger, but I am a harsh critic in this department, others might be more forgiving
- Primary plot path is by necessity shorter and more direct than most games, though their is a great deal that can be done outside that path.
tl;dr? Programming gameplay mechanic is bold and inventive, art style is quirky, music is retro, could be longer but as a whole, worth the money any day.

I like the game, but at $25 it's at the upper bound of what it's worth paying for.  It's got some problems but also has some seriously nifty mechanics that make me willing to put up with the problems.
Pro:
-Very maleable world where the game tolerates you doing very unexpected things
Associated Con:
- The 3rd-person camera is kind of derpy, and doesn't know how to avoid objects obstructing your vision., probably because their positions aren't set in stone  You'll have to manually move the camera around a lot to see what's going on.
Pro:
- Does the concept of "the matrix" right.  You don't alter the universe by just staring at an object and saying "there is no spoon".  You do it by actually having the power to alter the game's scripting code that defines how the spoon works, in-character.
Associated Con:
- It's nearly impossible for the developer to think of everything a player might do to hack the game in-character, and thus you can do stuff that breaks assumptions and makes bugs surface.
Pro:
- Unique gameplay mechanic that doesn't just talk about your character being a hacker, but actually has YOU, the player, doing the hacking, and not in a stupid "movie OS" sort of way, but in a way that actually feels like really programming - you actually type script code in-character, using a scripting language the game invented for its universe.
Associated Con:
- The game doesn't let you get access to this aspect of itself until a few hours of gameplay.  The apparent plot at first, the pure "dating sim", is kind of lame.  Especially since you apparently are a "salesman" selling soda by literally selling it one can at a time to random strangers you converse with, rather than by, say, selling it by the crate to restaurants like you'd expect.  That doesn't seem very viable as a job and feels like the sort of plot intended for an 8-year-old player.  But you have to go through that a while before the actual gameplay surfaces and the game suddenly gets a lot more mature and smart than it seemed at first.
Pro:
- You are expected to crack the mysteries of how to do powerful hacks yourself, and it is possible once you are given the tools to get started.  The universe's objects behave logically and consistently making it possible to reverse-engineer things to learn the system naturally in-character.
Associated Con:
- The game is VERY vulnerable to spoilers. The primary challenge of the game is learning the names of things so you can hack them, so it probably won't have good replay value unless someone starts making mods that add new plots.

Cities Skylines still remains one of the best city builders available in terms of flexibility, available space, mods, and so on.
In terms of available space you get a gigantic 9 tile area to work in by default. Which can be expanded with the 25 tile unlock mod. Since maps are different and inevitably cities get built different every time you play you don't unlock these tiles in any particular order either. You just purchase any tile that is next to another tile you already own. Which means you are not locked down to a simple square.
There is a LOT of community content now. The game has been out for a while and the workshop is full of mods, maps, and assets to make your game better.  Of course I always recommend first play throughs be straight up vanilla just to get a feel for the unmodded a game. However, there are some real benefits to using mods.
That said though I really can not recommend any of the paid DLCs other than After Dark. This was the first DLC they released and it still seems like the most impactful to date. I would have to say that what makes it better is that it provides things that are useful in building the city or in managing the city. This would be, as example, like the Bus Terminal which is an almost necessary thing for managing your city. Using it you can easily see how many of your citizens will travel between your various routes.
Snowfall and Natural Disasters on the other hand always seemed, to me at least, more gimmicky than really helpful. Like they were just put in to say "here is new content. enjoy!" but they really didnt help anything like After Dark did.
The Snowfall DLC pretty much only gives you the street car (tram) service to help with actually managing your city and everything else is just winter flavored Skylines. Actually one might even say that Snowfall is more hassle that its worth since you have to build in an all white zone which people have complained many times about this causing eye strain and headaches. Then you have specialized services for heating and road maintenance which eats up more of your city resources than you normally would.
Natural Disasters is kinda one of those things i remember from the first SimCity game I played as a kid. I remember working on my city and having the a tornado or godzilla go through the city and destroy things. Then I would have to rebuild. Seemed like might be interesting. Not so much though to be honest.
Where in that old game when you didnt have much else to worry about except placing power lines and roads... this game you have a lot more to worry about. Probably the least threatening aspect here is the forest fires, but everything else if it hits your city can really be a problem. The thing I find the worst about this, and I have seen this thought elsewhere too, is that I have to spend so many hours building up a great city then a disaster comes and smashes things. Which I am not even one that goes overboard with a huge amount of detail! I have seen streamers that really micromanage on the details and if I put that level of detail in only to have it destroyed I would quit playing.
Mass Transit Will be coming out soon and it promises to be another good DLC that will be helpful in many ways. What is known about it right now is that there will be new public transportation added in the paid DLC which will help in managing the city better and the free patch that goes along with the DLC release will have a LOT of quality of life changes which are focused on traffic and transportation.

Games that have such a larger player count, even years after release speak for themselves. I first touched this game when it was released and I was playing on consoles. Whether it was Unranked or Ranked I had a lot of fun. If you can get a group of friends together, it makes it 10x better.
I took a bit of a break and came back to it nearly a year later and the game is still the same, and trust me, that's not a bad thing when it comes to this.
Some pointers for new players or players coming over from console:
1. The game is worth it, but do not waste your money on the starter kit. There's a lot of grinding to go along with it. MY recommendation, get the standard and buy the year 1 or year 2 pass. Whichever caters to you. Or do what I did, wait 3-4 weeks and see the completed go for 50%.
2. Do not use a controller. Even if you want to convince yourself that you're a master with a controller, it doesn't matter in a game like this. Sure there's an odd few that are sucessful with it but start using that m/kb. Might take a couple games to  get used to, but it makes it much better. You also might want to remap some of the keys but that's all personal preference.
3. Don't expect a COD or CS:GO. These games are purely objective and team based. You need patience, and communication.
4. Do all the situations, you can easily get through them in an hour or so. This will give you enough renown (game's verison of currency) to unlock a few good operators.
5. Do not assume you have to grind. Win a couple MP games and you have enough to get another operator or two. And play around with them to see what your style is. Personally, I like to use ops with high speed/low armor on attack (ie. Ash, the japanese girl.. i always forget her name) and low speed/high armor on defense (ie. Rook, Mira).
I'm impressed how much I love the game after taking all that time off.
Final Verdict :
Story : N/A
Gameplay : 9/10
Soundtrack/Sound Effects : 9/10 (sound is important in this game)
Visuals : 9/10
Overall : 9/10

Offspring Fling! is a difficult platformer game about throwing chickens. I said difficult because it's hard to collect the flowers and some levels will only be unlocked after you collect the flowers (and those levels are harder than the rest of the levels). Each level will take less than one minute, except level 100 because of the long "cutscene" (but you can do it in less than 1 minute). Your time in each level determines which flower you'll get. Although the blue and golden flower might be easy to get, you can't say the same to the rainbow flower. The rainbow flower, which also can be called as dev times because it's the dev's time herself, is quite insane. Not only you need to finish the levels quicker (even with a difference in just one millisecond), you also have to master some tricks to do it faster.
I was planning to finish the game as soon as i get 100 golden flowers because i can't seem to get the rainbow flowers on the first few levels after several tries, but i ended up realizing that i can get them after doing a few levels. Some levels have more than one way to finish with; while some levels can be completed faster with an easier way, some levels can be completed faster with a harder way. Besides, you'll understand and master a few techniques as you play.
The graphics in this game is very cute. If you like pixels, you'll definitely love this. The pixel art is very nice to see, although the main menu might be confusing because the icons are not common.
For a difficult game where you need to hear the same music over and over, you'll need to have a great music which won't make the players tired listening to it and Offspring Fling! does a good job with it. Perhaps one of the reason i'm still playing the game despite of the difficulty is because of the awesome music.
I have to say that the controls are terrible. Especially if you are aiming for the dev times. Even the cursor is very slow (luckily, you'll only need mouse in the menu). There are delays between actions: jumping, throwing, picking up chickens--all of them. You'll need to time them right to do it. Some tricks require you to do a combination between actions, and it's not as easy as you think. One example is jumping + picking up chicken trick, which will need some time to get used with. You'll be raging everytime on your first few hour because of the "stupid controls", but you'll get used to it. At the next few hours, you'll realize that the "stupid controls" are not the thing that you need to rage about, it's the "seem-to-be-impossible-to-beat dev times" instead.
There are some design which you'll need to abuse to beat the dev times. You can actually jump a few seconds before falling on an edge, and you can actually flip a switch twice if you are fast enough. Although the second one won't be used that much, you'll have to abuse the first time a lot. There is even a level (level 44, uppercut), where people finish it with sick reaction time, as in.. jumping, picking up chicken, throwing, landing on an edge, jumping after you reach the edge, picking up the chicken (again), and throwing it in a split second. Luckily, the trick is not needed to beat the stage.
I was stuck in a level before because i didn't know that you can boost your speed while running in a small passage by banging the roof. Because of that, i have to stop playing the game for like 3 months before i start picking it up again. This makes me forgot most of the techniques, not to mention the slow down button (triggered with F12), which i usually used to play the levels, isn't working. I ended up thinking that it's impossible to beat the game, which just become possible today.
After emailing the dev with a hope that she'll fix this "bug", i only got a response with no luck in recovering my slow down button. She can't seem to reproduce the issue and said that she'll give me a build which has different key binding for the slow down. It's been a week and i haven't heard more from her. Luckily, i have already learned to play the game without that button in a hard way. Just fyi, the button strangely worked today and i found out that i can't seem to parry with it.
After playing the levels which are considered "very hard" by the others, i found out that those are true, especially during my ~3 months hiatus. I forgot most of the controls, resulting in doing trial and error for most levels until i somehow get used to it. Levels 101-110 will test your ability from the existing techniques, while level 111-120, the real hell, will introduce a new parry technique which have to be applied in a hard way. It'll be extremely hard if you didn't use the second character.
However, i have to say that the last 20 levels (especially the last 10), doesn't feel the same way as the first 100 levels. Sure, the game is more difficult, but i feel like i have to do the same thing over and over until i do things right, not because i'm not fast enough. This bores me quickly, especially when you die right after you started. In the first 100 levels, i feel the "one more level" feeling as i finished the game. However, for the last 20 levels, i got the "if i fail again, it's time to rest" feel.
After finishing all levels, i ended up knowing more technical things, like how you should parry when you are below the enemy (if you're curious, the answer is you don't, because you have to figure out whether you're in the left or right position from the enemy's center), how to press keys after free falling, and more.
Well, this has become long, but tbh, aside from the satisfaction that i finally can get rid of this game and how lucky i am to finish this game, i don't really feel anything after finishing this game unlike how i did after i beat level 100.

Cons:

- Requires to abuse a lot of "techniques" just to defeat the dev times
- No in-game tutorial for the techniques

Here's the problem with Duelyst.
TL;DR
The sucky thing about this game is you get punished for trying new things, and the meta is so stupidly flexible that really you just have to get lucky with match ups, and also draws. At this point, i would not say it's pay to win. HOWEVER, the major pro of this game is the ♥♥♥♥ing awesome animations and cards, which take forever to gain access to, and when you do, they're not even that good.
If you wannah succeed in this game, get the same boring consistent cards that the S players get, and watch as that major pro becomes so far out of your reach that the game is barely worth playing anymore.
---------
There's two things that i've noticed so far that influence this game quite a lot.
The meta is agro, and there are so many rad cards that never get played - because they cost so much.
By agro meta, I mean decks hit face AND control. So basically, you get rushed down by a whole lot of crazy strong cards, and then when you try to fight back, it gets immediately ♥♥♥♥ed by some bs.
Decks have 40 cards, which means the chance for you to draw a card that's useless in your current situation is stupidly high.  There is also significantly less card draw in this game, and most of it is situational.
This game was phenomonal when it first came out, completely balanced and well designed. Now there's so many random chance cards that are so strong you can't NOT put them in your deck - decks that win alot are extremely consistent.
Open a pack - get a legendary? Wow! How cool is that? Well legendaries are a lot more common in this game compared to hearthstone, but unfortunately, the chance to get a legendary you'll never ♥♥♥♥ing use it so much higher. A lot of faction legendaries in this game require you to build a deck around them, but because decks have 40 cards, the chance to draw one of these legendaries is... unfortunately, pretty low.  Even if you have heaps of card draw, you'll still fall behind because of how fast the meta is in this game. Once you get ahead, it's so easy to stay ahead that it takes a pretty amazing topdeck to get you out of the situation.
Most S rank players make decks that are consistent, meaning lots of low cost cards, minimal card draw, SOME healing, and maybe 1 or 2 high cost cards, but they're always the same high cost cards because the Duelyst devs don't seem to be that great at balancing the stupidly op cards they produce.
You have a card that costs 5, that's a 4/9. That's gamewinning in Hearthstone. In this game, it's not even played. You have a 7 mana 4/10 that gains 4 attack and does 4 damage to the enemy at the start of every turn, and that's not even played!
So what is played? Cards like the 7 cost 6/6 with RUSH that does 4 damage to the opponent for every minion it damages. What the ♥♥♥♥ is that? And you can have 3 of them? And in the same deck, you can discount them by using your bloodborne (hero power) ability, which summons two 1/1s, and using another card that costs 0 that sacrifices any card, (in this case, one of the 1/1s) to discount the next card you play by 2. That means that if you have one of these cards, you can summon a 6/6 with rush (charge) for 5(.5) mana that does 4 damage to the opponent for every enemy it damages.
That's nuts. But the worst thing? If the opponent happens to have a random♥♥♥♥♥card, it can ♥♥♥♥ that combo up just because you happened to get matched with someone who happened to have that card in their deck and happened to draw it and NOt replace it by the time you get the combo out.
Sure there's heaps of combos and cool possible things in this game, but no way to try them out without getting ♥♥♥♥ed up in the progress, and losing a bunch of games.
Despite what some people believe, the RNG IS higher, because with 40 cards alone there's so many more possabilities.
Hearthstone did not have more RNG simply because you could control and play around cards, in this game, there is no possible way to know what to expect.  In Hearthstone, you could also control what you get in your deck by adding heaps of card draw and that sorta thing, you can tailor your deck to the way you'd like to play it, and still succeed if you do it right. In this game, you can't. Atleast not until you get to higher ranks, where decks become a little more consistent so you can learn the meta.
There's MUCH LESS online help for this game - new players are gonna be confused and starved for content. Legendaries cost 900, but if you're gonna use a legendary, you need at least 2 of them in your deck to get anything out of them. That means 1800 spirit (dust) is needed. Disenchanting a legendary gives you ♥♥♥♥ing 350. Disenchanting a common isn't even worth doing, you get 10 dust. Rares cost 100 to craft, which is 1/3 of a legendary. Epics cost a whole legendary to craft. This is similar to hearthstone, but remember that this game has 40 cards in the decks - increasing overall crafting costs by a lot. It may seem cheaper, but this game is expensive af to play if you want variety.
Don't get sucked in, it's designed so you'll want to spend money and it's designed well.
Because the meta changes so quickly, it's hardly even worth investing all your time into a single deck.

My new favourite adventure game. Hands down.
Definitely not for those looking for traditional game design, this game does not hold your hand (except for the programming, it does teach you the basics of coding, so don't let that intimidate you).
In my mind, the lack of hand-holding is one of the game's strongest assets, the world and it's inhabitants feel alive and legitimately interesting.
The art direction is obviously well thought out, and executed perfectly. I love some of the more vibrantly coloured areas.
And the music. In the OST there's 56 tracks, and they're ALL amazing. Some very talented artists worked on the music for this game.
On a technical side note, the way in which the game object scripting is architectured and exposed to the player is particularly interesting and well implemented. Nearly all interactable objects in the world can be "hacked" and have their script altered. This leads to some interesting puzzles and equally interesting solutions.
All up, this is one of the most well fleshed out and immersive games I've played in years, with an incredibe size and scope for such a small team. It's clear how much love and dedication went into this project.
In short: not for those looking for a game that tells you what to do next, or one with a clearly defined ruleset. But definitely worth a shot for those who enjoy non-linear gameplay and creative problem solving, and don't mind getting their hands dirty with some basic scripting. Interestingly, it's probably a good way to learn basic coding, if you've been looking for a fun way to learn.

This is a very unique game that lets you go through a "King's Quest Style" point and click adventure but with the added gimmick of having you write code that affects the game world.

I've had things mess up due to being tired and falling asleep.  I've lost information on a quest and had to figure out what I'm supposed to do on my own.
All that being said, this game is great.  I suspect that someone who doesn't know how to program would see the little code snippets and functions they find around the world as items and if you run around and collect pieces of code that do things you will slowly "level up" by learning how to program. I'm guessing if this is you, you will spend a TON of time in game learning things.
If you already are a developer, you are going to feel that it is "too easy" which I did at first, but then I ended up feeling like I had unlimited powers!
Regardless of if you already know how to program or not, progression in this game is your every growing collection of code that you've written/assembled to give you powers in the game world.  This is unlike any other game I've ever played and I had a ton of fun playing it.  Definitely would recommend it to everyone.
For those that are wondering, I bet you could power through the plot of this game in about 10 hours or so.. but I believe there is easily 30+ hours of gameplay if you get into the programming mini-game.

Else Heart.Break ():
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Your name is Sebastian (Seb for short); you are sitting at the table with your parents on your special day. Yes, it is your birthday today! As you are about to have a serious encounter with your birthday cake, the phone rings…! You just got a job that nobody else wants (and you applied for it???)… You are about to become a Soda salesman for Wellspring & Co in a lovely place that goes under the name of Dorisburg.
Else Heart.Break () is a very interesting RPG adventure game set in a 3D/Retro world. You will explore the city of Dorisburg and meet its inhabitants and find out who they are and what you can do for them (get a can of beer or a smoke for example) but mostly how they can help you in regards to coding. As you explore the city, you will see a quite few floppy disks lying around the city or in apartments. On my first attempt (please be easy with me) I was trying to stick floppy disks in every computer I could find. Some had small monitors and the writing was going too fast and could not grab an understanding of “Sprak” programming language. Well, let me give you a tip… Find the modifier hacking device and everything will become clearer (remember, I am a gamer not a programmer). With this device, you will be able to read and study the coding language easily.
It is one of those games you will need to invest a little bit of time in to get the drift of it. Either you find it too challenging and give up or you will stick to it and try to figure it out.
Personally, this game intrigued me from the start and I am enjoying trying to modify the coding. At this stage I have had lot more failures than successes. Oh well, it’s my first attempt at modifying programming languages.

Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great artwork
-	Good and humoristic dialogue
-	Great soundtrack
-	Challenging
-	Learning “Sprak” Language
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Frustrating at time
-	No trading cards / No achievements
An unusual game to say the least. If you like a good challenge this game is for you.
8/10

Welcome to Transformice, you are a noob. Transformice is a 2D MMO online game where you are a cute brown rat. You need to get the cheese and bring it to your haven. Depending you on the amount of cheese you collected, you will earn titles to be displayed on your profile. Simple, right? NO. On some maps it is impossible to collect the cheese. Be it because the cheese is in a top of a building or behind a hidden wall. On every map, a random player with the highest score will be choosen to be the Shaman. Shaman is a rat that stands out for having powers. He is the guy who's going to help you, building ramps, bridges, stairs, teleports, boosting you with spirit or ruining your life, depends on how noob the Shaman is. Some Shamans love to troll players by not helping or completely destroying your chance to first. First is obviously when you reach the haven with the cheese faster than any rat. YOU NEED TO FIRST. Every first grant you extra points and count additionally on your profile. Firsting is VERY IMPORTANT on racing rooms. There are no Shamans there, only pro players that play for years. If you have a lot of firsts on your profile, they will know you are a pro and they will respect you, doubting before insulting you. MADNESS TO SPREAD TERROR AND TO MAKE YOU SUFFER. There you can see players cry and whine whenever they miss the chance to first. Yeah, even pro players miss the chance to first. Cities Skylines still remains one of the best city builders available in terms of flexibility, available space, mods, and so on.
In terms of available space you get a gigantic 9 tile area to work in by default. Which can be expanded with the 25 tile unlock mod. Since maps are different and inevitably cities get built different every time you play you don't unlock these tiles in any particular order either. You just purchase any tile that is next to another tile you already own. Which means you are not locked down to a simple square.
There is a LOT of community content now. The game has been out for a while and the workshop is full of mods, maps, and assets to make your game better.  Of course I always recommend first play throughs be straight up vanilla just to get a feel for the unmodded a game. However, there are some real benefits to using mods.
That said though I really can not recommend any of the paid DLCs other than After Dark. This was the first DLC they released and it still seems like the most impactful to date. I would have to say that what makes it better is that it provides things that are useful in building the city or in managing the city. This would be, as example, like the Bus Terminal which is an almost necessary thing for managing your city. Using it you can easily see how many of your citizens will travel between your various routes.
Snowfall and Natural Disasters on the other hand always seemed, to me at least, more gimmicky than really helpful. Like they were just put in to say "here is new content. enjoy!" but they really didnt help anything like After Dark did.
The Snowfall DLC pretty much only gives you the street car (tram) service to help with actually managing your city and everything else is just winter flavored Skylines. Actually one might even say that Snowfall is more hassle that its worth since you have to build in an all white zone which people have complained many times about this causing eye strain and headaches. Then you have specialized services for heating and road maintenance which eats up more of your city resources than you normally would.
Natural Disasters is kinda one of those things i remember from the first SimCity game I played as a kid. I remember working on my city and having the a tornado or godzilla go through the city and destroy things. Then I would have to rebuild. Seemed like might be interesting. Not so much though to be honest.
Where in that old game when you didnt have much else to worry about except placing power lines and roads... this game you have a lot more to worry about. Probably the least threatening aspect here is the forest fires, but everything else if it hits your city can really be a problem. The thing I find the worst about this, and I have seen this thought elsewhere too, is that I have to spend so many hours building up a great city then a disaster comes and smashes things. Which I am not even one that goes overboard with a huge amount of detail! I have seen streamers that really micromanage on the details and if I put that level of detail in only to have it destroyed I would quit playing.
Mass Transit Will be coming out soon and it promises to be another good DLC that will be helpful in many ways. What is known about it right now is that there will be new public transportation added in the paid DLC which will help in managing the city better and the free patch that goes along with the DLC release will have a LOT of quality of life changes which are focused on traffic and transportation.

I'ts a bit interesting coming from unity 3D into Godot. However programming wise, you're going to have to get use to the python style of no curly braces with the Godot's own custom scripting language. Other than that as a major difference it is quite similar to unity 3D.
the software has a MIT license meaning:
- you don't have to share the source code
- you can use for commercial purposes
- any game you make is completly yours
- no paying ANY fees for using the engine
the game engine is still in it's early stages so you don't have all the nice polish and ultra awesome stuff that engines like UE4 have. But the best part about Godot is that it is free, they give you the source code and pretty musch just let you run with it.
Downsides:
currently there is an issue where you cannot chane the logo/icon for the exported executable (i'm using windows version), however I'm confident that it will get fixed in the future (eventually). note- if there is a way to fix it via creating a build from source i'll probably do a tutorial on it.
another downside is the limited import options for 3d models. Godot (at the time of writing ver 2.1) only accepts .DAE for importing rigged models with animations. thankfully though on the Godot website they have a blender plugin :
Personally it takes some getting used to, but with all the lack of restrictions with licencing and fees its not a bad engine at all.

Godot Game Engine (GGE) is a simple 2D/3D game engine where it try to make learning programming and creating game as easy as possible with good, easy to understand documentation and simple interface, specifically crafted for a newcomer.
GGE have better, clear and easy to understand documentation especially for tutorial section compared to UE4 documentation. Especially for a newcomer, this will help them to learn and grasp the basic in programming, mechanic and developing their own game. Plus with GGE own interface, it won't make the newcomer feel overwhelmed like UE4 own interface.
Personal opinion, if you're aspiring dev who have a "big idea" to be realized then you better go for UE4 (or Unity5). Especially where UE4 itself is designated for epic 3D AAA game or simple 2D Flappy Bird-esque game, everythings is possible. With vast arsenal of useful tools like visual programming-esque language, profiler, real-time debug and WYSIWYG, it definitely will speed up and make your game development much easier.
Although the learning curve for UE4 is quite steep, in a long term investment it defenitely worth your time. Plus it's free (excluding 5% royalty on that amount after the first $3000 per game per calendar quarter).
Another game engine that sell like hotcakes among indie game dev or hobbyist.
Have been using UE4 for almost 1 year and GGE for 1 week before my friend ask me to help him create 360° video VR inside Unity5. Can't say much about the pros and cons but one thing for sure, Unity5 is easier than GGE and probably almost equivalently feature-wise like UE4.
The huge con for someone who reconsidering to get Unity5 instead GGE is the Unity5 license for Plus and Pro are quite expensive (with 12 month of continuous subscription commitment).
If you are the one who need a free, not license restricted (like Unity5) and looking for easy, not so hard game engine (like UE4), you should try GGE. If you like the game engine you should consider to make some donation to ensure that the developer can add more feature to this awesome software.

This is a great engine. Comes with plenty of out-of-the-box features for 2D. If you're choosing between Unity and Godot for 2D games, Godot is definitely the better choice. The only feature (that I noticed) that Unity has and Godot doesn't is a trail renderer. However, Godot has a much better rendering API, so implementing that should be pretty easy.
The language (GDScript) isn't my cup of tea-- I'm not a fan of dynamically typed things -- but it has the features it needs to get the job done. If you like Python, you'll like GDScript, if you don't... well, C# support is coming in 6 months.

So I will focus on the 2D engine as that is easier to learn and you can develop excellent 2D games at a fraction of the effort to develop 3D games.
While this is not a drag and drop game editor like some other higher level game making tools (which focus on a single or limited genre), this appears to be powerful enough to do what you want and how you want to. There is a solid physics engine available but you don't need to use it at all. The game script is very familiar for those who know Python, so it should be easy to get started with. Most of the features seem intuitive but it is recommend that a few basic tutorials are read first.
There are a few quirks which you need to work around. Tilesets need to be exported every time you change it (which happens frequently in game development) and you cannot use a single tile library file - you need to export each tile individually using sprites and set the tile region manually. Wish 2D tile-ripping feature would be automated in future versions.

Trying Unity's awful Linux build almost put me off visual editors altogether in favour of HTML5 frameworks ie Phaser for a while, but this has reignited my willingness to learn. A wonderful piece of software!
EDIT: For anyone wanting to learn how to use this:
READ THE STEP-BY-STEP GUIDE ON THEIR WEBSITE. IT HELPS.
