The game, even after all these years, is still full of bugs.  I've played a ton of the original SotS, and actually stopped mid game to give this one a shot, which I picked up for cheap on the winter sale.  I've convinced more than a few friends to buy the original, but I can't recommend this.
Its positives:
Tactical combat is better in many ways, worse in a few
Multiple planets aren't the pain they usually are to have in a game like this
Better system of handling damage in the game
New tech
Better graphics
The negatives:
That nice new tactical combat is hopelessly mired in a bad combination of bugs and the fleet system, which basically makes you fight the interface to get stuff done.  You'll have interesting experience like not being able to send a fleet from the closest star system to colonize, but only from ones half way across the galaxy, or have you invasion, listed as lasting 30 turns, mysteriously stop after 4, and because of the fleet system, you can't order your ships to turn around.
It has a very steep learning curve, is not balanced in terms of things like random events, the AI isn't very smart, and the game does a poor job of communicating what is going on to the player.  I wish they'd fix the game.  It could have been great but for a couple of dubious design decisions, and lots of bugs.
It's fun for awhile, but eventually you'll get sick of fighting the game more than your opponent.  Also, if you love extra layers of micromanagement, play the Loa, where you'll be continuously creating and destroying fleets, than making tiny fleets to send all on the same turn and reassemble someplace else, and try to figure out how to navigate the semi-functional battle manager, which is very bugged at least with the them.

It takes some newer hardware to run it well...for what you'd expect to be an easy to run game. Without an SSD and modern CPU the time to process a turn will take a while on a large map once there is a lot of traffic. The game is built on a database like system so there is a lot of disk I/O. Run it from a RAM disk if you can.
Deplomacy in AI games is completely missing for the most part. You might get a cease fire or even a non-agression treaty, but in a few turns they will declare war again. In my 200+ hour of game play I got an alliance once...and about ten turns after forming the alliance the AI declared war. So just keep that in mind...you will have no friends in an AI map.
The worst part of this game is the pirates. It takes a lot of infrastructure to reduce the chance of them occuring and even then they still will...and on large maps you might have ten pirate attacks to sit through in a game turn. That's at least 10 minutes of completely wasted game time and you can never do anything about them anyway. Even if you have defenses in range you only have 2.5 minutes so you will not likely be able to destory the ships and save your frieghter. Do your self a favor and edit your base chance for pirates to occur to -2.00 in the game's commonassets.xml file. You will also notice faster turn times and nothing of value will be lost.
The rest of the game is flat out awesome. I'd personalyl rate SoTS2 as the best 4x game on the market right now or the best modern one at least. The combat mehanics of ships not fighting as well when they take damage is really rare and makes it a cut above the rest of game alone. The weapons are ballanced pretty well...not perfect, but if your research options limts you one type you are not going to be dead in the water (though not getting point defense will make me just restart the game since you learn this early on, but that is it). The graphics are decent...better than they need to be. The fleet system isn't as bad as a lot of people make it out to be. The only complaint I have is that you have to have a command ship in every fleet which is always a less combat capable ship. I am sure the Admiral could radio the rest of the ships in the fleet from any ship. The combat is some what 3D...this could be better, but it is still pretty good.
So yeah...that was a bit of a mixed review, but I am still giving this game a thumbs up. I'd recomend it to any one, though pay attension to my warning on the hardware. Don't get this for your seven year old laptop.

Due to the nature of this being Open Source, which is *NOT* a bad thing, I have the luxury of creating my own TGA plugin due to the fact my asset maker relies on TGA for textures.  My only gripe with this software is if you need to use a proprietary dependency then you are at the mercy of someone making it for you or creating it yourself.
The major "con" out of the way this engine is quite powerful and easy to use.
To do anything substantial YOU do need to know how to code (in general terms - all languages have nuances but the same generalized constructs for logic, loops, and abstractions are the same)
The 3D component part of this is targeted primarily for mobile platforms where an engine like Leadwerks, for example, is geared for higher end PC.  The 2D aspect of this software is quite powerful.
If you wish to get into game development this is free, no strings, and quite capable.  If you are a veteran in the industry you can do some things with this as well but it does currently target lower end hardware devices; then again if you are in the industry you already heard of this engine and will not be reading reviews but sampling it yourself to see if it suits your needs.
It's free software regardless.  If you happen to read this review and you want to make a game this is a good place to start at the high end of beginning and intermediate level with no cost to you.   Until you can justify paying for an engine don't kid yourself trying to use the other AAA engines until you learn how to code.  You will never get away from being required to write code to make anything substantial that stands out.  Period.
This feature-packed game engine suits my needs with extra sauce!

***First Impressions Review***
Now ignoring the technical issues, this game is fantastic. The story is interesting and well written, the characters are all relatively believable (with the exception of the goofy "Wrench" character that has a sort of anime mask that displays his emotions at any given moment), and I'm really looking forward to seeing how events unfold.
The graphics are absolutely top notch. A lot of people complained about Watch_Dogs 1 getting downgraded, and it did without a doubt, but it still had some admirable graphical achievements, especially the water effects. Those effects return in Watch_Dogs 2 among other incredible effects including realistic looking wind, highly detailed textures, fantastic lighting, and an overall much more appealing color pallete. After lowering the extra details setting, the game runs pretty stable for me and looks fantastic as you drive around the city in a nice smooth 60fps.
The gameplay is also very well done. They've taken a lot of the complaints from Watch_Dogs 1 and clearly worked from there. Driving feels more akin to how the cars handle in GTAV, albeit they can feel a bit floaty at high speeds. The gunplay is more or less the same just now you're armed with "3D-Printed" guns which is a clever idea. The gadgets have a large presence in this game with little controllable drones that can drive around on the ground or fly high in the air only adding to the hacking insanity. The melee animations are also very cool, with a very unique signature weapon that's actually a billiards ball attached to a rope that the protagonist swings around.
The city feels alive this time around. Chicago was a dead city in Watch_Dogs 1 with only a few AI doing interesting things here and there but nothing to actually do. Watch_Dogs 2 however features lots of side activities including go-karting, sailboat racing, lots of hacking based puzzles and secrets to discover in addition to plenty of side missions that help you progress through the story. The clothing stores are much more varied this time, offering your character a large variety of outfits and are not limited to 2 types of trenchcoats with different ugly colors like Watch_Dogs 1. For example, I ran into a biker clothing shop and was able to choose from an assortment of leather jackets, jeans, leather pants, and ridiculous looking biker boots.
And finally, the clever online hacking modes have returned. These modes were the best parts of Watch_Dogs 1, allowing you to never feel safe even in your own single player save as anyone online could be stalking you at any given time. I was able to try the classic hacking competitive mode against another player (without me having to even search for a match or even accept anything) and immedietly began hacking the player when he was within range. I laughed as the player ran around the street destroying gas pipelines as he searched frantically for me as I drove a mini cooper slowly around the corner. They also added in a new bounty hunt mode that allows you and 3 other players to hunt down another player that's been causing too much chaos. If the bounty manages to escape or kill the hunters, he will be rewarded a large amount of points, making it a very fun game of cat-mouse.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. It's looking like they did a much better this time around and even optimization seems more playable than it was in the original game. I hope Ubisoft enhances the performance even more as I would love to turn up the anti-aliasing a bit to eliminate some jaggies as the game is not really utilizing the full potential of my system, but for now it's acceptable and plenty playable.

You dock in Dorisburg eager to start your new job after moving out from your parents. You, the player, will soon realize that everything in this city is connected and can be modified. You will also meet a lot of interesting people and activists which feeds you story elements.
From the point you dock, you are entirely free to roam the entire city and do whatever you feel like. There is no quest and/or journal system holding you back and you need to find the story-elements and pursue them at your own will.
Programming and Hacking
Everything in this connected city hold a bit of code which you can change. And with this freedom to do whatever you like, you can apply multiple approaches to solve a given problem.
Some very basic knowledge in programming beforehand – or a good willpower to learn something new – is advisable in this game.
The game will of course teach you a bit of programming by talking to NPCs, looking at the ingame manuals you can find and of course looking at existing source code in objects.
Story time
As mentioned, you make the story as you go along and you can also find multiple endings to the game. I feel however, the open and dynamic story element of this game fall a bit on the short side. There were moments when the AI would not let me talk to them about, what I feelt was, key story elements.
The quality of the dialogs also feelt somewhat second-rate.
I also found a few endings to the game, but I still did not have all the answers to all my questions. This begs for some replay value of this game, but I also think endings should give a decent closure.
=Not for everyone=
else Heart.Break() is unfortunately not for everyone. You must have the willpower to pursue stories and the knowledge – or desire to learn and understand – a bit of programming to succeed.
But if you are a bit of geek, enjoy or think you would enjoy some programming and find the thought of hacking the world itself from within to make your ends meet, then this may very well be the game for you.

And I still can't entirely dislike this game, because it has that kind of charm to it that only comes from people trying really hard to make something and completely and utterly failing to succeed.

Below you will read the most honest and truthful of game reviews, from someone who loved this game and played it hard.
Until I got to the end.
Below are some spoilers if you care about the story, or what little of the story you can interpret from the minimalist style of storytelling. No one speaks words. If you want to know what's going on, you will have to interpret dialogue from three vague pictures that an NPC will show you. If you want to know what happened to the world, you will have to collect all 16 monoliths and decipher the code language they are written in.
I spent 71 hours playing multiple saves of a story about a weak and vulnerable blue-skinned man with magic powers. The art is beautiful, the gameplay is creative, and the feel of the world is very unique. I'd say the environment is a combination of Dark Souls and Legend of Zelda. This is a game with so much potential. Even the story is strangely beautiful...
until you finish it.
You watch as the world is finally freed from evil. The sun starts to shine.
You see the Drifter. He appears to be fine. Slowly, blood starts to run from a deep wound...
then the credits roll.
You bring up your save file. There's a new slot next to it with a picture of the end of the game. You load that file...
It shows the mangled skeleton of the Drifter, similar to other drifter corpses you found in the game. It just rubs an entire box of kosher salt into your wounded emotions.
I invested a lot of time and effort into this game. I even beat the challenge arena. But in that moment when I finished it, I just wanted to flip someone off. I wasn't rewarded for my investment.
Now, if you don't care about story and you like a good challenge, then this game is for you. But if you're like me, and you don't like the feeling of being cheated out of a happy ending, then you might like to play this game as long as you never finish it. There's a part of me that thinks this game is a masterpiece; there's another part of me that thinks this game just exists to make you upset.
I don't even know how to feel about this game.

I told them they'll regret their decision because the game has a great potential of becoming interesting and competitive. Now I regret my words...
A clever game developer would think that when their game is relatively unpopular and their company is fresh on the market, they need to find a target playerbase and convince them that the game is worth playing and popularizing by providing content such as videos, streams, guides, exciting tournament matches, etc. CPG is full of people that think otherwise. In their opinion changing the game from being almost entirely tactical to being more "RNGstone-y", so luck-based and frustrating, was a good, profitable move. Is trying to attract casual "I drag random cards on the field and I can somehow win" type of players from other much more popular games when they've alredy collected cards there and some of them move to Duelyst only because there's no RNG a brilliant idea? You can answer that question yourself.
For me Duelyst right now is basically a hodgepodge of 2 different CCG styles, something in the middle of both. Players that don't lke RNG are like "I lost to Blue Conjurer giving my opponent Sparrowhawk again, I don't want to play this shhit anymore" and people who like casual RNG think "I lost, why is this game so hard? It will take me a while to get better and collect cards for playable netdecks, going back to HS", they're the ones that apparently would be confused by Zirix being able to place his BBS on a tile (CPG dev quote). Basically, they first baked a delicious cake, then they noticed (a bit late?) that pickled cucumbers are tastier to a bigger number of people, so they decided to forcefully mash some pickles into the cake...
Here's another aspect - trusting CPG as a company. Again, you'd think a smart dev would want to gather some trust at the beginning of the journey with a new, unknown company. Nope, letting "black boxes" and "discoverables" become memes in the community is definitely better. Let's start with Kickstarter. Not only did the game become something entirely different (e.g. paid -> F2P, happens), but also they cancelled/replaced some rewards and at least several people reported they didn't get some physical rewards while the support was either silent or delaying.
Then I had an awful personal experience - they closed official forums, I tried to create unofficial ones as nearly. I had nearly 0 support from developers (e.g. when it comes to advertising) and I learned why few months later - they planned to reopen official forums from the beginning! The dev I've talked to the most got annoyed  because I showed that I was surprised and disappointed - so much respect towards someone that tried to provide a service to the community after they made an arguable decision. It was the first "black box" experience of mine that started opening my eyes. It didn't take them long to disappoint again, twice, this time most of the community. FIrst they changed quests for worse and somehow "forgot to include it in patch notes", then they lowered Shimzar orb drop rates without letting anyone know before pre-orders. Sly. I don't think they'll ever get on the Chinese market because they won't be able to do such manouvers then, they require drop rates to be published.
A topic related to that is transparency - the lack of it. The lack of communication. They haven't talked about their design decisions in a while. Well, apart from an external interview where a dev seemed completely out of touch, speaking that people love Meltdown and frustration. A PR guy is not able to explain why they can't add simple features such as faction indicators on cards, as if he worked somewhere else or his dev co-workers ignored him and he wasn't able to ask them... People, including the few remaining streamers, were informed about Gauntlet (a competitive mode where you earn gold/dust) disappearing and being replaced by Rift (a more casual mode where you lose gold/dust) during the whole May like 2-3 days before the patch. And in the latest June patch they returned Gauntlet with 4 general choice that apparently was "a popular feature from The Rift". Yeah... Several people complained about it, including showing screens full of new decks that were needed to be created to get a general you'd like to play, I saw no praise, but I guess that's just a pretext for "fixing" poor general balance.
They made a lot of other poor choices, IMO - removing casual (it's the only popular CCG without casual, except Eternal I guess but they have rewarding single player content), weird promotion choices (including lack of promotion at some point), boss crates on timer for the psychological effect, etc. Good choices? I can't remember any lately, I guess aiming for mobile releases, if they were not delayed...
Lastly, they and their fanboys ([The]Bhawb, NecrogueFaust, walker_paranod to list a few) try to sweep every negative thought under a rug and get mad when people criticize the game because they're "discouraging new players" (a.k.a. they're scared that the game may die) - don't let them trick you. They will tell you that all the falling numbers - on Steam, Reddit, Twitch, anywhere publicly - mean absolutely nothing and there are 77% of Bronze (lowest ranks you can escape in 1-2 day[s]) players that sit on the non-Steam client and love RNG and everything else, even though they don't talk anywhere... They will tell you the game is in a perfect state and mobile will push it on Hearthstone's level. They will tell you it's the most tactical CCG, even though they clearly didn't touch other CCGs. Hell, they will even try to tell you that games like Gwent are less popular, even though it takes one minute to check that numbers on Twitch or Reddit are much higher for them. In the meanwhile devs are working on another game, gossips say and less frequent + lower quality patches confirm, some kind of a MOBA/ARPG or whatever - I guess they know that this ship is sinking. Or they think their small team can afford to navigate it and build a new one at the same time, which is even worse.
TL;DR: Duelyst is going downhill faster and faster because it's developed by a company that has no idea what it's doing. I still hope that one day I will have an incentive to change this review to "I recommend this game". But that's doubtful. In the meantime I'd recommend everyone to play some Gwent/Shardbound/Faeria instead.

I would really suggest that you read all that I have to say, as there is so much that I want to talk about as to why I play Duelyst that cannot fit into a simple TL;DR. I have played Duelyst for a long time (ever since the change from one draw to two draw- yet I made a late switch to the Steam version), and have made it to S rank ever since December (due to personal reasons however, I did not have time to make it to S rank in April and May). While their have been any bumps in the road, I have had an overall positive experience playing Duelyst.


One of the biggest things that gets to players is the meta. Duelyst is currently experiencing a control meta, where Vanar and Magmar (the two factions in the game with the most control tools) are on top. This is in part due to a general pendulum-shift in Duelyst ever since the release of Shimzar, where the game has gone from an Aggro-dominant meta (where Songhai, the faction with the highest burst potential, was on top), to a more Tempo-dominant meta (where Lyonar, the faction with the best tempo tools, was on top), to the meta's current state. I personally feel that this kind of affect is inevitable in any card game with multiple factions due to the diversity in their own gameplay. However, this doesn't mean that the other factions are out of luck. In fact, almost all generals see some form of competitive play (minus a couple of weak ones, yet that is more to due with their own Bloodborne Spell/Ability/Gameply in comparison to their counterpart). While metas can be frustrating, making it harder for players to dedicate time to the game, their is still a lot of unique gameplay styles and deck archetypes to be explored, and that can be achived competitively. I would highly suggest reading the following link, where a dedicated player developed a Zoo Argeon list after months of testing, and got it into the top 50 with it. The thread also shares his interesting take on approaching deck building and gameplay.





In terms of faction identity, I think Duelyst is doing pretty okay (-A or B+) in that you can kind of get a sense on what each faction focuses on (Lyonar is minion and heal based, Songhai is spell/burst and combo based, Vetruvian is artifact/value generation (obelysks) based, Abyssian is swarm and build-up (shadow creep and Dying Wish) based, Magmar is speed (fast with rush and slow with grow) and self-harm based, and Vanar is removal and synergy based).


I would also say that Duelyst is a lot more generous compared to its competitors. You can get about 100 gold from playing around 8 games, so players can at least get a core or shimzar orb daily. Gauntlet has also been improved, making it a more enjoyable experience as both a fun mode and a mean of grinding for players with a greater chance of getting epics and legendaries (with the new cards) and being able to win a crate key at 12 wins. While I haven't seen this comparison yet, I would also compare boss battles to Hearthstone's Tavern Brawl. Both are fun game modes that change weekly and give players 1 orb/pack upon their first win. However, Duelyst gives players the option to open a boss crate as well, providing 3 additional orbs, a crate key, a gauntlet key (free gauntlet run) and a legendary card(I believe) for about $5.00. Duelyst also has some pretty generous starter bundles to help players get into the game and catch up on their collection.


I also disagree with the argument that Duelyst has an issue currently with powercreep and RNG. Out of all of the RNG cards in Duelyst, only one card is problematic and sees competitive play (Blue Conjurer), but because CPG generally releases a blanace patch about every 2 months after an expansion, I do not believe it will be a problem for much longer. While other reviewers may say that they experienced powercreep in Duelyst, they fail to give a concrete example of one. This is because all cards are meant and designed to fill a specific role (for example, Katara, a 1 mana 1/3 with Backstab (3), is meant to be more of a combo tool for heavy burst, whereas Kaido Assassin, a 2 mana 2/3 with Backstab (1), fills a more general role as a solid 2 drop that can remove most early game minions with the use of his backstab ability). I also do not believe that powercreep can exist between two different factions, because they have different playstyles and different tools available to them, making the two cards being addressed as powercreep play somewhat different roles when deckbuilding.


While we haven't recieved a lot of cards that directly involve positioning, positioning is still a very crucial part to playing Duelyst. It is important to understand when to play offensively or defensively, and what early game positions are the best in order to make the best future plays. It is nearly impossible to play and position the same way against all types of decks, because every faction has accesss to different kinds of tools. For example, Magmar (and for the most part Vetruvian) have a hard time closing distances, and it can be difficult for them to deal with units at a distance. Songhai has high burst potential, yet has a very hard time dealing with large-statted minions and/or when backed into a corner. While Vanar has access to a wide range of flexible tools, healing is not one of them, and they can really struggle when faced with aggression. It is this type of mindset and thinking that is necessary for players to make the best choices when positioning their units, and understanding how to effectively conserve their resources.


Currently, Duelyst is preparing to release its next expansion (sometime in June or early-to-mid July). The period right before and right after an expansion release are some of the most enjoyable times in Duelyst, and with the recent improvements to Gauntlet makes now the perfect time to get into the game and prepare for it. I would also highly suggest going to the official Duelyst forums, reddit, and discord, as there are many experienced players that would be more than happy to help new players get into the game and understand it.

G'day all,
Things I've discovered:
1. For some reason the game seems to crash if I start it from the shortcut, but if I start it using the play button in steam library and then shift tab in and then out of steam the game seems to run stable as a metronome. Don't know why; it just works that way for me. Played it 14 hours straight over the Australia Day long weekend without it missing a beat.
2. THIS REALLY IS A GREAT GAME, I've been playing 4X since Supremacy - Your will be done and Imperium Galactic, both on Amiga 500 and this game is probably one of the best I've seen in a long, long time. Actual it’s a thinking mans (gals)  game.
3. The level of complexity and depth is amazing, it takes quite a while to fully grasp the mechanics of how this game works even after reading the manual/s cover to cover a couple of times and watching a boat load of YouTube.  Thank whatever deity you have, that the Devs didn't appear to go down the 'lets dumb it down for console path' like so many others have lately (Sid). For pity sake people PCs these days are so fast and can process so, so much that 4X SHOULD be about super micro management. I've been making spreadsheets like crazy, in order to track all the vessels in my fleets (by name, class, registry and assignment) my Fleet Admirals, my space station developments, OMG how amazing is this game.
4. It's such a pity that this game was rushed out and got the absolute thumping that it deserved, but I can tell you that all the fix up work that went in to it finally turned out a really good game.  Unfortunately it still doesn't look as graphically polished as it could, (UI and all), but the ships are superb and look amazing in the ACTUAL tactical combat piece. This alone beats so many other space 4X hands down.
5. Ship Micro-management Heavan :-) your ships have weapons, upgradable/exchangable (in real 3d not some 2d drawing/plan thingy), your ships have pods (marines, cargo, extra crew, extra energy etc) your ships have drive systems (upgradable with reasearch) and your ships have dorsal and lateral armour and shields (and forward facing deflectors if you research and build them). ALL these things are seen in tactical combat and you have to properly manage your ship's weapons, shields, direction that they are facing towards enemy (with spin and roll systems). ALL these things really, actually count towards not getting your backside handed to you in the few short minutes of (pausable) real tactical combat. [Love it, Love it, Love it]. Depth people, real depth.
I do wish that there was an easier way to mod this game, as that can sometimes make up a lot of the shortfalls in the graphics department, but the Devs chose to alter the format of the graphics files and having to covert simple .tga's is a complete pain in the ar_e.
I guess the lesson here is actually finish the game BEFORE release, make it mod-able from the get go and, at least have it pass a simple Beta testing before throwing it out to the unsuspecting public. If that had happened this game could have gotten the praise that it actually does deserve.
Love this game, so happy that I didn't buy it years ago when it came out, but I am so pleased that I finally took the chance and found an absolute gem.

This game is unfinished and a buggy mess. It may not work on some systems and it will require you to spend quite a bit of time messing with setting on your own system to keep it stable.
That warning being said, it is one of the best and most immersive 4x games I have ever played and unfortuantly probably ever will. This game's strengths lie in its nitch. If you like customization, detail and long term and large scale planning this game will scratch you just right. Here are the features which wowed me. Massive research tech trees, which improve and change the way you play, build ships, colonize and dominate. Arguably the games strongest feature is the modular ship system. Ships come in three scales, and each set allows for moduals of its basic parts, improvments from addons; to extra power generators, extra crew, more armor, better structural integrity etc.  If you like heavily customizing nearly every detail of your modular ships from replacing small cannon turrets to Point defence turrets (or anything inbetween) you'll like that.
The major aspect of this game which stands out to its peers? Meaningful Real time combat. Heavily tacticle, great graphics and impressive physics. Few things made me as giddy as watching one of my carrior ships launch dozens of fighter craft to swarm enemy supply ships. Or building a massive missle fleet dedicated to long range warfare of overwhelming the enemy defenses with missles barrages. Watch some youtube videos of its combat and you'll be stunned how well this game does it.
Unfortuantly, this game as much as I love it. Is awful. LIttle to no tutorials; you'll need to rely heavily on trial and error and online guides and refrences. I fully didn't know what the heck I was doing until maybe twentyfive hours or so of game time.
Game is unstable: keep to maps small and the amount of factions smaller. Turning on some features of the game such as a high amount of random encounters will simply make the game crash every couple of turns. There are known memory leaks and if you don't have a beefy computer you may have to close and reload the game after a couple hours to improve performance.
Elements of the game are just not there. The diplomacy is effectivly non-existant. You can do basic things such as, spy, ask for help/money and sue for peace and declare war and trade. It works as in it does just that and nothing else. All AI unless team setup at the beginning of the scenarios settings will eventually declare war on you and attack.
Several factions are missing units or don't have fully implamented technologies.
AI is weird: sometimes it is surpfisingly clever or even overwhelming. Other times its cripplingly dumb and easily beaten.
Mutiplayer is quagmire. Sometimes it works perfectly and some of my buddies and I will play a four hour sessions without one of us crashing or getting any bugs and we love it. Many times, we are unable to even connect to the host lobby: sometimes it simply does not appear, other times there are connection issues, some of us can see and or join the game while others can't. Weird problems like that. Luckily the game has save game for multiplayer and allows everyone to rejoin in case of crash or just done for the session.
In conclusion, this game had so much potential to be the best 4x hardcore game ever made. What is sadder still; in m any regards it actually is. The amount of detail and depth to this game is unparralled. So many factors and elements and so many diffrent ways to play and truely varied factions makes this game's ambition without equal. It is the only 4x game with an advanced combat engine which is both excellent in graphics and in gameplay. Ship designing, empire building and tech research are supurbly well done and will draw out the micro and macro manager of you. Unfortuanlty it was also never finished and severly suffers from its unfinished grand vision and pelthora of bugs, some being game breaking. Lacking core features such as diplomacy and scenarios (outside of open ended), I cannot recommed this game to the average player. If you are like me and actually like detail oriented games, grand strategy and tactics games, and with some patience, you may just find a gem here.

The Resident Evil series is fluid. They'd done survival horror, turn-based, first person, and action. This is the best of the action-based trio in my opinion. It improves on all of the combat aspects that I wished for since Resident Evil 1 as a child. Remember wondering why your SWAT (STARS) specialist couldn't jump on/over tables to avoid shambling zombies or worst, crimson heads and dogs? Ever wonder why that same specialist needed a knife to use close range combat on zombies? Ever wonder why you needed to wait for an incoming attack in order to evade danger (RE3)?
Yeah. This series gets a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥for going its action approach, but when Capcom makes these games they always manage to improve the gameplay. And that is where Resident Evil 6 shines. The writing is cliche, and not particularly interesting, but it's carried by the campiness of it all that had me laughing. The excellent voice acting, animations, and tensions portrayed by the directing of all of this sold the experience.

Offspring Fling is a puzzle- plaftforming game released in 2012 by Kyle Pulver.
The plot serves as justification for the gameplay. You play as a mother (of forest creatures resembling a certain pokemon) who has lost all of her children after a monster attack. The mother now has to search the woods and retrieve all of her lost children.
Gameplay is a mainly puzzle solving with some platforming elements. There are various levels (over 100). At the start of each one you will see where you (the mother), the children, exit, buttons and monsters are located on the screen. In order to win each level, you need to collect all the children and deliver them to the exit, which is done by walking up to the children and pick up each one and then either, drop, shoot or carry them to the door. For each child you pick up, your weight increases, which decreases your jump height.
The puzzle element comes into play when you have to figure out how to reach the all the children, which are trapped behind barriers or hard to reach places. Puzzles are generally solved by dropping your children on buttons (to remove barriers and decrease weight) which will allow you to reach the other kids. There are also traps and monsters which will kill you and the children. Should you or any child die, the level immediately ends and you have to restart. You and your children have only 1 life and no health, so anything dangerous will kill you instantlly.
There is also a timer which only starts when you move your character, allowing you time to plan out your movements beforehand. In order to unlock new levels you need to beat the recorded time for the level.
Audio is quite nice. The back ground music is cheerful and suits this game well. There is no voice acting. The sound FX for jumping and finishing a level sound similar to 'Mario' games.
Levels are quite unique, with the placements of children, obstacles and the mother, no levels look or feel the same.
Graphics are decent. The colours and 2D artstyle present a cheerful atmosphere.
If you are looking for a puzzle game with some plaftfroming, this game will not dissapoint.

A lovingly crafted monument to urban banality slowly collapses as the foundation of society is eroded away by a despotic cyberpunk conspiracy in this isometric point and click adventure game.  Heart.Break() presents the player with a world that is not so much interesting as it is wholly cohesive, much like its obvious predecessors Shenmue and Omikron: The Nomad Soul.  Ultimately the line between player and developer is blurred as they receive the power to alter the city of Dorisburg at its most basic structural level, its code.  Unlike other programming-themed games, here the player is not expected to laboriously logic out the solutions to difficult computer science puzzles, instead code is used as a tool to circumvent, subvert, and destroy the game itself.  Highly recommended to fans of atmospheric adventure games.

The game is a fairly slow paced, exploration based game with what appears to be a linear story thus far. Chatting to random people, stumbling around drunk, smoking indoors, going to raves, passing out on stranger's beds in communes and looting most things that are not bolted down is all quite possible but the game does hint at a darker plot teasing the depth of the story.
As for a world that feels alive, the soundtrack meshes with the game's vibe and atmosphere really well and I see it is available on Bandcamp now. As for the dialogue, I won't say it's super impressive by any means. The game doesn't always take into account which order you've spoken to characters in perfectly which can lead to a few strange lines of dialogue every now and then.
As a programmer by day, I do find the in-game coding to be a fairly decent balance for both newcomers and experienced developers. I'd be curious to see how players who have never coded actually grasp the mechanic. Some things are too easy in code like awarding yourself free money and I do wish the summary for commands was a bit more explanatory like actual APIs (Javadoc or Ruby/Python standard libraries). I know the focus of the game is "exploration" but that might be a big barrier for people new to programming.
My only real complaint is the camera controls. Luckily you can invert the camera rotation (feels more natural to me) in the Options screen but you can only zoom in and out with W and S not the mouse wheel which is bizarre. People who have played third person games like the Sims 3 or Cities Skylines might find the camera a bit weak in comparison. Whilst in the street, buildings between the player and the camera also don't go transparent so sometimes you find yourself messing around with it until you can see where you're going again. Really hope the developers patch this.
This is a niche game for sure, it's not perfect but I'm glad to see developers taking risks like this.

Well, let's compare the actual game to the things, which were promised.

1. "An expansive 3D world, begging to be explored."
If you call Dorisburg open world, then the cities in Path of Exile are open world as well. And I am not talking about lacking content, it is mainly about the quality of the content. I was excited to explore the supposed open world and before I was heading to my next step of the story line, which was checking in to the Devutchka hotel, I walked around the city to experience what is going on there. I talked with people, I looked for some buildings, but when I slowly started to change from randomly experiencing the map to finding my next story line objective, the city just got more and more annoying, because it was pretty hard to find the hotel after I explored other areas (btw. for me personally it was kind of immersion breaking, that you just look at a black void at the borders of the city, but that was not the only thing; the camera started to be really annoying at some point, because the perspective is just bad and you have to really work on seeing what you actually want to see, because your vision is either blocked by buildings or you are looking from the wrong perspective) and on the way I found like 500 floppies, 500 computers and a couple of people, oh and yes, you can kick lamps, for whatever reason. 2. "Many hours of engaging story, set in a meticulously simulated city, with people that feel truly alive."

I spoke to most people along my way and they either didn't want to talk to me at all, said some boring casual stuff, nothing special or weren't there because in the whole "open world" city there were like 20 people on the streets, and that number is generous. And most of them weren't special at all, or at least the "special" things were pretty boring compared to what imagination could have created. Also the dialogues sometimes were pretty stupid, since the people there are literally like AI and not believable at all (btw. when I looked for my room in the hotel, I found another room, which was open and it was really small and kind of ridiculous, because it had like two rooms, of which one was the main room with two sinks and a shower and the second room was like 2m² and had only a toilet in it. that's right, you obviously can stay over night in a hotel to get a room without a bed. I was really confused, when I saw that, well but finally I found my actual room and look at that, it was basically the same room, but only because it was Sebastians room, he shouted out "WHAT THE" and he was also "confused", when he saw the living conditions. for me this kind of scripted events aren't open world to me at all, since he should've noticed that♥♥♥♥♥♥in the previous room already, and when you make an "open world" you should expect, that people are gonna exploit this by reaching areas, that aren't supposed to be visited yet or at all, according to the actual story line), when they for example don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about you stealing stuff, which...

3. "A challenging game where your actions matter and nothing can ever be unsaid or undone."
brings me to my next point. Really? Really? Where do my actions matter? Please say the place and situation in the game, so I can check it out by myself. I break into houses of foreign people, and they are like "Hey, who are you? What's up?" or "Hey, what are you doing? What's your name?". I steal stuff in the front of the faces of the stupid AI and they do... nothing. Literally. Another example of how actions don't matter and you can undo them is, when you meet the guy, who speaks to an animal, or himself loudly so you don't have to talk to him, to see him talking. He asks you for a beer and you can answer no, no and then you can still give him a beer. Same with other people who ask you something about yourself and you still can change something about that, except the things, that don't matter. Like being called by your nickname for example. Which makes no difference. Many other answers don't seem to make any difference, except the different answer from the AI you are talking to, which has no actual consequence for you and your character, as well as the story. So meanwhile you talk to some boring guys and find loads of coca cola, booze and beer. You drink some of it, and oh, something changes... Wait, no, nothing changes. At all. Which...

4. "Tons of every-day objects and computers that work and can be modified."
...brings me to my next point. You can find many computers, that's right. You also can find many floppies, like the "DigitalCrap64", to have something to do on the computers. You also find tools for a computer, like a screwdriver. Well and that's it. I explored at least 20 houses and 90% of all things were those which I mentioned above. Oh, wait and you find beverages, like booze, coca cola or beer. Which btw. changes literally nothing about your character. I at least hoped him to get drunk after drinking some bottles o' alcohol, but mh-mh, no. What's the point of implementing something, that has no actual in-game effect or consequence? The only reason in this case could be: it is fun, or interesting, or something like that. It is neither of that though.
I know the motto of the game "...where bits have replaced atoms.", though I didn't realize, that most content is just based on the idea of doing something on vintage computers. And talking to people, that are supposed to be interesting, but I only met a couple of people in the city and the ones I was supposed to talk to, like the woman in the hotel. A guy on the street told me about a bar, which is supposed to be interesting. Also I asked the woman in the hotel, if there is something interesting in the city and she also mentioned bars. So, as I expected, the most interesting or action rich part of the "open world" is supposed to be the bars, which...

5. "A laid-back experience where you can just go to the café and have a coffee whenever things get too hectic."
...brings me to my next point. It is indeed a laid-back experience. Though not for us, rather for the developers, as it seems. And when exactly do things get too hectic? I know, I didn't play all of the game, but considering how the story went on and what the main "attractions" were, I don't expect much else. Feel free to correct me, if I am wrong. For me it just seems like the game is about going to the bar, hanging out with a couple of chicks, then go to your home and do some else heart.break() stuff on the vintage computer. The time in-between was just boring or there just was nothing really. This didn't get better, when I was even more driven by the game to get bored due to lack of some SOUND. It was really quiet and unexciting to listen to the game, which...

This game unfortunately is a huge mess
(TL:DR below)
On one hand, the levels and most of the gameplay is very well designed. The game is challenging and generally any mistakes you make are due to your own lack of precision. I made it through the whole game and had fun most of the time as I enjoyed the challenge.
The only reason why I would not ever recommend this game, which is a VERY BIG flaw, is that the ragdolls are very badly designed. For a feature that is so core to the gameplay (especially on the last few levels), it amazes me how random it gets. People seem to blame the games physics in general, but everything else in the game seems to behave normal.
When you, or any other object in the game, becomes a ragdoll, anything can happen. You can clip through traps meant to kill you, walls and platforms, or even get blasted outside of the map. Without the ragdoll mechanic the game would be amazing and fair, while still being very difficult. However you will often die, get stuck in a wall or fall off a platform for seemingly no reason and have to start the round all over again. This is most noticeable on one of the last few levels that is literally impossible to beat unless one of the ragdolled objects get stuck in the map, which seems like really lazy design for a game like this.
TL:DR Not the challenging game it is supposed to be due to poor ragdoll physics.

Pre-note: I will mention ways to fix most issues at the end of this review, if devs even see this they should at least read the improvments I propose.
FACTS:
Gameplay is fun, it is amazing fun when you and a friend start the game at the sametime and play against each other, BUT the fun really dies out quickly (explained in details below). You only get money to buy cards if you farm online game like crazy (at best 2 packs a day if you spend your day playing), but all you will get in those is bad cards or cards you already have. Good thing is you can fight your friends and gain levels (which gives free good cards) but only until level 10, which is incredibly low. So yes, you end up only playing ♥♥♥♥♥♥ online matchs against people with lots of way better cards than yours. Lucky you though, every week there is a boss fight you can do to get a pack of free cards, sad thing is, you need to own pretty much every good cards anyway to beat them, as they are near impossible to beat (used to be well balanced when they came out). If you are ready to spend money on a game, go ahead! After $100 you will be nearly be able to say you have a good card, yes their prices for cards are this terrible. The cards balance is simply non-existing, some legendary cards wins you the game instantly when you play it, others (those you will get obviously) don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥
HOW TO FIX:
Most important fix would be to award gold for playing with friends, doesn't need to be much. Do not cap the level at 10 when playing friends it has no purpose and only makes playing your friends pointless (thus uninteresting). Remeber that playing against random players in a competitive way is NOT what every wants, a lot of players do not want competition.
Award more gold per day with those daily quests and make them take less time, we don't all have 3 hours a day to spend on a game. Heavily rebalance the cards, you are doing the same mistake as LoL and Stacraft 2 WoL was doing, you are balancing the cards arround the "pro" players, not the majority of players. Reduce the price of the expension packs, it shouldn't take 3 days of farming to get only a few new cards, which most of them we will not like. You could reduce the price of your real money shop, the reason being I woulda bought, for example, at least 3 key for the boss boxes right now if they were half the price ($2.50) each instead of $5. $5 is A LOT for what little you get from it, but $2.50 is still a lot, but lots more reasonable. This game has a lot of potential, but nearly none of it is being used right now. As the game stand at this moment, I cannot recommand it to anyone for the reasons listed above. I bought this game 2 years ago, I came at it as someone who already had nearly 10 years of experience with guitar. I was good, but not a shredder and I definitely needed to tighten up many aspects of my playing. I had previously tried Yousician to help me with some sloppy playing, but the restrictive time limits and high pay wall really put me off. So I picked up Rocksmith 2014! I am immensely satisfied with it as a product; but there are also a few issues I'd like to address. These are not deal breakers, but fixing them would greatly increase the value proposition of the this game.
The main feature of this game is the "Learn a Song" mode, where you are taken through the songs with your instrument of choice, Lead Guitar, Rhythm Guitar or Bass. The new Dynamic difficulty update I found was spot on a good 95% of the time; I very rarely got hit with unexpected difficulty spikes. As such, the process of learning a new song is frequently silky smoothe. The selection of songs is pretty good as well. Although at first glance, they weren't really my cup of tea, I decided to use this as an opportunity to try some new music. This has lead me to discovering new bands as well as new styles of playing music. There are a plethora extra songs available for purchase to help you expand your experience. They may appear a little pricey, and you have to think carefully about the kind of mileage you might get out of certain songs/packs. You might be better off buying something a bit more difficult to master like Pantera or Dream Theatre than you would be Oasis if you want to get the most out of your purchase. The extra songs also come with "authentic tones"; where are essential simulations of the artists so you can best mimic their tone in the games' "Session Mode" (more on that in a minute). I have a few issues with the song selection and the DLC strategy. First of all, the song selection is made up mostly of the bands' singles; and given that the singles are meant to be the most palatable, radio friendly tracks, they are often the most musically uninteresting out of a band's discography. I understand this has a lot to do with track licensing and making sure the music is the most iconic and recongnisable to ensure people actually buy it. That leads into my second issue, the selection of bands I find are the most mainstream and visible in the public conciousness. There is a lot of fun to be had if they included bands like Korn, Slipknot, Tool and hell even some Animals as Leaders to let the best shredders indulge in their guitar playing fantasies. Unfortunately, for reasons such as bands not granting permission to use their tracks, the lack of mainstream appeal and requirement to have a different guitar/setup all hamper the possibility of having these types of bands in the library. I do wish Ubisoft could make it work so that we could have bands that use extended range guitars (i.e. 7 and 8 string) or some less mainstream metal and prog bands to allow us to REALLY test our playing chops. To reiterate, these issues do no hamper the product for me, but my mileage with this game would definitely increase if these things happened.
"Session Mode" is a game type where you play along to a band of your choice; either a preset or custom band. You can tweak a variety of options to make the band play and shift up their playing style to suit your preferences. It's a really nifty tool to practice your improvisation and just squeeze in some practice of your scales. It feels like the virtual band is responding to you organically and it feels pretty darn good to play!
The "Guitarcade" has a set of mini-games which test certain skills. My personal favourite is "String-Skip Saloon" on bass; it is great for practicing your finger picking, where you use a different finger for each string. There are others that test your ability to play chords and change between them quickly, change scale, slide and play harmonics. They are good fun and genuinely help tighten up your skills. In the guitarcade is a score attack mode where you can test everything you have learned in "Learn a Song" and get scored on the various different songs. Now I have spent a lot of time in "Learn a Song", I am spending a lot more time trying to boost my scores than I am learning.
There is a multiplayer mode, but I haven't been able to try it out unfortunately.
My personal opinion is that I feel like you get the most out of this game with a bass. I've found it is by far the most responsive. I have found that playing guitar with this game can be a bit frustrating at times; it all depends on what you are playing. I find playing complex chords to be the worst offender as Rocksmith does not easily decipher when you are playing a chord, and if you are playing it correctly. There are some strategies to overcome this, such as playing the chord very deliberately, gentely, ever so slightly ahead of the beat. But that does feel a bit unnatural. Playing power chords, riffs and solos are generally great fun to do. Make sure you are playing this on a moderately good PC to ensure that you can minimise the latency values on the audio; if it is running well you can play the game very naturally. If not, then you might have to alter your playing to account for that latency, which isn't fun! I have managed to have a great old time by plugging my laptop into a TV and didn't get any noticeable degradation in the experience. One word of advice, don't try it using the Steam Link, you will have a bad time! The network latency REALLY makes itself known with this game.
Overall, I certainly recommend this game, it has helped me tighten up my playing even though I've already had many years of experience. As long as Ubisoft keep supporting it with a strong library of great guitar driven songs to play; I'm not ready to complain.

First of all, I fully understand all negative reviews. I have rarely seen such a badly documented game. The description / explanation of critical features are either incomplete or totally missing (the official manual gets you started – but not more). A clear NO GO for an average gamer.
Having written that: why do I recommend buying this game at all?
Because after having spent really a lot of time to understand the game mechanics on my own (basically as part of a separate game), SoSt II (enhanced edition) turned out to be the best 4X Science Fiction game I have ever played. It even beats “Sins of a Solar Empire” (meaning a lot for those who know it). As far as the depth and complexity is concerned it can be best compared to “Hearts of Iron” (the latest versions).
Yes, the game crashes from time to time, but it is still playable thanks to auto saving before and after a combat. With my current HW configuration I can usually play around 10 – 50 turns without any issues – at highest settings. For beginners, the AI is absolutely sufficient. After you have achieved some game experience, I recommend playing primarily in a two player mode (without AI). Diplomacy is certainly not a strength of this game. However, the combat system with all the tactical possibilities is just awesome. Also, the fully 3D star map is unique with several different ways (drives) to explore. Designing ships and building up a reasonable economy is fun. In addition, the Tech tree is breathtaking (just note that a lot of technologies you find in other games from the beginning, have to be developed first – adding massive functionality and a lot of features you are not aware of at the beginning).
Bottom Line: an absolutely great game marketed in a very bad way. Only to be recommended for people who are willing to go the extra mile required to understand the undocumented features of the game (including some basic game mechanics).

I love 4x space strategy games and I tried to really give this one a shot but after 14 hours of struggling with this thing I just can't bring myself to give this any sort of a recommendation. On paper this game seems amazing with loads of great and complex elements but in reality it's all just horrendously designed trash. The menus, the UI, the battles, the Manager screens, the mechanics... literally EVERYTHING in this game is broken. I've got a mid to high range PC and this game plays at a silky smooth 4-7 fps in the Fleet Manager screen when I'm arranging a 6 ship fleet ffs. I once made the mistake of attacking an enemy's planet and ended up having to sit through a 3 fps battle for 14 minutes because of how horribly optimized this game is and because there's a complete lack of menus and other VERY BASIC things that can be found in any RTS made over the past decade (like an ESC menu, a Load Game option in the Campaign Menu, or even some camera hotkey options). This game has some of the worst camera controls I've ever had the displeasure of dealing with. No WASD or arrow key camera movement (everything is done using the RMB) which is literally the most basic thing in any game, let alone an RTS.
This thing is a rushed, buggy, poorly optimized, and completely half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥piece of sh*t. No tutorial, no explanations, no campaigns, and the list just goes on from there. I bought this thing on sale for $4.99 and I still feel pretty ripped off.

The second part of Sword of the Stars isn't what I expected, and as so many before me, I have to say it's disappointing in many ways.
Graphically a slight bit better than it's predecessor, it's giving a lot of pain in many details. But I will give that soon in Pros and Cons.
The game does lag a lot, even with lowered details, all special effects switched off and on lower resolution, you actually do need a lot of memory, even when you run the game on a quad-core System.
The player is factually drowned in information, you can do too much micromanagement of your empire - the same mistake that led to the downfall of Master of Orion III in public reviews. The Lore of your race can be looked up in the game 'cyclopedia, which actually is nice, because the information is given in digestible bits and pieces.
I was just glad, not to hear the strange squeal of shot down SolForce ships, that annoyed me in the first part, the sound was slightly more polished - and I will try to play a bit more of the game, but it's not the game I expected, neither has it anything good and barrier free as the first part... Oh, and german players, you will have a lot better playing experience when you play in english - fully free of strange artefacts in the descriptions because there was some issue with our ö,ä,ü, and ß in some words.
Even though I am a great fan of 4X games and especially space empire simulators, I can't recommend this game in good conscience. Sadly some things were overdone, putting the player into a frightful tight between overmanagement and minutae details, very finely crafted especially for perfectionistic buerocrats. But the fun of the first part with breathtaking  battles between fleets will come a bit short, and aren't as enlighting as in the first part.
Furthermore there are other issues, the lags, some of the bugs and of course the detailed aproach can scare off any newbie to the genre. I am quite the veteran in such games, but sadly, and as much as I first was very happy to have the game in my library, I am not quite accomodated with the game.
The only question that keeps me pondering, how would the game have fared if this one hadn't put Kerberos, the developers behind it, out of business? Hmmmm...?

A light puzzle game with one really neat twist of diving into cassettes to find elements of the puzzles. I definitely enjoyed it for the trippy little series of puzzles it is. The visuals are sharp, and the environmental storytelling honestly does more of the heavy lifting in creating this world than any of the interstitial scenes do.
I would like to see how else the core cassette mechanic could have been used. Perhaps making some greater level of interaction between the tapes and whatever given room you are in, or maybe magnets that affect the real world too? That might be something for Smaller Radios Bigger Televisions, who knows. Regardless, this was an enjoyable single-sitting puzzle game.

Knowing how bad Ubisoft PC ports usually are, I did not expect to like this game. Boy was I in for a surprise.
The game is so much fun. Gameplay is your standard 2D platformer fare. You run and jump towards the end of the level, collecting yellow "lums" for a high score, and defeating enemies by jumping on their heads, or slapping them silly. Nothing out of the ordanary.
What makes this game stand out is just how joyful and fun it is. The graphics have a beautiful hand-painted look that call back to the old hand drawn Disney films. Levels are all unique and colorful, with environments having distinct feels. The music is catchy, with a mix of orchestral symphonies, and western country banjo playing. Levels are difficult and may take a few tries, but are nothing compared to the unrelenting difficulty PC platformers like Meat Boy usually ask. But most of all, the game is just fun to play.
TL;DR: This game is New Super Mario Brothers, but on the PC.

Delightful is what I'd use if I had to sum this game up in one word.
It's an old school sidescroller with a lot of modern day polish. For example, the difficulty is extremely well balanced. Most levels are simple enough for a child to get through, yet only the most hardcore players will be able to collect enough Lums (the game's version of coins) to get medals in each level without a lot of deaths. But that's okay, because dying in this game is relatively painless. There are no lives to lose, and the game will place you in the beginning of the section you were in nearly instantly (possibly taking a cue from Super Meat Boy?)
The art is gorgeous, the animation is smooth, and it has good controller support. The only negative I can think of is the lack of online multiplayer. But that's a tiny negative in a sea of positives.

I'm not going to rant about how the Resident Evil series has changed over the years, that has been done extensively. I'm just focussing on this game by itself.
The singleplayer campaign mode is made up of 4 different stories that intertwine. In each story you play with a separate set of characters / weapons. Each story itself is made up of 5 different chapters, with each chapter lasting roughly an hours. So a full, non-rushed playthrough lasts about 20 hours. Take into account that there are 5 difficulty levels to choose from, and this figure can easily multiply. Especially when you have a friend to play co-op with (split screen is possible!)
All the campaigns have enjoyable gameplay; some are more survival horror oriented and some are more action packed. This change of pace keeps it fresh. All in all, just plain good zombie shooting fun to be had here. Some vehicle sections are encountered, those felt a bit lackluster to me.
When you're done with the campaign, you can aim for high scores in the Mercenaries arcade mode - also good fun. Can also be played co-op (both online and local) for some intense teamwork sessions.
I definitely recommend this game, you will get your money's worth of fun out of it. Note that it is on sale very frequently, so aim to buy it at a discount!

I bought this game 2 years ago, I came at it as someone who already had nearly 10 years of experience with guitar. I was good, but not a shredder and I definitely needed to tighten up many aspects of my playing. I had previously tried Yousician to help me with some sloppy playing, but the restrictive time limits and high pay wall really put me off. So I picked up Rocksmith 2014! I am immensely satisfied with it as a product; but there are also a few issues I'd like to address. These are not deal breakers, but fixing them would greatly increase the value proposition of the this game.
The main feature of this game is the "Learn a Song" mode, where you are taken through the songs with your instrument of choice, Lead Guitar, Rhythm Guitar or Bass. The new Dynamic difficulty update I found was spot on a good 95% of the time; I very rarely got hit with unexpected difficulty spikes. As such, the process of learning a new song is frequently silky smoothe. The selection of songs is pretty good as well. Although at first glance, they weren't really my cup of tea, I decided to use this as an opportunity to try some new music. This has lead me to discovering new bands as well as new styles of playing music. There are a plethora extra songs available for purchase to help you expand your experience. They may appear a little pricey, and you have to think carefully about the kind of mileage you might get out of certain songs/packs. You might be better off buying something a bit more difficult to master like Pantera or Dream Theatre than you would be Oasis if you want to get the most out of your purchase. The extra songs also come with "authentic tones"; where are essential simulations of the artists so you can best mimic their tone in the games' "Session Mode" (more on that in a minute). I have a few issues with the song selection and the DLC strategy. First of all, the song selection is made up mostly of the bands' singles; and given that the singles are meant to be the most palatable, radio friendly tracks, they are often the most musically uninteresting out of a band's discography. I understand this has a lot to do with track licensing and making sure the music is the most iconic and recongnisable to ensure people actually buy it. That leads into my second issue, the selection of bands I find are the most mainstream and visible in the public conciousness. There is a lot of fun to be had if they included bands like Korn, Slipknot, Tool and hell even some Animals as Leaders to let the best shredders indulge in their guitar playing fantasies. Unfortunately, for reasons such as bands not granting permission to use their tracks, the lack of mainstream appeal and requirement to have a different guitar/setup all hamper the possibility of having these types of bands in the library. I do wish Ubisoft could make it work so that we could have bands that use extended range guitars (i.e. 7 and 8 string) or some less mainstream metal and prog bands to allow us to REALLY test our playing chops. To reiterate, these issues do no hamper the product for me, but my mileage with this game would definitely increase if these things happened.
"Session Mode" is a game type where you play along to a band of your choice; either a preset or custom band. You can tweak a variety of options to make the band play and shift up their playing style to suit your preferences. It's a really nifty tool to practice your improvisation and just squeeze in some practice of your scales. It feels like the virtual band is responding to you organically and it feels pretty darn good to play!
The "Guitarcade" has a set of mini-games which test certain skills. My personal favourite is "String-Skip Saloon" on bass; it is great for practicing your finger picking, where you use a different finger for each string. There are others that test your ability to play chords and change between them quickly, change scale, slide and play harmonics. They are good fun and genuinely help tighten up your skills. In the guitarcade is a score attack mode where you can test everything you have learned in "Learn a Song" and get scored on the various different songs. Now I have spent a lot of time in "Learn a Song", I am spending a lot more time trying to boost my scores than I am learning.
There is a multiplayer mode, but I haven't been able to try it out unfortunately.
My personal opinion is that I feel like you get the most out of this game with a bass. I've found it is by far the most responsive. I have found that playing guitar with this game can be a bit frustrating at times; it all depends on what you are playing. I find playing complex chords to be the worst offender as Rocksmith does not easily decipher when you are playing a chord, and if you are playing it correctly. There are some strategies to overcome this, such as playing the chord very deliberately, gentely, ever so slightly ahead of the beat. But that does feel a bit unnatural. Playing power chords, riffs and solos are generally great fun to do. Make sure you are playing this on a moderately good PC to ensure that you can minimise the latency values on the audio; if it is running well you can play the game very naturally. If not, then you might have to alter your playing to account for that latency, which isn't fun! I have managed to have a great old time by plugging my laptop into a TV and didn't get any noticeable degradation in the experience. One word of advice, don't try it using the Steam Link, you will have a bad time! The network latency REALLY makes itself known with this game.
Overall, I certainly recommend this game, it has helped me tighten up my playing even though I've already had many years of experience. As long as Ubisoft keep supporting it with a strong library of great guitar driven songs to play; I'm not ready to complain.

At first, I was skeptical when I heard about yet another free-to-play card game but I am convinced now.
Duelyst is 100% worth it.
Visual and audio design are top notch. Stunning pixel art, as well as gorgeous backgrounds and paintings litter the game and will draw you in. The sound effects blend with the rich music to create a powerful, immersive atmosphere even when you're doing something as simple as browsing your card collection. The attention to detail is quite amazing. It's the little things that managed to exceed my wildest expectations. Like the terrifying earth-shattering sound effect a Magmar minion creates when it drops on the board.
From a gameplay perspective, the game should appeal to both veterans of the genre and newbies alike, it's very accessible. You can jump in, play less than a handful of games and feel like you accomplished your goals for the day or play for 3 hours straight and still find it enjoyable. The devs are very generous with rewards that come in all shapes and sizes. Free cards, bonus gold for the first win of the day, well designed quests, there's even free boss battles every once in a while that give you a chance to earn goodies.
For those interested in learning more about the lore, there's even an in-game book (and audiobook) called the Codex. I like to think of it as the last pages of a J.R.R. Tolkien book. The more you play games, the more you unlock chapters and learn about the history and races of the Duelyst universe (including a map of the world!). I'm constantly fascinated by the creativity that went in the fabrication of the game and its lore.
Bonus points for:
Try it for free, you won't regret it.

It really hurts to have to not recommend Duelyst after the long hours I've spent with it.
I received an alpha key from Decepticle back before he worked for Counterplay. My Steam time does not indicate the many hours I've wiled away at Duelyst.
In the beginning, I had become jaded with Hearthstone, and wanted anything more strategic and interesting than that mess of randomness. And I found that in this beautiful, well designed, and strategic game. In the beginning, hand size was smaller, but you drew 2 cards per turn in addition to your replacement. There were no hero powers. Duelyst, in those days, flowed unlike your usual DCG. You never felt that you were out of options, rarely ended up in topdecking scenarios, and had a more robust and accessible mid-late game. This fulfilled a great niche, and gave an options to folks like me who did not like the hearthstone style.
But I kept faith, even through the draw change, even through the addition of hero powers. But as time went on, the developer philosophy became clear, they were going to imitate hearthstone, instead of breaking from it. Expansion after expansion, season after season, player agency has been chipped at to make way for flashy, RNG based plays, early game rushdown, and a general feeling of frustration.
I would still have recommended Duelyst, but the inability to craft the most recent round of cards was the last straw. Unless Counterplay changes keel now, Duelyst is gonna become just another hearthclone, and I'll have to play Shardbound or Chaos Reborn or some♥♥♥♥♥♥

Godot, the underdog of the open scene of Game Engines Battle Royale. It's one of the least known game engines out there, which I myself discovered just mere month ago. Boy was I surprised to see something like this on the "market". It's an opensource 2D and 3D game engine, with a main focus on 2D (as of now, in version 2.0.2; 3D improvements and quite a lot more stuff! is coming in version 3) but which can also do 3D, though not as intuitive. But the best part of it all is the great community, responsive devs. (just try it out in their IRC chat: freenode - #godotengine & #godotengine-devel, like right now!) and best of all it's MIT license which basically means you can do whatever the hell you want with it. It is also poewrful enought to get you started in games ranging from simple to advanced. The editor itself is built in Godot! yah, you heard right, the editor is actually a game, how cool is that? Anyway, on to the more serious part (I'll focus more on 2D cause that's what I've been experimenting with):
Pros:
Cons:
Can't wait for Godot 3 which will a complete revamp of the particle system, it will be focused on 3D functionality and it will move on to the new Vulkan graphics API which is quite ambitious. So far the devs are on top of it and they have delivered every time! I guess it help that they are actually payed to work on this project, even though it's open source :). All considered I think this is one of the best game engines out there and on top of it it's open source! Definitely recommended!

After grinding months of endless unfruitful attempts with Unity 3D and other game engines, Godot (GD) is the most logically designed game engine to date.
It is relatively easy to learn. If you have just a little of programming knowledge, you already know how GD works. The best part, GDScript, GD's own coding language, is very Pythonic making codes extremely easy to read and write.
Definitely my favorite Engine! Really well designed and pure pleasure to use! :)
I'm using Godot engine in my game project.

First things first:
Although in steam I have just less than an hour of use time with it, I have been using Godot for months now and also tried my hand at Unity and some other less-known engines.
My background until Godot was basically using softwares from Click Team and also Scirra's Construct 2.
It is a fantastic engine, created from the ground up to be really modular. The nodes concept, something that just came to unity is a very handy and a really nice feature.
It also has so many features, it exports to pc, mac, linux, android, IOS and HTML5, although the HTML5 exporter has some catch-up to do compared to the other exporters.
You can create games as simple and as complex as you want, Godot uses a language that is basically python rebranded so, it is pretty easy to pick it up and make things...
The editor itself is packed with features to make awesome 2D and 3D games and the animation system deserves an entire review by itself. You can animate everything. Create cutout-style animation, animate opacity, position, any kind of value. In no time you'll have your character coming to life.
It is free and open source software, so you have complete control of your game, your code is yours only.
Have a look at the first game I made and also take a look at the game jam that happened during March of 2016, you'll be happily surprised with this engine.
Link:
