Unique thingies:
1. Dynamic Government Types, assigned based on economic, population, and military decisions, each government type with its own set of bonuses and restrictions
2. Automated empire population behaviors, spurred on with indirect economic stimulation, cause your citizens to act independently to colonize and set up trade routes
3. Fully rendered 3D ships with individually targetable sections, allowing advanced tactical warfare options (sniper weapons, heavy ballistic weapons, powerful beam weapons, drones, complex ordinance, you name it!)
4. Unique races, each with their own different FTL drive types. Different FTL technology significantly affects exploration and strategic warfare.
5. Random tech tree allows for a unique game each time
6. Research an A.I. to help your empire, but beware, it can TURN AGAINST YOU!! (Whaaat?!)
7. Randomized "Grand Menaces" (think "Borg" level galactic invaders) and encounters that make the game epic
There's a loooong back story on this game - an epic and confusing story of publisher vs developer. In the end, there were a lot of unhappy die-hard lovers of the original Sword of the Stars (an amazing game in its own right) who were severely off-put by what could only be called an unfinished game when it plopped out on release day. Because of this, you will no doubt be inundated by massive amounts of negative posts in forums and reviews. That being said however, from release forward, the developers continued to put out a fairly steady stream of patches and significant effort was made to bring this game up to "release" level by 2014. Unfortunately, this is where the story apparently ends as the publisher, after years slow improvement, decided to stop further progress on this game. Which is truly sad. Not sad, tragic. You can see the love for this game in the developers' forums, but politically (and I suppose somehow, legally) they no longer actively contribute to further patches. Some have hinted they will work on the product in their own time, unpaid, but very little has been seen to this end in recent time.
So where does this leave us? The game is lavish. It's complex. It's advanced. But you can feel overwhelmed because, simply put, the user interface just isn't where it should be. Tooltips are missing, documentation is limited (and in a game this complicated, detailed documentation is necessary to understand how things interact). Sword of the Stars seems to have always emphasized a fun-to-play engine on top of a complicated set of features. The player has (in the original Sword of the Stars game anyway) no immediate need to "understand" how all these factors work together to play - just set a slider or push a button and things "just work." That was okay in the first game, where your planet development and trade routes just made sense and were easy to understand graphically. But soooo much has been added to the sequel that it's mind bending to even try to guess what repercussions your actions might have. Browsing through the developer forums you will still get a sense that Kerberos intended things to "just work" and often you will see posts chastising users for asking detailed questions about mathematical formulas used to determine trade profit or population growth or morale, but without the necessary game feedback of what your choices in the game actually DO to your empire, it's hard not to want answers to the underlying logical questions of what's going on.
Still, Sword of the Stars is a totally unique series in an often sterile world of 4x games. It's ability to successfully merge tactical and strategic elements, with micro and macro management, and truly glorious 3D battles is so amazingly singular that you owe it to yourself to try this game. Few games allow you to actually implement strategic warfare to the point that it's possible to win against a superior enemy by focusing weaker units on strategic enemy ship components (each 3D element, turret, engine, etc is individually targetable), hiding in asteroid shadows, or annexing by indirect political power that it's without hesitation that I earnestly recommend this game.

Ben and Ed has that late night horror movie atmosphere that games today are lacking. It saddens me to see it at only "mostly positive" reviews; as this truly is a terrific game.
people are constantly complaining that it is too hard, and to that I say... git gud losers, because it has a fair amount of difficulty to balance the removable limbs power.
*edit:
people need to stop bubble wrapping themselves and play a game with some actual challenge.
If you watched the trailer before you bought it you knew what you were getting yourself into.

It's a crappy world and the little boy called Ben is alone and afraid until he meets a friend called Ed, who is also a zombie. The media takes an interest to this odd friendship and uses it to their advantage and so the zombie TV show, Rundead, is born!
This is the basic premise of Ben and Ed. The game is like Action Henk, you have a set amount of levels and you have to complete them one by one with some bonus levels here and there. However, as opposed to Action Henk, after a set amount of levels, there is a boss battle
Ben and Ed's premise is interesting, you have to run through a course filled with traps such as blades and cannons. As you progress you collect cans which accumulate an amount to unlock the next level. What is really interesting is that since you are a zombie, if your arm, leg or body gets chopped off, you can still play the level
That is mostly the most interesting game mechanic in the game, everything else is pretty standard. However, the game can be very unforgiving, especially with the jumping and the physics in the game
The music is okay but repeats over and over and over in the level and if you die multiple times, you're just going to keep on hearing the same music over and over and over again
Ben and Ed is an interesting game but can get very annoying with the amount of deaths in a level and the repetition of levels, however, if the game is in a price drop or you like this style of game, then why not try it!

This crossbreed between a Chocobo and Pikachu just looks cute as hell. Even the manliest men will feel warm in thier hearts when they see this thing. The game has a beautiful 16-bit artstyle and the best soundtrack when you like happy and cheerful music. OFFSPRING FLING is a cute little title that will bring a smile on your face.

A really difficult game to review - first thing to establish is that  lot of the negative reviews come from when this game was first released, which from what i can make out was one of the worst releases in game history! Second thing to establish is that whilst the game has been hugely improved since launch their are still problems, most notably for me was the lack of help provided by the game design, things like moving fleets which in most games is really easy in this is not intuitive at all! Balancing economies is also not easy and undertsnading the complexities of FTL travel variations and research options are also poorly explained in game.
However after struggling with a game which didnt explain itself i watched a couple of lets play episodes which helped explain the basics and tried again and i can safely say this is a fun and really detailed game! the races are significantly different, research is slow so you have to make big choices early game to figure out strategies, the visuals are cool, not amazing but you certainly get a feel for epic clashes going on in deep space, and flicking through finance spreadsheets is depressingly fun (who new data could be so exciting!)
If youre interested in space/4x games i would recommend trying this - it doesnt feel like a carbon copy 4x game (a genre of game i would love to love but also find becomes a bit stale and repetative), instead it brings new features to the table (the mission system which means you can only give your fleets in the strategic mapmode a single mission [survey, strike, invade, intercpet, construct, colonize, relocate etc.] before they have to return to refuel/restock - which sounds annoying but means you have to plan ahead and makes your fleets feel far more realistic than most strategy games where they ca just keep on going) - however I would also strongly reccomend watching a lets play video first otherwise poor UI could really drive you mad

With rayman origins being the first rayman game since rayman 3 released in 2003 I was understanderbly nervous that this game would not meet my expectations especially with it's coop.  I was afraid that it would be a coop only game or a game that had features locked behind a coop wall.  Thankfully this is not the case.
Rayman Origins is a game that you don't need a friend to play.  It'll make your life much easier in the latter half of the game sure but it isn't required (and honestly on a computer playing with a friend can be rather cramped especially if there's going to be four of you in total).  Unfortunately the coop system is local meaning you can't play with friends over the internet.  This is silly really because I know a couple that want to play this game with me but as I said playing at a computer desk is cramped.  You can always wait for a steam machine but you might as well get this game for a console if your going to do that.
The game itself is very difficult in the latter half.  If your inexperienced with platformers you may rage quit.  There isn't any lives in this game so you won't be getting any game over screens like in mario but your patience will be tested to the limit.
The levels themselves aesthetically look beautiful you'd be hard pushed to find a game that looks better (not counting the sequel Rayman Legends).  With many hidden objects to locate you'll having a lot of fun if your the completionist.  If your not a completionist and just want to get from start to finish each level then your not going to have much luck seeing as in order to unlock bosses you need to collect a certain number of electoons.  The electoons aren't hard to find if you look but if you don't like playing hide and seek you can always collect a certain number of lums per level to get electoons or beat the level under a time limit.  There are other rewards if you go out of your way but they are only for bragging rights.
I would like to point out that the game support gamepad support, kinda.  You see connecting a gamepad isn't enough for the game to register it.  You have to calibrate the button mapping which is something you really shouldn't need to do with a platformer and it's a shame because the game is easier if you have a gamepad.
In terms of story it's...enjoyable however there is a rather large plothole that comes at the end of the game that ruins it a bit for me.  Now the story is very bare bones.  The glade of dreams gets invaded by the land of the livin' dead after Rayman and the clan are snoring too loudly and thats really all you need to know.  The story doesn't go much further after that but my problem is at the end.  I won't spoil it but lets just say it raises more questions rather than answering questions.
I reccomend playing the demo first to see if you'll like it.  Be warned the actual game is much harder than the demo and the graphical settings are no where near as in depth as they are in the demo (not sure why either).
Personally I think this game is the best in the franchise but I am yet to play Rayman Legends.  If you want a comparison to other platformers then I would have to say it is better than the original sonic games for the mega drive.  This game is worth the full price.

* It uses (nearly) python for the scripting language, making it very. very easy to write code for.
* Great editor with code completion
* Has a dedicated 2D physics engine AND a dedicated 3D physics engine.
* Exports to about every platfor you can think of (iOS, android, linux, mac, and that Redmond stuff ;)
* Rapid developement
* An innovative and VERY useful inheritance structure
* Pluggins for Blender - model in blender, import to Godot
* Even isometric games are possible
* You wouldn't believe the number of built in object types (called "nodes") that can do things for you
* Good community
* Actively being developed
* Live Editing - you can apparently deploy to a tablet and change the level on the fly from your rig
CONS:
---------
* No one's ever heard of this thing
* Documentation is a little lite. It's there, but it's for the prior version, though most of it is still applicable
* Documentation needs more examples and use cases
* No documentation on how to set up the Live Editing
* The community, though friendly, feels like it's small - because no one's ever heard of this great product
Conclusion
-------------
Say goodbye to Unity3D, Constuct, and Stencyl - this thing is amazing. Every engine has a learning curve, once you get past that, this thing is very powerful and a joy to use.

I love Duelyst. I really do. Almost everything I've said in my original review still stands as true.
But they ♥♥♥♥ed up.
Recently, Duelyst fell under Bandai-Namco as a publisher and, in the announcement notices, under the guise of handling funding and publicity while Duelyst devs retain their ability to run the game the way they want.
Well, that was either a lie or the devs decided it's high time to cash in on their player base rather than stay their course. Since the change, Duelyst went from microtransactions costing exact amounts, payable through Steam Wallet, to requiring a special currency (diamonds) that you can buy a minimum of $7 worth. Want a skin that costs ~$1? Too bad, pay us $7! Can't imagine that will help them in the long run, since I was more than happy throwing an occasional $2-$3 for packs, but at $7 minimum, probably not.
Beyond that, they shadow restricted entire countries/regions from the game, meaning players that once had the ability to play (including many well-known players and spenders) now no longer have access to their accounts with no hope of a refund. There wasn't even an attempt at making it clear this would happen and, in fact, when asked about it after the fact, both the developer and Bandai-Namco refuse to reveal which countries/regions are affected, so no one has any idea if anyone else will be blacklisted or when. Why would they do it this way? Likely because if they announced it, the playerbase in those countries would immediately stop spending and thus they would lose revenue earlier than they would like. Basically, they want to milk them for all they are worth and kick 'em to the curb. Like gentlemen, truly.
I fear for Duelyst. What once was (and still largely is) a super enjoyable game and developer that showed how microtransactions and card games should be has now begun the standard spiral into free-to-play/pay-to-win oblivion. I fully expect future patches to reduce the ability to get free cards to force players into buying diamonds and future expansion sets to created a power-creep locked behind this new currency. Because that is the direction Bandai-Namco apparently wants for the game.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Duelyst is exactly what I want in a TCG-esque game. If I had more time (and less other games to play) I'd definitely be glad to spend more of it here.
The main thing that draws me to Duelyst is the gameplay itself. Unlike most card games, summoned unit in Duelyst get placed on a grid and can then move and attack through it. This changes it from games like Magic, where anything can attack anything, and Hearthstone, where there are lanes, into a game that is more about positioning than deck composition. Do not misunderstand me- deck composition matters a lot, as it should. The difference between a poorly built deck and a master deck can be glaring. But skill in tactics and positioning can make up some of the difference and, in many cases, trump better constructed decks ran by less skillful players. You can set up traps, force your opponent's moves, block lethal damage by just moving out of range... The game board does change the nature of the TCG for the better, in my opinion. It's not for everyone, but it is fantastic in my opinion and definitely worth checking out.
As for the card portion of the game, this is built upon the foundations of games like Hearthstone moreso than Magic. You and your opponent start out with a set amount of mana to spend on playing cards (2 for first player, 3 for second). This, like Hearthstone, increases by 1 each turn up to a default maximum of 9, allowing you to play better and better cards as the game goes on. There are three 'Mana Fonts' on the board that, when a unit touches, gives +1 mana for that turn, allowing a crafty player to get a jump start over their opponent if they position well enough to secure these. Again, positioning is a mainstay of this game.
Now, onto what seems to be the more controvertial topic of the game- microtransactions. Each of the five factions has a 'starter set' you unlock by using that faction's commander. These cards are enough to make basic (and somewhat decent) decks, but soon you're going to want to get other, and sometimes better, cards. You'll get 1 card for free daily, but that's still not enought o sustain a player, so you'll undoubtedly want to get packs, which there are a few ways to do this which ultimately boil down to two solutions- get gold, the in-game currency, or use real money.
I'll not lie, gold is harder to get in this game than in most I've played. The primary way to acquire gold is quests, which can range from as little as 25 to as much as 120 each (from what I've seen, there might be higher/lower ones I have not gotten). You will receive two quests daily and can re-roll 1, giving you up to three chances a day at getting quests worth doing. These range from getting wins with a particular faction's deck, defeating X number of enemy units, dealing X damage to the enemy player and so on. These do not reset unless completed, so there is no need to rush to complete them each day, but not completing them the day they are awarded will mean that you do not get another quest in that 'slot' the next day. I personally like this system, as it means more casual players can complete quests at their pace while more hardcore players can get quests each day, constantly earning gold, all the while keeping the gold gap between the two relatively low.
Beyond these quests, you get a first win bonus daily of 20 gold and every 3 wins (non-consecutive) gets another 15. Yes, this is very low, as packs are 100g on the low end and 300g for the most recent expansion sets. Quests are your go-to for gold making in this regard. Monthly leagues also award gold (among other rewards) depending on your final ranking, which is a decent drop each month to let you get some packs and cards, but some say that it's a bit too long a wait. I personally have no issue with this, but that's a matter of taste.
Also note that there is a puzzle-style mode that serves as a tutorial for game mechanics new players can play that also rewards enough gold for a few packs upon completion, allowing new players to add a bit to their collection before jumping into the leagues.
There is another way to acquire cards that I find can make up for the lack of gold and that is crafting them. All cards can be broken down into 'spirit shards' that can then be used to 'craft' specific cards you want/need, based on rarity. This means that you will never draw a useless card from a pack- you can merely break down the ones you will not use to get the ones you will. Spirit shards can be slow to get, especially if you're saving for a high-rarity card, but are a nice option to get cards beyond merely buying packs.
All said, Duelyst is a great game in my opinion and a well-done free to play one at that. Before spending a dime, I was easily able to reach mid-silver tier (~15 rank) in leagues just using the free cards and what packs I was able to earn through gold. Just looking around online, you can find a ton of budget decks that can be gotten for a small amount of spirit shards (depending on pack luck, maybe none) that can hit gold with a good enough player. I've never felt pressured to spend money to go higher in ranks, fully recognizing my cap now is not my cards so much as my skill in deck consruction and board control (I tend to overplay way too early, something I am working on addressing). In all, I've spend ~$20 on the special deals that pop up so that I can both add to my collection and show support for this wonderful game.
Bottom line- try it. It's free, a small download and can run on almost any hardware. If it's not for you, then nothing lost but some time. But you just might find a new TCG to fall in love with.

If you've been playing Duelyst since the early days, it's an amazing game, a lot of variety, no one or two decks really take over the meta like some games *cough cough* Blizzard take note *cough cough*
However, if you're a new player, and you don't want to drop about 200$ to get all the cards right away, don't even bother. You would be hard pressed to find a single player with even one bad or sub-par card in their decks. Getting cards in Duelyst is actually pretty easy. Getting a couple of packs is no problem and maybe crafting a legendary or two. However, when your experience of the game is just continuously losing at the very lowest possible rank maybe 50 times in a row, purely because of the fact that 99% of the players are using a "tier 1 deck," there doesn't feel like there's a point to collecting the cards at all.
A good thing to note is that like in most of these digital card games, you do not get a "pity prize" for losing (the winner can "tip" 5 gold to the loser if they wish, but i've yet to see it even once.), so your only income is from daily quests, which makes for a very long, drawn out grind of logging in every day to get the quest, play the games, and log out, only getting a pack every 2 or 3 days. While the expansions do not give out duplicates, the core set seems to do nothing but. Despite having 40 hours of gametime in Duelyst, I have only about one-tenth of the cards.
If you've got the time and dedication or the money, go for it, you'll probably have a blast. If not, there are Duelyst "clones" popping up now, try those instead.

Offspring Fling is secretly two games.
The first is the game you are presented with, a very light-hearted and somewhat simplistic puzzle-platformer where you pick up your babies and toss them around to get them to the exit. 100 levels plus a level editor go by relatively quickly.
Underneath that is a very technical speedrun game, almost like a classic speedrun game like Super Meat Boy or Dustforce. Lots of minor optimizations and hidden tricks that mean you can do a lot more than you initially thought, and do it much faster. It opens up every level to be re-analyzed again, this time looking for optimal strategies.
I recommend this game regardless of which kind of game you prefer.

Offspring Fling is a casual 2D game that consists of competing with yourself to beat a level quickly. It takes a lot of tries, but once I get that great time and that golden flower I feel extremely satisfied and proud. If you're a casual gamer but like a bit of a challenge, you should take a look at Offspring Fling.
The music was the first thing that took me, its beautifully simple and immersive. The only problem I had with it was the fact that it loops the same song and it can get repetitive. The plot of the game was introduced with pictures rather than words, which fits the game's style well. The controls are what make this timed platformer up, at first they feel unnatural and forced, but if you focus on where your character is at all times you start to adapt to them. The game's nature is simple yet competitive, you try to score a better time than a replay of yourself, that's it. The graphics are a unique simplistic 2D that also fits this game's theme perfectly, however it would help to make this platformer's graphics sharper from a gameplay perspective. The gameplay is fun for a while, but being that the game sticks with the same concepts for long periods of time make it tedious replaying the same thing over and over striving for the best score.
Offspring fling does very well at what it's shooting for, however if the devs would have introduced more game mechanics at a quicker rate, the game would be much better. The controls could be smoothed, and some new music would be well deserved. My overall score of this game is a 6.5/10, slightly above average.

Just know of you read any further into this review, you might end up spoiling the game for yourself. This one thing hate about alot of clever indie games that are trying to follow in the steps of games like Undertale. So just know, I might end up mentioning certain things that will spoil parts of the game. So, here we go!
I supported Pony Island when it started off on Steam Greenlight. When checking out the free Game Jam version and playing it all the way through, I saw potential in this game and made sure Steam knew that I wanted that game and I guess many others did too.
Pony Island, like Undertale, meta-games a decent bit but more towards the end than anything else. It is also kind of clever in it's execution of how game tells a different story then what you shown. From what some people have speculated, it shows how some game developers go through hell developing a game. I kind of support this idea but meh this is a review not an episode of Game Theory starring MatPat
The gameplay of this game is sub-par. The Platforming is solid and fun and the hacking minigames aren't too bad durning the first act. Then the second act comes in and then these parts of the game become repetive. They are really nice break though and give the player some interaction side from navigating a desktop or moving a pony across the world map. The first two boss fights aren't that great.
[SPOLIERS STARTING]
The first is just four hacking minigames where it's like Connect Four in a way as you and the demon take turns placcing certain code blocks. The final hack of this fight however, brings in the challenge and makes you plan your moves a bit better. The second boss fight is the platforming sections where you are chasing a demon as it throws down giant rock spikes and creating fissures for you to jump over while you shoot the glowly bits on the demon's face. The third fight however... lets just say it was clever. Really. Damn. Clever. This is where the meta-gaming truly comes as the demon uses your computer to mess with you durning the battle requires you to stay focused. The final fight is just another platforming section where you try to keep as many souls alive as possible while trying to survive the game having it's memory dumped.
The games plot is kind of cryptic, requiring you to really look at things from different angles to understand what is going and having you find the secert demons that lie with in the game. Also, to get the final ending, it requires you to collect 24 tickets that are hidden throughout the game. Some aren't that hard but others are like hidden to point that you need the guy who made the game tell "There is a ticket if you do X task and go to Y location."
The music in this game, as with alot of great indie games, are freaking amazing. The small 8-bits tunes you here as you play the game are very good and they match each situation well and can work well outside if their intended area if you want to play a different game with Pony Island's music.
I like Pony Island and it's great if you are looking for a game to kill some time with. It's not a life changing experience but it's good, different, and clever in what it does. However, I wouldn't say its the next Undertale.

Can't say enough good things about this game engine. I've been developing and re-developing my own game for a year or so. I started out using Unity, switched to jMonkey, but settled on Godot. It doesn't get any easier than this to make games, almost feels like cheating!
Unity is nice, but they 'shoe-horned' 3rd party "Mono-develop" in for the coding environment, I had several issues where they didn't stay in sync with each other.
jMonkey is a similar approach, they've taken open-source Netbeans and shoe-horned a game engine into it. It works fairly well, but being beta, still a few glitches, some quite bad ones. Eg. the sound system no longer works in 2.0. I reported this on the forum and got told off for not reporting it earlier!
Then comes Godot, still Beta, but very much more refined, very active development too, I monitor commits to the source code. I submitted a bug report/suggestion two weeks ago, it just got fixed and pushed out in the nightly build. Nice!
If you can't make a game with this engine, then maybe game developing is not for you, but you do have to put in some work, learning GDscript (which is basically Python) is the only hard bit.
Very intersting Game Development Tool. Check it out, it is completely free to use. ;)

I'd say the downside would be it's still new, so it doesn't do EVERYTHING for you.  The new version supports community plugins and community assets are coming soon, so this should improve.  An example of this would be something like a dialog system.  You are left to create it however you like, but by no means is it drop in place and go. Godot Engine has been a perfect fit for my project, RPG in a Box. The built-in scripting language, GDScript, which is similar to Python, was very easy to learn and I've been able to do everything I've needed to with it so far. Even so, it's nice knowing that if there is anything more advanced that you need to do, the source is available to be modified and recompiled. The UI system is great also, and keeps getting better. With the nature of my project, the visual editor has been extremely helpful in quickly and easily creating custom editors using the wide range of available UI components. The upcoming move to OpenGL ES 3.0 for rendering is also a plus.
I've been through trial and error over the years with various other engines and tools, but this time I am comfortable in saying that I will be sticking with Godot Engine! If you have any interest at all in developing a game, I would definitely check it out.

This game had so much potential. It could have scratched an itch that I haven't satisfied since Yu Gi Oh duelist of Roses. Tragically, I've watched this game go to hell. I've played in the desktop client outside of steam until now, even when it was still in beta, and am only getting it on steam to write this review.
The pros are gorgeous visuals, excellent sound design and OST, a smooth UI, and gameplay that really could kick some major♥♥♥♥♥ At the core is a wonderful idea. A collectable card game in the vein of yu gi oh or magic the gathering where you also have to move your cards around the board like chess pieces. They did it in Duelist of Roses for the PS2 and it was simply wonderful and about as balanced as Yu Gi Oh itself was at the time.
Speaking of balance, that's really the only nail in this coffin. However it is a nail roughly the size of a telephone pole. In the beta, something several of my friends and I noticed was that one particular class was really absurdly overpowered. It was understandable, since it was just the beta, and they needed time to feel out the stats they'd set up. Only problem is, it never really got better. To combat the balancing issue, their only strategy seems to have been to add more and more ridiculously overpowered cards and spells to the point where any deck could be absurdly overpowered, and the game became less about strategy and more about who could get the best card first. Ultimately, before you can even IMPLEMENT a strategy you're annihilated by your opponents bum rush because a bum rush is legitimately the most viable option most of the time. I tried to like it. I really did. I loved Duelist of Roses to death, and have been praying for an updated version for a decade. This game seemed like a gift straight from the heaven that R. Kelly's hit single "I Believe I Can Fly" descended from. Sadly, this game reminds me of Duelist of Roses the same way the bug from Men In Black reminds me of the man whose skin he was wearing.
I could get into the whole "Paid card drops" thing, but I honestly don't see a point. This is a free game, and I might have even been inclined to shell out some cash to fund it if it hadn't broken my heart so thoroughly.
Bottom line: Balancing a game is like cooking a steak. The solution to make one cut as good as another is to fine tune cook times and flavors to make a unique culinary experience for each. Not to char the hell out of them until you basically have vaguely meat flavored leather.

I loved Duelyst, and it was by far my favourite card game for a long long time. I was a S-Rank player, and have over 95% of the cards, including legendaries. I played the standalone version for much longer than my steam stats indicate.
I have recently uninstalled it, and quit playing. The game direction the devs are taking the game forms part of the reason many older players are leaving. The increased randomness of abilities, which reduces the importance of strategic positioning, the general power creep of recent expansions, and the inability to craft the last expansions with 'spirit' (dust) definitely has reduced my enjoyment greatly.
Many older players have saved up over 10,000 spirit, in anticipation for the last two expansions, only to find their time investments are cast aside, in an attempt to force players to purchase with money. It is a real shame, because this was one of my favourite games of all time, when it released.

Hello anyone interested in trying this game, do know that any review saying this game has a pay wall/ pay to win is complete nonsense. You can earn literally everything with in game money that they generously give as long as you play, there are monthly rewards based on ranking. If you're paying 300 dollars for cards  you can obtain for free and then saying there is a pay wall, you're doing something wrong. While you can obtain powerful cards and getting a head start by purchasing expansions you can still win through sheer tactics, with budget basic decks you can hit gold and possibly even diamond as your deck evolves from winning. Having all the cards does not guarantee you wins or high placement.
There is a replace mechanic, so Rng can't completely destroy you like other card games can. While Rng can be annoying it is also something that makes a game like no other. Rng can be healthy or completely ruin a game depending on how its done. While there are things that can be considered unhealthy rng in duelyst every game comes with their problems, and duelyst is constantly changing/improving to prevent the meta from being unhealthy. New cards and expansions or changes will obviously change the meta and make some of your decks less effective or noneffective, it something that comes naturally with a card game.
You will probably face your fare share of frustration, its a tactic card game. You will meet the most uncreative people because they're try harding. What game doesn't have try hards? Maybe they'll top deck an answer winning the game with what seemed like no effort, you could do the same. Rng might be on their side, but perhaps through your tactics you control the rng to do what you want it to do. Maybe through your tactics you punish your foe who only attacks your general. There might be certain decks that you see to often and are way too powerful to be considered healthy for the meta, build against them or wait till the meta changes.
End of the day, Duelyst is a card game and there will be always something that is frustrating, that is my guarantee to you but, it can be also quite enjoyable. Find a good pace, don't let yourself be worn out, don't follow the meta like a sheep >_> and have fun.

This game is somehow both ridiculously beautiful and utterly terrifying.

I think if you put Small Radios Big Televisions in a hundred peoples hands and asked them what the game was really about, you could get a hundred different answers. From God, Creation, Technology and its affect on our lives, the environment, geometry, expressionism, to a simple its a puzzle game with tape cassettes. Interpretation is the key word here and its required to really enjoy this title. This game at its simplest is a puzzle game for sure, but underneath the surface the developer is being duplicitous, and in a way tricking the player. How? Well, read on and we will break down this game together.
I am going to break this game down in two ways, the same way there are two sides to a cassette tape.(See what I did there?) Side A in this case is going to be all about the basic functions of the game, the puzzles, the graphics, and all the nitty gritty of game design.
Side B is going to be all about the key word I mentioned earlier, interpretation. What I took away from this game and my personal experience with its unique themes and how I think Fire Face is screwing with our heads. We are starting with Side A first.
Fancy Steam description or not, Small Radios Big Televisions is a puzzle game that is played from a side view but many angles/perspectives are visible at the same time. The visuals are something comparable to Fez, but less static. You can click around the screen to tweak and shift things to get a look at another side of a wall. The way you interact with the entire game is very reminiscent of a mobile game. You swipe with your mouse to move the camera and click/tap to interact with objects and the environment. However, one of cool things about this title is that it plays with your head and changes things constantly.
Anytime you load up a new cassette tape, you never know where you are going to end up or from what perspective you'll be seeing things. One second you are riding along in a forest, and the next on top of a mountain. This constant shifting assault always keeps you on edge but at the same time in awe. Small Radios Big Televisions is a beautifully made game that crosses into what I like to call Gamer-art. One of the reasons I said Geometry is that this game is very playful with its polygons and colors. The style is constantly blending Science fiction themes and beautiful fields and sunsets. While the graphics are simple they never feel unrefined, the game has a wonderful vibrancy to it all.
The game has you traveling across different factories that all have a unique shape/design to them. These areas are all played from the side view and that is where most of the puzzle interaction takes place. The real WTF moment comes when you collect cassette tapes and begin magnetically warping them. Your character, who remains unknown throughout the game, has a headset/VR set up that allows escape into these cassettes. In these virtual worlds are keys, which look like a twenty sided die, that allow you to get deeper into the factories and move along deeper into the game.
Any child of the 80's could tell you that a strong magnet can damage and even erase content from cassettes because of the way they are made. In this case, it warps the realities inside of those tapes and allows you to find more keys, albeit at the cost of things getting terrifying and weird.
If anything this game deserves your attention for its use of color and atmosphere in true artistic form and then twisting it into something that makes you uncomfortable.
The basic goal is just getting from factory to factory, solving puzzles and enjoying the art. The story presents itself through the levels and some dialogue in between stages. More about that on Side B. There are some hidden collectibles in the forms of Lenses, which I still don't know the point they serve. The puzzles themselves, while enjoyable are very easy. I beat the game in about two hours and replayed the game to find the lenses, which took me about an extra hour. Not a huge gripe but I wish a little bit more complexity was involved in the puzzles to give the a game a bit more length. It's a very short game but it packs a punch. The puzzles usually consist of moving some objects or pressing buttons. Nothing that will make your brain bleed.
Sound design and music are used quite effectively especially at the end. The ending scene of this game is miraculous and the music just elevates it further.
There is one particular scene that I will just call "orientation" where voice work, visuals, and sound effects all come into this perfect storm of creepy. That is what I loved most about this title, it was always one note away from beautiful, scary, and captivating.
Sadly, there isn't much to speak of in the way of replay, its a play it and leave it type of game. Like I said before, at two to three hours at the most of gameplay, the experience is short. It's something to keep in mind as you make your purchase at $11.99. This is probably the one thing that holds this game back. This is a bite sized experience in visuals, with great atmosphere and art. There are also a couple minor hiccups in the way the camera's controlled in the 360 degree areas. Other than that, no bugs or glaring issues.
I will say that I haven't ever played a game quite like Small Radios Big Televisions. It is innovative and does things in its own unique way for better or worse. I think these types of games definitely deserve our support. Personal kudos to the Developer and Publisher for this game
Moving on to Side B.
Simply put, this game has no actual story. The entire game is stringing you along with scraps of information but never gives any actual answers. The why, how, when, who, are never set in stone and even at the end, you're unsure of what really transpired. I think the developer is being sneaky is for a sole purpose. To get you thinking and come up with your own answer.
Even the dialogue between stages is rather vague as you're listening to two people speaking about some sorts of events. What those are, is never made clear. In the same room as the two people, are the lenses you have been collecting, which are magnifying light into one of the games keys. This is never explained and puts the games timeline in question as to when everything occurred.
Don't get me wrong, there are some things that are made clear but I feel like these are all red herrings. Fact is that these tapes drove their users mad eventually to the point of suicide. The tapes were made to hide from some sort of horrible truth that they couldn't accept.
Another fact is that these were being made for global use. The last factory shows hundreds, if not thousands, of tapes being made for a large amount of people. However, most of them are still in production and never seemed to reach the outside world.
Last but not least, let's not forget the end. On top of the final factory is a device that seemingly recreates earth and all its beauty and glory, using a mixture of all the cassette tapes. So how can they all be so bad, but be used to help in this miracle? This just doesn't add up. Perhaps a new reality was created or our protagonist finally faced the horrible truth which wasn't all that bad after all.
One point of interest is the tape labeled "Alpha" which once loaded shows absolutely nothing but a black blob that has no shape or definition. If you've read the book of the Bible, Genesis, the universe is described  "The earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep." Digging deeper into this, The word Alpha is used to describe the beginning and Omega the end. If this was intentional, I have no idea, but it is interesting to say the least.
My point is that this game aims to make you think about philosophy, technology, religion, and beauty. It accomplishes this in every regard.
Maybe I am looking to deeply into the game.

Small Radios Big Televisions is developed by Fire Face Corporation and published by Adult Swim Games. I’m surprised the dev team decided to release a purely abstract game as their first Steam project. Usually such titles are reserved after you’ve already built a fan base. Alas, “The Times They Are a-Changin'.

Much like its own title, the game really makes little sense from the get-go. As soon as you start, you’re transported towards a level that reminds me of Fez. And despite being more 3D than that one, the stages (referred in-game as “factories”) in Small Radios also benefit from a side swapping mechanic. Just like turning a dice, the sides of the factories offer new doors and puzzles that need to be solved before advancing to another level. The fully 3D environments are noticed as soon as you enter one of those previously mentioned doors. A maze-like series of rooms needs to be explored with the mouse cursor in search for compact cassettes which play a central role within this title. The puzzles are quite simple and most of them imply that you find way to unlock new doors that lead to even more cassettes. Reaching some of these tapes, involves powering back some of the rooms and doorways through gear manipulation that is quite simplistic by itself.
Despite being solely audio recording mediums, these obsolete exponents of magnetic tape offer blurry abstract visions once played back on a recorder. The tapes are not related to one another since they showcase everything from empty fields, forests, streams or roads leading to nowhere. They have to occasionally be rewinded in order to fully “understand” the meaning behind them. The one constant objective when playing the cassettes, is finding the green diamond/key that helps you get past some of the locked gates stading between you and even more barely passable or understandable content. I personally found the puzzle solving tedious (especially the sections related to gears), in this title and along with having zero explanation for what or why am I doing this, really felt less indie and more lazy as far as the devs are concerned.

I did enjoy the retro looks and perhaps that is why I’m willing to be more forgiving with Small Radios Big Televisions. Visual and audio glitches are a game design choice that I can support. The 3D transition between scenes is snappy enough and the frame rate remained stable as well. What I didn’t like, was the initial limited working resolution options. Major scaling problems, when playing over 1080p as the cursor was going haywire. Small Radios’ Steam Discussions threads weren’t helpful but I did manage to solve the 4K issue by using the same method I implemented on some older titles. You right click on the game’s executable->Properties->Compatibilty->check “Disable display scaling on high DPI settings”. There you go, running perfectly at 3840x2160 despite de dev claiming “The game has only been tested up to 1920x1080.” It’s almost 2017 and 1080p just won’t cut it anymore with contemporary titles.

+ Decent graphics and sounds
+ Novelty aspect, for some potential players
+ Steam Achievements (Store Page doesn't mention this)
- No story or even an explanation for the game’s purpose
- No Steam Trading Cards
- Slightly overpriced given what it offers
Small Radios Big Televisions had potential for so much more, if only it managed to convey a storyline along with its interesting gameplay that feels like a true novelty-type. It’s a bit overpriced but it's nothing a good bundle deal or special Sale can’t fix and I wish it had Trading Cards too. I’d almost stop recommending it, were it not for the fact that its art style and retro influences did hit right at home, in my case.

I also covered this game on YouTube:
When I was offered a review code for this, I looked at the trailers and had no idea what it was or what I was going to experience. I've never seen a game whose trailers explain almost nothing about it. Having gone in largely blind, what I've played has really surprised me. This is an "arty game" for lack of a better term and I'm someone who has pretty high standards for those. To me, something must be a compelling game first and an art piece second, otherwise it's already failed. I'm happy to say that this is both a good game and a good art piece but it still won't be for everyone.
Small Radios Big Televisions is at its heart, a puzzle game, if a bit of a simplistic one. You navigate into different rooms in these different factories, finding cassette tapes (for you youngins' with your iPods and your Spotifies, a cassette was a magnetic media we old people used to listen to music and sometimes, even play games from) that contain virtual reality worlds (no, I don't know how that works either) which you must travel to at different points to find clues to help you solve puzzles and progress. You'll frequently have to run the tapes through different sets of magnets (you see kids, cassettes were magnetic media so being near a magnet makes them do wacky things) to significantly alter these worlds in different ways as part of the journey. Unfortunately, these worlds are a bit one note and you don't really interact with them beyond getting some needed items on occasion. This does feel like a bit of a wasted opportunity.
There is a story in Small Radios Big Televisions, which is told a little bit through the environment but mostly through text-based cutscenes in between levels. It's a story of a failed planet and what the last remnants of humanity did to try to survive and be happy within it. The direct storytelling is minimal but it manages to convey a lot of narrative and even emotion within a small amount of dialogue. Things start off fairly easy but will quickly get more challenging, though even if you have a rough time, this isn't a long game and doesn't really have a reason to play it more than once.
You have to like puzzle games to enjoy this one but even as someone who tends to flame out on that genre pretty fast, I really enjoyed it and found myself driven to move forward. To be fair, the puzzles are not particularly difficult but for me, they didn't have to be as I wanted to see what came later. A lot of this was driven by the incredible style that Small Radios Big Televisions is drenched in. The developer did all of the music and the art and they blend together very well. The soundtrack is very heavy, baked synthwave that combined with the aesthetic and unique visual style, give everything a very dystopian, "analog" feel. You're alone in this world and everything feels haunting and uneasy, even though you're never under any pressure and are never given a reason to be scared. I've never experienced an audio/visual aesthetic like this in a game before and it's stuck with me.
As someone who will be harsh on art games that are more art than game (for context, I very much disliked Dear Esther and Gone Home), Small Radios Big Televisions really clicked with me and has been one of my biggest surprises of the year. If you don't like puzzle games, easier puzzle games or narratives that leave a lot to interpretation, this won't be for you. If you like games with a cool style, a moderate challenge and a story that is open but still gives you enough leads for you to know where it's going, I highly recommend checking it out. It is fairly short so the value proposition might be a concern but you but that's subjective based on your tastes. In my case, this one's stuck with me but it's definitely not for everyone.

A fling, a fling, a one time thing.
Offspring Fling is one of those unfortunate cases where a great art style, catchy music, and interesting concept (speed running x puzzle solving x tending to your flock) come together in a game bogged down by floaty, imprecise character movement and poor controller implementation. The real challenge here is getting the character to do what you want consistently.
Typically, one might be expected to adapt to the controls over time, but since the player is tasked with performing actions within a very narrow window, every second you're left fighting them, is time lost in your attempt to achieve the goal. The result is a very frustrating experience.
The inclusion of a level editor is a welcome surprise since this leads to an unlimited amount of extra content (stages) you could potentially create for yourself, or share with others online.
Graphics options are sparse, ranging from two preset windowed options to two preset fullscreen options. They serve their purpose but it's nothing fancy.
Bottomline: Unless you're proficient with just the keyboard itself, or prepared to configure a controller through third party software such as joytokey, I'd say pass on this for now (although there is potential for things to be fixed in the future).
edit: Join the beta branch for a build of this game with better controls that actually make the game enjoyable (although proper menu navigation is still lacking, you're at least able to control character movement with the dpad).

Been using Godot since early alpha. It's just come out on Steam.
It's not the kind of engine I can write a lot about. Not out of a lack of complexity, but out of admiration for the way it builds up on concepts others have thought of and addresses it's issues from the perspective of "how can our users achieve their goals better" as opposed to "how can we make an engine that is better than the other engines"?
That definement makes a world of difference.
Godot is an engine where you are a part of it. You don't download it and severe yourself from the development, hiding away with your application on your own. You contribute, you build it and you shape the future Godot holds. No matter what your goals are, there's a place available for you in this completely open source experience.
As for its functionality, the only limitation I have experienced is its struggle to make visually stunning 3D environments at a high level. Unless you're experienced with C++ I would suggest using Godot for 2D and non-graphically intensive applications. There's always room to learn.
In Godot, the main difference is the fact that all objects are "scenes", otherwise known as "nodes"; where everything is able to be called upon and referenced from anywhere in the engine. This makes it entirely fluent in any kind of global operations and instancing is extremely easy.
Updates are always happening. Tutorials are constantly being made. Do yourself a favour, and check Godot out.

Some days I wake up screaming wishing we went Godot.
Doesn't try to re-invent how you traditionally structure a game like Unity 3D forces on you... nobody wants another engine where there is an entirely new vocabulary for the same♥♥♥♥♥♥we've seen a hundred times. Godot's editor acts as more of a "scene/object" editor rather than something that entirely forces the structure of your code.
One of the most amazing concepts of Godot is everything is either a "Scene" or a "Node"... instead of in Unity you have: Scenes, Prefabs, MonoBehaviours, GameObjects, Components, etc. in a very contrived version of C# "faked OOP" based on horribly slow language Reflection.
Reading the wiki tutorial from top to bottom will get you up to speed:
Pros of Godot
* Open source gem. Top notch support on all OS's including first class Linux.
* Very active development, stable.
* Python dialect is a pleasure to work in.
* Collaboration way above Unity: Godots "Scene" format is easy to merge and work with a full team.
* Building from source (only if you need to!) is straightforward and fast... I've tried it: it works well!
* Signal to noise ratio: Unity really suffers from of "95% of my users are the greenest of green".
Cons of Godot vs Unity
* VR support is not good yet.
* Slightly slower physics engine than Unity.
* Not as many 3rd party plugins or "tutorials" as Unity (not a huge problem if you know what you are doing).
* No C# option. But if you love Python + can read C on rare occasions, you're golden.

I do game development since several years. I jumped from one engine to another. With Godot I finally can develop a game on Linux from the start to the end. It's still a young game engine but it has an incredible development pace. I follow its development since last year through GitHub, Facebook and I have to say what others say as a marketing term this game engine really does democratizing game development.
It's open source (MIT License) without strings attached, the main developer(s) listen to the community and welcoms everyone who wants to help in the development, documentation and growth process.
Some technical notes:
When we have to talk about the technical stuff right now the 3d stuff is really just at the start (although If I take a look around what people often produce with other game engines they could easily do the same with Godot) . One Problem as of now are the shadows and performance in large scenes. That said the 2d part, the custom scripting language, the editor (written in Godot and its GUI itself which proofes the power of it) everything fits so well together. If you come like me from a background with other game engines then you might need some days to fully grasp the concept and its underlying power. But then it makes just click and you see a really powerful game engine that has a lot of potential to become a serious competitor even for commercial grade games. The actual renderer is based on OpenGL (ES) 2.0, which as of right now is perfect for targeting Mobile,Webbrowsers (seems that most WebGL implementation are on par with OpenGL ES 2.0) and of course the desktop. There is an upgrade (and rewrite) planned for the 3d related stuff to OpenGL ES 3.0 which will come with Godot 3.0. In my opinion a lot of people underrate the possibilities with the actual renderer. I'm sure we will soon see some people prooving to be a good alternative to other game engines out there. (And let's not forget it's free to use without big restrictions like a lot of other game engines)
Scene nodes concept:
What I love about Godot is the scene node concept it follows. A lot of engines have some kind of scene node or scene graph based concept. But Godot makes it in a really simple and yet smart way. A scene consists of multiple scene nodes (of all sort of types of nodes for 2d,3d,gui, own defined with modules etc.) . A scene can also contain other scenes within its hierarchy. The keyword here is "instanced scenes", which allows to add scenes in other scenes and people can work on different parts of a big scene without having to fear to break the scene hierarchy, it's really great.  Together with Godots use of source version control friendly file formats this makes for me a great choiche for a collaboration. (Be it a collaboration for a  commercial game or a game for a game jam).  I love the scene node concept as it's main goal is that with one look at the hierarchy you already know where everything is and how it is organized (try that with componend based design where you have to first select objects (and find them first) before seeing which components they contain.
GUI:
In some simple words: smart, powerful, easy
The editor has everything you need to layout things. GUIs can be 2d on top of 3d content (like we see in every game) or it can be 2d within the 3d content. You need a menu on a display which is made as a 3d model? No problem. With Godot it is easy to set it up. I saw recently a demo where a guy made a 3d game where there was a tv and  game console in a room and you could start playing a 2d game  on that 3d modeled tv. So a game within a game. I know it's also possible with other game engines, but with Godot it's really easy to set these things up, the editor is just easy to use.
Everything can be animated:
With everything I really mean everything! Every kind of property can be animated (so it will be interpolated if the values are float based, set and unset if they are boolean like etc.),  But also function calls can be part of an animation track. Animating is so easy just some clicks and you have a animation ready to play. I made a simplistic day/night animation for instance in just 2-3 minutes lol
Extendibility:
You can write plugins in GDScript (Godots own scripting language which has some similarity with Python but is not Python as it is a scripting language made for game development).
And you can develop modules in C++. If you had problems integrating C++ libraries in other engines, you might be surprised how easy it is to do it with Godot, thanks to the nice binding functions offered by it.
My opinion so far:
My opinion is that we are seeing the start of what can become the Blender of the game engines out there.
If you need a high performance hardcore graphic solution for a game with large scenes then Godot might be the wrong choice rigth now. But it doesn't hurt to try it. It's easy to learn and you don't need to register any account with it.
I'm happy with it. Btw I used Unity, Unreal and Cryengine among other game engines and while I think that they are far superior in some areas especially in 3d rendering, I also think that they could learn a lot from Godot's simplicity of use and how it organizes some stuff.
As of now you can use it without any doubts for every kind of 2d game, 3d game (if not ultra realistic hardcore graphic is aimed- which will be possible only later on), mobile games  for iOS,Android and even Blackberry. Browsergames (so you can develop 2d and 3d games without needing a plugin).  And it runs on the typical 3 operatin systems for the desktop: Windows, Linux and Mac OS X plus people even made ports for FreeBSD, Haiku (which a lot don't even know it exists) and someone tested it on Raspberry Pi too. This is possible thanks to the permissive license.
I made my choice and I guess I will continue to use it for a long time. I feel that this game engine has potential to become really important. But again as said try it and valuate it if you need more or if it has everything you need right now.
What lacks is still the documentation but it's getting better and better, we'll see

This is in my opinion the best game engine ever made, and it has potential to become even better!
First of all, it is open source, and written in c++, meaning it's easy to extend the engine with your own code and libraries. Secondly, the engine is free and licenced under the permissive MIT licence, meaning you can actually do that and not have to worry about royalties. Thirdly, this engine is made in such a way that it's very easy not to make your project into a messy bowl of spaghetti, so that you can actually finish it.
The only thing this engine lacks is advanced 3D functionality, however, as the graphics API Vulkan has just been released, this is likely going to be worked on in the next update. In other words, if you're just starting out, or you want to make a 2d game, this is the engine for you!

I’ve heard it said that everyone has a little fondness for trains and this game is sure to appeal to that little bit in a big way.
Contrary to Sid’s flagship Civilization series, ease of use seems to be the secret ingredient behind Railroads and its engrossing gameplay. Setting up your first station is pips and in no time at all you’ll have an entire network of trains delivering everything from passengers, coal, food and automobiles to the various towns and industries looking to reward you for your efforts.
The scalable difficulty in Railroads is a real winner too as it allows you to tailor how in-depth an experience you’re after. The easiest difficulty will allow trains to pass through each other without delay whereas a harder mode will demand you route trains carefully, punishing you with delays should you mangle your track layout.
Once the money starts rolling in though, things get surprisingly addictive as you sit back and watch your trains dutifully trundling back and forth between stations and annexes, generating you cash with a very satisfying ka-ching! sound effect in accompaniment.
For less ruthlessly minded players at least, the multiplayer component in Railroads is somewhat muted, with not a whole lot of interaction on offer but the whole aspect of buying out other players on the stock market gives it some real teeth. I remember once hearing it described as a corporate deathmatch more than a train simulation; something that might not be too far away from the truth!
Railroads was well received on release and enjoys a small fan base to this day, but it’s a shame that the move to 64-bit computer systems has hampered this title’s ability to run effectively on newer computers. Just be sure that you check the online guides on how to get this title working properly!
Even so, it’s still a great way to waste a couple of hours on a Sunday afternoon that’s for sure.

Just know of you read any further into this review, you might end up spoiling the game for yourself. This one thing hate about alot of clever indie games that are trying to follow in the steps of games like Undertale. So just know, I might end up mentioning certain things that will spoil parts of the game. So, here we go!
I supported Pony Island when it started off on Steam Greenlight. When checking out the free Game Jam version and playing it all the way through, I saw potential in this game and made sure Steam knew that I wanted that game and I guess many others did too.
Pony Island, like Undertale, meta-games a decent bit but more towards the end than anything else. It is also kind of clever in it's execution of how game tells a different story then what you shown. From what some people have speculated, it shows how some game developers go through hell developing a game. I kind of support this idea but meh this is a review not an episode of Game Theory starring MatPat
The gameplay of this game is sub-par. The Platforming is solid and fun and the hacking minigames aren't too bad durning the first act. Then the second act comes in and then these parts of the game become repetive. They are really nice break though and give the player some interaction side from navigating a desktop or moving a pony across the world map. The first two boss fights aren't that great.
[SPOLIERS STARTING]
The first is just four hacking minigames where it's like Connect Four in a way as you and the demon take turns placcing certain code blocks. The final hack of this fight however, brings in the challenge and makes you plan your moves a bit better. The second boss fight is the platforming sections where you are chasing a demon as it throws down giant rock spikes and creating fissures for you to jump over while you shoot the glowly bits on the demon's face. The third fight however... lets just say it was clever. Really. Damn. Clever. This is where the meta-gaming truly comes as the demon uses your computer to mess with you durning the battle requires you to stay focused. The final fight is just another platforming section where you try to keep as many souls alive as possible while trying to survive the game having it's memory dumped.
The games plot is kind of cryptic, requiring you to really look at things from different angles to understand what is going and having you find the secert demons that lie with in the game. Also, to get the final ending, it requires you to collect 24 tickets that are hidden throughout the game. Some aren't that hard but others are like hidden to point that you need the guy who made the game tell "There is a ticket if you do X task and go to Y location."
The music in this game, as with alot of great indie games, are freaking amazing. The small 8-bits tunes you here as you play the game are very good and they match each situation well and can work well outside if their intended area if you want to play a different game with Pony Island's music.
I like Pony Island and it's great if you are looking for a game to kill some time with. It's not a life changing experience but it's good, different, and clever in what it does. However, I wouldn't say its the next Undertale.

What can I say, Duelyst combines the positioning aspect of a board game wiht the card manegment system used in games like Hearthstone and Magic the Gathering.  You need to mange your mana, your position on the board, which minion is most useful at what time, the attack and health of the enemy's minions, which enemies to prioritize first, how to make the best use of your minion's abilities, wether you should take the mana tile to not give your opponant an advantage next turn while also taking away any chance for you to use it in future moves. That's just everything you can do on the board. You need to choose a faction, then you need to level up that faction to get the other general, then you pick your play style and cards that suit it. You need a file balence of weaker cards that have a low mana cost and stronger (sometimes overpowered) cards that cost more mana, while making sure that everything fits well togeather because you don't know what cards you'll get at any one time. It's a fantastic game for anyone who likes strategy or tactics as Duelyst supplies both along with the most amazing pixel art I've ever seen. (Seriously if you like pixel graphics, you'll want to get it just to download the sprites files alone).

In gameplay, combat and exploration take the forefront. There is a satisfying dash-platforming mechanic involved that also can be used during combat. This skill is among the first you'll realize you'll need to upgrade. There are many elements to seek out to further the story and unlock zones. Exploration and success in combat leads to discovering the "gearbits" you need to upgrade skills and weaponry.

A lot of people will tell you that this game is not very good for beginners and that you should already familiarize yourself with the guitar before playing, but I have to disagree with those people. The only reason I ever started even using the guitar was because of the first Rocksmith. I used Rocksmith to get the very basics down, and then I started to learn my own music. Rocksmith, however, is a unique practice tool in which you can learn and practice music while getting down your technique. Do practice on your own though.
The gameplay itself is fun! If you're a rock rhythm game fan (like Guitar Hero or Rock Band) then this game is basically that but with a real guitar. You can use various tools to help you such as the Dynamic Difficulty setting which allows a song to change and get progressively harder as you play it. You also have arcade minigames that can help you get better at certain skills. As well as other tools to further improve your playing. I really think the gameplay in this game is fantastic.
The Hit Detection could be better, definitely.
When you use the per-song tuner, I'd recommend you (after tuning it once and you have to repluck all the strings) to pluck each string and mute right after. Give it a second. If the string does not immediately go to the next string you've got to retune because if you DON'T, then rocksmith will get certain notes wrong when they are really right. It happens quite often, and it sucks.
Alright, so, the songs that the game currently has aren't 100% amazing. However they have some great music nonetheless (Rise Against - Savior, Iron Maiden - The Trooper, Nirvana - Heart Shaped Box, and so forth). There are also TONS and TONS of DLC songs that you can purchase which provide a great variety of music choices... if you have the coin. A lot of people would hate this method of doing things, but I actually don't mind it. Rock Band is another game that does something similar to this. If you'd rather not spend money, there is something called Rocksmith CDLC (Custom DLC) which is a way to get custom user-created charts (?) if you're into that. However, keep in mind that these are COMMUNITY created, meaning things either may be correct or not.
I personally love this game and everything about it however the hit detection could definitely be improved. I'd say I have to give this game a

Hesitant recommendation. Like many smallish indie games, this is one that I would like a lot more if the serving size was bigger.
I liked the visuals and the soundtrack, but there's not much meat. The areas are small, and the game is very short overall. It took me 2 hours of leisurely playing to get 100%, and there's really not much replay value beyond replaying a chapter to get a missed item or leaving the music on in the background if you didn't buy the soundtrack.
It's difficult to discuss a game's length without also discussing its price. I wouldn't expect or insist that the price be dropped, but I must admit that the price is one of the major reasons why I was expecting more content.
That aside, there's some inconsistent execution within the gameplay. The majority of the game is basic point-and-click. Click on a door to go to another room. Click on a tape to put it in the tape player. Click on a key to get the key. Then there are parts where you're supposed to click and drag, but it's not particularly obvious. There are parts where you're moving along "on rails" and it's difficult to point the camera where you want it to go. There is one specific segment where you gain the ability to move around in first person with WASD. Each area contains ladders or stairs that would theoretically allow a human to get to any necessarily-accessible spot you can see, but there is no human model walking around in your view, so when you get to a particular area in which you have to move a platform up and down in order to "access" a completely unlocked door, it's hard to understand why you can't just go through the door. If my tape player is always with me, why can't I take my tapes with me to the next area? Why can I finish levels with extra unused keys left over?
Again, I LIKE this game, I just want the gameplay to make more sense and I want there to be more content.

Oh where to begin, On release this game was for lack of a better word an abortion. Something so devoid of functionality and entertainment it could only be called a game by the strictest legal definition. However I withheld my judgement and after an eternity away and countless patches here it is.
Pros:
In spite of its many flaws theres still some good to be found in this game. It was incredibly ambitious and attempted to expand upon its predecessor in every possible facet and had they done it correctly it would easily have revolutionized the genre. True to its predecessor you have several unique races that all certainly handle and feel different with plenty of customization in ship design far exceeding what was available in #1 with the addition of battleriders, psychic abilities, modules, new weapon mounts and ammunitions as well as commanders with their own traits and abilities it truly goes above and beyond as far as being able to micromanage your armies and strategy to perfection. The game is also pretty, for its genre, some people have managed to make some pretty sexy screenshots though its certainly not the game (or genres) selling point. Unfortunately this is about all they managed to get right.
Cons:
For starters, at launch it was buggy beyond all reason, to the games credit it seems to be all fixed now, I have not had even a single crash or bug in months, but your experience may (and probably will) differ. Along with all the cool new stuff added they also created a ton of needless, tedious addition, and draped it all in one of the most time consuming interfaces on the planet. Getting anything, even the simplest of things done in this game seems to take a minimum of 3 menus and at least 12 clicks. It's just insane. Combined with the new basing constraint on fleets and the 'mission' system which adds further unnecessary clicks and forces you're fleets to  return home for no real reason after literally every action they take is beyond monotonous. There's also the prototyping which is an abortion, costing tons of money and countless turns to redesign a ship from having a mass driver to a plasma cannon needs triple the time and all my money, even though I already have other ships using the plasma cannon. You can be an all intelligent dolphin thats mastered the art of space travel, can drop a plague on a planet turning all your enemies into zombies, and turn your opponents head into a blood pumpkin with your mind, but you're too friggin dumb to understand modular construction techniques. Lastly the game is just terribly optimized requiring a far more powerful machine than it should to run properly and even then at some point your still going to suffer massive slowdowns at countless load screens and menu transitions.
Overall this game had tremendous potential but it just fails terribly at living up to its own ambition. It's like wiping with sandpaper. Sure it might get the job done, but it's slow, gritty, and just downright painful at times. I loved the first one, and I can still find a bit to like in this one, just not enough to recommend it to anybody. Anyone who is wanting to experience the Sword of the Stars, I highly suggest you look at the first game instead.

Godot Engine is a true gem for those "in the know".
Being Open-Source, as an advanced user it allows you maximum flexibility and both Indie and Studio devs can benefit form it's design architecture based on nodes and scenes to create complex game flow. It certainly brings a unique perspective into the game development toolbox.
It's main scripting language is called GDScript which is very similar to Python, but has it's own Keywords to ease setting up several tasks through minimal code. If you are a C++ / LUA / Whatever language user, you can extend Godot with your advanced programming knowledge as well, but you would have to compile from source for that to happen.
However "true" beginner's, beware, if you don't have at least an intermediate foundation in computer programming you will have to study computer programming fundamentals, design patterns and object oriented programming to get the most of it, because this is NOT a DRAG & DROP / ASSET STORE program.  This is a professional tool for creating powerful Indie & A(AA) games alike, not a multiplayer creator sandbox with limited scope.
Making games is hard work, but when tamed, Godot can be an incredible helper or standalone tool for developing your own unique games.
p.s. Godot has been used to make commercial games.
p.s.2. Godot is not Unreal Engine 4, Unity, Construct2, or Roblox. Please stop thinking about how it doesn't compare.
