Amazing game engine with a huge set of tools. Its strength lies in the 2D engine. Once you are familiar with it, prototyping a 2D games is quick and easy.
The 3D editor has not received much love recently, and the renderer is stuck with GLES2, but it's planned to implement GLES3 for 3.0 (hopefully late 2016 or earlier 2017). Of course, this doesn't prevent anyone from creating great looking 3D games already.
The engine comes with a built-in script editor and debugger. The animation system is another of its strengths, allowing to animate almost everything.
In Godot you can instance scenes into scenes (this is the main difference over engines that use prefabs). This is a powerful tool for organizing your porjects.
The main fear you can find is the custom scripting language. GDScript is similar to Python, and new users tend to dislike learning a new language. But once you get used to it, you will understand the decision over other existing languages. GDScript and its debugger are really well integrated with the engine, making our life easier. If some parts of your code need better performance, you can write them as modules in C++.
The community is huge and very helpful. You can ask questions on the Q&A site, reddit, the facebook group, or the IRC channel. There are many community made plugins, modules and game examples (checkout
on GitHub), and hopefully we can get a asset sharing site soon.
Oh! Did I mention the engine is completely free and open source?

But it isn’t long until Hans, a big wig, millionaire and founder of the world’s hottest TV show, Rundead, kidnaps the duo. Ben is held captive, and if Ed wants to reunite with his friend and defeat Hans, he must defy death in the afterlife.
Since Ben and Ed is a plat former, you can expect a serious amount of jumping, running, dodging, throwing, crawling, limping, bleeding, and decapitation. Since you play as a zombie, you can take quite a beating before kicking the bucket. Limbs will be lost, but not your spirit, and this provides players with an extremely entertaining gameplay mechanic. If your legs are snipped clean by an oversized scissor blade, there’s no need to panic! You can adapt by waddling about with your arms and hands. Same goes for the loss of any body part. Instant death is almost always common place in these sorts of games, but Ben and Ed throws in these comical and engaging methods of giving players a second chance. Crawling to the nearest checkpoint with nothing but your head and torso in contact is nerve-racking, to say the least.
Not only that, but there’s a handful of boss fights to keep the action flowing. Speaking of action, it never relents. Each level is more daring and intense than the last, which is no small achievement. You will die… you will die many times, and many times more. But check points are placed at reasonable distances and I never felt cheated or at a disadvantage. Ben and Ed is not an easy game, but it is fair. When you ♥♥♥♥ up, YOU ♥♥♥♥ed up. There’s no one to blame but yourself for an embarrassing demise, and beating that level that had you pinned for over an hour… there’s no better feeling in the world. The motivation to save your best friend and defeat the bad guy in such a unique and original way enhances Ben and Ed’s overall entertainment value, and it really shines.
But gameplay and premise aren’t the only things done right. Graphics are top notch. I felt like I was trapped in some murderous child’s play box. The décor is spine chilling and ripe with pleasantly evil things to admire. Add in an awesome soundtrack and some silky smooth animations, and you’ve got yourself a pretty damn good video game.
This is the first positive review I’ve given on Steam without any negative comments involved. I tried to think of some criticism, I really did… but I can’t. Ben and Ed really is perfect in every sense of the word. With over 20 levels, bonus content, high scores and challenge stages, you really can’t go wrong with this title. It is plat forming done right. It is video games done right. End of story.

It is not a game, and that is one of the two negatives of this. More on that later.
First of all, I am using the cable from the original Rocksmith game. If you are confused, it is actually an audio to usb cable with a digitizer in the middle. Quite a good quality piece of equipment that you may want to have as a guitar player even if you dont play this game. So, if you need that, buying a physical copy is probably better idea than buying on steam.
So, if it is a learning tool why I am unhappy about it not being a game?
There is a concept called Gamification: Turning trivial or mundane tasks to a system of playing which with little positive feedback keeps you at it and make you improve the skill at the real thing / get a task done / etc. That was what original Rocksmith did amazingly well. I have been playing guitar for many years but playing that game was the only time I could have several hour sessions and only stop due to tiredness rather than boredom! The joy of "progress" that Rocksmith did bring very well, is quite lost at 2014 and 2014 remastered. That is the first negative of this game. It was "improve yourself at these songs and go to this concert and you may get cheered for an encore if you do well for bonus points". Now it is "This is your percentage number at this song, make it that percentage number and compete with other users online to get the 10,000th position in the rankings if you do amazingly well!" (yes I am exaggerating). Somehow it doesn't motivate as much.
Negative 2 is the company's money making model. Original Rocksmith came with a very well picked set of songs of different difficulty levels to truly improve your playing. This one, either deliberately didn't do that or failed at it miserably. This game is about paying more to get the DLC songs. There were so many songs I did not know of in the original which are now in my permanent playlist for my own listening enjoyment. From 2014's repertoire some songs, big names, were already in my playlist but it didn't introduce a lot more. They are there to make you buy the game. Not to teach you playing.
Now, a company needs to make money somehow and don't get me wrong, this is an amazing product, so, I'd give this second negative a pass. But I am still so disappointed how the first negative silently passed below almost everybody's radar.
So why am I not playing the first still? Most DLCs are not compatible with that one anymore.
How about positives? Yeah, well, elephant in the room: Are you gonna give yourself a wrist injury at a shooting game or show of your friends your skill at a plastic guitar with colorful bottons or enjoy fret tapping a real guitar? If you are offended by that comment, this game is not for you. Because despite making the learning easier and more enjoyable, you still need to build a skill which is still a painful and slow process, just less.
Other positives? The learning is more customizable than original Rocksmith. I am still amazed that it is not done to perfection but it is fairly good. Also a lot of frustrations of navigating the first game's menus are removed (but a few are introduced unfortunately).
Is it a good game? Hell no. Is it doing its job? Well, yes but could do it a lot better. Would I recommend it? If you are serious about learning, yes.

I like this game as it changes a basic rule of card games, the fact that there is no table and in it's place is a grid battle field where the players fight just as much as the minions.

Pretty fun.
PROS: The unique grid based movement genuinely makes each match a new experience. The huge skill gap makes each win feel that much more rewarding. Skill is much more observable and winning isnt hugely skewed by RNG.
CONS: There are alot of cards. Going in fresh, it may take a while to try out and build decks. Having disposable income definitely helps. However, this is a common obstacle in most popular card games. If you feel like the entry cost into building decks you enjoy playing is not worth your time or money, then simply do not invest your time and money.
The pixel art is an acquired taste. The music loop is ... decent
Cosmetics and loot keys/crates are an obvious money grab. Dont bother if you do not want to, but should not detract you from the awesome gameplay.
In terms of gameplay, this game is one of the most strategic and skill intensive card games I have ever played. (I have played Pokemon, YuGiOh, MTG, and Hearthstone) However, having reached S-rank (equivalent to Legend Rank in Hearthstone) the major downfall of this game is how uninteractive the board state, or even the oppenent's hand can be. One ranged, blast, or provoke minion can cost you an entire game if you do not have an immediate answer for them. Even worse, some classes have access to fairly gimmicky or hard to play around burst or "swingy" board clears from their hand. You will lose a few games to a divine bond Ironcliffe guardian or soulshatter pact + soul grimwar on turn 5. You will lose to a Spiral Technique from a Song'hai player after they backstabbed you the whole game. You WILL have your minions completely decimated by holy immolations and you WILL be impaled by makantor beasts.
Its still fun though.

Small Radios Big Televisions is a very short puzzle adventure game where you find cassette tapes containing worlds to explore.
I wanted to play this game in hopes of enjoying some good puzzles and exploration. You need to find cassette tapes, and each of these tapes has a different world on it. You also distort the tapes to affect the areas on them in order to find the items you need to progress.The gameplay is mostly solving puzzles to progress, with only a small amount of exploration.
I feel a bit misled by the game description and I had expected more in the way of exploration. When I heard the description say “boundless virtual worlds” I wanted more than just being stuck moving on rails, and panning the camera around to click on the same item every single time. I think they could have made the worlds better if they had some puzzles inside the tapes, had some sort of collectibles that give more insight into the story, or just made them larger areas to explore.
I like the ideas behind the game, but I am not at all impressed by the execution of it. The puzzles were the highlight of the game, and I still liked them, even though they weren’t that challenging. However, the frustrating camera angles, the lack of character movement while ‘exploring’ the areas, short playtime, and unsatisfying exploration took its toll. Small Radios Big Televisions just fell short for me. It just feels like wasted potential, and I think they could have done a lot more with it.

A very interesting engine, also one of the few that run natively on Linux for both exporting and editing.
It can be a bit unusual to get started with, but once you figure it out, it allows for very rapid progress. The engine works with "scenes", which are collections of "nodes". Such nodes are basic game entities like sprites, GUI controls or physics bodies, or more complex ones like audio output, cameras and such.
Every node can be given its own scripting in the engine's native language, known as gdscript. Gdscript itself is very easy to learn, and even easier if you are familiar with the python language. While it's a bit of a bummer to not be able to use, for example, Lua, the language barely takes an evening to learn if you can already code, and shouldn't take much longer if you don't. The editor contains a very competent code editor with all the bells and whistles, from bracket highlighting to autocompletion, which helps a lot.
Once your scene is set up, you can import it into other scenes, creating more complex scenes that you can alter dynamically with relative ease. For example, you can create a scene containing the HUD for your game, then import it into your main game scene, or custom widgets that you can include in said HUD. All very hassle-free.
The node system is also very good to write quick interfaces for debugging/development tools, saving huge amounts of time and allowing to provide suchs tools as modding tools once the game is shipped.
Once your game is complete, it's easy to export it to various systems, including the usual 3 (Win/Mac/Lin), Android and  HTML5 for in-browser games. It even allows exporting to...blackberry, for some reason.
The process is quick and simple, only requiring a few clicks, and includes various options allowing from open-sourced games to single-binary distributions, or even encrypted data.
Now, I have been using the engine for a while, and it's really solid for 2D games. And while it might not be as powerful as others for 3D games, it's competent enough if you use the features creatively. The engine is being developed at a rapid pace, and it gains features and improvements at a good rate, so if you find it lacking in some aspects, it might have just what you need for the next version.
Other interesting features include a very powerful animation system that allows keying almost every single element in your scene, allowing for easy cutscenes, skeleton-based animations and other cool visual effects. It also allows importing most common data formats used in development, international fonts, built-in localization features and other goodies, allowing for very easy prototyping or fully featured games. It also has a live editing feature allowing to change elements of your game in real time from the editor while the game is running, which can accelerate debugging and testing stuff like enemy logic in the project. A huge time saver.
The entire engine's source and issue tracker are hosted over at GitHub, allowing to easily keep track with progress, report bugs or collaborate with the project, which helps refining it further. The editor is also surprisingly stable, and I haven't encountered a single crash or data loss in months of use, even using bleeding-edge daily builds. It's also very easy to build in all systems, if you prefer to keep up with every single commit to the codebase or modify it to implement advanced features or alter core behaviors directly.
As the main flaw, while it has a number of step-by-step tutorials, some elements aren't completely covered by the available documentation, but the tutorials should be able to cover most basics, and the in-editor help covers almost all the classes and nodes without having to keep switching to a browser window for reference. There are a number of included demos which also can help giving you hints on how to proceed. Documentation is being worked on actively, so this flaw might be addressed sooner than later.

This is my first and only game engine, but my experience has been a great one!
I hadn't worked on a game for a few years, so I started looking around at engines. I was considering Unity, and reached out to them to see if they would ever release a Linux editor. They replied to my email telling me to just run Windows and export my games to Linux. No, thanks! So, I put my plans on the backburner...
...but not for long! A few days after my disappointing email exchange with Unity, news of plans to open-source Godot started making the rounds. I excitedly fired off an email to Juan Linietsky, who had offered to send out a pre-release to people wishing to try it and point out any immediate issues they found. Within a day, I was up and experimenting with an already-impressive, free, soon-to-be-open, game creation tool.
Previous to using Godot, I would make my game projects from scratch in C/C++ with SDL libraries. Godot was much different. It was kinda love at first tinker.
I admit that I was initially hesitant to invest much time into Godot because of the custom script language, GDScript. It's very similar to Python (which I had never used). However, after diving in, I found it to be very clear, clean, and fast. It's even easier since the syntax hinting and autocompletion were introduced. I see a lot of complaints around the web about how it should use C# or Lua or whatever, but I don't see the need. That being said, the engine is completely free and open-source (MIT license), so feel free to whip one up and contribute it so everyone else can use it, too. Or just keep complaining. Your call.
Speaking of contributing, the codebase is quite nice, even for people with modest C++ skills like myself. I was able to make a few meaningful contributions over the years, and hope to do more if/when I can. But this new release is a huge leap forward compared to a year ago. I think any of my minor complaints have been alleviated!
For 2D games, this engine is fantastic. 3D is limited to GLES2 right now, but a GLES3/3.1 rendering backend is planned for the 3.0 release, so that will bring over many capabilities that even the most demanding 3D developer will require. That being said, the GLES2 backend that already exists is capable of putting out some nice-looking pixels.
You can export your games to a variety of platforms with just a few clicks, and I've had no issues with that process so far (though i've no Apple devices to actually do any testing of those versions).
There are a lot of great things about Godot, and it's hard to list them all here (pointless, too, since it's going to continue evolving closer and closer towards perfection). It's free though, so you can jump in and try it out yourself.

I loved the first one.  It was incredible, and every expansion just became more in-depth. Backstory, artwork, tech trees... load of fun, gorgeous, and engrossing.  It made me want to support this company in any way I could; even the spin-off The Pit is fun and cute while being challenging and demanding.
This...  I just can't get into it.  I tried, I really did. I even came in after the bugs were fixed and enhanced was out, because the world-building and story here is just so engaging.  But... the magic feels like it was gone in the gameplay.
Everything is more complicated, micromanaging lots and lots of small space stations is now a core gameplay element. And now, half the tactics that were interesting in the old game are impossible (like parking Deep Scan picket ships in deep space to watch for approaching fleets). You can't send lone scouts anymore, you have to create a scouting mission first, make a fleet, maybe assign an admiral, and put a half dozen ships together. Some of those ideas (like automating missions and adding admirals) would have been INCREDIBLY interesting, and a great addition to another expansion of the first game (like how trade was expanded in aMoC), but now you're shoehorned into it, and the tense early game with a few lonely destroyers playing cat & mouse in uncharted space with unknown enemies is gone. It feels like a completely different company's product.

Not going to lie, this game can be extremely fun to play. Yet I won't recommend this game because of its absurd pay-wall tactics. I get it, it is a free to play game, and I understand the system. I am perfectly fine with having a system where someone with a heavy wallet can shell out a few bucks (or a bunch) to buy cards/cosmetics/ect. Yet the way this game makes you think you are going to get a "reward" and then hide it behind a pay-wall is very deceptive.
I just completed the special PVE boss event, which proclaims from the main menu that you get a unique reward upon completion. Spent at least an hour customizing my deck until I could defeat it. What reward do I get? A boss crate that can't even be opened unless I shell out an extra $4.99 for a boss crate key. This only adds to my collection of "rare" crates that I can't open because the only keys a free-to-play account can get are common crate keys (afaik).
Basically, the "rewards" the game gives to their dedicated FTP playerbase can't even be opened without spending money. Just another fun game ruined by a bad business model.

If you're looking for a fun and interactive city building and managing game, you've come to the right place! With many great maps to choose from right from the start, the game throws you into a challenging yet rewarding experience where you're expected to ♥♥♥♥ up again and again since learning from your mistakes teaches you far more than any tutorial could. Micromanagement is definitely on the highest priority as even the smallest mismanaged intersection can cause your entire city to be congested but don't let that scare you as the game is ever only as complicated and complex as you make it. If you want to build simple and easilly managed cities with minor issues that's definitely possible but the more challenge you want, the more you can create by expanding and growing your city.
And speaking of growing your city, Cities: Skylines is literally everything Sim City should have been. You're not restricted to a tiny plop of land but rather offered a massive playground to go wild on at your hearts content.
Best of all is, if there's something you feel is missing or you need an alternative to the 'same old' structures, the modding community is MASSIVE and you can find variations, improvements and even alteration mods for anything you can imagine.
This game can only be recommended as, perhaps, the best city builder game to date.

Ok well let's get this out of the way, Resident Evil 6 isnt a horror game, it's almost pure action. It's not like 1-3 in any sense but the characters,
Well that's done. Damn was this a fun action game. The game is broke up into 4 campaigns so I'll just list them below
Leon's:
The best of the 4. Has actual horror elements and traditional RE levels (an underground cave and lab, infected city). Feels like a modern day RE4, and we all know that was the best resident evil so that's great- 9/10
Chris:
If Leon's was an updated RE4, this is an updated RE5 (with a better AI) mixed with gears of war. Most of this campaign takes place in China, which has fun scenery and was really brought to life. The Bosses in Chris's campagin are also the best in the game. Story gets dumb, but dumb in the classic RE way, If the cover system wasn't utter trash, this would be on par with Leon's. But because of that 8/10
Jakes:
Ugh, everything that is wrong with the 2nd trilogy of Resident Evil games, in one 5 chapter campaign. God was this painful. Jake kung-fu's his way out of problems. Says more one liners that an 80's action flick, and is generally a boring character. Luckily his partner sometimes says things that add to the overall lore of the resident evil series. So that was nice. His boss, follows him around in the different chapters (similar to Nemesis) . It doesn't work, but it's not bad. So for this campaign, that makes it amazing. 3/10
Ada Wong:
A mix of Stealth and Chris. She fills in the gaps and explains what was happening behind the scenes of all the other campaigns. Fun to play, but pretty average. 7/10
So overall the average score of the game is: 6.75/10. Thanks Jake for ♥♥♥♥ing this up

God, where do I start? There's so much to choose from in this field that it's too difficult to pick just one without picking another simulatenously.
But I guess I'll start simple. After all, that's how the field started as well.
The game is amazing. There's a level of love made in this that you don't see often. It shows the difference between games made for money and games made for art/with love. It's like a comparing of when your neighbor just bakes cookies cuz' you ask for it and when your grandma bakes you cookies with love because she loves you.
First I'm going to explain what the game is. The game is essentially a heavily Dark Souls-based adventure game. Throughout the game you can upgrade your character by finding things along your travels. And speaking of travels, you'll probably wanna go somewhere first. The game is divided into the 4 cardinal directions. You can go either north, east, west, or south, however the south wing is blocked of until the north, east, and west wings are completed. Completing the wings requires that you beat the boss in that wing, raising a pillar on the center of the map indicating that the wing has been completed. When all bosses are beaten and all 4 pillars are raised, you can finally face off against your ultimate enemy.
Now that I've explained that, I'll explain the details.
The art design is what you'd see first in this game, given that it stands out with its bright colours and shininess unlike most other games before it. The design appears to take inspirations from that "a e s t h e t i c" 80s feel coupled with a nice chocolate coating of its own magic. The game is absolutely breathtakingly beautiful. Each wing of the world has its own aesthetic and each aesthetic is just marvelous. It kept me intrigued to move onto the next wing when I completed the one I was on.
The game design is very heavily based on Dark Souls. You get a gun, a sword, a quick dodge move, some potions, and a stamina bar. The stamina bar isn't important early game but later game if you upgrade your weaponry and whatnot it becomes very important. The gun and sword are your most useful tools for fighting off the evil that plagues the world. Potions are incredibly important if you're just starting. Potions can be found by finding secret areas or when they're given to you, which, keep in mind, isn't very common at all. Your "quick dodge move" (aka a dash) is a quick move that gets you out of the way of enemies so that you don't die.
All of these weapons and abilities can eventually be upgraded.
I've said before that the world is divided up into quadrants, corresponding to their cardinal direction. Each area has their own aesthetic and boss and enemies. And all throughout the game you can find a TON of secrets. And I mean an absolute TON. Exploration is a VERY key component of this game and it is INCREDIBLY rewarded. With exploration you can find potions, the currency of the game which can get you upgrades on your stuff, a module (which I'll explain what that is later), or, and this is incredibly rare, a new costume, or a new gun.
The music design in this game is amazing. It perfectly compliments both the aesthetic of the game in its entirety and the situation where it's used. It's very 80s/synthwavey, occasionally delving into being beautiful piano pieces. This perfectly matches with what the art design is based on and what the art designer added into the art design to make it special. It's all entirely beatiful and during writing this I am currently listening to the soundtrack.
Hyper Light Dirfter attempts to go for a story design that is not commonly used. It tries to tell a story without the usage of any words, much like Sonic 3 & Knuckles. I won't spoil anything but I can say that the story, if you know how and where to do your research, is incredibly deep and rich. The story uses elements with the boss names and the names of the cards to create a meaning that I've never seen before.
The main plot point is that you are a traveler in search for a cure for a disease. The disease makes you cough every now and then, and very occasionally makes you see "your greatest enemy" before you, killing you mercilessly in your dreams.
I played the game on Normal mode and I can say that this has been a very difficult experience. It's certainly a climb to find the skill to be able to take on the bosses and enemies. Occasionally I would find something to be kind of unfair but most of the time the difficulty is entirely fair. Besting the enemies and bosses are all very rewarding. Bosses will give you guns at the end of their fights that you can use and upgrade just like any other. Difficult enemy areas will end in you marking your dominance by stabbing a sword into the ground and then you can go pick up some potions nearby to heal you from that intense area.
Dying won't result in a lot of significant loss, just you being sent back to the last point where the game saved and any of the items that you picked up during that time will get lost unless you reached a point where the game saved (although picking up these items again isn't difficult). It's very easy to die and jump right back in. The respawn animation can be sped up by holding down the dash button to jump right back into the game.
If you haven't bought this game already then you're missing out on a lot. It's a great experience that drove me to absolutely loving the game in its entirety. Whereas previously my former favourite game of this type was Furi, Hyper Light Drifter easily bumps that game down to being my second favourite game.
Playing this game was an absolute blast and I couldn't be more excited to get angry at the game on the more difficult modes. When a game gets you pumped about being enraged, then you know it's doing things right.
Throughout the world there are many secrets to find. Finding secrets, like I've said, can result in you finding very many things. One of such very many things are guns. Guns, guns, guns. The most important meal of this game, lemme tell ya. Finding them all is absolutely reccomended, though not obligated. If you find a loadout with your guns that suits you, then good! But don't be afraid to mix it up a little.
Now onto the juicier bits; throughout the world in each quadrant, there are modules. I've mentioned these earlier, you may remember. Modules seemingly all come in fours for each of the cardinal direction areas. Although there are actually 8. There are 4 main ones, and then another 4 hidden ones to find on your own. I've yet to find these, personally.
Throughout the game, you can find variations for your costumes. There are 8 variations, and each one, minus 1 in particular, are very difficult to obtain.
Collecting everything gets you the Hoarder achievement.

I won't go over the plus points to this game; many others have done so. I'll give you reasons NOT to play it just in case it isn't up your street.
Firstly there is almost no text. Whilst this makes for a tranquil experience and little waiting around for pointless dialog, there are moments when it feels the developer has gone too far to stick to this principle. A smattering of text here and there would not have diminished the game yet made some parts of it a lot less frustrating.
As it is, knowing what to do is half the puzzle in this game. Be prepared to be confused, to wonder aimlessly, to die quite a bit (even though you get infinite lives in the game). It took me some time to work out how to upgrade my gear, as well as what the in game currency was.
Some of the maps are quite mazy, so just finding that route you need can be quite a big part of the challenge.
If those don't sound fun for you then maybe this won't be the game for you. Otherwise, with all its other amazing plus points it definitely is a worthwhile game to own and play.

Release Date: June 30th, 2012
Developers: Mike Bithell, Curve Digital, Bossa Studios
Publishers: Mike Bithell, Curve Digital, Bossa Studios
Platforms: Playstation Network, Xbox Live, PC, Andriod & iOS
Genre: Puzzle & Platform video game
Players: Single
Rated: 10/10
Synopsis:
Thomas Was Alone, like many other puzzle games, is actually quite enjoyable. Unless of course, you are stuck trying to figure out how to solve the puzzle. The game is quite simple though; you are a shape, or a multitude of shapes, and your end goal is to get all of the shapes into the corresponding outlined box that best fits to the shape(s) you aere
Thomas Was Alone takes place within a computer mainframe, where some unspecified "Event" has caused several artificial intelligence routines to run out of control and gain personalities. Each entity is represented by a simple colored shape; the game's eponymous character is a simple red rectangle. Each shape has unique abilities; while all shapes can move left or right across platforms and perform jumps, the height of these jumps may be limited by the shape, or may have other abilities such as being able to float on water. When the player has access to two or more of these shapes, they can freely switch between them, controlling one shape at a time.
Though the shapes themselves cannot be heard, the narrator describes the personalities and thoughts of each shape as the game progresses.
Story:
Say hello to your new tour guide, Thomas-AT-23-6-12. Don't worry, you can call him Thomas for short. As you can tell by the title, Thomas was alone. Or at least he thought it was! Thomas is the main "character" in Thomas Was Alone, and he is a small red rectangle. His job? To save the universe of course. While Thomas is observing the new world he has been put into, he eventually meets a friend, and more. See, each of these "characters" each have a unique ability, and so does Thomas. Thomas can jump, at a relatively high height. But, some of his friends might be able to jump higher, lower, fly or swim?! Thomas must encounter each character and they must work together in order to get to the end of the level, or puzzle. Each character has something to bring to the table as far as an "ability" so just because one character might not be able to jump at all, doesn't mean he is useless!
Thomas, is now no longer alone. He is joined by his gang of friends and together they can conquer anything together. But, you have to be able to solve the puzzle first to be able to beat it! Each character is able to be controlled by the player at anytime to help Thomas, and his gang get to the end of each level.
Click to View Content
Gameplay:
While Thomas Was Alone is rather quite a normal, average puzzle platformer, it does have a story that you will go through and learn. Each character has it's own personality, and you will learn to play around with their personality and their special traits. As said above, each player has a unique special ability that will ultimately help Thomas, and his friends get to where they need to be. While Thomas and his gang roam through the lands of the computer mainframe you will have to fight your way through puzzles, and while also trying to escape and protect each other from the mysterious, "pixel cloud" that seems to lurk in the distance as the gang acquires their new friend, Laura.
Graphics:
Thomas Was Alone is quite a simple looking game, you are a red rectangle, unless you are one of Thomas' friends, and the background is a fairly plain gray background, but. The sounds and also the narrator that voices over the game makes the game seem like such a better looking game than the simple game that is actually is. Even after playing it and beating the game completely, I would continue to play if. The game is just very appealing to the eye.
Controls:
The controls for Thomas Was Alone are extremely simple. You control each character using the arrow keys on the keyboard and simply switch between players using any button, that you can bind to your keyboard, it doesn't get much simpler than that. However, being able to learn how to control each character and use his or her powers to further progress through your journey of the computer's mainframes is a much more difficult task.

Addictive fun, if frustrating. Although I might just be really rubbish at it.
As with many similar games, the first few levels are a bit of a grind as you struggle/wait to unlock decent cards, but once you do it starts to get a lot more exciting; suddenly, Generals (who you need to keep alive - kill the opponent's General to win) with certain powers make a lot more sense when combined with certain cards/minions.
New card sets have brought expected balance issues, so your enjoyment may rest on how much you like seeing certain cards offering bonkers advantages that can be practically impossible to counter if you're 'playing with the wrong deck'. BUT...I don't mind this so much. There's a sense that DUELYST is on the cusp of being as mental as HEARTHSTONE - which can lead to some truly unexpected matches, if you like the idea of that.
However, DUELYST works best when it stays within its own identity (the different factions definitely have their own respective flavours). I would like to see more tactical tweaks made to the actual board - maybe alternate which squares can't be used, something like that. This should be DUELYST'S main selling point, rather than tumbling down the hole of 'buy better cards to win', which is a definite vibe I get from most matches.
On this point, I don't actually believe the game is 'pay to win' but it - again - feels on the cusp of this. 'Crates' are offered as rewards, which you need to open with Keys. Common Crate Keys are generally awarded after completing so many daily quests, but other Keys cost around $9.99 for not a lot of product. By comparison, Boss Crates also cost $4.99 to open and contain a ton of cool stuff, so there's a glaring disparity there.
And finally: BOSSES. I really like that DUELYST offers occasional boss battles, although these aren't without their issues ie. I've had a boss on the ropes multiple times only for them to magically draw a winning card that, for instance, deals direct damage to my General. Maybe I'm just really unlucky, but it's happened enough times that it feels like shenanigans.
So that's that. DUELYST certainly has its issues, but I still really enjoy it. I've only spent $5 on it to open a Boss Crate, and generally do okay with earning in-game gold to buy new cards. The community/other players seem really nice and I really, really like that you can 'tip' your opponent some of your gold if you win, which is a lovely way of promoting sportsmanship. Bad luck old chum, here's some pennies for your effort.

TL;DR: This is a fun, cheesy co-op shooter, not a horror game. Make sure to play on No Hope with a co-op partner.
Mandatory disclaimer: This is not Resident Evil 1, 2 nor 3. I'm OK with that, since I dont like broken controls, broken camera & broken puzzles. The love the original 3 get is 90% because of nostalgia, the remaining 10% is the love for the cheese those games had.
I've played through this entire game on No Hope difficulty with a co-op partner, that is the only correct way to play this game, as it's far too easy otherwise & the AI partner is brain-dead. Just remember to spam dodge buttons after cutscenes, lest you get insta-gibbed.
RE6/BH6 is fun, over the top action with a fair bit of cheese & interesting scenarios, but it's far from a horror game. This game is about the story, the characters & the action, which I feel it mostly delivers on, although you need to finish all 4 campaigns to get the full picture.
Pros: (assumes you're playing on No Hope, the only difficulty option)
+ Ammo presevation is important, if you miss more than 1 shot per 5 enemies you'll run out of ammo, as you should.
+ A single regular enemy is a genuine threat if not taken seriously.
+ You die in 1-3 hits.
+ You want to stealth & avoid battles whenever available. (not because combat is bad, but because it's costly)
+ It contains cheese & interesting scenarios.
+ Decent weapon variety.
+ Good enemy variety.
+ Severely punishes incompitent behaviour.
+ Approximately 30 hours of content split in 4 campaigns.
Cons: (also assumes you're playing on No Hope, the only difficulty option)
- You must hold the dodge keys to dodge, they're not instant, causing a delay & lowering the skill-cieling.
- Enemies can shoot through eachother in order to hit you, so sometimes enemies you can't even see shoot you.
- It contains quick time events.
- Sometimes difficult to get co-op to run properly.
- No item trading with co-op partner.
- Getting insta-gibbed/grappled to death right after cutscenes.
- You stagger like crazy every single time you're hit or you triggered a trigger.
- Contains bad driving segments.
- The worst aiming-style is on by default, you must change to laser-only yourself.
- Some shared events from different campaigns (due to characters bumping into eachother).
Others:
+/- Easy but fun bosses.
+/- Graphics & audio are acceptable.
+/- There are 2 states between healthy & dead, one making you slower & melee useless & another one where you crawl.
+/- Pointless passive skills system. (It's not in effect in No Hope, the only difficulty option.)
+/- There are invisible (for you) duplicates of all items in the game, so both co-op partners get everything.
+/- When in-game most menus are in the style of a phone, a poorly designed phone. It's immersive, but bad.

If you like to play games where you don't actually play the game, the sorts of games where you spectate more than you move. If you like to mash keys in quick succession to simulate playing a game, rather than actually playing a game. If you like to play games where you know you would be better off doing something else, but then you think nah... I will spectate my way through a little bit more of this game because uneccessary and intrusive immersion breaking cut scenes, copious amounts of QTE's and the game putting you on autopilot when it feels like it gets me hard.. then this game is probably for you.
As for me, it represents everything that is wrong with the series as it gets older. I love immersion and having a game break immersion by popping a set of instructions on how to move away from an enemy by rapidly pressing key sequences ruins the immersion. To be in control one minute only to have the game unecessarily yank control away from you, while it points out something you would have discovered on your own, had the game given you a chance to explore on your own, makes this more of a movie than a game.
Honestly I will keep playing the first four games over and over as I enjoy them immensely, however this series is dead to me beyond that!

Video games, being a medium relying on interaction; are probably the most effective medium for fourth wall breaking scenarios. Going way back from Metal Gear Solid to Batman: Arkham Asylum and currently climaxing with Undertale, you can see how much meta-gaming has become a thing.
I suppose it's accurate to say Pony Island is the aftershock of the earthquake that was Undertale, although unlike Undertale; its cutesy facade hardly lasts that long (just read page's description). On the subject of comparing Pony Island and Undertale (which I actually find unfair to both games), Pony Island really doesn't have any truly interesting characters like Undertale; instead what will fascinate you is the Pony Island inside of Pony Island and the tale of audience expectation versus the developer's limit.
It's hard to narrow down the appropriate genre for Pony Island. Best I could say is that Pony Island is a puzzle game (which is where Pony Island is at its best) and sometimes a runner.
All in all, Pony Island is a game that contributes to fourth wall breaks; but will probably be forgotten... or not.

The difficulty comes from the fact that you don't have extra lives, so if you die then you start the level with the health points you had when you arrived with from the previous level.
So if you start a new level with only 1 HP then don't save when asked upon death unless you know you can replenish your health on the current level.

This game has significant issues:
* There is an over reliance on instant death traps. While you have 10 health, and can recover health during the game, falling into pits and such will just kill you.
* Instead of a life or continue system, it has a save/load system. Every time you die, the game asks you if you want to save your game, then if you want to load your game, which gets annoying if you are constantly dying to a difficult section. It's even worse if you die in the first level of an episode, as it just dumps you into the high-score screen. (Asking you to save after dying makes sense in this game, as it will save whatever your state was at the start of the level.)
* I don't think the 10 health system works very well. You keep your current health from level to level, which, when combined with all the gotcha moments, means the smart way to play is to play through each level to find all those moments before loading your game and playing it for real.
* There are a lot of gotcha moments. For example, enemies are placed so that they hurt you immediately after landing a jump unless you know where they are. There are also a few levels that hurt or kill you almost instantly after entering a level unless you do some fancy moves.
* Even with all this, the game only takes 1.7 hours to beat, apparently.

Story: The story of this game was very minimal. A lot of it is told through the environment, and pictures produced by the non-player characters. The developer used a similar style of storytelling that is prevalent in the Souls series. The style leaves the player to use his or her imagination based on the visual feedback from the game to determine the story.
Gameplay: Controlling the player character in this game is fun. The protagonist moves around in swift motions using dash abilities. In terms of combat, it is mostly using guns and a sword. The game provides options to upgrade multiple aspects of the protagonist such as the gun, sword, armor, health, and more. It also has the option to do different moves such as holding the attack button while dashing to attack the enemies while you dash through them. I enjoy what I experienced. If there was one thing that I would change. It would be the aiming. It would have been better to have a lock-on option of some sort instead of freestyle. Oh, I should also mention that this game is challenging. The boss fights are great, and you have to pay attention. If you don't, you die. So... I recommend having an open mindset while you progress in this game.
Graphics: The art style is what attracts most people to this game I imagine. It is quite good, and it's simplistic, but it looks different from the usual games that one finds in the same genre. It is designed to tell the story of the game, and it does a good job at making the player wonder about what events lead to those changes in the environment. To put it simply, it's really good at what it was designed to accomplish.
Sound: I enjoyed the soundtrack of this game as well. Now, it's not something that I would listen to outside of the game. But it's good enough that it is something that you won't complain about this game.
I recommend this game for those that are looking for a challenging game that is designed well. There's plenty of content for one to absorb, and it has a proper ending that does not disappoint. It was updated to support 60fps, and the implementation is perfect. It also has a mode easier than normal if you want to experience the storytelling. The game was considered already pretty good, and with the updates it received. The game is even better than it was before. You won't be disappointed with this one. If you are a numbers person, I would give this a 9/10.

What you get out of Rocksmith® 2014 Edition - Remastered depends heavily on how you treat it. It's important to realise that it is not a complete learning program but rather the ultimate practice tool and is best used to supplement other learning avenues, be they YouTube videos, books, or classes with a tutor.

My parents' have spent more money on actual instructor lesson than they and I have spent on this game (base, and DLC). This is worth every $70-$80 depending on if you get the Realtone cable from the store. Either way both RockSmith 1 and 2 are worth the mone 100%.

Rocksmith 2014 is the kind of game everyone used to say should exist when Guitar Hero and Rockband were popular. "Wouldn't it be cool if like, you could play Rock Band, but like, it was a real guitar, man?"
Yes, it is cool. This game advertises as being able to teach you to play guitar. That's sort-of true. It's no substitute for taking lessons, but it will get your hands moving all over a guitar in a way that sounds like music to you and those around you. You may not learn much about music theory, but if you're committed you may still come out of a committed relationship with Rocksmith being able to play songs by many of your favorite artists.
I use Rocksmith as a tool to stay sharp on guitar and learn new songs more than as a strictly instructional device, so I can't speak to its value as a pure learning tool as much as a fun way to pass the time if you already know how to play guitar. However, if you look up Audrey on YouTube, the little girl who has been playing Rocksmith (for our amusement) for the last few years, you'll find that this game can very much make a guitarist out of anyone. The girl's better than me and I've been self-teaching for a decade.
The tracklist of the game is great, but things really open up when you start shelling out for DLC. It's only a dollar more per track than it would have been on Guitar Hero or Rocksmith, only the extra dollar buys you the added benefit of *learning to play a song you love on a real guitar* so I find it very worth the price.
There are lessons and exercise minigames, and a comprehensive and powerful "riff repeater" tool to slow down (or break down) phrases for you to learn at a comfortable speed. There are leaderboards and challenge modes, one of which is a feature that makes notes invisible the more competent you become at playing them, to really drive home in your mind how a song is played. It supports multi-player (provided you have two cords and two instruments) so that you and a friend can both play together. My room mate sometimes likes to pick up the bass guitar and pluck along with me while I play lead.
Rocksmith was a shocking thing to exist, and it worked well as a proof of concept. Rocksmith 2014 was a refined and nearly perfect improvement. Rocksmith 2014 Remastered somehow manges to tune up the original RS14 into an even better product. The only drawback is that by buying it on Steam, you'll have to order a cord online, and they never go on sale or anything. That said, once you've got your hardware in order, this is a game that just keeps on giving and you'll get your money's worth a hundred times over.

I have only played this game for a couple of hours. But here are some thoughts on it.
Performance:
I feared the worst and was pleasantly surprised. The game runs really really well. I am playing on Ultra settings, with NVIDA features turned on and Ultra textures on a 980ti @ 3440x1440.  At that high resolution and with those settings average 50-55 fps. The frametimes are super consistent, no stutters or hitches.  The multi-threading is very impressive as well. On my hexacore i7 all 12 threads are evenly busy at roughly 60-70% usage. Very CPU hungry game. But in motion it is really pretty.
Gameplay:

The world is a lot more interactive this time around. More hacking options and it deviates form the normal ubisoft openworld formula just enough to feel fresh.
Can't say anything about the long term value or multiplayer so far. But as a single player game, I am enjoying it a lot more than the first one. Definitely one of the better PC games this year.

Here is the point where you determine whether or not you’ll really love it or hate it let me get this out of the way I didn’t mind the original watchdogs at all I mean yea it was overhyped and it had tons of problems but I still managed to find things that I really loved!
Where Watch Dogs 2 really improves is in the section: “Character, Story and Gameplay”.
Those were the main aspects for me to like Watch Dogs or not. I LOVE the improvement on Watch Dogs 2!
The Gameplay is way less repetitive but its still an open world with bunch of stuff to cross off a list but combination of good progression systems and just more purpose and variety makes things feel stronger. What I really really loved about all improvements was the stealth system.
It actually feels like the game stresses stealth much harder, which means the game is sometimes pretty hard without using stealth. But it gets kinda frustrating when you don’t use stealth, get seen by a person and every other enemy knows exactly where you are. I don’t mind that at all but I know that some people may be frustrated about that.
Other than that you spend a lot of time on the rooftops of San Francisco. You can be running around you’re gonna be climbing stuff you’re gonna be parkouring which looks pretty cool but ultimately doesn’t really add anything “special”. It doesn’t re-invent the wheel you know. This♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of options that you have at your disposal I already mentioned even lends itself to getting to higher ground you know you can like fly your drone up somewhere you can hack a crane and do all weird stuff like that it’s just a good way pointing out that everything in this game can be improvised.
Now there are two things which I really don’t like about this game.
The Hacking relies way too heavily on these augmented reality pipe puzzles where you follow trials of line of code in the game and tweak pipes to get the data to flow the right way or something. Watch Dogs 2 does that waaaay too much and after a while they just feel extremely freaking grading ….
Second one is that the shooting doesn’t feel as strong as it did in the first game and basic stealth feels a bit odd at times and finicky. The stealth is extremely… unforgiving… Like I mentioned before. Running around -- Someone see you -- EVERYONE literally EVERYONE knows where you are… and that’s.. kinda frustrating at times.
But with all the other added elements it feels satisfying. The game world of san Francisco and the bay area itself look and feels NICE. NPC’s have a lot going on they can even photobomb your selfies. You can even pet dogs. Or you can run them over but.. Don’t do that. Lol.
Ubisoft captured the look and the feel of San Francisco pretty decent even if I just watched some Google Street View stuff and I kinda like what I see. The Game feels pretty decent and all in all a good Time waste and a good improvement on Watch Dogs 1.

I am reviewing the COSTS of this game as Duelyst caught my interest very quickly and I bought cards very fast too , making me aware of something I felt I needed to let other people interested in the game know.
Apparently a lot of people get upset by free2play games being "pay2win" . free2play means you can play and enjoy the game for free. Now if a game is all based on a PvP rank system, it is just obvious that at some point you will have to spend money - or you won't have the required tools to allow you to compete on an equal basis ( unless of course youre extremely talented etc but this review is aimed at normal/average players ).
Also , if the game is good I don't see why not spend some money on it ( even if very  little ) since people (  devs )  worked and keep working hard to develop it.
Now let's take a closer look at how this plays out in Duelyst. Aside from a very small amount of solo tutorial / challenge missions there are ONLY ranked matches available. The ranking system is pretty similar to a lot of other games. Each win earns you a star / point , with winning streaks getting you an extra one. You start at rank 30 - Bronze League, which decreases initially by 1 every two starts / points .  When you reach Rank 20 , you are promoted to the Silver League - and won't fall back to Bronze not maatter how much you loose until the end of the season ( end of the month ).  Considering the winning streaks bonuses, you could reach Silver in like 18 matches.
What happens when you hit Silver League ? You start running into better players with much better decks than Bronze, and it will be way harder to win if you only have a basic set of cards. With the need to purchase cards ( unless you do months of grinding ) and not being able to rank down , the game becomes effectively "PAY2PLAY" IMO. You either grind your way painfully and slowly with daily quests that do not require wins,  or you NEED to buy cards . Ok , pay2win is fine, but PAY2PLAY is the opposite of free2play. But let's suppose you are skilled and don't need to spend a single buck in the game. You can hit the top ranks without spending a single dollar. But you are a collector and want all the cards or just want to support the game developent buy buying all of them. Pretty muc the same as buying a game with all the DLCs.
What if I tell you that after spending a little over USD300,00 ( that's correct three hundred dollars ) you will still not be able to have all the cards ( you can have a maximum of 3 copies per deck , but I am talking about not having a single copy of some of the rarer cards ) of the game? How does that sound?
I definitively CANNOT RECOMMEND a game that so far has only 3 expansions and already requires you to spend like USD 500,00 to have all the cards.

Ben and Ed is a platformer with a wide variety of stages. You play as Ed, a zombie, who wants to save his friend Ben. The game itself is split into stages, which you try to finish by getting to the exit. During the stages, various limbs may be torn from your body, which cause you to run with one leg, on your arms, or even just roll your head around.
In general, the artstyle is consistent and with a neat morbid touch. Nothing feels out of place, yet there is a lot of variety.
The levels are interesting and again with lots of variety. While they do keep the "gameshow touch", the devs managed to make each level feel unique and interesting.
The lighting in this game is terrible. In each platformer, you should have the ability to see what's ahead of you and be able to react to it. However, in Ben and Ed, the stages are often so dark (with a spotlight on the character), you cannot judge what's ahead of you. So it might very well be that, out of nowhere, you get hit by a cannonball and have to start over.
This fact sadly plays in with the notion that checkpoints in the game are very rare. You have to complete large portions without being able to "save", so you might be stuck at a certain point and just wait for your ragdoll to fall juuuuust right so it activates a checkpoint. I'm looking at you here, laser pit.
Even more frustrating is the fact that its physics are a bit counter intuitive. Often hammers or similar barely grace you, yet send you flying across the stage. Other times you get knocked down from falling too hard and end up slowly sliding down a platform you should have had no problem landing on.
These three things make Ben and Ed feel arbitrary in either win or failure. "Winning" a stage feels more like "I finally glitched right", especially in the later stages.
I wish steam reviews had a "neutral" option. I do recommend it if you can look past these screw ups, if you look for a challenge in a sense that you can do everything right and still fail. If you're easily frustrated, you might be better off with a different game.

Recommended? Sort of.
I bought this at a steep discount years ago (less than 10 bucks), and have alternately loved and hated it ever since.
The game was originally released in a mid-alpha state, resulting in a lot of the rage evidenced  in some reviews.  After a free expansion, about 50 mid-sized patches and over a hundred micro-patches, what you have is basically a game in permanent mid-beta.
Most of what could be fixed without a complete redesign has been. What remains is an extremely time-consuming, mostly rewarding game that will occasionally infuriate you.
Put simply, the Mars2 engine is a paper tiger; anyone who's seen videos of a North Korean Parade knows what I'm talking about here. Yes, it can display some very pretty and entertaining visuals and doesn't do too badly handling most of the  strategic- or combat- layer graphics that make the game fun. No, it simply cannot handle the dataload imposed upon it by an eight-player game.
SotS 2's real saving grace is that it is extremely easy to mod, tweak, break, or bend to suit your gaming style. All you need is a basic grasp of English, some logical thinking skills, and a text editor. Most of the .entity, .section, etc. files are simple xml-coded text files. A free sqlite database editor will allow you to change almost anything in your saved games, too. Want to research everything? about 15 mins. with the .techtree file and my bugs -and bugs only- can play with every tech that matters to a bug (and some that don't). *Spoiler* This and some creative finacing gets me every tech in about 250 turns.
The bad news: This game is never getting finished, is a resource hog, and crashes whenever it bites off more than it can chew. The multiple redundant autosaves are a lifesaver, but getting past some turn-to-turn crashes will require you to figure out which event was the straw that broke the engine's back. If we want this game to work perfectly, we'll have to redesign it ourselves, XML is easy to edit, but extremely wasteful coding (Micro soft-in-the-head designed xml). If Kerberos had gone with a more machine-centric scripting language, This game would be an all-time bestseller but would be much harder to mod.
Tech Specs:
You don't need a datashredder to play this game well (at least as well as it can be played). gen 3 core i3's in quad-core mode, or fm2-based quad cores are probably okay on data processing here, Sots2 cannot fully utilize 6 or 8 cores, so your best bets are a decent i5 or i7 from Intel (not necesessarily new), Kaveri-based quad core, or Vishera based CPU from AMD. My FX-8350 occasionally reaches 20% load, but I've modded the heck out of most game files to make battles more exciting. My A10-4600 laptop can run the vanilla game well.
My old GTX 480 video card is overkill for the vanilla game at 1920x1080 with max detail, but I sometimes get a little hitching with all the extra ships and weapons I've modded into some battles.  Integrated video on an Intel chip won't get you anywhere, but the mid-range gaming qualites of an A10 laptop iGPU or A8 desktop iGPU is okay if you have extra RAM -see next-
Memory!!! This is why you must have 64-bit windows. Don't have 8gb? Don't bother!. Between the poor engine choice, the leaky and ineffecient coding, and the sheer amount of data that needs to be crunched, this game eats memory fast. At turn 200 on a medium-large map with 4 of 5 players still alive and about half the map occupied, I'm using 20% of the 32gb of DDR3 in my desktop. My modding has a role to play there, but years of trial and error have shown me that 8-player games are simply not practical on nearly any machine with this game engine, and 6-player matches  require a custom computer with about $1k worth of parts in them. An 8gb computer with dedicated graphics can run Vanilla okay most of the time with 2-4 players.
The Bottom Line-
Is this an extremely time-consuming game? Yes! -though it's really not as bad as 90% of mmos- Is Sots 2 often frustrating? Yes!  Is it rewarding to play for 3 days, get to turn 220 and take a huge nap? Yes!! Is all of this really worth the hassle and a sizeable chunk of money? Probably not for 70% of  gamers who like consoles even a little. This is a great game for guys like me who've been gaming on semi-high-end computers since the late 90's. Getting the game into the state I have it in now is like owning the Millennium Falcon: You spend a lot of time now and then figuring out what's wrong with your mod, or if it's even your fault or the devs. You put some real effort into understanding and modifying this rustbucket of a game, have a lot of fun and get really frustrated when you spend an hour getting your empire just where you want it for turn 221 and it crashes just before you get around to saving. (Think Escape from Hoth in episode 5 here).  The real fun is taking a mostly functional scrapheap of a YT-1300 and trying to make it really fly (metaphorically speaking). Actual gameplay is a little better than the reality of war: Most of what you do during a turn isn't all that exciting, but it's pretty wild when space-lizards, telepathic dolphins and rat slavemasters all decide they want to cook you in your chitin just before you get the chance to nuke their homeworlds.   Thanks for reading my super-long post. I think it says something that I recommend this game to at least some people right after the metaphorical Falcon decided not to enter hyperspace with Rat Vader coming for me. Just a heads up, you will have to fix the crashing issue by adjusting the size of the .exe header. If you are not comfortable with troubleshooting crash problems, I actually wouldn't recommend this game. If I find the file to adjust the size and the instructions again, I will post it.
Now for the second problem to get out of the way: the game automatically places trains on your tracks. Very often you will have open track for a train to use, and the game will unfortunately use track that already has a train on it, causing both trains to be stuck if set on the highest routing difficulty. There are also a number of smaller things to keep an eye on where a small slip might be confusing for a while at first. Sometimes you forget to put a depot somewhere at all, sometimes your track doesn't reach the depot, things like that. It will generally be frustrating at first.
Finally, multiplayer is based on Gamespy, and thus doesn't work.
However, once the crashing is fixed, and once you learn how to make up for the routing problems (which you shouldn't have to), it really is a fun game. At first I thought it was going to be too easy, as I quickly moved up the difficulty ranks until I was at all but the highest difficulty level. Then for whatever reason I started doing worse, so now I play on medium difficult (mogul). There is a fast forward option for the late game phase when you are often just saving up enough money to buy out another rr. You can also pause it, and do stuff while it is paused. It is generally very laid back, but not too easy. Somehow I want to compare it to a more skill-based version of monopoly, I suppose because you are trying to buy out your opposition. Unlike Monopoly, it is nice to have a certain amount of cash available instead of buying up everything right away, since other characters can start auctions at any time. The fact that you can keep an eye on your opponent's current cash can give you very helpful insight into their intentions, though.
In short, this game is not recommended for those who are easily frustrated. With a little work, both in getting it to work at all and learning the unfairly bad train placement, this game works fine and is pretty laid back without being too easy.

This game has shown me that not all stories require beautifully drawn and animated characters. It tells an interesting/cute story about Thomas the Red Rectanglular AI and his friends progressing through mystical 'portals' to see where they lead and exhibit their talents to each other. Starting slow with just thomas, the number of characters slowly increases, adding new rectangles to control with new abilities and flaws.
A major component of this game is trying to navigate each character to their respective exit using their own powers and those of others. John can jump really high, but has trouble reaching small spots. Chris can make tight squeezes but can hardly propel himself into the air, relying on others to stair him. The puzzles/levels are well designed to be challenging and require one or two occasional reelvauations of the solving approach, without being a mind-numbing difficulty.
Without giving too much away, TWA does a good job developing the personalities of each character. Some are benevolent and try to lend a hand, some are decietful and will use others to further their ends, some just want to progress in peace without too much interaction with others. One or two characters have a history. The entire story is detailed by a wonderfully acted narrator noting the thoughts and observations of the characters.
TWA is a game that will take 3-6 hours to complete depending on your visual/spatial puzzle solving skills. It is Wonderfully narrated with characters that are interactively interesting, though not visually. It has interesting and engaging challenges and an interesting story progression as the levels are progressed. The soundtrack is calm and relaxing, to ease frustration of the occasional roadblock. Whether it is worth paying the full $10 is debateable, but it is definintly a game worth playing.

This game is absolutley phenomenal in practically every aspect. I mean that from the bottom of my heart too. I went into the game with no idea what it was, armed only with the knowledge that it was a platformer and that it was supposedly a wonderful experience, and I wasn't just pleasantly suprised, I was blown away completely.
From the very first line of spoken dialogue, I knew it would be a good time. not only is the narrarators voice as smooth as silk, it fits perfectly with the game, and every line is spoken wonderfully, immersing you in the experience. I'm not trying to spoil anything about the story, so I can't talk about it much, but it is masterfully told from many dfferent points of view, giving lots of perspectives on the situations. I never thought I would be so invested in the lives and characters of rectangles without voices or features, but it is astounding what context can add to a game. Without the ongoing narraration, this game would be a simple platformer, but adding personalities, goals, dreams, and relationships, even simple blocks can be wonderful characters. Each one has strengths and flaws and feels relatable in different ways. When I'm pushing the blocks around a level, I don't feel like I'm solving a puzzle, I feel like I'm watching a group of friends help each other to get through a difficult situation. When characters came and left, I felt elated at the thought of a new friend, and depressed at the thought of losing any of them.
Even without the story aspects, this game is fantastic from a technical standpoint. The controls are responsive and handle beautifully, and the movement speed is perfect, never too fast or too slow. The puzzles are challenging, yet rewarding to solve. I never had a point where I was stuck and frustrated and was just angry at the game, no sir. There were so many "a-ha" moments and I loved how clever each and every level was set up. New gameplay mechanics were added smoothly, working with the story with just enough time to get used to each new one before it was applied to the upcoming puzzles. The game is short, yes, but it's as long as it needs to be. It's paced wonderfully, never plodding along or moving too quickly. I think it's the perfect length for a story driven game and I wasn't able to stop until i finished it. I needed to see what would happen in the story or what amazing puzzle I would be faced with next.
Any issues I had with the game are utterly minor and are more just little nags than anything. I had a few littles bugs, like when a platform moved upwards, you could get caught in the side and be pulled up with it, the shifters sometimes didn't change me at all until I ran back through them, just little tiny issues like that, nothing that impacted the rest of it. As far as story goes, it was a little convoluted, but easy to get caught up with by just playing more of the game. You are Thomas, while the game is a metaphor of life. Not only is the game endearing and emotional, but it contains valuable life lessons, and ideas that you can decide on your own of what this game tells it's players, depending on what you yourself have experienced in life. The shapes are not perfect, but each their own individual identity, and all have their own special talent, just as every other person on this planet. It symbolises that nobody is / can reach a state of perfection, some being better at things than others. The game teaches that we should however work amongst those around us to be the best possible version of ourselves that we can be. This game will engulf you, some it will captivate, but above all triggers you to think of yourself and those around you. A game worth every penny.

Well I sure never really even looked at any image related to this thing, the name itself didn't catch onto me until I played it for the trading cards.
Then I saw what a cute puzzle game it is.
You are playing as the mother whose offspring must be saved. That's the simple premise!
The controls are very responsive and the jump button especially in regard to how hard you press that jump button.
The goal is simple:  Bring your offspring into the exit along with yourself. This sounds simple at first, but several entities are required to take into mind, and here's a few of them.
Mother Fling (That's what I'll call her now) gets a bigger "hitbox" the more offspring she carries(You can't pass through narrow spaces), she becomes slower and finally also jumps lower.
Finally, you can 'fling' your offspring. This means tossing them straight ahead of you. This is what you'll be doing a lot, for most of the time you cannot simply carry your cute children to home sweet home.
Time to mention the story as I get on to obstacles: Various creatures are out to harm your beloved small offspring. One in particular seemed to just scatter them all over the place, a big mean one.
While it may not kill you, if a single off-spring is eaten alive or dies by the terrain such as drowning, you lose and must restart the level.
I should mention that I like the animation on Mother Fling if her offspring dies, she holds her face like she's about to cry from seeing her children dying.
Mother Fling must also survive, remember that. Even if all of your offspring have been thrown into safety, if you die at that point, you're back to square one.
The music in the game is nice! It's good to hear game soundtracks that doesn't make you want to mute the game instantly.
The sound effects? Neato.
In conclusion; a cute puzzle game that's worth paying the cheap price.
If there's a sale on this game, it's basically a steal.

Here is the point where you determine whether or not you’ll really love it or hate it let me get this out of the way I didn’t mind the original watchdogs at all I mean yea it was overhyped and it had tons of problems but I still managed to find things that I really loved!
Where Watch Dogs 2 really improves is in the section: “Character, Story and Gameplay”.
Those were the main aspects for me to like Watch Dogs or not. I LOVE the improvement on Watch Dogs 2!
The Gameplay is way less repetitive but its still an open world with bunch of stuff to cross off a list but combination of good progression systems and just more purpose and variety makes things feel stronger. What I really really loved about all improvements was the stealth system.
It actually feels like the game stresses stealth much harder, which means the game is sometimes pretty hard without using stealth. But it gets kinda frustrating when you don’t use stealth, get seen by a person and every other enemy knows exactly where you are. I don’t mind that at all but I know that some people may be frustrated about that.
Other than that you spend a lot of time on the rooftops of San Francisco. You can be running around you’re gonna be climbing stuff you’re gonna be parkouring which looks pretty cool but ultimately doesn’t really add anything “special”. It doesn’t re-invent the wheel you know. This♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of options that you have at your disposal I already mentioned even lends itself to getting to higher ground you know you can like fly your drone up somewhere you can hack a crane and do all weird stuff like that it’s just a good way pointing out that everything in this game can be improvised.
Now there are two things which I really don’t like about this game.
The Hacking relies way too heavily on these augmented reality pipe puzzles where you follow trials of line of code in the game and tweak pipes to get the data to flow the right way or something. Watch Dogs 2 does that waaaay too much and after a while they just feel extremely freaking grading ….
Second one is that the shooting doesn’t feel as strong as it did in the first game and basic stealth feels a bit odd at times and finicky. The stealth is extremely… unforgiving… Like I mentioned before. Running around -- Someone see you -- EVERYONE literally EVERYONE knows where you are… and that’s.. kinda frustrating at times.
But with all the other added elements it feels satisfying. The game world of san Francisco and the bay area itself look and feels NICE. NPC’s have a lot going on they can even photobomb your selfies. You can even pet dogs. Or you can run them over but.. Don’t do that. Lol.
Ubisoft captured the look and the feel of San Francisco pretty decent even if I just watched some Google Street View stuff and I kinda like what I see. The Game feels pretty decent and all in all a good Time waste and a good improvement on Watch Dogs 1.
