It is possible to play with a mic, but it is absolutely not recommended! You need the cable for proper note detection.
I only focus on the guitar part, as I do not play bass.
The game is very fun and intuitive. I let a lot of friends, who never touched a guitar in their life, play the tutorial and they understand the concept very quickly and have a lot fun doing so. It is certainly more rewarding and motivating than just playing by yourself. It kind of has a guitar hero vibe to it and who doesn't like guitar hero?
Ubisoft is not exeggerating when they say "The quickest way to learn guitar". (Keep in mind that this game does not replace a guitar teacher and regular guitar practice)
The game features dynamic difficulty, meaning that songs start out with just the most important notes, and as you get better more notes will appear, up until you can play the whole song.
The riff repeater is an awesome tool, which lets you repeat certain parts in a loop with a custom difficulty and speed level, so you can learn the parts pretty efficiently (although this is obviously not as fun as just playing the song)
There are other gimmicks, such as session mode, where you can jam along other virtual instruments, or minigames which train certain guitar playing elements, but for me it's always about playing the songs.
Currently the game only supports 6-string electric guitars and 4-string basses.
Because the cable's analog to digital converter is more on the poor side and effects such as distortion are simulated, sound quality is going to be average at best. Don't play this if you expect a good guitar tone, because you won't get one.
Note detection is OK, good enough for chords and fretted notes, but lacks behind with palm mutes (especially if you downtune your guitar)
Some riffs have a very annoying and loud hum, be sure to play with humbuckers as single-coils make it A LOT worse!
The game comes with a couple songs, which - in my case - became boring very quickly. The notes/tabs of each song are fine and I found them to be mostly accurate.
There is a lot of DLC out there, usually around 3€ for each song which is an OK price in my opinion. If you have the money you will have enough content to keep you busy ;)
If you own the original Rocksmith in Steam you can buy the Rocksmith Disc Import Tool (misleading name) to have all your original Rocksmith songs appear in Rocksmith 2014, which is a total rip-off in my opinion.
On PC and Mac you can download community created CDLC (Custom DLC) which you can "hack" into the game. The CDLC creators have to add their own notes to the song though, and that can be of very poor or very high quality. CDLC is great, but you cannot rely on it.
I dont know if CDLC is legal or not, so do your own research before getting into it!
The game itself runs very smooth on my system (144Hz, i5 6600K, AMD fury gpu) and rarely crashes. In my case the game also ♥♥♥♥s around with the sound drivers and sets arbitrary volume-level for completly unrelated microphones! It is very annoying to go into the windows settings to change it back to 100% when I want to voice chat with friends.
They force you into using a uPlay-Account but you do not need the uPlay-Software itself, it just asks for Log-In info when you start the game, so its not that big of a deal (still BS though)
Mouse controls in the menu work fine, but the menus themselves are very poorly designed. They have improved it a bit with the free Remastered update, but it still sucks.

The game is amazingly good. DLC is a bit pricey after a while, but i guess it's worth it as you literally learn the song forever.
Great for beginners and experts.. If you have NEVER touched a guitar before, I'd learn the basics before picking this up although there are practice modes in this game to help the newbies out.

Dueylst is a pretty entertaining card-game with wonderfully done art and character design, as well as an intricate story and lore-filled world found in various scripts on cards. That being said; the gameplay WAS fun. Of course you have to be lucky in order to have these cards in your hand because otherwise you are just going to spend the game prolonging your slow defeat. This basic strategy is of course viable in every deck; However, the Vanar are the living embodiement of this. All of their cards/spells are centered around dumping impecable amounts of dps on the battlefield, all the while disabling anything that could possibly save you..... Quite a problem indeed.
All of this could be remedied by tweaks in gameplay mechanics and nerfing  stupendiously overpowered cards so all the other wonderful and creative decks could actually be enjoyable to play. HOWEVER the devs seemingly prefer to simply pump out packs and even more packs absolutely brimming with cards more powerful and abusable than the last. Thus the problem that now plagues this game.
It's rather irksome and so i can't bring myself to reccomend this game to anyone, but it is a free game afterall, and you can tell much effort has been put into the design. In the end, the decision is yours to like or hate this game. Let my review be a warning, not something to inherently change your mind.

Rocksmith makes guitar practice fun, and it's very good at introducing you to concepts you may not have bothered playing with if you tried learning guitar by finding chords for your favorite campfire songs online. However, the game is best if you understand the educational limits of the game:
The input system is at times inaccurate, at other times too forgiving to compensate for this lack of accuracy. Sometimes you'll hit every note, but if you actually take the headphones off you'll realise that what you play sounds like crap because you're just barely hitting the notes, and you don't have the musical surplus to make the notes sound good in the process.
The game can only really track (and thus reward) your success replicating the note and chord progressions on the screen. Musicality is obviously beyond what a video game can teach you. The trap is that reading the notes on screen takes a lot of concentration off your musicality. I recommend plenty of practice outside the game where you focus on musicality, phrasing and everything else that the game can't audit.
Other flaws i've found so far:
- In the guitarcade, you spend a lot of time on "game over" screens. I'd love if there was a hardcore practice mode where you can't die but don't get a score either.

I'm a pretty big fan of SotS, and I got royally screwed when I purchased the hard copy of Prime.
Seems nothing has been learned from that experience. As with Prime SotS2 was as broken as it could on release with more features not working than did.
Kerberos made Prime into a great game with its DLC's (though kinda screwed over their initial customers). This seemed to be going into the same direction, but it isnt.
SotS2 is a very nice looking game with a number of really interesting features. However, it still is a very unfinished product and it is very clear Kerberos stopped development. Which would not be that bad if the AI would be able to put up a good fight, specially late game. The AI however can only seem to be able to destroy its own economy.
The default routine for the AI when set to hard is sort of like the following:
-Heavy on research, colonization second (you'll easilly outgrow the AI even if you allow the AI to start with 6 planets, even when playing as Hiver).
-When the AI meets you, 1-3 turns later it will declare war on you.
-AI goes into overdrive redesigning ships and kills its economy trying to build these redesigned ships.
-As a results you'll find yourself spammed with small/halfbuild fleets even when you have Leviathans on defense.
Also, research is basicly the same as in Prime. No you dont have to research cruisers, but it is still the same as in Prime as now you just have an extra stage attached to the end. However the extra strage (Leviathans) are boring, slow, strategicly only usefull on defense. Specially so since you can build as many Flagships as you like and below the math:
Leviathan: 54CP cost, can fit 2 in a fleet with 2 Dreads or add 5 Dreads.
Flagship: 18CP cost, can fit an additional 6 Dreads in the fleet.
Since the Flagship has better speed and is much more affordable you have the choice between a moderatly expensive 7 Dreads-Fleet (Flagship), or a hugelly expensive 1 Leviathan + 5 Dreads-Fleet.
All and all, as a game that should entertain I recommend you stay clear of this and try something else.
If you do not care about a (semi-)competitive game, or intend to only use it in MP, it sure is worth €15-ish.
I sure do advice you turn of random events and mod out pirates .. boy are those annoying features!

I have never really been able to play this game.  When it first came out, it was way too buggy.  Now it won't run for more than a couple minutes without crashing.  This was a huge disappointment considering how much I enjoyed the first.
There was a brief period of time near the release when I could play it, but the gameplay turned me off very quickly.  I hated the concept of the space stations and had a hard time getting into the game.

THE GOOD:
Basically a sci-fi Total War game. You have the campaign map where you buy ships, order fleets onto missions, and generally have a nice 4X time. When you encounter another player -> zoom into the tactical map for real time action.
The campaign map is beautiful, each faction gets a different movement mechanic from the standard warp drive of one race to instatanious gates and node lines of others. You really feel like a unique race not a re-skin. This keeps up with the ship designs, some races are hulking great beasts, slow and powerful, others are quick and fragile. Humans for instance have decent all-rounder ships, slightly less well armed than average but fast over the strategic map, unfortunately the drive section is very fragile and can strand your ships far from home.
Did I mention that? Yeah your ships are distructable in nice modular chunks, from individual turrets to command/mission/drive sections. Add to that a 4-facing armour matrix, shields that are very well balanced IMO, weapons that all have a use (though you will rely on a few favourites if you don't have a special need), and the tactical combat will keep you entertained alone.
THE BAD:
It's shonky, no two ways about it. The campaign UI is a bit slow to respond, after about 200 turns it takes quite a while for the calculations to play out and ocationally crashes (but that has got much better since release, in fact no crashes for ~ 3 months). Sometimes stuff doesn't update or doesn't work for no particular reason, and last but not least: THERE IS NO IN GAME WAY TO LEARN.
Yes that annoys me, you spend countless man-hours making a great combat game with a slightly shonky campaign layer and don't tell anyone how to use it. Thankfully the community has stepped up to the challenge and fixed this, creating beginners guides and guides on individual races (start with the Tarka, they are the most straight forward - or Hiver if you like to turtle). The guides are good, use them.
Another area that needs attention is the AI, it's pretty bonkers. It will declare war on your massive empire and send colony ships to bombard your planets which get killed straight away by planetary missiles (did I mention missiles, yeah there are missiles, and point defence for your ships, and weapons platforms... I like the tech). It will also be bestest mates with you but be mildly miffed you "stole that tasty planet near me" for 100 turns and then declare a holy war to wipe the stain of your civilization from the galaxy with 10 Leviathan class ships when all you wanted to do was trade with everyone and be a mecantile hippy empire (still sore about that).
When the campaign AI works it can be pretty impressive, I think it managed to plan an invasion once and pulled it off simultaniously against me and two other AI. That invasion was let down by the tactical AI (better but not exactly Sun Tzu) and a wall of torpedo platforms.
THE UGLY:
Three words, randomised tech tree. Some people hate it, some love it. I am in the second camp. But, I also loved the randomised discovery in Alpha Centuari (I don't care if it's not balanced, that's how science works guys, sometimes you miss a really obvious idea). Certain techs are always available, like cutting lasers, and dreadnought ships. Others, well, it's the luck of the draw. The Zuul are having an energy weapon bonanza and enslaving your planets? If you're lucky just research the "♥♥♥♥ you energy weapons" shield (only covers the front, not quite as OP as at first sight). If you're not lucky, well hopefully the cash you save in equipping that shield will let you build more ships and the Zuul run out of light to put in their lasers. It's about rolling with the punches, but it is pretty galling when those punches are a fleet of heavy phaser drones and your stuck with the crappiest point defence. It's also pretty horrible when your home planet gets glassed 10 turns in by a ghost ship.
Yeah, ghost ship I hate the ghost ship. Like a '90s RPG you are subjected to random encounters (I think they are not completely random but it feels like it). This mechanic is at the same time absolutely horrible and absolutely brilliant. It's horrible when 10 turns in, your economy is trashed by a giant wandering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (built by the humans and then lost forever to wander the stars... the lore is actually pretty cool). It's brilliant when your struggling colony, with only that admiral you should retire because he got the shakes (yeah your admirals have stats, some are mass murdering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, some just like to grow flowers) - but can't quite let go because he won that battle that one time - and a couple of second rate ships for support, is being slowly worn down by slaver attacks. Admiral shaky holds his battered squadron together while the new guy from the academy is bringing reenforcements in the form of the newest (and cheapest) system defence craft.
The random encounters make you feel like starfleet command, an ancient derelict in one system, a hive of wasp-like silicon lifeforms in another, colony alpha-nine has an incoming metor shower. More variety would make it perfect, an option to turn off mr ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ghost ship would be sublime.
THE SHOWDOWN:
Would I recommend this? Yes I would. Mostly because it deserves to do well. It improves on everything SOTS1 fell down on and expanded what it did well. It's not perfect by any means but it has ambition that alot of sequels lack. Paradox could have played it safe, they could have updated SOTS1, make a few fixes to the dodgy bits and called it a day. They didn't. They fixed the broken stuff and then said "You know what would be cool? Building science stations to observe pre-FTL aliens. Letting players build Bablyon 5. Treaties that real civilisations would make (re-create the treaty of Farixen). A ship that shoots asteroids at planets (actually in the first one but it's really cool)". Like I said some of it doesn't work, the science stations are better suited to sitting behind your lines researching important things, from what I can tell Bablyon 5 doesn't do much, the AI won't make interesting limitation treaties with me, but the asteroid gun is great.
The tactical combat is the best bit, the strategic map feels like a way to move ships to make fun battles happen. I really wish Paradox would release a single player campaign about a lost human exploration fleet, a load of linked missions with persistent officers who learned? Excellent. In the mean time, admiral shaky has some slavers to kill.

I know it's verbotem on Steam tocriticize a technically well produced, avant garde indie game, but Thomas Was Alone just isn't a fun game, or an experiential game, or whatever defenses one might try to clamour to defend this.
Thomas Was Alone at its heart is a platform game with some puzzle solving. By far its biggest problem is it's far too easy. None of the puzzles are challenging, and while nailing some jumps may be tricky, the platforming is not a reason to play this game. There just isn't any interesting gameplay to speak of and this kills the game. After reaching section 10 without any difficult stages - I felt like an employee moving boxes around a grid - I gave up.
Graphically its simple, but the style can't be faulted. You control geometric shapes, usually squares or rectangles, each with different jumping abilities. It's clean and has a nice interface for manoevring levels.
Despite its simply graphics, there is a bizarre attempt to narrate some sort of cohesive story. While the voice acting is a nice touch, simply naming and personifying these little shapes is not enough. They don't have any emotion to speak. How could they? These are not companion cubes.

I strongly recommend this game.
It's quite a nice city-builder, and if you enjoy this kind of simulation, you will definitely enjoy this game immensely. Other than Sim City or other similar games, it seems rather realistic, with the cityscape you create appearing like a real city.
I particularly enjoy the options for public transport, where you can create bus, rail, or subway lines and thus connect the different boroughs of your city.
There are some things which I think could be better, like e.g. more freedom in the way plazas can be built (the options right now being limited to a type of pulbic park that you just set into a given place - being able to create larger paved areas besides streets would be a nice bonus). A better utilisation of waterfronts or embankments would also be nice, however, I am told this is at least partially included in one of the DLCs (and thos DLCs could definitely be cheaper, but that's another issue).
All in all a great game, and by the way, the fact that traffic here is just as frustrating as in real life (only now from a city planner'S perspective) adds to the authenticity.

Updated review: 1/12/17
Updated review for Disasters and Snowfall DLC's (5/7/17)
Cities Skylines is the Sim City modern Sim City we deserved. Intuitive controls and mechanics, extremely malleable city building, tons of zoning and utility options and even the water is simulated and dynamic. Skylines really moved the bar up on city building games. It looks good, it plays smooth and on the technical side it seems to handle even massive cities without the performance suffering to much.
As for the AI, it's smart enough to function, but only as good as how well planned out your city is. Giving your citizens plenty of routes with well placed roads which range from simple two lanes, four lane, six lane and highways to guide your citizens to their destinations. I will note when it comes to high density districts, it can become quite a challenge to understand the nuances how your citizens destinations and needs effect traffic.
Another note on something I find special in Skylines is simulated water and the use of hydro electric dams which comes as it's own challenge beside having to manage a massive city. I recommend checking out the Steam guides, some of which do an excellent job at explaining some of the untold nuances on the subject.
Performance wise, I will say the game runs well with some frame drops once the city begins to become very dense. I found just fiddling with graphics options performance isn't much of a problem and doesn't compromise the detail of the game much.
Disaster and Snowfall DLC:
I was skeptical of the disasters DLC at first over what options were made available when planning, building and running my city involved. After some fair experience, the Disasters DLC is worth the price. Though it's not a massive amount of content, it really does add something in terms of planning out your city and always being prepared for things like massive fires, serious lightning storms, tornados, earthquakes, sinkholes, tsunami and in my opinion, the most frightening, meteorite strikes. It's almost a cathartic feeling when one of the more serious disasters hits. When your shelters have been packed full if an early warning came through, an entire district void of the usual noises and only silence grips that part of the city until the disaster strikes. Though most aren't enough to shut down your city, seeing a meteor slam into a dense district that rates a stright 9 on a scale of 1 to 10, you can only helplessly watch as a crater rips everything out of the ground, sending flaming debris spewing across the city. Any nearby forests are blazing and only your emergancy services can be seen scrambling to the rescure beneath the cloud of dust.
Now Snowfall.
Honestly? I haven't done much with it, maybe a few hours, so my opinion can't be formed quite yet. So I'll update this later.
Pros:
-Great controls
-Intuitive game user interface
-Practical but good looking graphics
-Tons of options for city management
-Disasters DLC is great
Cons:
-The news ticker could be in a better spot
-AI still needs slightly better route planning

This game is brilliant. It has one main strength that makes it a true gem, but it might be often overlooked: this game has two faces really.
At first glance it seems like a very casual but pleasant puzzle platformer. The levels are fun, they require a little bit of figuring out but nothing too complicated. You can pretty much play through the main 100 levels of this game like that without even realising there's more to it. This makes the game appeal to those gamers who just enjoy to chill out.
But there's a lot more this game is hiding... As you'll find out if you try earning fancier flowers, which requires completing levels within a strict time limit. You'll soon realise that for many levels those basic obvious methods of solving them that you used so far don't really work if you want to be fast enough. You suddenly learn the game has a number of undocumented features... little tricks you can do that may even look like exploits, allowing you to skip parts of the levels... But no! You're actually supposed to do all that! Those tricks aren't easy to pull off and getting good enough times is really challenging. Suddenly the casual chill-out game becomes a test of skill comparable to Super Meat Boy. And if you manage to get through all that too and you think you're done... Nope! Super-hard bonus levels are unlocked. If you manage to 100% this game, you're really really good.
This all makes Offspring Fling a great little game for both casual gamers and the most hardcore players. I'm very positively surprised, because initially when I started playing it, it seemed very generic and not standing out in any way. I saw very simplistic graphics and simple puzzles like in million other flash games published on various websites. I was wrong. I was completely wrong. Please take my word for it and don't get the wrong impression like I did. This game is a true masterpiece.

I'm new to the Crysis franchise, I started the first game a few days ago and finished the day I started Crysis 2. I'm not going to compare which had better aesthetics, I'll just say what looked good and what didn't in this game. However, my main focus will be on the gameplay and overall fun I had with this game.
[THE GOOD]
I'm treated to Hanz Zimmer's music for this game, and I already like the main menu design. I like that I can change the difficulty when I start a new game. The music and sound quality seem improved as well.
When playing, the environment seems more detailed and the city environment is an interesting approach and change from the last game, and when the environment takes damage it looks great (a concrete pillar fired on by an MG). The animations in the game are also improved, and there are better designed character models as well.
Continuing with gameplay, I like that I can finally toggle crouch mode on and off. You can finally climb over objects/through open balconies instead of just jump to, on, or over. For those that want to go guns blazing, you can finally detach mounted machine guns on cars, and use them to mow down enemies. Kicking cars in the direction of enemies is now possible for a more loud approach. Now if you want to to take the silent but deadly approach, they made a stealth kill option when invisible and next to an enemy.
[THE BAD]
Right from the menu options I noticed things that, although minor, is still unpleasant. You can no longer customize your suit's voice, you can no longer customize your suit's HUD color (military green, blue, red, or white), and there are no longer as many key customizations. The key customizations that are lacking which bother me most are leaning left and right. You can no longer disable blood.  Also, you can no longer save at any point any longer, it seems to now be checkpoint driven.
When playing, I was bothered by how the game had to hold my hand step-by-step in a linear enclosed environment, where everything is conveniantly placed (I'm talking trucks and debris) to prevent me from diverging a different path. I can't use stealth mode at the start until it gives me a prompt to do so at the beginning of the game, the same with armor mode.
Then there is the gameplay, let's start with the suit. From the start, all the abilities aren't unlocked (each ability has additional unlockable perks/upgrades that enhance stealth, armor, etc.), and I wasn't motivated to unlock anything. I just wanted to use the suit's powers and play how I wanted to with little restrictions in that regard. I also disliked how I wasn't able to choose strength mode and sprint mode any more (the abilities are now automatically used when sprinting and "hold" jumping), part of the fun in the previous one was in juggling around between each ability and knowing which is the best choice for a moment (whether combat or simply traversing terrain). Also, when looking at my HUD, I could no longer see a health bar, instead the screen effects were kept and a low health warning was added to the screen.
Now looking at gameplay,you cannot dual wield pistols anymore. The amount of weapons you can carry at a time has been reduced since pistols are considered a primary instead of a backup. Leaning left and right isn't the same anymore, it's replaced by getting behind something and aiming down your sights while using the camera axis to control you leaning over or past the cover. At one point I tried a lasersight weapon, but it was no longer it's own attachment like in the first game. Instead, it was a sight attachment which prevented me from using iron sights and instead zoomed in from hipfire. At one point I saw an enemy through the glass of a bus and shot at him, but the bullet wouldn't go through and would just spark off. I got some distance and shot again with the same results. I'm not sure if this is a glitch or if this is how it was designed to be.
[THE UGLY]
Part of the beauty of Crisis 1 was in it's very open environment and how you could approach different combat scenarios. It had its own charm with its story and gameplay. There were problems there, but even with those problems it felt fun. It felt like it had a lot of passion put into it. But something about Crysis 2 sets me off. I went into it with high hopes after finishing the first, wanting see where the story and action would go next. I liked how it started, but progressively I felt more and more annoyed, tired, and even bored with it. I'll admit I didn't play long and I didn't even finish it, because the truth is I don't even want to finish it.
They included collectables this time, which is a nice but unneccessary addition. If the other issues would have been fixed then I would have welcomed it. But without those issues being fixed, it only feels like a cheap attempt at having the player go on a scavenger hunt and make it more fun.
There were some fun moments where I could jump on a car, detach an MG from it, fire at the enemies, jump off, and power kick the car at another group of enemies. But those fun moments get overshadowed for me by all the negative aspects I found.
To each their own, to mine my own.

Playing SOTS 2 makes me want to play SOTS 1. I can see how they might have felt like they were making improvements to the SOTS concept. But they did such an unbelievably bad job putting the whole thing together that it blows my mind.
The user interface is atrocious. It's difficult to figure out how to do things that should be simple. I can't always tell what can and can't be interacted with. I'll give you a tip there by letting you know that most of what you see cannot be interacted with. The more I played the game, the more convinced I became that the game was intentionally designed to make gameplay as difficult and confusing as possible.
The game runs slowly in different ways. Even the game menu feels sluggish. It's even worse when you're actually in the game. The first time I clicked "next turn" it took 5-10 seconds to process the turn, which gives me nightmares about how long it might take in the late game when the map is fully populated.
The combat is much less intuitive than SOTS 1. It was very noisy, but I couldn't really see what was happening. I couldn't see any of the little laser beams or plasma cannon shots flying around. Just missles graphics cutting in and out. I think they redesigned things to look more realistic, but the end result was that it looked like garbage compared to SOTS 1.
Based on User Interface alone, I think the game developers should be ashamed of themselves. It's so bad, that I would actually rather do math homework.

There's no shortage of good 4X experiences out there, and this game just isn't one of them.
The game is an abject technical failure. It was completely unplayable on its release, and it's still riddled with performance issues and frequent crashes, even after the developer has finished updating it.
The game had good ideas, but the way in which they were implemented ended up generating way too much micromanagement, without actually expanding the range of meaningful choices available to the player. Star system management takes more time each turn now, not because you're making difficult choices about how to invest your resources, but because the game will punish you if you don't spend enough time fiddling with the dials.
The core gameplay of the first Sword of the Stars is still there, but it's buried beneath poor game design choices and technical issues that should've been fixed. All in all, that game is just a better experience than this one.
Its current price as of this writing is about half of its launch price, which is still more than it is worth. I would maybe suggest picking it up for under five dollars if it's on a generous sale, and you're already tired of the first SotS. Otherwise, steer clear.

Updated review: 1/12/17
Updated review for Disasters and Snowfall DLC's (5/7/17)
Cities Skylines is the Sim City modern Sim City we deserved. Intuitive controls and mechanics, extremely malleable city building, tons of zoning and utility options and even the water is simulated and dynamic. Skylines really moved the bar up on city building games. It looks good, it plays smooth and on the technical side it seems to handle even massive cities without the performance suffering to much.
As for the AI, it's smart enough to function, but only as good as how well planned out your city is. Giving your citizens plenty of routes with well placed roads which range from simple two lanes, four lane, six lane and highways to guide your citizens to their destinations. I will note when it comes to high density districts, it can become quite a challenge to understand the nuances how your citizens destinations and needs effect traffic.
Another note on something I find special in Skylines is simulated water and the use of hydro electric dams which comes as it's own challenge beside having to manage a massive city. I recommend checking out the Steam guides, some of which do an excellent job at explaining some of the untold nuances on the subject.
Performance wise, I will say the game runs well with some frame drops once the city begins to become very dense. I found just fiddling with graphics options performance isn't much of a problem and doesn't compromise the detail of the game much.
Disaster and Snowfall DLC:
I was skeptical of the disasters DLC at first over what options were made available when planning, building and running my city involved. After some fair experience, the Disasters DLC is worth the price. Though it's not a massive amount of content, it really does add something in terms of planning out your city and always being prepared for things like massive fires, serious lightning storms, tornados, earthquakes, sinkholes, tsunami and in my opinion, the most frightening, meteorite strikes. It's almost a cathartic feeling when one of the more serious disasters hits. When your shelters have been packed full if an early warning came through, an entire district void of the usual noises and only silence grips that part of the city until the disaster strikes. Though most aren't enough to shut down your city, seeing a meteor slam into a dense district that rates a stright 9 on a scale of 1 to 10, you can only helplessly watch as a crater rips everything out of the ground, sending flaming debris spewing across the city. Any nearby forests are blazing and only your emergancy services can be seen scrambling to the rescure beneath the cloud of dust.
Now Snowfall.
Honestly? I haven't done much with it, maybe a few hours, so my opinion can't be formed quite yet. So I'll update this later.
Pros:
-Great controls
-Intuitive game user interface
-Practical but good looking graphics
-Tons of options for city management
-Disasters DLC is great
Cons:
-The news ticker could be in a better spot
-AI still needs slightly better route planning

This is not a game, this is a learning tool.
And this is a very good one but you will not magically become the next Jimi Hendrix in 5 months, and you sometime need to practice outside Rocksmith
Pros :
The guitarcade games are really well designed to make you work certain skills and techniques
The lessons are okay, but it will not replace a real teacher or a friend with a good guitar level as the game cannot tell if you are doing any mistake beside playing a note wrong
The learn a song mode is where you are going to spend most of your time. And it feels very satisfactory to play along a song and it forces you to have the right tempo. The dynamic difficulty works generaly well, sometimes the gap between 2 difficulty levels is a bit strong but you can get use to it if you are practicing a single part of a song in the riff repeater mode
The session mode seems very interesting but my guitar level is way too bad to do anything interesting with it
Cons :
Playing along a song on the tempo can be satisfactory, but I tend to sometime rush or play approximataly some parts and the game still count it as played well and you can't really hear how bad you are. So sometime trying to play a song you practice outside rocksmith can really tell you if you are really good or bad at that song
The tone designer and tone switches doesnt sound really good imo, I have a Lag Imperator 66 (costed me 200€) and when I tested it on a real amp I found that the sound was more than correct for the price but on rocksmith I find it either oversaturated or really low
In conclusion : Rocksmith is definetly a good investement if you are struggling with traditional methods and it is worth the price if you consider picking it during sales (as you'll need to buy the realtone cable on your own + a real guitar if you dont own one) But it is not the ultimate and perfect learning tool. You'll still need to be motivated and work regulary if you want to progress. But after now a bit more than a month I realised how much progress I made. Before rocksmith I could barely play Between the bars by Elioth Smith and I tried recently playing it again (I need to tune my guitar to a standard D, and you will learn to hate tuning you guitar in something else than Standard E or Drop D) and I had much more ease playing it.

This game... There's quite a lot I can say about this. It would probably help If I sorted things into pros and cons
PRO:
-Controls
This game's controls are incredibly simple. WASD to run, shift to jog, turn with mouse, throw head with RMB, use with             E. Any doofus with a basic grasp of PC gaming can pick it up and play.
-Gameplay
Fast-Paced and EXTREMELY challenging, this game is a pretty solid 3D platformer, with enough goofy, blood-spattered antics to provide a fun experience.
-Graphics and Performance
This game looks great, with colorful semi-cartoonish visuals reminicent of
and runs smooth as butter even on my POS intel laptop.
CONS:
-Bugs
Yeah, this game is in need of a patch or two. I often caught myself pinned under a trap, not dead, but rendered completely immobile, or I ended up phasing through a wall and into a chasm. Not frequent enough to be a deal breaker, but still somewhat annoying.
-Soundtrack and overall Sound design
This is the game's biggest weakness. Its repetitive techno soundtrack sounds 'meh." at first, but it gets real obnoxious real fast. There is also the issue with sound effects that last too long, or repeat far too frequently. I won't give away too much, but if you've played the game, you'll know what I mean when I say: "WILL SOMEONE SHUT THAT DAMN CLOWN UP?!"
Overall, 7.5/10. Far from perfect, but a hell of a lot of fun. You get what you pay for with a $10 price tag, I guess.

Crysis 2 is a severely underrated FPS and a good successor to Crysis in most ways. Whereas Crysis was an exceptional shooter that had the biggest dip in quality I've ever experienced with a game once you start killing aliens, Crysis 2
does not suffer from the same issue and remains consistently brilliant throughout.
Btw, like the first game, I have way more hours than Steam states due to the vast majority of my playtime being on console and on disc. I have played this game consistently since release.
++The game looks absolutely gorgeous. Amazing first-person animations, gorgeous texture work and lighting and the detail in environments are phenomenal. Never has such a static enivironment felt so incredibly real in a game before. New
York might be deserted due to evacuation from alien invasion, but goddamn does it feel alive nevertheless.
++The nanosuit is lots of fun to use
++This game has a strong atmosphere
++Wayyyyyyy better optimization than Crysis
+Top knotch sound design, keeping the tradition from its predecessor that with gorgeous graphics amounts to unsurpassed presentation
+The story and writing are a big step-up from the previous game. The invasion of New York by aliens may be as cliche as you can get, but with strong characters and writing with a unique alien backstory makes the writing in the original game
look like a primary students' attempt at narrative.
+I really, really like the nanosuit upgrade system. It's simple and totally unobtrusive, but it helps you feel like you get progressively better as you unlock new functions or gain improvements.
+Switching weapon mods on the fly is innovative and just cool. Not a gimmick as it is actually really helpful.
+Weapon firing mode options are nice
+Environments are open, not nearly as open as the original, but are open enough and therefore retains the sandbox element I love about the series
+You can drive vehicles in unscripted events ala Halo style but without being anywhere near as prevalent
+Difficulty is well balanced
+Gunplay feels unique in the genre
+Good length
+Soundtrack is good with a great theme, even if repetitive
+Lots of unlocks and achievements
+Level design is great
+Full controller support
+-Animations (besides first-person) are shoddy
-+No more prone ;(
-Specific versions of weapon types now limit which gun can have which weapon mod, which is annoying
-Like the first game, has a severe lack of weapon variety
-Very, very glitchy game
-AI is braindead
-Multiplayer was never great and is now dead

I'm a patient person. I really wanted this game to be great. I payed for it, waited for the devs to patch it up, debug and finish it, so I could play.
It is broken. It may not crash anymore, but it is not playable. Almost everything great about the previous game is destroyed with the new design and this is not something you can patch away.
SotS1 was dynamic. You could build 3 recon destroyers and send them every turn, a little later send some tankers so the recon ships could refuel and continue exploring. By turn 20 you could have 20 explored systems and a couple colonized worlds.
In SotS2 yo ucan't send destroyers, you have to send cruisers, which are about 3 times more expensive - so 1 per turn, not 3. You can't send a recon ship alone, you have to have a fleet with a mission vessel, tanker and command ship (which was optional before) - so fleets are sent every 3 turns. Lastly, due to the awful mission system you have to send the fleet, wait for it to exlore the system AND return bofore it can be sent again. No more chain-exploring. The game drags on like torture.
SotS1 had great UI for its time. Since then there has been incredible progress in UI design, and the menu flow and information presentation could have been inproved, if the game designers had learned from the competition. They did not. The UI is a monster that has to be endured, not used.
It is all so frustrating, because beneath all this there is a game trying to shine. The battles are beautiful, the solar systems are big and complex.  If they make SotS Remastered with the design of SotS1 and the graphics and solar systems of SotS2 I'd buy it without hesitation. But in its current state, this game is not worth playing, even if given for free.

Coming from playing Simcity 3000, I thought City: Skylines would fill that niche category of games. It certainly has, but there are some shortcomings with the game.
It is a lot more modern, which allows for some very interesting things. Take into account the Steam integration, the Workshop has plenty of new things to add to the game, from advanced traffic systems, to buildings, this game is as close to the “next generation” of city builders as you possibly can get.
The game does push towards the DLCs a little too much for my liking, but I can see myself playing the base game in the future, due to it’s simplicity and modularity.
Graphics are great, but that really should not be the focus of the title. The way the simulation of a city works does not seem to be as accurate as SimCity 3000 did, but I guess that is just an unpleasant fact when titles become modernized.

This game is Sim City with everything that made Sim City remotely entertaining stripped out. It is more boring than Monopoly, possesses a terrible UI and the "tutorial" appears in text bubbles that are too small to read. Why do people play this game?

Well, i was having fun... was. See, the problem is, no one likes living near a dead body... and boy does this game have lots of those. If someone dies in a building, be it a one room bungalow or a 60 story high-rise, the city (thats's you) needs to dispose of the body. You can either cremate them or bury them, but you better do it quick. Otherwise, the building will become abandoned. Oh, and if that happens, so will the building next door (because no one wants to live near an abandoned building, either). And the building next door to that one will be abandoned and the one next door to that... You get the point. You might be thinking "no problem, I'll just build more cemeteries and crematoriums". That's what i thought, too. After a while, I noticed my hearses weren't picking up any dead bodies. They just seemed to be driving around willy-nilly, right past the buildings with corpses in them, and RARELY ever stopped to grab the corpses on the way by. It got to the point (since by now I had an almost $2 million cash surplus) that i was building crematoriums directly next to the infected building (that's next to EVERY infected building) in the hopes that it would curb the swell of whatever epidemic i was dealing with, but to no effect. I thought "very well then, I'll bulldoze every affected building." And I did exactly that until almost nothing was left of my city. The death wave never stopped. Now, I have no city. And I'm familiar with the effects of pollution and proper medical facilities, and the effect of traffic on various systems, etc. I'm not new to the Cities franchise, and I have read enough and played enough to know how not to mess up that badly. My conclusion-this game is glitched, possibly to the point of being uplayable. If you plan to buy this game, then you should also plan to mod it, or at the very least, wait until a patch is released that fixes some of the more glaring problems, such as total-city death. Yes, total-city death can definitely ruin your day.

Here's a game that is fundamentally difficult to describe because in order to do so, you would need to have exposure to a wide variety of niche genres.
You'd need to be used to abstract storytelling, where the use of pixels as an art style deliberately conveys or witholds information from you in the hopes of invoking either horror or the feeling of sublime.
You'd need to deal with "bullet hell" gameplay where care is necessary to quickly memorize attack patterns and counters.
You'd need to be comfortable playing on an isometric environment where danger can and will come from any and all directions, sometimes offscreen.
You'd need to accept that not everything will necessarily be explained in the end, and that the experience of the game relies more on a sense of accomplishment, than seeking answers.
You'd need to recognize that fuzzy feeling that occurs from finally seeing victory, after multiple attempts, without the sense of frustration.
Drift along, and see just why the light is hyper.

Magnificent tool for learning real guitar. I used to enjoy playing (and I mean "play" as in pretend) Guitar Hero and Rockband with my kids; now that I and my merry band of Wookies have real guitars and bass and can coax actual notes from our gear, it's hands-down the most fun we've ever had with a video game. Well, maybe a close second to the Mario Kart franchise. But you get my meaning. Tons of songs available and something that will appeal to everybody's musical tastes. Plus the awesome ability to introduce the next generation of shredders to giants of the industry like Bob Marley, Queen, the Stones, and SRV/Double Trouble. Highly recommended, though my daughter wishes there were more classic female leads, so a greater selection of songs from Heart, Janis Joplin, Joan Jett, etc were available (yes, she owns what's available and both Jefferson Airplane/Grace Slick DLCs).

The game itself is very fun and informative, ive only been messing around on guitar and this has helped tremendously. It has a plethora of songs you can get from DLC to suit anyones music taste which is a very good feature to have to keep people interested in learning the instrument.
I do have a few gripes though; these may be me doing something wrong as i am brand new at the instrument, but i think its the game.  I am currently using an sg g-400 guitar, before that i used a cheapo fender squire. On BOTH guitars it has an issue picking up what note im playing on the low E string. Its usually when it asks me to play something thats on the 2nd or 3rd fret that i have this issue, but its there nonetheless.
Also, the lessons, a fantastic learning tool and i thank the developers for obviously working hard in that field, but unfortunately, its not perfect. As of right now the biggest "problem child" of them all for me has been palm mutes. Palm mutes are something ive known, and i think everyone can pick up a guitar and do them, but in the lesson it constantly tells me im not palm muting and its ridiculously annoying.
All in all though, these are the only 2 problems ive personally had with this game, the 'learn a song' section is a blast that takes each song step by step. The riff repeater is a god send. guitarcade helps you learn fundementals without you even realizing youre learning.
Id recommend this to any beginner serious about learning guitar.
P.S. it'd be cool if we could somehow upload tabs of our own songs for other people to play...just a thought :)

Thankfully this is a problem only the first time going through a new maps since none of them are all that complex and so when you have rubbed your face once on all the walls it's easy to remember what is what.
Another questionable design decision is the semi-random level layouts. Whenever you restart a level all objects you need to pick up and remove(bodies and weapons) spawn in different positions. Which isn't bad in and of itself, but that thing that I think is a problem is that fact that some layouts are easier than others. So there is a slight incentive to a player to just restart a level till a favorable layout is generated.
Other than that it's a basic stealth game. Memorize which enemies do what, plan your rout and execute it. Good for 5 to 6 hours of fun.

I enjoy playing this game online with my friends (using a CD install, the 1.1 patch, the RailRoads.exe fix & GameRanger)  but its not my favourite game for making railway networks: Open TTD is (with its 32 bit graphics texture pack & the "Pineapple" trains texture pack enabled) because like in TTD, players can place signals for their trains to follow.
Things I like about SMR:
* Its 3D graphics and presentation.
* Its train engine selection screen.
* Its selection of trains engines with a different set of engines for different countries.
* Its sound effects & music.
* Its intuitive interface.
* Its economy and share trading gameplay mechanics.
* Its patent and town industry auction auctions.
* Multiplayer games can be saved (like in Open TTD)
Things I don't like:
* The Steam and disk releases aren't patched to allow it to use more than 2GB of RAM: so players who have a computer with more than 2GB of RAM must download a fan provided .exe patch to prevent their game from frequently crashing.
* A problem all the Railroad Tycoon series games have (except maybe RRT 1): Players can't make proper railway networks because they can't manually place signals for their trains to follow preventing them from making single direction railway lines and double line loops. Instead a train will always take the shortest route to its next station. So players must either make trains share bidirectional rail lines, stopping in passing places to pass each other (or driving through each other if easy/medium difficulty routing is enabled) or they can opt for the efficient, cost effective, unrealistic option of having one train per bidirectional rail line.
Internet gaming requires the use of free third party software like GameRanger or VPN software like Tunngle: this game's developers could have given its players a "direct IP connection" option. I've not been able to make my Steam copy work with GameRanger but my CD copy does.

Both had fantastic ideas, a bigger, better, and cooler - but failed horribly in execution and were relased with half the features missing and as buggy, broken pieces of crap. If you want an excellent 4x SciFi game, go buy Sword of the Stars I - but stay away from this sorry thing that wanted to be a sequel - you'll only be disappointed.

The game attempts to integrate real-time combat and turn-based strategy in a fairly good sized galaxy.  It does an ok job at it.
The real-time combat is very well presented, albeit somewhat frustrating.  The controls are wonky and imprecise.  The ships appear to "skate" across space, making the physics somewhat questionable.  The increasing levels of battle damage are nice to look at, but don't exactly give an accurate representation of your ship's status.
The turn-based strateg part is frustratingly complex.  The research tree takes entirely too long to work your way through with the possibility of not being able to research a technology a very real thing.  The economics of the game are probably the important aspect of it; requiring you to research that before anything else unless you want to be in debt up to your eyeballs.
The games themselves take entirely too long to load up once you start approaching the triple digit turn mark.  And once you finally do manage to get the game loaded, individual turns themselves take between 30 seconds and a minute to generate, even if you haven't explored the rest of the galaxy.  That's unacceptably long, in my opinion.

Most of the issues have been detailed in other reviews, so I'll keep this one short.
If you are a fan of the original SotS, just stick with the Complete Collection (Born of Blood, Murder of Crows, and Argos Naval Yard) and avoid this. The prettier graphics, bigger ships, and larger systems are not worth all the bugs, dreary gameplay, random crashes, and generally unfinished nature of the game (the in-game SotS-pedia help guide is mostly blank pages or just unhelpful). Trust me.
If you are looking into Sword of the Stars and want to buy this one because the graphics look better and the story seems cooler than the first one, don't waste your money; go buy the original Sword of the Stars Complete Collection and enjoy the game and the universe before it was left out in the cold to die. If you ignore this and figure that you'll pick it up anyway and give it a shot, and you end up being disgusted with it, do yourself a favour and pick up the first game and try it too.

1.  My biggest issue with this game:  Skill is not rewarded whatsoever.  Even if you do become great at the game, you will still be forced to play one of 3 modes:  duels, dom or tribute, because nobody plays anything else.  Duels have next to no reward.  You might as well throw rocks at a window for the same amount of time.  Tribute has no way to replenish health and requires immense team effort, which can't happen with randoms.  (If you try to queue with 4 people, you'll spend a good 20 minutes at a loading screen.)  Dominion is loaded with ganks, people gang attacking you and theres not a single ♥♥♥♥ing thing that can be done no matter how good you are.  Rep 14 Warlord?  Here, take two low level players.  You're dead.  Skill is not rewarded.
2.  Matchmaking is nonexistent.  You will, if starting the game, be matched with people who have been playing since the start and will demolish you.  The learning curve is immense, and the only people that play anymore have been playing since launch.
3.  Completely non realistic.  This is not a big issue for most people, but we were promised at launch that it would be a truly realistic game, and instead we have tiny assassins creed lookin girls that can stomp on big♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing vikings.
I suppose that if I had to give this game any credit, the only reason I've played for 500 hours is because overall the combat system is fun.  The graphics are good and in a fair fight, you can have a lot of fun.

Cost - 10/10  You can unlock the game by playing it.  The cards you are given at the beginning are fairly effective for the thrifty player.
Overall 36/40 for a 90%, or A grade.  Impressive.  Fun while it lasts.

At first the stealth puzzle gameplay is interesting, with an intriguing art style, concept and feel to the game. But as the difficult gradually increases it just stops being fun.
The single biggest problem is the police, who are the only real problem. Their cone of vision is absurd, they have ridiculous peripheral vision and can spot the player at the most stupid obscure angles. They have no turning animation, or indicator for when they are about to turn; which means an entire element of the behaviour of the police is not telegraphed to the player the police just snap from one angle to the next. Only some of the police patrol patterns have them turn predictably, some don't and if the police deviate from their pattern the player has zero way to anticipate them turning. The police deviating from their pattern every single time they go to investigate anything suspicious. The police can also hear the player walking, even through walls, which makes sneaking impossible. Players cannot sneak close range, they cannot, and the police will hear and be alerted even through solid walls by the player moving. If the player gets wedged into a corner with the police, they cannot move or they'll get caught, they just have to hope random chance doesn't have the police snap their neck instantly in their direction. Which makes close quarters stealth terrible as again players cannot sneak around the police and if the map is cramped that means the police can notice you through walls which you will constantly be surrounded by. Even more so because the player cannot walk slowly or crouch, their loud sprinting is forced. This is a huge part of the difficulty, is the bad or absent stealth mechanics. Players cannot sneak, the police can hear through walls, the police have no turning animations or smoothing of any kind and the police have massive peripheral vision.
Beyond that are the multiple design choices which just make the game literally less fun. The police investigate everything, everything. Anytime anything moves they stop to check it, anytime anything suspicious happens they stop and examine it. It gets so boring to have to wait for the police to move on because any time they see something out of the ordinary they stop everything they are doing to stare at it for several seconds. Over and over and over. Sometimes the player can't even function at all because the police are just camping one spot of the map and the player just has to wait for them to finish and move on before they can continue playing. The game also puts the police literally camping certain spots and the only way to get them out of there is to lure them out, which is just so sloppy and awkward because of how easy it is to get caught and how loose everything is.
The levels just keep getting bigger and more complicated, the patterns players have to adhere to in order to get through certain obstacles get more and more rigid, unforgiving and offer the player no room for choice on how to go about playing. And if you get caught once, everything resets. The amount of objectives which require players to transport a thing to another thing makes it all the more worse because of how many times players are demanded to cycle through the same map over and over transporting objective to objective around. You potentially have to lap the same map multiple times transporting things from place to place, everytime you attempt the level. Sometimes even random chance gets the better of things because some elements of the map are randomized; so sometimes it generates more difficult spawn locations sometimes it doesn't.
It's just not fun after the first few levels. The game straight up lacks certain fundemental stealth mechanics, while amplifying others beyond reason and fairness. And the amount of design choices which make the gameplay even more slow, chore-like and boring makes it even worse especially when you have to go through it all over again every single time you fail the level.

Thomas Was Alone is a parable. It's about accepting people who are different, helping those who can't do the things you can do, and being proud of your abilities while remaining humble. This game is about loneliness and finding people who will accept you no matter what, reminding you that regardless of how amazing you perceive someone, others are flawed and full of doubts.
All that from a minimalist game about squares.
I was extremely impressed with how, while the narrator spoke, the level usually reflected what was being said. Literal, unbreakable divides between characters, spikey, uncomfortable thoughts, and towering obstacles that would be impossible alone but you're /not/.
There's some glitches in the later levels (that you can use to your advantage). The music gets kind of clamorous, which isn't annoying at first, but I thought I somehow was running the game twice. It would probably grate on someone else.

Sid Meier's Railroads is a fun little game.  Basically you start off as a fledling railroad, with some starting captia, a starting railroad and station, and from there, the world is your oyster.
Pros:
- It is a railroad tycoon simulator, causing you to take time, pause the game, look around the map, figure out which towns/cities you want to lay track to to set up passanger, mail, and goods cars; all the while, looking around to find resources and facilities that process them to make a profit.
- You are always looking for markets, and industries to claim ownership over, provide materials, and export the produced goods to make a buck.
- Music and graphics are 7/10.  Nothing ground breaking but not horriable as well.  Also, the ability to be able to move the camera to "ride" the selected train is a nice touch.
- You are able to buy stock in your own company as well as your competitors, allowing you to buy them out, and either liquidate everything they owned or seize ownership and merge them into your own company to make money off of their "hard work".
- You are given the ability to build industries in cities and towns to help them grow, as well as expand your own industry base for your company
- Always have to think one step ahead, especially if you are playing against max AI on hardest difficulty level, which really adds another depth of thoughtful gameplay.
- New trains will always become available, causing you to think about which ones you can, need and must upgrade vs ones you can leave alone.
- There are auctions for buying new industries, and patents, which will give you a greater amount of leverage for your company and it's success in the game.
-Plenty of different maps, with different resources and industry chains to explore, plus time era challanges.  One map may be only for a gold rush in Californa USA, yet another would be weapons production in Britian.
Cons:
- If you want to upgrade all of your trains, you need to click your way down the list, no selection to change all all at once.
- Gameplay can feel a bit stagnent after a while and repititive.
All in all, I do enjoy this game.  It is a fun little game when you need a break from your main games and are looking to play a tycoon based game.

Crysis 2 is a rebalance for me. Where I recommended Crysis and Crysis Warhead for their world design, mechanics, and gunplay, but found the stories rather cliched (and contrived in Warhead); here I find the story rather interesting, but takes a nose-dive for world design. You originally played Nomad in the first game who was under the command of Prophet. Here you play a random soldier rescued by Prophet. Some sort of alien plague is infecting the world. Prophet gives you his nano suit to save your life and then tasks you with delivering the suit to someone who can pull the data off it for a cure. The story seems rather basic from this description, but the highlights and details would of course spoil it and it's these details that make it interesting. If you like a story-based FPS then do not pass this up.
Mechanically it's at least on-par with Crysis. Horrible MMS two weapon system with some trivial exceptions. Great gunplay with a solid sense of impact. Reducing the variety of weapons and making ammo for all of them more plentiful so you can stick to your favorites is a noticeable improvement. Weapon customization is gated behind finding the attachments on a per-weapon basis. You also have a psuedo-leveling system where you harvest material from certain enemies to improve your suit functions. This may seem slow but it's easily possible to get everything maxed out about 75% through the campaign on your first pass. It's not obnoxious or intrusive either. Suit functions have been somewhat automated into the actions they are relevant to such as jumping, melee attacks, and sprinting all auto-using the power modifier which is speed and strength from the first games combined. Cloaking is still manually activated though, and severely hamstrung until you've enhanced it quite a bit and then it's broken and overpowered moreso than the first games.
World design is as I already mentioned where Crysis 2 takes a nose-dive. The world is a city setting for the most part. You would think this offers some degree of tactical variety, but the little it does is obfuscated into pre-designated psuedo-scripted options on a per-battle basis. This is highlighted in a rather contrived UI element where your suit tells you to scan for tactical options trying to obfuscate this fact. Now I realize that this sort of setup takes effort; moreso than just strategically placing enemies and letting the player figure out how best to deal with them on their own, but it just makes the world and level design feel so confined and constrained in stark contrast to the first Crysis.
Ultimately it's still hard not to recommend this or any of the Crysis games (aside from Wars). Yet for different reasons that may make certain games in the series feel like an obnoxious necessity. The experience is still worth more than any let's play ever will be for these games.

Hyper Light Drift does a great job capturing the desperation of a world in recovery from a catastrophe, all without saying a word. I personally loved that the game let me infer the plot using only the environment and nonverbal communication.
The game is sometimes TOO effective at conveying this desperation; the environment with its looming music and the game’s difficulty is sometimes very lonely and oppressive, in excess. I found this particularly true in the western and northern areas.
Moving and fighting through the game often has a wonderful flow, especially as you gather more advanced abilities (which help keep the game fresh). You really do start to feel like a badass drifter who can do anything by the end.  The game is semi nonlinear, consisting of 3 linear areas you can freely choose to fight as far into as you want. That being said, I found bosses to be the most frustrating though, requiring many attempts. The music is somewhat ambient, but superbly conveys the mood and tone in this game, particularly in the lead up to the climactic moment.
Ultimately I enjoyed my playthrough, but I’d give the game  8/10 for the flaws highlighted above, and only recommend it to people who are patient and enjoy discovering things on their own.

Updated review for Disasters and Snowfall DLC's (5/7/17)
Cities Skylines is the Sim City modern Sim City we deserved. Intuitive controls and mechanics, extremely malleable city building, tons of zoning and utility options and even the water is simulated and dynamic. Skylines really moved the bar up on city building games. It looks good, it plays smooth and on the technical side it seems to handle even massive cities without the performance suffering to much.
As for the AI, it's smart enough to function, but only as good as how well planned out your city is. Giving your citizens plenty of routes with well placed roads which range from simple two lanes, four lane, six lane and highways to guide your citizens to their destinations. I will note when it comes to high density districts, it can become quite a challenge to understand the nuances how your citizens destinations and needs effect traffic.
Another note on something I find special in Skylines is simulated water and the use of hydro electric dams which comes as it's own challenge beside having to manage a massive city. I recommend checking out the Steam guides, some of which do an excellent job at explaining some of the untold nuances on the subject.
Performance wise, I will say the game runs well with some frame drops once the city begins to become very dense. I found just fiddling with graphics options performance isn't much of a problem and doesn't compromise the detail of the game much.
Disaster and Snowfall DLC:
I was skeptical of the disasters DLC at first over what options were made available when planning, building and running my city involved. After some fair experience, the Disasters DLC is worth the price. Though it's not a massive amount of content, it really does add something in terms of planning out your city and always being prepared for things like massive fires, serious lightning storms, tornados, earthquakes, sinkholes, tsunami and in my opinion, the most frightening, meteorite strikes. It's almost a cathartic feeling when one of the more serious disasters hits. When your shelters have been packed full if an early warning came through, an entire district void of the usual noises and only silence grips that part of the city until the disaster strikes. Though most aren't enough to shut down your city, seeing a meteor slam into a dense district that rates a stright 9 on a scale of 1 to 10, you can only helplessly watch as a crater rips everything out of the ground, sending flaming debris spewing across the city. Any nearby forests are blazing and only your emergancy services can be seen scrambling to the rescure beneath the cloud of dust.
Now Snowfall.
Honestly? I haven't done much with it, maybe a few hours, so my opinion can't be formed quite yet. So I'll update this later.
Pros:
-Great controls
-Intuitive game user interface
-Practical but good looking graphics
-Tons of options for city management
-Disasters DLC is great
Cons:
-The news ticker could be in a better spot
-AI still needs slightly better route planning

TL;DR - OK game if you're good at math, not good for kids. Could be much better with tweaks to difficulty. Not designed for controllers but I made a community config that works well for important functions (answering questions and pausing). If difficulty is changed (i.e. make easy easy and keep harder questions in harder difficulties) this would be a recommend.
FULL REVIEW
This could be a good game, but while it's clearly meant for kids, it's
designed well for them. The difficulty ramps up far too much and too quickly. Instead of easy being easy, it's easy for the first several questions, then it rapidly progresses to questions of increasing difficulty. A child with beginning math skills that can answer the questions at the beginning will quickly be in over their heads, making this game frustrating and very short. Easy should be easy; if they can do more challenging questions they should move on to the next difficulty setting for that. I'm not saying the difficulty shouldn't increase as they proceed, but this should be at a much slower pace and with a much lower ceiling per difficulty setting.
Some other issues I found with the game:
- Not made for a controller. Not really a negative since it doesn't state controller compatibility, but still, this would have been nice. I made a controller config and uploaded it to the community configs, so hopefully others will find it helpful, as it makes playing
easier with one, and faster than even a mouse would be which, in a game where a split second could make a difference, is important.
- When you unlock the next difficulty, the first time you start a game on that difficulty the achievement pops up and blocks the third answer. At least this is a one time per difficulty thing, but the achievement should pop when going to the menu, not during gameplay, both for this reason and the fact it's a distraction in a game where distractions aren't necessarily wanted.
- Far, far too often, several questions in a row have the answer in the same place. For example, the answers to 20 questions might be A, A, A, A, A, C, C, C, B, B, A, A, C, C, C, C, B, B, B, C. There needs to be more randomization of where the correct answer is. Basically, if you're running out of time, if you just select the same answer as the last time, you have an awfully good chance of being right.
- Once, the : (division sign) in a question was partially obscured by the number following it.
My rating reflects the fact this game appears to be meant largely for kids, but if you're an adult that's decent at math and want to improve or just want the mental exercise, I'd say go for it. Likewise, if it's for an older child that's good at math, it would probably be worth it. But for most children, it's not a good choice. Also, other negative reviews have pointed out the fact that very frequently the division elements of the equations lead to fractions. I personally am not against this as it adds a level of difficulty but not really that much, though I wonder if that's why the developer did this or if was more due to laziness. You don't have to know that 7/3 is 2.33333, just that it's a little more than 2, so as an example the question of 5 + 7 / 3 (or 5 + 7 : 3 as it's presented in the game) where the choices are 6.5, 7.3, and 9.3 is a lot easier than it looks. All you have to do is say 5 + 2 and change, so 7.something, and the answer is B. I will say, though, these should probably not be introduced so early in the game. Easy mode shouldn't have multiplication or division at all, medium should only have multiplication but not division, hard should have division that results in whole numbers only, and fractions should only start to appear in the hardest mode.

I watched the preview and picked up this game for my kids. On easy, even my youngest in first grade should be able to play (even if not well yet, but that's the point). There are in game power ups that are extremely easy to unlock (let a parent play on easy once) that extend the timer and allow additional mistakes. On hardest this reaches a point that is even challenging for me. It takes a second to think about some of the equations and you have to be able to read what cancels as you go to keep pace with the timer. The operations aren't hard, but you do have to be able to do them quickly on the highest difficulty. Good for the kids, but a worthwhile challenge if they want parents to jump in as well.
So I'm not misleading anyone about the difficulty, here are examples of the math involved:
9+1 with a 13 second timer (Easy, early question, in game power ups applied)
5+9:5-12+46  with a 5 second timer (Hardest, late question, no power ups applied)
With that one you basically have to read 7-12+46=41 then look at the options of 37.8, 41.8, 40.8 and realize that 9:5 is < 2, giving 40.8 as the answer very quickly. However, all the questions are multiple choice, so if math isn't your strong suit and you are running low on time you can blindly guess with a 1/3 chance of getting it right.

Weirdly fun, and surprisingly cute.  It's not much of a game, but it's worth the low price of admission.
Unless you hate math, anyway.  That could take the shine off of it.

Cowboy zombie is a game in which you have to count quickly, it uses additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions and negative numbers.
The very first few levels the game is enjoyable. Doing something like 10*7+4 in 5 seconds is reasonable. But this game... is way too difficult for the average human being. You see, i'm good at mental maths, but this game is impossible for me past a certain point, do you know why?
Because the divisions they use, do not care for decimals at all. It could very well be 3/7 which equals to 0.428571... in the middle of an equation.
If you find it enjoyable and totally normal to do calculations like 4*2*7*13/35 in your head, then this game is for you. Otherwise i'm sorry, but it is just unacceptable to think an human is capable of doing such things within 2-5 minutes in the game, or, ever, for that matter.
The graphics are great but the music is repetitive, the sound effects are just a joke... The song is cool, but there could be more than one, at least, one for each difficulty perhaps...
The game is cheap at $1, so you are to choose if you want to purchase it or not, but beware, the game is extremely unfair.

A fantastic platformer filled with charm, replayability and some dead-hard time challenges. You must navigate your little yellow Pika babies to safety (by throwing them violently across the world) and then get there yourself. A plethora of enemies, switches and hazardous ooze stand in your way.
The first so many levels introduce you to the game quite comfortably, but the difficulty soon ramps up. Or rather, not the actual difficulty of completing levels, but the satisfaction of completing levels FAST and attaining Gold and Rainbow flowers.
In truth, almost all of the levels are fairly easy to complete, but the true underlying challenge here is to complete each level in a quick time, which earns you a Gold flower. If you complete the level faster than the time the developer set, you earn a juicy and illustrious Rainbow flower. However, almost ALL of the rainbow flowers are very difficult to earn. Patience, some key tricks you can perform which you will need to learn and master, and downright skill are needed to rack up all 110 Rainbow flowers.
If you are a fan of puzzle-platforming and have some keen quick reflexes, this is the perfect game!

This game doesn't play like other third person shooters, and even less like previous Resident Evil games. Instead, it's one of the most rewarding action games out there.
There's a reason why Mercenaries is unlocked from the start, because it's the best way to experience the huge variety of enemies and weapons. Make sure you practice parrying, because nearly every attack in the game can be countered. It's a fantastic risk/reward mechanic, since you're punished for doing it too early or too late, but when done right is the best way to take out most enemies, especially the bloodshots (skinless zombies).
Even though Vanquish is still my favourite third-person shooter, Resident Evil 6 fixes my two problems with that game, which are the harsh punishment for using melee moves and the lack of extra content.
Co-op is also implemented really well, but when playing in single-player your partner is never the burden they were in RE6. They have infinite ammo and health, and you don't have to worry about their inventory either. You're capable of holding plenty of weapons and ammo, so there's no need to use your partner to hold all the stuff you aren't using.

So, I was waiting for this game for some time and I can't honestly say it matched my expectations, it sure is not bad, thats why I recommend, but not as much fun as I was led to believe it would.
The game concept is completly absurd and I really like it, but there is much inconsistency about it, for such an abstract idea (I mean come on, we play as a guy cleaning up crime scenes while sneaking up behind the police) with some real weird mechanics (like when you hide in a bush when being chased, and thought they can crearly see you do that they stop chasing you, just because, or that freakin vacuum cleaner for blood) the game takes itself really seriously, the story has no fun in it whatsoever, is icredibly dull and it really doesn't match the general absurdity of the game. So the plot is the weakest element of the game.
Beside that game is pretty solid, the art style is great, although gameplaywise it tends to mislead the player, not always is it clear whether or not you can walk through some object, sure it isn't much of a problem, but it can be annoying. Music is another really strong aspect, not like its Hotline Miami, but it matches the tone and some of it is really enjoyable, and it actually sets some rhytm for the gameplay, so its way better build into the game mechanics than the graphics.
When it comes to finally playing the game, it is a fine way to spend a few hours, I found it really satisfying when after trying for half an hour I have finally beaten one of the final levels.
