Overall, it is a solid game and if you like stealth games you would probably enjoy it, so why not give it a try? Just don't expect it to be a lifechanging experience

Short version: An amazing 2D stealth game where fighting is not an option, but instead you clean up after the fight, which leaves for much more exciting gameplay than the actual fights would be.
Story: The story is not the highlight of this game, but it isn't anything that is going to dampen my opinion of this game. The story is simple, you are in debt to the mafia, and in order to pay them back you clean up after their/other's crimescenes. Two of the clients end up butting heads, which eventually leads up to a challenging "boss fight."
Gameplay: In order to clean up the scene of the crimes you would have to dispose of the bodies, grab key evidence, and mop up some blood. The only issue is, there are cops everywhere. There are objects to hide in, barriers to move to change their course throughout the area, and objects that you can activate to make noise to atract their attention. To complete each level you must sneak by the cops and clean up the area, which I found to be a lot more fun than I thought I would have.
Stealth: Every time I opened up a new chapter I always scanned the map to see potential hiding places and try to come up with a plan before I dove in. If I messed up the plan, I would have to hide and almost always have to ditch my original plan to avoid being spotted again. What made this game's stealth a lot of fun for me was how it didn't seem like it was too tedious to do. I never felt like it was a chore to start a chapter over if I got caught towards the end, and instead I actually found it to be fun.
, If found, the items and bodies would move a bit and I would be able to try a different course/adjust my first plan slightly.
Is it worth it?: Yes, it definetly is. For 15 USD it is a bargan for the intuitive style of gameplay and all the fun that comes along with it.
Side notes: I am not usually a fan of 2D games. I have really only liked a couple of them in the past, so me liking this game really says something. I would definetly recommend this game.

Thomas Was Alone is a minimalistic yet charming platformer that delivers an experience unlike any other of this genre. Beauty in simplicity.
This is a wonderful game if you want just unwind and listen to a lovely soundtrack for a while. The story, centered around several artificial intelligences with distinct, if simplistic, personalities, is more absorbing than I expected it to be. I really started to grow attached to the characters and found myself playing for hours, hoping to finally reach the resolution. Speaking of which, the game may be a tad over-long. A story is only really satisying once the end is reached and this story seems to have two endings. The first ending is really touching and sweet and rounds things off nicely. The "actual" ending is somewhat confusing and left me wondering if I should be disappointed or intrigued.
Overall, the game is beautifully crafted, but I feel like it over-reaches itself. After the larger bit with the main characters, the game keeps going, introducing a slew of new characters, all interesting and enjoyable, who could have been made the focus of their own game. In this game, however, they don't really serve a clear purpose.
I still definitely recommend the game for its beautiful character development. It takes real talent and effort to make an audience care about visually nondescript geometric shapes and Thomas Was Alone pulls it off fantastically.

Thomas Was Alone is a fairly straightforward puzzle platformer with one of the most entertaining stories I've come across in ages. Yahtzee of Zero Punctuation fame wrote a novel called Mogworld that centers around the AI and NPCs of an RPG becoming self-aware, and TWA follows a similar track. Couple that with a number of soft plot twists that develop intriguing characters out of colored blocks and a string of underplayed jokes that keep you smiling throughout the experience, and you get a game that offers a truly enjoyable experience from begining to end. Some parts will make you rethink your strategy, but never will the end goal seem unachievable. There's just enough of a challenge intertwined with an amusing and intelligent story that I'd find it remarkable for someone not to take pleasure in the overall process.

I have been playing guitar for about  25 years now. I have had some formal training, but mostly just years of playing in various bands and practicing and learning theory over time, so I feel qualified to write an honest review here.
Before I go on, I will say  bottom line, if you are thinking about getting this game but are unsure, get it...period, just get it.
I also want to note, I highly recommend picking up  2014 remastered and the orginal rocksmith along with the conversion tool. This gives you access to all the songs and DLCs (DLCS still have to be purchased) from both Rocksmith games all within the improved UI of Remastered  2014.
I will start with the Cons list because there are a few but I dont feel they in anyway have any kind of dramatic impact on my overall perception of the game, its gets most everything right and what it gets right, it usually nails spectacularly. So these cons are more of a want list
Cons.
*Being that the amps and tones are all emulations, there really isnt natural feedback of course. Playing live, you get accustomed to natural feedback from gain and it becomes a part of your playing, particularly with solos...this game compensates by emulating the sound when you perform the technique correctly on songs which is fine but when you are jamming in session mode there is no real sustain, vets will notice this right away.
*Not all songs are created equally. Most songs are well done and each part is an accurate representation. However there are some songs where parts are omitted or the ones provided are lacking. I can think of a few examples where there are two guitars playing on the song but the game only shows one part....even more puzzling is the same song in game may have an alt lead and alt rhythm but they are almost the same as the primary lead or rhythm part and also lack the tab for the phantom guitar track heard, but not demonstrated in the game.
One point to note on this, the game does not start off by displaying all notes, additional notes get displayed the more you play  what is shown correctly, you can also manually choose what % of notes to display, this is NOT what i'm talking about above. Also, along the same thought, some songs are missing chord names for lead parts when they would be very helpful, its only after showing all notes at 100% and mucking around that I figure out a seemingly complicated part is really just picking two or three variations of the same chord.
*I find personally, despite Master Mode (which is really cool and helpful), with Rocksmith I do not retain songs I learn as well as I do when I have to sit down and figure them out myself (or consult sheet music). Something about being spoon fed what to play (and possibly a lifetime of lifestyle activities not conducive of improving short term memory) allows you to master a song without always retaining it.
*There should be some kind of chord and or tab bank on songs, a page where I can see all the chords or tab  for a song I am learning in one overview kind of like the way you would read sheet music, as opposed to only being able to see what I have to play right now.
* I would also love to see a scale mode....pick a scale and mode and be fed notes from all the positions in that scale/mode.
*The DLCs can get expensive, that is one benefit of getting on steam instead of console though. Recently Steam had a half of sale and for $20, I picked up roughly 15 new songs.
Pros
* It works. You see what to play in real time and when you play, you are playing that guitar part just as it sounds on the album. Its Rock Band or Guitar hero with real guitars.
*Incredible song list, over a 1000 songs spanning our favorite genres . KUDOS to the team as well as they are literally releasing new DLCs every week. Its not all mainstream radio friendly stuff either, the team behind getting bands to sign up and choosing the songs have pretty good taste in music. I was surprised to tracks from Dinosaur Jr, the Dead Weather and Tame Impala when i first got this.
*Out of the box, the settings are geared toward a new player. But i was happy to see I could fine tune the settings to fit my personal expertise which includes things like setting skill level which affects how many notes are displayed initially and how fast it escalates or settings that flip the neck display so it better resembled tab.
*Loads of technique tutorials that are extremely well done (a video of someone demonstrating then it gives you a riff to play and you follow along like a regular song)and some of the mini games are super fun and really do help with technique
*Huge fan of Master Mode - when you first start a song, not all notes are displayed, as you hit the notes presented to you correctly, more notes are shown until eventually you are playing every note in the song. With all notes (i.e. the entire song) displayed, as you get better and hit most of the notes with proper phrasing, it stops showing any music so you memorize the song. With Master Mode, you quickly (more or less depending on skill level) start playing basics of a song to playing the song as its played on the album without needing to see any music/notes.

It's a pretty good game for beginners, and will ease your stress about beginning for a while. The only problem it has, is the same as all other "learn quickly" tools, eventually the experience will be compromised by technical issues. A Realtone cable and microphone will never replace an actual amplifier and pedals; but still a great experience and some of the better DLC for a guitar game currently around. If you're thinking about getting a guitar and finally getting serious about learning, this is a great first step, just keep in mind, this is a stepping stone. You will learn much better and more rapidly/accurately here than you could spending money on Rock Band's pro guitar kit; plus you'll have an actual guitar that you can use outside the game. Pick yourself up a small amp and a guitar for a few hundred bucks and start practicing. The lessons are pretty well paced and after a time, you will get better at the techniques naturally, just make sure to practice without the game too. 10/10 for beginners, runs on probably a complete potato PC; intermediate and advanced guitar players, will probably show up the leader boards, and even if the tabs and tracking are better than some of the options available, they might be annoyed by the amount of content that they are already familiar with.

Rocksmith was the kick that truly got me into practicing playing the guitar.
Usually I'd be reading books about theory and trying to practice tabs of songs, while it made me a novice, I never
got anywhere with that. I couldn't do that for hours- , practicing chords, looking at tab notes trying to play it, rechecking, trying to understand why I keep ♥♥♥♥ing up etc. It just didn't provide the intensity of practice an in-depth class or hours of practice with fellow musical aspirants does. With theory I didn't really understand the terminology until I got my hands dirty with doing it in practice. Diminished fifths, sharps, flats, harmonics, tonics, semitones, oh god, what?
I'd say if you're practicing guitar: The more you spend not playing it, the faster you're going to get disenchanted with it. You can memorize all the note positions on the fretboard (BC EF don't have sharps between them, everything else does) , chords etc. but it's like getting a bunch of tools but never really understanding fully how to use them. To get anywhere with guitar playing, you really need to practice at least an hour a day. Rocksmith gives you the medium to accomplish that.
While rocksmith 2014 does not go in-depth into reading music or advanced music theory, it gives you the tools and yearning to research and get into music on your own. For example, I never really understood what scales were until I was shown the bare basics in the Session Mode; a whole new world opened up for me. It actually shows you the positions of the scale notes and playing those notes pretty much makes you sound like you're playing music with your band! Practicing jamming with songs or your digital band improves your sense of rythm and melody. The lessons teach you about different techniques you can improve your "phrasing" with, such as tapping, sliding, double stops, hammer ons/offs and so forth.
To put it simply, I never loved playing the guitar until rocksmith taught me how to love. Now I can't stop talking about guitars.
You have very small repertoire of songs you can practice on, unless you're willing to fork out tons of money on DLC (Really, all the rs2014 DLC is $4000 total). You can download custom songs from sourceforge, but you'll need to purchase at least one official DLC song for that to work. You can find the instructions on how to do this from sourceforge's site.
You need an expensive custom cable to hook up to your guitar in order to play this game. Though, on the positive side is, the cable can be used outside of rocksmith if you want to dab into recording and mixing guitar for fun.
You will need an actual guitar to play this game; acoustic, electric or bass. For not horrible and potentially hazardous quality, you will need to invest at least $100. Bear in mind that a decent guitar costs at least $300. I strongly advize against buying those 20 dollar fenders from alibaba.
To summarize, be absolutely sure and committed to playing the guitar to enjoy this game.

This is an first impression review, after playing like about an hour.
Most important thing: Buy the Ubisoft Real Tone cable and dont try another one. I did, and its only a mess. Ubisoft cable works perfectly, plug & play. The other calbe didnt work.
Second: People are complaining about delay. THIS IS JUST NOT TRUE. Maybe it depends on your overall system setup. Maybe you play too slow. Maybe you dont grasp the display and when to play. I didnt exerience any delays yet. Timing is good.
In the beginning the display is not easy to understand. I had the impression that they dont explain much and just throw you into the cold water. So you try to hit the right tones and understand the display while playing. Its ok, because you need to put some effort in terms of thinking and attention into it. So its a bit challenging in terms of usability in the first place. But its not bad and I had the impression its all thought through quite carefuly.
The software is quite smart. I tried the lead guitar mode. You pick a song you like. And it makes you play single tones of that song, but with a lot of time distance between the tones, so you have enough time to undestand what to do and when and find the right tone to play. When you get better or are good already the software increases the density of the tones successively and according to your progress. Quite smart.
Fun thing is: When you hit the right tones or several in a row, the audience is screaming in the background. Quite nice. After you completed the song, the software might even praise you. :D
The strings you have to play have different colors in the display, which is nice since it connects your visual imagination with your hearing. I like that very much. The whole experience also improves connecting listening, playing and singing at the same time. It really makes you want to sing and play all at once. Its all quite encouraging and makes your neurons connect and firing.
A small minus is, that for advanced players it might be interesting to see where to put several of your fingers at once, so you could increase the speed of playing and switching from one tone to another. The display only shows you single tones to play and if you dont know in advance where to put your fingures and are not experienced how this usually works you dont know how to play it fast enough.
Hence, I think the software cannot stand for its own. Its an addon to other. more traditional sources of learning. Get to know tabs or get a teacher or online learning.
I think the software is good to either learn some basics or have it as a kind of addon and it is a different playing experience with the features of connecting different of your senses. It makes you practice and play a bit, its fun to do and gives you some motivation and smiles.
Hence, it's a smart software with some nice features and ideas to it and I like it. For beginners it might be a good basic start and for advanced players a nice addon or different experience with some benefits to it.
If I had to rate it would get a grade "B"or maybe like a 7.5 out of 10.

Well, i was having fun... was. See, the problem is, no one likes living near a dead body... and boy does this game have lots of those. If someone dies in a building, be it a one room bungalow or a 60 story high-rise, the city (thats's you) needs to dispose of the body. You can either cremate them or bury them, but you better do it quick. Otherwise, the building will become abandoned. Oh, and if that happens, so will the building next door (because no one wants to live near an abandoned building, either). And the building next door to that one will be abandoned and the one next door to that... You get the point. You might be thinking "no problem, I'll just build more cemeteries and crematoriums". That's what i thought, too. After a while, I noticed my hearses weren't picking up any dead bodies. They just seemed to be driving around willy-nilly, right past the buildings with corpses in them, and RARELY ever stopped to grab the corpses on the way by. It got to the point (since by now I had an almost $2 million cash surplus) that i was building crematoriums directly next to the infected building (that's next to EVERY infected building) in the hopes that it would curb the swell of whatever epidemic i was dealing with, but to no effect. I thought "very well then, I'll bulldoze every affected building." And I did exactly that until almost nothing was left of my city. The death wave never stopped. Now, I have no city. And I'm familiar with the effects of pollution and proper medical facilities, and the effect of traffic on various systems, etc. I'm not new to the Cities franchise, and I have read enough and played enough to know how not to mess up that badly. My conclusion-this game is glitched, possibly to the point of being uplayable. If you plan to buy this game, then you should also plan to mod it, or at the very least, wait until a patch is released that fixes some of the more glaring problems, such as total-city death. Yes, total-city death can definitely ruin your day.

100 levels of platforming and baby throwing of cuteness. You play as a mother Pikachu thing that needs to get her babies out the door and then get out herself. To do this, you can pick them up, throw them to the left or right, jump, hit switches and so on. You can even put them down on switches or on door blocks so when you hit the switch, the door holds open. When thrown, the babies go across the screen until they hit something then they fall. That lets them be used to hit triggers from far away. When carrying a baby, you can't jump as high, nor can you fit through small gaps as you normally can when not carrying them. If one baby doesn't make it, then you merely restart the level with the quick restart button.
Even if the music and art style weren't top notch, this would be a great puzzle game. Most every level is only a single screen and you will blow through 40+ levels before you reach a real challenge. Not every level is meant to be a challenge though. Some are very simple to show new techniques and others are just fun in general. Each completed level unlocks others, but you can go in order and just keep playing the next level. It adds to the flow of the game. The levels are quick, simple, engaging and rewarding; all with a dose of adorability. Each level has a par time and keeps track of your best time. In fact the game shows you your ghost when you replay levels that you have completed.
Eventually, throwable rocks, adorable enemies, breakable blocks, crayon colored deadly traps and angled trampolines that change thrown baby directions get added to the mix. Throwing your babies into the adorable enemies is a way to stun them. Its a good way to keep amping up the challenge and diversity between level to level. Remember baby, mama loves you, no matter how much she throws you against the wall or into the face of a giant lizard.
This game goes by quick, and to pad it out, there is a level editor, along with the ability to download countless other levels made by other users. There's a lot of engaging fun here, but it all goes by so quick and virtually effortless that it feels like there's no reason to come back. 5 minutes of play can complete 10 levels.

I feel like this game serves as a nice contrast to the previous game I’ve played,
. It really highlights that you don’t need the prettiest graphics in the world to tell an emotionally engaging story.
While
managed to wallow in its narrative without ever drawing me into it in spite of its gorgeous scenery,
was able to make me care about a bunch of colored rectangles. This is the ultimate difference between good and bad video game writing. That, and the fact that the mechanics actually support the narrative instead of being a grudgingly accepted necessity of something being considered a game.
Each of the rectangles has a very clearly defined character and their abilities and shapes reflect their characters. This is interactive storytelling done right, because you end up using these characters in ways that feel congruent with their personalities. I’d even go so far and wager that this game does better character “roleplaying” than most RPGs, since their mechanics and abilities are so tightly intertwined with who they are. It’s an intriguing game that manages to take simple mechanics used in tons of Flash games – this having been one at some point in the past as well – and make them evocative in and of themselves. And I remind you, these are mere rectangles we’re talking about, they have no faces and they never speak themselves.
This is obviously helped with the excellent narration. And I know that in recent times, narration has become a go-to element for young indie developers in an attempt to connect on a more profound way with the player. Basically every walking simulator has narration and you could probably name half a dozen games as well just off the top of your head. But this is one of those cases where the narration intensifies the storytelling experience. It’s not used merely for expository purposes, it’s an integral part of the game.
That is not to say that I consider this game perfect. I feel like it’s a bit too long for its own good, even at barely 3 hours. The mechanics are fairly simple to understand and a few of the puzzles seem like Mike Bithell (am I the only one who desperately wants his name to be pronounced bit-hell?) is stretching the content to achieve an even 10 levels per level set to present 100 levels to the player. And certain levels can get a little frustrating as well. Some start off by showing you where you need to bring each of the characters, but some don’t and as a result it can get disorienting when you’ve managed to get one character to their goal and realize that you’ll be needing its unique mechanic to advance with a different character. I would’ve loved an option to zoom out and see the entire level at once with the goals highlighted.
But I don’t want to end this critique on a negative note so I’ll say that the soundtrack deserves special mention, since it so very nicely supports the narrative of the game and the personalities of the characters. It’s a gorgeous mix of orchestrated sounds and chiptune music that serve as the icing on the cake. While the
might not be perfect, it’s still a pretty damn excellent game regardless of its very few faults.
If you want a good story and don't mind slightly tedious level design, this game is for you.

Rocksmith 2014 is the absolute best way to learn to play guitar (and/or bass guitar). In my opinion, that makes it the best game ever!
7 years of drums/percussion in middle and high school. 2 years of "ukelele band" in elementary school. Zero knowledge of guitar-playing -- I didn't even know if I was holding the pick right when I started Rocksmith. I've now logged ~300 hours between original Rocksmith and Rocksmith 2014. And I'm still loving it (just played multiplayer with a buddy for 2 hours tonight).
Original Rocksmith was buggy and lacked a real "Riff Repeater", but I liked the focus on points and leveling -- it kept you trying to improve on specific sets of songs until you could perform them (at a certain level of skill).
What sets Rocksmith 2014 apart is 1) the Riff Repeater, and 2) Session Mode.
The "Riff Repeater" lets you pause a song, increase or decrease the difficulty and speed of sections of the song whenever/however you want. When you successfully play those parts on the speed/difficulty you chose, it can increase the difficulty and/or speed up automatically. This is perfect for learning new songs or working out the kinks in those tricky solos.
Now, "Session Mode" could be sold as a $20 game in and of itself: you pick the key, tempo, chord progressions, and backing instruments and start jamming away. The notes in your key and current chord are highlighted; the backing instruments (and there's a wide selection to choose from) will accompany your play style/syncopation. It's great for working on solos, rhythms, etc. (I wish the beginner guitar player in the high school jazz band had access to this!)
And Rocksmith 2014 keeps getting better! The "remastered" edition released recently includes tweaks to improve sorting and organizing your songs and favourites.
* Borrow your friend's electric guitar -- at least until you realize that you adore guitars. Then buy one on Craigslist.
* Commit to "60 days of rocksmith": play at least 15 minutes every day for 60 days. Take videos of your progress!
* After a few weeks, use your standard guitar to play "emulated bass", realize you adore bass, then buy one on Craigslist.
* Buy amps, pedals, and mics to build your own music studio.
* Get your friends to try Rocksmith, get hooked, buy their own guitars, and play multiplayer Rocksmith with them.
* Find a decent drummer and -- presto! -- you've got a cover band. :D
* World peace ensues.
* When I first tried to memorize a song above my skill level (Carry on my Wayward Son), I realized that my technique was counter-productive. Instead of memorizing, try to work on "sight reading" in Rocksmith first. (After completing my first "60 days of rocksmith", I set the "Level Up" difficulty to "faster".)
* Once you've built your chops a little bit, you can more easily return and pick up those awesome songs you love!
* To help with sight reading and chop-building, I usually choose "Nonstop play" mode, set to 20-30 minutes (often set to my faves).
* Keep a few of the Rocksmith DLC in your Steam wishlist so that you can get alerted/emailed whenever there's a sale (which happens several times a year for about 40% off each song DLC). I usually pick up a few more DLC songs/song packs whenever there's a sale.
* Setting a milestone (like a song you want to master) is a great way to stay committed. Also, doing the "60 days" with someone else can help you stay committed.
* Lastly, I recommend picking up both original Rocksmith and the "Disc Import tool" because they let you play *most* of the original song selection and any original Rocksmith DLC you own inside Rocksmith 2014 (which gives you the better Riff Repeater).
* More Muse!!! (I need all the Muse!)

Offspring Fling has brought many nice surprises to me, starting from the first moments I played it.  It's a puzzle-platformer with adorable visuals, smart gameplay, and challenging puzzles, all without deterring the casual experience.
I bought this game with a Humble Bundle, mostly because I wanted some the more expensive deals I would get from buying the bundle, and there Offspring Fling sat in my library, uninstalled, until those goshdarn trading cards showed up, encouraging me to give it a shot.  It was during the opening credits that I suddenly noticed: this game was made by Kyle Pulver!  This isn't the first Kyle Pulver game I've played, and I think I'm going to start paying more attention to the guy.  He first caught my attention back in high school as I was looking for tips on how to create my own indie games.  I stumbled upon one of his other games called BONESAW and said to myself "yes, this guy gets it."  The controls were intuitive and fun, the story was minimalistic, and the gameplay, while reminding me retro beat-em-ups like Double Dragon, blew them all out of the water!
Now, I can safely say that Kyle Pulver hasn't lost his touch.  The game is adorable with its visuals, and brutal in its gameplay.  The puzzles are that special kind of retro-challenging, but the controls are spot on and never frustrating.  To 100% the game is a gaming challenge equal to that of some of gamings greatest achievements, and recommended only to completely insane individuals (like myself).  It's the kind of unique experience that reminds you of a simpler time in gaming, where gameplay innovation and a solid setting were enough to make you undergo the toughest challenges you've ever faced.  Great work, Mr. Pulver!

This game is simple; it's just geometric shapes overcoming little platformer challenges and puzzles with a single narrator telling their story. However, perhaps because of that simplicity it manages to deliver each of those elements in damn near perfect form.
Gameplay-wise, the jumping is excellent and responsive. The characters all handle differently, but intuitively. The puzzles range from too simple to genuinely challenging, but never become fun-killingly frustrating. Overall I found the game just challenging enough to keep me feeling accomplished as I progressed, without stumping me on any levels to the point of breaking the story's momentum. That's a difficult balance to hit, but this game hit it dead on. (Though, I feel I should add as a disclaimer that I'm not....super great at platformers. It is a possibility that more experienced puzzle-platformer players might find the game too easy overall. Even with my limited skills I found the puzzles pretty obvious more often than not.)
The story is what makes this game come alive, though. The writing and the narrator make these simple shapes absolutely burst with personality. I loved pretty much all of the characters, even the more incidental ones, and soon found myself deeply invested in the victories, tragedies, and love lives of a bunch of quadrilaterals. Admittedly there were a couple of points the plot lost me  (namely,
). The story is just as carefully balanced as the gameplay, giving the player elements of humor, despair, love, and hope in perfect proportion.
Overall this is a game that surprised me. I wasn't expecting such a polished experience wearing such a simple aesthetic. I'd definitely recommend anyone give it a shot (and in fact I loved it so much I've already purchased a copy for my best friend.) Even if you can't justify the full price (which I think it's worth on the merits of its narration alone) then
snap it up next time it's on sale.

Otherwise, here’s a write up.
In this game you play as Bob, a freelance cleaner hired to get rid of bodies and evidence. Most of the story is delivered in your house, which is the only other place you’ll be in besides mission areas. You’ll always return back to the house prior to any contract and during that time you can interact with things like the TV, newspaper, and radio to hear the news that either foreshadowing your next contract or reacting to your previous one.
Most of the initial contracts are self-contained events but towards the halfway point a common thread will start to link the jobs together. Plot wise, it’s straightforward and easy to follow, similar to Bob himself. He gets a little bit of depth in how he reacts to certain events but the game’s not trying to make him an incredibly layered character.
Instead, he’s mostly a mildly sarcastic person that makes as many puns and pop culture references as he does regular dialogue. Overall, it’s a simple story that suits the setting, but you shouldn’t expect anything profound here.
Serial cleaner is a fast-paced 2D stealth action game. Your main job is to dispose of any bodies and evidence lying around and sometimes you’ll even need to vacuum up the bloodstains. Besides using your vacuum, you can only walk around the area an interact with a select few objects and you’ll have to complete the level without getting caught be the police. Cops will give chase if they spot you in their cone vision and they can also be alerted if they happen to hear you (something to keep in mind is how you make more noise while carrying a body or when you’re using the vacuum cleaner).
Since you can’t outrun most of them, your only hope is to get to a hiding spot (one of the level’s items that can be interacted with) before they catch you. You can definitely exploit this mechanic since hiding in front of your pursuer doesn’t blow your cover but this is counterbalanced by the fact that the game later on introduces faster enemies, not to mention that a hiding spot isn’t always going to be where you need it.
Progression wise, the game’s 20 story contracts introduce new enemies and mechanics every 2-3 levels. You’ll eventually get to move items to make new paths, make loud diversions using items on the map, and even access shortcuts in the area, all of which are crucial as the game ramps up in scale and complexity. You can keep track of them by using the Cleaner vision which essentially zooms out of the map to show you all the important items.
Enemies in turn include stationary foes that signal a group of cops to your last known position, faster grunts and guards that will shoot you on sight. Variety aside, one of the good things SC has is decent AI. While cops do have their initial patrol patterns, they’ll immediately change them to investigate any missing body or pieces of evidence. This is also the case when you move objects to block their path so it’s not as simple as just memorizing all their patrol routes since there is quite abit of variation to take into account.
The game is fast-paced in that you need to act quick when you’ve been spotted but it also rewards patience. Taking things slower is key to understanding enemy behavior and the levels themselves since each portion of the area normally has at least 2 entry points, so you’re not getting shoehorned into any particular path.
For replay value, you have 2 options. You can complete bonus contracts (10 in total), provided you unlock them by finding special items in the story levels, or you can undergo challenge mode which allows you to play all previous levels with unique restrictions. These include things like disabling cleaner vision and completing the level without ever being spotted.
Take that into account with the nice amount of progression, the emphasis on player choice through level design and the competent AI and SK is an enjoyable experience with quite abit of longevity.

Serial Cleaner es un juego de sigilo, con pinceladas de acción y puzzles en 2D, donde somos un Cleaner ("Limpiador" al traducirlo a Español); dicho apodo se le da a quien trabaja para deshacerse de evidencias y cuerpos de personas que fallecieron bajo alguna situación donde mediara el crimen. 
Nuestro personaje lleva el nombre Bob, o 'Bobby', como le llama su mamá, pero en el bajo mundo donde trabaja, es conocido como Cleaner. Bobby, es hogareño, solo sale para hacer su 'trabajo' y de vez en cuando va a jugar a las cartas con su amigo (y compinche) Joe. Bobby tiene un gran apego por su madre, se preocupa por ella, pasan mucho tiempo juntos viendo la televisión, y en especial, aman las peleas de boxeo. Los diálogos en general son entretenidos, y podemos interactuar con el televisor, la radio, y el periódico cuando estamos en casa, estos tres objetos siempre hablaran de cosas relacionadas con el argumento del juego y se vuelven un complemento interesante. A Bob le encanta coleccionar las evidencias que toma de las escenas de crimenes, y guardarlas en sus cuarto a modo de premios y recordatorios de sus hazañas.
Las mecánicas del juego son muy simples, camina, escóndete, recoge, limpia (literal) y lleva el cuerpo al auto. Así podríamos resumir Serial Cleaner. Su tono setentero y su estilo visual le vuelven lo hacen estéticamente llamativo, con un acabado parecido a cartón. Tiene una trama diminuta que le da un sabor especial, con ese aire de antaño que el desarrollador busca resaltar, y lo logra con éxito. Sumado a nuestro trabajo de recoger cuerpos y recolectar evidencias incriminatorias, tendremos la misión de limpiar la sangre de las escenas de los crímenes, y para esta tarea contamos con una super aspiradora chupa sangre. 
Los escenarios en el juego son variados, encontramos oficinas de periódicos, locaciones en bosques, granjas en las afueras de la ciudad, o el parque de alguna ciudad violenta. El juego ofrece una mecánica que nos permite mover objetos en los niveles, por ejemplo algún vehículo, puertas, etc, con el fin de alterar los patrones de vigilancia de los policías que custodian las escenas. Hay cajas de cartón, armarios y uno que otro conjunto de objetos que pueden servirnos de escondite en los diferentes mapas del juego.  
Cada policía cuenta con un rango de visión -siempre visible para el jugador, que nos permite establecer una ruta para poder evitar ser vistos. Además, podemos utilizar el botón LT en el mando de Xbox para tener una vista general del mapa desde arriba, donde podemos mirar toda la acción completa en el nivel, escondites, y lugares de importancia donde puede haber posibilidad de mover cosas. Si nos atrapan, toca comenzar todo el nivel desde cero.
Serial Cleaner tiene un sistema de spawn es aleatorio, lo que deriva en situaciones distintas cada vez que comenzamos una nueva partida o que reiniciemos un nivel por que perdimos o nos atraparon; este sistema hace que los cuerpos o evidencias que nos toca recoger, puedan aparecer en lugares distintos, lo mismo pasa con la sangre que nos toca limpiar en los escenarios.
El juego utiliza un sistema llamado Real-World Data, según el desarrollador del juego, este sirve para modificar los niveles de acuerdo con la hora actual del día en el lugar que se encuentre el jugador, este detalle se nota muy poco, y la verdad no tiene peso suficiente como para ser un gancho para el jugador. La exploración de los niveles siempre nos premiará con objetos escondidos y maneras divertidas de completar cada nivel.
Si tu sueño es encarnar a un personaje al estilo Ed de Breaking Bad, esta es tu oportunidad, con una jugabilidad sencilla, amigable y atractiva para todos los jugadores, Serial Cleaner es un buen Indie, no es fantástico, pero si lo agarramos en oferta es un buen trato. Directo, retador y de gran calidad visual, podemos recomendarlo.
Este divertido Serial Cleaner es desarrollado por el estudio independiente iFun4All S.A. y su editor es Curve Digital. Podemos encontrarlo en la tienda digital de Steam por $11.99 de momento en una oferta especial que acaba el 21 de julio, después tendrá un precio permanente de $14.99. De momento tiene una puntuación de Positive en la tienda de Valve, tras 39 análisis de distintos compradores.

Badly on the fence about this game, so consider this a cautious recommendation.
Downsides first:
- The gameplay is nothing to write home about. Basic mechanics are patrolling enemies with fixed patters and 'vision cones' plus some reaction to sounds and environment. Enemies are relentless and getting hit once means restarting the level.
- This is balanced by ridiculously cheaty 'hiding' system - you jump into a dumpster in plain view of three cops and they all go 'Huh, guess he beat us here, let's go back to stations'.
- The way storyline is presented (kinda) copies Hotline Miami 'back at your place' intermissions without being so laconic, forceful and remorseless. I guess this is more 'neutral' than downside.
Good stuff:
- Well, duh, artwork is nice, and the sounds don't make you want to turn them off immediately.
- Missions are pretty short and actually require some planning
- You can leave the game for a year and come back w/o needing to relearn metric ♥♥♥♥♥on of controls and mechanics.
My TL;DR would be, get this on sale and treat this lightly. This is the game to enjoyably kill half an hour here and there and then forget about the whole experience.

This is probably the most underrated game on steam.
There are so many people out there talking about how Cuphead might just be the best game that has come out in the past couple of years but I believe that Hyper Light Drifter is.
Many people adore the simple but beautiful graphics in Cuphead, and yes they are beautiful hand drawn animations, but I have to say this is one of the most beautiful games i've ever played. The gorgeous pixelated art style is just stunning and combined with the incredible soundtrack there are not many games that compare to this.
People also talk about the gameplay in cuphead and how difficult yet fun the gameplay it has, but then there is Hyper Light Drifter, with the satisfying and rewarding gameplay. It is also difficult like Cuphead but not AS difficult and rewards you with making precise movements and attacks to defeat all of the challenging bosses.
Lasty is the story. Yes I have talked about Cuphead a lot and it has many similarities but almost everyone who has played it knows about the story behind the game, like the developer actually selling his house to finish the game but this, the story behind Hyper Light Drifter is just amazing. The developer was born with a birth defect in his heart and always needs to think about it and he never knows how much time he has left until he dies, so he decided to make this game. He then incorporates his story into the story of the actual game following a character with death always following him and the ability to overcome some many challenges and it’s just amazing.
If you haven't yet, please try this game. Even if it's not on sale the money goes straight to the developers which is extremely helpful for them and they could possibly make a sequel. (Please make it happen) The only real complaint that you might face that I did is how many secrets there are. This isn't really a complaint though since it gives you so much to explore but it can be kind of tedious sometimes. But when you do find more secrets you feel accomplished so that's nice.
TLDR; Outstanding visuals/sound, gameplay and story = Must buy game

Hyper Light Drifter blows a lot of games out of the water when it comes to immersion, atmosphere, and presentation. The art direction of this game is absolutely nothing to understate--its pixel art, color design, and animation quality are all far above the standard, and its sound direction is an astounding, immersive feat itself. Every part of this game feels different, and every run will be different, despite the game not being rogue-like. The game can be taken in any order the player chooses and can be successfully beaten without upgrading your kit. Combat is solid and tight, encouraging melee bob-and-weave combat over gunplay by making ammo a resource based on hitting enemies with your sword, but allows you to use gunplay in between bursts of melee combat, and said gunplay is never necessary to complete the game.
This game is a masterpiece. God bless Alex Preston, god bless the team he lead at Heart Machine, and god bless the 24,150 kickstarter backers who funded this game to allow for its scope.

I played a little guitar in my 20's. Never got very good and while I never sold my 2 guitars I slacked way off for 15+ years. I still had some muscle memory for chords.  Got this game around Jan2014. This is a fun middle ground between Rock Band/Guitar Hero and real life. At this point I can plug in and have fun anytime. It definitely helps with motivation to practice. The dangers, that I have fallen into bigly, if you want to do more than just play a video game, include:
(1) keeping the Master Mode off and continuing to rely on the interface, when you should be MEMORIZING SONGS.
(2) skipping all the tutorials/lessons and guitarcade practice exercises. These will help you get better.
(3) plugging into your cheap Line6 or Squier amp and getting de-motivated because all the perfect guitar tones are in the game and not in real life
(4) learning poor technique and continuing in it because you 'made it work' in the game, but find it limits you when you want to play with more speed and complexity
(5) learning all kinds of rock stuff but gaining little exposure to other genres
But all that said, I continue to play the game week in and week out. It's definitely helped me get back into my instrument. It helped me learn bass which is so, so much fun. I highly recommend the song packs for Foo Fighters, Jimi Hendrix, classic blues and rockabilly, and Earth Wind and Fire.  The Remastered version brought some very helpful improvements. I really wish they would release more songs in non-rock genres, especially jazz, but I understand that Ubisoft has to make money and, and licensing can be difficult; and who knows how many people would buy 8-song packs of Django or George Benson or Jaco?
Bonus: you can use the Real Tone Cable with Garageband on MacOS. I assume it would work with similar software on Windows.
Now I'm taking baby steps into playing in the real world. It still takes discipline to learn and memorize stuff. Playing with real humans is (surprise) even more fun than the game. Also invest in a good amp - I'm borrowing a friend's inexpensive all-tube amp and it sounds so good.
Thank you Ubisoft for the game and continuing to support your user base.

If there is one thing Offspring Fling has going for it, it's charm. A childlike sensibility embodies every aspect of the game, from the beautiful crayon aesthetic to the heartfelt premise of a mother that has somehow misplaced here extremely numerous children. The music also does a good job at setting it apart, mixing classic 8-Bit sounds with classical instruments to great effect.
It's a shame then that the gameplay doesn't reach the same level, and in fact I found it rather dull and inconsistently challenging. This is mainly because of the jumping mechanics, which feel very much inspired by Nintendo's Kirby games (your character's appearance shares a striking similarity to him as well). They are simply too floaty and impressive for a game built so heavily around timing, and made some of the otherwise basic levels frustrating to complete. The spotty controller support didn't help, as anyone that has tried to play a platformer using a keyboard should understand.
If you can get past the controls you'll find a lightweight, mostly enjoyable puzzle platformer that never quite reaches its full potential, and is best appreciated in bite sized sessions to combat its somewhat repetitive design. If you are looking for a more well rounded experience however, you will probably be better served elsewhere.

Option to connect railway stations with Metro stations for a free transfer?

Railway stations with 2 middle tracks for trains passing through to bypass trains stopped at platforms?
Option to designate districts and/or neighborhoods as 24/7 centers of activity, such as entertainment, retail, bars, etc?

Just some suggestions that would make for a truly walkable, bikeable, and transit-friendly city.

Do not be fooled by the screenshots on the store page showcasing complex board states with multiple minions in formation.
The developers seemingly have no issue with the design of the game revolving around "Answer-or-die" threats kept only in check by cheap removal cards, having just printed an expansion featuring more of both.
Steer clear.

The Magmar faction reigns with too-strong minions and omnipotent removal, and any strategy has been removed in favor of gigantic swing cards that instantly win the game for you if you pull them off such as Alabaster Titan and Gate To The Undervault. Games have lost all tension because as soon as one of these is played the other person can just hit the escape key and concede instead of actually playing it out.

I definitely recommend that people give it a try if they enjoy these types of games.

Serial Cleaner is a unique original indie title where you take the role of a cleaner hired to clean up crime scenes by disposing of evidence and cleaning up blood. The game is currently in early access on Steam with more levels coming soon.
Serial Cleaner is a fun, fast-paced, puzzle game that feels unique compared to many other games in the genre. The graphics are beautiful with a 70's art style and the game feels challenging but not frustrating. However, the menus and control scheme are not well thought out and the game needs extra gameplay mechanics such as sneaking as the game feels basic at the minute. I would recommend the game to anyone who lives stealth games with a twist and don't get impatient quickly.
PROS:
+ Unique 70's art style
+ Challenging but not frustrating
+ Fun gameplay
+ Good level design
+ Music matches the mood
CONS:
- Bad control scheme
- Hard to navigate menus
- Only an hour or two of content
- Story behind the levels aren't clear

Yeah okay.  Changing this to a "Yes" from a "No".
Why did I start with no?  Well it has to do with threshold of pain.  Games shouldn't surprise players and then say 'well you should have read the manual' and you can read the full details of "No" way down there somewhere.
Reasons for "Yes"?  Because after you get past the surprises and understand the game - I think there's a good - maybe even awesome game in here.  Here are some pluses:
+ Massive tactical star battles that are player controlled.  Take that GalCiv.
+ Very deep and randomized tech tree.  This means some games will have more severe handicaps than others and you'll have to make due even when some tech isn't available.
+ Customizable ships.
~~~~~~~~~~~~ Ancient reasons for "No" below ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
This review was written to be sent on a time machine to the past to the "has not yet bought SotS2" younger, more innocent version of "huminado":  don't buy it.
And it's not because this isn't a great game.  Don't get me wrong - I like this game.  I like what the game is good at doing.  But I can't recommend it.  It's only to prevent myself that painful moment of having buyer's regret and believing I've been ripped off.
This will happen to most people who buy this game.  It might not be justified.  If they read the manual or the forums they might find out the game is fine, or they might run into other issues.
But I know that feeling of buyer's remorse.  If I can avoid it, even at the price of never playing a great game which has confusing surprises - I will.
To sum this review up: this game does not meet current standards of quality for TBS.  There's a very good chance players will run into problems which could easily be avoided if the game were finished.  In my case, if I had read the whole manual, I might have avoided an issue.  But I don't expect anyone to ever read a manual - I expect games to be intuitive on their own.
If you want the details, read my blog post on the anti-wiener game design pattern here:
------ Further observation ------
The longer I play the more it becomes clear reading the manual is not optional.  And some details are missing in the manual.  For example, the term PD is never explained, neither in the game, nor the manual, nor the wiki.  If you don't know what that term is (and maybe some people don't) - then you'll have to ask around.
I haven't played long enough to say, but this sort of missing detail doesn't mean bad game design, but it does mean assumptions are made about the player's level of expertise before they open the box.  It shouldn't discourage anyone from trying though.  I still have to give it thumbs down - at least until I see the game in a state that is more friendly to new players.

I have only one problem with this game:
Dynamic Difficulty.
If you are a beginner, TURN THIS OFF, IT WILL MAKE YOU HATE YOURSELF.
What Dynamic Difficulty does is, once you reach a certain level, it immediately bumps you up. For example, if you do OK on a 30% difficulty setting, even though you only played through it once and were decent,  the very next time it will be bumped to 50%, and I had no idea dynamic difficulty was on.
I kept thinking to myself, "I've been practicing for weeks, why the ♥♥♥♥ am I getting worse and worse and worse?"
And then I realized it's because the game was trying to bump me up to 100% difficulty within minutes. It will not wait for you no. I kept getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and discouraged because of this stupid, pointless feature. I never wanted to play guitar again until I finally learned what this poinltess, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ feature was. I love the game, and now that I can actually move at my own speed it's a lot more fun  and easy.
In short, dynamic difficulty is like an AP class, it will not wait for you to be caught up. If you can only play 20%, you'll do that once, get an okay performance, and then immediately the next time you play it will be changed to 40% difficulty, and if anyone here is like me, I can't learn 100% mastery in guitar in 3 hours from ground zero.
Horrible pacing and just a god awful feature to be automatically turned on, especially for beginners.
It'd be like after you beat a song on easy in guitar hero, the next song is medium, and then after that it's immediately switched to hard right afterwards. It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

Having Played Through The Main Missions and all of the side missions I can write a proper PC Review now.
Watch Dogs 2 has done what the first game couldn't which is meet expectations. It Gives us things that most other games this year couldn't and is easily one of the Top 5 games this year (opinion of course but to be honest it probably still is in this area). It offers the experience the first game should have offered but even better.
PROS:
The Port:
Lets think of one game this year that has had a really good PC Port, I'll tell you, There aren't many, Watch Dogs 2 has one of the best PC Ports this year which is why in terms of experience it was one of my favourites this year. I would always get a stable 60+ FPS never dropping at all. It runs smoothly and happily for me which is why unlike some other games with crap ports *cough* *cough* No Man's Sky, I can play it well and for long periods of time.
The Story:
The Story isn't top notch like for example Firewatch which is another candidate for my best game of 2016, but it is still good. I personally found the first Watch Dogs game to have good story but hey, Everyone has their own opinion. I liked the first game's story better than this one, but this one felt more unique. In the first game you simply went from one fight to the next, one hack to the next. In this game, it was more your choice. You Felt more like it was you doing these things. You would normally get 2 Main Missions to play and plenty of side missions which meant it felt like you were getting the choice. You really felt you were taking down all the corrupt companies and forces in this game which really appealed to me. The story is far from perfect but it is still quite good and worth playing.
Graphics:
Would you look at this? A game where Ubisoft didn't downgrade the graphics. The graphics look great in this game and if you want to go further and have a good PC you can get the Ultra HD Textures Pack. The game is beautiful in every way. All the textures really stood out to me and they enhanced the overall experience. If you want to know my specs I have a GTX 970, i7 6700K and 32GB RAM (more exact parts on my profile). The Graphics in this game are great and I'd wager one of the best games with these graphics that has come out this year.
Drones:
Something the first game didn't offer were these drones. These drones allowed you to do things you could never do in the first game which is really explore the layout of where you are trying to go. You can even use drones to do almost everything for you sometimes. They are really fun to use, especially the quadcopter (Have to buy that from 3D Printer) seeing as it can fly and gives the best view of the land around you. They add an element that the first game didn't have which was diversity of playing mechanics. With the drones you could distract people, hack things that you can't get to and even kill enemies (need an upgrade). The Drones are really fun and unique in this game.
The Driving:
Thank heavens. The Driving in this game is brilliant, better than the first game by a long shot. When you drive around you can actually get where you want to go relatively unscathed. It is very smooth and a lot more fun. It is very useful in car chases which is good that it is fixed.
The Open World:
If you included all the water, I think this map might be bigger or the same size as GTA V. Don't take my word for it. The game is huge, beautiful and far more memorable than Chicago was. With the big open world, the nice graphics and the good driving. It felt nice to just drive around everywhere rather than fast travelling which is always fun to do. It has a lot of unique environments and hey if you watched IEM Oakland you can visit the Oakland Arena (Blume Arena In-Game) and just take a look. You can visit the nudle campus (google of watch dogs) and steal the nudle car. You can do a lot of fun things in this massive open world. Edit: Isn't bigger than GTA V
Hacking:
There was a lot more options in this game regarding hacking.  In the first game you usually had like one option per hackable object. In this game you have four options in for almost everything. There is also a lot more to hack, vehicles for example is a great touch. You feel more how the game wants you to feel. In a world where you can hack pretty much everything.
Customisation:
The Customisation in this game was great. You could choose all kinds of clothing to wear, all kinds of skins (there aren't very many but still quite a few) to use with your weapons and drones that make the player feel like everything is theirs. Their clothes, Their guns, Their drones. It adds that bit of customisation which players will really like which is always great to see in a game and something that the first game didn't really use.
Negatives:
Enemy AI:
This always bugged me in my experience. The AI was always rather odd in certain situations and sometimes just unthinkably annoying. Sometimes an enemy would just lock on to me when he couldn't see me and kill me. Also the heavily armoured enemies are annoying if you don't have a good weapon. I have sometimes shot them 10 times in the face and they wouldn't die. This isn't really an issue but I thought I would address it.
Vehicle Distinctness and Variety.
There seemed to be a lot more vehicles then the first game but the problem I had with this game is that a lot of the vehicles looked very similar to even the same meaning there were barely any distinct features to tell them apart. The Performance cars were identifiable but apart from some motorbikes they were really the only ones. This isn't much of an issue either but it means the game has less memorability.
Conclusion:
Watch Dogs 2 succeeds where the first game failed and gave us a much better and more fun experience to enjoy. There are some negatives that may may annoy some people but from this PC port and the game itself comes an experience worth having.

My experience primarily from PS4 version (Focusing on gameplay, not performance) it is running great on my PC though - specs on my profile.
+Drones are incredibly fun and useful. The quadcopter should be your first purchase (second purchase after pants). Some missions can be completed entirely with the RC Jumper, it makes for more dynamic ways to take on missions.
+Fun new skills like hacking vehicles and calling gangs/cops on people.
+Co-op is great fun, you can team up and complete co-op missions, hacking events or just run around collecting moneybags/research points.
+I love the atmosphere, San Francisco looks incredible (even better on PC). Not to mention you can use the slides at Goo-uh, Nudle.
+Driving. I’m throwing driving up here, I’ve had no problems with it. Engine Override (boost) skill is great too.
+Very lenient achievements/trophies, was able to platinum it in no time at all (And I’ve only managed to platinum one other game).
+Story was definitely a step up from watch dogs and had a much brighter tone to it. It does get slow at times.
-The alert system is WTF: You can sneak around but the moment one guard (or dog) sees you, everyone will INSTANTLY be alerted of your whereabouts, even if you take them out a microsecond after they notice you. I assume the guards must press a button to alert everyone but the dogs!?
-The dialogue can get VERY cringe worthy at times. Some of the witty banter just comes off as awkward.
-Unfortunately missions can’t be replayed (aside from co-op ones). And, like in GTA V, many restricted interiors become inaccessible after a certain mission.
-The streets felt empty at times (on ps4 at least).
-No Steam achievements, only UPlay.
*Most missions are essentially ‘sneak into a restricted area, do something, sneak out’. Some may find it repetitive. Personally, I enjoy the challenges and like to try out different ways to tackle a mission.
*The controls (on gamepad) might take some getting used to, it's a little different from WD1. Expect to be pulling out a gun instead of your phone.
*The stun gun is very OP, especially once you research the “Amp Up” upgrade for it later on. I’m not complaining considering the alert system.

If you're looking for a difficult platformer  mixed with some puzzling, look no further.  On the other hand, the gap between the time-based ranks is sizable and may not be worth the required mastery and time, but the regular difficulty is still  enjoyable.
People who will truly love Offspring Fling: speedrunners and difficult game enthusiasts.   People who will probably like it quite a bit: puzzle fans, average players,  and fans of games done with retro sensibilities. Check it out some time.

While I was more than a bit skeptical when first launching the game, Serial Cleaner is one of those few games this years that honestly took me by surprise, in terms of underestimating its quality. It's by no means a perfect game, but features a really unique concept and lot of really interesting gameplay mechanics. Both the game's art style and gameplay manage to feel the same: Simplistic without being boring.
Pros:
-Great artstyle.
-Detailed environments.
-Challenging gameplay that revolves heavily around strategy and timing.
-Funny sound effects.
Cons:
-Some levels, such as the newspaper building level, offer too few hiding places, and can feel too linear in design,
while others are wonderfully open-ended.
-The movement speed of the police feels too punishing, and should be adjusted so they start off slower, but built up speed, giving the player a second or two to hide before the police are able to run at superhuman speeds, as they do now.
-The player's ability to distract police is limited exclusively to re-locating bodies or crime scene items. In the future, there should be additional ways to very briefly distract police. In short, a high-risk high-reward tool.
Overall:
A very fun, enjoyable game, that could easily become addictive, assuming it receives some mild re-balances and small gameplay improvements.

More bugs than an crackhouse mattress and crashes like a drunk chimpanzee in a demolition derby.  It gobbles down memory and then leaks it back out in a hundred places.  As we all know it was released unfinished.  Now, years later, it is still not finished and clearly never will be.
The saddest thing is that even if all of these problems were fixed it still wouldn't be a good game.  Clunky interface, a UI that is more concerned with neon than functionality, and a plethora of just plain bad design decisions make you wonder how the same people who created the masterpiece that was the original Sword of the Stars could live with themselves after putting their names on this overpriced disaster.
You can forget about balance anywhere.  Races, ships, technology, pirates, the economy - everything in this is completely out of alignment in some way or another.  Tutorials?  What are those?  The manual seems to have been written for a different game and is more concerned with giving background fiction than any usuable information.
Worst of all is that somehow, despite all the shiny new graphics and toys, they've made combat both look and play worse than the original (which was actually very good, by the way).
Metaphorically speaking, SotS2 is someone looking at a sports car that was SotS1 and saying "You know what this thing needs?  A piano tied to the roof!  Yeah!  And we'll save weight by removing one of the tires!"
Note that in sharp contrast the original SotS1 is a very good game, and I advise anyone considering this one to go buy that far superior product instead.  You won't regret SotS1.  You will regret this one, however.

Resident Evil 6 is a solid, powerful and substantial game that I never get tired of playing again and again, even after the three and a half years that have passed since its original release. Maybe not the perfection that Resident Evil 4 was, but Resident Evil 6 is very close to that.
We get to play as three of our long-known and favourite characters (Leon, Chris and Ada) plus a new addition to the saga, which is Jake, Wesker's son. As an alternative, you can also play the three main campaigns (Leon, Chris and Jake) with the characters' partners (Helena, Piers and Sherry), which is recommended as the experience is very different with them. Unlike the bad partner programming in Resident Evil 5, in this game the partners never cause you problems, they have their own inventory and they come to your rescue whenever you need them. But overall the gameplay is excellent anyway; each character has their own fighting style, others are quicker (Leon, Piers) others have better melee (Helena, Sherry) or are great at going stealthy (Ada).
There are four main difficulty levels, ranging from piece-of-cake kind of easy (Amateur) to really tough stuff (Professional) plus an additional extra hard mode (No Hope) which is basically of the Professional level, but without any perks and skills.
The story of the game is divided in four main sub-stories, and at some point these stories intersect. As a result, there are a few stages that you have to go through more than once (ie, you have to fight the mutated Deborah with Leon and then with Ada, or the creepy Ogromen with Chris and then with Jake). This may get slightly boring after some time, and there's a possibility that these particular stages may feel like a chore. However this doesn't really take the fun away, if you think about it, because with each character you may have to apply slightly different strategies and this is very interesting and enjoyable.
Atmosphere-wise, each campaign has a different feel: Leon's campaign is a strong reminiscent of the classic Resident Evil games, with all the zombies infesting the towns, the labs, the cemeteries and the cities and what not (there is even a police car to make your escape, and the - almost always present in zombie-themed stories - gas station in the first chapter), Chris's campaign on the other hand has a dominant feeling of war, mostly due to the overwhelming flashback, Jake's campaign is a refreshing change of pace with the two chartacters being constantly on the run and Ada's campaign is a lonely journey of our lady spy (well, unless you play co-op in which case you have a nameless and speechless soldier for partner) through most of the places that we have seen with the other characters.
Back to the gameplay, which is particularly important in this game, everything works perfectly; however there are a couple of situations and quick-time events that may cause issues. I don't know if these are bugs or something random, but I found out that in these cases fiddling with the screen resolution and/or the FPS fixes the problem. Other than that, the game is almost flawless; each character has unique melee attacks and counter attacks and a special weapon or fighting skill, and there's decent variety in weaponry as well. There are also many moves, other attacks and finishing moves that you can perform, plus the amazing quick-shot, which can be executed in different styles and ways depending on the character you are playing with. However the game is not so generous with ammo, which makes it significantly more demanding in this light.

BattleBlock Theater is an indie game developed by
, the creators of
.  Released on the Xbox Live Arcade on April 3, 2013, and on PC on May 15, 2014.
BattleBlock Theater is a simple to understand, but less simple to complete, platformer-puzzle game that can be played singleplayer, or multiplayer.
The story begins with you and hundreds of your friends, which includes everyone's mutual best friend, Hatty Hattington, sailing the ocean on the S.S. Friendship.  Due to a large storm, the S.S. Friendship wrecks and everyone is washed up on an island.  You and the squad are taken prisoner by large mobster cats, with something terrible happening to a good friend of yours.  You are then put through trials, or tests, for the cat's amusement, collecting gems, balls of yarn, and the occasional Golden Hat.
Combining the fantastically written dialogue, the talented voice of Newgrounds contributor, Will Stamper, and the silly popsicle stick puppets, every cutscene is one that will have you laughing hard enough you'll be "pooping yourself to death on the way to the bathroom".  The witty one liners and nonsensical sentences had me laughing, even when the cutscene ended and I started playing the game again.  One of my favorites has to be, "Even the word 'hopeless' has the word 'hope' in it! And if you rearrange the letters it spells 'peeslosh!'"
So many games today are trying to create a realistic feel.  When you start playing BattleBlock Theater, the vibrant colors, and silly animations make your heart feel giddy and excited.  It allows you to take a step away from the realistic shooters or intense MOBAs and have a good laugh while basically playing an interactive cartoon.
BattleBlock Theater features user-generated music from the Newgrounds community.  With an old swing feel, mixed with synth, the soundtrack of this game is by far one of my favorites.  It has very memorable beats and melodies that will get stuck in your head for hours on end.
Like most Co-op games, especially puzzle games, teamwork and coordination between players is crucial.  You can play through the main storyline with a buddy and try to A++ everything, or you can screw with each other accidentally and have a good laugh until it's been three hours and what they think is "funny" makes you want to commit heinous crimes.  BattleBlock Theater also allows you and your friends to play in 8 different multiplayer game modes giving you hours upon hours of fun.
I have spent 40 hours playing this game, and I still end up coming back to it when I don't know what I really want to play, or if I only have 15 minutes to spare.  I've beaten the game all the way through once, and I am currently going back through it trying to A++ every level.  Then after that, I still have the Insane difficulty to play through and then A++.  So that's another 40+ hours of great gameplay waiting for me.  I would highly recommend this game to you and your buddies.

Have you ever played Icarus Proudbottom Teaches Typing or Frog Fractions? If not, stop reading and start in on those free flash games; I'll wait.
If you've made it back with your sanity in one piece, or if you've already recovered from losing your mind, you'll probably have noticed the thing those games have in common, which is that they're not exactly what they appear to be. There's a simple mechanic at the core of each game, but the real game is more in the meta commentary about what the game actually is. Games about games, like The Magic Circle, are the decidedly postmodern expression of restless developers who aren't satisfied with the complacent feedback loops and progression curves of modern games, but unless they're literally making a point about the meaninglessness of control (The Stanley Parable), they're best when they actually manage to be a game, even as they deconstruct the entire notion.
Enter Pony Island, a self-described "suspense puzzle game in disguise," which basically establishes the game-within-a-game "Pony Island" as a limbo-like punishment for gamers, a one-trick...well...pony, in which you leap your magical pony/unicorn over gates over and over again until you agree to cede your soul to Lucifer. Pony Island itself, then, which does far more with its retro framing device than You Have to Win the Game or classic Strongbad cartoons, is a game of constant one-upmanship; players "cheat" at the devil's game, at which point Lucifer changes the code, forcing players to once again hack their way around his conventions. Along the way, the game pulls tricks from Eternal Darkness's book, cleverly attempting to convince players that the game is failing so that players will feel smart when they out-think the devil and progress to the next act.
Except, and here's the really clever part, the heart of the game really is "Pony Island." Even though you're aware that this black-and-white wireframe jumping simulator (which eventually gets two upgrades--a laser and wings--that don't add much to the difficulty) is a repetitive anti-game, there's so much framework built into Pony Island itself that you can't help but dive back into the original game. And along the way, you'll even get to see the various iterations of design, from a minimalist text-adventure rendering to a pathetic 3D version, and even a few different skins, including a cheery, full-color "modern" version. If the goal is simply to not play "Pony Island," players can simply quit at any point--Mullens doesn't go so far as to obfuscate your menu options. But because there are hidden "Pony Island" tickets to collect by completing cryptic tasks--along with equally meaningless Steam achievements--players soldier through the banal hopping in order to see what clever trick comes next.
And there's a lot of content here, from optional tasks like interacting with the desktop's "Settlers of sAtan" and finding passwords buried in broken option menus, to a series of "hacking" puzzles that involve placing basic operators into holes in faux-code. It's nothing overly strenuous. Even when loops and splitters are introduced, which calls for a lot of mid-routine micromanagement, the game isn't actually trying to keep the player from winning; it's just trying to convince the player that it is. That's the genius: "Pony Island" represents every repulsively designed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t time-suck, and Pony Island redeems them all. This even fits into the whole idea of games-as-limbo, in which players can either uselessly throw away their life/time/soul, or can find something of merit within the limns of all that code and thereby make something more of themselves. (It's one of the reasons I turned to criticism in the first place, as actively participating in entertainment is far superior to passively observing it.)
Even though there is no part of the final level that I even remotely enjoy, I couldn't put Pony Island down. It kept wrapping new and surprisingly devious tricks around the same-old-same-old pony express, and the context kept me going. Is there any practical difference between shooting a laser of corrupted binary data at demons or blowing a gust of wind at butterflies that just want to tickle you? No, just as "Pony Island" itself could be just about any game. What matters, then, is what's around the mechanics, and in that, Pony Island has found gold, and the fact that it doesn't settle for simply being a series of puzzles (like Please, Don't Touch Anything), is what elevates it to a Game That Matters--a game that, in finding both structure and absurdity, succeeds more than Frog Fractions. It's a joke that laughs with you, not at you.

Amazing blend of turn based strategy and card combat games.  I've actually played this game since beta, but only recently got it on Steam. Rewards are frequent and generous, so it doesn't feel as tedius if you were to earn your way rather than purchasing.
I've only gotten to high gold rank (7, you start at 30, diamond begins at 5).  I had only spent $10 by then and it was only to support the game at the moment in time, it was not at all necessary.  I don't know if you'd ever truly need to spend money to compete, but if you really needed the entire card library at your hands, chances are you're very high rank and very dedicated to the game by then and willing to spend your way.
This game also has a gauntlet mode similar to HS arena where you draft a deck so there is no way to buy better odds of victory.  You earn gold much faster than other games and can regularly buy keys (keys are purchasable with both earned gold and cash).
All in all this is both the best competive card game and competitive turn based strategy game on the market.
In addition to the ranked pvp, there are plenty of puzzles and challenges to both practice and earn gold without the pressure of playing against other players for those who stress that.  There used to be a new puzzle challenge daily, which are temporarily suspended for developments sake but are supposed to be returning later.  There are also special pve boss battle challenges that will really test your skill and teach you to deal with ridiculous odds stacked against you.
This game is also free, if you even remotely like either card or strategy games, just install it and thank me later.
P.S. when you make an account, get a referral code off of a friend or your favorite streamer.  You'll get 100 bonus gold to start with and if you stick with the game and rank up you'll earn them nice bonuses too!
