In my first review I commented that archery combat felt mehhhh and they did improve it. So the devs are listening. I still feel like combat is clunky. It might be because compared to other games in this genre there is a higher emphasis on attack speeds. Which might be why combat feels clunky since attacks are slower in this game then most.
That said this time around I decided to remap my controls because I didn't like the games controls by default. So here is a problem I noticed which isn't a huge deal but is fixable. When you remap your controls the game doesn't cahne the 'Y to pick up' or 'Press A to join'. The press A to join seems to be bound to your basic attack button, same with all menu option. I remapped it to X so as along as you remember its fine. Can cause accidental attacks on the friendly NPCs but that isn't game breaking since you decide if you want to remap them.
My recommended layout.
Attack - X
Strong Attack - Y
Special Attack - A
Use Item - B
Drop item - Dpad Down
Interact - Dpad up
Rest is the same as default.
So other then price, as a game why do I not recommend it?
Combat still just feels clunky and I'm not 100% sure why that is? Other games in this genre when I die I feel like I messed up and know what i did wrong. In this game half my deaths I feel like I was cheated.
What do I like about the game? The daily/monthly leaderboards is a nice touch so that a community can form around the game. I think later on if they added twists to the challenges like No items drop past arrows and weapons or you get all the pets from the start but you only get 1 hp. Or just something that spices up the game a bit would be cool. If they do have it already i dont see it.
I still dont like the doors and the terrain but all the other art has grown on me.
The comments from the developers on my negative review posting on updates when stuff changed was nice and gave me hope to try the game again. Would of done it sooner but i had to buy a new controller. Which I wasnt in a rush to do.
What would I like to change or add to the game?
Make it so when firing an arrow it's instant and you don't have to pull it back. That for balancing reasons you would have to wait for it to reload which would be the current pull back animation. If you do a melee attack it would stop this animation and the reload. I havent done PvP in this game yet so not sure how well that would work but projectiles are dodgeable in this game so it might not be game breaking for PvP
Staff combat is just hold left or right. Other then the staff ability there is nothing special. Might be cool to add a strong attack option for a staff that adds a 2nd attack variety other then the pellets. maybe it turns it into a flamethrower/gas spray type attack with a shorter range, has a higher attack speed then the pellets but lower damage or a cooldown after using. Some staffs could have a slower attack speed and stronger damage like firing an ice crystal or something. I don't know how many staffs there are but would make them more fun to use. Could make them broken if not balanced correctly.
I am not really sure what to change that would change my review though. It isn't something I would recommend yet for the price when there is other gaem for cheaper. This game is tough, but fair. When you start off, even the weakest goblins will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Prepare to die a lot. If you aren't comfortable with that, better skip it.
The game is a true roguelike - you die and start again. However, every new run is different because you get diffferent items, weapons and pets. If you are looking for something linear and easy like Castle Crashers, better avoid this game. There's a casual mode, but even if you play that, don't expect to beat the game on your first try.
If you plan to play with friends, make sure you first play a bit yourself, because you will need at least one skilled player to get anywhere. Otherwise, stick to Casual mode.
As you play more and get skilled at combat you will find that goblins are actually very slow and easy. You will beat the first boss like it's nothing. It just takes time to get a good handle on the combat, to you use rage and magic properly.
If you played games like Rampage Knights or The Binding of Isaac, this game is for you. The amount of different mechanics you can combine is amazing, and I'd say this game is already comparable in that aspect, even if it's early access. I mean, you can use the Antidote potion and a couple of Mushrooms to buff your Retaliator sword to insane damage level by getting hit by weak poison spitters in the castle and then one-shot the boss which ofterwise takes a lot of time to take down. I have yet to see such buildup in another game. Compare that to Isaac where once you get OP, the rest of the game is a walk in the park. In Witch, you can also get OP damage-wise, but you still need to use your items/weapons/magic wisely to survive.
Looking forward to see level 5 and the two remaining heroes.

I was contacted by the developers to see if I was interested in trying out Serial Cleaner and to possibly make a video of it for my YouTube channel. After looking over the game's trailer I thought it looked interesting enough so told them I'd be happy to have a look and if I enjoyed it then I'd be glad to make a video. Suffice to say there is, in fact, a video for Serial Cleaner on my channel!
I was given a copy of their PAX demo, which includes the first four levels of the game. I decided to record myself playing through for the first time, as I prefer to record my first reactions of going through games, and I felt if I didn't like it I'd easily enough just delete the footage. Luckily I found it a lot of fun.
The art style is great, with it looking both fun and (in some places) pretty gruesome. I absolutely love the music, though I do hope they'll include more tracks than I heard in the demo. The gameplay is really good, with easy controls and having two ways to view the "map" to help plan out your movements. The only thing I didn't quite get on with, controls-wise, was cleaning up blood as the movement seemed a bit loose, which made it hard to control the character and get the smaller bits of blood.
I will admit fully that I'm generally pretty rubbish at stealth games, but I was able to get through the first four levels (with some difficulty), and I didn't find it frustrating during the moments where I did get caught. I kind of felt it would be nice to have a short burst of sprint to help get away from the police when they do chase you, but then I guess this would lower the feeling of threat for getting caught. At the end of the day I definitely recommend the game - and, by the way, I wasn't paid in any way (other than receiving the demo for free) to cover the game.

The first half of the game feels a bit unclear, you're walking around shooting these guys, to get to this place to find someone who wants to look at your suit, but first get this thing in that building, or delete that yoke over that way ... what were we meant to be doing again? TL;DR - This is a good strategy game that doesn't require you to play the original to enjoy it (in fact you may be better off if you have NOT played the original). Just beware of the devs and fanboys.
Sword of the Stars II is a 4X strategy game with turn-based empire management and fleet movement coupled with visually stunning real-time space combat with ships that you, the player, can design. Now, when I say design, I don't mean you determine the length and silhouette and window placement or any of that. When designing a ship you pick three sections (in game described as a Command [front] Mission [middle] and Engine [back] section). Once you have selected your sections you can place weapons of varying size and modules which provide bonuses like extra crew, increased range, and much more.
But what about the factions? Well there are 7, the Humans, Hivers (insect like), Tarkasians (reptilian), Morrigi (avian/bird), Liir-Zuul Alliance (Liir are dolphin/whale like while the Zuul are genetically modified slavers that are difficult to define), Suul'ka Horde (Suul'ka are giant telepathic terrors of war that are allied with some more extreme Zuul) and the Loa (Artificially Intelligent race). Most of the factions have a very distinct system of faster than light travel (Morrigi, Tarka and Liir are all very similar with only minor differences) and each race has its own technological advantages and disadvantages.
The Tech Tree is randomly generated each game and most techs require you to perform a "Feasibility Study" during which you spend a few turns determining how likely you will be in achieving a certain tech. This is where alot of the faction specific technological advantages come into play (for example the Morrigi have a better chance of getting high end energy weapon techs than the Tarkasians). This "Feasibility Study" is a very divisive topic, however, I personally enjoy it as it means that you can't start a game and know that you don't have Shield techs despite playing as the Liir (the Liir have the best Shield tech chance, however, this still happened to me). This means that each game has an element of unpredictability that is maintained into the late-game whereas a simple tech tree where you could see all your paths would mean that at turn 1 you could plan your entire game.
Fleet Movement is also a divisive topic as ships cannot be moved unless they are in fleets with a dedicated command ship. I have personally had no issues with this system. You make a fleet and can then right click on a target, decide what to do and then select the desired fleet that is in range. Or, you can right click a fleet, select a desired action and then select a world in range.
Diplomacy, unfortunately, is essentially non-existent. The AI behaves erratically and while it may accept a peace treaty on one turn it may declare war on you the very next turn. I always wanted to rule the galaxy alone anyways but it is still a major eyesore on the game.
Finally, support for the game has, for all intents and purposes, ceased. The developers (which can be/are extremely difficult/stubborn) released a patch in August of 2014, however, there were no patch notes released and any comments on the patch were disregarded by the devs. As a result I cannot confirm or deny any of the findings, however, it is my suspicion that the AI was made more aggressive and everything else remained as it was before. But many people (fanboys?) will say that turn times are shorter and menus come up quicker and their cat came back from the dead after that "non-patch" as the devs deny any patch taking place.
So if you are looking for a grand strategy game with real-time space battles, stunning visuals, a handful of unique races and a learning curve that provides a sense of accomplishment then I recommend you give this game a try. It's come a long way from the opening day launch disaster.

Overall a good game.  When first released the game was unplayable yes but now it is extremely playable.
My only gripes are the radically changed command system lack of ability to change map sizes (without a third party program) compared to SotS prime.  My problem with the command system is that instead of just pressing “M” to move a fleet now you have to assign a “mission”.   My other issue is that when you “set up” a game you don’t have the ability to customize the maps like in SotS.  I really liked being able to set minimum distance between stars, star count etc but again with a 3rd party program you can do just that.
However all is not bad.  The new Loa race is fun to play, especially considering I can’t think of another game that lets you play as an AI race.  Another bonus is now you start off with cruisers instead of destroyers, you can still have destroyers but they are now drones carried on special hulls and act as little more than a meat shield.  Another benefit of SotS2 is that the tech tree is full but your ability to research tech is dependent on feasibility studies.  But this means that even with a 1% chance of feasibility you still have a chance to research and get the tech. Some people complain about the "end turn" times. Trust me those will save you much headache later down the line as while you have that period of time of nothing it gives you a chance to reflect about overall strategy.
This game also has a throw you to the wolves learning system.  Many players have created guides though so you aren't completely screwed but If you enjoy learning by yourself it can be quite enjoyable.

I really tried to give this game the benefit of the doubt. It's not the gameplay mechanics that is the games biggest flaws. It's in the presentation. The music and level design.
Jumping right in. The level design for me fell mostly flat. The levels are just so boring. Even when the game tries to mix the variety up it's still just as boring. "Deadly lasers again!?" The levels themselves look drab and uninspired. There are lots of collectibles in the form of stacks of cans through out all the levels to knock over or "collect".
The music in the game is probably the most horrible aspect about the whole game. Each level consist of a generic techno/80's style synth song that seems like it's only 20 seconds long. When levels usually take around 15-30 minutes to complete depending on how good you are you will hear the same song over and over again. My experience primarily from PS4 version (Focusing on gameplay, not performance) it is running great on my PC though - specs on my profile.
+Drones are incredibly fun and useful. The quadcopter should be your first purchase (second purchase after pants). Some missions can be completed entirely with the RC Jumper, it makes for more dynamic ways to take on missions.
+Fun new skills like hacking vehicles and calling gangs/cops on people.
+Co-op is great fun, you can team up and complete co-op missions, hacking events or just run around collecting moneybags/research points.
+I love the atmosphere, San Francisco looks incredible (even better on PC). Not to mention you can use the slides at Goo-uh, Nudle.
+Driving. I’m throwing driving up here, I’ve had no problems with it. Engine Override (boost) skill is great too.
+Very lenient achievements/trophies, was able to platinum it in no time at all (And I’ve only managed to platinum one other game).
+Story was definitely a step up from watch dogs and had a much brighter tone to it. It does get slow at times.
-The alert system is WTF: You can sneak around but the moment one guard (or dog) sees you, everyone will INSTANTLY be alerted of your whereabouts, even if you take them out a microsecond after they notice you. I assume the guards must press a button to alert everyone but the dogs!?
-The dialogue can get VERY cringe worthy at times. Some of the witty banter just comes off as awkward.
-Unfortunately missions can’t be replayed (aside from co-op ones). And, like in GTA V, many restricted interiors become inaccessible after a certain mission.
-The streets felt empty at times (on ps4 at least).
-No Steam achievements, only UPlay.
*Most missions are essentially ‘sneak into a restricted area, do something, sneak out’. Some may find it repetitive. Personally, I enjoy the challenges and like to try out different ways to tackle a mission.
*The controls (on gamepad) might take some getting used to, it's a little different from WD1. Expect to be pulling out a gun instead of your phone.
*The stun gun is very OP, especially once you research the “Amp Up” upgrade for it later on. I’m not complaining considering the alert system.

I'd llike to state before I start this brief review blurb that I am not the sort of person to really play Call of Duty. Check my profile - other than Black Ops, I've barely glanced at the series. That said... The sheer amount of content in this game is insane.
You've got a tightly constructed four-player cooperative campaign, an alternate version of that same campaign filled with zombies and corrupted machines, a new take on Zombies mode set in the 1940's with a star-studded cast all hamming it up beautifully, a competitive multiplayer that you can both play online and in botmode (YEAH! BOTMODE! REMEMBER WHEN THAT WAS A MAINSTREAM FEATURE?! Well, it's here, in Custom Games!), a free running trial mod inspired by Mirror's Edge, a top-down comedy shooter known as Dead Ops, AND mod support on PC.
Ignore the haters who insist this game isn't worth your time - they're just disappointed they can't curbstomp thousands of people with scorestreaks. Even with the smaller population online, the game's botmode AI is razor sharp and provides plenty of fun across multiple modes. All cooperative modes can be played solo, and BLOPS 3 even has PC split-screen support if you have a controller or two hooked up to your PC.
Launch day issues have been patched out, there's tons of progression and new tricks to discover as you play across the various modes... why are you reading this review at this point? Go get Black Ops 3! It's probably the most distinctive and interesting Call of Duty game in years. Which may be why it turned off its bro fanbase, but hey, at least the rest of us can dig it!

This game is GREAT!  But multiplayer is BROKEN!
I cut my teeth on Railroad Tycoon 3 which is also a very good economic simulator.  But it's missing one important detail: in RT3 the trains can't collide with each other - they just go through each other and there's no need to set up real railroad systems.
Sid Meier's Railroads takes care of that.  You can optionally turn on trains colliding with each other (set routes to "hard") and then they'll just wait until you build more track or figure out the right way to get them to cooperate.
It's also a fun economic sim.
But after reading other reviews and trying it myself, it LOOKS like multiplayer isn't working.
Pros:
+ Has a "tabletop mode" to play as sandbox with no competitors.
+ Good railroad building logic required (or you can use easy routing)
+ There's a frog in there somewhere in the audio
+ Nice cartoony atmosphere with all the historic millionaires to learn about
+ Fast paced
Cons:
- It crashes.  HOWEVER, crashing is fixed using the 3GBEnabler.  I haven't had any problems after running 3GBEnabler on the exe file.  To learn more, read this

- Trains get stuck more than they should (hard routing only).
- When placing track the lights will be buggy, have to delete track and replace until the lights are correct.  Unless you've played the game for a long time this won't be clear or intuitive.  Cluster-frack.
- A little (maybe a lot) too cartoony for my taste.  The buidlings and tracks are enormous compared to the landscape.  Especially if you've played Railroad Tycoon 3.  In RT3 The cities are miles and miles apart, while in Railroads! the cities are only a few trainlengths apart.  Go look at my screenshots for an example.
- no such thing as "X" shaped crossovers (diamond or scissors crossover).
- while hard routing is much better than RT3, it's still much lacking.  You cannot set up more than a 2 pronged fork.
- It looks like multiplayer doesn't work.  WTF

For Honor is a great realistic mood setting game, featuring fanstastic textures and great object collisions if your computer can allow, giving an extremely in-the-moment vibe. Though a common negetive review is lack of community and connection, those problems seem to only apply to certian areas and circumstances. Most players vs bots servers have a low body of overall players, and a very low amount of population of skirmish players vs players. The amount of player(s) vs player(s), in the following modes are high: Tribute (stealing and gathering relics for your team), 1 v 1 duel, 2 v 2 brawl, dominion, and elimination. Connection issues obviously do not apply to any player vs bot or player and bots vs bots, and rewards (leveling and items) are still present. Though connection differs from location and service, I've found only minor connection issues, and out of my current 18 hours, and each match only lasting roughly 10-15 minutes, only two in-game/aftergame connection issues have occurred. Further, steel, For Honor's currency, is given generously to begin, with 3500 obtained for simply completing the two tutorials. I am very pleased with this game and it's visuals, and look forward to explore what more it has to offer.

It's a basic puzzle-platformer for the casual crowd, but becomes a difficult, hand-straining game for those who want more out of it.
Apparently, with a controller, D-pad support is weird. In my case, I can't assign anything to it unless I use one of the supposedly supported third party programs like Joy2Key, or if I'm using the "Beta Branch". The game works find with a keyboard seeing as how it seems to have been intended for it in the first place.
Whatever engine this game is running on, it's pretty unstable on my end. It goes from 60 to 30-40 FPS a lot and it's a serious hindrance when tricky platforming may be required; it makes me unsure if some errors I make in-game are on my end or the game's.
On the surface, it's a cute little puzzle-platformer with some nice music and 100 levels to go through. You throw babies to flip switches, stun enemies, etc. You get every baby to the exit and you beat the level. You beat the boss on the 100th level and you beat the game.
The puzzles themselves aren't particularly hard and a bit of timed platforming is required in the later areas. Levels are fairly well-designed and they don't often have just one way of beating each one. They don't take very long to beat either, which can also be said about the base game so it might take only a couple of hours to get through the hundred levels.
While they're pretty short, having that many levels may make the game repetitive and it doesn't help either that the music doesn't change until after 10 levels. That said, the music in the game can be nice to listen to, and it can at least be turned off in the main menu.
What makes the game very difficult though, is when you decide to try and go for the "best time" to beat each level. You get a Blue Flower for beating it at any time, a Gold Flower for beating it at the listed time, and a Rainbow Flower for beating the "Dev Time." Beating the Dev Time requires serious platforming skills and a lot of knowledge of the game's mechanics – it can becomes its own puzzle on how you're to beat the level faster than the Dev Time. If you failed to beat the Dev Time by a bit, you can see a "ghost replay" of the Dev Time in action to see how they get that time – you can repeat what they do and do it better or find an alternative to getting a faster time, but finding one is uncommon. In case the "ghost replays" get intrusive in some way, their transparency can be altered from zero to full.
If you managed to get Gold Flowers in all 100 levels, you get access to 10 more levels. Beat the Dev Time in those 100 levels, you get 10 more levels as well as a new character with a small but very essential new feature added to it. These 20 levels are real tests on how well you can use the game's mechanics. All this is what makes the game a little more appealing to those who want a challenging precision-platformer, but it's not actually obvious that this kind of challenge is there to begin with unless you actually play the game.
There are some hidden mechanics in the game like picking up a baby mid-jump to go as high & fast as if you weren't holding one, and parrying. Parrying is a very useful mechanic but the game doesn't even tell you it exists until you get to levels' 111-120, where it's a requirement. Even then, you have to see the "ghost replay" of the Dev Time to know it exists. The mechanic works in the same style as Street Fighter 3 & CvS2 in that you have to press left or right just a few frames before a projectile or enemy touches you in order to cancel the damage and/or projectile, depending on which direction they may come from. Against an enemy, it stuns them for a few seconds.
It's a simple game for the regular crowd and a very challenging time-attack game for another; it's not bad either way.

Railroads will feel familiar to anyone who has played the previous Railroad tycoon series. This title represents a faster paced yet more streamlined game. You won't find yourself contemplating the most optimal route to avoid steep grades as the track laying is a lot neater without a grid overlay and you can curve your way around most obstacles easily. The real challenge is in using double and triple tracks from each station to supply every settlement with what it needs to grow and transport the goods between cities.
AI opponents aren't the brightest and make a few routing errors, but will frustrate your attempts to dominate the land. Scenarios have a variety of objectives that have time constraints, which keeps your focus on something more than just connecting everything and watching profits soar.

First, the graphics. compared to the previous railroad tycoon games, the graphics are much better.

Now, the gameplay. The gameplay is awful and nothing like that of the previous games.

You can barely zoom out. you can zoom in pretty close, but you can only get about a hundred feet into the air, unlike RT3 where you could zoom out to see pretty much the entire map. In the third screenshot they show of this game, that's pretty much the limit to your zoom.
In railroad tycoon 3, there was a detailed level editor and scripting feature so you could design your own scenarios to share, or play with your friends. After playing this game, I can't find any sort of level editor.
Overall, this feels like a game you would give to your kids and let them play it while they are still too young to understand what a good game is. It works like this. There are 6 factions and 2 generals per faction. They have names, but I never took the time to learn them. General 1 of every faction is the general you can pretty much play with from the get-go. To unlock the 2nd general, you will need to level that faction up to 10 or 11 by playing the first general.
1. Lyonar
General 1 - A pretty all-around style of play. Decent removal, minion buffing, and board control. Can heal with certain Lyonar cards.
General 2 - Focuses on healing self back up and benefiting from specific minion attributes that buff the general or offer unique abilities whenever something is healed.
2. Songhai
General 1 - Spell caster that burns his enemies down hard and fast. You can find yourself out of cards fast if you fire off too fast though.
General 2 - I've never played, so I can't comment too much. But, I think she's more geared towards doing ranged damage.
3. Vetruvian
General 1 - Places objects called "Obelisks" that summon minions (Dervishes) at the beginning of your turn. Certain Obelisks buff dervishes and if played right, dervishes can get out of hand and strong pretty fast.
General 2 - The play style revolves pretty much around equipping artifacts that have unique attributes to them such as stealing enemy minions, blasting from far away, or summoning harmful totems when a minion is killed.
4. Abyssian
General 1 - Used to be about swarming the board.. but it's kind of steered a different direction and not so much about massive swarms but getting a smaller swarm, and buffing it or killing all of your minions to buff one to ridiculous strengths.
General 2 - Removal and board obstacles. They lay 'creeps' which are more/less ground spikes that do damage, however certain cards have powerful abilities depending on how many creeps are on the ground often turning a very likely loss into an out-of-nowhere win.
5. Magmar
General 1 - Dropping minions that get stronger attack and health with every turn that they survive. Can spiral out of control VERY fast if you don't have an answer for it.
General 2 - More/less the same as general 1, but can draw an additional card and force enemy to draw an additional card which can work in their favor with certain minions on the board.
6. Vanar
Just NO.
Duelyst used to be fun. I've spent countless nights telling myself "Ok, one more match, I know what I did wrong last time." only to find myself playing 2 hours before I have to wake up for work. I had alot of fun with it, and to a fair amount of people, it still is fun... But, I really can't do it anymore and I can't justify supporting a company that has turned to such low standards.
With the addition to the newest expansion, things have gone so far over the edge that it has lost every sense of the meaning of fun. Counter-Play Games recently was aquired by Namco-Bandai Games which isn't so much of a bad thing. At first I was kind of happy for CPG. I thought, maybe it could improve the player base, which it may or may not have... Hard to say right now, but either way, there's never been much of an issue in finding a game. Maybe a full minute to wait at the very most.. But, here is my problem with the whole Namco-Bandai thing. For the past 2 expansions, Counter-Play released their expansions in the business model that is "Pay (x amount) and get all the new cards" like any expansion SHOULD BE. Generally it was 20$ and you got 3 copies of every card from that expansion. I think that's fair, right? However, they have implemented a new model that I can only sum up as a poor excuse for a money grab. They have stooped so low in the pool of game developers that they're now in the list of "Developers exploiting gamers wallets". Do you want all the cards from the new expansion? Ha, Suck it!, we've implemented a new currency that forces you to buy it in order to buy the orbs from the new expansion." But here's the kicker. You (literally, and I don't mean 'literally' metaphorically) can spend 20,30, even 50$ and not actually get all of the new cards from the expansion. How's that for a middle finger to their players? Can you craft the cards from disenchanting other cards and get their other currency for crafting a card you want? Yea, sure, but depending on the card, you may be destroying 10+ cards to get 3. It's a weird dynamic that doesn't make sense anymore.
They've been working on a mobile app for what seems like forever and even announced that they were post-poning it even more because of the newest expansion. Honestly, as a mobile game, it would make sense with their new business model. Pay a large amount for a small amount of content.
To sum things up about this game..
Pro's
+ The pixel art is incredible. Every general and minion have their own unique attack animations and none are dissapointing to look at.
+ 6 Factions with 2 generals each. Both generals of every faction play entirely different than each other, offering a pretty good variety of gameplay.
+ There are ALOT of cards to build decks with. Every faction has cards exclusive to them, and some are obviously geared towards 1 of the 2 generals, but CAN BE used with either to offer some pretty non-conventional decks.
+ The player base is steady. I've never waited more than a minute for a match.
+ Single-player tutorial challenges are awesome in teaching you the game and some of the potential that could be had for some pretty legendary combo's if you play your cards right. I would play the ♥♥♥♥ out of the game if their were a lot more. However, these can all be completed in 1 hour.
Cons
- The game is brutally unforgiving. One wrong minion placement, card replace, spell, or face attack can cost you the entire match.
- Vanar. The faction is so unfathomably broken right now that it's been possibly the #1 discussion on it's reddit page for months. The addition of some of the new expansion cards do not seem to be helping this by any means and in fact is only helping to make it worse.
- Magmar. Also a pretty broken faction that can snowball out of control after 1-2 moves if you don't have an answer to their drop.
- The in-game music is pretty repetitive, but can be switched off.
- The new 'diamond' currency to buy orbs from the new expansion is an obvious money grab. Don't fall for it.
- Depending on where you go to talk about the game (reddit, twitch tv, etc), the player base can be a little toxic.. There's a fair amount of BM'ing going on during matches, but I think I've been lucky in the fact that 95% of the people I talk to after a match have been rather nice.
- The developer does NOT listen to the community. They have their own agenda that they push on to the players and it's really kind of a 'take it or leave it' deal. There are interviews with them where they openly admit to creating cards almost solely off of the rage factor that they will get out of players... and there are A LOT of them.
- Songhai faction does not get love. Ever. I play Lyonar and Vetruvian exclusively, and have never played a Songhai deck against another human, but I can tell that they need a substantial buff. I rarely see them played anymore.
- No way to share a deck with someone in-game unless you export it, send it to someone out of game, and they import it in their game.
- The "RNG" is can be the worst element you've ever experienced EVER in a video game. Imagine you have your final 10 cards left in a match. In those 10 there are THREE of the exact same card that the RNG has not drawn for you out of the past 30. You replace the only card you have in your hand hoping to draw it and win the game, only for it to not come up. You've just drawn 31 out of 39 cards and those 3 duplicates NEVER showed. It happens and it really makes you question if the algorithms in the game are playing against you.
TL;Dr - A uniquely fun card game ruined by neglectful and money grabbing developers.

was an ARG, made by Capcom to promote the then upcoming Resident Evil 6. It featured pictures of "No Hope Left" graffiti around the world, and videos of "survivors" saying their last goodbyes, after a supposed viral outbreak that hit the globe. NHL set the mood for what could be the most terrifying RE title to date.
Too bad that the game failed to deliver on the expectations that Capcom set themselves, and "No Hope Left" became an inside joke in the RE community, pertaining to what what fans felt for the future of the series.
RE6 is an action game, and that's all there is to know about it. Ever played a TPS in the last decade? Chances are, you're already familiar with the game mechanics in RE6, albeit QTE-laden and includes an unreliable camera. Sure, there are zombies, mutated freaks, and hulking beasts, but I see no difference from the cannon fodder that runs into my view, while playing other action games. What used to be creatures that terrified me, are now minor obstacles that litter the path between point A and point B. This isn't the Resident Evil that I knew of, and it's bad at being one.
But of course, franchises change to better suit the modern trends, and what's hot in the market right now is the explosive Hollywood experience - something which RE6 emulated well. While it did throw off the tension and atmosphere out the window, RE6 kept the B-movie antics which became a defining trait for the rest of the series. Combine that with an over-the-top plot, and you've got yourself one hell of an explosive ride. Just don't wrap your hear around the fact that this is an RE game. It's better that way.
And there you have it.

Resident Evil 6 is a a good game, but not a great game.
It's something I'd recommend picking up on sale, but not even for the $30 price tag it has now. Its got plenty of action, a more convenient inventory system, and has a nice look; however, the story and gameplay is what doesn't make the cut.
The run and gun is probably one of the more satisfying changes I've seen (which is apparently what some people are agonizing about). While it could be re-worked a bit to feel smoother that's not so much the issue. The problem is, how the whole experience just works out. Obnoxious falling over after being shot, the tripping over bodies, crappy cover system, and  terrible camera angles/forced aiming for the sake of a in-game 'scene' all work against the game. That's just a few of the problems which have come with the game. Each campaign (4 all together) has a problem though in their own right. Leon's is probably one of the better one reminiscing more of an old schoool Resident Evil take. The constant falling over after being shot doesn't become apparent until you hit up Chris' campaign. Then, perhaps the worst of all is Jake's campaign. Which attempts to put you into a more cat and mouse type game which just works out terribly for the run and gun gameplay. Some areas where they try and encourage stealth can be laughably avoided by just sprinting past the entirety of it.
I applaud Capcom for trying to deliver so many experiences and different play-styles into one package, but it ends up just falling short. Instead of receiving one fantastic experience, we get four different mediocre ones.
Then comes the story. Terribly transitioned flashbacks, shallow characters and your typical 'conspiracy' stuff all show up in RE6. The story naturally requires you to play all 4 campaigns to understand it completely. Each campaign is a puzzle piece that doesn't quite make sense til you complete it. The part that really screws it over is just how they stick in details that apparently happen in the gap between RE4-5 to this. Things come up that make you say, "I don't remember that happening at all!" Which Capcom then tags in, "Oh, this happened in that 6 year gap between RE5 and 6 somewhere." The story isn't necessarily bad, but it's just okay. Since the story is split into 4 campaigns the experience is different and it shows that Capcom gave more love to one campaign vs another.
Overall, I had fun with the game. Coop is probably what became this games saving grace for me as my friend and I tackled it together. The segments of the game which have you "searching for a partner" are somewhat sad as you'll find pretty much nobody, but the AI that takes the players' place is great. The AI does their objective and they do it well without you having to babysit them.
If you're a fan of Resident Evil I'd say pick it up on sale, or if you're new to the series pick it up on sale too. It's a fun game with friends, but not worth the current price tag. Which is why, I will not recommend this game. I paid $10 and felt I got my money's worth (still am), but would not do it for $30. Just wait for one of the many Steam sales and have your fun too.

Resident evil 6 is the worst game in the franchise. Not because it’s an action game, but because it’s just a bad game in general. The story itself is very mediocre, the dozens of stupid set pieces that take place during the gameplay and cutscenes make no sense and is worse than a B action movie. The whole experience overall is even more cheesier than Resident evil 5, Chris boulder punching level of cheesiness multiple times. The world doesn’t feel believable, the levels themselves are just stupid with everything requiring more than one person to use. There is no immersion, tension, excitement or suspense during gameplay because it feels like the game is doing everything it can to take you out of the experience. The graphics are pretty poor, there is barely any detail in the environments and the textures are very muddy, probably so the console versions keep a steady framerate during the over the top action. This game is exhausting to play because of how long it is. The game has no right being 20 hours long because of how boring the gameplay is. Coop helps cure the boredom a little but it doesn’t save it. It’s probably as linear as a game can get, the game mostly feels like it’s playing itself, like you have no control over anything that is happening. I feel like this game did have some potential, I don’t mind that the series has gone the action route, I thought resident evil 5 was decent but because of how restrictive, simple, streamlined and scripted the gameplay is in 6, it does ruin its potential. I think the melee they added saves the game from being awful, it’s cool to pull off wwe moves and karate kicks on infected. I also liked the addition of aiming and shooting and being able to dodge around and roll on the floor avoiding attacks it made you feel badass. But none of that ultimately matters because the core of the game is trash.

Although very impressive in terms of graphics, and an attempt at innovation, I am forced to write this game off as a techincal failure. I considered this game to be the largest disappointment in 4X history since MOO3.
Also, be aware that there has been no updates since late 2013, which I think suggests that this game will not be getting any updates. From what I understand, the developers have no money to do so.
Pros:
- The graphics are some of the best ever seen for a 4X game, especially a space 1. The Mars 2 engine clearly was the centrepiece of their development.
- They did try to make the game something other than a sequel with beefed up graphics and it does show. Certain aspects like the combat are now more sophisticated, with a damage "grid" and the concept of "critical hits" (very important). This is good.
- If you've played SOTS 1, you'll know. There's a level of complexity here that you don't seen in other games, combining tactical and strategic combat. The problem is, a good deal of what made SOTS 1 outstanding is gone.
- Game will run acceptably well on a low end system, despite the graphics. At time of this review, I am running this on a fairly high end system (overclocked 4.5 GHz CPU, an overclocked AMD r9 290, which as of 2014 is a fairly high end GPU, and an SSD).
- Developers did make an effort to patch the majority of the issues and even offered a free DLC, the End of Flesh.
- There was some effort to make the game modder friendly, but it appears to be incomplete.
Cons:
- You still get crashes at times. Not often, certainly not as much as launch, but it still happens. Most bugs are gone, but you stilll sometimes get CTDs, so save often.
- The UI at times is hard to use and sometimes lags, even on a high end overclocked rig (and yes, I have tested this rig extensively for stability in my CPU, GPU, and RAM overclocks). An SSD does help somewhat I find though. The bigger issue though is the way the UI was designed. I've worked before in computer programming.
A good UI is one that requires as few clicks (or as few taps as possible for touch devices) to get things done. This UI seems to be the exact opposite. A long learning curve in and of itself is not a failure, but it must serve some purpose. I am unsure as to if the UI was left in this state due to lack of funds, or due to the design decisions made.
Another problem is that the game is very, very micro-intensive, particularly during late game. It's a much bigger issue than most 4X games.
- The mission system is very controversial. I really, really hate it. It adds a layer of micro that makes managing large maps very hard, slows down the pace of the game without adding any depth, and causes other complexities. The problem is not so much that it added depth, it's that it did so without adding much to the gameplay itself. A huge step back from SOTS 1.
- Certain features were poorly implemented or appear to be incomplete. For example, the private sector system was not very well done and adds micro problems at times. Given that there are no plans to patch this game, I fear that these features will remain this way. Another example of a feature that had to be axed was 64 bit (important I suppose for using more than 2Gb).
- Autoresolve is in real time, so everything has to be played out in real time. Although imperfect, I would have liked an option to accelerate an autoresolve system.
- There's a general lack of documentation with the game. You have to heavily rely on the wiki for information and to some extent the forums, although participation has since dropped since launch. I think that the wiki should be incorporated into the game somehow.
- The AI is quite dumb I fear and at times, tends to mismanage their own empire into bankruptcy. Often times, what ends up happening is that you expand into the game and you encounter your first player, only to discover that they have really messed up empire management and will not be a challenge.
In effect, this means that multiplayer is the only real area for challenge.
- Compounding the issue above, this game does seem to have issues with network connectivity. I am not sure why as other games seem to be stable. I have asked around and I am not the only person with these problems. I have also fairly extensively tested my network's speed, latency, and stability (works fine on other games).
- Worsening the issue further, this game does not have a very large multiplayer base, so your opportunity to play online is at times, limited
- Normally, I would not put this in a review, but I have found the attitude of the lead developer, Mecron to be highly unprofessional at times. Although I expect trollish behavior from some of the forum participators, it is completely inappropriate for the developer themselves to be acting in such a manner.
There's also a toxic atmosphere on the forums at times, where feedback, even constructive was not permitted and likely to be trolled. Essentially, I think what has happened is those who wanted to change the game for the better have been driven away by the cadre of people who believe the developers can do no wrong, and in effect you get this powerful "groupthink" mentality going on.
People who recommend changes at times are attacked and portrayed as "too stupid to understand why this game is a masterpiece". I will admit the conduct of some of the feedback has been less than admirable. But at the same time, the conduct of those very loyal to this title has also been less than admirable. The critics though have recieved a disproportionate amount of the moderation.
Recommendations: (Unlikely to be implemented due to the fact that this game is not getting patched and for reasons I have indicated above):
- Give the player the option at the start of the game to go for a mission or a SOTS 1 system. I suspect the overwhelming majority of gamers will opt for the SOTS 1 system, save for a very vocal minority.
- I get the impression that the developers did not understand why their first game, SOTS 1 was so successful. It was successful because it was intuitive, easy to play, had a reasonably good UI, but at the same time, a great deal of depth, particularly by the time AMOC and ANY was released.
- Separate the tactical combat into something like Gratitious Space Battles from the strategic portion of the game and let people play "Total War-style multiplayer". This will probably make for a much more engaging game in multiplayer, allowing for shorter combat sessions to take place.
Concluding remarks:
The biggest problem of this game, apart from the stability issues and the poor AI, is the fact that it was not fun to play for a very large percentage of the SOTS1 fanbase. As I indicated above, I think there's a total ignorance of what made SOTS 1 so well recieved.
The development team appears quite frustrated that their fundraising campaigns (they made a few additional efforts to raise money for development) have not been successful, but the issue I see is that they have demonstrated why they are worth additional funding to the majority. There has been a very hostile atmosphere towards feedback and an unwillingness to admit that certain problems exist, much less any indication that they will be addressed.
Complexity in and of itself is not a problem. Neither is a very long learning curve. But the issue is that in this case, complexity never had anything to offer save in tactical combat. It feels like complexity at times was made ... for the sake of complexity. That in many ways detracted from the game experience.
It's very painful for me to have to write this review like this. I really wanted to like this game. I can even see how this game could have evolved into one of the most awesome 4X games ever. But it's clear that in its current form, this game is the largest disappointment since MOO3 in the world of 4X gaming.

Momentum is a huge part of this game, and yet platforming needs to be done in places where the player doesn't have room to judge their own speed. It's shockwave attack affects the player while in the air, sending him or her into endless cycles of floating in the air. It was unplayable at worst, extremely enraging at best. Turning is very difficult, coordinating the camera is extremely difficult, momentum is incorporated and yet not accounted for in level design, and the ragdoll physics is much too intense. I do not recommend this game and am also asking for a refund.

TL,DR with Full Review below:
Pros:
-Interesting concept
-Interesting level designs
-Really good and appropriate soundtrack
Cons:
-Wonky controls for precise platforming
-Unreliable physics
-Camera can be poor
-Gameplay various from really easy levels to making you think you were playing a From Software game
Full Review:
Ben and Ed was a game I saw a preview for on Imgur a while before its release. Those screenshots got me really interested and I was excited to play the game myself when it dropped on Steam. I finally got the time and picked it up on sale for $7.99 and actually enjoyed the first couple of levels. Around the first Boss Level is when things turned sour. It became clear that the games controls were a bit too wonky for the platforming it expected. Also, the physics system is just unreliable. Sometimes I would find myself getting hit by a blade and simply falling down. Other times I would be hit and fly across the arena, meaning the whole dismemberment system wouldn't work. Being able to continue the level as a torso or reattach to my body was cool, but didn't matter if I was thrown across the level to a place where I was forced to restart.
The camera can also be frustrating. There are pendulum style obstacles which pose little threat when presented swinging side-to-side. But When they swing front-to-back the pendulum can get behind you and completely obscure your view. Essentially making those moment of blindness a crapshoot. Will you make it? Or will some other trap come out and annihilate you while you can't see?
This is a game I would have really loved to recommend. The premise is interesting and I really enjoyed the levels with pure platforming, rather than trap avoidance. But I just can't. I played for 80 minutes and probably only enjoyed myself for about 30 of those minutes. The only thing keeping me sane for the other 50 minutes was the game's surpsingly good soundtrack. Maybe another installment with more finely tuned controls and more dependable physics would have me recommending the game.

Pony Island is reminiscent of some old experimental Flash games, adhering to the genre which mischievously bullies the player and encourages exploration in a sort-of-point-and-click interface, albeit more refined and containing elements which would be technically impossible in a Flash container.
The story is cute, amusing and not overly serious, although the game did have some welcome, unexpected points of intrigue. The writing could be better, one may feel that the concept of the game could have been realized much more convincingly had the writing been wittier, but I found it to be adequate.
The game is fairly short, but fitting for the type of experience it offers: it is not so short that it feels underwhelming, and not so long that it outstays its welcome. Secrets are plentiful for those with a keen eye and creative mind. Additional playthroughs to uncover more secrets rewards those with a completionist mindset, although the replayability of the game is lacking, with little to no variation.
The soundtrack is catchy and appropriate, bearing (largely) a sense of doom and desperation, with flares of ferocity and determination; erratic and enjoyable.
If the premise of the game and its promotional material appeals to you, then I think that you will likely find Pony Island to be a fun, novel experience.
Easily my favorite pony-themed non-pony game.

So, the first thing you need to know about this game is that this is in fact the original Railroad Tycoon, it's just been renamed and updated to play on modern OS such as Vista and Windows 7 (see other reviews about compatibility with newer).  There's a version of RT1 on Steam that DOES NOT play on modern OS.  But don't buy it if you're not working on an antique; you don't need it.
As for the "RAM-filled" crashing glitch, definitely dowload the patch mentioned in other reviews, but before that turn off autosave.  It saves every minute for some god-awful reason, which pushes you towards the ram limit quickly.  With that turned off, I've played for six + hours without a hitch (though I also downloaded the player-made patch, so I can't tell which did the trick, if not both).
As to gameplay, as another reviewer said, there are about 15 maps, each with scenarios that take about an hour.  However,  you can play them on three different difficulty levels, with 0 to 3 AI players, and each has gold, silver, and bronze victory conditions, so there are quite a few permutations available to keep you interested.  You can also randomize the town locations, but even without that, each time you play a map, the msc resources (lumber mills, cattle pastures, grain farms, etc) randomly generate their locations.
The most fun part about this game for me is efficiency of transport.  You can have up to four tracks per station, upgrade engines, stations, and towns to make them faster and with higher return values, and also buy properties in the towns for extra income.  This diversification of investments is more important when you're playing against AI---basically, you can own a piece of your competetor's pie! (Or they'll fight you for yours....)
The game is one of Sid Meyer's best from back in the day, and it balances well the ability to play as a sandbox builder vs a super-competitve crazy land.  (Part of the point of the game from the competitve pov is clearly to make 900 foot high roman-arched bridges over your competetors' tracks.)  If you play it like that, it's downright zany.  Truly, early Sid Meyer.  But it's also got great mechanics and logic, as per par for SM games.
The graphics are also super cute, which I particularly like.  They stand the test of time.
A couple of tips to players: There's a feature that lets you go-to cities (bottom left of control panel), which is really helpful for maps that center around places you've never lived/been. (Like various parts of Europe, in my case.)  Too, you can press + or - to increase or decrease the elevation of your tracks.  There's no other way to get a tunnel when it wants to auto-build you a bridge.  Also, holding the mouse wheel allows you to swivel the map, which you can't do in RT2.
If you're wondering wether to get RT1 or 2, I like both, but for different reasons.  I think RT1 is a better game, though I remember playing RT2 way more as a kid.  RT1 is more about building and logistics, whereas I'd say RT2 is more about making money.  It's also a way harder game.  The graphics in RT2 use the Tropico engine, which is actually rather frustrating for that game.  The camera also doesn't swivel; you get four fixed viewpoints.  I could never find a satisfying map angel in RT2, and I don't know about you, but that just drives me absoutely nuts.
All in all, a very solid game, a favorite oldie, and definitely worth the tiny price.  It's one of my top favorites of all time, right up there with Roller Coaster Tycoon.  Go ahead and buy it!

Resident evil 6 is the worst game in the franchise. Not because it’s an action game, but because it’s just a bad game in general. The story itself is very mediocre, the dozens of stupid set pieces that take place during the gameplay and cutscenes make no sense and is worse than a B action movie. The whole experience overall is even more cheesier than Resident evil 5, Chris boulder punching level of cheesiness multiple times. The world doesn’t feel believable, the levels themselves are just stupid with everything requiring more than one person to use. There is no immersion, tension, excitement or suspense during gameplay because it feels like the game is doing everything it can to take you out of the experience. The graphics are pretty poor, there is barely any detail in the environments and the textures are very muddy, probably so the console versions keep a steady framerate during the over the top action. This game is exhausting to play because of how long it is. The game has no right being 20 hours long because of how boring the gameplay is. Coop helps cure the boredom a little but it doesn’t save it. It’s probably as linear as a game can get, the game mostly feels like it’s playing itself, like you have no control over anything that is happening. I feel like this game did have some potential, I don’t mind that the series has gone the action route, I thought resident evil 5 was decent but because of how restrictive, simple, streamlined and scripted the gameplay is in 6, it does ruin its potential. I think the melee they added saves the game from being awful, it’s cool to pull off wwe moves and karate kicks on infected. I also liked the addition of aiming and shooting and being able to dodge around and roll on the floor avoiding attacks it made you feel badass. But none of that ultimately matters because the core of the game is trash.
3/10 (Bad)

It's not Resident Evil, but the game itself is solid and great with friends. Will you be scared? No. Will the gameplay mechanics frustrate you? This time, not really, because Capcom made it comparable to other third person shooters. No tank controls, aiming movement, and easier melee. It's not trying to masquerade as a horror game, and I don't judge it as such.

Resident Evil is not a survival horror saga any longer, but this has advanced combat system and an excellent Mercenaries mode. Unfortunately Capcom have once again spent too much time fixing what didn't need to be fixed and not enough time addressing the real issues of this series. The game is long because it's drawn out or challenging because of a flawed control system rather than displaying these positive attributes through balanced game design. Resident Evil 6 is not a bad game, but it's not a great game either and this is a real shame. Despite this however, it still has many amazing elements that should not be overlooked and at its core is a decent horror experience.

Was it for the gameplay? The cinematics or the style? Or simply because it was a Resident Evil game?
It was for all the reasons.
I can understand if alot of old school fans might get a bit upset over just the fact that these 3 games have a whole lot of action. But since I grew up with Resident Evil 4 and 5, I'm used to this mixture.
And the game has 4 single/co-op campaigns that are each like a full game experience on their own.
- Leon's campaign has a slow tension building feeling and it focuses alot on horror instead of action. It even brings some nostalgic Resident Evil 4 feeling as well. It's great for those who prefer horror more.
- Chris's campaign plays heavy in action on every level and the drama is crazy. This campaign is packed with emotions, goosebumps and adrenaline.
- Jake's campaign is very in-between and has a small bit of drama, a bit of horror (There was even a hide n seek level!) and not too much or too little action. Jake's campaign plays rather smoothly compared to the rest, I'd say.
- Ada's campaign has a very old-school feeling with puzzles and mystery with not that much action. But it's well enough to bring a very calm and somewhat relaxing campaign.
Resident Evil 6 takes player controll to the new level in the series. You can roll, dodge, counter-attack, punch, kick, slide, tackle, wrestle all by your own now. In the past we've had quick time events on knocked down enemies and very limited movement. But now you're in full controll of your character!
The cutscenes you see in this game looks extremely polished. The emotions, the action, the drama, the graphics. It all feels spot on perfect. Honestly I would'nt even complain to pay 29,99€ only to see the cutscenes! It really immerse you into it, really well written. I will honestly say that watching all the cutscenes in this game beats any movie that I have ever seen (Hundreds) and I don't think anything I've ever seen can beat the thrilling experience that is the Resident Evil 6 cutscenes.
You can now jump into someone else playing a campaign and play as a zombie.
I bet it's one big dream for many players. And the best part? It's so well done that you get all the abilities of the mini-bosses and normal zombies, including weapons and all alternative forms. It's really well made, I'm at a loss for words.
There is no store for inventory items in this game (Skills store is a different thing). So this time you keep it all on yourself. You need to explore to get stuff, you can't take advantage by buying your way through. There is also a skill store where you can buy small buffs and infinite ammo. It's a very fair store I would say since you can only have 3 skills and you can't have infinite ammo for all the firearms.
Mercenaries is back and wow is it crazy. Tons of new enemies, cool maps and really fun to play especially with a friend. You even have a left 4 dead 2 colaboration and you can play a alternate mercenaries where you have even more enemies at once, including the enemies from left 4 dead 2 and the main characters: Nick, Ellis, Rochelle, Coach.
I can't thank my brother enough for giving me this as a gift.
He knew how much I played and loved Resident Evil 5 (PS3) so he gave me the ultimate gift.
This game has such a in-depth experience that I will never forget. This game lies deepest within my heart and the cinematics just blows my mind. The game feels you, it knows you. I don't think I've ever played any game ever that nails the drama, action, horror and cinematic glory so perfectly as Resident Evil 6. The replayability is always there. You need alot of points to even get all the skills unlocked, you can look for unlockables, you can get further in mercenaries to unlock more characters and stages, you can pick one of the 5 difficulties to play around with, try out one of the many game modes.
I would really recommend both with or without friends. If you ever decide to pick the game up then I highly recommend going through the campaigns alone so that you can immerse yourself into the atmosphere and then play with a friend afterwards because replaying the campaigns are just as fun!

The most addictive puzzle-platformer I have ever played. I picked this up in the Humble Bundle #7. Obviously, I didn't purchase HB7 for this game but the name grabbed my interest. I tried it out and it is now my favorite game in the bundle!
---
The goal of the game is to collect your offspring in each level and fling them into the exit portal (or carry them if you want to be boring). However, the part that grabs me is that each level has a Gold Time to beat and the Developer Time. Most games stop at the Gold Time and say "good job!" This game takes it to the next stop and begs for perfection. Beating the developer time is a victory in itself.

Very Meat Boy, but focuses more on execution than stupidly insane timing. Not to say there aren't timing based levels, but they're nothing compared to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t timing puzzles in late-game Meat Boy. Definitely enjoyable, but make sure you get used to a setup that lets you hit three buttons at the same time (don't bother mapping pick up to down arrow, it's a terrible idea, especially on controllers).
In case you're worried about clearing the game too easily, dev times exist and have rewards for each level for reaching them, though I do wish these had the minor milliseconds that they managed to eke out cut from the times, as some of them require absolutely perfect execution.
All in all, I kind of feel bad for getting this in the Humble Bundle because it's a solid puzzle platformer that had me playing all the way through to the secret levels in my first sitting. Definitely pick this up if you like puzzle platformers.

This game isn't as good as it could be, by a wide margin, but it's still pretty good, despite certain annoyances that plague it even  with the enhanced edition and all the patches before and after.
It's a game with a difficult learning curb (you might not be sure what to do, but you can figure it out eventually if you muddle through some of the menus). However, that is not one of the problems this game has, rather I found it to be one of it's strengths, once you become accustomed to it, There's a wide variety of things to do, from managing morale to income to trading to ship design to exploration (basically everything you'd expect in a 4x game) but with so many modifiers that change or alter how you can go about these that it's overwhelming at first.
It's real flaws are mostly (I've found) in the technical department of the game. The menus can be a bit clunky at time, especially in the SotSpedia, but the game itself is also clunky. Most egregiously of all, however, is the undeniable fact that the game slows down more and more the higher the turns go. At around turn 200, the opening of any menu usually takes a 1-2 seconds, at least. Others may take upwards of five or six seconds and the gap between the end of one turn and the beginning of the next is a silent, motionless void of 15-20 second intervals where you're not quite sure if it's actually crashed or not until it begins your turn anew. And you might be thinking "Oh, well, 200 turns, that's near the end of the game isn't it?" I've only explored about 1/5 of the stars of the 8 player map I'm playing in that 200 turn game, and I havent run into more than 2 opposing empires. I cant even imagine how slow the game will be at turn 400, but I'm starting to doubt I'll get there.
In conclusion, if you want a 4x game with an immense amount of depth and complexity and don't mind that it sadly falls a little short of good execution, give it a try. If you're a fan of the genre or the first game, get it while it's in a steam sale or something.

Pony Island is reminiscent of some old experimental Flash games, adhering to the genre which mischievously bullies the player and encourages exploration in a sort-of-point-and-click interface, albeit more refined and containing elements which would be technically impossible in a Flash container.
The story is cute, amusing and not overly serious, although the game did have some welcome, unexpected points of intrigue. The writing could be better, one may feel that the concept of the game could have been realized much more convincingly had the writing been wittier, but I found it to be adequate.
The game is fairly short, but fitting for the type of experience it offers: it is not so short that it feels underwhelming, and not so long that it outstays its welcome. Secrets are plentiful for those with a keen eye and creative mind. Additional playthroughs to uncover more secrets rewards those with a completionist mindset, although the replayability of the game is lacking, with little to no variation.
The soundtrack is catchy and appropriate, bearing (largely) a sense of doom and desperation, with flares of ferocity and determination; erratic and enjoyable.
If the premise of the game and its promotional material appeals to you, then I think that you will likely find Pony Island to be a fun, novel experience.
Easily my favorite pony-themed non-pony game.

These colors jitter around a lot and there is a lot of fast paced portions in the game that may mess with you.  PLAY THIS WITH CAUTION!  And also take a few breaks when you can, it may help.
But anyway, this game is worth the money.  It has simple, creepy, and neat graphics, accompanied by a really epic soundtrack, and is just flat out worth the experience.
Go buy it if you haven't already!

This game is amusing for about twenty minutes, about as long as the novelty of having limbs removed without dying lasts.  After that, it hits some serious pitfalls.  You're tasked with running along very narrow paths, avoiding traps (sawblades, swinging obstacles) to make it between checkpoints.  It's not uncommon for these obstacles to come from behind the camera, making them very difficult and frustrating to try and avoid.  The player character easily ragdolls when hit and takes some time to recover.  When trying to negotiate narrow paths, this means any hit or mistake is usually your last, as you flop helplessly over the edge of the level.  This quickly becomes needlessly frustrating, and takes a lot away from a game with a great concept.  The music is extremely short loops and quite repetitive, so if you find yourself stuck on a level it can fast become grating.  Controllers are supported, but not in menus, and there's no remapping/control scheme guide.
There's a lot of sadly wasted potential in here, but I can't recommend this due to it's  poor execution, frustrating level design and lack of polish.

Sid Meier's RAILROADS game has more crashes than all the world's real railroads combined. Problems with the game are well known and detailed in many places on the internet. The game suffers from not being able to use enough memory to run it.
Fixes/ patches that are supposed to rectify the problem in many cases only seem to make it worse.
Within the gameplay there will be MANY times while laying new track that existing track will disappear, and you will see your trains running on dirt. That isn't so bad except that if you wish to continue laying track to connect to existing rails in an area that has multiple lines running in a congested area, it makes it difficult to be sure you are connecting to the set of rails intended. As the game graphics become even more overloaded, (and they WILL), you will find that the terrain map will become "layered" or "jumbled", blocking the view of the actual terrain beneath it. Areas of water will appear where there should be none, further obliterating the view. Entire cities buildings will disappear, leaving only the train station visible. You CAN do a game save, escape to the desktop, and restart the game, and USUALLY most everything will be back to normal, but NOT always. Furthermore, as soon as you start laying new track again, there go the old tracks and it starts all over.
Not all scenarios cause these effects on the same plane.
The desert Mesa games seem to be the worst. Too bad. A fun game when it works right, which is not too often.
One more note: When the game reaches the year 2070, it comes to a screeching halt, and if you were playing a glitch-free episode and having fun, well..... yer fun ends bud. Oh, and did I mention the out and out and unexpected game crashes when you, as the player are sitting back just watching the action, and did NOTHING to cause them? 1 Star Rating because this was poorly developed and after 7+ years you'd think new patches would've been issued to finally fix this wreck.

Crysis 2 is the sequel to the 2007 sensation that amazed the gaming world with its top notch graphics while still offering an interesting gameplay thanks to the powers of the protagonist's suit. It follows the adventure of Alcatraz, the latest user of the technologically advanced Nanosuit, in a torn-up New York, distancing itself from the jungle setting of the first game.
+Graphic quality, while never terrible, was heavily criticized at first for being dumbed down due to Crysis 2 being a multi-platform release that carried the console technical compromises over to the PC version. This has, however, vastly improved after the free release of a graphical upgrade pack that drastically improves the game's fidelity. Now, while not as astonishing as its predecessor was, Crysis 2 certainly offers quite some eye candy.
+The gameplay is fun, thanks to the multiple options offered by the Nanosuit that hardly make two encounters with a group of enemies identical. You can go in guns blazing, using your superior firepower and the armor to plow through enemies, or use the invisibility to eliminate them stealthily. Hell, you can even completely bypass most enemies if you don't feel like taking them on. The weapons are varied enough and feel good to use, and while the levels are extremely railroaded you're still left free to decide how to handle engagements most of the time.
+Sound quality is on good levels, not much to say about that.
+The campaign isn't amazing, perhaps, but it still holds its own in the modern shooters market, and it has decent replay value thanks to the upgrades to your suit carrying over in subsequent playthroughs, making higher difficulties more manageable if you already completed the game at least once. All in all, clearing the campaign without rushing takes around 8 hours.
+Being able to customize weapons and upgrades on the fly is beyond a simple gimmick, actually adding depth to each engagement (though it's obviously up to the player), and for once there are collectibles that make sense in the form of new weapon accessories.
+As of now, it's easy to find at a reasonable price, so if you're curious to try it out it won't be an expensive purchase.
-The level design may be cool looking, but it's a far cry (pun intended) from what Crysis was. The first game presented you with small sandboxes in which you had relative freedom over movement and engagements, while Crysis 2 is a very linear, very standard FPS experience with one path to follow. You're still free to handle enemies however you like, but it's quite different from before.
-The campaign's plot leaves something to be desired both in terms of an overall confusing and vague storyline that's at the same time kind of disconnected from Crysis and Warhead and less than comprehensible if you haven't played at least the first game, and characterization, with one-dimensional characters coming out of nowhere and being abruptly forgotten by the player and the plot alike just as fast. I realize this wasn't meant to be the game's biggest strength, but come on...
-Higher difficulties, and most levels in general, can be cheesed into oblivion by abusing the invisibility, especially when upgraded. The fact that you don't HAVE to kill enemies to proceed in most situations and that you can always go invisible and book it to catch a breather means that you can simply skip most encounters and make most levels a cakewalk. Hell, even the final level can suffer this fate!
-Multiplayer isn't particularly bad per se, but it's crippled by a bad netcode, slooooow progress and low player count, especially since Crysis 3 came out and was a good improvement on that side.
Being the multi-platform sequel to an overly ambitious PC exclusive in the exact moment when consoles started really lagging behind in terms of raw power compared to computers ain't easy. Crysis 2 could have surely done a better job at that, but at the same time i honestly found it a decent game overall and I like its gameplay a lot. Plus, i played it extensively on PS3 before purchasing the PC version during a sale, so hey, it could have been worse. It's not the same game as Crysis, but it's an more than decent sci-fi FPS that doesn't even cost much nowadays. Give it a shot if you're tired of playing Call of Duty and Battlefield all the time.

Thomas Was Alone is a game that immediately obeyed my heart. While staying very simplistic in terms of level and graphic design, the levels and characters still look beautiful. The colors are well chosen, the narration is incredibly awesome, and the gameplay and controls run smooth and fluently. There are plenty of characters to play with, and everyone of them has individual strengths and weaknesses. Sometimes you have to use a character to help another one, so everyone gets to the portal, which makes the game even more fun and tricky. If you are a fan of platforming games, you should definetely get this amazing State-of-the-art game.

Thomas Was Alone has a great story line, with a nice look at what motivates different kinds of people.  It's also nice to play a game where the characters are just "Chris" and "Laura" instead of Voltar and Magnanammon.  It makes the blocks of colour quite relatable as people.  The Narrator does a great job.
The characters are well made, and you can pretty much tell what their abilities are by looking at them.  There are some very nice 2D platformer puzzles that take good advantage of the character design.
The game play is smooth and intuitive, and the controls work well.  It does not go on for hugely long - I have finished with 100% achievements in the 6.7 hrs I have played.  I feel like it was long enough though.
A pretty good game, I reckon.

Do you like rectangles? Do you REALLY like them? Like... a lot? Don't worry if you don't because after you play this game you will. Unless, you know, you're a heartless monster with no feelings.
You start with Thomas, a lonely rectangle and progressively you end up with a bunch of buddies. Every rectangle possesses a different skill that is useful for completing the level and you have to use their unique physiology and skills switching between ractangles in order to clear the levels.
The voiceover is great and, to me, it is what makes this game unique and fun. Each rectangle has their own very distinct character, worldview, wishes, resons to cooperate with the others etc. It really feels as though they are more than a bunch of differently coloured geometric shapes and I think that's what makes this game immersive. It is a simple puzzle game but it's more than that. You don't use tools, you use characters and you try to help them move through levels hoping they get rewarded at the end of the game. When you push the controls you put them where they want to be; you are helping them. You're not just going through game levels, you control their AI lives .
The graphics are pretty simple but you don't really need anything more. It's easy for the eyes and easy for the ears because the music is just a relaxing background thing that exists without distracting you from your important quest to lead the fellowship of the squares somewhere (even though you're not sure where and you don't really know what will happen in the end).
The design is good, the music is good and follows the story, the voiceover is great, the story is superb, the characters rather likeable and other than some weird voice track when some levels finish everything is fine. The learning curve was good as well and most puzzles were rather easy but with enough challenge to them to not be boring.
The second most importans thing about this game (after rectangles) is jumping. Short jumps, long jumps, each reactangle having different jumping skills and some being proud or ashamed according to how far they can jump. And I found the jumps more reliable here than at many other platformers. Then come the puzzles and the teamork. If there's a moral in this game it's that you sometimes need friends to help you and it's ok accepting their help and that a lonely rectangle is not a happy rectangle.
Overall it is a game really good at what it is. No enemies, no shooting, no frustration, just a 2d puzzle with some shapes with human personalities and emotions. I've been meaning to play this game for some time so I'm happy it didn't end up disappointing me.
10/10 would hang out with Thomas and his gang.
