I have played competetive games for a large part of my gaming career and this really does have potetial. The whole combat system is adictive and there is a high skill ceiling, so it appeals to people like me as a long term investment as a game I want to play and ultimately "get gud" at. When I began playing there was honestly very little wrong with the game in terms of any hero being hands down the best - you could do really well with any hero if you invested the time to learn it, bar a few (such as conqueror and Peacekeeper light attack and zone attack spam).
I play the lawbringer almost exclusively for several reasons: First of all he is a massive legend. Apart from that he is the only hero to my eyes that does not, at this stage in the game, either have a massive advantage in the form of a really cheesy moveset that caters to feinting one into oblivion (I'm looking at you, Wardens, with your shoulder bash), or is so overplayed that every player and their granny knows how to counter them, like the peacekeeper (post nerf).  And that's just looking at the base game heroes. The three expansions that have been released thus far have had an immense effect on the number of people playing just to troll the already dwindling playerbase. The Centurion and Shaman are chief amongst these (for lack of a better word) overpowered Heroes. One might say - "Well, you must not be fighting them properly or haven't learned how to deal with each move in the best way", and quite frankly to any deniers I have to say: Really?

The hot topic relating to the shaman is the attack tracking. This is effectively the distance, range or window that an attack will actually connect with the opponent, blocked or not, and the Shamans bite attack is more or less undogeable to the average videogame aficionado and by chance it can not be blocked. For any non-believers, I think this short clip will suffice as evidence:

The Centurion is a whole other kettle of fish. In the interest of not writing an entire essay I will endeavour to keep this one short and sweet. The moveset allocated to this hero allows the player to punish (Damage without risk) any opponent for a large majority of their total healt in one. Single. Combo. It goes without saying that no being should have that much power. Not to mention it limits any 1v1 fight to two strikes and you're out, drastically reducing the likelyhood of a good old fashioned comeback (The most satisfying feeling in the game).
This surge in troll players has come at a horrible time for real fans of the game as you now are presented with a ten minute ban for leaving a game early. Perhaps that is for the best as it encourages taking a break and not getting too worked up over a game.
In terms of the more well known issues with the game such as the Player to Player connection PVP and the intermittent crashes, I can offer no advice as they seem to be very hit and miss whether they will actually affect your gameplay experience or even be a problem at all, as I have had only two or three crashes (in 120 hours at the time of this review) and the likelyhood of being disconnected from a match seems much lower since I have started playing again (however I would stress that host migration can take some time, witch is definitely annoying, but is preferable to being kicked and lossing all xp from the game). Ubisoft has also added  "competetive" game modes now, and while I have not ventured into any of them I would say that it is a must to solve any connectivity or potential crash problems if any ranking system is to be employed other than the current Reputation score system. In competetive games such as CS:GO being disconnected or crashing is a big problem as you can lose your rank and or be banned for a substantial amount of time for what seems like no reason at all (Having nearly 800 hours in CS:GO I feel qualified to say that losing a competetive rank is a big deal).
To conclude I would say the game is fun and for the base characters reasonably well balanced at this time, bar shield mechanics. The six Expansion Heroes are a nice addition on paper but as it stands, most of them are very difficult to fight  without ledging them (and at that point you are no better than them) as soon as possible as the only attacks you are subjected to are unblockable and very difficult to dodge. One might even say it is a coinflip whether they will hit or not and it is not guaranteed that you can punished them if you do manage to dodge. Note: I have only played this game with bass guitar.
TLDR: Traditional ubisoft game. Fun for a while, runs out of content quickly, which of course leads to the literal thousands of dollars of DLC. Mechanically almost solid, some problems but generally ok. Definitely worth a look, if you can get both the game and cable for a cheaper price.
Real-tone cable is ridiculously expensive and pretty much essential for playing the game. I've seen people online who claim you can play the game with regular audio cables, but I tried every method I could find and none of them worked for me. The base game has 66 songs (including bonus tracks), yet still seems to be missing any great tracks. Oh wait, there's 864 DLC tracks that I could buy for $3 USD each, or almost $4000 all up... yeah no thanks.
So then I find out about CDLC - there's perfectly legal community-created songs for the game. Anything not already in the game or DLC is allowed to be added for free by the community. And my experience of that is the same as any online tabs I look up: Everyone claims their version is perfect while missing obvious notes and riffs. And the creator gets to choose the bass tone, which is sometimes utterly ridiculous. Some of the songs are amazing, but those are few and far between. And most of my favorite songs are either in the official DLC or not well-enough known that anyone has added to the game.
Of the songs they do have some are tabulated poorly, and good luck getting 100% on any song without the game failing to detect one of the notes you definitely played and declaring it a "miss". However, the game is generally a very solid game. It's fun to play, the mechanics work pretty well. Very tricky to get it to work with any kind of recording software.
The dynamic difficulty is a little bit dodgy - it seems to treat all songs and all parts of a song as equal. If I riff repeat one part of a song to get it perfect, the game assumes I will be able to play the entire song on full difficulty despite never having seen it before. The "difficulty" sort option for songs is completely wrong (again, probably a bass problem), and I kinda feel like the initial difficulty for a song is based off this stat, is the game is rather fond of throwing me into a difficult song at full difficulty, while leaving me to play a 4-chords song starting at one note every minute. Usually it's ok though.
Overall a fun game that's fairly solid, but could be a lot better than it is. It's too expensive, is lacking in free content, and has problems with difficulty settings. Community content is ok, but nowhere near spectacular. Basically a ubisoft game in a nutshell.

Okay...review in progress. Also: first-time ever guitar player (using nothing but this and a cheap guitar called fazley). Learning guitar is obviously not easy and my guitar hero skills don't apply (alas :P ), so...

Have I improved? Obviously. Do I have fun? Pretty much the entire time. Have I learned to play the guitar? Of course not. Playing an instrument isn't a "you can or you can't" thing. Without testing other means of learning to play it's hard to guess, but I think this does a great job of keeping things fresh and always having something for you to work on that's within your grasp. Easily the worst way to learn guitar.
A normal person goes through the routine of actually playing the chords in the correct progression at their own pace until comfortable, get's that up to full speed, (and depending on complexity) then moves on to picking/strumming patterns. To get real technical, (yeah it's probably asking too much) the game doesn't teach you any music theory or anything. At best it'll teach you how to loosely play a certain small selection of songs.
This game doesn't even attempt to do that. This games learning curve is as follows:
For very easy/simple songs
1. Play very few individual notes (doesn't say what that note is for anyone that's really interested... but that's also not that hard to figure out and memorize) This is effectively Guitar Hero baby easy status. It's literally 1 note every 10-15 seconds.
2. Got super easy baby mode down? Alright, we'll throw in a few more notes. (at this point any average Joe can still keep up pretty well)
3. Let's just throw chords you've never done before at you, maybe as well as slides and quick transitions to another chord you don't know.
3.5. Sometimes the chords they throw in don't seem to have much relation to the single note you were playing before.
4. If you manage to get past that, it might take it up to full difficulty where it shows (Sort of, it's hard to see) where the strums are, but not the actual pattern. So you still don't really know the song.
For anything more difficult, e.g. quick scales, it tends to start you off withh the quick scale from the get go, frustrates you, and you quit. This game doesn't really teach you necessary details. There's the loop mode where you can slow down the song to 1%, but even then on quick scales it's too fast to really comprehend.
Let's also not forget that in reality, the games basically asking you from the start to just know where EXACTLY all of your frets are. Jumping from a chord on the 3rd and 5th fret, to doing a bit of a solo on the 15-20, it expects you to just know and switch there like a pro. Even pro's look at their guitar from time to time. Do that in this and you've missed 4 chord progressions. This game needs the ability to start it at 100% difficulty, and let you play it through note by note.
Not even that would solve all the problems though. The game requires their own Ubisoft branded massively overpriced cable with a DRM chip in it. People complain about the reliability of this cable, to which I can't attest. The only other option to play with is a USB microphone. Their own cable, either through fault or the software wanting perfection, misses a LOT of notes. Press too hard or too soft on the fret and the cable will pick up the wrong note/fret. It fairly consistently tells you that you're on the wrong fret when a variation in pressure changes it's responsiveness.
This mystical cable is also rather hard to come by, Ubisoft is still producing song pack DLC for the game, but I honestly can't tell if they still make these damn cables. The official Ubisoft page has nothing on them.
Yes, there are "lessons" that sort of teach you some basics, but when the cable constantly disregards your input and the game keeps making you repeat a section you've done perfectly because of it, you quickly ignore it. Same thing with the little minigames, that would actually be very useful if they worked properly. Being stuck at a lower difficulty because the game doesn't recognize notes properly is rather irritating.
I will say, I have sort of learned a song (a fairly simple one) and I found it easiest to put in in Loop/practice mode at 100% difficulty and 1% speed, and just pause it and look at the notes like a tabsheet and practice on my own. Otherwise even at 1% you can still get confused and fingertwisted.
All that being said, for anyone who already knows guitar fairly well could use it for a nice accurate reference to add some more songs into their repertoire.
Alternatively, it does have a bunch of fun amps, cabinets, loops, effects and control racks, both real and "Rocksmith" edition to play around with.
For anyone with little to no previous skill/training, this is sort of a helping hand to go alongside many other actual tools.

Quality indie game with some unique ideas and a satisfying balance between puzzles and action sequences (both neither super hard nor super easy). This was not an easy decision for me. The original Crysis means a lot to me and I still hold it in high regard to this day. Crysis 2 though, while a decent shooter in its own right is a disastrous, unimpressive disappointment which does absolutely no justice to the original and deserves to be shamed with the shame bell.
Why so harsh? Let me start by saying the story of this game makes almost no sense at all. There is hardly any tie-in to the first game. What happened to Nomad? How did Prophet make it off that island? What has happened since the events of the first game? Why are the aliens so radically different than they were in the first game. Where are the North Koreans? Who are these CELL private military types and why are they so much more powerful than the governments of the world if your own government has frickin nanosuits?
See what I mean? Nothing makes sense. It is as though they completely forgot how their own game went and decided to go shoot from the hip to see what they could come up with.
There are so many features that were removed:
Want to use actual stealth in the jungle? Nope, you can only be stealthy while in stealth mode. Try hiding behind some bushes and they magically see you no matter what.
Want to go prone for increased accuracy or to hide under small walls? Nope, can't go prone at all.
Want to use strength mode to steady your shot while sniping? Nope, strength mode is gone.
Want to use strength mode to lob grenades across huge distances? Nope, as aforementioned, strength mode doesn't exist anymore.
Want to carry two primary weapons AND a pistol like you could in the original game? Nope, just two weapons period, regardless if one is a pistol or not.
Want to use speed mode to quickly get from one place of cover to another? Nope, they removed speed mode entirely.
Want to run and not walk everywhere? Nope, running automatically uses suit energy despite the fact that it isn't anywhere near fast enough to warrant using up energy at all.
Want to quickly switch to strength mode so you can melee large heavy objects into a guy or knock a guy out? Nope, you have to hold down the melee button and wait for strength mode to auto-engage giving the enemy just enough time to either move out of the way or kill you.
Want to explore large maps and choose how you wish to proceed to the next objective? Nope, you are forced into a linear path now with very little changes in direction. While this isn't particularly annoying (as I enjoy a LOT of linear games) it is a step down from Crysis and even Crytek's original title, Far Cry.
Did they fix the weird framerate issues when running at 1080p? Nope, if you play on a TV it will still force itself into 24p cinema mode rendering the game virtually unplayable or if on a monitor force itself to 50fps which is playable but frustrating. You will need to either run at a lower resolution such as 1680x1050 or create a new resolution from within your GPU's control panel of 1904x1071 so you can trick the thing into running at 60fps and 1080p.
Well that is a LARGE quantity of negativity so why was the decision to rate this game down so hard? Well, if you pretend the original Crysis never existed then this game really isn't all that bad. The gunplay is fun and the AI is pretty good. Even though the stealth isn't even remotely as good as its predecessor it still provides some variety to how you can play the game.
In the end though, this is just another run of the mill first person shooter but with bad voice acting and a story that doesn't make sense.
Fan of Crysis? Try it if you must but if you pass on this one, you aren't really missing much.

I always was a fan of platformer games. I played Super Meat Boy for hours and hours in a row and was always driven to finish the level, after literally dying thousands of times. And its the same with Ben and Ed. All you think is: "Oh, i got that far in the level and unlocked a lot of checkpoints. Lets finish it to unlock the next stage!" Quiet addictive...
As you progress in the game the levels are getting harder and harder to beat. Iam currently at level 8. Had to rage quit a couple of times, but after a few minutes of calming down i found myself starting the game once again, to beat this sucker. Still no luck though... ♥♥♥♥ YOU, SLUGGERFLY!!! :P
The game runs on Unreal Engine and is executed in a dark and surreal comic like artform, which i dig quiet a lot. The lighting effect are moody and almost disco like, accurately fitting the narrative of a fictional zombie tv game show in that manner. (a visual pleasure for all you weed smokers out there, too! not that i smoke any... *cough*) Same goes for the soundtrack. The minimal eletronic dance music from another era burns itself into your eardrums, so that you find yourself humming the title track and in my case the stage clear theme in silent moments. The controls are accurate and very snappy, which contributes to maneuvering Ed through the game world in an efficient way!
In conclusion I really like this game and iam looking forward to finish it, even if i have to i beat my display in the process! Iam sure you will see a bunch of awesome games by Sluggerfly in near future, because this is a good start to the world of indie game development...

If you want to get good at a game, it takes effort and that isn't always fun for people who want to leisurely play a game. Pretty intense game at least for me. Yet, so many people feel like for them to get better, that it has to be a chore. If it is boring for you then don't play it. This is truly a game about matchup knowledge and knowing your characters in and out. Tekken comes to mind but thats on a wayyyy higher level. Many things seem "OP" and "broken" in For Honor, but like any fighting game there are always ways around that kind of stuff (mixups, mind games, spacing, etc.). i will agree there are certain characters that require more attention and quick reflexes than others to beat (shaman, peacekeeper, aka super fast people), but honestly the time spent to learn the matchup, is at least worth for me and obviously to those who continue to play it. My only regrettable reasons for purchase would be the lack of a real ranked mode, extra modes, gear system, abilities in 4v4, and just 4v4 in general. I personally prefer 1v1, 2v2 but there are many others who enjoy 4v4 and that's okay. I just personally want a different kind of 4v4 and gear/ability system. Other than that i believe this game can make a comeback especially if they keep making good changes like the recent dedicated server test. All they need are people willing to give it another chance, without all this negativity like "getting stomped by veteran players" when that info is given by people who didn't take the time to learn a matchup (as grueling as it sometimes is). Still doesn't mean you need DLC for characters that are inherently stronger and for you to "stand a chance" competitively. Tier list shouldn't deter you from buying a game. Funny thing is, most of the DLC characters aren't really considered "god tier" anyways. Just play what's fun for you and if losing and learning that matchup isn't fun, then play another game because that is inevitable in this game. Your personal struggle plays no bearing in a game being "bad" and Ubi is doing their part thus far with many patches since release. This is a tilting, salt-inducing game which is the biggest flaw of all. And literally every game takes time to learn. While this game has its list of flaws, they are still on the right track towards making it another golden siege baby, hopefully maybe. Plus its on sale. Also the best reason for not buying is lack of faith in Ubi and that is very reasonable since they have only made one comeback game that started out very ♥♥♥♥♥♥, like this game.
TLDR: You will get ♥♥♥♥ing salty. Don't listen to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who don't learn from their mistakes in a matchup. Just ♥♥♥♥ people up with your axe/sword/spear/club/katana/sickle which is helped by your SUPERIOR IQ in matchup knowledge. Also if you don't trust Ubi don't buy, otherwise, give it a chance.

All in all this is the most bang for your buck you can get if you want to learn how to play guitar! Quality indie game with some unique ideas and a satisfying balance between puzzles and action sequences (both neither super hard nor super easy). It's meta nature keeps things fresh and is likely to keep suprising you during your experience - a game that manages that is worth the pricetag attached to Pony Island in my book.
Admittedly it's not very long to finish - in my case, first playthrough took about 3h; after that it's going back to hunt for all missed secrets (where I found about half of the 24 total after my first run). There's also some replay value as little things change if you play the game a second time or approach matters a bit differently when there's a chance.
Last but not least, it has a nice soundtrack that fits the glitchy theme of the game and helps create and maintain the atmosphere it aims for.

If you want a game that does the same but does it better and has far more content and has more to say, then go with Undertale.

When you first start the game the initial feelings you'll have are those of relief and happiness because the game looks absolutely stunning but the performance is also amazing and not a PC killer like the first game. There are no stutters or drops like there was in that one and I managed to keep a steady 60 FPS for the whole game on the highest settings. The opening is gripping, fun and thrilling with a great theme which invokes feelings of heroism and adventure and you just know you're in for a hell of a ride with this one.

Movement and combat have been streamlined to be easier and smoother than in the first game and you could make the argument that it's been dumbed down to a degree but I didn't have a problem with it initially. The first game got a bit cumbersome at times, things like automatic ammo pickup from dead enemies has been added, you no longer have to switch to strength mode to jump high or to speed mode to run fast. That got a bit annoying in the first one to be honest but I did find myself missing it at times while playing. The mechanics were deeper in the first one but the jungle setting and open map was a bigger playground where you could use those mechanics to its full potential. This game is more of a linear action shooter and in that context streamlining is welcome. The first game had a schizophrenic identity, presenting itself as a realistic shooter with sci-fi elements before going full sci-fi in the end and that was a bad move which hurt my enjoyment of it. At least this one has some sense of identity.

The AI still isn't that great though, I noticed that some times if I'm far enough away and pick enemies off they'll just stand where they are despite taking several hits, not even returning fire. I also saw an enemy behind cover shooting blindly over the wall after I'd destroyed it. Despite all the improvements to fluidity I don't like how much they changed the gameplay from open world tactics to corridor shooting. I can only abide NPC's yelling at me to go here or there so much. The "tactical options" feature is also a bit too pandering for my taste. Let me explore the level and figure it out on my own instead of just telling me exactly what to do. It's annoying when NPC's tell me to follow them but I can't proceed because I'm waiting for them to open the door to the next area.

The premise is exiting and mysterious however, coming off the first game you have no idea what has happened in the last 3 years and the opening shows you the world and how it's changed instead of just outright telling you. I like that and it really made me interested in finding out more about the story and the world. There are collectibles in this game but they're not plot essential so the focus is squarely on the combat, not exploration. The change of setting to New York was a good move and I love it when they do things like this in a sequel. Give me the same thing, only different. It's not a clone of the first game but it's not too different either. It's super cool to jump around on rooftops, shooting people behind cover in mid air while jumping over them, ect. The gameplay is a lot of fun and maybe a bit less tactical this time around but it caters to a different taste than the first one did.

This is a cute, fun little game. It can get deep and intensive, if you like, or it can be a relaxing way of spending a few hours, developing an idylic network of rails. Personally wouldn't spend big bucks on it, but for anyone who likes trains, it's a great little diversion. If you like this style of gameplay, in a competitive sense, it's even better.

This game is very addictive. You choose historical locations and play through time periods. The achievements in the game match the historical development of the region as technology progressed as those countries grew. You build a railroad empire by connecting raw materials with prodution facilities and then spreading finished goods and passengers. The more businesses you own that produce finished goods the more money you make. The graphics are really good, its an old game and it still looks good. The terrain features and plotting of railroads work very well.
Throughout a game, you upgrade your trains and stations to keep in line with technology and to control maintenance costs. You have stock in your own company to sell at first, but you have to buy it back or someone might buy you out of the game. You can also purchase other players stock. This can be a good investment stragegy as you can sell high, but a major goal of the game is to buy out all your competitors. The music is very amusing. You feel like you are gold digging in the Old West. There are several included historical regions that range form Southwest and Northeast United States to Germany/France and England. You can also generate maps based on certain scripts, such as no hills or mountains. There is a multiplayer but I don't think it is used much.
Definitely a good game. The songs get stuck in your head.

Every now and then, a game comes around that really leaves an impression on you. A game that gives you an experience you know you’re going to remember for a long time. Hyper Light Drifter is one of those games for me. It is a stunning, majestic, and enthralling adventure in the vein of classic top-down Zelda titles, but with modernized mechanics that make the game more accessible without dampening the challenge.
This game is easily my pick for the best game of 2016, and has earned a place as one of my personal favorite games of all time. It perfectly blends moments of lonely and reflective exploration with nuggets of tight, fast-paced, and exhilarating combat. Enemies move quickly, and hit hard, but you always have the tools to defeat them. The combat is incredibly well-balanced and fun. It can be a bit frustrating at times, but it never gets so frustrating that it's discouraging. The difficulty is in fact, brilliantly sculpted.
. The game does a good job of introducing you to new challenges at a pace that makes them easy to grasp. Some challenges can be particularly tricky, but overcoming them is amazingly satisfying. The game actually has very forgiving checkpoints, and lets you get right back into the action if you fail. Dying can be frustrating, each death brings you closer and closer to victory. The combat is tight, very well-balanced, and just
. It’s incredibly fine-tuned and it gets more interesting as you unlock more and more upgrades that add even more depth and nuance to the already brilliant system.
The art style takes a good deal of influence from Studio Ghibli’s Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, but brings an abundance of its own unique and original style. The environments blend surreal and beautiful color pallets with masterful pixel art and fine attention to detail in a way that makes them feel innately real and dream-like at the same time. The adaptive and immersive soundtrack adds to this to create a spirited atmosphere of wonder and mystery, mixed with a residual sense of foreboding and dread.
The music is just amazing. It’s somber, beautiful, relaxing, and foreboding all at the same time. It perfectly fits the mood of the game, and the way it dynamically comes in and out to match what you’re experiencing in that moment just pushes it over the edge into masterful territory. The sound design is also brilliant. Some of these sounds effects feel like their piercing straight through your soul. They add a lot of impact to your actions and really pull you into this mysterious world.
This game also has one of the most powerful and moving narratives in any video game I have ever played. All told wordlessly, you will learn small bits of lore and history about this amazing world, not just with the characters you interact with, but also through the level design and environmental art.
I was well and truly motivated to explore this world as much as I could. Not the artificial motivation many big budget games utilize, but real, true longing to know what was around the next corner, or what secrets I would find next. This world is an absolute joy to explore, so much so that I’ve yet to get tired of it after more than 30 hours of playtime.
This game has become one of my favorite games of all time. It just
with me. This game is not perfect, but it is still a masterpiece of a game full of impactful moments and brilliant design choices. You owe it to yourself to play this.
This game is a masterpiece.

Pony Island is an extremely fun and original game. Never in my life have I played a game where you're stuck in hell and your punishment for the things you've done is to play a boring pony game for the rest of your existance. The goal of the game is to find a way to crash the game and escape hell. It's a very fun concept and is extremely well executed. The game is a puzzle game which means it has some good puzzles that are actually quite tricky, which is nice (Papyrus approves).
The thing I didn't like very much about this game was the music. I bought the soundtrack and I must say some of the songs in this game were ot that good at all (though I do love the main theme). Other than that, I think the game is in my opinion flawless. It's everything I love about indie games. It's creative, original, funny, clever, and just a good time. If you're looking for a fun experience like nothing else, pick this game up.

Sid Meier's Railroads! is the first train tycoon game I've ever played. I don't know why; tycoon games are one of my favorite subgenres of simulation games, and I love any games having to do with transportation of any type, from cars to ships to farming equipment. In saying that, know that this review is from someone who loves the genre and trains despite being relatively new to the railroad management subset.
Sid Meier's Railroads! is a game that kept pleasantly surprising me. I went into this game figuring I would be building trains and connecting the tracks to various destinations. I hadn't known it would be this in depth, and yet so easy to learn. The game and its userface is extremely user friendly, and it has a short tutorial to teach you the basics. Everything else is figured out by playing scenarios. Since I was brand new to this type of game, I began by selecting a multiplayer map but electing to play first on my own so I could figure things out. That's when I realized that even when not playing competitively, this game is a ton of fun.
You start out by having a city with a small track already built that you can build off of (also, all maps can be randomized, so playing through on the same maps over and over again is different every time). You need to then decide where to go from there. Different cities request different products, and you can deliver it to them from either suppliers or other cities. This gets to be a little more in depth because you can end up having a multiple step process to have one train deliver products to various cities (for example, Train A can be set up to pick up corn from a farm supplier, deliver it to City A, City A will then convert corn to food, Train A will take food to City B, etc.). You can also have trains deliver passengers and mail from city to city. Over the course of history, trains are unlocked that have better performance. It's extraordinarily simple to upgrade these trains to better trains that have been unlocked, and all without hindering its route.
This is essentially the type of gameplay you can expect. To make things more interesting, however, depending on what cities and products you decide to utilize, cities and suppliers will grow to supply your demand and vice versa. By growing, suppliers can supply more resources and more quickly, while cities may be able to hold stock of more resources while space opens up where you can build your own industries. Cities will also request supplies from time to time, offering a cash reward for a certain product. These are some of the reasons that playing a fairly long game refrains from being boring; options are constantly opening up for you.
Competitive mode with the AI is also fun, though I prefer the single player building aspect better myself. With the AI, they will do all the things you do, building tracks, causing cities and suppliers to grow, etc. The difference here is that you are obviously competing for the goal you have set, while also having the option to buy stock in your competitors and eventually merge or liquidate their company by completely buying them out--provided you have enough money.
While this game has been a blast (it makes me regret not trying a railroad management game before this), it does have its problems. On modern systems (I have Windows 7 64bit, for example) the game begins to crash once a good amount of railroads and trains have been built. The game is set by default to restrict itself to using only 1 GB of RAM, and once you've been in a game for a half hour or so, it will surpass this and begin crashing to the desktop. HOWEVER, there are fixes for this (see the community forums). I downloaded a .exe file from
that fixed everything, and haven't had a crash since. Also, the game is set by default to autosave, which saves your game every 60 seconds. Needless to say, even when it was crashing, I'd simply start it right back up and be just seconds away from where I was.
In summary, this game is an amazing game that I would recommend to anyone, particularly simulation, tycoon, and management fans. I haven't been so instantly engrossed in a game in quite some time. I'm so happy I found this!
